texts.chapter:volume0-prologue-no-rewind:title: Prologue: The Reversal That Never Happened
texts.chapter:volume0-prologue-no-rewind:event:
Emergency council record · Common minimum measures (same-day handling · copy):
I. Suspend the White Tower access qualification assessment for all trainees in this cohort indefinitely.
II. Examine the two separately.
III. Reclaim access credentials

and confiscated evidence.
IV. Until a long-term decision is made, leaving the village and the two meeting alone are prohibited.
Supplementary clause: The above are minimum measures; no conclusion has been reached regarding long-term handling.

My mother did not sleep that night. By order of the council, she was responsible for keeping watch over me inside the house, while the footsteps of the night watch could still be heard faintly through the cold wind outside.
She sat beside the stove, the half-mended garment spread across her knees. Not one stitch had advanced through the entire night. Only when dawn was close did she finally lean back against the chair
and close her eyes, as if drained of all strength. The firewood in the stove had burned through, compressed into a layer of dark-red ash, and the air in the room was growing cold and hard by degrees.
I took off my shoes and carried them in my hand, keeping my steps as quiet as possible. Barefoot on the cold wooden floor, I held my breath and passed in front of her.
When I climbed out through the window, cold wind rushed down my collar. I clung to the outer window frame and looked back once.
She had not woken. The faint, dark-red glow from the stove fell across her exhausted profile.

The meeting place was a low wall behind the chapel. The sky before dawn was a heavy blue-gray. A thin layer of frost covered the blades of grass; beneath our feet, it first gave a faint brittle crackle, then yielded softly into mud. The cold air entered my lungs like a swallow of ice water.

I had been waiting by the wall for less than four minutes when a shadow climbed over it. She stumbled slightly when she landed. The cat ears that were always held alert and upright gave a small twitch, and both hands came down hard on the gravel-covered frozen

earth. She had known how to climb every wall in the village since childhood, but today her movements were unusually stiff. When she stood again, a small patch of skin had been scraped from her palm, a thread of blood showing through. She did not even look at it.
“The shift-change gap is only six minutes,” she said under her breath, speaking quickly. “It’s our only chance to avoid the surface patrols and slip into the lower levels of the White Tower.”
“I’m ready,” I said quietly.
“If we don’t touch the machine beneath the White Tower, we can only wait here to die.” She slapped the frozen dirt from her knees. “If the conservatives gain the upper hand, we’ll be executed
at noon today. Estelle is already dead on the boundary line, and the evidence she carried out will be erased completely. We have to go back to yesterday evening and save her. It’s the only way.”
She stared into my eyes, speaking extremely fast.

“Your reading on the old tester yesterday was ten thousand and eighty. According to the theory in the books, one unit of capacity corresponds to five seconds of reversal. If it really converts to nearly fourteen hours, that’s just enough to take us back to last night. We go back, stop her, find another way, and leave this place together. All three of us.”
She rubbed the scraped hand against her clothes and her expression darkened.

“But all of this is just calculation on paper. That piece of junk has been abandoned for over a hundred years. If it malfunctions, you could be burned to ash inside it. Arno, have you made up your mind?”
I nodded heavily. If we did nothing, all we could do was wait for fate to pass judgment; and Estelle, who usually treated every rule as iron law but crossed the boundary for us
in the end, would remain dead forever. If we accepted the investigation step by step, the truth she had traded her life for would also be completely erased by the people above.
This was something only the two of us could decide in private. If we were going to wager our lives on whether this piece of junk was worth it, neither of us could blame anyone else.
From the outside, the White Tower looked like a gigantic dead bone driven into the frozen earth.

We used the six-minute gap to cross the perimeter and crawl into the tower through a rusted maintenance hatch. Keeping to the edge of the huge shadow in the entrance hall, we descended two levels without a sound.

By the time we reached the access control point in the inner corridor, the six-minute gap on the surface had already run out. She reached habitually for her waist, only to find nothing there—our identification badges had been confiscated the night before.

“According to the investigation procedure they announced last night,” Yuna said quietly, “they were supposed to escort us inside today and make us repeat the standard investigation route. So the passages along the way have already been opened in advance.”

She pressed her lips together and waited in silence. Sure enough, the heavy metal door clicked and released itself. Before the search could spread toward the perimeter, we used the procedural gap prepared in advance for the investigation escort.

The spaces farther down were older still. The air was cold and dim, with the astringent smell of old metal and dust. The sensor lights came on in sections; wherever we went, a patch of murky yellow would reluctantly wake. Because we had to avoid various old security scans all the

way from the chapel, through the outer wall, and deeper into this level, the journey took us nearly three full hours. By the end, only one thought remained in our minds: put one foot in front of the other. She walked ahead, her shoulders rising and falling unevenly from exhaustion.
At the end of the long staircase was a broad, lifeless hall.
A heavy seat frame stood in the center of the hall, facing a whole wall of control panels. The ancient numeral displays on the wall gave off a dim green glow and showed the time: 7:50.

I walked toward the machine from the stories. The binding position was a dark recess. I drew a deep breath and sat inside. The seat was cold. A thin line was pressed against the back of my neck, its touch like a cold worm.
The grip, calibration, and long waiting delay were all operated by Yuna from the panel outside the seat frame. There was nothing I could press on my side.
“Ten thousand and eighty.” She watched the screen, her voice carrying a faint echo through the empty hall. “It confirmed your reading. Ten thousand and eighty.”
She copied the number from the screen into her palm with a finger.
“From here, the machine has to finish the process on its own.”
Following the interface instructions, we retreated to the corridor outside the calibration area and waited after the scan finished.
The system required a ten-minute delay. We sat pressed close together against the cold metal wall. She lowered her head, both hands buried between her knees, trying to draw out a little warmth.
“Almost there.”
She stood and walked over to an external control interface beside the adjacent unit. I retreated to the other side of the heavy metal door I had just come through.
Eight o’clock sharp.
The White Tower’s breath changed.

It was a low hum pressed against the ground. In that instant, it sank half a note. The vibration beneath my feet grew heavy, passing through the soles of my shoes and reaching my heart. The sensor lights in the corridor suddenly brightened by one level. From somewhere extremely deep and distant came the click of an outer door lock releasing.
Three steps apart, she and I looked at each other beneath the glaring lights.
There was no dizzying flash. No storm tearing open space.

The corridor was still the same dust-covered corridor. I was still standing outside the door, and she was still standing beside the interface. Our positions, our rigid postures, and the direction of the shadows on the wall had not changed at all.
“Wait.” She stared fixedly at the door. “Wait another thirty seconds.”
Thirty seconds. Then another thirty seconds. The air solidified.
She hurried back to the console, her fingers sliding rapidly across the panel.
“The system record has written a new line.” Her voice was dry. “I can’t read it. Only one line.”
“Did the machine take effect?” She turned to look at me. “Did you feel anything just now?”
“No.”
She stared hard at me for three seconds. Then the spirit holding her up seemed to scatter, and her shoulders sagged.

“Maybe this isn’t the machine proper at all, just a calibration device. The real activation terminal is somewhere else.” She lowered her eyes. “Or maybe everything in the old records was a lie. Or the machine is broken.”
“What do we do now?”
She raised her head and looked toward the dark staircase leading deeper underground.
“Go find the real activation terminal,” she said through clenched teeth. “If we still can’t find it down there, we’ll accept our fate and go back to face the investigation.”
The sound of boots striking metal grating poured down from two levels above us. Then someone shouted my name.
That person called my name the way our mentor used to call for a child who had wandered off while playing: deliberately drawing out the ending.
She grabbed my sleeve, her fingers cold.
“We can’t go up.”
“I know. Even if our mentor wants to protect us, people from the Investigation Hall must be following behind her.”
Immediately afterward, the people above called Yuna’s name in the same tone. Without looking back, we fled into the deeper darkness.
The metal doors in the abyss opened one after another, making a path for me.
When the second sealed door opened without a sound, she stopped and pulled me back. She stepped forward, but the door gave no response. I approached, and a green light came on.
“Between 7:50 and 8:00, you were the only one who sat in that position.” She looked at me. “This machine recognizes only you.”
I walked ahead in silence, becoming the key that opened the doors for her.
The closer we drew to the bottom, the more instruments lit up on the walls. In an outer chamber, she stopped before a huge metal plaque and read the incomplete ancient script by the dim light:
“‘A certain system must remain continuously lit. Once it disperses, the underlying restart operation must be performed again.’”

The pursuers’ footsteps stopped outside that sealed door and never sounded again. The door had become a complete barrier against everything above. We were now truly trapped inside a grave with no way back.
“Don’t just look at the words. Look at the surface.” She pointed to two glaring filing marks on the plaque. “The modifiers before ‘system’ and ‘continuously lit’ were scraped away with
a file. And the ‘Safety Regulations’ we memorized in class happen to be missing the most important page too. I asked our mentor yesterday what to do. She said there was no such page.”
She clenched her teeth.

“They taught us for ten years how to read the instruments, but erased what this machine was meant to maintain and what would happen if it dispersed. We don’t even know what kind of monster we’re touching.”

At the end stood a massive iron platform. A huge rust-covered iron cage hung over the abyss. Without the slightest hesitation, I stepped inside, and she followed. The cage door grated harshly and slammed shut. Trembling, the cage descended into the abyss.
Not long afterward, the steel cables snapped with a shriek.

Weightlessness seized my insides. During the first two seconds before the final crash, the old shaft’s emergency resistance calipers produced a string of piercing grinding sounds. Amid violent sparks and jolts, the cage

suddenly slowed. She slammed me to the floor. My cheek was pressed against the cold metal cage bottom, and through the twisted bars I stared at the seam in the cage door. With one final boom, the world became silent darkness.
The echoes of metal grinding in the old shaft continued to reverberate through the empty abyss. I realized I was still lying with my cheek against the floor. As my vision slowly focused,
the first thing I saw was the cage door several steps away, its bars badly warped by the crash. A small patch of dim yellow light seeped through the gap, painful against my eyes.
A dust- and blood-streaked hand was pressed hard against my forehead.
“You’re awake. Don’t move yet.”
She sat on the metal floor beside me. A strip had been torn from the hem of her shirt and tied tightly around my forearm to stop the bleeding.
“You’ve been unconscious for a long time. Probably more than half an hour.” She looked at me.

I pushed myself upright, my head splitting with pain. The iron cage had fallen into a deeper underground hall, twisted and deformed, with the instruments on all four walls glowing densely in the gloom.
“Somewhere in the middle just now… you actually woke up once, for about ten minutes.”
“I did?”

“The person who woke up didn’t seem much like you.” She stared at my face, as if deciding whether she should say it. “You suddenly opened your eyes, staggered to your feet, and had me help you pry open the maintenance side—the service passage behind the panels of the large machine outside.”
She pointed to the disassembled machine in the corner of the hall.
“You looked exhausted, and some of the words you used were… hard to understand. Then you felt around inside that passage for a while. You seemed to alter the records on the main panel and connect

something.” Her brows drew together. “After that, you had me come over and pointed to the metal sliders hidden deep inside the service opening, telling me to look at the interlock indicator on the outside.”
She drew a deep breath.

“I couldn’t understand what you were doing. But when you finished making the connection, the outer interlock light really did go out because of what you had done. You had me push the slider all the way in myself.”

“As soon as I pushed it in, you let out a great breath, like all your strength had left you. You said, ‘No matter what happens, I’ll come back and fulfill my promise.’ After leaving me that sentence, you collapsed again.”
“I said something hard to understand? Fulfill what promise?”
“I don’t know. You even looked at the time on the control terminal.” She looked at the twisted metal on the floor. “Whatever happened, we need to get out alive first.”

I sat on the floor as an icy chill climbed up my spine. I not only had no memory of standing up, I had no idea how I could have connected wires and pushed the slider. But looking at her scraped knees and this desperate ruin, I could only force down my fear, brace myself against a nearby metal pipe, and stand.

A section of passage farther down split in the middle, divided by an extremely thick blast-resistant glass wall. I was diverted into a cramped corridor on the left, while she entered the spacious control room on the right. The structure of the passage forced us to take separate sides.
We had not gone far along the glass before we discovered a sealed security door on each side. We could only gesture through the transparent glass.
She watched the geometric patterns change on the console over there, then drew them backward in the air for me to see. I followed the instructions and turned the mechanical dial on my door.
The heavy gears engaged four times, and the blast door on my side burst open. Immediately afterward, the door on her side also lit up green. The linked mechanism had passed verification.
Through the glass, I saw her relax on the other side and make a mischievous face at me, exaggerating the word with her mouth: Idiot.

We continued downward through the underground depths, which resembled a grave. Over the trek, the beam of the flashlight grew yellow and weak, until it could illuminate less than half a meter of metal grating beneath our feet. Dehydration had left my throat dry as

if packed with sand, and every breath carried the taste of blood. While detouring around a collapsed section, my foot slipped and half my body hung over the abyss. Yuna grabbed the collar of my shirt from above with both hands. I climbed upward using her strength,

while she leaned almost her entire upper body out over the edge. Just as my right foot found firm footing on the grating, her foot slipped and she pitched forward. In that instant, she instinctively released me to grab the railing beside her, and my collar came free.

I gripped the sharp edge of the grating with all my strength. My palms were sliced open and streaming blood, but I barely kept myself from falling. Yuna crawled back on hands and knees, seized my wrist, and pulled me up with everything she had.
The two of us collapsed against the cold iron wall, gasping violently, our hearts pounding in our throats. A few seconds later, fear turned into anger.
“Were you about to let go?!” I shouted at her.
“Who told you not to watch where you were going?!” she shouted back without yielding, her eyes red. “You nearly dragged me down with you!”
After we shouted, the abyss returned to silence. Only our heavy breathing remained. She turned away, took the canteen from her waist, and shook it. Only a little water remained
at the bottom. She did not drink it, but handed it straight to me. The acid in my stomach seemed to burn through the lining; even swallowing saliva felt like swallowing a knife.

The drive we had in the morning had long since been drained by the cold of the abyss. Later, we stopped speaking altogether. I had no idea how many levels we had crossed; I only felt the smell of dust grow heavier with every

stretch downward. The entire world became nothing but the mechanical sound of our footsteps and the heavy breathing she made while supporting me. We trekked through the dim underground passage for nearly three hours, relying

entirely on instinct except for several extremely brief rests. During that time, the despair hidden beneath everything grew heavier and heavier—we had no idea how much farther we had to go, or what this machine actually wanted.
Before the final fork in the passage, she stopped, leaned most of her weight against the wall, and breathed in quick, shallow gasps.

The metal door on the left bore a circular marking; the large door on the right was engraved with ancient script. She went to the right and read it. Her expression changed slightly. When I approached the door on the left, the indicator on its frame instantly turned green, lighting only for me.
“The right one says ‘control corridor.’” She looked at the circular marking on the left, her voice tense. “And this marking is the ‘operator’s room.’ This door recognizes only you now.”
“If it’s a dead end, we won’t go in,” I said. “We’ll take the right-hand door together.”

“The right side is an airlock. Only one person can enter at a time, and it has to verify—” She stepped forward and placed her hand against the reader on the right. A beam swept over it, the lock clicked, and the indicator turned green. She stepped back and turned to me. “You try.”
I stepped forward and pressed my hand to the same place. A red light flashed, and the reader gave a sharp, sustained tone of rejection.
“This door recognizes only my biometric information. Your authorization in this area has been completely erased.”

No matter how we tested it, the system’s conclusion was rigid and unchangeable: the airlock would not allow anyone to follow. I could not enter the control corridor, and she could not enter the operator’s room.

“You sat inside during that scan in the hall at 7:50. I started it.” She raised her head and looked at the partition wall between the two doors. “It bound your identity, and it bound mine too. Both positions have to be occupied at the same time. They can’t be switched.”
She turned to look at me.
“Level by level, it split the authorizations apart this completely. From the beginning, this machine was designed so no one could complete the operation alone.”

“Look on the bright side. Maybe there’s a passage straight to the surface in your room.” She suddenly smiled, her smile clean and clear. “If either of us finds a way out inside, don’t wait for the other. Run out and find a way to get help.”

She held out her right hand. It was the old rule we had followed whenever we made bets as children: a hard slap of the palms, then hooking our little fingers together. I met her hand. When our fingertips touched, her hand was cold as ice.
“Arno. No matter what happens, we have to come back.”
With that, she turned and pushed open the door on the right. The heavy metal door closed behind her with a dull locking sound.
I pushed open the left-hand door that belonged to me.
I slid down a narrow, slanted shaft and landed hard in a completely white room.

The walls and floor had been cast as one piece, without seams. The room was pitifully small. I took seven steps forward, and my toes touched the end. I raised my head. The one-way shaft I had just slid down opened three meters above, in a

sheer wall. At the edge of the ceiling was another maintenance duct with an iron grille. It was black inside, and a line of extremely faint reflected light seemed to travel down the metal pipe from an unknown depth. Aside from those two openings,

the walls were smooth, with no handholds at all. There was no way to climb back. In this pure-white space, there was no button, screen, or seat that could be called an “operator” station. There were only four empty walls and a smooth floor.

In this room built specifically for the so-called “operator,” there was no operating equipment—only absolute confinement and waiting. It did not feel like a place for someone to start the machine. It felt more like a place to load some kind of fuel, or imprison a dangerous object that could never be allowed out.
A long, narrow window was embedded in the wall to my right. Its surface was like a sheet of transparent ice. On the other side was a narrow control-room corridor. I saw her walk
to the enormous main console. The moment she touched the panel, her left wrist was forcibly locked into a metal ring. Several slender probes sprang out and bit deep into her skin.
She frowned from the pain, then saw me through the glass and raised her right hand in greeting.
I struck the glass hard. She shook her head and pressed the metal grille switch in the corner. After being filtered through the communicator, her voice was thin, as if separated by a layer of water.
“Can you hear me?”
“Yes. What happened to your hand?”
“Authorization verification. I can’t pull it free, but I’m fine. Don’t knock on the glass anymore. Save your strength.”

A long, dead silence took over this underground grave. At first, we tried to communicate through the glass about ways to escape, but every lock remained as unresponsive as an iron wall. As time passed, an indescribable sense of

depletion began spreading through the control corridor. I watched her on the other side of the window. At first, she could still stand by leaning against the console. Gradually, she could only slide down along the console to sit

on the floor, forcing herself upright every few dozen minutes to look at the unchanged screen. Her lips cracked from extreme dehydration. Several times she tried to gesture something to me, only for her hand to fall helplessly

halfway up. In this absolutely silent white room, I could almost feel that time was not passing, but settling into something with weight, pressing down on her little by little. This desperate standoff continued for an entire day.
System time: 20:36.

At that exact moment, the equipment underground began to behave strangely. One of the main screens in the control corridor on her side went dark without warning. I looked up toward the end of the maintenance duct at the edge of the ceiling. It was impossible to tell how deep

it went. Deep inside the pipe, where there had been only darkness, a layer of ghastly white light suddenly reflected downward. There was no direction to the light source. It was as though something blindingly bright had erupted at an immense height, whitening the entire duct.

Immediately afterward, the absolute white of the wall on my side dimmed slightly once, as if an invisible hand had lowered the light of the entire world by one level. Yuna lurched sharply on the other side and caught herself against the console with one hand.
Over the next hour or more, the long standby finally began to slide into an irreversible decline. I watched the screens that had been continuously lit in Yuna’s control
corridor go dark one after another. The lights throughout the underground hall also dimmed layer by layer, until only a few weak red lights remained, barely clinging to life.

The probes were still clamped tightly into her wrist, the dried blood around the punctures turned dark red. As the power around us drained away, the instruments on her console emitted a dull, low hum. Yuna’s breathing grew lighter and lighter. The violent impact of the fall, the extreme

dehydration from going without water for more than ten hours, and the lack of oxygen at the bottom of the abyss were rapidly draining her strength. Each time she managed to straighten herself to look at the main panel, she soon lost her strength again and slumped against the console.
Until the system time shifted to 21:50.

“The underlying record on the main panel…” She stared fixedly at the screen, her body swaying uncontrollably as she gasped for breath. She watched the faintly fluctuating line at the edge of the screen. “The real-time monitoring of the operator’s neural state—this line hasn’t changed shape at all from eight this morning until now.”
She turned and looked at me through the glass.

“It’s still watching you. And the environmental compatibility status here at the control terminal has fallen from full capacity at dawn to two percent now. There’s also that half-command left at eight this morning… its annotation says ‘Not yet completed.’”
“So it isn’t broken? The scan this morning only completed the first half of the activation?” I asked urgently.

“The same record… yes. The machine never stopped. It’s been waiting in the active state for fourteen hours for us to confirm it.” She raised her reddened eyes to look at me. “The fourteen hours of remaining capacity hasn’t changed,

but it’s already ten at night… Even if we press the confirmation key now, subtracting those fourteen hours can only barely take us back to eight o’clock this morning, when it began waiting. We’ll never reach yesterday evening.”
“If we can’t get back to save Estelle yesterday, then don’t press it!” I struck the glass hard. “While you still have the strength, let’s find a way to pry the door open and get out!”

“Everything outside is shutting down.” She pointed to the last few darkened sections on the main screen. “Before that main screen went dark just now, I saw the power and telemetry data from the outer stations. It isn’t

that this machine has run out of power. The world above has cut the connection. This machine is turning into a dead grave. Once it goes completely dark, we’ll be locked in and unable even to get through this door.”

Her left wrist was locked in place. She could only run her right hand along the console, trying to reach the row of locked levers and force the operation to stop, but they were too far away. She tried twice and could not touch them. The emergency stop button beside them was blocked beneath by a rusted metal latch and could not be pressed.

The probes in her left wrist severely restricted the movement of her hand. Her breath caught sharply, and cold sweat slid down her forehead. She did not waste even a second struggling. Instead, she pressed the weight of her entire body onto the console and tipped herself toward its far right end.
“There’s only one road left. The final confirmation key for the main procedure is over there.”
She stretched her right hand as far as she could, her fingertips hovering above the cover.
“Once this activation is completed, the probes will release. At least we can return to eight this morning. I’m going to press it.”

“Wait! You can’t hold out in your condition! If starting the machine still requires you to expend your strength, you’ll die!” I smashed the glass like a madman. “Don’t press it! I’ll break through and get over there!”
“I told you. I’m the only one who can press it from outside.”
Her knee gave way and struck the metal console hard. With her left hand locked in place, she could not fall to her knees. She could only hang half-folded over the edge in an extremely
twisted posture, gripping the edge of the console with her right hand to keep herself from collapsing. The cat ears atop her head drooped uselessly into her hair like wet rags.
“Yuna!” I slid to my knees in front of the glass. “Rest for a while, okay? Just rest first!”
“I’m a little sleepy.”
She closed her eyes briefly, then forced them open again.
“Arno.”
She lifted the plastic cover and held her hand above the confirmation key. The veins stood out clearly on the pale back of her hand.
“Arno, tell me—those times you promised to buy me meat, from when we were children until now… you never actually welched on any of them, did you?”
“No… Never.” Tears welled up uncontrollably in my eyes.
“Yeah.” She closed her eyes. “If the one who woke up was you too, then I believe you… You must have had your reasons.”
Using the last of her strength, she pressed her palm down.
The system made no tremendous sound. Only the tower’s breath, as if coming from the center of the earth, took an extremely long, deep breath beneath my feet.

Immediately afterward, the metal ring locking her wrist gave a dull click and released. Yuna slid down the metal console, all strength gone. She fell into a seated position on the floor, her face turned toward my window.
She was still looking at me. Her lips moved with difficulty, but her voice could no longer pass through the grille. I desperately tried to read her lips.
Only two syllables. She was calling my name.
Then her eyes lost focus, and her breathing stopped completely.

All I remember is my fists hammering the blast-resistant glass, blood coating it. The white room was like a black hole, swallowing every sound I made. On the console beyond the window, the screen quietly lit one square an eye-searing green.
The system time shifted. Ten o’clock p.m.

As I understood it, this was simple arithmetic: the system executed fourteen hours of retreat, returning exactly to the eight o’clock when it had begun that morning. Back to eight o’clock, when Yuna was still standing safely beside me.
Ice-cold morning light.

The sensor lights above the corridor were shining with perfect steadiness. The ancient display panel on the wall gave off a green glow. Eight o’clock sharp. From somewhere extremely deep and distant came the click of an outer door lock releasing. Exactly as I remembered it.
Yuna was standing three steps away from me, leaning against the corridor wall and staring fixedly at the door behind me.

I stared straight at her. The cat ears atop her head were standing upright, just as they should. More importantly, the little tuft of unruly fur at the tips of her ears—made impossible to flatten by the way she slept—was sticking up, alive and well.
Thirty seconds passed. Then another thirty seconds. The air seemed to solidify.
At that exact moment, the corridor lights flickered once. Yuna turned to look at me.
“…What’s wrong?”
“…” I stared at her like a dead man.
“Arno? You look awful, like you’ve seen a ghost. Did the machine’s shaking make you feel sick just now?”
I looked at her lips, still flushed with color, and the rise and fall of her breathing.
“It’s been a full minute.” She glanced at the time. “We said we’d wait thirty seconds and see if anything changed. Nothing happened.”
She looked suspiciously toward the console.

“I’m going to check the panel. I heard the record-refresh chime just now.” She hurried over and read the screen with a frown. “Only one command. The annotation says ‘Not yet completed.’ I don’t understand what it means.”
The door leading to the reversal was pushed open by the two of us with our own hands.

For the full seven days before we entered that tower, we thought we had uncovered the horrifying secrets of this land. This story has to begin seven days earlier. It has to begin with that strange classroom, and those three entirely different sets of formal clothes.
Seven days earlier.
At that time, there were still three of us.

texts.chapter:volume0-first-lesson:event:text-:
Page One of The Picture Book of Convergence:
Once upon a time, giants lived beneath the sky.
Giants did not need lamps—they plucked the stars down and hung them in their

rooms.
Giants did not need to walk—they could step from sunrise to sunset in a single stride.
What happened next?
What happened next is written on the pages that follow.
That morning, I woke at six-thirty.

As long as a person knows that something they have waited ten years for will happen today, their body will wake them first. If I could make it through the next seven days of examination, be formally selected, gain access to the

White Tower, and perhaps even touch the old facilities that kept the settlement running, I would have the highest status a village apprentice could attain—and the only chance to find out what secret that long-dead man had been hiding.

I lay in bed for a while, listening to the sounds in the house. Mother was already up. I heard her moving around by the stove, rustling very quietly—the kind of quiet meant to avoid waking her son, even though she must have known perfectly well that there was no way I could sleep that morning.
When I got up, it was still dark, and the formal robe was already hanging over the back of the chair.

The candidate uniform was mostly standardized, but each family supplied its own details. The way we were taught to put it was: pure white belongs to the divine, embellishment belongs to people. The divine part was not to be given color. As for the part belonging to people, you could embroider as much as you liked.

Yuna’s formal robe was covered in crimson and gold. Hers was the boldest embroidery in the entire village. She had said proudly that since the regulations allowed it, she intended to fill the part belonging to people completely.

On the surface, mine had only the lapis and crimson embellishments required by Church regulations. My mother did not like making a show of things. Apart from those two permitted colors, she had hidden all the other multicolored

supplementary threads in the lining and inside the cuffs. In addition to the robe, the formalwear came with a narrow metal arc-ring as a head identification device, marked only with segmented gradations and the candidate insignia.
When I had put everything on properly, the door creaked open and she came in carrying a basin of hot water.
“Wipe your face. Then turn around.” She set down the basin, wrung out a hot towel and handed it to me, then wiped her hands on her apron as she spoke.

I took it and wiped my face carelessly, then turned around. She carefully smoothed my collar, leaned closer, picked out a loose thread that only she could see from my cuff, and then pulled something from her pocket.
It was a dark green tool belt.

It still had the old-era fasteners and repair scratches, and the woven edge had come loose in places. It had lain at the bottom of the chest in our house for many years. I had found it once when I was little, but she immediately took it away without explanation.
“Wear this today.” She held out the belt, her tone flat.

I looked at the belt. Against the uniform with its lapis and crimson embellishments, it was the only dark thing. And it was no ceremonial sash. It was a work belt that had truly been through grease and machinery.
“This isn’t regulation.” I did not take it.
“The section on belts in the candidate formalwear regulations says ‘self-supplied.’” She looked me in the eye. “I checked.”
My mother never broke regulations. She would not even step on the edge line of the village road. Yet she had checked the wording for this belt.

Without waiting to see whether I would take it, she leaned over and wrapped it around my waist. Her hands were practiced. Her fingers went around twice, and as she tied the knot, her movements suddenly paused.
“His?” I asked softly.
“Mm.”

I waited for her to continue, even if only by one sentence. She did not. She pulled the knot tight, stepped back half a pace, looked me up and down, then reached over and smoothed once more the spot on my collar she had already flattened. Only then did she nod in satisfaction.
“There.” She turned to pick up the basin.
“Mom.”
“Not today.” With her back to me, her voice hardened. “Today is a good day.”
She carried the basin back toward the stove.

The things I had heard about my father from her added up to no more than twenty sentences. I knew that he had died young when I was seven, and that he was good with his hands. As for why he had not even left an official record of

cancellation, no one had told me. Whenever I asked, her answer always had the same shape: a sentence neither long nor short, without a single adjective, followed by her turning away to do something else and leaving me with her back.
By the time I was sixteen, I had learned not to ask anymore.
Yuna did not knock on the window.

When I pushed open the door and stepped outside, the morning wind was cold, and the frozen ground still gave off a chill. She was already standing by the roadside, her back to me, looking up at the sky.

Yuna had had her own way of knocking on windows since she was eight: one tentative knock, then two impatient ones, and finally her whole face pressed against the window gap to make a face. But today, she was actually standing quietly by the roadside waiting.
I stopped in the doorway.
She caught the sound of the door opening at once, but did not turn around.
“What are you staring at? Let’s go.”
Those two lines of hers were always joined together. There was never any space between them, like a gust of wind sweeping past.
“Why didn’t you knock?” I walked down the steps.
She turned around.

Only then did I get a clear look at her. She was wearing a metal arc-ring around her head, fitted around her cat ears. Her formal robe had an extremely high stiff collar, locked high around her neck. Once it was on, she could not turn her head freely.
She thought she looked ridiculous too, so she laughed first, her eyes curving into two crescents.

“Couldn’t.” She pointed at her head. “Whenever I move, this metal ring knocks against the window frame. My mom said I wasn’t allowed to knock around someone else’s window this morning. It’s bad luck.”
“So you just stood by the road.”
“I stood very properly.” She deliberately thrust out her chest. “I’d already been standing properly here since your mom got up to light the fire.”

We followed the village road toward the White Tower, our soles striking the stone pavement with a hollow sound. The route from the mill to the central square, then through the old residential district, usually took only twenty minutes. Today, it seemed unusually long.

It was barely light, but there were already early risers in the village. By the chess stand, Old Baro was methodically setting out the pieces. From the direction of the mill came the dull sound of the waterwheel turning.

On the road outside the yard, six people were huffing and puffing as they lifted something very long onto their shoulders. It was wrapped tightly in gray cloth, with a little rust-spotted metal showing at either end.

They were arranged in two rows, thick pads of straw beneath their shoulders, their steps heavy. All six wore the same gray smocks, each with a square of cloth sewn onto the left shoulder—same position, same size.
Yuna laboriously turned her body and lifted her chin.
“Morning.”
The burly man at the front looked up, recognized her, and gave a muffled reply. He did not stop walking. The thing on his shoulders could not stop.
As we passed, everyone by the road stopped what they were doing and watched us.
It was a very formal, slightly solemn kind of looking. Old Baro set down the chess piece he had just picked up and gave us a solemn nod.
“They’re looking at us,” I said quietly.
“They’re looking at today. Only once a year.”
She said it lightly, but her fingers were clenched around the edge of her clothes, and her breathing was quiet.
When we were nearly at the central square, a child shot out of a side alley like a cannonball.
It was Milu, Yuna’s younger sister.
“Sis!”
She skidded to a stop and looked up at the metal arc-ring on Yuna’s head and the high stiff collar, her eyes wide as saucers.
“Wow.”
“Wow what?” Yuna said irritably, unable to bend down freely.
“Is it heavy?” Milu reached out to touch it.
“Heavy.”
“Then why are you wearing it?”
“Because it looks good.”
Milu went halfway around her, seriously evaluating her from every angle, then reached a conclusion:
“It does look pretty good. But you can’t move your neck. You look like a pillar.”
“Go home.” Yuna rolled her eyes.
Milu giggled, ran a couple of steps, then turned back, her expression becoming unusually serious.
“Sis.”
“What?”
“You’re going to win today, right?”
Yuna paused, her breath catching for an instant.
“What are you talking about? This isn’t a competition.”
“That’s what everyone says. They say only two people will be kept this year. Big Brother Arno has the first place, and you have to compete with the other person for the second.”
The formal announcement had not yet been made, but news about the allocation of places had been spreading through the yard as though it had grown wings for a week.
Yuna did not answer right away. She laboriously bent down and expertly pressed down the tuft of hair sticking up over Milu’s forehead.
“Go home. Tell Mom I’ll be back for dinner.”
Milu ran off, her back quickly disappearing around the mouth of the alley.
We walked for only a few minutes before stopping at the steps beneath the White Tower. It was much quieter here than in the village. Only then did Yuna speak again.

“In the end, only two of the three can stay. As long as they do not cross the red line, a lineal candidate is guaranteed to inherit their parents’ place. That rule hasn’t changed in decades. You were only temporarily entered

into the records as ‘Internal—Lineal,’ but since the system accepted you, your first place is secure.” She sounded as though she were chewing over the thought. “I have to compete with the one from the outskirts for the second.”
“You knew already.”
“I confirmed it yesterday. Elder Sera told me herself. Three candidates this year, two internal and one external. The main competition is between me and that external candidate.”
“External?” I was a little surprised.

“From an outlying settlement. Seventeen years ago, the Church compromised and said it would bring in new blood. It was only a resolution that passed on paper. Until today, this place had never actually been honored all the way to the step of an adult entering the Tower.”
As she said this, she raised her left hand and pressed her thumb against the metal clasp on the inside of her wrist.
It was an old cloth band faded to reddish brown, wrapped twice around her wrist. When she was thinking, she would unconsciously turn those two loops. From the outside in, one loop, then the other.
“I’m thinking about seventeen years. If this were an open road, someone else should have made it to the end by now. But there’s only this one.”
She turned one loop halfway, then stopped, her fingers tightening around the cloth.
“That door only opened a crack seventeen years ago, then got jammed shut. Now someone has decided to push that crack a little wider. I want to know who decided to push it this year.”
It was seven forty that morning. Twenty minutes remained before the first lesson began.
The White Tower’s front hall was even brighter than I had imagined.

From the outside, the building looked like a thick white bone planted in the frozen ground, cold and forbidding. From the inside, it was a very clean, very empty room. Light poured evenly from the ceiling, with no visible source.
There was already someone in the front hall when we entered.
She sat at the very end of a row of benches against the wall, her back perfectly straight, both hands placed properly on her knees, a small booklet spread across them.
She wore a purple-base formal robe, originally an old work uniform from the Watermarsh settlement, temporarily fitted with the candidate regulation’s patternless white collar and metal
arc-ring. Ice-blue and silver threads formed symmetrical rope and geometric patterns against the purple. In a room where even the air seemed pale, the vivid purple was impossible to ignore.

When she heard our footsteps, she stood and walked toward us. At exactly three steps away, she stopped, crossed her arms, and inclined her head slightly—a complete Church bow, without a fraction out of place.
“Estelle. Watermarsh settlement. This year’s external candidate.”

Her hair and ears were pale gold, arranged in immaculate low twin ponytails. The tips of her ears pointed steadily upward, unlike Yuna’s, which occasionally trembled restlessly when something happened. This was a person who had forced splendor into order.
“Arno. Mill apprentice.”
“Yuna. Chapel apprentice.”
Estelle nodded and lifted her gaze from her booklet.
“You arrived at seven forty.”
“…Did we?” I was momentarily stunned.
“There’s a time display in the front hall.” She pointed to an inconspicuous dial in the corner.
“What time did you arrive?”
“Six thirty-five.”
“The first lesson starts at eight.”
“Yes.”
There was no boast in it, and no complaint. She was simply answering a question.
Yuna looked at her for three seconds.
She looked at Estelle’s neat collar, at her unguarded certainty. Yuna let go of her casual attitude and straightened slightly. Her gaze at Estelle changed.
“Why did you come an hour and twenty-five minutes early?” Yuna’s tone had turned aggressive.

“The external-candidate entry inspection and preliminary review took forty minutes.” She opened her booklet. “I spent the remaining time checking the schedule posted on the wall. It, like the notice I received

before leaving, requires candidates to complete material collection before class begins. I didn’t know how long these procedures would stall at the site, so I estimated the lead time using the longest possible case.”
The booklet was filled with dense writing. She had copied the schedule posted on the wall word for word, leaving a blank space beside it for her own time marks.
“You copied it down.”
“Things posted on walls can be replaced. Things copied into your own booklet can’t.”
Yuna abruptly straightened her neck.
“How old are you?”
“Seventeen.”
“I’m seventeen too. You look more like thirty-seven.”
There was no ripple in Estelle’s gray-blue eyes. After a moment, she spoke:
“Thank you.”
Yuna stared for a moment, then laughed aloud. Some of her wariness faded.
The registration desk was at the other end of the front hall.
After checking my wristband, the middle-aged woman behind the desk handed me a packet in a white envelope.

Could I receive it directly because my category was the ordinary “Internal—Lineal”? But according to the regulations, an apprentice counted as lineal only if their parents possessed execution authority over the old facilities

inside the White Tower. That long-dead man had not even left a cancellation record. No one in my family possessed that authority. On what basis had the system identified me as lineal? I did not ask. I silently accepted the envelope.
It was Yuna’s turn. The screen flashed green, but the woman behind the desk stopped moving.
“Yuna, your category is ‘Internal—Non-lineal.’ Your materials require an elder’s countersign. Elder Sera will sign before class.”
Yuna stepped aside. Her fingers dropped unconsciously and found the old cloth band around her wrist.
Estelle stepped forward. The screen lit up white.
“External candidate. Every room you enter and leave today requires a hand press on the registration panel by the door. Materials will be distributed in the classroom.”
Estelle nodded, opened her booklet, and wrote it down.
As the three of us headed down the corridor, Estelle closed her booklet.
“Go ahead and ask what you want to ask.” She turned to Yuna. “You’ve been watching me since the front hall.”
“Have you been to the White Tower before?” Yuna stared at her.
“No.”
“Then how did you calculate in advance that there would be this many absurd rules designed to trip people up, and leave exactly an hour and twenty-five minutes?”
Estelle thought for a moment, her brow drawing slightly together.

“I can’t calculate whether something is designed to trip people up. I only estimated from the longest times listed on the schedule. If I were late, I would be disqualified. If I were early, I would only waste my own time. So I chose to waste my own time.”
She tucked the booklet neatly into the crook of her arm.
“Our margins for error are different.”
The classroom was on the underground level, and the corridor held only ghastly white permanent lights.

At the end stood a heavy metal door. The six burly men in gray smocks whom we had seen in the yard that morning were there too, silently leaning the heavy metal frame against the wall. It gave off the stale, metallic smell of iron.
Elder Sera approached from the other end of the corridor. The burly man at the front respectfully called out, “Elder,” in a low voice.
Sera did not respond. She pressed her hand to the registration panel, and the door slid open without a sound.
“Come in.”

Yuna and I walked over. Estelle stopped at the doorway, glanced back at the registration panel beside it, and pressed her hand down. Only after the screen lit white in confirmation did she cross the threshold.
The door slammed shut behind us.

The classroom had no windows. A long table stood in the center, with three metal chairs behind it. All the square panels in the ceiling were dark. Only a small screen on the wall directly ahead was lit, displaying a line from an old text.
We sat down in the chairs.
Elder Sera walked to the far end of the table. Her plain white uniform did not have a single crease. The difference today was a dark red metal insignia on her cuff.
First she took an envelope bearing a red seal from the folder and handed it to Yuna, then pushed another, blue one, toward Estelle.
“This year, an exception has been made. An external candidate is sitting here.” Her gaze swept over us. “But the rules have not changed. In seven days, only two of you will remain.”

“I’ll start with the unpleasant part. I’m not going to coax you into this room with a warm opening. At the registration desk today, the three of you were still ordinary village apprentices. But from eight o’clock—from the moment you stepped into this room—you officially

became ‘candidates.’ That status can be terminated on any day during the next seven days. Termination does not require you to make a mistake, and you will not necessarily be told why. If anyone has taken today for a ceremony where you receive a badge, you may leave now.”
No one spoke.
“Induction is not a day. It lasts seven days and proceeds in layers. Each layer delivers part of the knowledge, and each layer reassesses your qualifications. If you are suspended on any
day, you will remain a ‘candidate’ forever. Only after making it through the seventh day will you be formally selected. After suspension, the Church will not make up anything you missed.”
Estelle recorded it rapidly in her booklet.
“In today’s lesson, I will deliver only three things. Listen carefully, and write them down.”
She raised one finger.
“First: candidates will be granted access to the old facilities in stages. Today is the first stage.”
She raised a second finger.
“Second: knowledge is not personal property. Anything candidates learn must not be repeated to anyone who has not been selected. Must not, including
to family.” She looked at Yuna and me. “Being selected means that from today onward, you share responsibility with us. You are part of ‘us’ now.”
She raised a third finger.
“Third: any breach of boundaries may terminate your candidacy. The examination does not consider your motive, nor whether you caused any actual damage. One wrong step and you are out.”
“Because there are things in this building that, if understood incompletely, will harm the person who understands them—or even destroy that person.”
Yuna raised her hand.
“Speak.”
“Why would understanding something incompletely destroy a person?” Yuna stared at her. “Is that why you sealed them away back then?”
“You are not yet qualified to know.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
“It is an answer. I am telling you that I will not answer, and telling you why I will not answer. It is not a riddle. That is the rule.”
“Will you tell us on the seventh day?”
“If you’re still here.”

The materials placed in our hands contained no sacred doctrine, only cold data: how many floors the White Tower had, which floors had been sealed, and which areas remained inaccessible because of contamination. This was not the preaching we were used to hearing in the outskirts. It was a disclosure.
“A considerable portion of the space in this building is inaccessible even to us. It contains secrets we forgot long ago.”
When she reached a floor deep underground, she stopped.
“An old research project was preserved on this floor.”
The screen on the wall flickered. An extremely simple diagram of a mechanical structure appeared, accompanied by a line of blurred text.
Estelle immediately raised her pen and drew the components that could be made out in the diagram.
Yuna leaned her upper body forward and stared fixedly at the blurred mechanical structure.
“What research?” Yuna blurted out.
“That exceeds the permissions granted to you today.”
“If we’re not allowed to know, why put the diagram up?”
“It is displayed so you can recognize the danger in advance. If you encounter a similar structure—do not investigate it. Under no circumstances touch it.”
“Remembering the shape of danger is safer than pouring the whole picture into you at once.” Sera did not engage with her provocation. Her gaze passed over the three of us.
Yuna did not ask again. But I saw her hand clench into a fist beneath the table.
“Set the boundaries first, then survive within them. This is the Church’s protection mechanism.”
Before dismissing us, she handed out a card printed in poor-quality ink.

“Question: A person claims to have heard an instruction in the silence of the dice-roller. This cannot be verified against the shared record.
　　How should the candidate handle it?
Answer: Statements of this kind are meaningless. Do not pursue them further.”
The dice-roller was the specific divine name used in the Church’s scriptures for the creator who determined the world’s probabilities and operating paths. It was not a metaphor.
“Copy it once in your own handwriting. Return it to me for the records.”
“Which line?”
“Both lines. Without changing a single word.”
I took out my pen and copied it. Estelle copied it fastest.
Yuna copied it too, but pressed the paper flat against the tabletop.
“But what if he really did hear it? Not being verifiable and being ‘meaningless’ aren’t the same thing. That’s a logical problem.”
Sera reached out and pulled the paper away.
“We are not discussing this question today.”
After we handed in the cards, Sera operated the control panel beside the door. A hidden compartment opened, and she took out three temporary access permits.

“The common-knowledge portion of the first stage is complete. Now comes a practical exercise. The decommissioned cable bridge outside the corridor is your task today. Move it to the recycling area on sublevel two. But your permissions are different.”
She looked at Estelle.
“External candidate. You have the complete transfer procedure. You are responsible for checking the execution order of every step. Miss one, and the alarm will lock the door.”
She turned to Yuna.
“Non-lineal internal candidate. You have only a public safety card. When you encounter an access-control error, you must determine the conditions for passage from the device’s actual feedback.”
Finally, she turned to me.
“Arno, you are the only one who can connect to the sensing terminal on that metal frame. The physical lines are your responsibility.”
Sera looked at us coldly.
“How you coordinate across different permissions is your concern. The exercise begins the moment you step through this door.”
We left the classroom. Estelle carefully pressed her hand to the panel outside the door. Yuna did not.
Beside the heavy, old metal bridge in the corridor was a control terminal embedded in the wall. Beneath it was an old mechanical authorization slot, exposing heavy
copper reeds and a gear-locking mechanism. I recognized it at a glance—the old water pump in the lower level of the mill used the same obsolete mechanical structure.
Estelle looked down at the sheet.
“Step one: environmental safety verification. Before connecting, we must confirm that the gas valve in this area has been closed.”
Yuna inserted the public safety card into the terminal. Red text appeared on the screen: “Gas valve response timed out.”
She followed the wiring behind the terminal upward, all the way to the bare ceiling. There was only a blind end of ventilation ductwork there, with no sign of any mechanical gas valve.

“There’s no gas valve on this level.” Yuna pointed at the rusted metal blind end. “It’s honestly waiting for a signal that doesn’t exist. The equipment isn’t broken, but the error has stalled the procedure here.”

“According to procedure, when the safety verification cannot be satisfied, operations must stop and the matter must be reported to a superior.” Estelle immediately took half a step back and reached for the communication key beside the terminal.
When she pressed it, there was only a harsh electrical hiss.

“The procedure sheet says the exercise limit is fifteen minutes.” Estelle pointed to the words on the sheet. “I assumed that the ‘report to a superior’ specified in the procedure would always connect before the time ran out.”
“The communication is down.” Yuna stared at the terminal and slapped its casing twice. “Go back and knock. Sera can’t have gone far.”

I turned and walked toward the heavy metal door we had just come through, then pounded on it twice. No sound passed through. The red light that had been lit on the door went out. It had not closed. It had locked itself.

We froze around the terminal. Estelle rapidly flipped through the booklet, searching for other compliant clauses. Yuna circled the bridge, checking for a physical switch. I crouched beneath the terminal, checking whether a wire had come loose. We found nothing.
The red text on the screen flashed silently for almost ten minutes.
“There are no other clauses.” Estelle’s voice finally showed signs of agitation. She pointed to the sheet again. “Once the fifteen minutes are exceeded, the system will automatically judge us to
have failed. If we stand in the corridor without working, then when the fifteen minutes are up… During the seven-day examination, a failing result in any exercise means losing our qualifications.”

“The communication is down, and the door is locked.” Yuna’s voice tightened. “So if we just stand here and wait for the countdown to end, we’re eliminated today? If this is the ‘boundary’ she drew, then there’s no way to survive inside it.”
“Yes. Pressing the elimination key beside it means withdrawing voluntarily; waiting fifteen minutes means failing on timeout. The result is the same. This is a dead end.
” Estelle stared at the row of red text. “‘If any safety check is omitted, the corridor access control will lock immediately.’ If you force it now, we’ll be trapped here.”
“We only need to short the gas-valve detection interface with copper wire and trick the machine into thinking the valve is closed.”
“No! ‘Tampering with the gas-valve detection line is prohibited. Otherwise, the bridge’s built-in anti-fall deadlock will trigger.’ Touch the wire and the whole frame will lock in place.”

Giving up would eliminate us directly. Waiting for time to reach zero would eliminate us too. Forcing it would lock the door. Rewiring it would lock the frame. The fifteen-minute limit was running out.

I looked at the old slot beneath the terminal, my palms slick with sweat. The old tool belt Mother had fastened around me that morning was tight against my waist. I had waited ten years to enter this building. I could not be sent back the way I came because of a sentence saying, “The procedure doesn’t work.”

“We can’t damage the line, but we can bypass its brain.” I drew a deep breath and gripped the heavy, rough brass connector. “The mechanical slot in this terminal has the same structure as the old water pump at the

mill. I’m betting their startup logic is the same too—the system will be forced to restart if we pull and reinsert the main power line beside it. In the two seconds after it wakes up, before it starts reading the

peripheral sensors, only the core verification module will be working. If I force the connector in and make the gears bite… it’ll directly recognize the connection as successful and won’t have time to check the gas valve.”

“That isn’t in the procedure.” Estelle flipped through the pages rapidly, her fingers trembling slightly. “Using a power interruption to bypass the initialization check is a nonstandard action. If the equipment is damaged…”

“What standard action is left? We’re out of time.” Yuna stepped closer. “Estelle, either go press the elimination key now and declare that the chance you waited seventeen years for ends here, or shut up and help!”
Estelle’s gray-blue eyes fixed on the rough brass plug in my hand. She bit her lip. After several seconds, she slowly closed her booklet and stepped aside.

After a brief standoff, Yuna seized the thick black main power cable. “Get ready. Forcing it in will definitely push back. I’ll count to three. Pull the cable and plug it back in, and you force this thing into place.”
I gripped the connector tightly with both hands.
“Three, two, one—pull!”

The screen went black instantly. Yuna moved with incredible speed, then drove the cable back in with a low growl. The power returned, the machine flashed a blinding mess of codes, and as it restarted, I shoved the brass connector into the recess.
Before the heavy internal gears could engage, tremendous mechanical recoil surged back through the plug. The spring catch on the brass fitting made a harsh scraping sound. The force numbed
the web between my thumb and forefinger, as though an entire gear array were resisting my entry. I clenched my teeth, put my full weight behind my arm, and forced the plug into the final inch.
Green authentication text appeared on the screen.
“Forced authorization complete! It didn’t check for the gas-valve signal!” Yuna shouted.
“The corridor access control didn’t lock!” Estelle looked up.
A dull sound of gears engaging came from deep within the bridge, followed by a crisp click from the bottom rollers. The deadlock released.
Together, we pushed the bridge. With the heavy rumble of its wheels, it slid forward half a meter.
At that moment, Sera’s cold voice came through the loudspeaker overhead.

“Rollers unlocked. You used the restart interval to bypass the gas-valve safety verification.” Sera’s voice came through the loudspeaker like an iron block striking down. “You were trapped by the rule that withdrawing meant elimination,

so you chose to damage the safety line and force your way through. In a real lower-level environment, what you just did would have exposed you to lethal contamination. The system has recorded the noncompliant operation in full.”
The air in the corridor suddenly fell silent.
Yuna’s hands were still braced against the rust-covered bridge. She had frozen.
Estelle snatched her hand back as though shocked and hugged the booklet filled with procedures tightly against herself.

A faint hiss of static came from the loudspeaker. Sera’s judgment hung above us like a blade. But after more than ten seconds, the locked corridor door did not open to throw us out. The blade did not fall.

“But this is the first lesson. The Church tolerates your first mistake.” The voice from the loudspeaker lowered slightly. “This was only an exercise. There was no real contamination. You kept your qualifications today.”
A soft hiss of an airlock releasing came from the door deeper in the corridor, and white light shone through the gap.
“Push the bridge all the way, then get out of here and rest. Same time tomorrow. Second lesson.”
The loudspeaker cut out.

I looked at my palms, flushed from the force I had exerted. The tendons on the backs of my hands were still taut, and the dull pain at the web between my thumb and forefinger was clear. The door had opened. We had not been eliminated. I

looked at Yuna. She was still braced against the rust-covered bridge. Estelle had lowered her head, her knuckles white around the booklet filled with copied safety procedures. Her first day had ended with a “violation” recorded in the system.

The veins stood out on the backs of her hands as she forced the winch to stop reversing. Using that brief relief, Yuna regained her footing, silently placed her blistered, bleeding palms back on the rough wooden lever, and followed us in lowering the rope inch by inch.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s10-1: No one told us whether we would be allowed to stay after dragging the thing into the recycling area. Estelle’s black-covered booklet recording our violations hung above our heads like a guillotine poised to
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s10-2: fall. We held out through the morning in silence and exhaustion. It was not until the afternoon that Sera took us, dehydrated and with our palms rubbed raw, directly toward another timed practical exercise.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s13-1: Sera led us to a small room beside the classroom on the outskirts of the White Tower. It had no windows. The air smelled of old machine oil and dry dust. In the very center sat an old piece of equipment, like a metal
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s13-2: beast crouched on the floor. A wide, semicircular control console surrounded the space in front of it like a moat. There was an opening in the middle of the console, just wide enough for one person to walk through.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s14-1: Strangely, two gray metal partitions rose stiffly from the semicircular console, taller than our heads. They were inserted into the console like a large capital “V,” with the point of the “V” pressed against the center of the semicircle’s inner edge—the empty space where the operator was supposed to stand.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s14-2: The two sides extended all the way to the outer edge of the console. In this way, the entire console was cut into three sectors from which the others could not be seen. If three people stood before the three sections, they could only hear one another through the uneven little holes in the partitions.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s17-1: Sera stood by the door and read the three names once first, as if taking inventory.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s18-1: She always did that. Before issuing an instruction, she had to name, one by one, everyone responsible for it. Only when those names had been driven into the air like nails did the matter truly begin.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s22-1: “The main power source for this thing was dismantled long ago, so none of the mechanisms inside can turn.” She patted the machine casing. “But the control panel is connected to backup power separately. Its operating sequence is still there.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s24-1: “You’re going to run through the startup sequence in order. Three people, one station each.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s25-1: She paused, her gaze sweeping over the three of us.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s27-1: “First, the rule: you cannot see the other side’s hands, or anything on the other side’s console.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s30-1: “Exception: there are holes in the partitions. You can speak.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s31-1: She pointed toward the three separated stations, indicating that we should move over.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s33-1: “Each person can see only the part in front of them. None of you has the complete version of this machine’s sequence. If you want to complete the procedure, you’ll have to talk.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s34-1: She stepped back toward the door and drew a pocket watch from inside her robe.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s40-1: I walked to the station on the left. The blisters rubbed raw while we dragged the bridge frames still burned with pain, and my fingers trembled slightly. A layer of dust covered the surface. A row of brass toggle
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s40-2: switches and a graduated dial in the upper-left corner stood out clearly. Beneath each switch lever was a small metal plate that should have been engraved with an inscription, though its surface was mottled and worn.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s41-1: I crouched down and tried pushing at the bottom of the partition in front of me. It was wedged firmly against the console, sealed tight. Not even a sliver of light from the other side came through.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s43-1: “I have a circuit diagram over here.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s44-1: Yuna’s voice came through the small holes in the partition, carrying a slight echo from the enclosed space.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s46-1: “It’s engraved on a metal plate. There are six lines. Four run toward your side. The other two are cut off. I don’t know where they go.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s50-1: “There’s a column labeled ‘Switch Number,’ corresponding to each operation instruction and its prerequisites.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s57-1: “First item: Confirm that all switches are at zero.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s59-1: “Arno?” Yuna called from the other side.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s60-1: I looked down at the row of brass levers. There had originally been a metal nameplate beneath each switch, but the writing on them had long since worn into indistinct smears.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s62-1: “Count from left to right,” Estelle added coldly. “Look at their positions. Ignore the writing on the nameplates.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s63-1: I started counting from the far left.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s67-1: “Then move them back. Set them all to zero.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s74-1: “There’s a mark beside the first item on the table.” There was no inflection in Estelle’s voice. “It says: ‘Confirmation must proceed by the official numbers entered in the register. After each switch is reset, repeat it to a second person.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s75-1: There was a pause on Yuna’s side, as if she were turning the sentence over in her mind.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s77-1: “But I can’t see his side.” I heard her tapping on the console through the hole. “If I can’t see it, I can’t catch him even if he fails to report one. What good is repeating it?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s79-1: “The only way to verify it is exhaustive checking,” Estelle said coldly. “I can’t see your hands, but my table has the official numbers arranged from left to right. Arno,
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s79-2: start with the first one on the far left. Report each switch’s physical position and current state aloud. For example, ‘First, zero position,’ or ‘Second, not at zero.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s81-1: “I’ll compare the positions you report against my table one by one. If the one you report isn’t at zero, I’ll order you to reset it. You’ll move it back and
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s81-2: verbally confirm, ‘Reset,’ and then I’ll cross it out. If tampering has created a position that isn’t on the table, we skip it and do not touch it. Begin.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s84-1: The other side of the partition was silent for two seconds. I could imagine Yuna pouting behind it.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s91-1: Time was short. I felt my way along the levers one by one to the right, loudly reporting each position and state.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s93-1: “Number one, zero position, confirmed,” Estelle responded from the other side.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s96-1: I forced it downward. The brass mechanism made a dull click. “Reset.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s98-1: That was how we moved forward, one command and one action at a time. When I felt my way to the middle, my hand stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s100-1: “Fourth, zero position.” After reporting that one, I moved my hand farther right. “Fifth, not at zero.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s102-1: “Stop,” she said without hesitation. “My table has no record of this fifth physical position. The official number in the first column jumps directly from four to six. The slot for five is blank.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s105-1: I lowered my head again and examined my row of switches carefully.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s106-1: The middle switch was indeed the fifth from the left, but it was different from all the others. Beneath every other switch was a metal plate running horizontally. Even where the plates were badly worn, traces of former engraving could still be seen. Beneath this fifth switch, there was only a bare, smooth metal surface.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s107-1: It was not a matter of blurred writing. Even the metal plate that had carried the words had been forcibly pried away, leaving only several irregular scratches on the console.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s109-1: “There’s a fifth one on the console.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s111-1: “But someone pried off the metal plate beneath it.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s113-1: “I’ll feel how deep that scratch is. Maybe I can—”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s117-1: Her voice suddenly came from the other side of the opening, a beat faster than when she had been reading the numbers, carrying an unquestionable force. My finger stopped an inch above the nameless switch.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s125-1: “Because the row for number five on my table is blank,” she said.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s127-1: “If it isn’t written on the table, we can’t touch it?” Yuna’s voice carried a trace of impatience. “People wrote the table. People can miss things when copying a table. Since there really is a switch there, why not let him try touching it? What if the sequence won’t work without it?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s129-1: “Arno said there are pry marks there, which means it was altered by someone,” Estelle said coldly. “Until we know exactly what it is, we do not touch unknown things. That is an iron rule. Don’t count it as part of this operation.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s131-1: “But the first item on the table says to confirm that ‘all’ switches are at zero.” I looked at the lever without an inscription plate in the middle. “If we skip it, does that count as completing the first item?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s133-1: “Since it is not in the current sequence, the ‘all’ required by the table includes only the ones written there,” she said without hesitation. “Skipping it is not a violation.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s136-1: The other side of the partition was silent for two seconds. I heard Yuna take a deep breath.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s139-1: “…Okay. I’ll listen to you. We’ll skip it.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s140-1: We continued checking the steps below.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s144-1: The procedure went slowly, with everyone proceeding carefully. When we reached the eleventh instruction on the table, we came to a complete stop.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s145-1: That step required me to adjust the dial, but the condition it gave was not a fixed number—it said to “refer to the log.” The problem was that none of us had seen any damned “log.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s146-1: Estelle read the prerequisites for that step three times. Yuna examined the circuit diagram on her side three times. Separated by the gray panels, the three of us each fell silent. We could hear only one another’s faint breathing through the holes.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s147-1: Yuna was the one who broke the deadlock again.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s149-1: “Estelle, read the item before number eleven again.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s151-1: “Item ten: Enter the reading in the log,” Estelle read.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s155-1: “It isn’t written on the table, and there are no other documents nearby.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s159-1: “Arno, is there anywhere on your console that you can write?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s161-1: “No. It’s all rusted metal plates.” I ran a hand over the console.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s162-1: Time passed second by second. The cold sweat in my palms seeped into my torn blisters, making them ache sharply. Small, broken sounds came from Yuna’s side, as if her fingertips were searching over some rough surface.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s164-1: “The partition,” she said suddenly. “Feel downward. Near the middle section of the console, the holes form two neat rows, and the edges have been polished.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s165-1: I felt downward where she indicated and, sure enough, found the two unusually regular rows of holes.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s167-1: “These panels separating us were added later, forced into place with whatever scrap metal was available.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s171-1: “Arno, how far is your row of switches from the outermost edge of the console?” Yuna asked rapidly.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s173-1: “Far. About two arm lengths,” I said. “All the controls are crowded toward the inside.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s179-1: “That’s it. This wasn’t originally made for three people at all.” Yuna’s voice echoed through the holes, carrying a suppressed urgency. “If the partitions were removed, the three stations would form one complete semicircle. One operator standing in the empty space at the center could reach everything with both arms spread.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s181-1: “Then something like a ‘log,” which needed to be written down at hand, could only have been placed somewhere within the operator’s reach.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s184-1: “Arno, follow the base of the partition on your right. It’s where these two panels form a point and converge at the operator’s position! If someone left a recessed slot at the edge of the console for storing a log, it would definitely be blocked by this panel that was forced into place later!”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s188-1: At the deepest point where the partition meshed with the edge of the semicircle’s inner rim—in the dead corner formed where the two panels converged—I felt an inconspicuous recessed slot. I
