texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s188-2: hooked my finger around its edge and pulled out a foreign object. It was an old record board that could be repeatedly written on and erased with chalk, still covered in a layer of white dust.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s190-1: “Found it,” I said, blowing gently on the dust.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s194-1: “Good. Back to item ten: Enter the reading in the log.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s196-1: “That means entering the current reading on that board, not in my booklet.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s197-1: I looked at the brass dial in front of me. The mechanism did not move, but its mechanical pointer was fixed hard against one mark. I called out the number on the dial. In
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s197-2: the blank space at the very bottom of the stone board, I scratched that number into the remaining white dust with my fingernail. When I finished, I read it back to her.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s198-1: Estelle repeated it in a low voice from the other side, confirming that it was correct.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s199-1: Then she read out item eleven.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s201-1: “‘Turn the dial to the previous reading recorded in the log,’” she said.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s203-1: “Arno, what was the previous reading on the board?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s204-1: I looked above the line of numbers I had just written. It was originally the last line on the board. It had been wiped relatively clean, but because someone had pressed too hard, the traces of the old number had been etched into the grain of the stone. One number could still just barely be made out.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s206-1: Then I gripped the brass dial and slowly turned it to that mark.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s207-1: There was a faint click. At the very top of the device, a small light covered in a thick layer of dust came on with a weak green glow.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s210-1: The other side of the partition was dead silent at first. Then Yuna let out an uncontrollable “Yes.” It was extremely short; she must have remembered that we were still in class and forcibly covered and swallowed the rest, turning it into a strange muffled sound, almost like a hiccup.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s211-1: The door creaked open. Sera stood by the entrance and tucked the pocket watch back into her robe.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s219-1: When we came out of the stuffy little room, a thin sheen of sweat covered all three of our backs. The day’s exercise was over.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s220-1: The corridor was much cooler than the room. A draft moved through it, cold against our bodies. Yuna went straight to the wall and leaned her back against the chilled stone, drawing both hands
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s220-2: into her sleeves. Estelle did not lean against the wall—she stood properly, holding the record booklet against her chest, just as she stood during lessons all day, without the slightest lapse.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s221-1: Yuna watched her for quite a while, then spoke first.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s223-1: “Estelle. If we had actually touched the fifth switch just now, what do you think would have happened?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s226-1: Yuna pulled one hand from her sleeve and lightly tapped the stone wall behind her twice, producing two hollow beats. She looked at the stubborn Estelle, then suddenly smiled.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s228-1: “You,” she said, shaking her head, “are really hard to deal with.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s231-1: “I have a question too.” Estelle ignored her assessment.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s236-1: “When we were in the room, how did you determine that you should look for the original operating position?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s237-1: Yuna tilted her head and thought for a moment, as if recalling her own line of reasoning.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s239-1: “When you can’t find something, think about what it looked like when it was first built,” she said slowly. “The division of the operating area was added later. So the blind spot it blocked was precisely the place the original operator was most accustomed to using.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s242-1: After listening, Estelle took the booklet she had been holding against her chest, opened it, and began writing. When she wrote, her wrist stayed fixed, and the pen moved only under the guidance of her fingers. The letters were tiny and precise.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s244-1: “What are you writing down again?” Yuna straightened from the wall and leaned over to take a look.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s245-1: One line was written in the booklet with perfect order:
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s249-1: “Question: Why use temporary partitions to deliberately block the device’s original operating center?”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s254-1: “You wrote a question. I just gave you the answer to finding the log.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s256-1: “Inference is not fact. So the answer column stays blank.” Estelle snapped the booklet shut and brought it back against her chest in a defensive posture. “Something whose meaning we don’t know should first be recorded as a question.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s261-1: We had to part there. Estelle had to walk back to the place where she was staying—the empty grass-thatched hut arranged for her at the eastern end of the village, the place farthest from the White Tower in the entire village.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s263-1: “See you tomorrow,” Yuna said to her back.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s268-1: “See you tomorrow,” she answered evenly without turning around, then walked away with her back held perfectly straight.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s271-1: Yuna leaned against the stone wall and watched her back disappear into the night.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s273-1: “If it had only been the two of us just now, I would have let you touch the fifth switch,” Yuna said suddenly, without context.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s277-1: “Whatever the consequences, I would still want to know what would happen. I can’t control that problem of mine.” Yuna gave a self-deprecating laugh. “There are only two places for people who get to stay. If there’s something like this again—something concealed from us, or deliberately left incomplete—she’ll probably live longer than I will.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s283-1: Yuna had been in a hurry to complete the registration procedures—the packet given to her at noon on the first day had not finished processing, and Sera had temporarily stamped it and handed it
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s283-2: to her. She had to go to the White Tower’s main hall and have the clerk on duty enter the missing materials into the system. That night, she climbed out her window and quietly came to my house.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s284-1: To avoid the night patrol’s line of sight, we sat in a corner of the front porch. With her back turned toward the White Tower, she lit a hooded windproof lantern.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s285-1: This was plainly forbidden by the strict disciplinary rules. But she matter-of-factly pulled out the packet bearing the supplementary signature stamp, along
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s285-2: with mine. In the dim yellow light, I immediately saw that something was wrong—they were not the same thickness. Mine clearly contained an extra section.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s288-1: We spread the materials out in the lantern light. The first several dozen pages were exactly the same: dry access-range tables, complicated floor plans of the White Tower, and a long string of disciplinary regulations. Although
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s288-2: the packet clearly stated, “During the selection period, displaying the contents of this packet to anyone is strictly prohibited,” in the latter half of the table of contents, her copy skipped over a large section entirely.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s290-1: “You have an extra section here: ‘Candidate Physiological Specifications and Preliminary Assessment.’” Yuna pointed at the extra boldfaced line. “When I went to complete the registration, I pressed that woman for an answer. She said, ‘Although the candidates come from different origins, all three candidates follow the same procedure.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s291-1: Yuna stared coldly at the papers.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s293-1: “But if the procedure is the same, this entire stack of materials was sent straight to you. As for Estelle, I saw her collect her access credentials for the White Tower outskirts with my own eyes. She had to be checked and registered again every time she entered a new door.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s295-1: “So the external-candidate materials Estelle received might be missing even more?” I guessed.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s298-1: Yuna turned my materials to the extra section. It consisted of more than a dozen pages of elaborate blank forms and operating protocols. My name was printed at the top of the forms, followed by several indicators concerning fluctuations
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s298-2: in brain activity. Most strangely, it contained a complete set of observation procedures for the central nervous system and tolerance limits of an operator—the documents called the person occupying this position a “recipient.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s301-1: The pages were filled with interaction assessments between the human nervous system and the White Tower’s mechanisms. One page showed a human spinal column, with dense markings around the
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s301-2: back of the skull and cervical vertebrae indicating puncture points for inserting metal probes. The final metric the form required was an irreversible damage rate marked only by a code.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s302-1: The night wind passed through the village. I stared at the spinal diagram covered in probe points. This was not an interview for some heir. Suddenly, the back of my neck went cold, as though those icy metal probes
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s302-2: had already aligned themselves with the gaps between my bones through the diagram. This looked nothing like an employment examination. It was more like an assessment of a consumable that could burn out at any moment.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s305-1: I folded the pages and put them back into the envelope.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s307-1: “Think about how she was this afternoon. She wouldn’t even make a guess. She had to write down the unanswered question exactly as it was.” Yuna turned to look at me. “If she found a similar blank space in her materials—”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s308-1: I remembered the icy way Estelle had said, “I don’t guess.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s310-1: “She won’t come ask us about it,” I said. “She’ll verify it herself.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s312-1: “So tomorrow morning, we need to look at her copy,” Yuna said decisively.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s315-1: She tilted her head toward the night sky. The true main structure of the White Tower stood behind layer upon layer of inner walls. Under the starlight, it was white as a gigantic bone, looking down coldly on the outlying village and barracks.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s318-1: She rose from the steps and dusted off the dirt clinging to the hem of her robe. Then she bent down, picked up the heavy metal identification arc that served as part of the candidate uniform, and slipped it over her forearm.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s320-1: “Starting tomorrow morning, I won’t come knock on your window anymore.” She looked down at the human diagram marked with puncture points. “Nothing unexpected can happen during the review period. We need to get through these six days steadily.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s323-1: She turned away and waved at me with her back turned.
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s325-1: “When the results come out in seven days, I’ll come knock on your window again.”
texts.chapter:v15-z01d:event:text-s326-1: Then she left, walking a little faster than usual. I stood in the doorway. The night wind swept through the village, and the medical spinal diagram covered in puncture points rustled on the table beneath the lantern.
texts.chapter:volume0-appendix-two:title: Interlude: Appendix Two
texts.chapter:volume0-appendix-two:event:text-:
Candidate Process Sheet (issued to the three candidates, one copy each, consecutively numbered):
“...7. Termination: Candidate status may be terminated at any time following evaluation and assessment by the White Tower. The termination decision will disclose neither

the specific grounds nor the itemized scores.
Appendix One: Anyone whose status is terminated will no longer attend classes or receive new access credentials.
Appendix Two: Termination of candidate status does not affect existing residential, labor, or rationing status.”
This happened on the evening of our first day inside the White Tower.

Although Elder Sera had said “Once the practical test is over, get back and rest,” before we could leave the basement level, we were still required to remain by the long table in the front hall and complete the final task of the day—transcribing the regulations.

For ease of copying, Elder Sera switched on the ceiling light. Its stark white glare fell across the long table, pulling our shadows very short. She handed out the printed seven-day candidate process sheet, along with blank paper for transcription, and required us to copy it exactly, without leaving out a single word.

That morning, we had copied the day’s schedule posted on the wall and filled out answer sheets to be returned for the records. The document in our hands now was the general rule covering the entire candidate period.

Elder Sera said that once we finished copying the process sheet, we were to keep it ourselves. Her reason was that “rules you write down yourself, stroke by stroke, stay with you better than anything you hear ten times.”

The three of us bent over the classroom’s polished wooden table and copied separately. Yuna’s palm had blistered from the afternoon’s drills, so she could only awkwardly grip the pen between her knuckles.
Even so, she wrote the fastest, her handwriting always tilting toward the right edge of the page. I was comparatively slow, each stroke carved out one at a time. But Estelle was slower than I was.
She wasn’t slow because she wrote slowly. She was slow because after every passage, she had to stop and look at it for a while.
When she reached item seven, she stopped for a long time.
She stopped for so long that even Yuna, who had been focused entirely on the page, put down her pen and looked up at her.
“Stuck?” Yuna released the pen from between her knuckles and shook her aching wrist, asking casually.
“No.”

Estelle’s voice was very quiet. She set her pen on the table, placed her fingertip at the beginning of item seven on the original, and traced along the lines all the way to the end of Appendix Two. She moved very slowly, as though feeling the texture of the paper with the pad of her finger.

Then she did something I didn’t understand at the time. She held the printed original beneath the ceiling light, tilted her head, narrowed her eyes, and carefully examined the portions of the page that reflected the light.
“What are you doing?” Yuna knit her brows in confusion.
“Looking at the typesetting and the ink.” Her eyes remained fixed on the page.
“It’s a black-on-white printout. What are you expecting to find?”
Estelle did not answer. She laid the paper flat on the table, then turned toward me, her gaze settling on where I sat.
“Arno, lend me your printed sheet.”
I pushed the original over to her. She placed the two printed sheets side by side and firmly pressed her index finger against the same spot.
“Look at the spacing here.” She motioned for me to come closer.

“The edges of the type in item seven above are blurred, and the ink is matte. But these two lines in Appendix Two reflect more brightly, and the letters are slightly slanted. Their line spacing doesn’t match the lines above at all.”

I leaned closer and examined it carefully. The difference was extremely slight. Without deliberately comparing them under the light, I would never have noticed. But those two lines really did look as though they had been forced into the bottom of the page.

“If they had been printed together in the same run, the ink wouldn’t suddenly change at this point, and it wouldn’t be crooked.” She pressed her index finger against the page. “This was added after the sheet had already been printed. They found something missing, then used another machine to press it onto the old paper.”
“She’s right.” Yuna had been listening from the side. She leaned over for a look, then shrugged.
As long as it didn’t involve specific operations or procedural blind spots, Yuna had little interest in typesetting or printing.

“But that’s normal, isn’t it? If they find something missing from the procedure and don’t want to waste the paper they already printed, they just run the old sheets through again and add it.” Yuna picked up her pen again.

“And look at what it says.” She tapped the two lines of Appendix Two with the shaft of her pen. “‘Does not affect existing residential, labor, or rationing status.’ It’s a safety net for the people who don’t make it. That’s a good thing for us.”

“The grain and housing we receive in the village are already distributed according to labor.” Estelle stared at the page. “If we’re washed out, even if we go back to the village and continue doing hard labor, none of that would be reduced. The White Tower handles selection. Rations are the village’s baseline responsibility.”
“If they wouldn’t be reduced anyway, why find another machine now to print this in, then restate it as some kind of benevolence? And why force us to copy it out by hand and carry it with us?”
Estelle curled her finger and lightly tapped twice on the first half of item seven. It said, “will disclose neither the specific grounds.”
“If someone is washed out for no apparent reason, without even receiving a written determination, they might feel it’s unfair.”

“But at that point, if the White Tower points to this sentence and tells them: You haven’t lost anything. You can go back to the village and live as before. Maybe, maybe no one will keep asking about the reason they can’t obtain.”
Yuna hesitated. Her gaze moved back and forth between the two lines on the page.
Estelle pushed the printed sheet back to me and folded her transcription in half.
“I don’t guess.” She smoothed the page and slid it into her booklet, her voice softening. “If there’s no evidence, I don’t guess.”
When class ended that evening, Estelle deliberately stayed behind.
I had to wait by the door for Yuna to finish putting her things away, so I happened to see the whole scene.
Estelle walked quietly to Elder Sera’s desk and patiently waited for her to sort and put away the record books before breaking the silence in a soft voice.
“Elder, sorry to bother you. May I ask a question about the process sheet?” Her tone was respectful, but her back was perfectly straight.
“You may. Ask.” Sera did not even look up.
“I wanted to ask: what year was Appendix Two of item seven added?”
Sera was holding a pen. At the question, her movement paused. She slowly placed the pen back into the wooden holder. Only after the shaft made a faint clicking sound did she turn
her head. Her gaze first dropped, resting for a moment on the lower-right edge of the process sheet in Estelle’s hands, and only then slowly lifted—but it did not meet Estelle’s eyes.
“Why do you ask?” The elder’s voice was like a bottomless old well.
“Because I’m transcribing it.” Estelle faced in the elder’s direction.

“The procedure says that we keep our transcriptions for reference. I thought I’d note the year it was added in the margin, so I could compare it properly when I looked back later and understand the institutional changes of that time.”
The reason sounded perfectly reasonable. There was nothing to pick apart.
Sera looked at Estelle in silence for a full two seconds.
“Appendices are not dated.” That was all the elder said. Cold, with no explanation.
“Okay.” Estelle nodded.
“Then I won’t date it.”
Coming up from the basement level and heading toward the White Tower’s front hall, Yuna impatiently tugged at Estelle’s sleeve on the stairs.
“What were you whispering to the elder about just now? Did you get anything out of her?”
“Nothing.”
“I told you it was a waste of effort. Aren’t all important people like that? They can’t be bothered to explain anything to us.” Yuna sighed.
“She wasn’t too lazy to explain.”
Estelle stopped on the landing at the turn of the stairs and looked back at the shadowed steps leading down to the basement.

“If you’d looked carefully at the edge of that paper just now—” She lowered her voice. “There are very faint fingernail scratches at the lower-right corner. Someone tried to scrape off that layer of matte ink and see what had originally been printed underneath.”

“She didn’t look me in the eyes. That means what mattered to her wasn’t my question, but whether that piece of evidence had been disturbed. From today on, apart from the operations I’m supposed to learn, I won’t ask the instructors a single unnecessary question.”
“When you run into something you don’t understand, aren’t you always determined to figure it out?” Yuna looked utterly bewildered.

I was just as surprised. Estelle was obsessed with how things operated. She could squat in the village for two hours just to figure out how the pipes in the dehydrator were connected. For her to hold back a question

went against her nature. But I watched her standing on the half-lit stairs, the line of her shoulders drawn slightly tight. She moved the hands holding the process booklet behind her back and avoided my gaze.
Estelle offered no further explanation. She turned, finished climbing the remaining steps, and pushed open the door to the front hall.
In the front hall, the evening sun cut diagonally across the stone floor through the high windows.
Estelle stopped and waited quietly for Yuna to catch up. She kept the process sheet with the appendix pressed flat inside the record booklet, and for many days afterward, she never took it out again.
texts.chapter:volume0-second-seat:title: Chapter Two: The Second Seat
texts.chapter:volume0-second-seat:event:text-s:
Candidate Process Sheet · Day Two (copy, copied by: Estelle):
Morning: Low-clearance lessons (continued). Afternoon: One item of candidate practical work.
17:00: The elder on duty announces the results of the preliminary assessment

covering the first two days.
Addendum: The results of this assessment will not be itemized. Anyone who fails the preliminary assessment must immediately return their badge and have their confidential access suspended, becoming restricted.

(Copyist’s note: This addendum consists of only two dry sentences. It does not state what happens after someone becomes restricted. In a place where everything must be entered into the record, this deliberate vagueness makes me uneasy.)
Early on the second morning, with the morning mist not yet fully dispersed, I opened the door. As expected, Yuna was already waiting by the roadside.
She wasn’t wearing the narrow metal arc that represented a candidate. Instead, she was pinching it in her hand like a hot potato.
“You were the one who said we had to be dignified.” I looked at the hair the morning wind had tousled around her ears.

“I tried it in front of the mirror last night.” She sighed and gestured above her ears with one finger. “This thing has to go around my cat ears. It makes my scalp go numb. I’ll put it on when we get to the front hall.”
We walked toward the White Tower side by side. The only sound on the flagstone road was our footsteps. After a dozen or so steps, she suddenly began speaking without any apparent connection.
“I didn’t sleep well last night.”
“Because of the differences between our two sets of materials?”

“Yeah.” She kept her eyes ahead, her brow slightly furrowed. “Your set has the puncture points and damage rate. Mine doesn’t. If there’s already this distinction between us on the inside, then what does

the third kind given to external candidates look like? How much unequal treatment was hidden by the registration office’s ‘different sources, same procedure’? My brain kept turning it over all night.”
She tossed the metal arc lightly in her hand, as if shifting the burden in her mind from one side to the other.

“So I changed my mind.” She let out a long breath, and her steps grew lighter. “You can’t untangle this by letting your brain spin in place. I’m done thinking about it. I’ll wait for the lessons ahead.”

That was Yuna. She could wrestle with a thought all night, grind her pillow to pieces, then throw it into the wastebasket rationally and coldly the next morning, simply because she judged that continuing
to spend herself on it wasn’t worth it. She called it “cutting losses.” She first learned the phrase from a passing peddler when she was fourteen, and afterward treated it as a blade for living.
“So what’s our main quest for today?”
“Listening to lessons.” She turned her head, her eyes shining. “Listening properly.”
She looked so serious saying it that a thread of suspicion suddenly rose up my back.
At the White Tower’s front hall, Estelle still arrived before us.
But today, she was only twenty minutes early.

She sat on the bench at the edge of the front hall, precisely in the same spot. Even the posture of her hands folded over her knees was exactly as usual. Catching sight of us from the corner of her eye, she stood with the precision of a wound clock, smoothed her skirt, and bowed.
“Morning.” She inclined her head slightly.
“Why are you only twenty minutes early today?” Yuna walked over and sat down, familiar as ever, at the other end of the bench.
“Because I now know exactly how long the registration process takes,” she replied, with perfect precision.
Yuna laughed without making any attempt to hide it.
She leaned forward with it, eyes fixed on the back of Estelle’s hand, wanting to see what reaction this person, meshing as tightly as a gear, would produce next. Estelle
merely drew her folded fingers in slightly, neither acknowledging nor objecting to the unrestrained laughter, maintaining a perfect fit with the literal meaning of her words.
This was the rhythm peculiar to the two of them. Yuna never tired of it. That pause was exactly what she was waiting for.
“What did you do after you went back yesterday?” Yuna propped her chin on her hand and looked at her.
“Organized my notes. Until eleven. Then I went to sleep.”
Estelle answered in a flat, straightforward manner, then keenly noticed the ambush hidden in Yuna’s question. She paused, and her gaze focused.
“What are you trying to ask?”
“I’m asking whether, before you return it intact later, we can borrow that external discipline manual and take a look.”
Estelle did not answer immediately. She opened the cloth bag she carried and handed over two thin sheets of paper.
Yuna took them and skimmed them quickly. Her expression slowly darkened. She handed the papers back to Estelle, then turned to me and lowered her voice.
“It’s thin enough for a gust of wind to blow it away. It doesn’t mention the puncture points. It doesn’t even have the access-area list that mine has.”
Estelle looked at her quietly.
“After I received it, I read it four times,” she said calmly. “I also copied the key points of the discipline rules into my notebook.”
“Because this external manual may only be borrowed overnight. It had to be returned intact this morning.”
Yuna’s expression stiffened little by little, as though a cold wind had passed over it.
“It had to be returned intact this morning.” She chewed slowly over the sentence, then turned to me. “Our materials can be kept until the selection is over.”
“I know.” Estelle’s tone did not change at all. “That’s why I read it four times.”
From the corner of my eye, I saw Yuna’s fingers find the edge of the metal arc, her knuckles whitening with the pressure.
The second morning’s lesson was still in that poorly lit classroom.
Elder Sera wasn’t there. Standing behind the long table was another elder, Otto.

I had only seen him from a distance before. He was very tall, with broad shoulders like a wall. When he spoke, he habitually folded his two large hands together in front of him. A string of wooden mediation tags, which he never went anywhere without, hung from his waist. That morning, he taught us about access within the White Tower.

Which doors could be opened by scanning a badge, which would leave a record in the files, and which would bring guards immediately if touched. He explained everything in detail, in enough detail to make people drowsy in the stuffy air. In the middle of it, Yuna couldn’t hold back a yawn, and it fell directly into his view.
“Tired?” He stopped speaking.
“No.” Yuna immediately sat straight.
“If you’re tired, say you’re tired. It’s nothing to be ashamed of.”
He slowly unhooked the string of wooden tags used to mediate disputes from his waist, his rough thumb rolling over one of them.
“These rules and regulations are boring. I know.”
His thumb rolled over another.
“But boring rules are most useful on the day something goes wrong. You’re perfectly welcome not to believe the one I’m explaining yet.”
With a turn of his wrist, the tags gave a dull clack as he hung them back at his waist.
“Remember it. That’s enough.”
He cleared his throat and continued.
When he reached the divisions of the White Tower’s underground levels, his voice stopped. His gray eyes passed over the long table and looked at Estelle.

“An external candidate’s access range differs from the rules issued to internal candidates,” he said flatly. “After class, come look at the external-only access map here. You may only look. No copying. It will be collected immediately afterward.”
“If the materials given to her already have to be returned intact, why separate the map out and deny her even the right to borrow it as an attachment for one night?” Yuna frowned.
Otto looked at her. The room was silent for two seconds.
“Because the public provisions on those two pages tacitly permit her to take them back and relay them orally in her home settlement,” he answered in a low voice. “But this map shows the boundaries
of the White Tower’s deeper levels. It must not leave this room. Not even as a map she cannot take out of the White Tower, not even for her to borrow for one night in her temporary lodging.”
“And if she accidentally takes a wrong turn…”
Otto folded his two broad hands together in front of him again, each finger distinct.

“If an internal candidate takes a wrong turn, it goes in the record. If an external candidate takes a wrong turn, her confidential access is suspended immediately and she becomes a restricted visitor.” He looked Yuna in the eyes.

“To prevent information from leaking directly to neighboring settlements, she must remain within the White Tower’s monitored area until the weekend, when an appointed village official will arrange her return to Watermarsh.”
The air in the room seemed to stop moving.

I instinctively turned toward Estelle. She did not raise her head, as though she had not heard the sentence at all. Only the tip of her pen moved across the notebook with a soft scratch, recording the two places she could not go.
“Then what if I’m eliminated today?”
“You’ll still wake up in your own village tomorrow morning. You’ll rot in this village. You and her are separated by two different distances.”

“So this has nothing to do with whether someone is trustworthy or not. It’s only that once she’s eliminated, she still has somewhere to retreat to, while the White Tower can’t keep her under observation forever.”
“The risk of letting her out. Once she leaves the White Tower’s village boundary, if she doesn’t follow the unified procedure, even a three-hour journey will create a gap in between.”

His rough fingertip slowly rubbed the mediation tag at his waist. It was a callus built up over years of settling quarrels between villagers, watching people crack each other’s heads over half a foot of boundary.
“I don’t like speaking this way,” he said heavily.
Yuna looked at the tall elder. Faced with that cruel honesty, she eventually only nodded.
“Thank you,” she said.
That afternoon’s candidate practical work involved no examination, only tedious cleaning.
On the White Tower’s underground first level was an abandoned storeroom that had never seen daylight. When the door opened, the smell of dust, rust, and mold rushed out. The room was packed with
dusty old storage boxes and decommissioned instruments. Our task was to pry them all open, inventory them, record the useful things, and move them to the new room at the end of the corridor.

The discarded instruments were strangely heavy, and locked. Some looked like chairs, some like cabinets covered in spikes, and there was a large pile of iron lumps whose names we didn’t know. Their surfaces were cold, their edges polished unusually smooth. The three of us spent the entire afternoon there.
The division of labor came naturally: Yuna handled the inventory, I used the crowbar to open the rusted clasps and heavy iron shells, and Estelle recorded everything with a pen—at her own request.
“Can’t counting and recording be done together? Why do you have to write it separately?” Yuna wiped the dust from her forehead.
“Because if one person counts and writes it down themselves, no one will notice if something goes wrong at either stage. Only two people checking each other can lock down mistakes.”

Yuna silently curled her lip. She didn’t answer, only reached out and deliberately scattered the stack of yellowed files Estelle had just painstakingly squared up, pushing them slightly toward the middle.
Halfway through the work, we found an old wooden box with no name on it in the corner.

It was crudely made, wedged into the gap between two rows of iron shelves, with a thick layer of fluff-like dust covering it. When I dragged it out with all my strength, the rusted clasp came loose, and the lid opened a crack by itself.
There were no secrets inside, only a pile of scattered old things. An old pen with its ink long since dried, a stone polished warm and bright by someone’s fingers, and
several broken buttons that could not make a pair. In the corner was a pair of dice, carved from scraps of wood, with shallow and deep indentations cut into all six sides.
“Looks like someone left their life behind here when they left.” Yuna fished out the wooden dice.
Estelle wiped the yellowed registration form pasted to the box. “This whole batch is old property sealed away last time.”
Yuna tossed the dice twice in her palm. Then, with a sudden flick of her wrist, she threw one at me.
“Let’s play a round. Guess odd or even.” The corner of her mouth lifted slightly.
“We’re working. If the inspectors see us, they’ll deduct points.”
“We’ve been working in this airless hellhole for two and a half hours. Taking five minutes to breathe isn’t a crime.”
She turned and tossed the other die toward Estelle.
“I know the rules. But I don’t play.” Estelle looked at the wooden block as it rolled to a stop by her foot. “Because I can never stop myself from calculating.”
“Rolling dice is pure luck. What is there to calculate?”
The equipment room fell silent for two seconds.

“The last time I played this, I was seven. I played with my mother.” She spoke slowly. “She covered the dice with a bowl and had me guess odd or even. I guessed wrong six times in a row. Because I was always calculating in my head, thinking, ‘The last one came up odd, so this time it must be even.’”

“She looked at me and told me that if I tried to find a pattern, I would lose to the pattern. Dice have no memory. They never remember what they rolled last time. Every roll starts over. But I can’t break the habit of calculating, so I don’t play.”
“Your mother saw through things pretty clearly,” Yuna said softly.
Estelle seemed to suddenly realize that she had brought a private emotion into the workspace. She did not respond, only hugged the notebook in her arms a little higher.
“Let’s keep moving. There’s a quarter of it left.”
Yuna did not try to hold on to those five minutes of rest. She bent down, picked up the die, and put it back in the wooden box. I put mine back too.
After we cleared away several more heavy objects, Yuna suddenly spoke through the sound of our heavy breathing.
“Estelle, which direction is the Watermarsh settlement?”
“North of the White Tower. Go past the boundary stone and follow the waterline. It takes three hours.”
“Then where do you usually stay after you go back?”
Estelle set down the iron frame in her hands and looked at her with those eyes that always seemed to be assessing things.
“Why are you suddenly asking about that?”
“Just asking.” Yuna shrugged.
“I’m not recording that. ‘Just asking’ does not constitute a reasonable motive. Give me wording I can put into the record.”
“Fine.” She leaned against the wooden box. “The truth is, I just want to know where I should knock if one day I want to find you.”
Estelle considered the logic of this carefully, then accepted it.
“The public distribution station in the very center of the settlement. If I’m not at home, I’m usually helping there. If you can’t find anyone in either place,
ask someone named Kolai. I signed out with Kolai. As for my mother, she counts the days I’m away. If I don’t return for too long, she’ll also ask Kolai about me.”
Yuna quietly rolled the three elements—north, the waterline, Kolai—over and over in her mouth.
At 4:50 p.m., we finally dragged the last instrument into the new room. The three of us sat side by side on the high wooden threshold, panting.
Yuna furtively looked left and right, then pulled three pieces of dried ration wrapped in oiled paper from inside her clothes and gave one to each of us.
“I slipped these off the kitchen counter this morning.” Her cheeks bulged as she chewed. “I left a note. It said, ‘Taking three pieces, Yuna.’”
Estelle was examining the ration in her hands. At this, she stopped.
“In the operating regulations, that isn’t called taking. It’s called ‘named requisition.’”
Yuna froze for a moment, then leaned against the doorframe and laughed recklessly.

We sat on the dusty threshold like that and finished the dried ration with a jug of cool water drawn from the well. A large patch of black had rubbed onto the cuff of Estelle’s purple jacket. She did not complain. She simply rolled the cuff up once, turning the dirt inward.
When we returned to the classroom, the White Tower’s time bell rang at exactly five in the afternoon.
Elder Sera held a thin sheet of paper in her hand.

“Today is the day of the preliminary assessment,” she said, her voice carrying a cold echo through the empty room. “I’ll restate the rules first: the assessment results will not be itemized, specific scores will not be announced, and no on-the-spot challenge will be accepted.”
I heard Estelle, standing to my right, draw in a very slight breath of cold air.
“Arno. Preliminary assessment passed. Internal candidate status retained. Entering the First Seat’s practical operations process.”

I instinctively stood at attention and answered, “Yes.” I had waited ten years for this ticket to investigate the records of what happened to my father. Whatever the First Seat’s later practical assessment might be, at this very second, I finally had one foot inside the door.
But I felt no wild joy. Instead, my palms grew damp. Had I survived this round on the strength of my performance over the past two days, or had the medical
materials filled with “puncture points” and “irreversible damage rate” happened to fit some hidden need they had for expendable assets in the First Seat’s
practical work, getting me passed from the very beginning? In that quiet room, survival brought only the exhausted relief of boots finally hitting the ground.
“Yuna. Internal candidate status retained. Entering the subsequent process for the Second Seat. Continued evaluation.”

“Arno, this isn’t a preliminary assessment at all…” Yuna’s voice was rough. She stared hard at the thin list in Sera’s hand. “‘First Seat practical operations.’ ‘Second Seat subsequent process.’ They didn’t even conduct a token cross-assessment. They put you straight into

practical operations and put me straight into the Second Seat. Your medical materials, filled with ‘irreversible damage rate,’ had already fixed you as practical operations’ expendable asset. They had turned our circumstances inside out before the selection even began.”
Sera’s fingers moved an inch lower on the paper.
“Estelle.”
The classroom suddenly had no sound left in it but breathing.
“External candidate qualifications terminated. The elders on duty jointly announce that the decision takes effect at this moment today.”
In that instant, in that suffocating room, I heard three sounds.
The first was the dull sound of Estelle’s notebook sliding half an inch downward from weakness, then being pressed hard against her waist by her hand.
The second was the sound of Yuna drawing in a sharp breath and failing to release it, caught in her throat.
The third was the frantic beat of my own heart.
“Please provide the written grounds for the ruling.”
Her voice was perfectly steady. Not a trace of a break.
“The comprehensive risk assessment result was unsatisfactory.”
“Which specific item in the risk assessment?”
“This stage’s assessment is not itemized.”
“If there are no items, did I personally do anything in the White Tower over these two days that was serious enough to terminate my qualifications?”
“No.”
Sera spoke extremely quickly. The two words were forced out almost before the question had fully landed.

“May I ask one last question?” She looked at Sera standing on the raised platform. “If I had performed more flawlessly in every practical task over these two days, would today’s result have been different?”
Sera looked at her. For the first time in my life, I saw an elder so visibly selecting words in her head.
“Candidate qualification assessment incorporates consideration of multiple factors.” In the end, Sera settled on that sentence.
“Elder, where would you like me to record this?”
Estelle slowly raised the notebook an inch. The veins on the back of her hand stood out clearly.
“‘Multiple factors’—these six words are a fog I can’t grasp. I have no way to enter them into any column on the process sheet.”
“This is the only answer I can give you.”
Estelle nodded. She did not press the matter any further.

She slowly lowered her head and removed the badge from her waist, carefully straightening it so that the side engraved with her name faced upward. Only then did she extend it forward respectfully with both hands.
“External candidate badge, returned. My access record shows that I never took this badge out of the White Tower.” She looked Sera straight in the eye. “As for
the two pages borrowed last night, they were returned intact before class this morning. If you consider the copies in my notebook a risk, I can destroy them now.”
Sera reached out and took the badge.
“No need. The explicit provisions were permitted to be taken away in the first place.”
“Thank you.”
Estelle stepped back and bowed with perfect form. Exactly the same as when she first met us.
Yuna sprang to her feet. The chair legs shrieked as they dragged across the stone floor.
“Elder. Read out her assessment report.”
“The assessment process is not public.”
“Then read it to her alone. She can stand here and hear it before she leaves. We’ll go outside.”
“Stand down, Yuna.”
“‘Comprehensive risk’—those four words are for fooling ghosts! Not one of them corresponds to anything she actually did over these two days! She didn’t do anything wrong!”
“The rules state clearly that termination of qualifications does not require a violation.”
“That’s an excuse for ordinary elimination, not an excuse for pinning an imaginary crime on someone!”
Before the words had even finished, she tore off her own badge, swung her arm in a full arc, and hurled it hard toward the long table.
With a sharp crack, the wooden badge struck the tabletop.
“Yuna. Pick up your badge and put it back. Stop making a scene here.”
“Yuna. Stop it.” Estelle shouted, sharply cutting her off. “If you anger them, I won’t be the only one thrown out through that door today.”
Yuna stubbornly raised her chin and did not move.

Sera came down from the platform, shoved the badge back into Yuna’s collar without allowing any argument, seized her arm, and forcibly dragged her out of the classroom door. The sound of Yuna’s furious struggle drifted faintly through the corridor.
The heavy wooden door swung behind them. The room suddenly felt empty.
Estelle did not look at me. She turned and walked out alone.
I drew a deep breath. I was a First Seat candidate still under evaluation, yet I had not even dared to say a word of protest. Forcing down my pounding heart, I chased after her.
By the time I caught up with her in the White Tower’s front hall, she had stopped there.
“Estelle.” I called after her.
She turned around.
Her eyes were webbed with red, but she had forced the tears not to fall. Her jaw had drawn into a rigid line.
“You don’t need to come out to see me off.”
“I didn’t come specifically to see you off.” I denied it instinctively, trying to cover up my silence in the room. “Your water jug is still in the underground storeroom.”
Estelle looked at me silently for two seconds. Then she pulled at the corner of her mouth and smiled. It looked a hundred times worse than crying.
“Thank you for reminding me. I borrowed that water jug. Please find a chance to return it for me.”
Before I could answer, Yuna came running up from the corridor, gasping for breath.
She clutched the narrow metal arc tightly in her hand. She came to an abrupt stop, her chest heaving violently.
“I wanted this seat, but I don’t accept a win that comes from a result like today’s.” Her voice trembled as she stared hard at Estelle. “What exactly makes them think you’re a risk?”
The front hall was utterly quiet. The evening sunlight stretched the shadows of the three of us long across the floor.

“I don’t know.” Estelle was silent for a long time. “If it’s fair, I want to know where I lost. If it’s unfair, I want to know where it’s rotten. But all I have is the four words ‘comprehensive risk.’ They don’t even give me an excuse that would let me finally accept it and be done.”

“Yuna, be in that classroom on time tomorrow morning. I’m already out. If you give up this seat too, then whatever was pulled out from between us will truly become a rotten account forever. Don’t let yourself be ruined over this dead end of mine that can’t be saved.”
Yuna did not take the advice. After leaving the classroom that evening, she dragged me to the prayer room no matter what I said.
“Elder. I want to ask you face-to-face and make it clear. What exactly is ‘not itemized’ hiding?”
“The literal meaning.” Sera spoke coolly, her hands never stopping as she arranged the books.
“But we took the same set of lessons! If the rules can be interpreted however they want, how am I supposed to know that this blade won’t fall on my neck tomorrow?”
Sera stopped working and looked down at her from above.
“Yuna, out of generosity I can treat this as excessive concern for a companion. But I can also treat it as something else. For example, contempt for the rules.”
After saying this, she naturally opened Yuna’s register, rapidly wrote a line in the blank space with a dip pen, then closed it and returned it to the shelf.
“That’s enough. Go back. Don’t be late for class tomorrow morning.”
By the time we were driven out of the prayer room, it was completely dark. Yuna stopped on the steps.

“Estelle warned me.” She looked at her hands, trembling slightly in the night wind. “And I was actually mocking her in my head for being a coward. Less than half a day passed between her being driven out and me being watched too.”
Early on the third day, Estelle went to the records office outside the elders’ council chamber and submitted a written appeal.

On the strength of the appeal, which was temporarily accepted for review, she was permitted to continue using public areas such as the chapel front hall and visitor reading table during the days she waited for the end-of-week review.

When we found her beside the reading table in the chapel front hall, she sat there staring at a visitor map. She had changed back into the old purple work clothes she had worn when we first met. The candidate’s white collar had been removed from the neckline, and the metal arc was gone.
“If you have to stay until the weekend, why not hide in your temporary lodging instead of sitting here enduring everyone’s looks?” Yuna sat down across from her with unusual care.

“Because I just submitted a formal written appeal. I want to take a conclusion in black and white back with me.” Estelle did not yield. She gripped the map she had received from the records office, her knuckles pale. “And I don’t want to sit in a corner and wait around doing nothing.”
She raised her head. There was a nearly obsessive stubbornness in those eyes accustomed to examining things.
“Since I’ve been made a restricted visitor, I’ll sit where a restricted visitor is supposed to be—the visitor table in the front hall, directly facing the outer courtyard corridor.”

“I can’t see the inner layer from here, but I can see every cart going in and out of the First Seat’s practical operations area. Since Arno was assigned there, if the next exercise involves large physical objects or new equipment, there will inevitably be movement in and out. If they’re moving

discarded instruments, the wheel tracks will vary in depth. If they’re moving new equipment in full crates, the corners of the dust covers will hang very low. Whatever you go and do, I only need to watch those wheel marks and the dust on the covers to work backward to one or two points.”
Yuna’s lips moved. She seemed about to say that she had already gone to see Sera last night, but Estelle spoke first.
“You look awful. If you did something impulsive last night, stop now.”
Yuna stiffened.
“If you notice anything strange from now on, remember it in your head. Whatever you do, don’t put it on paper.”
She turned her eyes back to me, their rims red with blood.

“I’m completely out already. Whether my record is clean or not can’t change anything. But you’re still on the candidate list, and you still have access privileges.” She paused. “I also know the rule from the candidates’ first

lesson: knowledge must not be relayed to anyone who has not been selected. If you tell me about irregularities aloud because of the acquaintance you’ve formed with me these past few days, you’ll end up like me if you’re discovered.”
Yuna gave a cold laugh.
“Give me a break. Ever since yesterday, when she couldn’t produce any itemization, that rule has been a joke to me. I want to see exactly what shameful thing they’re hiding.”
Estelle looked at her, her eyes softening slightly.
“If you find anything that doesn’t add up, decide for yourself whether to tell me. I’ll be sitting here, waiting for you.”
On the third morning’s lesson, we were still sitting in that classroom.
For the entire lesson, while Elder Sera stood at the lectern and read out the new candidate rules, Yuna did not say a word.
Only when the lesson ended did she follow me back to the mill. That day, Master Galon saw that we had somehow survived the first stage and excused us from the afternoon’s work.
We sat beside the moss-covered water channel behind the mill.
Yuna rested her chin on her kneecap and watched the foaming water.
“Yesterday in the storeroom, when I asked where the Watermarsh settlement was…” She suddenly spoke, her voice pressed low beneath the roar of the waterwheel. “A
very dark thought had actually gone through my head. I thought: if she were swept out of here, there would be one fewer strong rival for the internal position.”
I turned toward her in astonishment.

“Yesterday afternoon, when I threw my badge and shouted about the injustice for her, how much of it was true loyalty, and how much was me covering up that ugly little thing in my own heart?” She bit her lip hard, her eyes reddening. “Arno, I really did hope for it.”
The waterwheel continued to roar without tiring.
At last, Yuna let out a long breath, stood, and forcefully brushed the mud from her skirt.

“But having the position someone else should occupy handed to me in such an opaque way—I don’t accept it. Sitting in a position given as charity makes me sick.” She wiped at her eyes. “Estelle deliberately warned me

this morning because she was afraid I’d investigate like a mad dog. They’ve clamped their mouths shut like clams, so I’m not going to ask. As long as we look closely at what they hand down, we’ll eventually find a flaw.”
She dug a pebble out of the mud and hurled it into the rushing channel, splashing a brief flower of water that was swallowed almost at once.

“Fine, then. I’ll leave the grunt work to you. You handle the dead memorization, and I’ll search for targets. Once we find something, we’ll go to the chapel front hall and settle the account with her.”
She came to stand in front of me, her eyes clear.
“But there’s one rule of hers I absolutely will not obey.”
“You’re planning to copy?”

“Exactly. I know evidence in black and white is more dangerous than something kept in your head. But if we don’t take it from Sera and put it on paper, then when they turn around and deny everything, we’ll be like Estelle—we won’t even have anything to confront them with.”
That morning, the water roared, and the sunlight was brilliant.

Yuna was doing everything she could to find a loophole, while the image that would not leave my mind was of the three of us sharing those three pieces of dried ration over a jug of cool water in the underground storeroom the previous afternoon.
Now only Estelle’s back remained, alone at the visitor table, her hand gripping the visitor map tightly.
“Fine,” I said softly. “I’ll remember.”
texts.chapter:volume0-ageless-person:title: Chapter Three: The Ones Who Do Not Age
texts.chapter:volume0-ageless-person:event:tex: Yuna arrived on time for class on the afternoon of the third day.
It was our first class after talking beside the water channel that morning. When I entered the classroom, she was already seated there, her materials spread out in front of her and a
pen held in her hand. No one mentioned Estelle being struck from the rolls—Sera entered the classroom as usual, Otto sat at the back sorting papers, and Yuna did not mention it either.
She only turned to me when I sat down and said:
“Starting today, we look at things twice.”
“What do you mean?” I slowed my hand as I reached for my notebook.
“The first time, we look at what they want us to see.” She looked toward Sera, lowering her voice. “The second time, we look at what else is beside it.”
That afternoon, Sera issued the second phase of our access authorization. It was part of the candidate procedure: as time passed, the places we were allowed to visit would increase.
Sera stood at the front and read out a list. It contained seven places, five on various floors inside the White Tower and two in the village.
The two in the village were the storeroom behind the chapel and the Controlled Archives.
“Where are the archives?” Yuna raised her hand.
“The innermost room in the row of houses behind the chapel,” Sera answered without looking up.
“I spent ten years in the chapel,” Yuna said, frowning as her pen stopped over the paper. “I never knew there were archives there.”
“Because the door says ‘Odds and Ends.’”
Yuna looked at her, slowly lowering the pen in her hand.
“Why does it say ‘Odds and Ends’?”
“Because if it said ‘Archives,’” Sera finally raised her eyes and looked directly at Yuna,
“someone would ask what archives were inside.”
She said it in an entirely ordinary tone, without mockery or defensiveness, as though explaining something obvious—something as self-evident as the sun rising in the east—that required no defense.
Otto, seated in the back row, stopped writing. His gaze moved across the faces of everyone present, as though silently recording our reactions to what we had heard.
“Today you may enter the archives.” Sera put the list into a folder. “There are three categories of files you may not access. The shelves are marked. You may look at anything else.”
“What are the three categories?”
“The three categories with marks on them.”
“I’m asking about the contents. They must have names.”
“I know what you’re asking.”
“But the category names are classified too,” Sera said calmly. “Once you know the names, you already know half the secret.”
Yuna opened her mouth, apparently wanting to argue, but quickly closed it again.
“Noted.” She lowered her head and drew a line on the paper.
After class, Otto gathered his things, and Sera left the classroom with the register.
“To the archives.” Yuna slipped her notebook into her bag as she spoke.
“What are we looking for?”

“Even though Estelle was struck from the rolls, we still don’t know the exact reason.” Yuna looked toward the end of the corridor. “I want to see what her file actually says. I want to see what legitimate reason they used to erase her.”
We went to the archives whose door was marked ‘Odds and Ends.’

Three categories of files had red marks on the shelves, just as Sera had said, and could not be accessed. We searched through the outer section, but found no records at all related to this year’s candidates. Instead, inside an

iron cabinet marked with a red strip, we found a brand-new black file resting on top, not even touched by dust. The side of its cover bore today’s date, along with half of a character not fully covered by the red strip: ‘Es—’.
“It’s Estelle’s file, but it’s sealed with a red strip,” I said quietly. We had just arranged that morning to reconcile the accounts in the front hall. Now there was only this half-sealed character.
Yuna walked once around the archives and opened the transfer register in the ordinary section.

“She isn’t at the temporary residence. The transfer records say that two files concerning her were taken away at noon today, destination: the Special Review Committee.” She stared at the black file for a while,

then rapidly copied two long strings of numbers from the register. “The red-tagged originals can’t be removed. Since we have the numbers, we can search the ordinary section with our second-phase authorization.”
Unexpectedly, the system provided the locations of the public versions of both files without any obstruction.
One was the Candidate Procedure Evaluation Report, signed by Sera, the course supervisor. Its conclusion clearly stated: “Passed the current-level assessment.”

The other was in an entirely different risk directory, titled Risk Review Attachment. It was an internal document additionally signed by the security administration. It stated: “This candidate has complex peripheral relations and poses a risk of converting core secrets into political mobilization. Immediate removal is recommended.”
The two documents concerned the same person. The first confirmed her capability; the second directly overturned the result.

“Two files, two repositories.” Yuna stared at the signature on the risk attachment. “The formal course evaluation clearly confirmed that she passed the assessment. The thing that actually removed her was

this political-risk attachment, which bypassed the evaluation system. If she didn’t know this parallel risk directory existed, she wouldn’t even know what reason she had supposedly been eliminated for.”
She took out a charcoal pencil and quickly copied the central conclusions of the two reports onto opposite sides of a sheet of paper.

“The risk attachment is signed by Otto and Barro.” Yuna put the paper away and looked toward the old archive shelves. “Let’s check the earlier records and see when this practice of removing candidates across repositories under ‘political risk’ began. I don’t want to be erased without explanation one day either.”

We searched for a while in the farthest corner of the old archive shelves. We found no historical records of the candidate procedure, but in the process of moving things around, we pulled out an entire

set of Annual General Supply Ledgers, bound together with coarse hemp rope and compiled continuously by year. The pages went from brittle and yellowed at the bottom to relatively recent paper at the top.

She spread the thick consecutive ledgers across the table, starting with the one from seventy or eighty years ago and working forward to the most recent one from this year. She laid out every countersignature approval page from each ten-year interval side by side.
“Arno, look.” She pointed at the pages spread across half the table, her finger trembling slightly.

I lowered my head to look. Across the continuous ledgers spanning seventy or eighty years, the countersignatures of Sera, Otto, Barro, and Toma—the four Elders of the Inner Circle—were astonishingly identical.

Not only were the names the same; even their habits of joining strokes and their distinctive ways of moving the pen had not changed at all over the long years, despite the traces that should have shown age.
“Could the seats be hereditary, with the descendants deliberately imitating their elders’ signatures? Or could they be stamped seals?” I asked.

“Look at the impressions on the back.” Yuna turned the pages over and pointed to the paper backs showing through with ink. “A seal applies pressure evenly, but the pressure varies from stroke to stroke in these characters. They were written by hand. And

since we have a complete set of ledgers, if this were a master training an apprentice, or a family succession, there would always be a period of awkward imitation, gradual improvement, and eventual stabilization. When two generations changed places, there

would absolutely be a transitional period in the force of the strokes and the habits of lifting the pen. But across these continuous years, there was no transition. Not a single year breaks. These four people signed every ledger from the past eighty years.”
She drew a deep breath, her voice trembling with something close to disbelief.

“They’ve continued living on paper under the same names, in the same seats, with the same handwriting, every day throughout these seventy or eighty years.” She raised her head and looked at me. “They haven’t aged?”
I looked at the signatures spanning most of a century, and a cold sweat slowly seeped across my back.
“If the Elders are like this,” Yuna said, her eyes filled with extreme unease, “then what about the people in the village?”
Instead of relying entirely on memory as she usually did, she took a charcoal pencil and a sheet of white paper from inside her clothes.
“Didn’t you say this morning that if we discovered anything, we should remember it, and never leave it on paper?” I watched what she was doing.

“Because this suspicion is too frightening, Arno.” Without looking up, she quickly traced the countersignatures from those pages. “If I rely only on memory, by the time I walk out that door, I’ll definitely wonder whether I saw it wrong. I have to carry the evidence with me.”
She shoved the files back into the bottom of the wooden chest.
“Come on. To the chapel’s front hall to find Estelle.”

There was no one else in the hall that afternoon. Morning prayers had ended long ago. The rough kneeling stools had been pushed neatly beneath the benches, and the wax in the wind-shielded candle stand
on the dais was from yesterday; no one had come to clean it yet. Yuna had grown up here—when she had first started working with Sera, she had recited scripture here, learned to record visitors’ words

verbatim in confession forms, and scrubbed every inch of the floor. When she walked in, her steps were natural. When she reached the third row, she automatically went around a slightly loose flagstone.
But when she reached the visitor’s table where Estelle had been sitting, she stopped for a moment. It was empty, with only a bench left there.

“She isn’t at the temporary residence, and she isn’t here. There’s no signature from her in the front hall visitor log either.” Yuna stared at the empty tabletop, her brows drawn tight. “They even skipped the step where she would receive the public reason.”
“Was she taken away by force?” I lowered my voice.

“And no one knows where.” Yuna bit her lip. She touched the paper in her pocket, the one on which she had copied the truth of Estelle’s elimination. Estelle was not here. The arrangement she and Yuna had made that morning ended here. There was no one to hand it over to—not even the trump card that determined her fate was of any use.

Since the normal process had not been followed, the girl from outside had not only been driven away; before leaving, she would not even know that she had been eliminated because of peripheral political risk. The thoroughness with which she had simply vanished quickly chilled the small spark of resolve Yuna had kindled in the archives.
She silently withdrew her gaze and took me to the wall behind the hall.
The Inscription Wall.

I had come here many times with my parents as a child, but I had never really looked at it. It was a massive stone wall built from the floor all the way to the high beams, its rough surface densely covered in carved names.
“How many names?” I tilted my head back and looked at the varying depths of the lettering.
“One thousand one hundred and forty-seven.”
“You counted them when you were eleven. That was six years ago. There haven’t been any additions?” I was a little surprised.

“Every time I’ve been punished by being sent to scrub the wall over these six years, I’ve counted again.” She looked at the wall, her eyes cold and sharp. “The total hasn’t changed once. Not a single person has been added.”
She walked to the middle section of the wall, raised her head, and searched among the names.

“The wall is divided into sections. Each section represents a period, arranged from left to right.” She raised a hand and gestured. “The section farthest to the left has the oldest writing. This is the fifth section, the one covering the thirty years closest to the present.”
Suddenly, her voice stopped. Her finger moved down along the rough stone and came to rest at one spot.
“Here. The third section.”
I leaned closer.
A line was carved into the stone, the lettering still clear: “Canal Watchman Garon.”
“What year was this?” I asked.

“According to the calendar markers on the left, the first section to the present covers one hundred and thirty years.” Yuna stared at the name. “This is in the lower middle of the third section. By the rules of this wall, it was probably about eighty years ago.”
“Garon.” I read the name aloud. There was only one Garon here.
“Mm.” She gave only that one response.
She did not say, “My father.”
Then her finger moved a long way to the right, past the dense rows of names, across the distance of two sections, and returned to the fifth section.
“Tower Repairer Garon”
“That was ten years ago. When the village repaired the foundation of the White Tower,” Yuna said softly.
We stood in front of the massive stone wall without saying anything. The air held a faint mixed smell of old paper and cold smoke. The two inscriptions were separated, unmistakably, by seventy years.
Yuna took paper and a charcoal pencil from inside her clothes, and made rubbings of the two names.
“The village rules require anyone who has done work for the community to carve their own name into the wall by hand.”
She held the two sheets with the names rubbed onto them side by side.

“Look at the finishing strokes of the initial characters in these two names, and the turns in the final characters.” Yuna pointed to the ends of the lettering. “At the same positions, both have an extremely unnatural, rigid hesitation.”
“The wall has been re-engraved. Could that have been the repair worker’s own habit?” I said.

“I looked at more than a dozen other names in the third and fifth sections just now.” Yuna rubbed the rubbings in her pocket, her voice tightening. “Not only is the force used at the beginnings and ends of those two characters exactly the same, but look at these two instances of ‘long’—the final stroke of ‘隆’ is carved more lightly than usual in both.

That habitual easing of pressure at the end is the hardest thing to imitate deliberately. If a descendant with the same name were copying it, he might reproduce the hesitation, but he would definitely put force into the final stroke too, to make it clear. These two places were carved by the same person, using the same physical habit to chisel the stone.”

That evening, we sat beside the water channel behind the mill—the place was far enough away, and the roar of the turning waterwheel loud enough, that even speaking loudly would not make it easy for outsiders to hear us.
She squatted on the ground, rhythmically tapping the dirt with a short length of charcoal. “Knock, knock.”

“Grandfather and grandson with the same name, or a craftsman’s copying habit. The simplest explanation can gloss this over. We should have gone back and continued tracking down Estelle’s whereabouts.”
She straightened.
“But it doesn’t make sense.”
She turned the charcoal around and struck the mud hard with the unsharpened end.
“There are one thousand one hundred and forty-seven names. I never stopped to think about a single one of them. I just counted them one by one. Just like—”
She stopped suddenly, as though something had caught in her throat.
I waited patiently. The current rushed past, scouring the channel walls.
“Just like I’ve never thought about how old my mother is.” She finally said it, her voice very quiet.

The roar of the channel nearly drowned out her words. But her voice did not change. It still had the same calm, analytical tone she used when sorting through materials, and the contrast made it unsettling.
“My father is thirty-one. My mother is twenty-nine. I’m seventeen. My little sister is twelve.”
“These four numbers get larger every day. I could write down the ages of my own family with my eyes closed.”
She lowered her head and stared fixedly at the ground.
“Thirty-one minus seventeen is fourteen. Twenty-nine minus seventeen is twelve.”
My heart sank.

If twenty-nine and thirty-one were their real biological ages, how had the whole village managed to ignore and never mention, for these seventeen years, something like twelve- and fourteen-year-olds giving birth to her?
She shifted the charcoal back into a normal writing grip.
“If those two people on the wall really are the same person—” She pointed at the ground.
“Then seventy years between the two inscriptions isn’t strange. Though that means he must be at least over a hundred now.” I followed her line of thought.
“It isn’t strange. Garon looks only a little over thirty now. We need to confirm whether his mind contains memories of that time.”
“How do you confirm it?”
Yuna squatted there, the charcoal in her hand no longer tapping. The huge waterwheel rumbled nearby, stirring up waves of mist.

“The inscription in the third section says ‘Canal Watchman.’ That was eighty years ago, when the canal burst its banks.” She lowered her voice. “Ask him whether it rained that day. Then ask him how the iron shovel he used to dig the mud got its blade bent over.”
“What would that tell us?”
“There was no iron shovel at all. I looked at the supply ledgers for those years in the storeroom just now. No iron tools were issued for that breach. They used wood cut on the spot.
” Yuna threw the stone in her hand into the channel. “Ask him. If he only heard the story from an elder, he’ll follow your question and invent a reason for an iron tool breaking. But
if he dug through the mud himself, that wrong detail will make his hands remember what he held before his mind does. He won’t be able to hide that instinctive physical contradiction.”
She raised her head and stared at me, her gaze burning.
“What if he experienced it himself?”
“Then ask him a third question.” She looked at me. “Ask him how old he really is now.”
“You’ve worked at the mill for three years. You go ask.”
I froze and looked at her.
“You’re not going?” She was the one who had raised the issue in the first place.
She drew her gaze back from the rushing water.
“If you ask, he’s only facing the apprentice at the mill. If I ask, he’s facing his daughter.”
“How am I supposed to bring it up? I don’t even know when it happened.”

“The first section to the present covers one hundred and thirty years. The lower part of the third section was probably about eighty years ago, by the rules of this wall.” Yuna thought for a moment. “Just ask him about when the canal burst its banks eighty years ago.”
“What about you?”
“I’ll wait here for the result.”
I went to ask him anyway.

When the mill was nearly finished for the day, Garon was bent over the millstone platform, inspecting the old machine—the mill’s main shaft had a set of heavy iron drive components, and because they had gone so long without proper maintenance, they had to be thoroughly checked once a month. His entire upper body was inside it, his hands covered in thick black machine oil.

I stood beside him, handing him tools. I had done this job with him more than thirty times. I knew which section needed the large wrench and which needed the pliers. He did not have to speak, and I did not have to ask. We worked together perfectly.

But that day, I handed him the wrong tool once. He pulled his hand out of the machine, and absentmindedly I placed a six-point wrench in it. He did not take his hand back or say anything. It simply stayed suspended in the air. I suddenly came to my senses and hurriedly handed him an eight-point wrench instead.
“Your mind’s not here,” he said in his muffled voice from beneath the machine.
He did not even look up as he said it. His tone was flat, the same tone he used when cursing at a jammed waterwheel.
I stood behind him for a while, my palms slightly sweaty.

I had spent the entire walk from the channel back to the mill thinking about what I needed to ask. I had imagined all kinds of excuses for starting the conversation and worked through his possible reactions. But when I actually stood there, I realized that all those approaches had been prepared for a stranger.
The person in front of me was the master I had worked with for three years.
“Master Garon.” I took a deep breath.
“Mm.” He answered, still straining to turn something in his hands.
“I went to the chapel today and looked at the Inscription Wall.” I tried to make my voice sound casual.
“Your name is on it. In two places.”
This time, the clanging of metal stopped. Only for half a second, then it began again.
“An ancestor’s.” His voice was muffled.
“Which elder?”
“Can’t remember.”

The movement of his hands did not pause. The drive components inside had to be checked one section at a time. From outside, I could see exactly which section he had reached—he did not touch the wrong place, nor did he slow down because of what I had said.
It was only that he did not say those three words as fluidly as usual. There was the faintest pause in the middle, as though half a breath had come between them.
“Can’t remember” was not technically a lie in the village. It was a universal shield. Anyone could say it, and once they did, everyone understood without speaking that no one would ask again.
I handed him the next tool. My palm was wetter now.
“The inscription in the third section says ‘Canal Watchman.’ According to the calendar, that was eighty years ago.” I brought up the first fact, feeling my voice tighten.
“Did it rain that day?”

The evening light slanted through the dusty western window, fine flour dust floating in the beam. Outside, the huge waterwheel roared. Garon was bent over the oil-stained machine, both hands buried deep in the dark drive components.

He did not answer immediately. His hands continued feeling their way along the drive components, one section at a time. He finished one section, then the second. At the third, his hand stopped there, frozen, and went no farther.
Then he spoke.

“It did. For three full days. It didn’t stop until the morning of the third day. When the sun came out afterward, vapor shot up from the bottom of the channel, and the whole channel was stifling, like a pot coming to a boil.”

He did not brush me off as he had just before. He bit down firmly on every word, with a trace of exhausted concession. After saying it, he fell completely silent, like a machine whose power had been cut.
He remained bent over in that awkward position, motionless. One hand was still thrust deep inside the machine’s gears.
I stood behind him with every muscle tense, afraid even to breathe.
The waterwheel outside continued turning tirelessly, once, then again, the sound of water striking the wooden trough heavy and dull. The wheel struck once, and he did not move;
it struck a second time, and the hand inside the machine still did not come out. Only after the third heavy splash had sounded did the water fall back into the bottom trough.
Garon slowly pulled his hand out of the machine. He sat upright and began rubbing his hands hard against his oil-stained apron.
He wiped them with extraordinary care, rubbing one finger at a time, as though cleaning some precious, fragile object.
“Arno.” He finally called my name, his voice hoarse.
“Here.” I instinctively straightened.
“Which phase did you enter today?”
“The second phase.” I answered truthfully.
“Mm.” He nodded and stopped wiping his hands.
He untied the apron from around his waist and casually draped it over the tool rack beside him.
“You’re not supposed to ask that in the second phase.” His voice had turned cold.

He did not show any anger when he said it. He did not look at me even once. He simply sat beside the machine he had only half-finished inspecting, his head lowered as he looked at his hands, which he had finally managed to clean.
“Go ask Sera. She should be the one to tell you about this, not me. If I say it, I might say it wrong, and she’ll be the one left to clean up the mess.”
He braced himself against the machine and stood, his movements somewhat heavy.
“Don’t come tomorrow.” With his back to me, his voice sank lower. “Focus on going through your candidate procedure from now on.”
I silently lowered the wrench in my hand. When I was seven, I had timidly entered this roaring room for the first time, and he had lifted me onto the millstone platform. That
man, who repaired machines with me every day and occasionally complained about sluggish gears, had just described a rainstorm from eighty years ago in an utterly distant voice.
But I still clenched my teeth and turned to leave. When I reached the door, I stopped.
I turned back.
“The iron shovel they used then.” I looked at his back and put forward the second question.
“How did the blade get bent over?”
Garon’s back stiffened, but he did not turn around.
