“There was no iron shovel.” A trace of weariness entered his voice. “They used wooden poles. The village hadn’t issued any iron tools. More than two hundred people had to use wooden poles to pry at the stones.”

He remained facing away from me as he answered. The apron that marked him as a worker had been taken off, and he had already told me to leave. He had no reason to answer me at all. But he answered anyway.

Not only that. He could have followed my lead and invented a reason for an iron shovel’s blade bending, just to brush me off. But he didn’t. Faced with that wrong detail, asked through three years of familiarity, his body

remembered what he had held back then before his reason did. It was the instinctive contradiction of someone who had been there in the mud and water. Even if he had wanted to deceive me, he could not hide it in that moment.
Only after speaking did he slowly turn around to look at me.
“How many questions did she teach you?”
He had seen through me, and for a moment I could not speak.
“How many did she give you?” he asked again, his tone heavier.
“Three,” I said.
“You’ve used two.” He nodded, as though everything were exactly as he had expected.
He reached out and slowly smoothed the crumpled edge of the apron on the rack.
“You don’t need to ask the last question.”
Garon raised his head. His eyes were like a dust-covered room whose windows had not been opened for decades.

“The first time I woke up in an unfamiliar body was after that rainstorm.” He looked at me, his voice as though he were talking about someone else. “You’ve now seen the continuity of the memories and touched the edge of changing bodies to stay alive,

but you only know half of it. Don’t stay in the middle. Something will happen. Either ask Sera why only the Inner Circle can keep changing bodies, and find out why it’s done that way… or keep your mouth shut and focus on going through the procedure.”
He turned around and continued gathering the tools scattered across the floor.
I left the mill and stood in the mud outside. Behind me, the huge waterwheel continued to roar tirelessly. The heavy sound of the water, one I was used to
hearing every day, now sounded like a ruthless iron door, shutting me completely away from the familiar world. Who, exactly, was the man who had just answered me?
The wind grew colder on the way home.
I had always believed that everyone grew old at the normal pace. But if Garon possessed memories from eighty years ago, what about my family? And my father, who died when I was seven, whose
body was quickly taken by the White Tower under the reason of “internal direct lineage,” leaving no record of his name being struck from the rolls—where did he stand within this arrangement?
I stood in front of my house, my hand resting on the wooden door.

A dim yellow light leaked through the crack, and I could hear faint sounds from inside: my mother, Rena, clearing the table. The clinking of bowls and plates was exactly the same as it had been on every evening I could remember.
My hand remained on the rough wooden door for a long time.
I pushed the door open.
Rena had her back to me, stacking several washed plates on the shelf.
“You’re back? A little late today.” She did not turn around. Her voice carried its usual gentle weariness.
I stood in the doorway without moving. The familiar checkered tablecloth covered the table, and in the corner sat the old kettle I had seen since childhood. Nothing had changed.
“Mom.” I looked at her back, my voice somewhat dry. “Are you… still you?”
A plate made a faint clinking sound. Rena’s hand stopped in midair.
She slowly turned around and wiped her hands on her apron. She looked at me without surprise, only a deep calm in her eyes.

“I remember you having a fever when you were seven, crying in the middle of the night for water.” She spoke softly, slowly walking to the table. “I remember the day you first went to the mill, when you scraped your knee before leaving.”
She placed her hand on the checkered tablecloth.
“I remember all of it. I have always been myself.”
Her voice did not tremble, and she did not evade the question. It held an unquestionable confirmation: she possessed every memory of the life we had shared.
“Then what about my father?” I stared at her. “He doesn’t even have a record of being struck from the rolls. If even Garon can… why did my father die young?”
Rena’s hand tightened slightly on the tablecloth. The calm certainty from a moment ago disappeared.
“He died young.” She avoided my eyes and turned to take the kettle.
“He was internal direct lineage. He worked in the White Tower. He could have, like everyone else—”
“He died young, Arno.” She interrupted me, pouring water with her back to me. Her voice had become stiff and distant. “There’s no need to ask about this again.”

She was like a door that had suddenly shut, sealing away every possibility concerning my father inside one thin assertion. Standing in the room where I had lived for seventeen years, looking at her familiar back, I felt a deep, bone-level strangeness for the first time.
I did not drink the water. I turned and stepped back into the darkness.
We found Sera in the academic affairs office on the second floor of the White Tower. She was sitting at the desk, marking the records from the day’s class.

“Garon told me to ask you.” Yuna stood in the doorway without any preamble. “If the endpoint of the candidate procedure is to change into a new body and live forever like the Elders of the Inner Circle, why do we first have to guarantee lifelong secrecy before we can learn that this is what we’re competing for?”
The pen in Sera’s hand stopped.
She did not look flustered. She simply watched Yuna in silence, as though evaluating something.
“Because if the people in the village knew that the right to continued life existed, order would collapse.” Sera’s voice remained perfectly even. “The Dice-Thrower permits selected guardians to share
in continued life. But this is a transaction. You must first prove that you can keep your mouth shut and stand on the side of the greater order before you are qualified to receive this privilege.”
“What about you? Have you changed bodies too?”
“Yes.” Sera admitted it without reservation.

“Where did the old body go? And where did the new one come from?” Yuna clenched her fists, her voice tightening. “Why can only people from the Inner Circle keep changing bodies? With so many people in the village, why are only you allowed to enjoy this privilege?”
“That is not something you need to know yet.” Sera picked up her pen again. “First, I will not tell you the technical details. Second, candidates are responsible for obeying the rules, not

questioning those who make them. And third—if you think every signature that has remained for a long time belongs to an Elder who changed bodies, then you haven’t carried your subtraction far enough.”
Sera’s cold refusal was like a wall without a single gap. Yuna did not argue again. She turned and walked out.
I did not go home. I followed her to the road near the mill.

Yuna had not gone home either. She was sitting on the stone steps outside her house. It was completely dark. A dim oil lamp was lit inside, and the light leaking through the doorway illuminated a square patch on the steps in front of her. Her whole body was curled up in the darkness outside that patch of light.
I sat down beside her and told her everything that had happened at the mill, including Garon’s answer and my mother’s unquestionable confirmation that she possessed all our shared memories.
After I finished, I kept waiting for her to speak.
But she didn’t.
A long time passed.
“My mother’s inside.” Her voice trembled in the night wind.
My little sister Milu’s clear laughter came from inside the house—she seemed to be reading from some booklet, stumbling over the words and being corrected twice, in the gentle voice of Meru.
Yuna buried her face deep in her knees, her knuckles whitening with the force of her grip.
“Arno.” She did not raise her head. “When I came back just now, I pushed the door open a crack. I asked her if she was still herself.”
I held my breath and watched her.

“She said she remembered me having a fever when I was ten, clinging to her hand in the middle of the night; she remembered the first day she taught me to recite scripture, when I hid behind the door and refused to come out. She said it while looking

into my eyes. She said she had always been herself, that she remembered every day.” Yuna’s voice trembled even more violently. “But that voice… it was the voice of a twenty-nine-year-old woman, and that face was the face of a twenty-nine-year-old.

Since Sera confirmed with her own mouth that my mother had changed bodies, but if that last thing she said was true—that not everyone whose age doesn’t add up survived by changing bodies—then what price did those who aren’t Elders pay to stay alive?”
She did not wait for my answer. Her eyes snapped shut.
“I didn’t dare go in.”
I clenched my hands and sat at the edge of the patch of light. The chilling certainty I had received in my own home crashed down heavily onto the ground once again.
Yuna finally raised her head, her eyes red.
“If this is a transaction that trades secrecy for the privilege of continued life…” She clenched her teeth and stared hard at the patch of light on the ground. “Why them?”
“What?”
“The Elders. Garon. My mother. And your father, who worked in the White Tower and whose body was taken under the reason of direct lineage. These people form the skeleton that
keeps order in place.” Yuna’s voice was soft, but carried a sharp, icy edge. “Where exactly do they stand within this arrangement? Were they deceived like everyone else, or…”
She turned her head toward the blurred outline of the White Tower in the night.
“…are they part of the arrangement itself?”

I fell silent. Garon’s words echoed in my ears—“You’ve now seen the continuity of the memories and touched the edge of changing bodies to stay alive, but you only know half of it… figure out the other half too.”
We sat there in the darkness outside the house, listening to the familiar laughter of our relatives on the other side of the door, but neither of us took a single step inside.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:title: Appendix to Chapter Three: Miscellaneous
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s1-1:
Archive Room · Shelf Labels (Door Sign: Miscellaneous):
1. Lesson Plans and Courses (Old Copies). 2. Registers and Batches (Duplicates). 3. (Red Cloth Strips). 4. Unclassified.
Note: Borrowing does not require registration. Except for shelves marked with red cloth strips. Report any contact to whoever is on duty.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s3-1: On the afternoon of the fourth day, we pushed open the iron gate bearing the “Miscellaneous” sign again.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s5-1: Deep inside the room, among the tightly packed ordinary case files on the wooden shelves, ledgers bearing red seals were scattered here and there. When we came yesterday afternoon to look for the delisting registers, we nearly pulled out the wrong ones several times because they were mixed in with the ordinary files.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s6-1: After entering, Yuna went straight to the areas marked with red labels.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s7-1: She didn’t reach out to touch them. She simply stood there in silence, her gaze jumping from one red label to another as though combing through loose threads. She studied carefully what was exposed—the damaged spines of the ledgers, and their distinctive binding.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s9-1: “What are you doing?” I asked softly from behind her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s11-1: “Memorizing what they look like.” Her eyes continued moving among the marked ledgers. “If I see files of the same format somewhere else later, I’ll recognize at a glance where they were supposed to be kept.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s12-1: She turned around. There were pronounced dark circles beneath her amber eyes. Last night, we had sat stiffly on the stone steps outside her house for the entire night. The sound of her mother moving around occasionally came through the wooden door only a few steps away, but in the end, she still hadn’t dared to open it.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s14-1: “Let’s get to work,” she said, forcing the words out on a single breath as she patted her stiff cheeks.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s16-1: The room fell silent except for the rustle of turning pages. We sat opposite each other at the two ends of the long table and began carefully avoiding the red labels as we carried down a stack of ordinary population-change files.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s17-1: The process was tedious and trivial. The ledgers recorded a jumble of things: duty rosters for the chapel, running records of marriages and funerals, even minute field allotments. Dense dates and names struck at my eyes like dull rain.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s19-1: I was going through an old household-register ledger. When I reached a spot low on one page, my finger stopped abruptly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s20-1: My eyes moved along the line to the right and stopped at the column for household address. I scanned it word by word all over again, afraid I had read across the wrong line. Just yesterday evening, he had driven me out of the mill. The heavy sound of that wooden door closing still seemed to be beside my ear.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s21-1: Yuna sat at the other end of the table, bent over the stack of files that belonged to her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s23-1: “Yuna.” I heard the roughness in my own voice.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s25-1: “Mm.” She answered only with a nasal hum, her fingertips still moving quickly across the pages.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s26-1: I turned the ledger halfway around on the tabletop and pushed it toward her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s29-1: The rustling of paper stopped. She stood, went around the table, and came to my side, her eyes settling on the place I was pointing to.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s30-1: The entries were arranged strictly by year. On the curled, withered-yellow pages, a line of inconspicuous ink was squeezed in:
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s31-1: Name: Garon. Residence: East Mill. Status: Deceased.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s32-1: A date specific down to the day followed those words.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s34-1: “Forty-three years ago.” Yuna read the year aloud in a low voice.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s35-1: We stood side by side, staring hard at the line. It wasn’t only the name. The address matched exactly too.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s37-1: “The register says he died forty-three years ago,” Yuna stated flatly. “But he clearly looks only a little over thirty now.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s41-1: She took the ledger from me, then flipped through it, her fingers tightening slightly. After turning through more than twenty pages, the rustling stopped abruptly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s44-1: “Same year.” Her finger pressed beneath the two words, the knuckles whitening with force. “Four months apart.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s47-1: Her finger remained there on the rough paper, completely motionless.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s48-1: Absolute silence settled over the room. Outside, the faint rasp of a broom passing over the yard reached us, distant as though it were happening in another world.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s50-1: “Yuna.” I watched the tension in her profile.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s52-1: “Wait for me a moment,” she answered quickly, but her voice sounded as if it had come from some kind of machine.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s53-1: I waited quietly. I didn’t know how much time passed before she finally lifted her hand. Instinctively, she rubbed her palm hard against her apron—as though the shriveled page had burned her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s57-1: “What does ‘induction’ mean?” I broke the silence.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s59-1: “If they’re descendants born to people from the village, the term used in the register is ‘birth.’ Someone from the outskirts, or a wanderer, being entered into the village register—that’s what they call induction.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s60-1: She raised her head and looked straight into my eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s62-1: “Arno, our village has never accepted outsiders. Cain, the boundary guard responsible for watching the boundary stone, guards the border like he’s keeping thieves out for exactly that reason. An adult outsider who has never appeared in the village would be watched by hundreds of eyes even if he moved into the mill carrying a formal seal from the council hall.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s68-1: “I don’t know.” She cut me off.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s69-1: Slowly, she set down the heavy ledger and braced both hands against the peeling edge of the table, leaning forward as though she were kneading all the clues back into fragments.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s71-1: “One isolated case doesn’t count. The person who wrote it might have mixed things up.” After a while, she straightened, forcing her voice steady. “Find a second one.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s73-1: She pushed aside the entire stack of files she had just gone through and began carrying over a new one. The heavy paper ledgers struck the wooden table, raising a choking cloud of dust.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s76-1: I left the archive room and went outside for some air.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s77-1: The sunlight had already begun to slant. Estelle was sitting on the stone bench in front of the chapel, its surface worn smooth and bright, with a large ledger spread across her knees. There was no one else around. Even the servants who handled the sweeping had already left.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s78-1: Hearing my footsteps, she closed the ledger halfway.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s79-1: I knew how dangerous it was to reveal an anomaly in the archive room to an external candidate facing selection. But in this sealed-off chapel, only those eyes of hers, eyes that had seen life outside, could see through the household register to the hard accounting of survival behind it.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s81-1: “I want to ask you about a word.” I walked up to her and stopped at a distance where we could hear each other clearly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s83-1: “Go ahead.” She leaned back slightly, a trace of instinctive wariness in her expression.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s85-1: “Induction. If someone was explicitly recorded as dead first, and then a few months later the same name underwent induction at the same address, what could that mean outside, or in a refugee camp?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s86-1: She looked at me in surprise, then at my empty hands. I had just come out of the controlled archive room in the deepest part of the chapel, a room even she couldn’t enter. Empty-handed, I had thrown a potentially lethal administrative loophole at her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s88-1: “When one more person is added to the household register, the distribution station’s master ledger needs another line. The village’s rations are fixed. A portion has to be divided out, and everyone else gets a little less in their bowl.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s90-1: “That’s never as simple as writing a name on paper. That’s real food watched by hundreds of eyes. During the months you’re checking, did the distribution station have one extra person come asking for food? Or did the ration that originally belonged to that person never stop at all?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s91-1: I stood in front of the stone bench, feeling as though an invisible net had suddenly tightened around my thoughts.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s93-1: “Check the distribution slips for those months.” She reopened the ledger on her knees and stopped looking at me. “No matter what the household register says on the surface, as long as the person was still eating, there would have to be a trace in the granary’s disbursements. But I can’t check it from here. I can’t get through the gate outside your archive room.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s95-1: By the time I returned to the archive room, several ledgers were already spread across the long table.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s96-1: I repeated Estelle’s reasoning about the rations to Yuna. When she finished listening, she pressed the charcoal pencil hard into the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s98-1: “Find the ration details from forty-three years ago in the wooden boxes below.” She made her decision without hesitation. “Check the account under Garon’s name. I’ll keep looking for a second one.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s99-1: To find that ledger, I nearly emptied the three wooden boxes at the bottom, each half-eaten by termites. The years on many of the account books had blurred beyond recognition. I could only work downward by calculation until I finally pulled out the distribution slips, resewn with hemp thread.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s100-1: The ink in the ledger was cold and conclusive: throughout the four months when the archive marked Garon as “deceased,” the ration assigned to his name had not been canceled. It was allocated every day as usual. Before
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s100-2: the “death” entry, the recipient’s fingerprint was pressed in the signature column after his name; during the four-month blank period, the method of receipt changed to a seal used exclusively by the elders’ council hall.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s101-1: More importantly, on the day before fingerprint receipts resumed, the remarks column of the distribution slip contained a glaring annotation we could never have seen in the ledgers of ordinary villagers:
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s102-1: “New body activated. Approved for standard ration allocation.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s103-1: After “renewed induction,” the receipt column returned to fingerprints. The whorl patterns of the prints left before the death and after the induction ran in exactly the same direction.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s105-1: “‘New body activated’…” I looked at the glaring words and felt a chill run down my back. “Did Garon change into another body during those four months?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s106-1: If it was another body, why were the fingerprints identical? The question had barely surfaced before another horrifying flaw covered it.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s108-1: “And everyone in the village had just attended his funeral. If they watched him move back into the mill four months later, they would have thought they were seeing a ghost.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s109-1: Yuna stared at the seal beside the fingerprint, her lips pressed tightly into a line.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s111-1: “If he came back looking the way he originally did, he would certainly be recognized as dead. But if he had a different face no one had seen before, given how guarded this village is, how could he have swaggered back in and taken his own identity without anyone questioning him?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s112-1: She raised her head sharply, deep fear in her amber eyes. For the decades that followed, this body, bearing the same fingerprints, would lead her from childhood into adulthood. Yet in her memory, its appearance had never grown older.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s114-1: “And Arno, he hasn’t only been like this in recent years. For the seventeen years I can remember, he’s always looked exactly as he does now—like a man in his thirties. Looking further back, he has the same face in the old photo albums my mother left behind. He has never aged.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s115-1: Seventeen years of memories and the fingerprint printed on paper forty-three years ago were like two nails locked into each other. What had that man gone through during the four-month blank period after he was
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s115-2: delisted? What exactly was the so-called “new body” he changed into? Or… in the year the dead man returned to the village, had the memories of the entire village simply been forcibly erased and uniformly implanted?
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s116-1: The daylight outside darkened by degrees.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s117-1: Throughout those long dozens of minutes, she did not turn a single page. She only stared at the shriveled ink, as though watching the father who had carried her on his shoulders since childhood slowly shatter into some kind of cold component. Then the wooden table gave a dull thud.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s118-1: She slammed the register she had left untouched onto the table and drew a deep breath.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s121-1: Dozens of household-register ledgers she had searched lay scattered across the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s123-1: “The elder who taught me. Otto.” She looked at the name. “Deceased, sixty-one years ago. Induction, the same year, five months apart.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s125-1: She stood and pushed the newly found file toward me.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s127-1: “The wooden boxes below.” Her hand pressed against the ledger, her fingertips white. “Find the distribution slips from sixty-one years ago. If we can find the same seal and annotation under his name…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s128-1: But the archive room did not generously yield every answer. Twenty minutes later, deep inside the bottommost wooden box, all we could pull out was a mass of paper pulp chewed to pieces by termites. Not a single
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s128-2: complete page remained of the ration details from sixty-one years ago. There were no fingerprints, addresses, or annotations left for us to verify whether this was a record belonging to Otto, the current elder.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s130-1: “Same names on the ‘deceased’ and ‘induction’ entries alone can’t prove he went through the same procedure. They can’t even establish that he’s the old man who taught us to read and write.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s130-2: ” Yuna stared at the pile of scraps, then turned toward the two records in the household register, nearly twenty years apart. But the next moment, her tone shifted. “But what if he is?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s132-1: “If they really were changing bodies, why go to so much trouble?” I looked at the ledgers on the table. “Why kill them completely in the public register for several months? Then add them back into the village under the same names?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s134-1: “Because whatever was going to happen to them during those months absolutely couldn’t be seen by anyone else.” Her fingers gripped the corner of the table tightly. “Do you remember what you told me on the steps last night? Garon admitted outright by the water channel that when they
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s134-2: breached it back then, they used wooden poles because the village wouldn’t approve iron shovels. He could even correct you about the rolled edge on the shovel you deliberately used to test him. He didn’t hear that story from an elder. He dug mud in that water channel himself back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s135-1: She looked at me, the dim light from outside reflected in her eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s137-1: “Arno. If he was the one digging the channel with a wooden pole more than eighty years ago, and the person who came back after the four-month blank period forty-three years ago was still him… Add in these suspicious same-name entries in the household register… The people running the council hall may not have been elected term after term at all.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s141-1: “But in the village, once someone is recorded as ‘deceased,’ there has to be a funeral. The whole village watches the coffin get buried in that dirt
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s141-2: slope behind the hill.” I looked at her. “But if what came back a few months later was a ‘new body’… what exactly did they bury in that slope back then?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s143-1: “They either used a false funeral to blind the whole village, or…” Yuna’s brow drew tightly together, her voice dry. “It was a real funeral. The old body was actually left in the coffin.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s145-1: “We need to go to that slope behind the hill.” She braced both hands on the table. “The gravestones on the back slope were built row by row downward, arranged by year. We’ll count along them and find the rows from forty-three and sixty-one years ago. We’ll see whether the names ‘Garon’ and ‘Otto’ are on them.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s147-1: “What if their gravestones are really there?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s148-1: Yuna released her grip. Her eyes were cold as ice forming.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s150-1: “Then we have no choice but to bring shovels,” she said. “We’ll dig it up under cover of night. I want to see what was actually lying in the coffin they buried when they delisted my father. Stones, or his old corpse.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s151-1: Digging up the graves of elders was an unforgivable capital crime in the village. If discovered, the offender would be thrown straight into the underground water gate. But there was not a trace of fear of the death penalty in her eyes now. The vast black hole running through her father’s entire life, and reaching even further into the lives of others, was waiting beneath that slope.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s153-1: “If their gravestones aren’t there at all…” She forced the words out through clenched teeth. “Then they didn’t even dare raise proper graves at the time, afraid the truth would come out later. We’ll follow the soil pits from those two years and investigate downward. That slope must still hold traces of how they concealed the truth back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s154-1: I watched her fingers clamped tightly around the edge of the table. She was digging up the graves of her elders, and also digging open the home that had been stable for her for seventeen years.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s155-1: She said no more. Her breathing was light, and her fingers pressed pale marks into the edge of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z03b:event:text-s157-1: “All right. Bring the shovels.” I did not try to stop her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:title: Chapter Three, Supplement Two: Face to Face
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s1-1:
Periodic Medical Examination Records · Reporting Standards (copy):
Basic physical indicators (such as height and weight) must be measured in person every year.
Skeletal development and crown-wear status may be left blank after adulthood. For any blank field, carry forward the previous conclusion, to conserve medical supplies.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s3-1: After night fell on the fourth day, we reached the cemetery on the back slope with shovels in hand. But when we found the row of gravestones from forty-three years ago, Yuna drove her shovel into the soil.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s4-1: “Digging up an empty coffin would only prove that the funeral back then was false. But if we dig up bones, we’ll have even less way of confirming whether they’re Galon’s discarded old body, or someone else’s, brought in to make up the numbers.” She
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s4-2: looked at the gravestones in the night wind. “If bodies are being replaced, the dead can’t tell us what exactly changed over these decades. To find out how he used this identical body to live until now, we need to search the living people’s records.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s5-1: So we left the cemetery and headed toward the “Medical Records Room” on the second floor of the White Tower under cover of night. Although it was listed on our access credentials, that applied only during the day. The White Tower was still closed at night.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s7-1: It was an extremely cramped little room on the second floor above ground in the White Tower. Apart from just enough space for a person to turn around, it was filled with rows of metal filing cabinets reaching all the
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s7-2: way to the ceiling. The air smelled of old paper fermenting together with insect repellent. Inside the cabinets were the medical examination records of everyone in the village—once a year, from birth all the way to death.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s8-1: With hundreds upon hundreds of drawers lining the walls, there was no way we could spend the entire night in here. We had used the keys issued during the day to open the door, but in the dead of night, the light from the lantern in our hands could draw the night patrol from outside at any moment.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s9-1: My own was in there. So was Yuna’s.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s11-1: “We’ve been examined since we were little.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s13-1: “Every autumn, in the chapel. We lined up to have our height measured, our weight taken, and our teeth checked, then got a prick of the finger at the end.” She ran her hand over the rows of cold drawer handles. “I always thought it was just some kind of rule.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s14-1: Using the alphabetical index, she pulled open a lower drawer. The runners made a dry scraping sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s16-1: “It’s all here,” she said softly, brushing her hand over the yellowed cards. “All the data on every one of us, from birth until now, gathered here.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s17-1: We did not look at our own records, nor at my mother’s. Those could wait. We went straight to Galon’s.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s18-1: His cards were bound into a booklet, a thick stack whose paper edges had frayed from frequent handling.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s19-1: Yuna carried it beneath the wall lamp and turned the pages one by one in the dim yellow glow. At first her movements were steady, but as she went on, her fingers paused for longer and longer stretches.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s28-1: She turned the booklet around and pointed to the two pages in the middle.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s29-1: Between two routine autumn records, someone had inserted an irregular table in a different hand, dated the following spring.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s30-1: “Besides the four-month disappearance forty-three years ago, when he was ‘re-registered after death,’ this abnormal table from eleven years ago interrupts the normal record cycle again.” Yuna pressed her finger against the inserted year, her voice tightening. “The
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s30-2: village requires every adult to visit the ration station once a month to collect a fixed amount of purified water agent. The receipts are pasted into this booklet month by month. But between the autumn examination and this new spring table, there isn’t a single receipt
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s30-3: for four whole months. Children aren’t given this medication. Starting on the day they become adults, they’re required to take it every month for the rest of their lives. If they stop, they get blood-fever. Four consecutive months without a medication record makes it
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s30-4: look as though a person simply wasn’t in the village at all. Worse, compared with the old autumn table on the previous page, his height on this new spring table differs by less than a centimeter. His body fat and muscle mass shifted by an extremely small amount as well.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s31-1: Such slight shifts in physical indicators might ordinarily be dismissed as measurement error. I leaned closer to look at the line.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s32-1: “But the part that truly can’t be covered up comes next.” Yuna’s finger slid toward the columns for skeletal age and crown wear. “In this inserted record, his skeletal
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s32-2: age directly went backward from over forty to twenty. In every record after that, these two fields became completely blank. They all say, ‘Carry forward from old file.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s33-1: Then she found her mother Melu’s record booklet. The same kind of discontinuity appeared in one of the examination intervals from eight years ago.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s34-1: “This afternoon, you said you compared the grain-allocation records from before and after the period when he was unregistered. The whorl patterns in those fingerprints were exactly the same. If that was a forgery made when he replaced his body forty-three years ago…” Yuna abruptly closed the booklet and looked up at me. “But now we’ve seen the regression in
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s34-2: skeletal age from eleven years ago! If Galon has been using a twenty-year-old body for the past eleven years, his face and voice still haven’t changed at all. Even the breadth of his skeleton is almost exactly the same. If the body was replaced, how could this new body, replaced eleven years ago, happen to carry fingerprints exactly identical to the original ones?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s35-1: I went rigid. A chill shot up my spine.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s36-1: “Unless someone made an identical set of patterns on this new shell that looks exactly the same.” Yuna stared hard at me, her eyes red. “Or simply replaced the skin on the entire fingertip…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s38-1: She pulled paper and a pen from her pocket and quickly copied down the data before and after the two discontinuities. Then she hurried back to the cabinet, put the booklet back in its place, and shoved
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s38-2: the drawer closed. After that, she stood rigidly before the drawer, without moving. There was only one dim oil lamp in the records room. Her outline remained frozen in the shadows for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s44-1: When she finally turned around, her face was frighteningly pale, but her eyes were bright enough to hurt.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s46-1: “There’s something I need to say.” She looked straight at me, speaking quickly. “I need to say it now, because if I don’t, I’ll start lying to myself in a moment, telling myself it isn’t true.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s50-1: “The inscribed wall, the household records, and now the discontinuities in the medical records.” She drew a deep breath, her chest rising sharply once. “Galon and Melu… at least two adults we see every day in this village have replaced their bodies under this system.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s51-1: She said it all in one breath, then paused for two seconds in the dimness.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s53-1: “I said it.” Her voice finally steadied. “Now it’s no longer some frightening idea I made up in my own head. It’s real.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s55-1: “So are you going to refute it?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s57-1: “I’m going to find someone and ask them face to face.” She lifted her chin and walked toward the exit. “Right now.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s60-1: The first person she meant to question face to face was her own family.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s61-1: When we pushed open the door, Galon was wiping oil from a wrench with a dry cloth, while Melu washed dishes beside the sink. Everything was exactly like every evening of the past seventeen years.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s62-1: Galon heard us and looked at me. He was the man who had thrown me out of the mill just yesterday. A complicated shadow passed through his eyes, but I could no longer tell whether it was a warning or guilt.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s63-1: Yuna walked to the dining table and slapped the records she had just copied from the White Tower directly onto the mottled wood grain. No preamble.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s65-1: “Minor shifts in physical indicators. Regressed skeletal age.” Yuna looked at Galon, her voice taut with extreme restraint. “And this face that never changed, along with those perfectly matching fingerprints.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s66-1: The water was still rushing beside the sink. Galon set down the dry cloth. Yesterday, those very hands had pushed me out of the mill. I stared at the rough whorl patterns on his fingertip and felt my stomach twist.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s67-1: Melu slowly turned off the faucet, wiped her hands on her apron, and turned around. Neither of them looked at the copied records on the table. There was no shock at being exposed on either face.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s69-1: “It’s the same face, but not the same shell. So who exactly is in this house?” Yuna looked at them. “You replaced your bodies, didn’t you?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s70-1: Galon looked at her. His lips moved, but no sound came out. Melu came over and reached toward Yuna, but Yuna suddenly recoiled.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s72-1: “Yuna.” Melu looked at her own hands hanging in midair, her voice trembling. “The body was replaced. But I’m still me. That has never changed.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s74-1: “What kind of explanation is that?” Yuna stared at her. “How am I supposed to believe that someone who put herself into another shell is the mother who woke me every morning for the past seventeen years? Who did this body originally belong to? Where is she?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s76-1: “Even if this body once belonged to someone else, I don’t have any of those memories.” Melu spoke softly, a sheen of water gathering in her eyes. “When you were eight, you secretly took apart the big clock at the village office. You couldn’t put it back together, and you were
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s76-2: so frightened that you hid all the gears in my flour jar. I helped you keep it from Otto. Every night, after Galon went to sleep, I sat with you in the kitchen with the lamp lit, trying the springs and gears one by one until they fit. Those are the only things I remember.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s78-1: Melu took a step forward, and her hand finally touched Yuna’s shoulder. Yuna flinched instinctively, but in the end she did not pull away. As she had every time Yuna got into trouble in the past, Melu reached up and smoothed the loose hair beside her temple.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s80-1: “That wasn’t someone else. That was your mother.” Melu’s voice caught. “I don’t remember any other identity. I only remember that I’m Galon’s wife, and your mother.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s81-1: Yuna pressed her lips together, her chest rising and falling slightly. She looked into Melu’s reddened eyes and felt the warmth of that hand. The room was utterly quiet. Every so often, a drop fell from the sink and struck the metal basin.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s82-1: I saw Yuna’s eyes soften for an instant. It seemed that if she only nodded and admitted that the past seventeen years still counted, this nightmare could end.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s83-1: But her gaze eventually dropped back to the copied records on the table, the ones bearing the height discontinuity. When she raised her head again, the mist in her eyes was gone.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s85-1: “…If you’re still you, then where did this new body that looks exactly like you come from?” Her voice trembled slightly, but every word was heavily enunciated. “A body like this takes time to grow. Whose life did you take?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s86-1: Melu’s shoulders jerked inward as if the words had burned her. Her face went deathly pale. She turned toward Galon in panic, her lips trembling uncontrollably. It was a kind of shuddering fear so deep it was almost instinctive.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s87-1: Galon sighed, came over, and placed a hand on Melu’s back, gently pulling her a little behind him.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s89-1: “Yuna, let’s stop here.” He looked at his daughter, exhaustion deeper than I could see in his voice. “This is all we can tell you. The rest… we can’t say. We don’t dare say.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s90-1: The room fell into silence again. Melu leaned against Galon and buried her face in his shoulder, muffled sobs coming in broken bursts. Galon held her without a word. The large hand that had just been repairing machines, rough with calluses and
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s90-2: oil, now soothed his wife’s trembling back again and again. These were the people who had raised Yuna. Now, in this homely kitchen, they clung tightly to each other, as though something outside the door could tear them apart at the slightest touch.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s91-1: Yuna stood by the table and watched them for a long time. She did not slam the door as she would during an ordinary argument, nor did she demand answers loudly. She only slowly placed her hands on the tabletop, her fingers tightening little by little as she gripped the copied records. The pages crumpled in her hands with a dry, brittle sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s93-1: “Fine.” She roughly wiped at the corner of her eye, shoved the crumpled evidence into her pocket, and turned toward the door. “I’ll find someone who can talk.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s96-1: We went to the chapel to find Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s97-1: She had just finished evening prayers. A very dim wall lamp burned beside the intercession room door. She stood before the stand, checking and aligning the day’s communal prayer slips and stubs one by one, then binding them together with thread.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s98-1: Yuna walked straight over and pushed the copied records in her hands across the wooden stand in front of Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s99-1: Sera stopped tying the thread and lowered her head to look through them. She glanced over the discontinuity data. Then, without hurry, she returned them to the tabletop.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s101-1: “You spent four days?” She raised her eyes, her tone as calm as if she were asking what they had eaten for dinner.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s108-1: “You expected us to investigate this.” Yuna stared at her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s110-1: “The Medical Records Room is already on your current access list. It isn’t a confidential archive. The moment the counter on the door ticks when it’s accessed, we know how far you’ve gotten.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s112-1: “Judging by your expression, you found the discontinuities, went home to force your parents to admit it, and then came here, didn’t you?” She nodded, with even a trace of approval. “That’s much harder than hearing me admit it aloud yesterday.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s115-1: Yuna’s hand hung at her side, clenched into a fist so tightly it shook.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s117-1: “How many people in the village are like this?” she asked again, her voice hoarse.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s119-1: “All ten seats on the Council of Elders.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s121-1: “Who else is on the list? Where did the old bodies go? And where did those new bodies come from?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s123-1: “The list, the source, and the destination are not on the materials being delivered to you today. I refuse to answer.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s125-1: “How long has this system been going on?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s126-1: The air in the chapel seemed to solidify for two seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s128-1: “For more than a hundred years,” she said softly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s129-1: The surroundings were terrifyingly quiet. In the distant wall lamp, a little remnant of wick flickered in the darkness, burning at an extremely slow rate.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s132-1: “More than a hundred years…” Yuna repeated it unconsciously, as though weighing the four words in her mouth.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s136-1: “Then how old are you, really?” Yuna suddenly raised her head and looked directly into Sera’s eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s138-1: “If you mean the body standing in front of you now, thirty-four. But if you mean ‘me,’ that is exactly what you’ll be learning in the lessons ahead.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s140-1: Yuna raised her head and stared somewhat blankly at the vaulted ceiling.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s142-1: “When I was little…” Her voice was very soft, as though recalling something from a distant past. “You taught me a passage of scripture called ‘The lamp must not go out, the people must not scatter.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s148-1: “It’s a doctrine meant to be recited. It serves no function in itself. Carrying consciousness into a new body is merely a medical procedure. Wrapping this system in the sanctity of divine grace is meant to make accepting it a little easier for you.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s149-1: Yuna’s jaw tightened instantly, her masseter standing out beneath her pale skin.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s151-1: “If we’re going to learn all of it anyway, and you already told us yesterday that we could exchange secrecy for continuance, why do this today? Why divide access to the evidence into stages and hand it to us piece by piece?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s153-1: “Because we paid a price and discovered a pattern. Those who piece these things together little by little, in the prescribed order, and those who are given the whole truth at once eventually grow into entirely different kinds of people.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s154-1: She picked up the stack of papers she had just bound, straightened it perfectly, and then turned to face us.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s157-1: “You went to the kitchen just now, didn’t you? You should understand what this net for selecting people is actually screening for.” Sera looked at Yuna. “Those names you didn’t see in the records, and
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s157-2: their original bodies… Without this strict screening to eliminate people unworthy of the qualification, how could your parents have had the chance to replace their bodies with the ones they have now?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s159-1: In that instant, the aggressive tension Yuna had carried all this time seemed to strike an invisible wall. Yesterday, she had still been angry at the bargain of secrecy for privilege. Now Sera calmly tied that bargain to the lives of Yuna’s parents.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s161-1: “The fact that you can see them alive at home is the result of this system’s selection. This is what the induction examination is truly meant to deliver to you—the qualification to appear, like them, on the list of those allowed to continue by replacing their bodies.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s162-1: Yuna’s fingers dug hard into the edge of the wooden stand, her nails nearly sinking into the wood. She stared at Sera, opened her mouth, but no words came out.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s164-1: “If the people who remain on the list are conspirators…” I took a sudden step forward and slammed my hand onto the stand, my knuckles whitening with the force. “What about my father? He died without even a cancellation record, and
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s164-2: you’ve always brushed me off with ‘he died young.’ You never said a word about the cause of death! Was he disposed of because he refused to keep your secrets, or did you simply take his body to fill someone else’s place on the list?!”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s165-1: Sera watched me lose control in silence. She did not take half a step back.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s167-1: “Every batch that reaches this point asks this question after hearing that promise.” Her tone remained even.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s169-1: “Since we have it, what happens to the people who aren’t on the list?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s171-1: “It is the hardest question in a system that has continued for more than a hundred years. It has no answer that will make you feel comfortable or satisfied. So I won’t fob you off with an excuse today.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s172-1: She turned back and picked up the lantern from the stand.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s175-1: “Go back to sleep.” The lantern light illuminated half her face. “Tomorrow’s lesson is in the morning. Don’t be late.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s177-1: When we turned around and were nearly at the main entrance, she suddenly called out behind us:
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s182-1: “Your mother came to the chapel this afternoon.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s184-1: “To see you?” My heart gave a sudden lurch.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s189-1: Sera looked at me quietly from several steps away.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s191-1: “She only came to ask me,” her voice echoed through the empty passage, “whether, given how far you’d gotten consulting the records these past few days, you would happen to turn over that hidden card tonight.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s195-1: There were only a few dozen steps from the intercession room to the chapel doors.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s196-1: I walked one step at a time. The night wind poured into my collar, but it could not disperse the roaring in my head. My mother had known long ago what would happen tonight. These past few days, she had maintained her silence about my father, yet today she had gone to Sera of her own accord to ask how far we had gotten.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s197-1: Outside the doors, on the two rough stone benches, Estelle was sitting on the one to the west.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s198-1: She sat in the night wind, rose, and brushed off her clothes. She asked nothing, only watched us quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s199-1: Yuna drew a deep breath of night air and walked straight up to her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s201-1: “I’m laying all my cards on the table for you now: all ten seats have replaced their bodies, and this system has continued for more than a hundred years.” She looked at Estelle, speaking extremely quickly. “And Sera even
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s201-2: coaxed and deceived us by saying that as long as we pass the seven-day examination and prove ourselves conspirators capable of keeping their secrets, we’ll be on that ‘list’ of people allowed to replace their bodies too.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s202-1: When Yuna said “more than a hundred years” and “the list,” Estelle’s face did not change at all. After Yuna finished, she remained silent, simply rubbing the notebook in her hands again and again.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s204-1: “If it’s only about bringing in conspirators, they could choose people at any time. Why force the examination to happen at the point of adulthood?” The resistance in Yuna’s eyes was hard as ice as she stared
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s204-2: at Estelle. “Unless adulthood means more than being eligible for induction. It also means the body has finished growing. If someone fails the examination, then this body can conveniently be treated as…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s205-1: She did not say the word.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s207-1: “Why aren’t you saying anything? Aren’t you going to say something?” There was a trace of undisguisable agitation in Yuna’s voice.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s209-1: “I can’t verify the source of the bodies tonight.” Her tone was as flat as if she were discussing tomorrow’s weather. “I don’t have a second solid piece of evidence to cross-check against Sera’s words.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s212-1: Estelle lowered her head and thought seriously for a while.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s214-1: “If she really used the word ‘list,’ then this isn’t some sacred gift. It’s matching.” She raised her head. “Matching donors and recipients. If she made up excuses about where
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s214-2: the bodies came from, there would be gaps. But if she can admit that bodies are being replaced while precisely blocking off where ‘the people who aren’t on the list went’…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s215-1: She opened the notebook on her lap, but did not write anything.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s217-1: “There’s no shortage of bodies, only identities. Your parents replaced their bodies eleven years ago, taking on adult shells that looked exactly like them, even down to matching fingerprints. And they themselves can accept those bodies without the slightest misgiving, even use familial love to defend them…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s220-1: “That means they don’t think those bodies originally belonged to someone else with an independent consciousness at all. Add in the fact that they specifically select people who have just
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s220-2: reached adulthood as conspirators, and there’s really only one answer left—the young people who fail the examination, the people outside that so-called ‘list,’ are the material themselves.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s221-1: The words went into the wound that had just split open in me because of my father like a cold needle, exactly where it hurt.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s222-1: A gust of wind passed through, making the notebook pages rustle.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s224-1: “As for my most practical concern right now—”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s228-1: “If we can’t take something with us, then no matter how thoroughly we investigate it, it amounts to nothing.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s230-1: “Once we’ve figured everything out, will I still be alive to leave this village?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s232-1: “There’s still a lesson tomorrow morning. It’s late. Go back to sleep.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s233-1: We said nothing more and turned toward our quarters. After walking a dozen steps, I could not help looking back.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s234-1: The chapel’s towering shadow lay over the square. Estelle sat alone on the stone bench at the edge, the notebook open across her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s235-1: The night wind made the pages rustle. She held her pen suspended in midair for a long time. In this night laden with dangerous evidence, in the center of a village that might be under surveillance at any moment, she looked up at us, then at the chapel.
texts.chapter:v15-z03c:event:text-s236-1: In the end, she slowly capped the pen and put it into her pocket. That night, faced with immense fear, it was the first time she had retreated.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:title: Chapter Three, Supplement Three: The Stove
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s1-1:
Village Storehouse Issue Slip · Day Four (storehouse copy):
Issued: one coarse grain, half a bundle of firewood.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s3-1:
When I pushed the door open, the cold night wind carried a little ash and scattered it across my feet. It was almost ten. Most of the village had long since gone completely quiet, with only a few dim lights still burning here and there.
On the short cabinet beside the door lay the half-strip of receipt paper I had brought back with the supplies that morning.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s4-1:
My mother was sitting beside the stove. The slender needle went into the coarse cloth, then came back out, making a nearly inaudible sound. As far back as I could remember, her hands seemed to have grown into this kind of work. They had hardly ever been idle.
The half-bundle of rationed firewood we had collected that day was burning in the stove.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s5-1: I didn't hurry inside. I just stood there by the threshold.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s6-1: The needlepoint paused. She looked up.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s7-1: The two of us quietly looked at each other across those few steps of darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s8-1: I knew this room too well. The crack in the wall on the left had been made when I ran into it in mischief at seven. The old wooden table on the right always had one leg a little
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s8-2: too short, with a blackened scrap of wood wedged beneath it year-round. As soon as the thin sheet iron on the stove cooled even slightly, it made a faint clattering sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s9-1: I looked at my mother sitting in the middle of all this. Her face, in her early forties, looked somewhat haggard in the firelight, and there was already obvious gray at her temples. Everything was the same as yesterday. And everything was different.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s13-1: “You're back.” She wound the thread once around her finger.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s17-1: This time, the slender needle did not go back in.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s18-1: She pinned it to her collar, then slowly spread the half-sewn piece of cloth flat across her lap. Then she covered it with both callused hands and held perfectly still.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s19-1: She didn't ask what it was.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s20-1: I walked over and sat down on the low stool across from her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s24-1: My mother looked at me. Her eyes slowly reddened, blood vessels spreading little by little through the whites.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s29-1: “I don't know,” I said. “A person can replace their body and go on living under the same name. I don't know whether this was actually the body you had when you gave birth to me.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s30-1: She slowly stood up and gently placed the piece of cloth from her lap on the table beside her.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s32-1: “Arno,” she said, calling me by name, “I've been waiting sixteen years for you to ask that question.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s36-1: “Candidates in this village will eventually reach the age when they begin to come into contact with these things, and sooner or later someone will ask that question out loud.” She turned her head
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s36-2: and looked at the crack in the wall. “I knew a day like this would come. I just didn't know, among the children your age, whether you would be the first one unable to bear it and come ask an adult.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s38-1: She walked over to the stove and prodded the firewood inside. The flames suddenly leapt up, lighting her profile. Then she turned around again.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s40-1: “Let me answer the parts you can know for certain first,” she said. “You are indeed my child. This body.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s41-1: She slowly raised both hands and spread her palms beneath the firelight.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s43-1: “This is the one you're looking at now.” Her gaze moved from her fingerprints to me. “It was raining hard outside a little after three in the afternoon on the day you were born. Old Nona delivered you. The pain that day, the cold that day—I experienced all of it myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s45-1: “What about before that?” I pressed stubbornly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s57-1: “How long?” I stared into her eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s58-1: The firewood cracked in the stove, sending a line of sparks into the air. She watched me across the firelight.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s60-1: “Arno,” she finally said after a long time. “I'm more than a hundred and forty years old.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s62-1: More than a hundred and forty.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s63-1: The number struck the floor and made the familiar air in the room vibrate with a buzzing sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s64-1: I looked at the face of a woman in her forties before me, trying to overlap it with more than a century of time. Had she already been here when the first section of the village's inscription
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s64-2: wall was raised a hundred and thirty years ago? What about eighty years ago? How many years had this person lived before, sixteen years ago on that rainy day, she gave birth to me with this body?
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s65-1: Seeing my stiff expression, she walked back and sat down again beside the low stool.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s67-1: “I know what you're thinking. That I look like a monster, right?” she said. “That every single thing in this room is, to me, only an insignificant fragment of a long life.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s68-1: She reached out. Her fingertips traced the old wooden table, scarred by the years, and finally came to rest very lightly on its edge.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s70-1: “Sometimes I wake up suddenly in the middle of the night and feel this body, and I'm afraid too. Where this body was made, what you have to face when you change bodies…” She paused, the corners of her eyes shrinking slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s70-2: “I can't tell you. That's a rule the Inner Circle does not speak of. As long as you don't keep climbing upward—as long as you haven't obtained a seat in the Inner Circle—you should never touch it in your entire life.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s71-1: Little by little, she spread her fingers flat across the rough grain of the wood.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s73-1: “But no matter how afraid I am inside, there hasn't been a single day when I've thought of myself as someone else.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s76-1: “As for what you asked me—whether I'm still your mother.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s77-1: Her spread hand pressed hard against the tabletop.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s81-1: “These sixteen years of raising you, every callus worn into these hands, every bit of hardship this body has endured—all of it is real. If I were given another empty shell, could it take on the hardships of these sixteen years for me?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s84-1: “This afternoon I was panicking, so I went specifically to the chapel to find Sera. I was terrified—terrified that, following the way things were going, you would discover this tonight. Terrified that you would stop recognizing me.” Her eyes glistened. “I really lived through every single day of these sixteen years.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s86-1: I reached out and seized the hand she had pressed against the edge of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s87-1: It was a rough hand covered in calluses, the knuckles slightly deformed from years of work. Its warmth was still familiar. As long as she was herself, I didn't even dare—or want—to look too closely
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s87-2: into how this body had come to be. It was an intensely selfish relief. After learning that changing bodies might conceal a terrible price, all I could think was: Thank goodness. I still have my mother.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s91-1: “Mm.” She patted the back of my hand in return.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s92-1: I slowly raised my head. In the relief of having something returned to me, another black hole that had always hung in the back of my mind suddenly became painfully bright.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s96-1: For an instant, the air seemed to freeze. The hand she had placed on the table suddenly went rigid and pulled away from mine.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s99-1: There was only the crackling of the firewood in the stove. She pressed her lips tightly together and did not answer a word.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s101-1: “He left when I was seven. All these years, you kept telling me he died of a sudden illness.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s103-1: “But there isn't even a grave. If people in this village can replace their bodies and go on living, then he didn't really die of an illness, did he? Where did he go? Did he take on another identity?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s107-1: “Was he simply not eligible to change, or did he—”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s110-1: Her voice rose abruptly, sharp enough to hurt. After shouting, she seemed startled by her own loss of control and forcibly pressed her breathing back into something steady.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s111-1: The room fell silent, with only the shadows on the wall moving.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s114-1: “He wasn't assigned a turn for a body change back then.” She lowered her eyes to the hand pressed against the rough tabletop. “It was a sudden illness. Until the day he died, he never got to wait for the next assignment.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s117-1: “He wasn't assigned a turn?” I demanded, unwilling to let it go. “If he could have gone on living, what happened to his body? There has to be something behind it, doesn't there?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s120-1: “No one forced him, and there was no conspiracy. He simply didn't make it through that night. As for where his body was sent and how it was handled, that's a rule from above. I can't say.” She closed her eyes and shook her head. “Nine years ago, when he fell ill, he didn't make it. That's all.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s121-1: She sat across from the old table, both rough, callused hands tightly folded over each other. Her eyes were even redder than before, but they were completely dry. Not a single tear fell.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s123-1: “That is the only thing you need to know.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s125-1: “There isn't even a place where his ashes are buried. How am I supposed to believe you?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s128-1: She cut the conversation off hard, stood up, and walked over to take the small iron pot warming on the stove down. The sheet iron scraped with a dry sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s130-1: “You've been through too much today. You found out something enormous.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s131-1: With her back to me, she spoke softly as she prodded the coals.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s133-1: “I know you're not hungry.” She filled a bowl with clear broth and pushed it into my hands. “Have something hot. It will help settle your heart.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s134-1: I held the scalding rough porcelain bowl and lowered my head to take a large drink. The boiling broth ran down my throat and into my stomach.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s138-1: I set down the empty bowl, pushed the door open, and sat on the cold stone threshold in the yard.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s139-1: The village was exceptionally quiet at night. In the distance, the enormous White Tower stood silently in the darkness. The extremely low hum from deep within its base traveled through the soil and across the ground, transmitting without loss into the bluestone I was sitting on.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s140-1: It was nearly eleven when a burst of light footsteps suddenly came from the dark mouth of the lane.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s143-1: She came running through the moonlight and only slammed to a stop at the threshold, breathing hard. Behind her, in the darkness of night, followed a silent shadow.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s144-1: It was Estelle. As a restricted visitor whose eligibility had been revoked, she had only been allowed to move between the front hall, the visitor table, and the temporary lodging at the edge of the village these past two days. For them to have made it out of the core district at this hour, they must have slipped out during a shift change.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s146-1: “It’s late. What are you two doing out here?” I moved aside and looked at Estelle. “If the night patrol catches you—”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s148-1: “I couldn't stay there.” Yuna cut me off. Her voice sounded dry and hoarse.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s149-1: Without bothering with formalities, she sat down right beside me on the stone step. Estelle hesitated, then silently sat down on Yuna's other side.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s151-1: The three of us sat shoulder to shoulder on the narrow threshold. The night wind was cold. Yuna drew up both legs, gripped her knees tightly, and rested her chin on them.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s152-1: I looked at their pale profiles beneath the night sky. My palm was slick with cold sweat inside my pocket. What my mother had said beside the stove—the more than one hundred and forty years, the manufactured shells, the body-change assignment my father had failed to receive before his death—each thing burned
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s152-2:
against my nerves.
But I couldn't say anything. Once I spoke the terrifying answer that the Inner Circle could turn people from the outer district into new bodies, it would do nothing but plunge them into despair and panic right now. We did not yet even have the strength to protect ourselves from that enormous thing.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s154-1: “After Estelle finished saying that outside the chapel earlier, I couldn't stand what I'd been like anymore.” She hid the side of her face in shadow.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s157-1:
Yuna turned to look at me.
“What if ‘who gets to go on living’ and ‘who gets processed as material’ are really just the two sides of the same sheet of paper?”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s158-1: When she said it on the stone bench outside the chapel not long ago, I had taken it as a hypothesis blurted out in despair. But now, in this night gone cold through and through, the chill rising from my bones could no longer be suppressed.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s159-1: Yuna slowly tightened her arms around her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s161-1: “When Sera stood on the platform and promised, in her own words, ‘You’ll have this right too, someday’… my first reaction in that instant was actually happiness. I thought, Thank goodness. As long as we were both eligible, I could stay with you forever. We would never have to part.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s162-1: She paused, her voice dropping until it was almost inaudible.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s164-1: “I shouldn't have felt relieved about being eligible, not even for a moment, after hearing that Estelle had been screened out.” She stared hard at the shadow on the ground.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s165-1: I reached out and covered her cold hand with mine. It was trembling slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s166-1: Estelle had been listening quietly the whole time. She turned her head and looked at Yuna's knuckles, gone white from the pressure.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s168-1: “You don't need to feel guilty, Yuna.” She looked down at her boots, damp with the night's dew. “At a time like that, there's nothing shameful about wanting to live, wanting to stay with someone you care about. You don't owe me anything.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s169-1: Yuna said nothing. She only buried her face more deeply in the crook of her arms. The night wind grew colder. The question of the “material” weighed on the three people sitting on the threshold like a heavy piece of lead.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s172-1: I looked at the White Tower in the distance. The hum from its base refused to fade into the night.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s174-1: “Yesterday afternoon in the archive room,” I said, “Yuna said she wanted to check the files and find out why Estelle had been screened out. We saw then that the red-cloth sections had been marked as restricted-touch areas. But if…”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s177-1: “What if that guess about the material is true?” I looked at them. “What if those who fail selection really are made into some kind of ‘material’? Then we can't keep
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s177-2: looking only at personnel records in the archive room. A person can vanish from a list, but what we need to find is where large numbers of living people are being sent.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s180-1: “This morning, when I went to collect the firewood, I saw that everything moving in and out of the village storehouse had a copy kept by the storehouse. If the people above really are treating people as material, whether to make new bodies for the long-lived or for some other reason, something on that scale couldn't be completed out of
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s180-2: thin air. It would require transport and consume supplies. With physical goods moving in such quantities, there will always be one link that can't be hidden. We shouldn't investigate the people. We should investigate records that show physical consumption, like the outer-district transfer slips and unusual issues in the village storehouse.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s182-1: “Check the records…” Yuna wiped her stiff cheek with the back of her hand, her gaze slowly turning cold. “As long as there was large-scale movement and consumption, there has to be a trace.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s183-1: Yuna turned her head and looked at Estelle, who had remained silent.
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s185-1: “If we can't figure it out before the return pickup this weekend… Estelle, we don't know what you'll be facing. I can't just watch you board that return vehicle without knowing where it's headed.”
texts.chapter:v15-z03d:event:text-s186-1: Estelle looked at us and silently clenched the corner of her clothing, damp with the night's dew.
texts.chapter:volume0-outside-the-list:title: Chapter Four: Outside the List
texts.chapter:volume0-outside-the-list:event:t: Dawn had just broken, and the fog had not yet lifted. As we had agreed on the stone steps outside the night before, Yuna and I met at the entrance to the controlled archive room in the junior section.

As a restricted visitor stripped of her eligibility, Estelle could no longer enter the interior. She could only remain in the visitor reading area in the front hall. Yuna and I stood before the access gate leading to the inner shelving area.

Last night, we had agreed to look up the intake details for Estelle as “material.” But when we met, Yuna had already added three more items to the note: the allocation lists for the ten seats across the generations, the disposal rules for old bodies, and my father’s de-registration status in the civil registry.

“Scanning a badge leaves a trace in the backend,” Yuna said in a lowered voice. “We’ll avoid the red-marked restricted areas. For your father, we’ll only check the ordinary paper registers to see whether he’s there. We absolutely won’t use a terminal to query above our clearance. We need to move quickly.”
