I nodded. We passed through the access gate and entered the dimly lit controlled shelving area. Estelle sat down beside a reading table in the front hall and waited quietly.

To avoid crossing the line, we silently agreed to steer clear of the restricted shelves deep in the room, marked with red danger signs. Without the help of a search terminal, we had to search blindly among rows of

wooden shelves that rose to the ceiling. At first, we tried following the labels for “Logistics” and “Materials Intake” to find traces of Estelle as material, but found nothing. In the end, Yuna changed tactics.

We went back through the dusty paper-card cabinets, following labels for “Asset Write-Off” and “Depreciation” to narrow down several rough divisions, then slipped into the cold-smelling aisles. For more than an hour,

we dug through miscellaneous records from across the years beneath thick layers of dust. Several times, Yuna’s fingers hovered before red-marked storage slots, but each time she forced herself to pull them back.
In the bottom slots of the second row, where the dust was thickest, beneath a label reading “Material Depreciation,” Yuna pulled out a dark-blue volume: The Carrier Allocation Sequence.
This ledger, which should have recorded inanimate objects, conspicuously recorded the body-transfer batches of members of the Church’s Inner Circle.

Position｜Duty｜Current Name｜Previous Allocation｜Scheduled This Time｜Basis for Ordering
One｜Practical Operations｜Nona｜Fourteen years ago｜TBD｜—
Two｜Knowledge Archives｜Barrow｜Forty-three years ago｜TBD｜—
Three｜Resource Allocation｜Otto｜Thirty-five years ago｜TBD｜—
Four｜Candidate

Selection｜Sera｜Nine years ago｜TBD｜—
……
Ten｜(omitted)｜(omitted)｜Twenty-seven years ago｜TBD｜—
Deactivated Numbers｜Eleven, fourteen, seventeen (struck through)
Note: The Basis for Ordering column has not been filled in since the eleventh revision. The original entries are stored separately.

“These are the ten active seats.” Yuna’s finger moved across the page. “But the intervals between body transfers are completely inconsistent. Barrow’s was forty-three years ago; Sera’s was nine years ago. This isn’t a queue arranged by any fixed interval. And…”

The “Basis for Ordering” column had been cleared outright, leaving only a cold, hard line. The crossed-out numbers eleven, fourteen, and seventeen at the bottom meant that this register had once contained more seats.
The second thing was The Asset Management Register, found in the back half of the same slot. Under “Level Three: Special-Control Assets,” it contained a single line:

Inner Circle Active Carriers (full complement: ten seats): Special-Control Assets. Ownership belongs to the Church. In the event of aging, the old asset must be surrendered according to the allocation sequence in exchange for a new asset.
Note: After the old body is surrendered and written off, no tracking record will be maintained.
“‘Ownership belongs to the Church’…” Yuna’s finger hovered over the line. “They don’t even own their own bodies.”
I looked at the words “full complement: ten seats.” These past few days, we had assumed that being assigned to “First Seat Operations” or “Second Seat Procedures” meant competing for a
seat left vacant by death. But the Inner Circle had no vacancies at all. The so-called candidates were only selecting the next batch of spare parts for those already occupying the seats.

When they wore out, they were surrendered. As for where the discarded old bodies went, this register offered no explanation. At that moment, the archive room’s cold smell seemed to grow slightly viscous. The ten seats worshipped by everyone were, in the system’s underlying ledger, nothing more than parts waiting in line to be depreciated.
Yuna silently turned the register back to its first page. A document number was printed there: CL-02-0045.
“The CL prefix for Civil Logistics.” Yuna looked at the number. “It’s in the same classification sequence as the headers on the materials lists Watermarsh issues
every day. In the Church’s eyes, Inner Circle body transfers aren’t some taboo that needs to be sealed behind red markings. They’re ordinary asset management.”

“But the old bodies’ destination has been cut off.” She closed the register and looked at us in the darkness. “If they put the discarded bodies back into ordinary parishes as some kind of ‘material,’ then the civil

logistics system would have a weight that appeared out of nowhere. To balance the books, the bureaucracy would have to fabricate an intake record for this batch of ‘material.’ Come on. Let’s check the files in the

ordinary archive outside. Estelle is about to be ‘repatriated.’ We need to find which materials shipment her body will be entered into next, and that means finding the index number for the file under her name first.”
We left the controlled area and went to the ordinary miscellaneous section inside the access gate, where we found a brick-thick volume on the bottom shelf: the Parish Residents’ Register.

The register included the storage location of each person’s file. Using Estelle’s civil number, Yuna found the index number for the file under her name and copied it onto a sheet of paper. Then I drew a deep breath and searched downward through the alphabetical index.

Yuna’s hand pressed against the edge of the page. Rena’s name was right there. Last night, she had admitted herself that she was more than a hundred and forty years old and had changed bodies once. If we followed the trail, the record of that transfer might be in the file indicated by this register.
I looked at the name, then turned the page. The secrets of the living could wait. Some things could not. I continued turning the pages in alphabetical order and found my father’s name.
But where his name should have been, the entire section of paper containing his life record had been cut away by hand, leaving an unnaturally glaring break in the page.

This was more than a missing file. If he had died of ordinary illness, there would at least have been a de-registration record, or a stamp reading ‘DEATH.’ But there was nothing here. The part that should have proved he had existed within this system had been dug out along with the paper.
To find out where the rest of his records had gone, I took out my badge and walked toward the search terminal in this section.

Yuna seized my wrist. “No.” She lowered her voice. “This has red-mark restrictions. If you exceed your clearance, the system will not only automatically record the access source; it will also report your badge number to the Central Inspection Team.”

But all I could think about were the edges of paper cut apart by a blade. In this system, where a badge controlled everyone’s life and death, every trace that my father had truly lived had been erased, leaving behind only a hollow name.

I pulled free of her grip. A voice in my head told me what this would lead to, but I could not stop. Only here could I see whether he had been assigned a new body before his de-registration, or transferred somewhere else. I scanned my badge and entered the name in the search field.
A cold line of text flashed across the screen: 【Search anomaly. This person’s record is frozen. Current clearance insufficient.】
And it did not stop there. After flashing for two seconds, the terminal’s indicator light turned directly to warning yellow.
【Logging anomalous access source: entering session initiator’s badge number……】
Yuna slammed the terminal’s physical cutoff switch, forcibly interrupting the session. Her face had gone deathly pale. The screen flickered once, then went black.

“It’s no use. The moment the yellow light came on, it had already reported it.” She stared at the black screen, her chest heaving. “The inspectors will come tomorrow morning and use the logs to find out who exceeded their clearance.”

I stepped back to where I had been, running my fingers once more along the torn edge of the page in the register. The edge was rough. When he died nine years ago, I was only seven. The adults took away his

body. There was no gravestone, and no ashes. Throughout all the years I was growing up, Mother had always vaguely said that he had fallen ill and failed to make the body transfer that had originally been

scheduled. I had believed her. But these pages cut away by a blade, and that glaring word “frozen,” told me that what had happened here was far more than simply “not waiting long enough for a body transfer.”
Yuna did not hurry me. She only stood beside me, quietly looking at the ruined page. At last, she slowly reached out and placed her hand over the back of mine.
“Arno.” She looked at me, her voice very soft, but with enough force to pull me back. “Deal with what’s in front of us first. Estelle’s still outside waiting for you to get her index number.”
I closed my eyes and drew a deep breath of the archive room’s cold air. I did not answer her. I simply closed the register and turned around.

Carrying the copied index number, we passed back through the access gate into the front hall. Estelle was waiting at the visitor terminal. She saw that something was wrong with my expression. Her gaze paused between Yuna and me for a moment, but she asked nothing.
“We found your index number. But something went wrong inside.” I handed her the note. “My badge clearance may have been downgraded or flagged. Use your visitor interface to search.”
Estelle entered her civil number and tried to follow the route Yuna had just indicated to trace where the file would go.

Two index records appeared on the screen.
The first: 【Capability Evaluation (Candidate Program): Below Standard】. Status: Returned.
The second: 【Special Investigation Risk Alert】. Status: Core Restricted Area access only. External access denied.
Estelle stared at the two lines on the screen. They were the final verdict that had closed the book on the first fifteen years of her life.
“Sera’s public reason was that my ‘candidate capabilities were below standard.’ So there really are two things here.” She looked at the words “Special Investigation Risk Alert,” her
voice hard. “My capability evaluation was only ‘returned.’ That meant losing candidate eligibility, but it wasn’t enough for them to put me on the earliest return freight vehicle.”

“That ‘Special Investigation Risk Alert’ locked inside the restricted area is the reason they’re in such a hurry to send you away,” Yuna said quietly. “Special investigation risk… They weren’t evaluating your capabilities at all. They were evaluating how dangerous it would be if you remained as material.”
Just then, the indicator on the visitor terminal in the front hall, which had been glowing green, suddenly flickered without warning and turned yellow.
A system notice appeared in the corner of the screen:

【Warning: An unresolved unauthorized access record has been detected on an Inner Circle search terminal in this area (initiator: Arno). All online visitor terminals in this area will be forcibly linked to the unauthorized session……】
There was no shrill alarm, only the continuously flashing yellow light and the synchronization progress bar flickering across the screen.

“It’s imposing collective liability through the search permissions!” Yuna suddenly pressed the master power switch behind the terminal. With a sharp click, she forcibly cut the power. “Don’t let it capture Estelle’s number!”
The screen went black instantly. The front hall fell silent again. But one second before the power was cut, the network indicator on top of the terminal had still turned green.
“Too late. The linkage request has already been sent.” Yuna watched the green light slowly fade. “Whether or not it got Estelle’s number, the anomalous query from Arno’s badge has already triggered
the red mark. The system will automatically report the unauthorized session to the Central Inspection Team. Once the inspectors find an anomalous reconnection to this area tomorrow morning…”

Estelle stared fixedly at the black screen. She did not step away at once.
“Watermarsh’s autumn harvest won’t last through the winter. I want to enter the White Tower. I want a seat. And I need the technology and material quotas they have. She turned and looked at the

access gate leading to the Core Archive Division. “If the so-called risk is that they’ll send me back as dangerous material as quickly as possible, then I need to know what exactly was written in that alert. Even if I go back, I need to bring back more than I had before.”

She looked at us.
“The elders on duty are all upstairs during the day. Now that the red light has come on, we absolutely can’t touch this ordinary search system again. Once the inspectors

investigate the uploaded record tomorrow morning, we won’t even be able to enter this area. We have only one chance left: physically infiltrating the Core Archive Division in the middle of the night.”

Yuna did not object. She only turned to look at me. We both understood our situation clearly: the forced query of my father’s file had already been caught by the system. Once the inspection began tomorrow morning, our unauthorized activity in the archive room would be exposed in full, and the candidate evaluation of these past few days would be terminated along with it.
Under the fading afterimage of the still-flashing yellow light, Yuna tightened her grip on the strap of her shoulder bag.

“We need to redo the route.” She drew a deep breath, her voice pulled taut. “The access controls for the Core Archive Division are much stricter than these. We can’t rely on a nighttime break-in alone. We need to think of another way.”
I put the badge flagged by the system into my pocket. The rough sensation of the torn page’s edge seemed to remain on my fingers. I looked at her and nodded.
“Let’s go.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:title: Appendix to Chapter Four: General Index
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s1-1:
Controlled Archives · Candidate and Personnel Index (copied from the front page of the volume):
I. This index contains files on candidates from every term and files subject to special restrictions by the Church.
II. Once an entry has been assigned a number, that number shall not be changed by subsequent
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s1-2:
events.
III. Anything not entered is not in this index.

(A line was added beneath the third clause, then crossed out. The ink of the crossing-out is newer than the main text, and pressed down hard; four characters can still faintly be made out through the scratches: entered in another register.)
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s3-1: The archives wing was dead silent in the night.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s4-1: Estelle’s words that afternoon—“Come tonight”—had ultimately fallen to Yuna and me. She had wanted to come with us at dusk, but Yuna had stopped her with grim determination—the unauthorized query during the day had triggered an alarm, making the identity of an
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s4-2: eliminated external candidate extremely sensitive. Yuna said the patrol dogs could easily distinguish the scent trails left by clothing from those left by a living person, and Estelle was the only person from Watermarsh to have entered the Inner Circle in the past
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s4-3: few days. If the dog followed her footprints and started barking, it would amount to placing direct evidence of “infiltration from the outer settlements” into the White Tower’s hands. She could only remain in the temporary house at the east end of the village.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s5-1: We lay low in the cold back courtyard for two full hours. Yuna had calculated the timing during the day: midnight exactly. The night-shift guards would change over then, and the gray patrol dog would be led to inspect another
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s5-2: street. But this night seemed different. The priest taking over stayed by the back door with his lantern for another fifteen minutes, and Yuna held my head firmly against the dirt until the faint halo of light finally moved away.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s6-1: Less than six hours remained before the inspectors restarted the power in the morning and arrived to examine the site with the day’s unauthorized-query alarm.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s7-1: After confirming that the night patrol priest carrying a lantern had followed his fixed route away, Yuna climbed the high wall through the dead angle cast by the great bell tower. She had noticed an exhaust vent left behind from a period of repairs. Its
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s7-2: outer louver had already come loose. Using the paper knife she carried, she pried up the rusted clasps bit by bit, afraid of making even the slightest shrill scrape of metal. Once the cover was removed, we squeezed one after another into the dust-filled duct.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s8-1: The immense silence pressed down above our heads. By the time I crawled out through the vent, I was covered in cold sweat. We landed between rows of wooden cabinets reaching up to the ceiling—the deep archives. According to what the terminal
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s8-2: had displayed during the day, both the ordinary basic database and the specially controlled files restricted to the core zone were housed in this sealed physical space. Even the air carried the stale smell of paper and preservatives.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s10-1:
A heavy black Candidate and Personnel Index sat on the long table, almost painful to handle. Yuna opened it and followed the alphabetical order until she found Estelle’s name.
After the name was a string of filing numbers for ordinary files, along with the corresponding physical location: third row, second slot.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s11-1: That was precisely the physical file we had not been authorized to touch during the lawful search that afternoon.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s14-1:
Yuna walked to that row of wooden shelves and looked into the shadows at the back.
A red strip of cloth bearing the Church emblem barred the compartments, its two ends fixed beneath thick wax seals. A thin layer of dust had settled over the cloth.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s17-1: “She said, when she left, that she wanted to see with her own eyes what had eliminated her.” Yuna’s voice was quiet, but hard. “What they announced this afternoon wasn’t enough. She needs the actual scores, and every word they wrote in the risk attachment.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s19-1: “This is how they enforce that line of theirs: ‘Touch it and it’s reported.’” I looked at the dust. “As soon as the original is pulled out, it will leave a trace. The routine inspection tomorrow morning will definitely find it.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s21-1: “Even if the boundary guards come knocking on our doors the moment dawn breaks tomorrow, this is what we owe her now.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s26-1: Holding her breath, Yuna avoided the red cloth and drew a thin procedural file out through the gap above, extremely slowly. A few grains of dust fell softly onto the red cloth, unnervingly conspicuous in the shadows.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s27-1:
Yuna took a small flashlight from her pocket and covered most of the lamp with her hand, leaving only an extremely narrow halo of light.
We opened it in the dim light.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s28-1: The first page was the basic registration.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s32-1: The second page was the annual assessments. From the year she entered the preparatory academy onward, there was one line per year, each followed by an extremely concise evaluation.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s33-1: Yuna’s finger hovered in the air, tracing down the writing. From the shadows in the corner came an almost imperceptible buzzing—the sound of the exhaust fan turning in the deep of night.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s34-1: Five and a half hours remained before the power was restarted in the morning.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s36-1: “‘Stable memory.’ ‘Strong procedural awareness.’ ‘Able to revise judgments after correction.’” she read softly.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s37-1: Her finger stopped at the note from a year ago.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s43-1: “That’s the highest compliment there is.” She looked at those few words. “Whoever wrote that knew exactly what they were doing.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s46-1: The third page was the summary of this round’s Phase One assessment.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s47-1:
There were seven assessment dimensions: “Logical Reasoning,” “Psychological Pressure Tolerance,” “Instruction Compliance” … each followed by a precise number. All were scored out of 100.
The three people’s numbers were arranged in parallel columns. Mine, Yuna’s, Estelle’s.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s48-1: My eyes went involuntarily to my own column first. Logical Reasoning, 72. Psychological Pressure Tolerance, 68. Instruction Compliance, 75 … I had not exceeded 80 in a single one of the seven
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s48-2:
items, and my total was only 512, still well short of the usual passing requirement of 560. Dead last, without suspense.
Yet in the classroom announcement three days ago, I had been ranked first.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s49-1:
The numbers in the other two columns were astonishingly high. Yuna had scored a perfect 100 in three items, and 95 in two. Her total was 640.
Estelle’s scores were
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s49-2: exceptionally even: Logical Reasoning, 96; Psychological Pressure Tolerance, 98; Instruction Compliance, 95. None of her scores was below 85. Her total was 644.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s54-1:
At the very bottom of the score sheet, a conclusion had been written in the blank space:
“Additional Risk Determination: See Special-Control Zone Risk File R-409.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s55-1: Beside the filing date was a seal indicating that the registration had come from Sera, but pointing elsewhere. Beneath the signature was a line of small print: “Phase One Procedural Assessment Entered
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s55-2: in Register: 18:30, Three Days Ago.” That was the time it had been entered, one and a half hours after the classroom formally announced that Yuna’s eligibility had been retained on the second day.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s58-1:
Yuna turned around. On the other side of the archives was a row of gray metal cabinets used specifically for files under special restriction. These drawers likewise had only catches to prevent accidental opening, not keyholes.
In the corresponding drawer, we found the complete file numbered R-409.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s61-1:
At the top of the first page, the title was printed in bold: Supplementary Opinion on Candidate Political Risk.
Apart from the conclusion, it also recorded the detailed reasons:
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s62-1: “2. After completing all examinations, this term’s candidate will continue to obtain permissions involving governance of the core … Should an external candidate obtain such permissions and subsequently be interrupted for any reason, her return to the outer settlements will constitute
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s62-2:
an ongoing risk, and that risk cannot be eliminated through procedural means.”
“3. Under equivalent circumstances, the risk posed by an internally born candidate is controllable, because her social relationships, material foundations, and future eligibility all lie within the village.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s63-1:
Otto’s name was signed at the bottom. Beside it was a deep-red seal representing the Ten Seats’ authority to veto internal political reviews. Under the Church’s rules, that seal carried the power of a single veto.
And above the seal was a clearly marked signing date: “11:45, Three Days Ago.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s64-1:
Yuna stared fixedly at the date. Three days ago at noon, she had still been anxiously waiting to see whether she might be eliminated. She suddenly clenched the edge of the pages.
She did not return either file to its original place. Instead, she stacked them together and shoved them straight inside her coat.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s66-1: “The dust on the shelf has already been disturbed. If the originals disappear too, the risk of discovery is too high.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s68-1: “She has the right to see the scores of the three of us clearly with her own eyes.” Yuna zipped up her coat. “Go.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s72-1:
Once we crawled out through the vent, Yuna loosely fastened the louvered cover back against the wall as it had been.
Moving through the village with two originals was entirely different from sneaking in empty-handed. Every bark from the patrol
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s72-2: dogs seemed to explode directly against my scalp. When a night patrol priest passed the intersection with his lantern, and its beam swept across the stone wall where we were hiding, Yuna pressed both hands tightly over her coat pocket, afraid
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s72-3:
the pages might make even the slightest sound.
Using the cover of the night fog, we ran along the outer wall of the preparatory district until we crossed the little square and reached the east end of the village in one breathless sprint.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s75-1: The temporary house for external candidates at the east end of the village had no lights on. By the faint moonlight coming through the window, I saw Estelle sitting beside the bed, her luggage already packed at her feet. She raised her head when she heard us push open the door.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s76-1: Yuna went over and locked the door from the inside. She took out the small flashlight, switched it on, and covered most of the light with the back of her hand before slapping the two originals from the deep archives down on the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s78-1: “These are the actual itemized scores, and the full text of R-409, the file that eliminated you.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s79-1:
Estelle walked to the table and opened the file in the small pool of flashlight light.
She looked at the three-column score summary, her gaze stopping over the three sets of numbers.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s80-1: “512 points. You’re first.” Estelle looked up at me, then turned to Yuna. “640 points. Your eligibility was retained.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s81-1:
Then she opened the gray R-409.
Her gaze passed over the lines explicitly stating that “internal social relationships are controllable,” and finally settled on the date beneath Otto’s signature.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s85-1:
“Three days ago. 11:45.”
She read the date aloud.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s87-1: “The procedural assessment was entered in the register at 18:30 three days ago.” Estelle’s voice was unnervingly calm. “That means the risk veto had already taken effect before the elder responsible for the procedural assessment
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s87-2: entered the final score summary. My scores had already been voided at noon on the day of the assessment, but when they made the announcement in the classroom at five that afternoon, they never mentioned this supplementary file.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s90-1: I looked at the date beneath that signature, three days ago at noon. 512 points, dead last without suspense. I had always thought this assessment was measuring me, but the veto’s red seal, stamped long beforehand, and the fact that I had smoothly entered the more central first seat left my stomach feeling
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s90-2: as though it were packed with cold gravel. My father had never let me enter the White Tower district, yet his file had been frozen deep inside it. And now I was standing here too. I felt that I had not won within this mechanism, but had been treated as some kind of usable material and selected in advance.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s91-1: Yuna stared at the page filled with numbers.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s95-1: “I told you during the day …” Yuna’s voice was trembling, her eyes full of anger. “I thought that, at least in the end, this system would calculate clearly who deserved to stay. I thought that even if the result was eliminating me, I could accept it as the judgment of the rules.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s96-1: She pointed at the three columns of numbers on the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s98-1: “Now look. I didn’t even beat you.” She looked at Estelle and pulled the corner of her mouth into a self-mocking smile. “And Arno is ranked first without even needing a passing total. Second place … I used to think that was my qualification, my right to remain in the Inner Circle, to remain …”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s99-1: She did not finish. She only looked at me.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s100-1: Yuna pressed her finger hard against the page, the tip bloodless.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s102-1: “‘Deserving it’ was never on their game table in the first place.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s108-1:
Estelle’s hands remained on the two originals for a long time. Her fingers pressed against the numbers in her own column on the score sheet, her knuckles faintly white with the effort. Her breathing was somewhat heavier than usual.
That afternoon in the reading room, she had said she would take
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s108-2: a conclusion in black and white back with her. This file, bearing an anti-counterfeiting seal and detailed scores, was more than a conclusion. It was hard evidence. It was what she had earned through ten years of flawless performance, spread out on a rough wooden table in the middle of the night.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s109-1: But slowly, she let go. She closed her eyes and drew a deep breath, as though forcing something on the verge of breaking back into her chest.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s111-1: “When you brought them out, you disturbed the dust on the red cloth, didn’t you?” When she opened her eyes again, the slight fluctuation in her voice had disappeared. She looked up at Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s112-1: Yuna bit her lip and nodded.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s114-1: “That is the White Tower’s red-seal boundary. If the report of the missing originals is filed tomorrow, this won’t be unauthorized reading. It will be theft.” Estelle’s fingers tapped slowly against the table. “The White Tower is only missing a
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s114-2: reason to enter Watermarsh. Once the originals are gone, together with the unauthorized-query alarm from the terminal today, they can isolate me directly under the pretext of containing a risk. I can’t sacrifice the settlement for these two files.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s116-1: “Even if you only copied one and took it back?”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s118-1: “A handwritten copy is useless, Yuna. Without the red seal representing authority over risk vetoes, they can accuse us of spreading false claims with a single sentence. But I’ll remember every number on these pages.” Estelle closed the two files and pushed them back toward Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s120-1: “Put them back. Before dawn. As long as the originals are still in the cabinet and nothing has actually gone missing, they can only investigate this as an internal disciplinary violation. Without the grave charge of theft, the elders’ council has no excuse to immediately make an issue of the outer settlements.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s122-1: “What about you? Are you going to go back alone, empty-handed, and let them think you were merely an unsuccessful candidate who lacked the ability?”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s124-1: “Even if I proved that I wasn’t inferior, what would that change?” She lifted the strap of her luggage, her gaze falling on the two pages that had shut her out. “It would only show that here, an outsider will always come after an internal option. But I won’t treat my failure as a private defeat. If the
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s124-2: originals inside can’t be taken out, I’ll go to the outer settlements and look for something else: irregularities in supply quotas, the whereabouts of past external candidates, or accounts showing that Watermarsh was shorted. I’ll find public evidence that can prove the injustice without needing a red seal.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04b:event:text-s125-1: Yuna shoved the two originals back inside her coat and zipped it up. The second hand on the wall clock ticked on. It was almost two. Only four hours remained before the power was turned on in the morning.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:title: Chapter Four, Appendix Two: A Place to Stay
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s1-1: On the sixth day of the candidate period, before dawn, dense fog locked the Central Village in place.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s2-1: Using the dead angle cast by the great bell tower, we climbed back into the controlled archives through the abandoned ventilation outlet. We had to return the two files borrowed over the past night before the routine inspection began at dawn. Yesterday’s forced power outage had already put us on the edge of being watched.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s3-1: There was only the faintest light in the archives beneath the ventilation outlet. Yuna carefully closed Estelle’s grade file and pushed it back into the wooden slot behind the red cloth strip.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s3-2: Then she turned toward the gray metal cabinet on the other side. She opened the drawer marked with an “R” and prepared to put back the Political Risk Supplementary Opinion on Candidates.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s4-1: But before she pushed it all the way into the drawer, she stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s5-1: Yuna was about to slide the kraft-paper envelope back into place when she noticed that two unbound sheets of thin paper had been stuffed into the gap that originally belonged to the envelope.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s6-1: “When we pulled the envelope out just now, the space underneath was definitely empty,” she said in a lowered voice. “Someone calculated that we would come back to return the files sometime during the past half-night and deliberately left these archive stubs underneath.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s7-1: She pulled out a short piece of charcoal and a blank form, then pressed them against the metal cabinet door in the faint light before dawn. At the bottom of both stubs was a dark red “internal cc” stamp, with the routing marked beneath it: specially approved sedatives and peripheral transport.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s8-1: Yuna skimmed the writing on the fronts of the stubs, her expression shifting slightly, and copied it onto the form.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s9-1: When she was done, she stuffed the two loose sheets deliberately left behind into the drawer, then pushed in the kraft-paper envelope and pressed it flat with force.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s10-1: “The original is back in place.” She looked at the outer edge of the metal cabinet. “And whoever left those papers for us already knows we came here—the dust along the edge was disturbed.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s11-1: “The morning inspection won’t measure the dust too. As long as the original is still in the cabinet, there’s no evidence to classify it as stolen,” I said.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s12-1: She nodded and drew a deep breath.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s13-1: “Come on. Let’s take what we copied to Estelle.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s15-1: When we left the corridor on the north side of the chapel and circled back to the main entrance, the rising sun had just cleared the White Tower. Its glare made it hard to keep our eyes open.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s16-1:
A new notice had been posted outside the records room:
Restricted Visitor · Stage Access (subject to review before the end-of-week review):
Permitted: the chapel front hall, temporary borrowed houses, reading tables in the
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s16-2:
outer ring.
Prohibited: the teaching area, controlled archives, all levels of the White Tower.
Note: All restricted visitors will be sent back after the end-of-week review. No one may lend materials on another person’s behalf.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s17-1: Estelle sat on a stone bench in the corner of the front hall. To avoid looking too conspicuous, she kept her head lowered and patiently rewound a hemp-fiber strap whose end had frayed. It was used for tying luggage. Inner Circle members passing by occasionally glanced her way, but all of them deliberately looked away.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s18-1: We walked up to her. Yuna used her body to block any eyes that might turn toward us and handed over the folded sheet.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s19-1: Estelle did not take it immediately. First she pinned the strap beneath her thigh and rubbed her palms hard against the coarse fabric of her trouser legs. Only then did she accept it carefully.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s20-1: “I copied this from beneath the risk-assessment attachment,” I said.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s21-1: She looked at the two entries on the form:
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s22-1:
“Four days ago, high-dose sedative issuance record: sent to temporary storage points along the route toward Watermarsh, for the reclamation and long-term transport under restraint of peripheral irregulars.”
“Attached cancellation list: includes three people, among them former name
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s22-2: Sarah (female, 22). Having fallen below the baseline due to failure to meet evaluation standards, their identities were erased from the date of cancellation. Classified as live human products produced in this batch, they were assigned as cargo numbers 42, 43, and 44, awaiting receipt.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s23-1: Estelle’s eyes remained on those two lines for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s24-1: “Sarah…” Her voice was very low. “Those of us from our batch assigned to Watermarsh were numbered according to our evaluation rankings at the time. I was the stupidest, at the bottom in position
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s24-2: 45. She was number 42. She slept in the bunk above mine, and every morning she would braid my hair for me. She did that through all three years, even when we couldn’t get enough to eat.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s25-1: “When we were fifteen, the person leading the Watermarsh group sent her away, saying she was slow with her hands and feet and would work somewhere else. On the day she left, she put half a corn cake under my pillow.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s25-2: Estelle looked at the new designation where her name had been erased, her eyes reddening and her fingers trembling slightly. “She didn’t go somewhere else, did she? She was cancelled as number 42. And 43 and 44 were too.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s26-1: She raised her head, her vacant gaze passing over us. Yuna and I looked at each other, and neither of us interrupted the brief dead silence. To this immense system, stripping a living person of their name meant nothing more than replacing it with a two-digit code convenient for transport.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s27-1: “I’m the forty-fifth person from that batch, and the last one who hasn’t been cancelled.” Estelle drew a deep breath, forced her gaze away from the name, and refocused on the objective record on the form.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s28-1: “The medication order issued four days ago says it was for long-distance transport under restraint…” She pointed to the final half-line. “From Watermarsh to the Central Village, it only takes three
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s28-2: hours along the water route after passing the boundary marker. If they needed to give them high-dose sedatives and still took four days, that means this convoy didn’t come here directly from Watermarsh.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s29-1: “This medication was probably sent out with some large convoy as supplies for transport under restraint.” Yuna quickly followed her reasoning. “They picked people up in settlements along the route, then detoured back to the nearest Watermarsh when they were done, using Watermarsh as the final stop on the transport circuit?”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s30-1: “Before I came to the Central Village, I spent three years as a registrar at the Watermarsh distribution station. I handled the master ledgers for supplies sent to all the peripheral settlements.” She gripped the hemp strap
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s30-2: in her hand, her voice gradually returning to its calmness. “Road allocations to the periphery are locked. Fuel consumption, access credentials, and the checkpoint gates are all constrained by the quotas in the master ledger.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s31-1: “So they couldn’t send several transport vehicles out onto the roads for no reason. The fuel consumption wouldn’t match,” Yuna said.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s32-1: “If they wanted to transport the cancelled people back here, they could only hide them inside this official supply convoy taking the long loop.” Estelle handed the form back to Yuna. “And people breathe. They need sedatives, and room has to be left
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s32-2: for them to move. When a vehicle carrying living people passed through Watermarsh, its cargo volume had to be larger than that needed for the same weight of grain. Only the public logistics records from these three days contain clear load assignments.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s33-1: “Even if they didn’t bring them into the village, but unloaded them at a concealed transfer point near the outskirts of the Central Village,” Estelle stood and pointed toward the area beyond the records-room wall, “the vehicle serving as cover would still have to return to the Central Village logistics hub and report in.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s34-1: “As long as I can see the public schedule and check which long-route vehicle left Watermarsh on its return with an unreasonable amount of empty volume and unloading time, I can identify the suspect vehicle.” She retied
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s34-2: the luggage strap. “Once we know which vehicle it is, we can examine the hidden vents beneath the cargo compartment at night and look for scratches around the latches. Then we’ll know whether it really carried people.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s35-1: “But your terminal access has already been suspended. You can’t get into the hub,” I said.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s36-1: “A handwritten paper backup of the schedule is posted on the outer-ring noticeboard every day at noon.” Estelle turned her head. “Right now, I’m only allowed to stay in the front hall and at the outer-ring reading tables. That’s the only place I can see it.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s40-1: He stood at the edge of the front hall, tall, broad-shouldered, and rigidly upright. His iron-gray short hair and matching cat ears were groomed without a stray hair. There was not a single unnecessary crease in his uniform. When he saw us approach, he indicated the two wooden chairs beside him with his chin.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s43-1: “During the day yesterday, the system logs recorded not only the command you issued to query restricted-control data beyond your level, but also another record of a terminal being forcibly shut down—right when the restricted
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s43-2: badge came close enough to trigger the alarm.” His procedurally imposing voice echoed through the front hall. “By this morning, the routine inspection had found that the dust in the deep archive section had been disturbed.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s44-1: He stared at us. Estelle remained seated to one side, gripping the luggage strap without saying anything.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s45-1: “The physical break-in must have happened later than the daytime terminal record. You crossed sections.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s46-1: Yuna pressed her lips together and did not argue.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s47-1: As he spoke, he calmly took out a folded sheet and opened it. It was a standard form, most of its blank spaces already filled.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s48-1: “But the original hasn’t gone missing.” He tapped the page with a firm finger. “Since the material is still there, this matter will be classified together with the terminal violation. This is a formal disciplinary violation confirmation, putting your transgression into writing.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s49-1: The substance of it was only one sentence: “Accessing materials beyond the scope granted for the current stage.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s50-1: The document before me forcibly combined the nighttime physical break-in with the daytime unauthorized query. I did not respond. He had pressed the risk of the break-in into an ordinary violation record. Since the theft had not been reported, the line that would trigger immediate repatriation had not been crossed.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s51-1: We signed our names without hesitation.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s52-1: He put the signed sheet into his inner pocket.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s53-1: “Here’s a reminder for you.” He pulled out a copy bearing the marks of the carbon paper and pushed it in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s54-1: “As an elder, I can tell you something everyone should know. One formal violation does not directly suspend an Inner Circle candidate’s eligibility. To suspend it, you need three joint signatures.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s55-1: “Then why could you reject Estelle’s eligibility outright just by writing a risk assessment yourself?” Yuna asked sharply.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s56-1: “Because she’s from the periphery.” Otto looked at her without expression. “For a peripheral candidate’s risk assessment, the elder responsible for the evaluation effectively holds veto power. Once I determine that she has failed, the Inner Circle’s countersignature becomes nothing more than a public procedure that cannot
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s56-2: be challenged. But the procedure is different for you. After two violations, you’ll only be watched by a designated person. If there are three, the joint-signature process will be triggered automatically. But joint signatures do not mean automatic removal. The cliff is at your feet, but there’s still room to maneuver.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s57-1: He stood. When he reached the front-hall door, he stopped with his back to us.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s58-1: “You must be wondering why the list yesterday said ‘thirty-five years ago’ beside my name, but why here…” He pointed toward the archives deeper in the front hall, which were not open to restricted visitors.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s59-1: I raised my head in surprise. According to what I remembered from yesterday morning, we had only looked through the Carrier Allocation Sequence on the ordinary physical shelf, avoiding the red-marked restricted area. And because we had consulted the physical copy directly, there should have been no terminal search record. How did he know?
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s60-1: “In the second row, fourth slot of the primary section, where the ordinary registers are kept, the dust line along the outer edge of the shelf was broken. Once you went in, there was no way you didn’t look through that ledger.” He paused. “But only people with
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s60-2: higher clearance know that the sealed previous edition of the red-backed ledger records my last allocation as having taken place sixty-one years ago. In other words, the Church believes that sixty-one years ago, I had already received the new carrier assigned to me.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s61-1: He turned and pointed to his chest.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s62-1: “But this carrier of mine is only forty-eight years old.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s63-1: A dry hatred showed through in his voice.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s64-1: “Between the roster’s record from sixty-one years ago saying that I received a carrier and my accepting this body, which was only thirteen years old at the time, thirty-five years
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s64-2: ago… there is a long gap spanning the previous allocation and the later actual receipt. Where did the carrier that should have belonged to me, the one assigned under my name, go?”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s65-1: He reached out and pushed open one half of the heavy wooden door.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s66-1: “The person who crossed over me, crossed over everyone, and inserted himself into the line…” He turned back. “It isn’t only you two. I want to know who he is too.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s67-1: The door opened, and he walked out. Only the dull echo of the wooden door closing remained in the chapel front hall.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s68-1: “Why… would he hand this gap over to us?” Yuna turned her head after the sound of his footsteps had disappeared completely, her voice very low.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s69-1: “Because he wants to know who crossed over him, but he doesn’t dare investigate the red-backed ledger that isn’t included in his clearance.” I looked at the copy of the violation confirmation left on the table,
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s69-2: the sheet that reduced the break-in to an ordinary terminal violation. Now, the price of this temporary alliance was printed clearly on it. We had to explore the abyss he himself did not dare to search directly.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s71-1: Near evening, we accompanied Estelle to the reading tables outside the front hall. The backup of the public logistics schedule posted at noon had been pinned to a pillar.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s72-1: Estelle’s eyes moved rapidly across the schedule. Her finger calculated the returning vehicles’ load weights and travel times above the page.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s73-1: “Tomorrow morning, three heavy supply vehicles that have just completed a long route will leave the Central Village from the peripheral distribution station and set out again.” Estelle turned and
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s73-2: pointed to a line on the form. “But the schedule shows that when these three vehicles entered the village from the direction of Watermarsh to report in yesterday evening, two of them arrived three hours
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s73-3: later than the other. There are no border inspections along this stretch of the water route, and the convoy has no repair record. The road conditions couldn’t have swallowed three hours for no reason.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s74-1: “So during those three hours, they ran into loading delays, or left the main road to unload something?” Yuna looked at the form. “Then they set out again and came to the logistics hub to hand over the shipment.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s75-1: “They’re the two most suspicious vehicles now.” Estelle lowered her voice. “As long as we can reach their undercarriages before they depart tomorrow morning and use the gaps around the vents to check whether there are scratches from nonstandard latches on the inside of the cargo compartments, we’ll know whether they really transported living people.”
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s76-1: If we wanted to know Sarah’s current situation, if we wanted to know where the transfer station holding the cancelled people was, this was our last chance before the review.
texts.chapter:v15-z04c:event:text-s77-1: Tomorrow morning, when these suspect vehicles stopped at the gate preparing to leave the Central Village, we would have to inspect them ourselves.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:title: Interlude: One Li
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s1-1:
Out-of-Village Notice · Blank Form (copy kept in the Records Room):
Reason｜　Accompanying observation　/　Accompanying a transaction　/　Other (specify)
Person leaving｜Name　　　Current assignment　　　Number
Escort｜Name　　　Current assignment　　　Number
Time of departure｜　　　　Time of
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s1-2:
return｜
Approved｜(signature of elder on duty)
Note 1: The current assignment field must not be left blank. A blank field is treated as failure to file.
Note 2: Two copies of this form are made; one is handed to the boundary-stone guard for safekeeping when leaving the village.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s5-1: On the sixth night, after Yuna finished briefing me on our plan to inspect the carts outside the village tomorrow morning, I went out to find Estelle.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s6-1: Yuna was still in the kitchen. The lamplight was dim. She spread the copy of the list brought out at dawn across the table and said she wanted to go over it once more, and that I should go ahead. When she said “go ahead,” she did not say where to. But we both knew.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s7-1: Estelle was sitting on the cool bench outside the chapel, the little booklet she always carried lying flat across her lap. There were two stone benches here, set side by side. The one on the west, shielded from the sun during the day, was always cool by night. A thin layer of dew had seeped onto the stone’s surface.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s8-1: The night wind moved through the chapel’s broken window lattice, very quietly. I walked up behind her. She did not turn around.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s10-1: “Arno.” She called my name while looking out at the empty courtyard.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s12-1: “How did you know it was me?” I stopped.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s14-1: “You land on your heels first when you walk.” Her voice had no more rise or fall than the night wind. “Yuna lands on the balls of her feet.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s16-1: I sat on the other bench. Between us was bare mud without paving stones. During the day, ants crawled all over it. At night, nothing could be seen there. Only the astringent smell of earth rising from it.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s17-1: The ash on the chapel’s outer wall flaked off very slowly. When it landed on my shoulder, I felt no weight. It only left a layer of pale powder on the cloth.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s20-1: “You’re leaving tomorrow morning,” she said suddenly.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s22-1: “Yeah.” I said, “Yuna’s going to the distribution station outside the village tomorrow to see whether the insides of those supply carts have any unusual marks from locking mechanisms.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s26-1: “She’s taking care of it.” I shifted on the bench. “Although we kept our candidate status after filing the report, this trip can’t use the regular accompanying arrangement. She gave the logistics team’s Chico half a
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s26-2: strip of smoked meat to vouch for us on the out-of-village form. We’ll put ‘odd jobs’ in the assignment field. As long as we get the form to him before Otto’s shift ends tonight, we won’t have to worry about questions.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s27-1: She nodded once. The way she nodded was a little like Sera’s, very slight, just confirming a fact.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s29-1: “I’m not asking about my own business tonight.” She kept her eyes on the darkness ahead and spoke calmly. “I’m asking about Yuna. You’re going to inspect the carts outside the village tomorrow. What makes her think you can get close to them without being noticed, when it’s that dangerous?”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s34-1: “That’s because of Chico too.” I answered as Yuna had instructed me. “Carrying cargo beside him will be our cover. If he changes his mind tomorrow and refuses to take us, the cover won’t hold, and Yuna won’t go. She won’t take a single step farther.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s36-1: “That is exactly what I need to know. When she decides whether to go, what is she comparing in her mind?” She lowered her head, her finger tracing the edge of the booklet. “Starting tomorrow, I won’t be able
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s36-2: to see what you’re doing outside. This copy in my hands will have to pass through you to be checked on site. If you run into an account that makes no sense, I need to know what rules she is using to calculate.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s39-1: Her voice stayed level as she spoke. There was no panic in it. It had been the same on the day the names were withdrawn.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s42-1: “Can you leave the village yourself, or not?” I suddenly remembered that form. “Didn’t you say before that if you could personally inspect those carts outside the village, you’d definitely be able to see where the discrepancy was?”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s45-1: “I can’t go with you tomorrow.” The corner of her mouth pulled up in self-mockery, but the smile did not reach her eyes. “The person leaving on that form has to have a current assignment. After my name was withdrawn, my status on their rolls became ‘restricted visitor,’ waiting for the unified return
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s45-2: transport at the end of the week. That status isn’t an assignment. It’s a cage. Chico dares to vouch for you as ‘odd-job labor,’ but he would never dare vouch for a candidate who has already been struck from the rolls. I can’t even enter my name, much less get off the cart to investigate any ledger.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s47-1: “What if we didn’t need the notice?” I looked at her. “There’s open ground between the boundary stones. If you avoided the main road, you wouldn’t have to wait for the end-of-week repatriation review to get out…”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s50-1: “The guards at the village entrance might ignore two children running around in the wasteland, because they know you won’t get far. But I’m someone whose file has been locked. The moment I leave the escort party and appear on an outer road, any inspection team that finds me will treat me as a fugitive.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s51-1: I sat on the stone bench, cold seeping through it. The chill of the night passed through my clothes. Her words brought a lot of old scenes to mind. That experience
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s51-2: had proven it: even without stones to block the way, a wilderness without water or supplies became a wall that could eat people by the end of the journey.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s52-1: I followed her gaze toward the heavy darkness. She had explained the reason rationally enough, but there was a weight in the eyes fixed on the booklet—a weight from not being able
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s52-2: to investigate it herself. I finally decided to speak. Not only to answer her question about what Yuna used to make her choice, but also to tell her we were not entirely unprepared.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s53-1: I told her about that time.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s56-1: It happened a year ago. That night was cold, and the sky was still dark.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s57-1: She knocked on my window. It was the same method she had used since childhood. By the time I looked up, her face was already waiting outside the gap in the wooden frame.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s58-1: I was sitting on the edge of the bed, about to put on my shoes, when she lowered her voice outside the window and said, “Bring the waterskin.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s59-1: It was an old goatskin waterskin hanging behind the kitchen door, and the only one our family had. So I wouldn’t wake Mother sleeping in the inner room, I went barefoot into the outer
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s59-2: room, took it down, and hung it at my waist with the half-skin of cold water still inside. I moved very quietly. Only after I returned to the bed and tied my shoes did I open the door.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s63-1: There was dampness in the wind. We used the darkness to skirt the mill and slip out through an unused path north of the village.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s64-1: I had always thought leaving the village necessarily meant crossing the boundary stones. In my understanding, that was an iron rule. But where she took me that day, there was not a trace of a boundary stone anywhere in sight.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s66-1: “The boundary stones are on the road.” She walked ahead, parting waist-high weeds without looking back. “Go count them. Seven to the north, nine to the east. I counted eleven to
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s66-2: the south, then there were no more, because there’s water that way. Every one of them is set in the road, plain as day. But there are no stones in the wasteland between the roads.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s68-1: “So they don’t stop anyone.” My heart tightened. A trace of excitement began to rise, beyond my control.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s70-1: “I don’t know whether they stop anyone.” Her tone was like a statement of a known condition. “I can only say the stones aren’t set here. What that means, I don’t know.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s74-1: We climbed across the slope between two boundary stones. Loose stones were hidden in the grass. Before every step, I had to probe with my toes, or I could easily twist an ankle.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s75-1: Before we reached the top, she grabbed me and pulled me down behind a dead tree. Dawn had begun to break. From there, we could look down onto the person sitting beside the boundary stone on the main road.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s76-1: Kane was sitting on his stone.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s77-1: In my memory, whenever I saw a boundary stone, Kane was sitting there, perfectly still, like something the stone had grown.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s79-1: “Can he see us?” I lowered my voice. My throat felt tight.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s83-1: “Then we’ll wait for him to leave.” My instinct was to retreat.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s85-1: “He won’t. I’ve watched him three times. He doesn’t leave from morning until noon.” She stood and brushed the dirt from her trousers. “If we can’t avoid him, we go.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s86-1: We crossed the slope above him in full view. I kept my head down, afraid that if I turned and met his dead-water eyes, my legs would give out.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s88-1: She told me later that when she looked back, he was still sitting there, his back stiff as stone. He had not turned his neck even once.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s92-1: Beyond the slope was a pathless wasteland. We went deeper and deeper. Waist-high weeds clung tightly to our ankles. Each time we planted a foot deeper, wet mud beneath the grass smeared against our shoes, slowing us down. As the sun rose, the wet mud gradually dried, hardening into gray-white clumps stuck to the soles.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s93-1: Yuna was counting her steps. She walked ahead, her lips moving in rhythm. Every time she reached one hundred, she pressed hard against the side of her thigh.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s95-1: “Why are you counting that?” I couldn’t help asking.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s97-1: “We’ll need it on the way back.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s99-1: “Can’t we just follow the flattened grass?” I thought she was wasting her effort.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s101-1: “The grass will stand back up.” She stopped and pointed at the trail behind us. “Once the sun comes out and the dew dries, it’ll return to its original shape very quickly. Once it stands up, everything will look the same. I won’t recognize the way.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s102-1: I looked back. The trail through the grass really was very faint. Farther away, the weeds were already swaying in the breeze as they recovered, and the way back was gradually disappearing.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s105-1: The sky was high. The north wind was dry and harsh against my face, without a trace of moisture.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s106-1: At the flat edge of the wasteland, enormous shapes swallowed by vegetation could be seen far in the distance. Farther still were intermittent gray-white traces, like abandoned old roads. Nearby, there was nothing with which to measure distance.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s107-1: After we walked for a while, the stretch of ground ahead changed color. It was paler, like bleached bone. The soil also looked harder. The sound of the wind passing over it was hoarse and grating.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s109-1: “What’s over there?” I stopped, a sense of awe rising in me.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s113-1: “Let’s go take a look.” The heartbeat of facing the unknown gave me courage.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s115-1: “How far is it?” she asked back.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s119-1: “Things that don’t look far often aren’t the same once you start walking. This place is flat as far as you can see. There’s nothing nearby for reference, and the ruins in the distance are far too large. Your eyes will lie to you.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s122-1: Even so, she walked forward another few dozen steps. Then she stopped without warning.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s123-1: She turned around and walked silently up to me. She took the goatskin waterskin from my waist, weighed it, and frowned.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s128-1: I really didn’t know. The wind was so dry that whenever my mouth felt dry, I had simply pulled out the stopper and taken a couple of swallows. I hadn’t counted at all.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s129-1: She put the light, empty waterskin back into my belt and tightened the cord.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s131-1: “That was half a day’s water for both of us. I thought you’d keep track of how much you drank.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s133-1: “I’m not thirsty.” I felt somewhat guilty and wanted to keep walking.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s137-1: “You’re not thirsty now.” She reached out to stop me. “We have this far to walk back.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s138-1: She pointed toward the direction we had come from.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s140-1: “How long have we been out?” She stared at me as she asked.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s144-1: “Almost half an hour.” She glanced at the sky. “We’re out of water, and the way back is uphill. If we go any farther to explore that ground, we definitely won’t make it back before lunch. Once the family starts looking, this road without boundary stones is over.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s145-1: She looked at the pale ground and added:
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s147-1: “I don’t know what’s really ahead. Something could be buried there. Or it could be dead ground.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s151-1: I was unwilling to go back in every possible way. I was fifteen, and this was the first time I had reached a place without even a footprint, a place beyond the reach of rules. The unknown ground ahead shone strangely beneath the sun, as if calling to me.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s153-1: “Just a little farther.” I gritted my teeth and pleaded with her, my voice tight.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s155-1: “How much is a little?” she asked—the fatal question.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s156-1: I couldn’t answer. What was “a little”? Ten steps? A hundred? Or until I saw what was on that ground?
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s157-1: She waited quietly for a while. When I had completely run out of words and still couldn’t answer, she turned around decisively, without the slightest hesitation.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s162-1: It was uphill, just as she had said. The grass had also stood back up in places, covering the faint traces of our path. Twice we nearly went astray. She relied on the sun to find
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s162-2: our direction. From memory, she worked backward step by step: after two hundred steps there should be a pit, or after one hundred steps we should have crossed a gentle slope.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s163-1: Whenever the terrain and the step count did not match, she firmly led me back to the last point we were certain of and started again.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s164-1: The empty waterskin swung against my waist the whole way. Its sound against my hipbone was dull and hollow, as though constantly reminding me that there was nothing inside.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s165-1: Later, I really did get thirsty. A sharp pain ran deep through my throat when I swallowed. I clenched my teeth and said nothing. But on the final, most exhausting uphill stretch, she looked back at me without a word and quietly slowed her steps so I could steady my breathing.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s168-1: That was how we returned over the slope between the boundary stones. When we stepped back onto the gravel road, we were about twenty or thirty steps from the boundary stone.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s169-1:
Kane was still sitting there, in exactly the same position as before dawn.
But this time, his face was turned toward us.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s170-1: My heart contracted sharply. Yuna pulled me along, hard. We pretended to be calm and kept walking as usual.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s173-1: When we passed him, he actually spoke.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s175-1: “There’s water beneath the grass to the east.” He was still looking at the dirt road ahead. His voice was dry and hollow. “Don’t step there.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s176-1: Neither of us answered. Yuna gave a slight nod.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s177-1: We had gone a long way before I dared to speak, my voice trembling.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s179-1: “He saw us. He mentioned the grass to the east. That’s where we crossed.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s181-1: “There’s water beneath the grass to the east. That has no causal connection to whether we crossed there or not. The water has always been there.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s183-1: “Then why did he say it today?”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s185-1: “Don’t know. He sits there all year and only reports a few road conditions.” She stopped and looked at me. “Arno, I don’t guess about him. I can’t guess at things that make no sense.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s188-1: That was where the story ended.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s190-1: Outside the chapel, Estelle listened quietly the entire time. She did not interrupt me once.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s194-1: “Don’t know. I never went there again. We avoided everyone, but when I got home, my mother recognized the gray-white dry mud from the outskirts stuck to the soles of my shoes at a glance.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s195-1: I paused, remembering what happened then. Mother did not report me, but she privately flew into a terrible rage. It was the first time I had seen her lose her temper like that. She took the goatskin pouch we had emptied from the kitchen and hung it on
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s195-2: the highest nail under the eaves. For the next half-month, whenever I reached for a cup of water, she pointed at that empty waterskin and made me stare at it for a while. After that, that stretch of ground became a forbidden place we never mentioned again.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s198-1:
After we returned that day, Yuna converted the steps and directions she had recorded on paper.
The straight-line distance we had traveled was actually less than one li.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s199-1: That morning, with the waterskin empty and afraid of being discovered by our family, we had not even seen what the outside world really looked like before being forced to turn back.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s201-1: “As long as it’s water and stamina she can see, she knows when to stop.” She repeated it softly, flattening the booklet on her knees.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s205-1: She closed the booklet in her hands.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s207-1: “I’m not afraid of her acting on impulse. I’m afraid that once she’s outside, she’ll run into something she absolutely can’t give up, while the cost on the other side of the scale is too great to calculate—”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s209-1: She did not say the rest.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s210-1: The ash on the chapel wall fell soundlessly. I did not dare think any further.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s212-1: After a while, she lowered her head, took two cut sheets of paper and a short piece of charcoal from inside her clothes, and began to write by the faint candlelight leaking through the chapel’s broken window.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s213-1: When she finished, she folded the two sheets twice each and held them out to me.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s214-1: I reached out and took them. The paper carried the chill of her fingertips.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s216-1: “The first sheet says 802, 804, and 807.” Her voice was very quiet. “Regular freight from Watermarsh has always been assigned numbers by ten-day period, seven carts per period. But I checked the departure forms from the past six months. At the beginning of this month, six carts suddenly
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s216-2: appeared that did not follow the sequence. I worked downward from the intervals between those departures. These three numbers correspond to tomorrow’s cover carts. There will be many carts at the distribution station tomorrow. With these three numbers, you can identify them directly.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s217-1: “As for Sarah and the other two, the copy says they were classified as ‘midweek transshipment goods,’ and that high-dose sedatives and this batch of goods were sent together to an outer temporary storage site. People and drugs could not have been loaded together with ordinary village supplies.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s217-2: That means after they were transported out four days ago, their first stop was most likely some specialized transfer point along the way. But that is an old account from four days ago. To find out where they went afterward, you’ll have to get close to the carts and see whether, besides
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s217-3: the scratches from the interior locks, there are additional strap marks along the edges of the undercarriage—marks left by straps installed to secure cages for transporting living things. Ordinary cargo boxes have no use for those straps. I need to confirm exactly which cart was modified.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s218-1: “The second sheet shows the structure of the cargo-box undercarriage, with the four places where you need to check for strap marks. When you come back tomorrow night, each of you will draw the shapes of the marks you saw. Draw them separately. Don’t discuss them.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s219-1: “And,” she looked at me, an unusual seriousness in her eyes, “tomorrow, once you’re outside, if you come across an account that could get you killed, you’re responsible for calling her back.”
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s220-1: I looked at the two folded sheets in my hands and drew a deep breath.
texts.chapter:volume0-one-li:event:text-s222-1: “Okay.” I clenched them tightly in my palm and tucked them inside my clothes.
texts.chapter:volume0-manufactured-people:even: At five on the morning of the seventh day, the morning fog had yet to lift. The air by the boundary stone was cold as iron soaked in water, and breathing it into my lungs brought a dull ache. We waited for Chiko in the dense fog.

The night before, in the chapel courtyard, Estelle had given us two sheets of paper. The first listed the three batch numbers we had inferred the previous day were possibly used to transport people. The second listed

four observation tasks for the outskirts: what they checked when distributing grain, whose name children were registered under at birth, what title the person in charge held, and what they called themselves in private.

Those four unanswered questions were what we stood here carrying with us, along with the purpose of finding the three large carts on the schedule. Those three carts were supposed to be the breakthrough we had agreed to use for verifying the batch numbers.

Chiko was the liaison who specifically ran deliveries to the outskirts for the village, and the only channel the elders had authorized for going there. The sound of wheels crushing gravel came from deep in the fog, but what he pushed out was a two-wheeled handcart with boards polished bright from use, and a donkey with drooping ears.
Yuna stared at the small cart without moving.
“Why is it you? What about the three large carts on the schedule? They’re supposed to take this route today.”
“They don’t take this route at all.”
“Then which route do they take?”

Chiko stopped the cart and showed no intention of answering. He only untied the reins from the donkey’s back. Yuna suddenly took a step forward, and I grabbed her sleeve. The three carts that might be carrying people had vanished right before our

eyes. It was too late to block another gate, and Chiko was about to leave the village. If we missed him, we couldn’t get to the outskirts. Yuna bit her lip hard. After a moment of struggle in her eyes, she could only force the question back down.
“Give me the report.” He held out a hand without looking back.
He shoved his hands deep into his coarse-cloth sleeves and let out a breath of white vapor.

“Yesterday afternoon, you brought me half a strip of smoked meat and said you wanted to leave the village. But I should remind you: although you kept your candidate status after being written up, the proper form for leaving the village can’t be approved.

Even if you use the excuse that you’re helping me work, by the time I finish this cart’s rounds at several distribution stations tonight, the entire outskirts will know that two Inner Circle children came by.” His narrowed eyes studied us through the fog.
