“You decide whether you want to go.”
Yuna did not hesitate.
“I’m going. The form is here.”
“Signed by Otto.”

That was true. Although we couldn’t go under a regular accompanying-work order, she believed every step after this had to be taken openly and properly. Her exact words had been: “I want them to know I’m

investigating, and I want every step of the investigation to comply with the village rules. If they want to stop me, they’ll have to write down their reasons for stopping me, clearly and in black and white.”
Chiko took the report from Yuna. He read it slowly, his gaze lingering over the paper for a long time, as if searching the ink for some hidden nail.
“It says the position is ‘odd-job laborer,’ and the purpose is ‘loading and unloading from the cart.’” He finally spoke, his voice slightly hoarse.
“That’s right.” Yuna met his gaze.
“Two children. Loading what?”
“Helping you move the goods, and seeing how you conduct your trades.”
Chiko stared at her for another two seconds, then folded the slip and handed it back. He asked nothing more. He only turned to untie the reins from the donkey’s back.
“Get on,” he said.
We left the boundary stone behind before dawn.
Kane, who guarded the boundary, sat on the enormous boundary stone like a stone carving. He looked over the slip in the faint light, nodded, and didn’t say a single unnecessary word.
“How’s the waterline past the bridge?” Chiko asked, lifting his chin.
“Passable.”
“Don’t step in the soft mud on the right.”
The wooden axle gave a dull creak, and we officially left the village.

Two li beyond the boundary stone, the ground felt completely different from the village roads. The village’s dirt roads had been trampled by generations, packed firm and soft at once, carrying the breath of the earth. But here,

an enormous gray-white structure pushed stiffly out of the ocher soil, like the spine of some dead giant beast. Its cross-section was incredibly thick, with massive rust-red iron bars embedded inside. Beneath it was a hollow

with no visible bottom, and I could faintly feel gusts of cold air rising through it from underground. Its upper surface was so level it defied nature, stretching back toward the village until it disappeared in that direction.
Yuna jumped down from the cart and walked to the edge of the bottomless break to look down.
“The road we came on was built.” She raised her head, a strange clarity in her eyes. “Look at these iron bars—they laid out the framework first, then poured some kind of slurry over the whole thing.”
“Who would pour a foundation this thick in a wasteland like this?” I looked at the desolate terrain around us, unable to make sense of it.
“It extends all the way toward the village.” She stood and dusted her hands.
She turned and looked back in the direction we had come from.

A howling wind swept across the wilderness, lifting gray-white dust. I stood on the high ground and looked over the boundless, cold, lifeless ruins. In the distance, the village was only a small halo of reassuring warmth. In this vast silence, it was so small that a gust of wind seemed capable of scattering it.
Chiko was focused on driving ahead of us, his back perfectly straight. He didn’t look back at all.
“Don’t look around so much.” His voice lashed back like a whip, cold and hard, without a trace of inflection.
“Why?”
“If you look too much, you’ll start asking questions.”
“If you ask too much, it has to be recorded.”
What the people from the outskirts called the “distribution station”—the trading point where Chiko met them—had been set up on the leeward side of a massive old building.

Only half of the building remained, as if some tremendous force had sliced it cleanly in half. The fallen rubble had been cleared by hand, gouging a flat patch out of the earth. Several crude tarpaulin shelters stood there.

When the wind blew, their roofs rattled loudly. Beneath them lay heaps of things: bags of coarse grain, rolls of homespun cloth, metal tools still caked with mud, and several viscous raw materials I couldn’t name at all.
Dawn had only just begun to break, but people were already there.

About a dozen of them. Men and women, old and young, gathered in small groups beneath the shelters. When they saw Chiko’s familiar wooden cart appear on the horizon, they stood one after another. Someone waved at us from far away.
“Morning,” Chiko called, raising his whip.
“Morning.” The replies rose one after another, carrying the distinctive clamor of ordinary life.

Before then, my impression of the daily lives of the people from the outskirts had been almost blank. The strange stories passed around by the children were even more bizarre: some swore they weren’t human at all, while others said they could stay awake at night without sleeping, like bats.
But that morning, through the light of the rising sun, all I saw was a group of entirely ordinary people.
Their clothes were older and coarser than the villagers’, patched in many places, but freshly washed. Their faces bore the marks of years spent in wind, sun, and hard labor. Nearby,
a woman held a child who wouldn’t stop crying. She patted the bundle gently while turning in a steady circle. On the other side of the shelter, two men were arguing red-faced and
neck-veined over how to divide a pile of old lumber, swearing the whole time. When they were done, they squatted down as if nothing had happened and each took out some tobacco to smoke.
At the edge of the clearing, an old man with graying hair leaned against a post, eyes narrowed as he enjoyed the warmth of the first sunlight. A thin yellow dog lay listlessly at his feet.
But among this crowd, so full of the heat and noise of ordinary life, there was another group that seemed completely out of place.

There were six of them. They stood silently in the open ground outside the shelters. They did not squat or sit casually like the others, but stood rigidly upright. I realized they were the same laborers we had seen in the

village before, still wearing those gray smocks. But only today did I notice that a narrow strip of metal two fingers wide had been sewn firmly onto each of their left cuffs, with a deeply etched horizontal bar across its center.

As soon as the sky grew fully light, the six moved in silent agreement. Without saying a word, they formed a line and marched toward the desolate road leading west. The curve of their backs and the distance between their steps were uncannily identical, as if years of severe discipline had unified even the instinct of walking.
I asked Chiko quietly where they were going.
“The outer districts,” Chiko answered casually as he unloaded the goods.
“The outer districts are the outer ring of the old site. They’re going to repair some roads and move out whatever they clear from inside.”
“They go a few times a month. The shifts are fixed.”
I followed his answer to its implication and asked: What about inside the old site?
Chiko’s hands, busy sorting the ropes, paused for a moment. He turned his head and glanced at me.
“They’re not responsible for inside the old site.” He turned his gaze back and lowered his voice.

“They have passes for the outer-ring door, so they can get through. They don’t have one for the heavy iron door inside. Once a month, they go into the outer ring of the old site to repair roads, sweep, and move things. The shifts are fixed. If they don’t go, their rations are cut off.”

“They have to stop when they reach the iron door. Not one step farther. There’s a gap beneath it as wide as a hand. Stray dogs from the village can slip through easily, but even a child couldn’t squeeze through.”
At the mention of animals, Yuna’s gaze fell involuntarily on the yellow dog at the old man’s feet.
“Dogs can come and go freely, but people can’t?” Yuna sounded as if she were confirming something.

“Yes. The machine controlling the door is stubborn. It doesn’t detect whether anything living passes through. It only recognizes passes. Without one, it won’t open. So people can’t get in, but dogs can slip back and forth and it doesn’t care.” Chiko grabbed a handful of beans.
Yuna withdrew her gaze, but I saw that she had fixed the fact firmly in her memory.

Chiko began trading with the people from the outskirts. His movements flowed with practiced ease, carrying a persuasive rhythm: he placed each item on the scale, glanced at the mark, and announced the number in a perfectly level voice. Beside him, someone immediately scratched the figures onto a wooden board with charcoal.

Throughout it all, I kept my eyes fixed on the packaging of every batch unloaded, trying to find the three inferred batch numbers Estelle had told us to verify. None of them matched. The supplies sent out from the village and the receiving slips here seemed to be two entirely separate sets of accounts.

The three large carts that had vanished that morning showed no sign of having appeared here either. The coarse grain and homespun cloth on Chiko’s two-wheeled cart seemed to be the entire supply line connecting the

central village to this place. This trip had failed to trace the dedicated route for transporting people. We could only search for the answers to the four observation tasks in these most ordinary exchanges of goods.
Just as Chiko finished counting the third batch of cloth, the woman holding the child walked toward us.
When she came close, her gaze passed over me and settled on Yuna.
“You’re from the village,” she said, using a statement rather than a question, with a trace of barely perceptible awe.
“Yes.” Yuna nodded.
“Why are there two children here today?” She looked curiously over our thin frames.
“Odd-job laborers,” Chiko put in while busy with his work, without even looking up. “They’re here to help move the empty sacks.”
The woman gave an enlightened little “Oh,” but the awe in her eyes did not lessen.

Next, she deftly shifted the child into the crook of her left arm and freed her right hand. She rummaged for a long time in the pocket of her patched clothes. At last, she took something out and carefully held it toward Yuna.
It was a small piece of candy.
“Take it,” she said with a smile, the wrinkles on her face relaxing into a plain, ingratiating warmth.
Yuna clearly froze, her hand stopping in midair.
“I can’t take it.” She instinctively drew back.

“Take it.” The woman pushed her hand forward stubbornly. “People from the Inner Circle are all honored guests. Even if all eight generations of us were added together, no one here could enter that gate in this lifetime. Since we happened to meet you today, let us share in your luck and take it as a good omen.”

Yuna lowered her head and stared at the sugar. Its surface was rough, covered in large crystals, with a cloudy yellow tinge. It was not made in the central village workshops. She slowly extended her hand and accepted it.
“Thank you,” she said softly, looking directly into the woman’s eyes. “Do you have names you call yourselves in private?”
“…Me?” The woman seemed not to have expected an Inner Circle child to speak to her, and grew somewhat flustered.
I broke out in a cold sweat standing beside them, because Estelle had specifically told us last night to verify it once we reached the site. We had assumed there would
be a more tactful way to broach the subject. But Yuna had bluntly thrown out the exact wording of the observation task in front of a mother who had just given her sugar.
“Malda,” the woman answered.
“Malda.” Yuna repeated the name, her gaze falling to the bundle in the woman’s arms. “What about the child?”
“They have a name in private too. But it doesn’t count yet.” Malda patted the child’s back and answered naturally. “We’ll count it after registration.”
“How long does registration take?”
“Soon.” Malda glanced up at the sky. “The official from the central village will be here next month.”
“What title does this official hold?”

“We don’t know that.” The woman shook her head. “We only know he’s coming specifically to take fingerprints. He wears the Inner Circle’s white clothes. Once he nods, this person will be added to our ration accounts.”
After saying that, she smiled at us, turned, and walked away patting the child, merging into the noisy activity nearby.

Yuna stood where she was, the rough sugar clenched in her palm. She waited until Malda was more than a dozen steps away and had turned her back completely before slowly opening her hand and looking down. Then she carefully put it into the pocket close to her body.

“‘We’ll count it after registration.’” She recited the half-sentence as if chewing on a stone. “Arno, here, the name a mother calls her child doesn’t count. The official has to take the fingerprint, and the ledger has to gain a share. Only then does this body count as alive within their rules.”
A little after ten, as the sunlight grew increasingly harsh, I noticed the second thing.
I saw this one myself. Yuna was watching other people unload cloth at the time.

Chiko was counting a batch of coarse grain with a short man around forty.
“Bak, your grain. Mark it.” After announcing the count, Chiko handed over the wooden board.
The man called Bak
was thin as a bundle of bones, but strong. His large hands were covered in thick calluses, like dry tree bark. He picked up the charcoal and prepared to press his mark onto Chiko’s board.
At the instant he forcefully rolled up the sleeve of his left arm, I caught sight of something strange on the inside of his wrist.

It was a small mark noticeably darker than the surrounding skin, a perfectly regular square that clearly had not grown there naturally. Several symbols I couldn’t understand had been faintly etched into that dark square.
When Chiko had distributed the grain just now, he had also made Bak expose this spot for a look first.
“What’s that?” Unable to hold back either, I pointed at the man’s wrist and asked Chiko.
Chiko was looking down as he calculated the accounts. At that, he only glanced up.
“Batch number.” His tone did not change at all.
“What’s a batch number?” The term sounded cold and metallic.

Chiko stopped writing. He turned and looked silently at me for a while. Then he lifted his chin toward the gaunt man. The man obediently rolled his sleeve higher. A square mark was plainly visible on the inside of his wrist.
“Chiko.” My throat felt dry.
“Hmm.” He looked at me calmly.
“This thing… was he born with it?” The words escaped me.
“When he was a hundred days old, people from the central village came down and branded it onto him.” He looked at me as if stating something obvious.
The sun was already high that morning, its heat baking the shelter roof. The yellow dog from before rolled over in the shade of the post and let out a heavy pant.
Estelle’s image suddenly flashed through my mind, always wearing a long-sleeved coat fastened tightly to the wrist. Though she came from the Watermarsh settlement and
had a name of her own, she still carried an origin from the outskirts. In this system that divided people into ranks, was there a similar brand hidden on her wrist?
Before this, I had worked alongside the laborers from the outskirts and seen them obediently move things, but the outskirts had always remained a vague concept to me. Today, watching that
mother offer the rough sugar with my own eyes, then watching Bak roll up his sleeve as if displaying a livestock mark, I finally matched the rumored “outskirts products” to living people.
“But… you manage the contact with them.” My thoughts were confused as I tried to recover the logic. “You just watch them get branded like objects?”
“I’ve been running this route for more than a hundred years.” He looked at me.
“More than a hundred… You’ve changed bodies? Are you one of the Ten Seats?”
“Why else do you think the elders have always kept one seat open for the errand runner?”

I jerked my head up and stared at his perpetually sunburned, peeling face in disbelief. Deep lines, carved by wind and weather, marked it like knife cuts, but the direction of the muscles clearly belonged to someone in his early twenties.

Before this, although Mother had told me she had changed bodies, and I had always known that all ten members of the Ten Seats had changed bodies, I had assumed they were all elders seated high above us in the council hall. I had never

imagined that this peddler, spending every day in the wind and sun of the outskirts, was one of the Ten Seats. When he confirmed the astonishing fact himself, his tone was as flat as if he were talking about the price of cabbage today.
“They feel pain when they fall. They get sick too. I know that.” Chiko ignored my shock, his voice flat as still water. “But the village’s rules allow no exceptions.”
He turned and continued sorting the empty sacks on the cart.
“How much grain is needed this year, how much labor the outskirts must provide, which lives are to be kept and which are to be crossed off—those quotas are fixed in the ledger, locked tight.”

“I can give them a straight answer while they’re waiting in line, and I can make sure no one skims their share when the grain is distributed. But no one can change these rules. I’m able to stay alive doing this because I follow them. The people who dared to ask why are long gone.”
At some point, Yuna had come over and was now standing behind me.
Her gaze locked onto the man called Bak. After watching him for a while, she slowly raised her eyes and looked straight at Chiko.

“Chiko.” Her voice was quiet, but carried a force that allowed no evasion. “That man unloading the grain, Bak—he has a number on his wrist. If he dies, how will the village ledger record it? Will it only cross out a string of digits, or will it note that he had a family?”
“The ledger only crosses out the number.” Chiko did not avoid her gaze.
“And you? You’ve been running this route for so many years.” Yuna pressed him step by step. “Do you know whether he has any brothers or sisters?”
“He has an older brother.”
“Dead.”
“When did he die? How?”
Chiko stopped everything he was doing. He turned and faced Yuna completely.
“Nineteen years ago. A mine shaft in Outer District Three collapsed. His brother didn’t make it out.” He stressed the words, biting down hard on each one.
“I know what you want to ask.” Chiko sighed like a tired traveler. “You want to ask: if I remember all their names, and who’s alive and who’s dead,
how can I still stand by and watch them treated as tools? I’ll tell you. It doesn’t help. What I think can’t change a ration of coarse grain.”
He raised his rough fingers and scratched hard at his sunburned, peeling cheek.

“There’s no record like that in the candidate materials you memorize at school. Other curious candidates have asked me the same question before.” He pointed toward the village. “But under these rules, everyone has to follow procedure.”
In the afternoon, we followed Chiko’s empty cart back toward the village.

Yuna did not say a word on the way back. She sat curled up on the swaying cart bed, both arms wrapped tightly around her knees. Her gaze passed over the rear of the cart and fixed on the old pavement, pitted and uneven from being crushed beneath the wheels, receding behind us as if she were trying to find some pattern in those gray-white remains.
She finally spoke when the enormous boundary stone came into view in the distance.
“Chiko.”
“Hmm.” Chiko answered from ahead.
“You’ve talked with them before. How exactly is the ‘baseline compliance’ review judged?”
Chiko’s hand, swinging the whip, stopped abruptly in midair.
It was an extremely slight pause. If I hadn’t been watching his back the entire time, I almost wouldn’t have noticed.
“Where did you hear that term?” He did not look back, and kept his voice very low.
“Estelle mentioned it.” Yuna tossed out a lie.
Chiko maintained his driving posture, watching the boundary stone ahead.
“Once a year.” He recited the sentence mechanically. “I go down to the outskirts, ask each of them a few routine questions, and write a few notes in the register.”
“What do they ask?”
“As long as they can answer like a person and their emotions seem normal, they pass. But I know what you want to ask.”
“You think that ‘pass’ is too simple, don’t you? Because you didn’t understand the phrase ‘like a person.’” He lowered the whip and scratched irritably at his cheek. The cart slowed.

“What the village wants is for them to have some hope for tomorrow, some concern for their neighbors, and anger that occasionally erupts over a mouthful or two of grain. That’s the human quality we can keep hold of. But if—” He looked straight at

Yuna. “If someone suddenly decides that, as a ‘person,’ they shouldn’t be given so little; if they suddenly want an explanation for something that was never meant to belong to them… then they’re no longer a person. They’re a thorn in the system.”
“Let me give you some advice as an elder: don’t ask people from the outskirts questions like that again.” He did not answer Yuna directly. Instead, he turned and looked at
her with a rare severity. “A careless question from you, if you ask it in front of them and let them follow the thought downward, will take root in their minds like a plague.”

“If they fail, they’ll be taken away for disposition. How? Do you really want to know?” He drew a deep breath. “At most, I can make sure their grain isn’t shorted by a measure. But I can’t save the people

from the outskirts who suddenly wake up because of one extra question you asked today and want to pull out the thorn. I’ve been running this route for years. No one knows their fate better than I do.”
Chiko raised the whip again and cracked it hard through the air. The report rang out.
“Your report says, in black and white, ‘loading and unloading from the cart.’ Whatever you’re really doing here,” his voice turned cold, “the part I let you see today ended with that last question.”
That evening, as night settled over the village, we slipped into the archive room by now knowing the way. This was already our fifth time entering the controlled shelving area this week.

This time, we didn’t have to sneak around like thieves. As soon as we returned to the village that afternoon, Yuna had gone straight to the council hall and asked Otto to sign a consultation slip, because she wanted to take the matter of consulting the regulations properly through the open channels.
The document called the Regulations for the Management of Peripheral Personnel was not thick. It had only three chapters.

Chapter One was the tedious “General Provisions,” a long discussion of the need to establish liaison officers, the grid-based division of the peripheral regions, and the principles for locating trading points and scheduling patrols.
Chapter Two was titled “Registration.”
Halfway through that chapter, those lines drove themselves into our eyes.

Article 7 Peripheral personnel shall be registered by batch and serial number. This number is their sole identifier, remains unchanged for life, and shall not be altered due to relocation, marriage, or a change of name.
“‘Registered by batch and serial number.’ ‘Sole identifier.’” Yuna pressed her finger against the page, the tip paling slightly.
She raised her head and looked at me.
“There isn’t even a name field in these regulations.”
Her finger slid down the page and came to rest on the article immediately below.
Article 8 The children of peripheral personnel shall be registered under their mother’s batch and serial number, with an additional secondary serial number.
“That child in Malda’s arms is, under the regulations, only a secondary product number extending from its mother’s production batch.” Yuna’s voice grew hoarse.
The archive room’s specially made, shadowless cold light poured plainly across the yellowed pages.

“Combined with the list of people written off for ‘failure to meet the baseline compliance standard’ that we copied out yesterday… No wonder there are only numbers. This isn’t a population ledger at all. It records the consumption and derivatives of a kind of object.”
The second chapter continued downward, ending with two rules standing there by themselves—

Article 9 The annual review of baseline compliance shall be conducted by the liaison officer. Those who fail the review shall be reported for disposition.
Article 10 “Disposition,” as used in these regulations, does not include the circumstances stipulated in Article 19 of Chapter Three.
We turned back to the table of contents. After the title of Chapter Three, only three words were printed: See separate volume.
Yuna searched the entire second row of unmarked public shelves from beginning to end, checking every volume. She found nothing.
She stopped, stood before the tall wooden shelves with dust covering her hands, and looked up at the topmost row.
“It’s in those three rows of restricted shelves with the red marks,” she said through clenched teeth.
“Are you going to cross the line and get it?” I clenched my fists, ready to keep watch for her.
“No.”
Unexpectedly, she refused with absolute finality, without the slightest hesitation.
“Why?” I stared at her in disbelief.
“I don’t know exactly what Article 19 is, but I can see where this ledger draws its red line.” She turned and leaned her back against the shelves.
“How could you possibly guess? We haven’t even seen its shadow.”
“Precisely because we haven’t seen it.” She pointed at the shelves. “I know where it sits in the system’s ledger.”
She returned to the table, extended a dust-covered finger, and tapped the end of Chapter Two.
“‘Disposition, as used in these regulations, does not include the circumstances stipulated in Article 19 of Chapter Three.’” She pronounced each word clearly.
With a sharp slap, she closed the volume, stirring up a small cloud of dust.

“As long as it says ‘does not include Article 19 of Chapter Three,’ that means there’s another special circumstance among those who fail the baseline compliance review, one exempt from ordinary ‘disposition.

’ It could be a way out, or it could be a more secret destination—whatever it is, the red line is drawn before it.” She picked up the volume and put it precisely back into the empty space on the shelf.
“You’re not taking it because you’re afraid of being caught?” I asked.

“It’s because of the report.” Yuna patted the dust from her hands. “Otto and the others are watching me from the shadows now. If I cross this door and touch something on the restricted shelves now, they can immediately accuse me of ‘unauthorized violation’ and permanently strip me of the right to investigate.”
When we pushed open the heavy archive-room door, we ran straight into someone. It was Sera.
She wore a heavy pure-white cloak, half her face hidden in the shadow of its hood. She had clearly been waiting for us in the early-autumn night wind for a long time.
“Finished?” Her voice was calm, impossible to read.
“Finished with Chapter Two.” Yuna faced her without fear.
“The missing Chapter Three is on the marked shelves. I locked them.”
“I know. I didn’t touch it.”
Sera seemed satisfied with that answer. She nodded slightly and stepped out of the shadows.
“Come with me.” She gave the brief order, then turned and walked into the night.
She did not take us to the council hall. Instead, she went around to the back of the chapel by a route she clearly knew well.

It was an extremely secluded courtyard, one almost no one usually entered. I remembered coming here only once—long ago, when Yuna had mysteriously taken me by the hand and climbed over the wall to show me

a litter of wild kittens she had hidden in a haystack. In the center stood a well that had been dry for years. An old tree grew beside it, with several cold stone benches scattered beneath its branches.
Sera walked to the benches, sat down first, then pointed to the place opposite her.
“You left the village first thing this morning. Chiko’s cart.” She came straight to the point.
“Yes.” Yuna sat perfectly straight.
“You saw the people at the trading point.”
“We did. Old people, women, and children.”
Sera did not look at Yuna. Her gaze passed over the well and fixed on the old tree’s twisted branches in the moonlight.

“You’re probably wondering why, since I know the Inner Circle’s defenses don’t withstand scrutiny, I would willingly sit here and answer you.” Sera looked at her. “Because this afternoon, you could have consulted the

regulations directly, but insisted on getting Otto to sign that unnecessary slip, simply so you could lay your archive investigation out in the open. Someone who has only begun to investigate is most likely to mistake

themselves for a hero full of righteous passion. If I don’t open this account and force you to see how this village has survived, with your temper, you might go smash the restricted door to the archive room tomorrow.”
Yuna drew a deep breath and straightened her back.
“The people at the market, registered as assets—are they human, or are they machines?” She threw the question bare onto the stone table.
Sera looked at her and answered without hesitation:
“They’re human.”
Yuna’s chest rose sharply.
“If you know they’re human, and Chiko clearly knows that man’s name is Bak!” Yuna’s hands clenched into fists on her knees. “Then why can the village ledger record
only the batch numbers on their wrists when grain is distributed? Even if the village doesn’t have enough supplies, what would it cost to write down their names?”

“The moment the official ledger writes down their names, they stop being ‘asset consumption’ and become ‘starving fellow humans.’ What do you think will happen next when those softhearted people from the Inner Circle watch their kind starve?” Sera stepped closer, her gaze intensely oppressive.

“The hydroponic farms beneath the central village have a fixed output, just enough to feed the Inner Circle. The outskirts have several times as many laborers as we do, and they eat industrial synthetic waste that consumes no hydroponic resources. Once the ledger recognizes them as fellow humans, someone will propose improving their treatment, and someone will demand that hydroponic grain be distributed to them.”
Sera looked at us coldly.

“The moment those few mouthfuls become available, everyone’s rations will fall below the survival line. What happens when everyone starts going hungry? Someone will propose sacrificing the old people in the village who don’t work. Someone will

question why the elders who have changed bodies deserve double portions. Once the crack of ‘equal treatment’ is torn open, this order that has held for a hundred years will collapse completely over the scramble for food within three months.”

The wind stopped in the courtyard. Only the monotonous sound of dripping water came from the depths of the dry well. I looked at Sera’s profile in the moonlight and felt my stomach churn with nausea. But I also knew that as long as I continued eating the hydroponic food distributed by the village, I was indisputably enjoying the profits of their being treated as consumable materials.
“So to protect those rations, you can pretend they aren’t people.” Yuna did not retreat. “Then what about the beginning? If they couldn’t be fed, why create so many people from the outskirts?”
“Who do you think created them?” Sera gave a cold laugh. “More than a hundred years ago, the survival systems in these ruins were nearly paralyzed. To clear land and fill
pits, the first generation of us who woke up restarted a biological production line left over from the old era, manufactured the first batch of adult laborers, and used
rules to press them firmly into the lowest position. Later, the outskirts reproduced and made up the numbers themselves, so the Inner Circle stopped mass production.”
Sera placed a hand on the stone table and slowly sat back down.
“Once they’re born, they remain consumable materials registered under their mother’s batch. That’s the truth. This is the order we’ve maintained to this day.”
Yuna stared at her, her eyes cold as ice. There was no shock, and she did not answer. She seemed to be using all her strength to digest the enormity of the fact.
After a long while, Yuna finally spoke again.

“If there were even one person from the Inner Circle who couldn’t bear this bloody account, who stood up in front of everyone and said, ‘I’m going to expose this secret to the world,’ what would you do to them?” Yuna asked. “Would you activate Article 19?”
Sera looked at Yuna, bristling like a small animal with its fur raised.
“The Inner Circle doesn’t need Article 19.” She spat out the result cruelly. “The people from the Inner Circle who can access these core secrets have long had
their vital point seized by the elders—their allocation of a next body. If anyone betrays this survival system, the road to their ‘new life’ is permanently cut off.”

“In this system, a traitor doesn’t need to suffer physical punishment. When the body they have now naturally grows old, they simply lose every qualification to obtain new life. Do you think everyone will rebel for the sake of the secrets

they reveal? No. Everyone who knows and hopes to change bodies will compete to report them in order to keep their own allocation. Their friends will rush to sever ties with them. Even the evidence they produce will be destroyed by those

around them to protect themselves. They can only watch their peers regain youth while they themselves gradually grow old in isolation. Along with the truth they spoke, they will be buried by the entire village, united in its will to survive.”
I heard my own heartbeat pounding violently against my ribs.

Nine years ago, Father died because there was not enough medical allocation. The adults took away his body directly. There was no gravestone, and they left us none of his ashes. Yesterday, we couldn’t find anything about him on the terminal screen. Even the page belonging to him in the archive room had been cut away by a blade.
I suddenly remembered Sera refusing to answer my question about Father’s whereabouts in the isolation room a few days earlier. If the final fate of an Inner
Circle rebel was to have every trace erased, then had Father really not been ill? Had he been stripped of his right to live because he refused to be an accomplice?
“My father…” I suddenly stepped forward, my voice so hoarse it sounded strange even to me. “Was the page cut from his file because he produced some kind of evidence?”
Sera stood. She did not even turn to look at me. She simply walked around Yuna toward the courtyard gate. When she reached it, she stopped and turned halfway back.
“So, little girl, don’t think too highly of the people in this village. In this resource-monopolized village, all it takes is saying, ‘No.’”
When we came out of the back courtyard, Estelle was still waiting for us on the cold stone bench at the chapel entrance.
“Same as usual. One at a time.” She held the battered notebook and pointed toward the chapel’s side door. “Yuna, go wait inside. Arno speaks first.”
Yuna said nothing. She pushed open the door and entered the chapel.
I stayed in the courtyard. The matter of Father was a lump of pig iron lodged in my throat, but I knew this was not the time to ask Estelle. I forced myself to recount everything I had seen after

leaving the village that morning. When I told her that we were supposed to investigate the three carts, but Chiko had explicitly said they did not take that route at all, Estelle’s expression changed.
The hand holding her pen hung suspended in midair, the knuckles paling with the force. Those three carts had been our last lead in tracing Sarah’s whereabouts, and now that lead
had been cut off right before our eyes. But in the end she clenched her teeth and forced the rising emotion back down. In a hoarse voice, she said, “Continue with the rest.”
Only after I finished did Yuna come out and piece together what she had seen.
Estelle drew a deep breath and forced her attention back to the notebook.

“So,” she summarized, looking at us, “the supplies are checked against the wrist brands, and the child follows the mother with a secondary suffix. The official comes next month, wears only white, and we couldn’t find his title.”
Yuna leaned wearily against the wall, her hands in her pockets, and nodded.
“Last item. The woman today told me her name was Malda.”
Estelle’s hand stopped halfway through making two marks on the paper. She raised her head and looked at Yuna.
“You asked her.”
“Yes.” Yuna did not avoid the question.
Estelle watched her for two seconds, then wrote the name firmly beside the fourth item.
“Arno, who signed those regulations?”
“No one. Just three bare words: ‘Current Edition.’ There isn’t even a seal.”
“Every entry in the central village’s comings-and-goings accounts leaves a trace. Yet the highest rule governing the life and death of the entire outskirts doesn’t even have a signature.”
After leaving the chapel, I walked silently along the night road, taking Yuna home.
Neither of us spoke. Sera’s account of the manufacturing history, the dissenters whose traces had been erased, and the unresolved cause of Father’s death weighed on our backs like slabs of pig iron.
When we were almost at the gate of her shabby courtyard, she stopped. She did not open the door, only stood silently in the shadow before it.
After a long time, she slowly took the piece of sugar from her pocket and looked at it in the dim night.
“Sera has calculated this account very clearly,” Yuna said quietly, her thumb rubbing the rough edge of the sugar.

“As long as we keep eating the village’s food, we’re accomplices. But, Arno, I won’t accept the idea that we have to eat people in order to survive.” She turned around and pressed her hand hard against the mottled wooden door of her house, the knuckles paling with the force.

A cold wind of early autumn swept in from the end of the village road, stirring the dead grass with a rustle. She carefully put the sugar back into her pocket, then pushed open the door and stepped into the courtyard.

“These regulations have no signature.” She turned around, her back to the dim yellow light. “But if, over the past hundred years, there really was someone who thought this account was wrong and didn’t want to be an accomplice… those whose names were erased must have left traces.”
I had watched her read the ancient book in the chapel ever since she was old enough to understand what she was reading. She stood inside the doorway, her gaze calm and stubborn.
“Sera said the traitors would be buried together with the truth. Their words would never appear in ordinary records.” She gripped the doorframe tightly.

“First thing tomorrow morning, I’m going to look through the Scripture. Only something that everyone in the village has to read, and that no one would dare destroy on their own, could have preserved dissent.”

texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s16-: “Nothing. Reading it four times doesn’t add any words to it.” Her voice was level. “But the fact that I read it four times is itself a new record. That was the only thing I still had the right to do today.”

texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s21-: Sera reached the dry well, glanced at her, and sat on the stone bench on the other side of the dead tree. Between the two benches was a stretch of bare earth without paving stones, crossed by the tree’s tangled roots.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s26-: “I’m still here,” she replied, a little hoarsely, but without retreating.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s28-: “The escort on the supply cart a few days ago privately said he could take you out of the village, but you didn’t get on.” Sera sounded as if she were checking an account, without any hint of reproach. “As soon as he crossed the village boundary,

texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s36-: She looked directly at Sera and added, “That’s what the receipt says. As long as the elders’ final review hasn’t reached a result, everything remains ‘to be discussed.’ I’m waiting according to the literal meaning.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s40-: The backyard fell into a brief silence. The wind passed through, and the dead tree’s shadow swayed between them. Then Estelle asked the question.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s42-: “If I don’t return to the rented house on time tonight, or if I suddenly disappear here in this backyard, will the people responsible for the morning roll call notice?”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s45-: “No. The village’s accounts are divided into permanent residents and village candidates. Those two groups are checked by roll call every day.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s49-: “What about me? People who come from outside—where are they recorded?”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s51-: “The third set of accounts isn’t checked by roll call. It’s only a static record kept on file.” Sera looked at the dead leaves on the ground. “External security only handles whether anyone crosses the village boundary.

Inside the village, your current status is waiting to be sent away. Until the moment everyone gathers for the coordinated return trip after the end-of-week review, you won’t be among the people actually counted each day.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s54-: When she left, Sera lightly brushed a dead leaf from the stone bench. Before walking out of the backyard, the elder, who was always hard-edged, looked back at the charcoal and notebook in Estelle’s hands. Her gaze lingered there for several seconds. Then she said nothing, turned, and left the yard.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s57-: After Sera left, Estelle sat alone on that stone bench for a long time. Only when the sun shifted and the shadows in the backyard stretched longer and longer did she put away the notebook, stand, and return to the rented house.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s60-: Estelle stopped there and looked up at me.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s62-: “But today, I really was sitting there.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s64-: “So I record it myself.” She patted the notebook beside her. “I can’t record anyone else. I can’t manage the system’s accounts either. I only record myself.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s65-: On the yellowed pages, six lines were arranged in neat order. Each line briefly recorded what she had done that day: first day, initial assessment; second day, name withdrawn; third day, appeal; fourth day, restricted

waiting.
The fifth line was what she had written the day before yesterday: “Fifth day. Awaiting review, still here.”
The sixth line was what she had written yesterday: “Sixth day. Awaiting review, still here.”

In front of me, she picked up the charcoal and carefully added today’s entry:
“Seventh day. Awaiting review, still here.”
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s67-: The rented house was very quiet.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s68-: I looked at the short row of writing on the tabletop. In this village, my father had died, and the page about him in the register had been cut away in its entirety. He had disappeared like that, without even leaving behind a single line in his own hand.

Last night, Yuna and I had seen the severed edge left by the blade with our own eyes in the controlled archives. In the faint halo of light now, the sentence still sounded like an empty mutter in a dream.

texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s73-: “Then keep a record for him.” After a moment, she said it softly.
texts.chapter:volume0-backyard:event:text-s74-: She closed the notebook and tucked it carefully into her arms.

texts.chapter:volume0-doctrine-reversed:title: Chapter Six: Doctrine Turned Inside Out
texts.chapter:volume0-doctrine-reversed:event:: In the pitch-black sky, the distant White Tower was only a blurred outline. The long preliminary screening period was drawing to a close, and the formal post assignment review could be issued at any time.
I sat on the threshold of my house, the soreness from trudging beyond the boundary stone these past few days still lodged in my bones. Yuna came over through the darkness and sat down beside me.
She was clutching a book. It was a very old booklet, its cover rubbed soft by countless touches, its edges frayed.

“I lay down, and I closed my eyes.” She looked at the dirt beneath her feet, her voice hoarse. “But my head was full of things that didn’t add up. The consumables lists, the gaps in the medical records—they kept turning. I want to know whether the scriptures really hide traces left behind by the people who opposed them back then.”
She placed the booklet on her knees. Printed on the cover, in flaking gilt letters, was the title: The Church of Convergence Primer: The Dice-Thrower Watches.

“When I was seven, Sera gave me this primer. I memorized the doctrines in it for ten years.” Her fingertip traced the faded letters on the cover. “Once we pass the review, we’ll be assigned specific posts and placed under round-the-clock surveillance.”
I watched her in profile.
“Tomorrow afternoon’s candidates’ self-study period is our last chance. But think it through,” I said quietly. “After signing the acknowledgment with Otto, we’ve
already received one violation warning. If we’re caught during another intrusion, they’ll trigger a full isolation review. Then we won’t be able to investigate anything.”
Yuna silently looked down at the battered primer in her hands.

She lowered her head, fingers gripping the metal clasp of the old cloth band around her wrist, unconsciously turning it inward once. If we passed the review, this old cloth band would be taken away and replaced with a wristband equipped with real-time positioning, cutting off any possibility of unauthorized investigation for good.

“If we don’t find out where the rules that have always been wrapped around our necks came from, those internal qualifications are worthless to me. I’ve been looking at this primer for ten years. I don’t care about risking it one more

time.” Her voice was low, without hesitation. “I observed the condensation tower behind the hill these past two days. Every afternoon, there’s a maintenance window when the condensation tower on the north side of the controlled area

shuts down. Estelle also confirmed from the abandoned building plans that the connected backup ventilation shaft leads at its far end directly to the climate-controlled zone where the archive is located. We’ll investigate it tomorrow.”
The next day, 13:40.

The condensation tower’s blades had stopped turning. This was the only window when the connected backup ventilation shaft wouldn’t shred a person to pieces. The maintenance period lasted from 13:30 to 15:30 each day. We used the gap at noon, avoided the guards at the main entrance, and

crawled inside through the narrow maintenance duct. The disturbance we caused outside another abandoned exhaust outlet had already been discovered, and an additional ring of seals had been added around the perimeter. This new route, however, led directly into the depths of the archive.

Our toes touched the floor without triggering the alarm. The deep archive smelled of old paper and machine oil. Dense cabinets filled an entire wall, arranged like a maze and packed with records from years past.

Finding anything among that mountain of documents was like searching for a needle in the sea. We searched between the dusty cabinets by the faint glow of our flashlight. Most drawers had no clear labels. Yuna stubbornly

searched through revision records and drafts of the scriptures from past years, hoping to find a few words left behind by the erased dissenters in the marginal notes, but found nothing. During the first thirty minutes,

all we turned up were soulless official documents and abandoned pipeline layouts. As the wall clock passed 14:15, the maintenance window was slipping away minute by minute, and cold sweat began to seep across my back.
Yuna pulled open a drawer in an area marked “General Affairs and Logistics,” only to find rows of equipment purchase orders. We had no choice but to change tactics and search along the base of the
wall for the classification guide left behind from that time. At last, Yuna found a damaged Classification Index beneath a cart used to store discarded stationery. Following the blurred numbers in
the index, we pried open the bottom compartment of a cabinet deep inside marked “Local Settlement Planning” while searching for the lost Management Regulations, Chapter Three, and the dissenters’

manuscripts. Yuna found neither the manuscripts nor the regulations. Instead, she pulled a blueprint from a stack of damp, yellowing papers: Draft Physiological Specifications for Peripheral Populations.

We spread the blueprint in the shadows between two cabinets and examined it in the weak halo of the flashlight. The dense charts were divided into two broad categories. Yuna’s eyes stopped at the lower-left section, “Genetic Intervention Items for Peripheral Laborers.”

“Modification of the auditory cortex: forcibly induces strong neuronal resonance at specific low-frequency bands of the bell, triggering instinctive avoidance and panic.”
“Endocrine and neural compensation: locally increases susceptibility, lowers the reward threshold

for repetitive labor and collective prayer, and strengthens neural feedback.”
“Cognitive and memory regions: no knowledge preinstalled at manufacture. Obedience to instructions and common-sense systems must rely entirely on postnatal environmental conditioning.”
Yuna stared at those lines. Her fingers trembled faintly as they pressed against the cold printed text.

“So they… carved weaknesses into the body.” She murmured, her voice dry, trembling with a trace of disbelief. “No wonder. The groundless reverence in Marda’s eyes whenever she looks at me—it’s because her instincts are

more easily subdued by those above her and by rules. The irresistible fervor when they go to prayer, the way everyone instinctively shrinks back whenever the town’s great bell rings… If their bodies have been adjusted for

stronger reward feedback, and they instinctively panic at specific frequencies in the bell, what kind of devotion is that? What kind of reverence? They’re just exploiting physiological interfaces that have been altered!”
She drew a deep breath, as if trying to suppress the churning in her stomach, then turned sharply.

“But this isn’t enough. The draft says ‘no knowledge preinstalled at manufacture.’ A little neural feedback tuning can’t produce a complete doctrine and set of taboos.” Gritting her teeth, she swept the flashlight beam toward the

indoctrination archive opposite them. “Specific commands to obey, and the objects of fear, still have to be established through postnatal conditioning. I want to see when the doctrine they put into everyone’s heads was actually written.”
She placed her own primer, its edges curled, on the desktop and carefully opened it to Lesson Two. The footer of the page was stamped “Fifth Edition.”

Then, in an archive box, she found a stack of Textbook Revision Approval Sheets filed by year. As she went through them, she noticed several policy-setting dossiers from the early period: “Confiscated books left over from the old world, Compendium of Church of Convergence Doctrine

and related ritual materials. By decision, the original doctrinal system is to be retained as the foundation for peripheral settlements. Attached: minutes from the initial compilation of the public curriculum: remove all entries concerning advanced technology from secular textbooks.”

So that was it. They had not invented a god from nothing. The Church of Convergence had already existed in the old world. They had simply inherited the complete religious shell, using it to fill the void left by the removal of scientific knowledge, then crossed out with black ink in an office whatever parts they did not need.
She kept following the dates on the approval sheets backward and finally pulled out a yellowed piece of paper.

[Revision: Primer, Lesson Two (updated from the Fourth Edition to the Fifth Edition).
Assessment: As the peripheral settlements expand, directional guidance must be strengthened to unify procedures and reduce the cost of maintaining public order.
Resolution: Replace “In the face of the unknown’s arrangements, one should feel reverence” with “Obey without reservation.”]
Yuna glanced down at the line “obey without reservation,” printed clearly in her children’s book, then looked back at the assessment on the approval sheet. The doctrine that had once made her
doubt herself was merely an amendment approved in an office to reduce the cost of maintaining public order. She clutched the old children’s book tightly, her knuckles turning faintly white.

Immediately afterward, in the Defense Zone Infrastructure Approval Dossier from the same year, Yuna pulled out a voided old notice. It was the Safety Warning Notice for District Seven, and it read plainly: “The wasteland north of the setting sun: absolutely no passage. This is the wasteland upon which the gods have brought down their wrath.”
But on the approval sheet for the latest version, this boundary-crossing prohibition, regarded by countless people as sacred and inviolable, had been crossed out cleanly:

[Resolution: Revoke the northern warning.
Explanation: Phase Four of the high-voltage physical grid in this area has recently been completed. With the barrier active, there is no further need to rely on safety notices to prevent crossings.]
Yuna’s eyes swept over the densely packed approval-routing records. Every textbook revision had a procedure. Every prohibition imposed in the name of the gods had a signature.
A faint vibration of military boots striking the floor tiles came from deep in the corridor. The wall clock pointed to 14:45. It was nowhere near the normal end of the maintenance period.
This might have been a random surprise inspection—or perhaps the disturbance we had caused at the abandoned exhaust outlet a few days earlier had made them shorten the patrol intervals.
“The patrol team’s here.” I lowered my voice and pressed down on the edge of the dossier. “The originals have to go back.”
Yuna turned sharply toward me, her hand pressing hard against the approval sheet bearing the written directive, her eyes full of unwillingness to let go. She knew this was the most direct evidence.

“Memorize the approval date and the project number.” I stared into her eyes, speeding up. “Since Phase Four of the high-voltage physical grid has been completed, the barrier must really exist. If we ever get

the chance to go to the northern boundary, trigger that physical barrier in front of the others, and combine it with the date the Safety Warning Notice was publicly revoked… If those two dates line up exactly,

we can prove to everyone else that the so-called divine punishment never existed. It was only a high-voltage grid to keep people out, and the notice was just a tool to cover up the construction schedule!”
The boots drew closer. We could already hear belts rubbing against fabric. The electronic lock on the main door gave a faint preheating sound. The patrol team was preparing to open the door.
Yuna clenched her teeth, quickly committing the information from the draft and the notice to memory. Then she shoved all the documents back into place and smoothed the creases from the dossier.

At last, her eyes fell on the battered children’s book. Her hand paused in midair. I watched her, waiting for the tearing motion she might make. But she only squeezed her eyes shut, folded the booklet carefully, and slipped it into the pocket against her body.
She noticed me watching, but did not stop moving.

“The words in this book were changed on a whim.” She said softly, pressing a hand over the pocket through the fabric. “But ten years ago, on that afternoon when Sera held my hand and taught me to read from this booklet—that was real.”

The heavy iron door was shoved open, and flashlight beams swept into the dark archive like swords. We had already retreated into the ventilation duct along our original route one second earlier. As we crawled outward through the narrow duct, Yuna took one last look through the

grating at the row of cold, densely packed cabinets. The shadows of two guards fell across the cabinet doors as they checked the seals row by row. We did not dare stop. Before the condensation tower restarted, we followed the duct and vanished into the shadows behind the archive.
