texts.chapter:volume0-quarter-hour:event:text-:
Yuna’s booklet · The page for Day Seven of the first week (copied verbatim):
“Today: initial check of the relevant files.
I read the copies. Arno checks the originals.
Initial review of the first batch of suspicious names complete: the forty-four

people marked in bulk as ‘died of illness’ in the labor registry also appeared on the ‘Destruction List for Discarded Machinery Parts’ sent outside the village on the same day.
The outer-settlement laborers have no graves. If these forty-four people

really died of illness, then by convention they could only have been taken to the old pits in the back hills where diseased livestock was buried; if they were transported as discarded machinery parts, the destruction list should contain a receiving

acknowledgment from the destination station.
There are no new pits, and no receipt for scrap metal. On paper, all forty-four records simply end in midair.
Return: original shelf, original position.”
Appendix: End of page. The reverse is blank.
That was the evening of Day Seven of the first week.

As soon as we returned to the village that afternoon, Yuna went to Otto and had him sign out an access form. That evening, under the pretext of “reviewing after class,” we went straight into the reading room. In a blind corner, we completed the comparison of the first batch of suspicious files—some of the original documents concerning the falsification of the labor registry.
After we finished checking them, neither of us got up right away.
She sat hugging her knees on the stone steps behind the reading room, her chin resting on the back of her hand. I sat half a step away from her.

A breeze passed beneath the eaves, carrying the astringent scent of moisture. From the distant chapel bell tower came the dull sound of the evening bell. Closer by, I could hear the faint tapping of flying insects striking the glass of the street lantern

at the corner. She stared motionlessly at a tuft of weeds growing between the paving stones, her chest rising and falling slightly with the exhaustion of days spent under intense strain. I felt a heaviness seeping through the gaps between my bones as well.
We sat in silence like that for a full quarter of an hour. In the tense, covert investigation of the past few days, it was one of the few blank spaces we had. Neither of us said anything.

After a quarter of an hour, she lifted her chin and braced both hands behind her on the rough stone steps, tilting her head back slightly. There were no clouds that night, and the starlight was faint.
“Arno,” she said suddenly.
“Yeah.” I turned my head.

“If we really manage to find out where all those dozens of people went, and piece together the complete ledger…” She gave a small shake of her head, her eyes still fixed on the night sky. “Where are you planning to put it?”
“One copy is with you. One is with me.”
I realized only after answering that something was wrong.
She straightened and turned fully toward me.
“One copy tucked against my chest, one tucked against yours.” She looked at me, her eyes startlingly bright in the dimness. “And both of us are inside the boundary stones.”

“If one day someone inside the boundary stones decides to erase all of us, or take the papers from our hands, then everything that happened these past few days—all those people whose whereabouts were unknown in the registries—will be nothing but a hallucination that never happened.”
She extended one slender finger and pressed it hard against the hard, cold stone of the doorstep. It made a faint “knock.”
“We’re inside the game. Checking against each other ten thousand times won’t help.” She shook her head. “There has to be someone with both feet outside this ring of boundary stones, a living person
who isn’t part of this village’s system, to serve as our witness. They have to take this thing, carry it out to the outer settlements, and lay it out again in another parish or a Watermarsh camp.”
She slowly drew her finger back. Then she lowered her head and rubbed her sore, gritty eyes hard with the back of her hand. Her formerly straight back collapsed with exhaustion.
“Someone outside the boundary has to know… Inside this ring of boundary stones, power is the end of the line. There’s nowhere for us to appeal.”
She spoke slowly, her voice roughened by days of staying up late. She did not look at me, only at the blurred paving stones beneath her feet.
“Do you know anyone like that outside the boundary?”

“I don’t know. Maybe an old laborer from one of the outer camps, maybe someone who used to handle deliveries from them.” She looked at me. “I only know that when the ledger is complete, there isn’t a single higher

office inside this ring of stones that can rule in our favor. Leaving a ledger that could be confiscated at any moment inside the boundary stones overnight is more dangerous than handing it to just anyone outside.”
Yuna stood and dusted the dirt from her skirt.

Later that evening, we completed the final cross-check in the archive room. Just as we were about to leave, we ran into Sera in the hallway. It was 18:06 on Day Seven of the first week. A member of the Inner Circle seized all three of us on the spot.
It was a long standoff. Our request to formally leave the village was rejected outright.

By the time I had taken Yuna home and walked back to the yard where I lived, I was still going over and over what she had said on the reading-room steps, along with the situation after the evening’s confrontation.
It was already after eleven that night.
Before I reached the door, I heard Estelle’s footsteps. She had come around by the secluded path behind the house.

The path wound all the way from the chapel’s back courtyard, more than twice as far as taking the main street. The first thing I heard was not her breathing, but the faint sound of her soles crushing gravel. She did not walk quickly. Every step was steady, and she had deliberately chosen a hidden route.
At last, she stopped in the darkness outside the door.
“Still awake,” she said, her voice kept low.
“No. I can’t sleep.”

She did not sit on the doorstep. She stood in the shadows two steps away from me. Since returning her belt badge on the day her name was withdrawn, she had always held a frayed strip of burlap, its edges worn smooth. But in the middle of that night, her hands were empty, and her fingers dug hard into the back of her other hand.

“I can’t stay long.” She spoke quickly, with a trace of caution. “I took the chance to clear the leaves from the chapel’s back door, avoiding the eyes around the perimeter all the way back along the rear wall. I’ll have to go this way when I return, too.”
“That far? How long did it take you?”
“A little over a quarter of an hour, I think.”
I shifted to the side, making room for her on a clean stretch of doorstep.
She looked down at it but did not move.
“If we sit down to talk, it feels like we’ll be here a long time.”
Her clasped hands loosened for a moment, then tightened again.
“This afternoon, the deacon handling expulsion matters came over to the temporary lodging to check my file. While I was waiting in the hallway outside, I saw the clerk who came with
him casually throw out a curled, discarded approval slip from the stack for the 5th—the mark wasn’t from any of Watermarsh’s regular supply points, but the date matched exactly.” She
went straight to the point, watching me. “I know you went back to checking the accounts tonight. When you take notes in your room, are you keeping your inferences separate from the data?”
“I am,” I said. “The inferences never go on the same sheet as the original copies.”
“Not even with the central village archives?” she pressed.
“No. They’re physically separated.”
The tension in her shoulders eased slightly, and she gave a small nod.
“Good. They have to stay separate. Their origins are completely different. If someone asks later, you need to be able to say clearly which point was verified and which one we came up with ourselves.”
“But I made this trip tonight for something else.”

“Go ahead. This evening, Yuna and I cross-checked the first batch of names. The records for forty-four people who supposedly died of illness overlapped with the destruction list for machinery sent outside the village. Their whereabouts are unknown.”

“That’s exactly what I came to talk about. Checking only the central village archives isn’t enough. I know where all of Watermarsh’s supplies go. Those forty-four people you found records for didn’t go into the burial pits outside the village, and they

never entered any of Watermarsh’s regular receiving points.” She took a deep breath. “This evening, I looked along the chapel’s rear wall. The old pits where diseased livestock used to be buried don’t have a single deep track from a heavy vehicle. If dozens

of people had gone through there, the regular routes couldn’t hold them. If you can keep tracing the village’s outbound records and compare them against the blind spots I’ve checked, we can narrow it down to a route that exists only outside the accounts.”
“What are you trying to say?”
“If we really can get this complete ledger, where exactly are you planning to take it?”
Her hands, which had been clasped tightly in front of her, shifted against each other with force. The knuckles had gone slightly white.
I opened my mouth.
“Yuna just said that the moment we had the complete ledger, we should find any outsider who could serve as a witness. We couldn’t wait.”

The words had already risen to the tip of my tongue. But when I looked at Estelle’s whitening fingers, I stopped. In the dead of night, she did not even feel safe sitting beside me, and she had repeatedly

asked whether the records were physically separated. If I told her now that Yuna intended to leave the central village and intercept someone outside the perimeter the very day we obtained the complete ledger…
I clenched my teeth and swallowed Yuna’s name.
“Nothing’s been decided yet.”

“Since it hasn’t been decided, I’ll tell you what I think first.” She did not seem to notice my hesitation. “What I need to warn you about is that you absolutely cannot count on any existing verification procedure.”
She moved half a step forward without meaning to, nearly stepping onto the edge of the doorstep.

“You may be thinking that one day, once you’ve finished investigating all this in the village, you can put the ledger on the desk of some elder or office.” She shook her head. “No. You only have to open the access list for their system to understand—there is no appeals threshold

higher than the central village hall. Once something deadly enters an ordinary channel, whoever takes it up, it will ultimately be closed within the same access structure. It will immediately receive a number, be locked in a cabinet, and be signed off by whoever is on duty.”
Her chest rose and fell slightly. She stopped to catch her breath.
“Once it’s locked in a cabinet, the only thing announced to the outside world will be: ‘This matter has been handled according to procedure.’”
“You… You’ve actually seen something like that?”

“I once tried to verify the provenance of an old file concerning the allocation of funds for an external assignment. There was no signature on it, only a seal.” She was silent for several seconds before speaking slowly. “The date on the seal indicating that the matter had been closed was absurdly earlier than the day the first

receipt had been issued. The matter hadn’t even happened, and the conclusion had already been stamped, sealed, and locked in a cabinet. During my report at the beginning of the week, I asked one extra question about that file. At the candidate eligibility assessment that afternoon, they unanimously voted to withdraw my name.”
She looked at me, her eyes holding a bone-deep coldness.

“Sera only told people outside that it was ‘not itemized,’ but I secretly checked that vote. Unanimous. I offended the entire council of elders with one sentence, and they unanimously threw me out. I’ve experienced this black box that buries living people inside a stamping procedure once. I won’t gamble on a second time.”
“After you were caught this evening, your previous plan to ‘wait for a gap in the procedures’ no longer works. What are you planning to do now?”

“I’ll take it out myself.” She looked into my eyes and spoke each word distinctly. “Since the official road out of the village has been sealed off, we can’t keep waiting passively. If there’s no gap within the procedures, I’ll carry the ledger myself across the boundary stones and find a witness outside.”
It was deep into the night, and the silence around us had become frightening.
“As someone whose name has been withdrawn, you’ll have eyes on you everywhere. What if they stop you on the way?”
“Then that’s still better than leaving the ledger in the village and waiting for official procedure to destroy it,” she answered without hesitation.
“Do you think… what I’m doing is too reckless?” she suddenly asked, a trace of panic showing in her voice.
“No.”

“But I’m afraid too.” She gave a bitter smile. “This evening, as I looked toward the chapel, I hesitated too. But I have no idea what chance these extra two days could possibly bring. I’m just afraid that if I keep waiting, I’ll lose even the chance to make this choice.”
I looked at her fingers, clenched white from digging into her own hand, and said nothing.
“You should go back soon,” I said softly. “When we reach the final step of the investigation, I’ll tell you.”
Estelle glanced at me.
“Okay,” she said.

She turned and walked back along the secluded path. The sound of her soles crushing gravel rose again, receding from near to far, until it vanished when she stepped onto the soft meadow behind the chapel.

After I went inside, I felt around in the dark and pulled out a blank sheet of trimmed paper. I wanted to record the situation tonight, to sort out some kind of thread. But as soon as I picked up the pen, I stopped.
I sat there in the darkness.

Just two hours ago, Yuna had been desperate to hand the evidence to any outsider who could serve as a witness. Now Estelle likewise did not trust the ordinary channels, but had decided to carry the evidence across the boundary herself, gambling on the chance of making it through the boundary stones.
If I told Estelle now that Yuna intended to hand it over the moment she obtained the complete ledger, or told Yuna that Estelle intended to carry the ledger out herself…
In the darkness, I slowly crumpled the trimmed sheet, still blank of even a single word, into a ball and clenched it tight in my palm.
texts.chapter:volume0-fourteen-hours:title: Chapter Seven: Fourteen Hours
texts.chapter:volume0-fourteen-hours:event:tex:
Candidate Course · Third-Stage Delivery List (classroom wall, same day):
I. The soul-fire and the promise of continuance.
II. The old-city ruins and restricted directions.
III. Baseline capacity.
Addendum: After this stage, candidates enter the end-of-week review.

After making it through that night, we sat down in that classroom on time at eight in the morning of the seventh day of the candidate process. The morning sunlight had not yet reached the narrow windows high above, and a penetrating chill seeped through the stone walls.
Sera was there. Otto was there too. He held a piece of charcoal and a writing board, his face set as stiffly as it was when mediating disputes.
Today, the small section of the classroom wall illuminated by a special device bore three lines.

“You’ve been hearing it since birth. The villagers call it the tower’s breath, and tell the children from the periphery that it is the sanctuary breathing.” Sera stood at the head of the long table. “The catechism says it is the soul-fire granted by the Dice-Thrower. As candidates, you must protect this flame.”
She paused and let her gaze pass over us.

“If you pass the review at the end of this week, you will be inducted. The Dice-Thrower will grant you the ‘right of continuance.’ You will gain the qualification to cross beyond this mortal body and share eternity with the Inner Circle.”
She spoke of the immortality promised by divine grace, but her hands were doing something entirely different.
She reached out and opened the heavy hardbound folder on the table. It did not contain a catechism, but an engineering ledger from the elders’ court, its pages yellowed with age and untouched
by religious embellishment. She spread it directly across the table, as though testing whether we would show a crack when faced with the technical reality beneath the sugar coating of faith.

The ledger was divided into four columns. The first was an encrypted batch number, the second read “reserve reading,” and the third “loss replenishment.” The fourth had no heading, but was covered with controlled red stamps used to approve intake. There were

no prayers, only long strings of dense, fluctuating raw data. Every sharp drop in the reserve reading was followed by a note of a massive replenishment allotment, while the bottom of every fluctuation was held up by a glaring red line at the bottom of the page.
Yuna reached out and turned the ledger toward herself. Her eyes moved quickly over the pages, her finger tracing down the rows of plunging readings.
“What are you looking for?” Sera asked.
“How many times it drops.” Yuna did not look up.
“When you’ve counted them, say the number aloud.” Sera watched her. “We need to record your reactions to this genuine ledger.”

Yuna’s finger stopped at the edge of a page. I sat beside her and followed her fingertip. It was an especially steep drop. In the third column, a massive replenishment batch had been entered immediately afterward, with the number “B-73.”

I recognized the number. It was the code the Inner Circle security force had used to identify the detention batch during last month’s unrest in the periphery. Two full rows of peripheral people had been marched away in a long line, never to return.

Yuna continued flipping upward. Beside the replenishment batches associated with the massive plunges in the readings, the dates all matched, precisely, the points over the past several years when large numbers of laborers had disappeared from the periphery.
This naked technical ledger did not explain what material was used for replenishment. But alongside the disappearance records, every deep pit left by a plunging reading came with the
disappearance of living people. Sera had deliberately brought it out to test us—the ordinary candidates who had never seen the lower-level records would see only a mass of abstract industrial loss.
Yuna’s finger hovered over the page.
“Not saying.” She did not look up.
The air suddenly turned colder. Otto frowned, and his charcoal dragged heavily across the writing board. I straightened my back without thinking.
The red line on the ledger remained glaring. Yuna pressed down on its edge, her knuckles whitening.
Sera neither pressed her nor objected. She only gave a cold nod on the candidate assessment form.
II. Mortal remains and restricted directions.

It was Otto’s turn to take over. The tall, broad-shouldered, rigidly upright middle-aged man stepped forward, pulled a wrinkled parchment terrain map from his sleeve, and spread it across the long table. Three areas had been marked with heavy black circles.

“The first: the area below the fourth underground level of the White Tower. The second: the old city’s central district to the east. That is where the mortal remains of the sinners of the old era are sealed away. It is filled with contamination.”
He took the long string of wooden tokens used for mediating disputes from his belt. His long, strong fingers rolled them, rubbing one loose with a faint click.

“The third.” His finger touched the edge of the map to the northwest. “That is an old facility no one is permitted to approach. Any person from the periphery, once they come within a certain distance, will begin to feel dizzy and suffer heart palpitations, and finally develop an irresistible urge to turn around.”
Another wooden token slipped free.
“These are the words used in boundary files from decades ago. But there are no checkpoints around the third area, because checkpoints simply aren’t necessary.”
Yuna’s back went rigid.
“No checkpoints because they can’t approach it.” She stared at Otto. “Is there some kind of interference source near that old facility that triggers physiological abnormalities in them?”
“People born in the Inner Circle don’t have that reaction. I went there myself once when I was young. I felt nothing unusual.”

This confirmed what we had seen yesterday in the Peripheral Physiological Specifications Draft: peripheral people were written at manufacture with a defect that triggered instinctive avoidance in response to specific frequency

bands. If that facility happened to emit signals in those bands, peripheral laborers would instinctively want to flee as soon as they approached, while people from the Inner Circle could pass through without obstruction.
“What exactly is hidden there that requires a physiological barrier aimed only at people from the periphery?”

“I’m only responsible for delivering the directions,” he answered stiffly. “Why these measures are used is outside the scope of my delivery. Not a single page of the catechism requires me to answer you.”
Yuna’s fingers clenched around the edge of the table. Otto glanced at her and said, without making it clear whom he was addressing, “I’ll remember that.”
III. Baseline capacity.
Sera took over again for the third item. She pulled two sets of materials from the bottom of the folder and pushed them directly toward us.
This was the physiological specifications table that had finally been issued. It was filled with requirements concerning bone density and neural reflex thresholds, but every
parameter had already been stamped with a cold verdict: “Compliant.” And in the identification field at the top, a classification prefix had been added before my name: “N-.”

At the very bottom of the last page, there was one solitary term, followed by an empty box for a number.
The term was “baseline capacity.” The box was blank.
“What does this mean?” Yuna stared at the empty field.

“It is simply a standardized form copied from another source. As candidates, you are required to have this field on your forms, but I have no authority to explain its meaning, and I cannot tell you what number

should go in it.” Sera’s answer left no opening. “As for the comparative data you would need to fill in the number, that belongs to the controlled maintenance catalog. It is not administered by the course.”
Sera closed her heavy elders’ court lesson plan.
“That concludes today’s lesson. To prepare for the end-of-week review, go over your catechisms.”
She said nothing else, turning and leaving the classroom with Otto.

We spent a long time in the classroom going over those fragmentary surface materials again and again. When we opened the door and stepped into the corridor, Estelle was standing in the shadow of a torch.

Her name had been withdrawn. Under the rules, she had now entered the appeal waiting period and was staying in the village as a restricted visitor until the group returned at the end of the week. But she absolutely

should not have been allowed to remain near the candidate classroom. She was looking down at her toes; she had no idea how long she had been standing there. A patrol had just passed by without stopping to drive her away.
That deliberate, tacit permission was terrifying.
Estelle raised her head and glanced toward the far end of the corridor.
“The patrol has circled back. I’ve been standing here too long. I can’t stay any longer.” She stepped back.
“We’ve matched some of the material we pulled yesterday.” Yuna lowered her voice. “Let’s talk somewhere else. Where can we find you later?”
“No. Piece together the rest yourselves. You don’t need to come tell me what numbers you calculated.”
“Why?”

“The fallback has to be physically isolated. If all three of us know the core secret at the controlled level now, then once the reckoning comes, there won’t even be one person left alive outside to maneuver.”

She paused.
“For the next few days, I’ll stay in the peripheral area and wait for the return vehicle at the weekend. Don’t come looking for me. I won’t contact you either.”
Estelle did not wait for our answer. She turned and hurried into the shadows at the other end of the corridor.

Watching her back disappear, Yuna gave me a signal with her eyes. We immediately left that exposed corridor and went down the stairs to an abandoned storage room. After confirming that no one was nearby, Yuna took out what I had brought from the Inner Ring archive transfer area at dawn.

It wasn’t an infiltration. The door to the deeper area remained firmly locked. But during a five-minute gap between shifts, I pulled these scattered scraps through a gap in the cart used to transport files awaiting destruction. I hid them in my sleeve and handed them to her before the morning lesson.
Now, in the weak light, we spread them out.
The first scrap was a crumpled Table Comparing Carrier Types.

It contained only three rows of extremely simple data:
The category name in the first row had been neatly blacked out, and the capacity field contained a very small single-digit number.
The second row read “ordinary surviving

old-era people,” with a baseline capacity of approximately 1 unit.
The third row read “high-capacity carriers,” with a baseline capacity of approximately 10000 units. The identification-code prefix on the left was N-.

The identification prefix on my physiological specifications table from class was N-. Yuna took out hers as well. Exactly the same.
“This isn’t just our identification number.” Yuna stared at the table, her voice tightening.

She meant Remy, the patient in the southern district who had been bedridden for years. Apart from the pre-catastrophe old personalities bearing old-era codes, Yuna, Remy, and I were the only three naturally born people of our kind in this village, from the first

round of natural births roughly seventeen years ago to the present. Remy had never taken part in the candidate process, but when Yuna brought her medicine before, she had confirmed that the prefix on the nameplate beside her bed was exactly the same as ours: N-.

“If ten thousand is a specification even someone paralyzed like Remy possesses, then this ‘capacity’ is absolutely not an ability gained through health and training. It’s a fundamental structure built into the few of us at

manufacture,” Yuna said in a low voice.
On the surface, the Inner Circle’s candidate courses demanded extremely high neural reflexes and physical fitness. But over the past few days, what they had actually spent so much effort

testing was our judgment and our reactions to classified information. In the end, they were calculating which of those carrying this fundamental ten-thousand-unit structure could keep a secret, and which posed the least political risk.
They were only selecting heirs who could be safely absorbed into the Inner Circle—or operators for some dangerous device.
But Yuna did not let the feeling of being examined as a tool linger for long. Her eyes fixed themselves on another scrap I had brought out today.

The second scrap had no heading or signature. In the upper right corner was the red intake stamp of the elders’ court controlled archives. The footer read “Laboratory Abandoned Documents / Destruction Group-4.”
Yuna read the passage aloud in a low voice.

“‘…The old device’s retroactive limit is positively correlated with the carrier’s baseline capacity. Measured results show that, under standard configuration, the maximum usable duration of this limit for ordinary carriers

(baseline approximately 1 unit) is approximately five seconds. When the baseline capacity of a high-capacity carrier reaches approximately 10000 units, this limit expands proportionally. See Appendix 1-A for the projection diagram.’”
She raised her head, pressing her finger against the illustration in the appendix.

“Look at the coordinate system in this diagram. The horizontal axis is time offset Δt.” She pointed to an arrow extending in the reverse direction. “The origin is the moment the device starts, and this curve is entirely on the negative side. That means its direction of action is interference into the past.”
Her fingertip slid along the line to its lower end.

“The limit for an ordinary carrier is five seconds, expanded proportionally by a capacity of ten thousand…” Yuna stared at the estimated interval on the horizontal axis and spoke under her breath. “Approximately fourteen hours. And the chart notes

also say that the limit of a single activation cannot be accumulated iteratively. This capacity data isn’t consumed as fuel. It’s more like a fixed physical scale that determines the maximum window in which this device can interfere with the past.”
“Approximately fourteen hours?” I looked at the chart. “If this document is talking about some machine that can interfere with the past, then fourteen hours is its physical dead line…”
“Fourteen hours. No matter where this device is or exactly how it’s operated, it has been marked with this limit.” She clutched the pages.
Now and then, wind passed through the ventilation opening of the storage room with a low moan.
The transfer cart from dawn today. The old scraps scattered in the gaps, within reach of my hand.

“This isn’t a coincidence.” I thought of Sera taking out the engineering ledger just now to test our reactions. “They knew what we were investigating all along. Those scraps were deliberately left on the cart.”
“This was bait before the net closed.” Yuna raised her head, her eyes cold enough to frighten me.
No wonder they had allowed Estelle to stand outside the classroom door today. No wonder the cart had been left somewhere unattended. That incomplete file was both a warning and an open card.

The Inner Circle was showing us the card in its hand, displaying that fourteen-hour interference window. And Estelle had just cut off the flow of information between us, staying alone in the peripheral area to wait for the return vehicle at the weekend. She thought physical isolation

could protect the secret, but did not know that the isolation had turned her into an isolated target that could be removed at any time. We could not follow her physically, and we had no way of knowing exactly where she would go or whom she would contact over the next few days.

If the Inner Circle decided to move against her before the weekend, then as long as it locked the situation in place for more than fourteen hours, no matter where the device shown in the diagrams actually was, or whether it truly existed, every possible interference would already have fallen beyond the physical dead line.

texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s1-1:

in the time of departure.

(There is another entry beneath the last line, in a different color of ink: This line was filled in by the officer on duty. The person who filled it in did not sign.)
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s5-1: It was evening. The setting sun stretched the shadows along the village road. A little after two this afternoon, we had pieced together the scattered copies from the past few days in the outer reading room. Now, on the way back to our lodgings, Yuna and I looked over the final record we had assembled.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s7-1: “The dates all line up.” I looked at the dark-red road ahead and lowered my voice. “The changes to the freight-truck schedule fall exactly on the days the doctrine was revised.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s9-1: “But all we have are copies.” Yuna walked beside me without looking at me. “If we accuse them with something we wrote ourselves, they only need one sentence to dismiss it—‘You forged this.’”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s12-1: She raised her hand and turned the clasp on her sleeve once. The metal made a faint scraping sound.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s14-1: “We have to get the originals out—the ones bearing the Inner Circle’s signatures.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s17-1: She put her hand into her pocket and pressed down on the notebook inside, filled with new notes.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s19-1: “We only entered the outer reading room this afternoon. We have to go back into the core restricted zone and get the original signed revision order. That’s the only way this hand can stay alive.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s20-1: So we turned around and headed back. We intercepted Estelle along the route she took after her shift and brought her with us. She knew which cabinets in the restricted zone held the supplies and risk reports. Taking someone without
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s20-2: authorization along with us already violated the separation agreement we had made that morning, but with less than twenty-four hours until tomorrow’s final review, this was our only chance to turn a lone piece of evidence into proof.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s21-1: All three of us knew there would be risks if we went in. None of us suggested going back to our lodgings.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s26-1: When the three of us entered the Controlled Archive Room together, the hands on the wall clock had just passed half past five. The air inside was dry and heavy.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s28-1: The door closed behind us. Estelle turned and pressed down on the bolt. With a click, she locked the door.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s30-1: “The people outside have already seen us come in.” She glanced through the crack in the door, her voice suddenly taut. “There are lookouts watching both ends of the corridor. Just before we came in, someone had already filled in the entry time and ‘three persons’ on the register outside…”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s31-1: “Then why didn’t you say anything before we came in?” Yuna blurted out.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s32-1: “There was no way back in the corridor. If we stopped to whisper at the sign-in desk or turned around and ran, the hidden posts would have arrested us immediately.” Estelle leaned against the door, her knuckles white. “Once we came in and locked it, they wouldn’t rush in right away.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s33-1: We had already stepped onto the line.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s34-1: “Why aren’t they arresting us right away?” I lowered my voice.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s35-1: “They’re waiting to catch us in the act.” Estelle said, “They’re waiting for us to pull out the classified originals, or put the copied material into our pockets. Only hard evidence of theft can make the capital charge stick. They’ll hold the corridor outside and search us when we leave.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s36-1: “Then we’ll put down what we brought and leave empty-handed,” I said at once.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s38-1: “If we go out now, they’ll question and search us. We’re finished if they find the copies on us. We can’t hide anything in the room either. Once they decide to close the net, they’ll tear up even the floorboards.” Yuna lowered her voice. “This
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s38-2: afternoon, when I went to the prayer room, I deliberately checked the security maintenance schedule on the wall. 6:06 is the power-outage self-check for the restricted zone. The security monitors and corridor lights will have a two-minute blind spot.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s38-3: And… evening prayer in the chapel next door ends at exactly that moment. During those two minutes with the lights out, the lookouts’ vision will be blocked. If we blend into the crowd leaving prayer, that’s our only chance to leave the central zone.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s39-1: In other words, we had to endure inside this trap, under the watch of the hidden posts outside the door, until 6:06, and gamble on those two minutes of darkness and the departing crowd.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s41-1: “This is the supplies schedule I copied outside.” Estelle pulled a slip from her pocket and pinned it beneath the corner of the table, then stepped back two paces, deliberately avoiding the manuscript in Yuna’s hands.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s42-1: The only sound left in the room was the rustle of pages being turned rapidly.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s45-1: It grew dark. I took down an oil lamp, lit it, and placed it in the center of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s46-1: We went through the records of deletions and revisions one by one as quickly as we could.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s50-1: Afterward, following the clues in the copies we had made over the past few days, Estelle went to the gray metal cabinet outside where the risk assessments were stored. She searched through a stack of files for a moment, then pulled one out and placed it on the table. Yuna voluntarily moved the consolidated manuscript she had brought beyond the safe distance at the very edge of the wooden table.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s52-1: “Found it. File R-409, ‘Supplementary Opinion on Candidate Political Risk.’” She pressed her palm against the paper she had just pulled out. “Five days ago, this was what kicked me out of candidacy. The violations attached to you two were added by him afterward, too. The signature at the bottom is Otto’s.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s55-1: Yuna reached for the file. Estelle’s hand stayed pressed on top of it.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s57-1: “Before you look at it, note how it’s arranged. We’ll have to put it back in the metal cabinet exactly as it was.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s58-1: Only after Yuna had confirmed it did she take her hand away. The file opened to reveal, on the first page, the clearly written reason: “External candidate… her return to the outer settlements would constitute an ongoing risk.” From the moment she opened that page, I felt that
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s58-2: her eyes remained fixed on the spacing between the lines on the first page, never moving down to the body below. She did not touch the second page. Instead, she pulled two more sheets from another stack of archived files and placed them side by side at the corner of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s60-1: “Look at these two original revisions. They were changed on the same day. One moves the legally prohibited boundary inward on the map, and the road it opens is exactly the shortcut used by the freight trucks. The other deletes the entire section on prohibited directions from Lesson Nine of the doctrine.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s61-1: Yuna swept her eyes over them once, her brows drawing together.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s63-1: “They changed the boundary of the prohibited zone to clear a path for the freight trucks, then changed the doctrine to make the boundary fit.” Yuna reached out and tapped the two sheets. “This isn’t just concealment. It’s systematic erasure. The signatures on the backs of both sheets are still Otto’s.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s68-1: The wick in the oil lamp spat. The hands passed 5:50.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s72-1: “Arno,” Yuna asked as she turned a page, “if tomorrow we pretend we saw nothing, pass the review, and accept our posts, what then?”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s74-1: “I’ll get access to the White Tower.” I looked at the flour stains that would not wash from my knuckles. “I’ll find out what’s really behind my father’s record, stamped ‘Archive Frozen.’ It’s a chance that opens only once every ten years.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s76-1: “Fine. What about me? Go read the machine’s daily readings to seven-year-old children and tell them it’s worship?”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s79-1: She watched the pages, her voice calm but without warmth.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s81-1: “When I was seven, no one told me it was a lie. I don’t want to tell them that now. I’m taking these two originals to the outer settlements tonight to find someone.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s83-1: “The people we ran into in the alley last night.” She watched the pages, her voice calm but without warmth. “The receivers who aren’t governed by the village rules, or the outer patrols. As long as they still believe in the original doctrine, these hard proofs of tampering can set the outer settlements alight.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s84-1: I looked at her. Once that path beneath the surface was brought into the light, I would not only lose my access to the White Tower. I would stand directly against the Inner Circle.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s85-1: The version of me who had spent his hands in mill oil and calculated how to win the candidacy had been cracked open by fact after fact over these past few days. The freight trucks whose routes had been cleared, the doctrine erased systematically, and the two originals on
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s85-2: the table bearing signatures from the same day. Even if I took the post and investigated the frozen record from back then, the things they had covered up would not change. But if I withdrew now, the moment Yuna stepped out of this room, it would become a capital offense.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s86-1: The cold sweat was clammy and icy. I closed my eyes for a moment in the dim lamplight, dug my fingers into my palm, then opened them and looked at Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s88-1: “I’m going with you.” I looked at her, my voice hoarse. I knew that saying those four words meant burying with my own hands the chance I had waited ten years for—to investigate the old records. But I couldn’t watch her push that door open alone.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s89-1:
Yuna’s tightly pressed lips moved. She stopped turning the pages and looked at me. After a long moment, she nodded hard.
“We’ll go together,” she said softly, but her voice was steady.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s92-1: Estelle stopped at the corner of the table, squared the original R-409, and slowly put it back into the gray metal cabinet.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s94-1: “Then I can’t go with you either.” She turned to look at us. Her expression was much calmer than when she discovered we were being watched, as if she had confirmed something she had expected all along.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s96-1: “I told you last night that I wouldn’t expose myself before the repatriation appeal was decided.” As she pushed the cabinet door shut, she said, “But if you’ve decided to meet the elders in the outer settlements tonight, I have to stay here. I can’t leave.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s97-1: “As long as I don’t touch the prohibited copies or originals, I’m just someone who wandered into the restricted zone. Since my repatriation appeal is still in its waiting period, even if Sera sends people in to arrest me, she won’t dare strip me of my
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s97-2: right to go through the procedure.” She straightened, her fingers leaving the metal door, and pointed at the two originals we had just examined on the table. “But if I’m the only one left in this room with the prohibited originals on the table, then
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s97-3: to stop me from continuing to look through them, the people who come in will have to complete the on-site sealing procedure according to the rules and freeze everything. At least that will ensure the originals in this room aren’t destroyed in secret.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s98-1: Neither Yuna nor I said anything. Yuna looked at the notebook in her hands, her fingers tightening slightly. I turned instead to Estelle. She had deliberately returned the file to its place, carefully avoiding every touch of the manuscript.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s98-2: Now she was invoking the rules governing an appeal’s waiting period, trying to remain here on the strength of her awkward status as someone awaiting judgment. She wanted to become a living lock, securing this room full of originals.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s100-1: Time passed six o’clock. The expected guard change never came. The corridor outside was utterly quiet. There was not even the sound of footsteps. Time was running short.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s101-1: “The final new note has been checked and folded into the file.” Yuna closed the manuscript and let out a long breath.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s102-1: The black hands on the wall had already moved toward 6:04.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s103-1: We hurriedly tucked the copies into my and Yuna’s pockets separately. At the edge of the wooden table, only the two original revisions we had just examined lay quietly beneath
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s103-2: the oil lamp. Yuna still held the consolidated manuscript in her hands. We had to prepare to blend into the crowd immediately; there was no time to restore the two originals.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s105-1: The corridor lights gave a barely audible hum as the power grid began its self-check, then went out. The red light on the surveillance camera outside the door disappeared. The two-minute blind spot had begun.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s106-1: The half-closed wooden door was pushed open.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s110-1: Bright light from the lantern in his hand poured into the room. The three of us stopped at once.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s111-1: His eyes swept rapidly over the original revisions left at the corner of the table and the supplies schedule Estelle had set down earlier, then fell on the obvious bulges in my and Yuna’s pockets, and on Yuna’s hand clenched tightly around the consolidated manuscript.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s116-1: “What time is it?” he asked, speaking very quickly.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s118-1: “6:06.” Yuna looked at him, one hand pressed against her pocket.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s119-1: Otto came over. His lantern cast wavering light and shadows across the table. The blind-spot window was shrinking second by second.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s121-1: “This morning you asked me what exactly was hidden inside the old facility. I told you that wasn’t within my scope of delivery. So you came here to search the originals for the answer.” He stared at Yuna’s pocket. “And you finished copying them.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s128-1: “You don’t have permission to enter this room.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s130-1: “Someone outside filled in ‘three persons’ for me, and there was no way back through the corridor. I came in myself.” Estelle did not retreat.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s131-1: Otto pointed at the file in the corner of the table. “Not confiscated cleanly?”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s135-1: Otto slammed the lantern down on the table. The glass chimney gave a dull knock.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s138-1: “Besides these three sheets, what else did you find?”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s139-1: Yuna suddenly straightened, both hands behind her back.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s141-1: “Evidence of how the village decides who gets to live.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s143-1: “Everything in your pockets and in your hands—put it all out and leave it on the table! Follow me. You’re coming with me now.” His voice was low, but sharp as a blade.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s145-1: “I’m not going.” Estelle’s hands pressed hard against the wooden edge of the table. “As long as I don’t touch the copies or originals, you can only treat me as someone who wandered in. My appeal is still in its waiting period. You can’t strip me of my right to remain at the scene and demand the sealing procedure—”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s147-1: “Why should we hand it over to you?” Yuna gritted her teeth and took a step back, shielding the manuscript against her chest. I stepped forward and stood in front of her.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s151-1: “Because Sera’s people are outside that door.” Otto’s voice was like cold iron, cutting through Estelle’s fantasy at once. “They’re waiting in the corridor because they’re here to catch a theft in the act. If you stay here and get caught, you’re not someone
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s151-2: who ‘wandered into the restricted zone.’ You’re ‘aiding and abetting theft of classified information.’ Your right to appeal will be stripped immediately. You won’t even have the right to go through the procedure. The originals will be taken away anyway.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s152-1: He pointed at the tabletop, leaving no room for argument.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s154-1: “Leave every copy written in the new notes’ handwriting, along with the originals here.” He spoke rapidly, pulled a key from his belt, and locked the archive room’s front door with a click. Then he pointed at the ventilation
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s154-2: shaft inside. “Once they break through the front door and discover that the classified contents have been searched, Sera’s rule is that they must first surround the entire room and inventory every original. No splitting up.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s154-3: The front door is locked now, so it’ll take them some effort to break through. I can use those ten minutes while they inventory everything and smash the door to get you out through the ventilation shaft and onto the back route.”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s155-1: Only a few dozen seconds remained in the blind spot. If we carried any copies or originals on us, there was no way we could pass through the net of searches outside. And Estelle’s trump card had been mercilessly exposed by Otto.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s156-1: Under the dim yellow light, we gritted our teeth and pulled the two copies from our pockets. Yuna also pressed the consolidated manuscript onto the table. Six things remained on the tabletop: the two copies, Yuna’s consolidated manuscript, Estelle’s
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s156-2: supplies schedule, and the two original revisions we had not had time to put away. R-409 lay exactly as it had before in the metal cabinet Estelle had returned it to. The evidence was still there. It had simply become a bomb locked inside this room.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s160-1: We followed him out in silence.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s163-1: We entered the back route through the ventilation shaft. As we stepped through the side door leading to the north wall, the surveillance camera above the main corridor flickered once, and its red light came back on. The two-minute power self-check was over.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s164-1: Yuna glanced back through the side door.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s165-1: At the end of the corridor, the door to the archive room stood half-closed. The oil lamp was still lit. Otto had not touched the originals, had not touched the copies, and had not even put out the lamp.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s170-1: Outside the back door, the night wind rushed into my collar.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s173-1: It was fully dark. The White Tower stood quietly in the distance. The extremely low hum beneath its base passed tirelessly through the hard ground and rose to us. I listened in silence to the vibration of that machine.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s174-1: We walked over the uneven dirt road, without heading toward any guarded gate. Otto went ahead along the blind path beside the north wall, avoiding every patrol post.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s175-1: The work of the past few days, along with the two copies meant to be made public, had all been forcibly left on that table. We had no leverage in our hands now. We had completely become people being taken away by him.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s176-1: As we moved through the darkness, I gradually recognized the road. This was the freight-truck shortcut he had drawn himself on the revision notices, avoiding the boundary-stone inspections. It cut directly through the old northwestern prohibited zone and led all the way to the base of the White Tower, deep within the power grid.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s177-1: The wind grew colder. Estelle, walking ahead, began to take heavy steps. As the dull lowing invaded our ears from deep in the night, she slowed more and more. It was not a physical expulsion,
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s177-2: but a huge, invisible pressure, like a wall blocking the way ahead. She gripped her collar tightly, as if merely approaching the tower rising in the night had already exhausted all her strength.
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s179-1: “That sound…” She hunched over, her voice trembling. “It’s too loud…”
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s180-1: I watched her struggle to move before the lowing of that machine. Was this one of the reasons R-409 had listed her as a risk? Even this invisible pressure made
texts.chapter:v15-z07b:event:text-s180-2: her seem so out of place. But instinct told me that the file’s real reason—or rather, what they were truly guarding against—ran far deeper than this pressure.
texts.chapter:volume0-simplest-exchange:title: Chapter Eight: The Simplest Exchange
texts.chapter:volume0-simplest-exchange:event::
Disposition Record · Night of Day Seven (excerpt, held in the Controlled Archives):
Three declarants. Obtained separately, recorded separately. The three were not present together during the formal statements.
Arno’s statements (excerpted, recorded verbatim, not consolidated):
　　1. Estelle relinquishes her appeal and accepts withdrawal

of name.
　　2. Revoke Arno’s and Yuna’s candidate qualifications.
　　3. Permanently renounce any future possibility of being selected again, undergoing a body exchange, or entering the Inner Circle.
　　4. The three leave the Central Village on their own and go to the outskirts.
This record is copied in duplicate in accordance with precedent.

Otto escorted us out of the archives and immediately searched all three of us roughly. The original documents and copies we had left on the table had supposedly bought us “ten minutes to escape the central

district,” but that time was never granted. Otto had no intention of letting us move freely. To keep the villagers from seeing us, he deliberately took back routes, avoided the night patrols, and led us

all the way to the base of the White Tower. By then, the outer defenses had certainly been locked down completely. If we broke into a run halfway there, we would only become fugitives to be shot on sight.

There was a windowless review room here, probably normally used for storing odds and ends. It always smelled of old dust mixed with damp stone walls. The outer room held a rough table made of unfinished timber and

two benches. Several rust-covered old locks hung from iron nails in the wall. A lamp burned on the table. Presumably to save oil, its wick had been trimmed very short, leaving a flame no larger than a fingernail.
He shoved the three of us into the cold, gloomy room, said only, “Stay here,” and went upstairs by way of the stone steps along one side.

Yuna sat at one end of the bench, staring at the seams between the floor tiles. Estelle sat at the other, her back perfectly straight. I did not sit. I stood with my back against the stone wall beside the door. The room was too small. Even if no boundary guards were stationed in the outer room for the moment, the entire White Tower was an iron barrel with no way out.

“If they separate us for questioning later,” Yuna suddenly said in a low voice, speaking extremely fast, “we can only hand over every right we currently hold. Estelle, you give up your appeal and accept withdrawal of name. Arno, the two of us give up our current candidate qualifications, and add

one more condition—we permanently renounce any future possibility of being selected again, undergoing a body exchange, or entering the Inner Circle. We trade all of that for the three of us going to the outskirts together. Every condition has to be tied together. If even one is missing, we refuse.”

“But we’ve already violated the rules. We’ll be stripped of our qualifications anyway, and we won’t be able to undergo a body exchange anyway. Why list this separately?” I asked through clenched teeth.

“Because stripping our qualifications alone still lets them keep us in the village as laborers, or as reserves.” Yuna stared fixedly at the floor tiles. “We have to cut off our future value as ‘vessels’ completely, on paper.”
“More important is ‘voluntarily.’” Estelle spoke coldly. “Removal through the normal process requires a hearing and would leave a record visible to the
entire village. If we voluntarily give up everything on paper, they can settle the matter quietly. That is the last bit of convenience we are offering them.”

“Right. We trade that last convenience for leaving the village.” Yuna stared at the floor tiles as if she meant to see through them. “That is the only bottom line that might keep us alive. If they won’t agree even to that…”
Yuna did not continue.
What were we supposed to do if they refused even this final concession? In that cold, cramped room, we had no escape route planned in advance. Estelle still sat perfectly straight. Her
position had always been to preserve the evidence and wait for a gap in the procedures. But if the Inner Circle simply tore up every procedure, then beyond this bottom line was only darkness.

Not long afterward, low voices came from upstairs, muffled and heavy. After a while, hurried footsteps left the White Tower and headed toward the village. Boundary patrols did not walk with steps like those. It sounded as though someone was rushing to summon somebody.
Otto came down the stairs.

He held a hard wooden board with several sheets of paper clipped to it with iron clamps. He walked to the table and slammed the board down with a sharp crack. He did not sit. He looked down at us from above.
“Candidate tags. Hand them over.” There was no emotion in his voice.

I reached inside my collar, touched the wooden tag warmed by my skin, removed its cord, and placed it on the table. Yuna took hers off too. The two wooden tags struck the rough surface almost at the same time, making identical dull knocks.
Otto’s gaze passed over us and landed on Estelle.
“I don’t have one.” She looked at Otto, her tone calm.

“I returned it the afternoon of the second day,” she added, enunciating every word clearly. “The day the instructor stripped me of my qualification in front of everyone. Elder Sera took it herself. It should already be entered in the register.”
Otto stared at her for a moment in the dim light, then gave a slight nod and quickly drew a line on the paper with his pen.
“Then what am I?” Estelle asked suddenly.
Otto’s hand, preparing to write the next word, stopped. He raised his eyes.
“What do you mean?”
“They’re candidates. I returned my tag long ago. I’m not on your candidate roster. In the general register for outsiders, my status is ‘appeal pending.’” Estelle looked straight at him.
“I have no villager status, and I’m not a candidate who has violated the rules. I’m being forcibly kept here. If I speak from this point on, in what jurisdictional capacity am I speaking?”
Otto did not answer immediately. The atmosphere in the room tightened at once.
He instinctively reached to his waist and touched the string of wooden tags he usually wore, rolling it hard between his rough thumb and finger. I had watched him mediate field-boundary
disputes for villagers since I was little. I knew it was a habitual gesture—whenever he encountered a difficult situation and needed to weigh his wording, he rolled those tags.
“You’re a party to the matter.” Those were the words he finally gave her.
“Then write that down.”
“Write what?” His brows drew together.
“Write what you just said on the paper.” She pointed at the tabletop. “I want it to have a clear source. If, in a future case file, one of the three parties has no formal jurisdictional
status at all, anyone reviewing it will ask: what gives this person the right to be held here? If you don’t make it clear today, no one will be able to answer for me then.”
Otto narrowed his eyes and looked deeply at her for two seconds, as though trying to see through the stubbornness in the bones of this outsider girl.
“Wait for Sera to record it.” He shoved the matter back to her stiffly.
“All right. Then I’ll wait for Elder Sera.” She withdrew her gaze and did not speak again.
Then Yuna stood up.
“What about the things we left on the table in the archives?” she asked, looking at Otto.
“They’re still where they were. Someone is counting and registering them.”
“After they’re registered, will you show us the list?”
“No.”
“Then how do I know that what’s sitting there tomorrow will still be what we put there today?”
Otto impatiently picked up the hard wooden board from the table and slammed it back down.
“The record will contain the exact number,” he said coldly.
“But I can’t see that record.”
“Correct.”
Yuna’s hand hanging at her side clenched hard once, the knuckles turning pale.
“Arno.”
She called my name suddenly, but did not turn to look at me.
“Two copies, one compiled manuscript. And Estelle’s supply-batch schedule, plus two confiscated original draft documents.”
“What?” I froze for a moment.

“Those are the things left on the archives table. Six items in all.” She spoke quickly, every word striking the floor. “Everything else is locked in the metal cabinet, untouched. I counted them one by one before I left.”
Only then did she turn around, her gaze sweeping over everyone in the room.
“You heard me. Estelle heard me. Otto heard me too. Now all four of us know the number.”
Otto’s hand holding the pen paused in midair.
The pause lasted perhaps one second. Then he pretended nothing had happened and continued writing on the paper. I had no idea whether he ultimately wrote that “six” into the record.
“What use is counting it out now?” He did not raise his head. A concealed irritation showed in his voice.
“It’s no use now.”
She dropped the words and sat down calmly.
I leaned against the door, watching the two girls before me. Estelle remained perfectly straight-backed. After stating that precise number, Yuna did not say another word.
When people are driven into a dead end, they are supposed to shout, to vent. In that stifling room, the only person who almost failed to hold back a shout was me.
I wanted to speak. I wanted to argue loudly about so many things—I wanted to say we had never harmed anyone here; I wanted to say we had not taken a single original from the archives; I also

wanted to say to Otto, You’ve watched me grow up for sixteen years. Don’t you know what kind of person I am?
Anger and grievance surged into my throat, pressing the sound down inside it.
“Arno.”
She called my name again, quietly, without even raising her head, but it was like a basin of cold water poured over red-hot coals.

I abruptly closed my mouth. Maybe she had seen my flushed face from the corner of her eye. Maybe she was simply telling me that venting my emotions here was meaningless, that all she needed was for me to stay quietly on her side of the line. I followed the call and silently retreated to the wall.
Elder Sera did not arrive until after nine that night.

She was still wearing the completely undecorated plain white clothes from the day, the dark-red duty marker symbolizing her status fastened tightly and precisely at her cuff. When she pushed open the door, her gaze swept over the tags surrendered on the table, then over the faces of the three of us in turn.
“Three people,” Sera confirmed.
“Three people,” I replied in a low voice.
Sera walked to the table and slapped down the thick ledger she had brought with her.
“From now on, the three of you will give statements separately,” she announced in a tone that allowed no objection. “One enters, one leaves. No one is permitted to hear anyone else’s
testimony. The three separately obtained records can be compared against one another someday in the future. This rule exists so that what you say next may retain at least a little value.”
Hearing her announce these severe procedures, I found it absurd. Otto had kept us hidden from the villagers by shoving us into a room for so long, while the
elders upstairs apparently had no idea that we had already had enough time in the cold review room below to coordinate all our bottom lines and statements.
Kane stood blocking the doorway like an iron tower. The light from the courtyard fell in from behind his broad back, leaving his face entirely in shadow. His gaze deliberately avoided Estelle.
“You go first,” he finally said to Estelle.
Estelle stood. Just as she was about to walk outside—
“Estelle.”
Yuna suddenly spoke. Her voice was not loud, but in the dead silence of the room it was unusually clear. Kane stopped moving, but did not immediately intervene.
“No matter what they ask you in there,” Yuna said, looking straight into her eyes, “if the official route out of the village is completely sealed, if they insist on keeping
someone here… remember this: Arno and I will never let you bear the charge of violating the rules alone. We’ll share all the consequences with you. The three of us are together.”
Estelle’s ice-blue eyes looked at Yuna for two seconds in the dim light. She did not nod or say yes. She only turned and followed Kane outside.
After a long while, Kane came back to take Yuna away.
I was the last one.

During that long interval, I sat alone in the review room. Counting from the moment I was caught red-handed at 6:06 p.m., the so-called “fourteen-hour” countdown was already draining away irreversibly. I knew what they were waiting

for—if the retrograde model was real, then as long as they delayed the closed-door ruling past the deadline around 8:06 tomorrow morning, even if we later reached the machine, we would no longer be able to rewind to this roundup.

As those forcibly consumed hours passed, I desperately searched for something we could exchange with the elders to break the deadlock. But there was nothing. After counting and recounting, the only thing we

could give up was everything we possessed in the Central Village. Leave the mill, sever our identities, say goodbye to our families, and pay all those costs in exchange for one chance to “walk out alive.”

I didn’t know whether Yuna and Estelle had already been crushed by the elders’ formation in the council chamber upstairs. But I had made up my mind. When I went up there, even if the sky fell, I had to bind the three of us together so tightly that we became one indivisible piece of leverage.
The White Tower’s council chamber was on the third floor.
It was a vast room, spacious enough to make me uneasy. A very long blackwood table stretched across its center. Several people who held power in the village sat sparsely along both sides.
Near the door stood another chair by itself, outside the long table’s area. My mother sat in it.

The elders had clearly summoned her in the middle of the night—to use her as a card to break me apart if necessary. When she heard the door, saw me brought inside, and recognized me, she sprang to her feet.
“Sit down,” a cold voice came from beside the long table.

She flinched, then slowly sat back down. Her hands were locked over her knees. The force of it had drawn her knuckles white. From the moment I entered until I came to a stop, she did not raise her head to look at me once.
Yuna’s parents, Galon and Meru, had not come. The elders

probably knew perfectly well that the two of them could not persuade Yuna and might instead cause a scene on the spot. Estelle’s mother was far away in the outskirts and could not appear here. Tonight, in this great room, I was the only one who had family come to take me home.
“Arno. Come to the middle.”
I walked into the open space before the long table beneath all their gazes.
Sera sat upright directly before the long table, the thick ledger open in front of her.

“Before questioning begins, the person in question will make three declarations,” she said in an official, procedural tone. “First, every word you utter here tonight will be entered into the record. Second, after you

finish, the person in question will read the record back to you and confirm that it is correct. Third, you will not hear the other two people’s statements, and they will not hear yours. They have already finished.”
“What did they say?”
“I won’t tell you.”
“Now, the person in question asks and you answer. Do you have a disposition request to make?”
“Yes.”
I drew a deep breath of the cold air in the great room.

“First, Estelle relinquishes her appeal and accepts withdrawal of name. Second, revoke Yuna’s and my candidate qualifications. Third, permanently renounce any future possibility of being selected again, undergoing a body exchange, or entering the Inner Circle. Finally—the three of us leave the Central Village on our own and go to the outskirts.”
Sera’s pen point paused above the paper.
“Do the two of them agree to these four conditions? Did you discuss them in advance?”
I met her gaze.
“Yes. This is a decision the three of us made together. These conditions are bound together and cannot be separated. If one is missing, none of them counts.”

Sera showed no emotion. She only lowered her head and wrote rapidly. When she finished, she read in an even voice: “Answer: The declarant confirms that the three people jointly request that these four items be treated as an indivisible exchange condition, surrendering their qualifications in exchange for permission to leave the village.”
“The record is correct.”
Then she deftly pulled an old copy from the stack at her right, slapped it onto the table, and pushed it in front of me.

“If you choose to leave the Central Village for the outskirts, your name and identity here will be revoked,” Sera said, looking at me without a trace of warmth in her eyes. “This article will apply to you. Read Article Seven.”
I stared at the rigid official document and began to read aloud.
“Outskirts personnel are registered by batch and serial number. The number is their sole identifier, remains unchanged for life, and is not altered by relocation, marriage, or a change of name.”
“Do you accept this regulation?”
“I refuse to sign this regulation,” I shot back coldly. “But I am not withdrawing my request to leave the village.”
“If you do not register according to the regulation, then even if you get out, you will only be an identityless exile. Why? Be more specific.”
“Then an exile is what I’ll be. Wipe us out of your internal ledgers however you like.” I stared hard at her. “The word ‘batch’ is used for things. Bricks fired in one kiln
are called a batch. Grain hauled in one cart is called a batch. But people aren’t things. We are leaving as people, and I will never sign a paper admitting that I am an object.”
Sera picked up her pen again and began writing. When she finished, she read: “Answer: Do not accept. Reason: A batch is a way of measuring things and does not apply to people.”
“My exact words never mentioned ‘measuring things.’ I said it was ‘used to refer to things.’” I stared hard at her.

“Correct it.” She did not become angry. In front of me, she roughly crossed out the words “a way of measuring things” with her pen, clearly wrote “used to refer to things” beside them, and even pressed a bright red fingerprint onto the crossed-out section.
After correcting it, she pulled the copy back and pressed it beneath the very bottom of the stack.

“Since you’re requesting to leave the village, answer this question.” Her gaze locked onto me again. “Once you reach the outskirts, how will you ensure that what is in your heads does not leak out? There is no oath in this world capable of locking a secret away completely.”

I clenched my teeth and offered the greatest concession I could think of. “I can swear a solemn oath. If that still isn’t enough, the Central Village can send people to the outskirts every year to monitor and review us.”
Sera recorded the sentence like a machine, then read it back to me: “Answer: Willing to swear an oath of secrecy and accept regular reviews in the outskirts by people sent from the Central Village.”

Hearing my concession become cold ink on paper, I felt as though a millstone were pressing on my chest. Only a few hours earlier, Yuna and I had been planning how to carry every sentence from the bottom file outside. Now I was

actively asking them to put shackles on us. I watched Sera record without raising her head. I did not know whether Yuna would have nodded at this result if she were here, or whether she could have thought of another way out.

“But this method is not feasible.” Without raising her head, she delivered the verdict. “Chico goes to the outskirts every year only to check provisions and headcounts. If someone were deliberately sent to check whether you had leaked anything, how could that person check? If he

did not know what the secret was, he would not know what to listen for or guard against. If he did know, then the moment he was detained in the outskirts, the secret would escape with him. As long as it depends on communication across the boundary, it carries an uncontrollable risk.”
I opened my mouth to argue, but found that I had no argument to make. They had no intention of taking even the slightest risk. They would not accept even this submission.
“Then what do you actually need before you’ll consider it enough?” Driven into a corner, I felt my voice begin to shake.
“The person in question does not know what, in this world, can make anyone feel that it is ‘enough.’”
“You can’t keep the three of us locked up here like criminals forever.”

“Tonight, the person in question’s duty is only to record your statements and requests. As for how you will ultimately be dealt with, the elders’ council will deliberate tomorrow and naturally reach a decision.” She forced my impatience back down.
At that suffocating moment, my mother spoke.
She sprang to her feet to say it. The heavy chair legs scraped hard against the solid floor, producing an intensely shrill sound.
“My son was born here,” she said toward the long table. Her voice was not loud, but it was firm.
Not one of the people seated along the long table answered her.
“He was born in this village,” she repeated, louder and without fear. “He’s only sixteen this year! He’s lived and struggled in this village all his life. His master is Galon.
Even now, he carries water every morning and fills my jar. He knows nothing about those settlements in the outskirts. He has no idea how he would survive alone if he walked there!”
Her chest heaving violently, she finished shouting at the elders, then suddenly turned to look at me.
“You have no idea what you’re facing! Do you think this is a negotiation?” Her voice carried an unmistakable trace of fear, directed at the people
across the table. “You’re coming home with me right now. You have to come home with me tonight. Tomorrow morning, you’ll go work at the mill properly.”

I stared at her blankly.
Every word she had shouted was the truth—I really was a native of this village, really did carry water for her every morning, and knew nothing about those settlements
in the outskirts, much less how to put down roots and survive there. She was doing everything she could to pull me out of the dead end facing the three of us, to sever my connection with them.
“If your father were here—” She looked at me, and her voice suddenly caught.

She did not finish the rest of the sentence.
She almost never mentioned my father. She had lived longer than I had and knew much better than I did how far the people across the table would go to protect their secret. But at a moment like this, she brought up that sentence to drag me out.
“Rena.” A cold warning came from the other side of the table. “It is not your turn. You should not interrupt.”
“I know perfectly well that it isn’t my turn.” She gritted her teeth and pushed back.
Sera raised her head again.
“The person in question will not record your mother’s words just now as a joint request from the three of you. She was speaking only to you.” Her tone was purely procedural.
She fixed me with a stare that chilled the blood.

“If you personally request to go home with her now, the elders’ council can treat you as someone who was misled. You can return to your mother’s strict supervision and renewed internal review, and sever your connection with them permanently. You can survive. They may not. Choose for yourself.”
I stood alone in the center of that great room for what must have been a full ten seconds.

During those long ten seconds, I looked at my mother’s reddened eyes. I knew Sera’s words were the final chance: if I nodded now and went to stand beside her, I could avoid the death penalty. I could go home, keep fetching water every morning, and return to work at the mill. The

temptation was enormous—so enormous that the tips of my feet shifted half an inch toward her without my willing them to.
But if I left, what would happen to Estelle? To Yuna? In the situation facing the three of us, only the two of them would remain to bear all the consequences.
I dug my nails into my palms, straightened myself again, and said, “I’m not changing it. If one person is missing, none of it counts.”
“That is all you intend to say?”
“My request does not change. I can’t abandon them by myself.” I held fast to the words.
I watched my mother sink back into her chair. She sat as though all the strength had been pulled out of her at once, without making a sound. She folded both hands
together again and placed them on her knees, lowering her head deeply. From that moment until I was taken out of the room, she never raised her head to look at me again.

Sera began writing rapidly in the ledger again. Then, as usual, she read it back: “Question: Is there a separate request to be placed under family supervision and sever association with this case? Answer: The declarant refuses to separate himself. The four requests remain bound together. The answer remains unchanged.”
She slammed the thick ledger shut.
From the moment I entered until now, Otto had sat at the inner end of the long table like a ghost, without saying a word. Now he rose from the shadows.
The sheet containing my four requests lay spread across the table before him.

“There is no need to wait for tomorrow’s deliberation. You want to trade the concession of voluntarily giving up your qualifications for the last ticket out of the village.” His voice was slightly hoarse, then turned cold. “I’m

responsible for the outer defenses and approval for leaving the village. The moment I determine there is a risk of crossing the boundary, I alone can lock down the village boundary. I can answer you here and now—absolutely not approved.”

“You just said yourself that ‘batch’ is used to refer to things. Now the three of you have minds full of secrets that cannot see the light of day. The moment you cross the village boundary, people in the outskirts can use you as weapons! The three of you will become living explosive packs!”

“If you have no intention of letting us go, then revoke Yuna’s and my candidate qualifications! Elder Sera can stamp it right now and throw us out of this process! That’s simply dealing with us according to your own rules. It isn’t sending us straight to the outskirts!”

“Withdrawal of name is also the village’s punishment.
