Don’t even think of using it as an excuse to delay!” he shouted over me. “If you are to be dealt with, your responsibility for violating the rules will be assessed first, and you will be punished accordingly. You have no right to pick and choose now!”
He reached out, turned over the sheet bearing the four lines, and pressed it face down onto the table without mercy.
“None of your requests will be approved.”
“The village boundary remains closed. Hold the three of them separately. Do not move them tonight. Reconvene the full elders’ council tomorrow morning and decide the final punishment!”
When I heard “the village boundary remains closed,” my heart sank completely. This was the outcome we had feared most—it meant that even after surrendering every part of our
identities, even after being willing to swear like condemned prisoners, we had not obtained a single legal route out of the village. The official door had been locked shut.

Sera reopened the thick ledger and wrote at great speed the decision to hold us separately that night, then stamped it with her private seal. She immediately took out two blank sheets and began making copies with practiced efficiency. When she finished, she placed the two copies into two different hard-paper folders.
“Take him downstairs,” she ordered.
Kane waited silently at the stairwell like a massive ghost.

We began descending from the third floor. The White Tower’s stone steps were very old. The center of every step had been worn by countless soles into a smooth, shallow hollow. I walked mechanically, counting the steps silently. When I reached twenty-three, we arrived at the landing at the second-floor turn.
Estelle was still sitting on that landing. She sat on a long wooden bench against the wall.
A boundary guard other than Kane stood beside her like a wooden post. Her hands remained properly placed on her knees, exactly as they had been when she was waiting in the
review room at the base of the tower several hours earlier. Even the folds in her clothes had not changed. Hearing footsteps, she raised her head slightly and looked at me.
I stopped. The guard stepped forward alertly, blocking the space between her and me.
Looking over the guard’s shoulder, I watched her remain seated perfectly straight.
“All our requests were rejected. The official road out of the village is closed.” I spoke quickly to her.

The guard had clearly heard me, but only shoved me viciously, driving me downstairs. I stumbled down, then, using the momentum of the shove, quickly looked back over my shoulder for one last glance at her.

When she turned her head, I read a terrifying resolve in her still-perfect posture. Since the village had sealed off the exit it offered, what leverage could she possibly use to smash open a crack in this White Tower, with boundary guards everywhere?
I forced myself to keep going down. After descending two steps, I heard her speak behind me.
“I’ve already been waiting a long time.” Her voice was quiet but clear. “How much longer do I have to wait before I can go in for questioning?”

At those words, my head gave a loud buzz. Sera’s cold statement upstairs—“They have already finished”—had been a complete lie. Kane had taken Estelle out of the review room first, but instead of bringing her into the council chamber on

the third floor, he had dumped her in this corner halfway there to wait for several hours! They had never intended to hear the conditions of an outsider with no jurisdictional status. Sera had only used information isolation to trick me.
The boundary guard watching her was like a deaf man. He did not even look at her, let alone answer.
“If you won’t let me go in immediately, can I have a sheet of paper?” she added stubbornly. “Just one is enough. Any kind of paper. A pencil is fine. I don’t need a pen with ink.”
Still, no one answered her. Only the empty echoes remained.

When I finally reached the first floor, those few sentences were still buzzing in my eardrums. When we left the archives, Otto had searched all of us thoroughly. She sat there, slight and alone on the cold, hard wooden bench, without a single means

of self-defense. I did not know what she intended to write on that one sheet of paper—an official accusation, perhaps, or some statement that had to be entered into the records. But since even her qualification to enter the room had been stripped

away, that paper was the last bit of noise she could make, however slight. Whatever she wrote, I had to cover for her. Yuna and I had no other choice. We had to hold fast to the testimony we had given that night and buy her every bit of time we could.

They locked me in a narrow, dark room on the west side of the White Tower’s first floor. It was cold as an icehouse. There was only a bare wooden bed board and a rough ceramic water jar. There was not even a transom here; a little of the outer room’s dim yellow light leaked in beneath the door.
Strangely, the heavy wooden door was not locked.

I tested it myself. I sat motionless on the bed board for a while, then stood, went to the door, and gently pushed it open a narrow crack. A stool stood outside, with a man responsible for guarding me sitting on it. At the sound of the door, he raised his head warily and glared at me.
“Get back in there and sit down!” he barked in a low voice.
I silently retreated into the room and closed the door firmly again. Then I returned to sit on the cold bed board.

Was this unlocked door simply because someone was watching from outside, or because the elders’ council could not be bothered to lock a room at the base of the White Tower that no one could possibly escape from?

I looked at the door. Though I had just closed it so firmly, now it seemed as if it would open with a single push. If I could no longer endure the silence and pushed the door open to run into the night, this door would immediately strip me of the last bit of standing I had while waiting for them to give their verdict.

I sat upright on the bed board in the darkness. The night wind moved outside the wall, passing over the White Tower. Every second slipped away toward the deadline around 8:06 tomorrow morning. All I could do was stare hard at the unlocked door.
texts.chapter:volume0-fourth-route:title: Chapter Nine: The Fourth Path
texts.chapter:volume0-fourth-route:event:text-:
Village Boundary Patrol Roster (excerpt):
West-line night shift: thirteen people in total.
West One (four). West Two (four). West Three (four).
Supplementary clause: This log covers only the routes marked on the public defense map.

By the time that suffocating council session ended, it was deep into the night. As persons under review, we were held separately, and I was pushed into a narrow, windowless room facing west on the White Tower’s ground floor.

The room had originally been used for storing odds and ends. There was no iron lock; a guard simply sat outside, bracing the door. In the darkness, cold seeped outward through the stone walls. I pressed
my palms against my knees, trying to suppress that difficult-to-name trembling. Our lawful request had been rejected. Now our only hope was the desperate plan we had settled on in the archive that

afternoon. If Estelle could obtain paper and pencil during the interrogation, if she had really written down all the connections from memory—then she was the only vessel that could carry our evidence out.
What broke the dead silence was a sudden, tremendous commotion from upstairs.

Someone was running wildly down the stone stairs. The heavy cart of miscellaneous objects had been overturned and came crashing down the steps, followed by the dull thud of bodies colliding. The guards were shouting.
“The draft was taken by her! She went toward the western main road!”

That was Yuna’s voice. This was the division of labor the three of us had decided on together: if things came to the worst, Yuna and I would serve as bait, drawing every pursuer in the White Tower toward the western main roads shown on the defense map, while Estelle crossed the boundary through the concealed route.

I sprang to my feet, my body moving toward the wooden door before I had time to think. The door opened outward. I slammed my shoulder into it. The guard outside had been leaning against it, half-asleep, and was caught off balance, staggering backward. The door opened a crack. I pushed my way through and kicked the bedboard over, making a tremendous noise inside the room.

“Don’t let her get onto West Two!” I shouted, bracing myself hard against the door, playing along with Yuna’s lie. As long as the guards believed the target was on one of the three western main roads, the pressure on Estelle would drop to nothing.
The guard reacted. Heavy force pressed against the door, pushing it back.
“Go back.”
I couldn’t push against that force. My shoe soles scraped harshly across the floor tiles. With a bang, the door slammed shut in front of me, tight as a seam.

Outside, I heard the bolt being fastened. But then a tremendous crash came from the end of the corridor: Yuna had smashed open the White Tower’s side door. Cursing, the guards’ chaotic footsteps were quickly drawn away by the commotion in the west.

The guards ran off. I backed up two steps and hurled myself at the wooden door like a madman. The wood around the bolt had long since rotted. On the second impact, the plank gave a sharp tearing crack, and the bolt flew out together with its screws.
I rushed into the empty corridor and ran out through the smashed-open side door. Outside was a steep flight of stone steps. My foot missed one, and I rolled all the way down.
When I landed, my right foot twisted hard against the sloping side of the drainage ditch, and a stabbing pain shot through me. I lay on the wet grass for a few breaths, then forced myself upright.

I shifted my weight onto my left foot and dragged my injured right leg through the weeds in the Tower’s shadow. I turned into a narrow path along the wall, with no lights, and left the village road entirely.

Flashlight beams swept everywhere across the main roads, all drawn westward by our earlier shouts. Dew on the grass soon soaked through the uppers of my shoes. The swollen ring around my right ankle began to burn. I dragged my leg along at a fast pace, making a one-deep, one-shallow rhythm in the darkness.
At the far western edge of the village was a gentle slope with an open view.
Following the slope upward, I could faintly make out three broad, trampled main roads—the West One through West Three recorded in the roster. Flashlight beams crisscrossed
there now, with nearly every guard searching the main roads for the target we had invented. I didn’t go near them. I plunged straight into the thickest patch of wild grass.
In these seven days, we had never actually surveyed this stretch of wild grass together. But that afternoon in the archive, Yuna had pointed out a fatal gap to Estelle and me.
The roster listed thirteen people in the west-line night shift. Yet the shared internal map used by the Ten Seats clearly showed only three roads in the west line, with four people on each.

Yuna had drawn the lightest mark with her fingernail across a blank area where a contour line broke on the map. “Four times three is twelve. Where is the extra person? The fact that even the Ten Seats’ shared map doesn’t show this road

means it isn’t merely being kept secret from the villagers. It’s a concealed route handed over verbally within the boundary guard system alone. That roving sentry is stationed in this gap, outside the shared oversight of the Ten Seats.”
This fourth path, beyond every line of sight and every shared authority, had become Estelle’s only blind spot through which to cross the boundary.

It was so dark I couldn’t see my hand in front of my face. I groped blindly through the soft weeds, dragging my injured leg, my shoes sinking deep and shallow into the mud. After struggling through the grass

for more than ten minutes, my foot suddenly stepped onto something hard and completely unyielding—the hard strip made by the boundary guards’ boots over years of trampling. I had found the concealed route.
I struggled uphill along the hard strip. After about two hundred steps, I heard the faintest footsteps beside the irrigation channel on my right.
I turned around. In the blurred darkness, I recognized the outline. It was Yuna.

She was soaked through, her trouser legs clinging tightly to her calves. I could just make out abrasions on her palms—she had probably felt her way through the mud after shaking off the pursuers on the main road.
“Most of the guards have been drawn onto the main roads,” she panted in a lowered voice. “But Kane isn’t there.”
“He didn’t go after you?”
“He wasn’t drawn by the commotion at the White Tower at all. He may have been on this concealed route from the start.”
She said no more, and I understood at once what that meant. Our baiting plan had fooled the ordinary guards, but not Kane, who held final authority. Estelle was walking toward
him completely undefended. Without a word, Yuna took hold of my left arm and carried half my weight. Together, we pushed toward the top of the slope with everything we had.
Supporting each other like that, we walked farther uphill.

The upper half of the slope rose sharply. The concealed route hidden in the grass wound upward beside a waist-high stone ledge, eventually meeting the broad western main road at the same boundary-crossing pass. Night wind blew in from the village boundary ahead, carrying a dry, harsh smell, as if the sun had scorched the land all day.
That was when we heard voices from above.
It was Kane.
“I’ll say it one last time. Stop.”

His tone was pressed flat, without a rise or fall, but the pauses between his words were precise, as if measured with a ruler. This was no warning issued at their first meeting. The confrontation had reached its final ultimatum.
We lowered ourselves at the same time. Crouching beneath the stone ledge, we looked up.

At the top of the slope was a flat, open stretch wide enough for vehicles to pass. On the left, a huge section of the roadbed had collapsed, with a steep slope below. On the right was a patch of knee-high grass. Beyond this open stretch lay the world outside the boundary.
Estelle stood alone on the path.

She was very close to the slope’s edge, beyond which lay the boundary. Kane stood in the middle of the path like a mountain. He carried no lamp. In one hand he held something small, hanging beside his leg, its heavy front end pointed at the ground.
“Put the thing on the ground and come back with me.”
Estelle stood perfectly still, like a statue.
“I’ll count to three.”

But he never counted. The moment he finished speaking, he shifted a small step to the right. It was an extremely short step, but it perfectly sealed off Estelle’s attempt to circle around through the short grass on the right.
Estelle stopped. She knew the right side was blocked, so she slowly backed to the left, all the way to the edge of the sloping drop on the left.
She stopped before the edge and slowly raised one hand, pressing it slightly below her chest. That was where she had hidden the thing.

She took out a roll of paper. In the moonlight, I recognized what she had asked for upstairs. After the first round of searching, when the guard had mockingly thrown the statement paper and half a pencil onto the

table, she hadn’t tried to write an appeal. She had no original draft hidden on her. What she carried was something she had written from memory during the gaps in the interrogation, in the blind spot of their gaze.
“What are you carrying?” His voice remained steady.
“A sheet of paper.” Her answer was just as calm.
“What’s written on it?”

“The five things you took,” she said, pausing before adding, “not including my roster. Only the numbers of those two copied documents, the summary manuscript, and the two originals, along with the relationships between them.”
“You copied them?”
“I wrote them from memory.”

Kane fell silent. The pause was probably only two seconds, but in the night it seemed extraordinarily long. I knew Yuna’s memory was good enough to reconstruct the ledger, but I hadn’t expected Estelle, simply by handling those materials, to have carved all those complicated connections into her mind.
“You shouldn’t have come out,” he said at last.
“I know.”
“Once you leave this stretch, you won’t be able to come back.”
“I know.”
The next second, Kane raised the thing hanging at his side.
His movement was slow but oppressive. He leveled the heavy end at chest height and aimed it at Estelle. He didn’t change any of its settings. He only pressed somewhere on the handle.
Then came the sound.
It wasn’t loud at all, like a thin, insubstantial line whose frequency never changed. The sound had no direction. It clung over the entire open ground and continued with extreme steadiness.
I heard it too, and so did Yuna crouching beside me. Apart from hearing the sound spread through the air, our bodies showed no discomfort.

But at the top of the slope, Estelle seemed to have been struck hard. One foot staggered half a step backward. She waved her hand and barely caught the rough rock at the edge of the break. Her whole body sank to one knee along the rock, her thin shoulder hunching forward once.
It was a dry heave of extreme pain.
She knelt in the gravel, humiliated, one hand braced against the ground and the other clamped over her ear. Her knuckles were distorted in the moonlight.
The sound continued.
Suddenly, the sound vanished. Silence settled over the top of the slope again, broken only by the night wind rustling through the dry grass.

Estelle knelt rigidly for more than ten seconds, as if all her strength had been drained away. Then she lowered the hand covering her ear, braced both hands against the ground, drew a deep breath, and pushed herself back up.

She was extremely unsteady. As soon as she straightened her legs, she tilted to the left, awkwardly rubbing the soles of her feet against the ground to find her balance again. Swaying, she backed toward the left. Her heel reached the sloping drop at the edge of the roadbed. Two more steps down, using the slope for cover, and she could get around Kane.

Below the stone ledge, I clenched my fists. Estelle could barely stand now, her body already wavering at the edge of the steep slope. My right foot could no longer exert any force. There was no way I could knock Kane down across those

dozen-odd meters—and Kane’s finger was hooked around the instrument’s handle. The moment we made the slightest sound, he could press that switch again. At this hopeless distance, we could only stay nailed to the spot, utterly helpless.
She laboriously stepped down once.
“Stop.” Kane’s command was as cold as before.
“I can still walk.” She forced the words out through her teeth.
She didn’t look at Kane. Her eyes fixed on the ground, she stubbornly moved forward another step.

At that moment, I could hide no longer beneath the stone ledge. I stood up, wanting to rush forward and put myself between her and Kane, wanting to shout for him to stop. But the instant I stepped with my injured leg, my knee buckled. I slipped awkwardly into the grass on the slope, able to produce only a hoarse gasp.
Kane at the top of the slope didn’t look at me at all. He lowered the thing he was holding until it hung at his waist, then lowered his head to look at it.

At that moment, Yuna violently pulled free of my arm. She grabbed a piece of gravel beside her, stood, and hurled it toward the top of the slope. The stone struck the ground in front of Kane with a dull thud and bounced into the grass.
Kane glanced at the gravel on the ground without even lifting his head.

Then, from the darkness, came two extremely faint metallic clicks. The first sounded like some latch being pushed open by a thumb; the second was the sound of some kind of knob being forcibly twisted halfway around.
He raised his arm again. The heavy end locked onto Estelle, tottering on the slope below the break.
The faint sound began again, just as expected.
A few seconds later, Estelle’s head suddenly tilted backward for no apparent reason. The movement was very gentle, as if an invisible hand had lightly lifted her chin in midair.
She sat down.
Her legs folded at the knees as if their support had been taken away. Her whole body fell backward, her back striking the sloped surface below the break. Her head tilted toward her left shoulder.
I dragged my injured leg and crawled toward the top of the slope like a madman. By the time I threw myself over, the movement of her chest had already stopped.

I caught the back of her neck and laid her flat on the ground, then clasped my hands and pressed down hard on her chest. Once, twice, ten times. Her bones made faint, muffled sounds beneath my palms. I desperately forced air into her lungs, then watched it disperse without any sign of life.
Yuna climbed up and knelt on the other side of Estelle. She didn’t stop me. Instead, she opened Estelle’s eyelids, and the stray light from the flashlights swept across them. Her pupils
were already fully dilated, without the slightest response to light. Yuna pressed two fingers hard against the artery in Estelle’s neck. After a long time, she slowly released her hand.

“It’s no use, Arno.” Yuna’s voice trembled with hollowness. “This isn’t suffocation, and it isn’t blood loss. All muscle tension vanished in an instant. Her autonomic nervous system has been completely destroyed.”

I wouldn’t listen. Gritting my teeth, I kept pressing. But the body beneath my palms was soft as an empty shell stripped of all support. That sensation, devoid of any neural response, was despair itself. There wasn’t a single physical wound on her, only the redness left when she braced herself against the ground during the first attack.
“Arno, you heard the sound the first time too, right?”
“I heard it.”
“I’m not dizzy. I don’t feel anything.”
After saying this, she snatched her hand away from Estelle’s neck as if shocked.
“Neither am I.”
Heavy footsteps sounded on the gravel.
Kane calmly hung the instrument back on the belt at his waist, walked over to Estelle, crouched beside her, and expressionlessly reached inside her shirt, pulling out the paper folded into thirds.
With one hand, he unfolded the paper, casually scanned its contents, folded it back exactly as it had been, and tucked it inside his coat. Then he stood upright.
“I killed her.”
As he said it, he looked past us toward the village sleeping below the slope. There was no attempt to conceal anything, and no unnecessary explanation.

I lunged at him like a madman, dragging my leg through the pain, and hit him. He was like a stone without a sense of pain. He neither struck back nor stepped away to dodge; he only raised both arms to shield

his head and face. Yuna wrapped her arms around my waist from behind and dragged me back. We both fell into the sharp gravel. Yuna said nothing. She only clutched my clothes tightly, her hands trembling.
The patrol guards were coming up the slope from below, carrying glaring flashlights.
Blinding beams swept across the top of the slope one after another, casting countless shifting shadows across the grass.

Yuna held me tightly in the gravel. No one paid attention to my screams. They only closed the circle around us in silence. I looked at Estelle’s hanging hand, her fingers loosely curled, less than an inch from the rough slope.
We were taken back to the village in profound silence and separated.

Only much later did I learn that, deep inside the White Tower’s archive, the paper had not been destroyed on the spot like the other prohibited materials. The central village treated it as evidence from that night, assigned it an archive number, and formally filed it.
Kane’s statement, along with the emergency order issued that night by Otto, the village chief—“intercept using non-lethal means”—was filed alongside it.
The front of the paper was filled edge to edge with the words she had written from memory.
At the very top, she had written a single summary line:
“Five in total.”
Below that line, she had neatly listed the characteristics and contents of the five documents, along with the relationships between them.

One record had been crossed out violently. She had pressed so hard when crossing it out that the pencil lead carved a dark, shallow groove into the paper. Beside the mark, she had written three characters with force:
‘Uncertain record.’
The three characters were crooked and heavily drawn, the point nearly piercing through the back of the paper. They were like a brutal scar, forever carved into the end of this chain of evidence.
texts.chapter:volume0-these-children:title: Chapter Ten: This Batch of Children
texts.chapter:volume0-these-children:event:tex:
Inner Circle Emergency Proceedings · Night of Day 7 (Front Matter):
Matter: One fatal disposition at the western boundary.
Boundary Guard involved: Kane.
Eyewitnesses: Arno, Yuna.
Recorder: Toma.
Yuna and I were forcibly pulled apart on the loose-stone path up the long slope.

The night wind was cold, needling my skin. Six or seven people came up to meet us, carrying windproof lamps, their halos swaying through the darkness. Two of them came to either side of me, each taking hold of one arm, and dragged me up from the freezing stones without a word. My right ankle, which I had

twisted, was badly swollen and throbbing. My right leg could barely bear weight, so I could only let them drag me forward. My toes stumbled against the stones. It took more than a dozen steps before I barely recovered some balance, putting all my weight on my left leg as I staggered along with their pace.
Both my hands were shaking uncontrollably. The punches I had thrown at Kane had torn the skin from the knuckles of my right hand. My mind had been full
of Estelle collapsing. I hadn’t felt any pain at all. Only now, walking down with them, did the night wind bring that piercing pain crawling up my arm.
Yuna was being escorted by several others walking ahead, more than twenty paces away from me.

I raised my head and watched her back. She walked between the two of them, looking very thin. She didn’t struggle or look back at me. She simply followed in silence. After they had gone a short distance, her steps suddenly

faltered, as though she were trying to make something out in the darkness, or had remembered something. The two of them immediately tugged her impatiently, making her stumble. She steadied herself and kept walking.
“Where are they taking Yuna?” I called out, my voice somewhat hoarse.
The person holding me kept his eyes forward. His rough fingers clamped around my arm like iron pincers. He said nothing.
I took a deep breath and raised my voice slightly.
“Where are they taking Yuna?”
There was only the rustle of leather boots on loose stones. Still, no one answered me. In the eyes of these adults carrying lamps, we were already objects whose value could be assessed separately.
We came down the western slope, went around the usually empty assembly square, and reached the main road.

At this hour, the village would normally have been completely dark. But that night was different. The lamps in every house along both sides of the main road were lit. Yellow light seeped through the window lattices, joining into an

ominous band. The doors of several houses were not fully closed, left ajar by a crack. As we passed them, I could feel eyes silently watching us from behind those gaps, watching this midnight escort brought on by a death at the boundary.
When we reached the foot of the White Tower, I stopped and looked back once toward the direction we had come from.
There was still lamplight high on the long slope. Four or five windproof lamps clustered together, perfectly still in the night wind, like vultures guarding the carcass of their prey.

After we returned to the White Tower, we were separated immediately. At the staircase by the tower’s ground-floor entrance, two tall guards escorted Yuna toward the side room on the second floor.
As for me, they took me straight up to the third floor.
The door opened, and they brought me into the council chamber.
This was my second time in the room. Only a few hours had passed since I left it before.
The council chamber was stifling. All ten people who governed the village were present.

Six people sat around the long table. Three additional seats had been set up at the end of the table for the family members summoned overnight. By the rules, as the families of the parties involved, Garon, Milu, and my mother had lost the right to make proposals at the long table tonight. They could only sit separately and observe,

though they still retained their voting rights. Boundary Guard Kane stood at the far end of the long table, in the place reserved for the accused, at the center of all the light. There had originally been ten people in this room who could decide matters of life and death, but because Kane was under examination, his vote was void tonight.

Every lamp in the room had been lit. Flames licked at their shades, illuminating the yellowed village boundary map on the wall. The three red lines on its western side, symbols of life and death, cut across it in an eye-searing row.

The people who brought me in released my arms and pointed to the spot by the door. I obediently leaned against the rough stone wall. My strength had been exhausted long ago. I could only press my weight into the wall, bracing my shoulder hard against it for support.

My mother sat less than three steps away. Because Yuna and I were involved, the council had apparently summoned both our parents overnight as family members. So she had not taken a seat at the long table. She sat in the

battered chair outside the long table’s designated area, withdrawn into the corner nearest the door. From the moment I entered, her eyes remained fixed on the tabletop in front of her. She did not turn to look at me once.

Garon and Milu also sat awkwardly beside her. The six members seated at the long table kept a subtle distance from the three people who were likewise members of the Ten Seats but could only sit separately and observe as family members tonight.

Kane was still wearing the dark gray coat he had worn when stopping us on the slope. His heavy leather boots were covered in the white dust of the loose-stone path. Before I entered the room, someone had removed the standard-issue weapon of his that could decide between life and death. But from the look of things, no one had thoroughly searched him.

Toma sat to Sera’s left, the thick proceedings ledger spread open in front of him. Freshly dipped ink pressed over the dried ink in the joints of his fingers, its edges catching a faint glimmer in the lamplight.
The heavy oak door was shut tight. Ten people who decided matters of life and death, plus me, the eyewitness, sat here with so many lamps burning. Every breath carried the scorched smell of lamp oil.
“Speak.” Otto, seated at the head of the table, looked at Kane and spat out the single word.
“You’re the witness.” Sera turned her head, her cold gaze falling on me.
“Take him next door. By the rules, a witness cannot hear the accused’s initial statement.” She turned her back to me.
“After dawn tomorrow, we’ll question the two of you separately.”
The person who had brought me in roughly seized me by the back of my collar and tried to drag me out the door.
“I killed her.”
Kane’s voice rang through the council chamber. It was flat, as though he were reciting a list that had been written long ago.
The hand gripping the back of my collar loosened involuntarily at those words. Everyone’s gaze locked onto the voice standing at the center of the light. Even Sera stopped.
“I stopped her at the dry ditch outside the boundary.” He looked at the air above the middle of the long table, at no one in particular, speaking extremely quickly. “I told her to stop and put
the paper on the ground. She didn’t listen, and she didn’t stop walking. I went over and blocked her path with my body. She tried to go around me. Whichever way she went, I moved to block her.”
I leaned against the wall, my heart suddenly tightening. He was lying. Estelle hadn’t even reached the dry ditch fifty paces beyond the boundary line. She had been stopped on the
slope at the break in the roadbed. And when she heard the order, she had clearly stopped like a statue. He had altered the location and erased the fact that she had obeyed the order.
I jerked upright, wanting to shout, but the guard behind me immediately seized the back of my collar and slammed me against the cold stone wall. His elbow pressed into my
back, hard enough to leave me choking. In this council chamber, the long table had not given me the floor. I had no right to speak yet. All I could do was grit my teeth.
He paused, his chest rising and falling slightly.
“I used the handheld repulsion device assigned to the guard post on duty there, as required by the rules. It works on people coming in from outside, and on people like her who carry blood from the
outlands. She couldn’t withstand the vibration. She dropped to her knees and dry-heaved in pain. When the shock passed, she pushed herself back up and continued toward the outside of the boundary.”
“I used lethal force.”
Within a few seconds, he rattled off the entire process in a rapid stream.
Toma, who was also serving as the recorder, paused his pen briefly before continuing across the paper.
I leaned against the wall, my breathing growing rapid. A few hours ago, Estelle had still been running with us. But now, in this room, she had become a withered noun: one fatal disposition.
“Enough.” Sera cut him off coldly, her face livid. “You’ve poured out the entire statement in front of the witness. What meaning is left in taking testimony separately?”
She turned her head toward Toma.

“Record this: the suspect voluntarily confessed in public, and the statement was heard by the eyewitness. Separate testimony is no longer valid.” She sat back down, her gaze scraping across Kane like a knife. “Since you’ve already shattered the rules, we’ll continue questioning you in front of him.”
“When you acted, you knew it would kill her.” Sera lightly tapped the tabletop with her fingertip.
“I knew,” Kane answered crisply.
“Who gave you that order?”
“No one.”
“What was Otto’s original order to you?”
“Seal the boundary. Recover the material that was taken. Intercept them using nonlethal means.”
“Before you used lethal force, was it put to a vote of the Ten Seats?”
“No.”
Sera slowly placed her hand on the edge of the ledger.
“Then what makes you think you had the authority to do that?”

“If she crossed that dry ditch, I wouldn’t have had a second chance to intercept her.” At last, he offered one defense, his voice still utterly even. “At the outermost edge, the Boundary Guard has the authority to make that judgment. I only used the authority I was supposed to use.”
“That’s for outsiders crossing in. Does it apply to this batch of children too?”
“Once they reach that point, it does.”
At that moment, Toma, who had kept his head down writing, raised it.
“Location. Point it out to me on the map. Which one is it?” He looked at the line he had written and addressed Kane.
Behind him, the village boundary map with its red lines was clearly visible in the lamplight. There were only three lines on the western side.
“It isn’t on the map. The dry ditch fifty paces outside the break in the roadbed is the fourth line.”
“If it isn’t on the map, what gives you the right to define it there?”
“It’s written in the handover message. The person on watch tells the person taking the next shift. That ditch is the last physical edge outside the village boundary where you can actually stand.”
“In the location column, record it this way: fifty paces beyond the western boundary line. Not on the map.” She addressed Toma.

“Record Otto’s original order and Kane’s statement strictly separately,” Sera instructed. “For the original order, copy only the exact wording of Otto’s written order, without changing a single word. As for the statement he just gave, divide his

exact words into three lines: that he intercepted her fifty paces beyond the boundary line; that he used lethal force knowing it would kill her; and that he acted on no one’s instructions. Leave a space at the end of each line for him to sign himself.”
“Yes.” Toma bent over the ledger and wrote furiously.
When Toma finished writing, he stood and walked over to Kane. No one had searched Kane that night, and no one had confiscated the belongings on his person.
“Take it out. Whatever’s in your coat.” Toma extended a withered hand toward him.
Kane said nothing. He reached into the breast of his dark gray coat and fumbled for a moment, then took out the paper folded into thirds and handed it to Toma. No one had
confiscated his personal belongings. The paper that had originally belonged to Estelle had remained pressed against his warm chest all night. Toma carried it back to the long table.
“One item recovered.”
He carefully unfolded it.
“It has a number written on it.”
“Register it as it is. For the crossed-out parts on the paper, draw them exactly as they are crossed out. Understood?”
After finishing the transcription, Toma opened another ledger, one containing forms specifically for accidents.
From where I stood by the door, I could see the edge of the original paper forced open beneath the lamplight. But the deep crease in the middle still arched stubbornly upward.
“The time column.” Toma pointed to the blank space on the form. “The time you decided to kill her. What time was it?”
Kane looked at the paper for several seconds.
“I didn’t look at the clock then. I don’t know.” He shook his head. “It wasn’t light yet, anyway.”
Toma’s pen hovered above the blank for two seconds, then passed over it, preparing to move directly to the next box.

“That box cannot be left blank.” Sera reached over and tapped the edge of the ledger. “Since he said he doesn’t know, enter his exact words: ‘The undersigned does not know.’ This ledger cannot contain an unverified mess.”
Toma stopped his pen and filled the four characters into the box that had been left blank.

“It’s obvious what happened.” Barro, seated in the middle of the table, suddenly spoke, pressing both hands heavily against the table edge. “As of today, one of this batch of children is dead, and the remaining two spent half the night running outside the village. We recovered what they had. We can’t recover what they remember.”
He glanced at me by the door, then looked straight at the head of the table.
“I move that we deal with the remaining two immediately as well.”
As soon as the words left his mouth, Toma’s pen stopped on the paper.

“Toma, record this: proposer Barro, motion to kill the two remaining candidates.” Sera immediately took over, her cold gaze sweeping over him. “Barro, with Kane under examination, only nine valid votes remain. Six votes are enough to pass. In

other words, excluding Garon, Milu, and Rena in the family seats, even if they vote against it, your motion must receive every remaining vote at the long table. Before the vote passes, anyone who acts on their own will bear the consequences.”
“Then record it. It’s something that will have to be done sooner or later.” Barro did not back down.
I pressed myself hard against the stone wall behind me and heard my own heartbeat pounding desperately in my ears.

“No one can die again tonight.” Chico, by the door, spoke up and laid his hands flat on the table. “The people outside who take our goods only recognize that we keep to the rules within our boundary. If they hear that this entire batch of children was killed in one night, they’ll take us for madmen who could lose control at any moment.”

“Don’t forget what happened on the West Two Line back then.” Nona, seated in the shadows, interrupted him by picking up a chess piece. “That time, someone crossed the boundary in secret and was stopped. The long table later ratified the Boundary Guard’s action. Besides, this time they were carrying something deadly. The Boundary Guard wasn’t insane.”

“Record this: Nona advocates ratification, citing the West Two Line precedent.” Sera spoke rapidly, without hesitation. “Add my opinion: the West Two precedent did not result in anyone’s death and cannot be treated as equivalent.”

I leaned against the stone wall, listening as they weighed our lives with the cold precedents of years past and the risks to their outside trade. I hadn’t even had time to recognize all their faces before life and death had already been broken down into a series of motions entered into the record.
At that moment, my mother stood up. The battered wooden chair scraped heavily against the floor.

“The investigation isn’t finished. No one can touch them.” She stared hard at everyone around the table. “But before the vote produces a result, I request responsibility for watching them. From now on, my son stays under guard in my house, with a guard posted outside as usual. If he runs or meets Yuna in private, the responsibility is mine.”
“Fine. Then do you dare take responsibility for the other one too?” Barro asked coldly.
My mother fell silent. She glanced toward the door, then back at the tabletop.

“I can’t keep two people under guard in my house, and I won’t make grand claims.” Her voice dropped. “The guards are already responsible for watching her. Until the final judgment, I guarantee she enters the cell alive. Nothing happens to her along the way.”
She sat back down.
Yuna’s father, Garon, had been sitting at the end of the long table all along.

“Let’s not wander off topic. First, let’s talk about the Boundary Guard killing someone alone. If all authority over life and death when judging a boundary crossing remains with one person on the scene, something will happen again sooner or later. It’s time to take that power back. From now on, using lethal force must require two people to confirm it together.”
Sera gave him a cold look.

“Garon, your status tonight is that of a summoned family member. You’re not in your seat at the long table, so you have no standing to propose a motion concerning the boundary defense.” She cut him off without mercy. “And the emergency

authority of the Boundary Guard has been an iron rule since the village was founded. If it is to be permanently changed, it must go through a formal amendment vote. The people at this table cannot change it tonight. Don’t say useless things.”
“Fine. Then I’ll say something useful.” He remained seated, his rough hands lying flat on his knees.

“I’m not asking for any disposition that would exempt her from punishment. The mill I manage is desperately short-handed this year. Carrying flour beneath the waterwheel is hard labor. I propose that Yuna be handed over to me. I only need beasts who can perform hard labor at the mill for the rest of their lives. Who she is doesn’t matter to me.”

I whipped my head toward him. Garon’s face was as numb as stone. He said the words “hard labor” as though they were a form of execution. He didn’t look at anyone. He only pressed those rough hands hard against his knees, facing the weighing and scrutiny of the long table.
The moment Garon finished speaking, Yuna’s mother, Milu, turned her head.
“Where is my daughter now?” She ignored Garon and addressed Sera directly at the middle of the long table, her voice carrying a trace of tremor.
“She’s in the side room on the second floor. Two guards are watching her,” Sera answered without expression.
Milu’s fingers gripped the edge of her chair. The joints went white with the pressure. She closed her eyes for a second. When she opened them again, the tremor had been forcibly pressed down.
“I oppose hard labor. A place like the mill can’t possibly be kept under strict guard. Who knows whether she’ll find another chance to run outside?” She addressed Otto directly
at the head of the table. “I demand that she be locked up. Put her directly in the cells below and assign people to guard her without relief. You decide how long. I’ll accept it.”

I leaned against the wall, breathing heavily. The execution motion was still on the table and could be brought up again at any moment. Milu’s back was rigidly straight. In this council chamber thick with the smell of lamp oil, she and Garon did not exchange a single glance, yet together they pushed Yuna toward the death cell and hard labor.
Otto remained seated at the head of the table for a long time, then finally rose slowly.
“There are too many threads. We’ll take them one at a time.”

“First. The companion who caused this trouble is dead, and the item has been recovered. I guarantee that no confidential information will get out. The aftermath on the long slope will be cleaned up before dawn.”
“Second. Regarding the two remaining people. There aren’t enough votes for execution tonight, so the death sentence is postponed. But Toma, write this bottom line into the copies for them: execution
remains on the table. Even if they are spared death, the gentlest outcome for this batch of children will only be long-term isolated examination. Cut off any thought that they might be released.”
I leaned against the corner of the wall and listened as he settled the dead end awaiting us.
“As for tonight’s arrangements, I approve the families’ proposals: Arno will be escorted home and guarded by Rena; Yuna will be locked directly in the cells below.”
“Third. To prevent the situation from spiraling out of control, certain powers that should not exist must be frozen.”

“Tonight, the entire western boundary defense will change shifts. The new shifts will only carry out interceptions. For the time being, the authority of the Boundary Guard on duty to decide life and death independently is suspended.”
“In addition, there are several minimum measures for control.”
He slowed his speech, giving Toma time to write.
“Suspend candidate evaluation indefinitely. The induction process for this batch of children ends here.”

“Arno and Yuna must be examined separately. They are absolutely forbidden from coordinating their statements. Confirm that the identification badges and all access credentials they handed over several hours ago have been sealed and stored.”

“Finally, until the Ten Seats makes a final long-term decision, these two are strictly forbidden from taking even half a step outside the village—and they are absolutely forbidden from meeting each other alone in private.”
Toma finished writing and read it aloud once.
“These temporary orders do not require a vote. They take effect now. Toma, arrange tonight’s shifts.”
At that moment, Toma set down his pen and picked up the duty roster in front of him.
“I’ll rearrange the shifts going to relieve the western boundary, the shifts guarding the two of them, and tomorrow’s gate duty now.” He crossed out the old list as he spoke.
Barro watched him with a dark expression.
“What if the execution motion I proposed just now passes in the future? Will you arrange the execution shift?”
Toma looked up without expression.
“If it really passes, find someone else to arrange it. There will never be a post under my command for sending them to their deaths. My people won’t do that.”

Silence settled over the room. No one accused him of defiance. Sera gave a slight shake of her head. No one asked for those words to be entered in the ledger. They simply slipped through and went unrecorded.
The emergency proceedings ended. Sera personally escorted me to the stairs on the third floor.
The corridor was dim. She held two copies of the temporary control measures Otto had just announced and folded each one in half in front of me. Then she pulled one out and held it toward me.
“Take it.”
I reached out and took it. The ink was still damp. My thumb left a clear fingerprint on the white paper.
“What about the other one?” I looked at the copy remaining in her hand.
“For the other one among you.”

“The two of you have survived tonight. But the village has not reached a final decision about your long-term disposition.” She fixed me with a warning stare. “Both of those statements are facts. You’d better keep both of them in mind. You are absolutely not allowed to choose only the one you want to believe. Understand?”
She turned sharply and walked deeper into the corridor.
I gripped the stair railing with both hands and slowly made my way down.
When I finally reached the first floor, I saw them. At the far end of the corridor, two tall guards were escorting Yuna toward the cells on the eastern side, one on either side of her.
Almost at the same moment, she turned her head and saw me.
That was how we looked at each other from far away, across the long stone corridor. I saw that she too was clutching a sheet of paper. Its fold lay in exactly the same place as the one in my hand.
At that moment, she opened her mouth slightly, as though she wanted to call my name. Before she could make a sound, the guards roughly shoved her forward.
As we passed each other in the corridor, we didn’t have time to say a single word.
I stepped out through the White Tower’s doors. The night wind cut to the bone. My mother was waiting for me in the tower’s shadow.
Without a word, she came to my side, caught my shoulder as it swayed faintly from exhaustion, and half-dragged, half-supported me forward.
A new guard assigned to us was already sitting on the old wooden bench outside our house.

After we opened the door, my mother opened the stove and added two pieces of dry firewood. Then she brought over a basin of cold water and had me wash my badly swollen ankle and the torn skin on the knuckles on the backs of my hands.

I dipped my stiff fingers into the cold water. The torn skin on the knuckles of my right hand sent a piercing pain through me at the slightest touch. I don’t regret hitting him. But I couldn’t shake the look in Kane’s eyes when I tackled him to

the ground—the way he had stood there woodenly after being hit, waiting for something. He insisted that no one else had ordered him, yet he lied about the details of the interception. Did he also know that he needed those punches as punishment?
She crouched beside me, one hand resting on the rim of the basin, watching the surface of the water, interrupting my thoughts.
“Arno.”
“Mm. I’m listening.”

“I’ll go and plead with the people at that table. Even if I die, I won’t let a resolution to kill you pass. As your mother, I’ll do everything I can to take responsibility for keeping you alive.” She raised her head and fixed me with a burning gaze.
“But I can’t promise they’ll set you free.” Her eyes dimmed. “I can’t promise what the village will ultimately do with Yuna, either.”
“I have to make this clear to you tonight, so that later, sitting alone in this room, you won’t waste time imagining things with hopes you shouldn’t have.”
The bright fire in the stove reflected across the water.
“As for Yuna…” My mother’s voice turned cold again. “I don’t know how to handle whether she lives or dies. And I can’t handle it.”
She stood and turned the stove down.
I was still gripping the sheet Sera had given me tightly in my left hand.

The final order was written clearly on it: until the Ten Seats makes a final long-term decision, these two are strictly forbidden from taking even half a step outside the village—and they are absolutely forbidden from meeting each other alone in private.
I folded the paper sharply along its existing crease. The crease fell directly in front of the two words “and they.”
The black fingerprint I had pressed onto it at the stairs was still clearly there. I stared hard at the red line drawn in black and white between Yuna and me. It couldn’t stop me.
Outside the window, the sky was still black as ink. The night watchman outside shifted his position, and the heavy bench leg gave off a harsh echo.

texts.chapter:volume0-remaining-road:event:tex:
End-of-Week Review · Escort Order (Same Day, Copy):
Two persons under review. To be escorted separately, hearings held separately.
Route: White Tower underground restricted-zone passage, via the antechamber.
Time: To be determined after the day’s shift handover.
Note: Route to be opened in advance of handover.
The night was heavy. Dawn had not yet come.

I carried the shoe from my left foot in my hand. The upper of the right shoe had already been torn apart, so I could only tie the sole against the sole of my foot as a layer of padding. With every step, the instant my unweighted toes

touched the ground, a stab of pain shot up along my shinbone into the back of my head. But I could only bite down hard on my tongue and swallow every gasp. The short iron rod hidden inside my sleeve pressed its coldness against my wrist.

If I could not make it back before the day-shift handover, the little room for mercy my mother had fought for in the council house last night would all come back down on her as a heavier punishment. I glanced back at the path behind me, then limped into the darkness.

The chapel stood on the higher ground north of the village. The new guard sitting on the old wooden bench outside my house when I was escorted home last night had been Toma. At the instant my mother pushed open the door, he had quickly whispered one sentence in my ear: Five o’clock. The chapel’s low wall.
I had been waiting by the low wall for less than four minutes when a shadow climbed over it.

Yuna stumbled when she landed, both hands striking the gravel-covered frozen ground. Like an alert little animal, she immediately came toward me when she saw who it was. One side of her collar had been violently torn open, exposing a horizontal scratch beneath the neckline.
“Your neck.” I stared at the wound.

“Sera’s guards scraped it against the wall while holding me down during the council meeting. Nothing happened to my airway.” She yanked up her collar and roughly covered the wound. A ring of deep red marks encircled her wrist where it had been bound, the skin rubbed

raw in places. “There was a loose long nail in the leg of a wooden chair in the broken cell downstairs. I used its edge to scrape the clasp open. The wooden latch on the outer window had rotted long ago. I climbed out while the guard was in the corridor smoking.”
She shook her wrist, then fixed her gaze on my right foot, which could not touch the ground at all.

“Toma couldn’t get close when he brought the food, so he left a note under the plate with this meeting point.” She spoke extremely fast, cutting straight to the point. “It said Otto had found something missing while rechecking the six relics

confiscated from the archive-room table on the long table last night: a handwritten log mentioned in the initial inventory of the scene. The hardbound notebook Estelle always carried, the one where she drew the machine’s structure. He

suspected she had dropped it near the boundary when she escaped, and ordered a search of the village outskirts. That will leave a short blind spot on the west side during the shift change. If we can get inside, find the machine, and start it—”

“No matter how many of us it can throw back into those fourteen hours,” I took over, drawing a deep breath, “as long as we intercept the three of us in the archive room then. There has to be some way to leave this place.”
“This is the only route.” She nodded firmly. “But if a patrol catches us in the village now, the consequences will be worse than staying in the house.”

There was movement ahead. Five or six people carrying storm lanterns were spreading in a fan toward the west and north sides of the village. Otto’s order had taken effect. During the shift arrangement, Toma had only pointed out the temporarily open blind spot left after these people were pulled away.
We immediately pressed ourselves against the wall of a family’s yard and held our breath. Yuna’s hand rested against my forearm, her grip light.
The lantern light swayed away toward the boundary.
“We go inward.”

We turned toward the silent tower at the very center of the village. There were guards at the main entrance, so we kept close to the wall and circled into the shadow behind the tower. Yuna tore open the ventilation grating with her bare hands; half of it had already rusted through.

Climbing through this maintenance opening into the tower connected us to the underground route that had been opened in advance for the morning’s interrogation. Just as the blind spot ran out, the heavy metal door inside

the underground restricted zone gave a faint click, and the indicator light changed to passage permitted. That was probably why Toma had arranged to meet at five—he knew the door had been set to unlock at a specific time.

But beyond that door was no clear path into the depths. The normal route that should have led downward was completely sealed by a mechanical deadlock, disconnected even from the system. The only route beside it was an underground maintenance passage with its iron grating removed. It was pitch-black inside, thick with the smell of machine oil.
She did not know where the endpoint was. She could only follow the direction of the pipe layouts and choose the downward branch through the maze of crossings. Yuna glanced at my foot.

“If you crawl through the maintenance passage in that condition, it’ll take several times longer.” She looked into the depths of the passage, then back at me. “That was her theory, drawn in the hardbound notebook. Estelle never used it, and she doesn’t even know

how. And even if the old experiment records are true—the people who sat in it died. They left behind only brainwaves or other fragmentary reactions. The records don’t even fully say how they died. If the machine really reacts, we won’t even leave ashes behind.”

That meant that when the day-shift guard pushed open my mother’s door, she would not even have a single sentence left with which to defend herself. It also meant Yuna’s parents would be taken away immediately because of her disappearance, and Milou would wake up alone. There was no way we could return to our respective houses before the day-shift handover.
I swallowed the dryness in my throat and clenched the short iron rod in my left hand. “Whatever it sends back, it’s the only way out of here. I’m taking this half-step.”
Yuna was silent for two seconds. Then she took my left arm, draped it over her shoulder, and said, “Go in.”
Dragging my right foot, I crossed into the maintenance passage with her.

For more than two hours, we moved slowly through the cramped underground passage. The heavy smell of machine oil mixed with the stale, moldy air. Every breath carried the taste of blood in my throat. My right foot had lost all sensation. There was only a heavy weight hanging from it. I leaned half my body

weight onto Yuna’s shoulder. Her clothes had long since been soaked through with cold sweat. Her slight shoulder trembled faintly each time I leaned on her, but she did not make a sound. She only clenched her teeth, feeling her way through the darkness, supporting me one step at a time as we went down.
Partway through, while avoiding a patrol, footsteps in the corridor on the right suddenly came straight toward us.
Yuna seized me and pulled me behind a pillar. I was a beat too slow. The short iron rod clenched in my left hand struck the stone pillar with a dull thud.

The footsteps stopped at once. The person raised the lantern, and its dim yellow glow swept directly across the pillar where we were hiding. I held my breath and gripped the short iron rod tightly, my knuckles whitening with the force. If he leaned around to look, the stealth we had bought with our lives would become a bloody confrontation.

The beam paused at the edge of the pillar for several long seconds. Then the footsteps began again. But he did not come around. Instead, he walked faster and faster in the opposite direction, fleeing the corridor away from

us. Deep beneath this tower, rumored to be a place of no return, the dull sound from the darkness had clearly stirred some unsettling story. The guard did not even have the nerve to lean out and confirm what he had heard.
Farther down was a heavy metal double door. On the walls to either side, a recessed compartment held a heavy lever.

The instruction plate on the right doorpost said that pressure had to be released. Most of the plate on the left had been scraped away, leaving only a few old words painted in white directly onto the wall: “Both sides simultaneously.”
“You take the right. Listen for my command. Pull it all the way down and don’t let go.” She walked to the recessed compartment on the left.
I braced myself against the wall and hopped to the right. I reached into the recess and gripped the old metal lever.
“Three, two, one. Pull!”
We exerted force downward at the same time. Hissing pressure-release sounds came from inside both walls at once. The heavy metal door gave a dull clunk as its bolts withdrew, and the door leaf sprang
inward by a crack. We braced our shoulders against it and pushed hard. After crossing the threshold, we pulled down the reset slots on the inside. With two muffled clicks, the door locked behind us.

Beyond the door was a vast, uncanny space divided into several levels by a complex network of pipes. When we were nearly exhausted, we pushed open an inner door whose number had been erased completely.
At the end of the corridor was a small high-set ventilation window, letting in a thread of gray-white light.

Dawn had come. The light fell on a mechanical punch clock forgotten beneath a dust cover in one corner of the hall. Its hands pointed to 7:45, and every second it still gave off an almost imperceptible sound of gears meshing. The day shift was about to take over.

Once the day shift completed the handover, or once the village began counting the residents of each household after eight, my mother would be unable to hold out any longer. The moment the guard outside realized

I had escaped, she would be dragged from the chair and interrogated. I drew in a deep breath of cold air smelling of machine oil and followed Yuna from the corridor through a half-open metal double door.
The instant I crossed the threshold, the enormous machine in the center of the hall entered my view. It was a black device covered in giant cables, its outline perfectly matching the
one Estelle had drawn in the hardbound notebook. To bring us before it, she was still lying on the lightless slope at the western boundary, with not even a peaceful burial to hope for.
Yuna stopped abruptly, her breathing tightening at the sight before her.
“This is the hall.” She looked at the machine, then back at the daylight entering from the corridor. “It’s not yet 7:50. We found it.”

An Official Illustrated History of the Past, Volume Six:
The fall of the Old Human Race began with that silent extinguishing.
It was the bitter fruit of the Old Human Race’s unchecked technological

expansion.
There was no storm, no tsunami, no geological disturbance.
The sky was enveloped in an unknown radiance, taking on the color of a disordered dusk.
Then people quietly fell, one after another.

There were no wounds, no torment from illness.
Cities, machines, and production facilities continued to run blindly for the following months, but no one in this world could ever again say the word “I.”
Only a second ago, I had been outside the deep-level control room, with the first cycle nearing its end. From 20:36 onward, through the thick blastproof glass, I
watched Yuna below continue to wither for more than an hour. We spoke our last words over the communicator. Then the long darkness swallowed every last light and sound.
At exactly 22:00, time threw me back to this merciless starting point.
My vision came back into focus beneath the steady sensor lights overhead in the corridor. Eight o’clock in the morning. We had thought that if the system performed its delayed startup at this
moment, time would immediately return to yesterday so we could save Estelle. But the first cycle had shown me that this morning was only the beginning of fourteen hours of futile waiting and death.

Yuna was alive—truly, fully alive—three steps away from me. She had just finished checking the error record on the secondary panel, the line that read “incomplete,” and was turning to ask why I looked as if I had seen a ghost.

The knuckles of my right hand still ached faintly—the skin had been scraped when I threw those punches at Kane while searching for Estelle at the edge of the ruined village last night. My right ankle, twisted during

that search, was now swollen and shining with taut skin. The pain in my body reminded me that the world before me was real, but the memories of the deaths I had just experienced surged through my body like a tide.
I forced myself through the pain in my ankle and lurched a full step forward, throwing half my weight onto her as I suddenly seized her hand.
“...Whoa.” She flinched and instinctively braced herself against me. “Why is your foot worse?”
Her hand was warm. Tears struck the antistatic floor without warning. One drop, then another.
“Arno?!”
“Go.” My voice was so hoarse it didn’t sound like mine.
“What?”
“They’re here. Now.”
The words had barely left my mouth when the heavy tread of boots on metal grating rang out without warning through the empty corridor outside the hall. Then Kane’s rough shout
echoed through the empty tower: “First team, seal off the chapel and bell tower! Second team, go to Otto’s and get the work-hour cards! Everyone else, follow me and search the rear!”

A flash of shock crossed Yuna’s usually self-assured face. She immediately realized that I couldn’t run in my condition. Without asking another word, she hauled my arm over her shoulder and dragged me into the hidden maintenance passage beside the hall.
We held our breath in the narrow, dark maintenance passage. The search party’s footsteps thundered over the iron grating outside, pursuing us deeper in.
After a brief dead silence, Yuna clasped my pulse in the dark.
“Okay.” She spoke at last, her voice pressed low. “Arno, listen to me. I’m going to ask you a few questions now. Bear with me.”
“First question. The search party—did you hear about their deployment last night?”
“No. It’s because I’ve already lived through today once.”
Yuna’s breathing paused for a second.
“At 22:00 tonight, time will reset to now. In the first cycle, after we started the machine this morning, the search party went everywhere arresting people.
Estelle was confirmed not to be coming back. At noon, we were trapped. That desperate standoff lasted the entire day. And you won’t even make it to 22:00.”
Yuna’s fingers remained on my wrist, feeling my pounding heartbeat.

“If you were fabricating a delusion, your most direct reaction right now would be to drag me away from the White Tower. But you accurately predicted the footsteps in the corridor outside, and you know clearly that they’re a search party, not a routine patrol.”

“But that isn’t enough. Last night, you and I had just worked through the possible consequences of starting the machine. The possibility that ‘once it reaches the endpoint, it automatically throws a person back to the starting point’ is still within the range of that analysis. You could have used that possible mechanism to imagine an entire return.”
“To prove that you really went to the future, you have to tell me one thing that is impossible to verify now, but certain to happen in the future.”
I drew a deep breath and searched through that brutal memory.
“There’s a communicator switch on the deep-level blastproof glass. The night sky outside will begin to glow a ghastly white with no physical source. Yuna, you’ll continue to wither
for more than an hour. The world above will cut the connection. This machine didn’t send us back to yesterday at all. It’s draining something else. It’s even demanding your life.”
“This isn’t only about what will happen today. It’s also the only way to prove that what I’m saying isn’t a fabrication: if everything happens tonight exactly as I’ve
said, it will be evidence of a future that cannot be fabricated. Most importantly, it will begin precisely when the electronic display on the wall reaches 20:36.”
Yuna’s fingers stopped on my pulse. She slowly released my hand.
“Okay. If that abnormal drain you described really happens tonight, I’ll accept this hypothesis: you really did go to the future.” Her voice was somewhat hoarse.
She leaned against the pipe wall and let out a long breath.
“But Arno, if your landing time was eight o’clock sharp, then the theory I drew out on paper last night was entirely wrong.”

“The machine didn’t immediately throw you back to before Estelle’s accident.” She rapidly reconstructed the logic. “It ran from eight this morning until 22:00 tonight. During those fourteen hours, the ‘starting point’ was bound firmly to the instant the system was powered on just now.”
She drew a deep breath.
“If we can’t cancel this operation, then it means... we’re locked into today.”
“Yesterday...” Something seemed to clog my throat.

In the dark maintenance passage, that brutal possibility finally crashed down with full weight. We had risked our lives starting the machine, dared to violate the greatest taboo in the village, all to return to yesterday and prevent Estelle’s accident.
But now, that point in time seemed to have become a past suspended across a chasm.
“If we can’t find another machine to undo this binding... then she really is dead.” I gritted my teeth. “We can never save her.”
Yuna was silent in the darkness for a long time.
“...Right. If we can’t find another way, Estelle really is dead.” Her voice trembled faintly, but she quickly forced it down. “Our model from last night was entirely wrong. If this is the end of the
road, then today is the only battlefield we have left. Come on. While the search party is still heading into the deep levels, let’s go back to the hall and try once to overturn the starting point.”
Forty minutes later. The search party’s activity had long since shifted to the lower levels.

We quietly returned to the stretch of corridor outside the hall where we had started the machine that morning. Yuna stood before the secondary panel beside the door and pressed her hand flat against the sensor plate.
“You have to reconfirm the operator’s position inside. I’ll try to override it from here.”

I nodded, drew a deep breath, and walked back into the depths of the hall. I sat once more in the cold recessed seat and pressed the sensor wire against the back of my neck. This was what we had done when we started the machine that morning.
Yuna pressed the scanning sensor outside. But the scanning light did not come on, and the secondary control panel showed no response.

I climbed out of the seat and returned to the doorway. Yuna was forcefully working several toggle switches on the panel, then tried pressing the confirmation key from that morning again. The screen gave

no new response. The record reading “incomplete” remained lit. She gritted her teeth and tried pulling the emergency cutoff lever beside it. The lever was locked in its slot and would not move at all.
“No. The lever’s stuck.” She released it, breathing hard, her face pale. “There’s no manual keyboard on the secondary panel for going back to yesterday, either. We can’t cancel the operation.”
We withdrew to the outskirts of the White Tower. The sun hung at an angle in the morning sky.

“We can’t just leave it at that. If it can’t be stopped now...” I thought back over last night. “When that ghastly light comes on tonight, what exactly is the underground system draining from outside? What did the panel actually say when you started it?”
“We need to split up. First, that extra line from this morning is trying to complete some kind of external demand. I’ll dig through the comparison tables in the bell tower archive
and decode it, to see whether I can find the specific conditions that trigger that demand. Second, you need to test the adults’ limits in the village. Tell them what you experienced.”

“You’re certain to hit a wall. You may even be arrested. But you have to walk through the process yourself. Only then will we know in the next cycle how the adults’ institutions respond to something like this, and what leverage to use against them.”
She gave me an escape route: “If things go well this evening, meet behind the mill.”
I circled back toward the village along the edge of the wheat fields, dragging my swollen right foot down from behind the mill onto the field ridge, then limped home.
I slipped through the gap in the courtyard wall like a thief. On the clothesline, the two pieces of clothing that should have been taken inside long ago were still hanging there.
Mother was standing with her back to me beside the stove. She heard my footsteps and turned around calmly.
“You still dared to come back. Captain Kane has already brought people to search here twice today.”

She walked to the courtyard gate, closed the half-shut door completely, and slid the bolt into place. She picked up a rough baked flatbread from the cutting board, tore it in half, and set one half on the wooden table in front of me. My ankle throbbed fiercely. I pulled out a chair and collapsed into it.

“Mom, there’s something urgent.” I didn’t touch the bread. “I’ve already lived through today once. Tonight, you have to do whatever it takes to keep Yuna from coming within a step of the White Tower.”
Mother’s hands stopped as she untied her apron.
“Why?”
“Because I’ve already lived through today once. If nothing is done about her, an irreversible disaster will happen tonight.”
Mother listened to my absurd story like a statue.
She pulled out a chair and sat across from me, both hands resting steadily on her knees.
“What I say doesn’t count. I have no independent authority to enforce anything.” She shattered my hopes without mercy. “The Ten Seats argued all night, and there’s still no result on the final
disposition of the two of you. I took advantage of the brief recess just now and made an excuse to come back and bring you bread. But this deadlock is the only thing keeping you alive right now.”
She walked to the courtyard gate and looked outside warily.
“Sera is on duty today. If you really think it’s necessary, go to the council site and find her yourself when the recess ends. But before that...”
She stood.
“The only thing I can do for you today is this. You will sit obediently in this room and not set one foot outside the courtyard!”
I stood from the chair. Pain shot through my right foot, making me stagger. The half of the dry bread remained on the table.
“I’m sorry. I have to go.”

She instinctively reached out to grab me, but when she saw my swollen, deformed right leg trembling even as I stood, her hand stopped in midair. She stared at me, knowing that a forceful prohibition could no longer hold back someone determined to leave at any cost.
She slowly drew her hand back, followed me silently into the courtyard, and watched me drag my foot through the gap.
“No matter what happens, you are absolutely not going back up the White Tower!”
That was the last thing she had said to me in the first cycle. Now everything was repeating itself without the slightest deviation.
I followed the back wall through the drying yard.

Elder Otto stood beneath his doorframe, in front of the administrative board. He removed an old wooden tag from the board, glanced at it, then selected a new one from the long string at his waist and hung it up.
Hearing my footsteps, he straightened the tag and turned around.
“If you risked your life to come here, spit it out.”
“Elder Otto, I’ve already lived through today once! No matter what, tonight we have to cut the external connection to the White Tower’s deep levels! If you don’t believe me, you can
verify it immediately—Kane is taking the search party to seal off the chapel and bell tower right now, then he’ll come to you for the work-hour cards! I know every step of their search!”
Otto wasn’t shocked by my prophecy. He only tapped the blank wooden tag irritably with his knuckles.

“That’s the public mobilization order issued before the search party set out. The whole village knows Kane is going to check the chapel and bell tower. You came here to use that as evidence for your ravings?” He frowned. “There was no advance

warning, no verifiable basis! On the strength of one piece of nonsense from you, I’m supposed to order the White Tower’s facilities forcibly shut down? If a large-scale power failure occurs halfway through, who is going to answer for it?”
“Then forcibly pull everyone out first, and fill in the basis afterward!”

“Taking an old facility offline requires a maintenance report. I’m not on duty! The only compliant thing I can do is write an abnormal-incident report and send it upward, where it can queue at the council site. It absolutely won’t arrive today.”
I stood there in despair.

“And your evacuation request means nothing coming from me.” He sighed. “The White Tower’s deep levels were fully sealed by Elder Sera last night. Your request to clear them has already been a settled fact for some time.”
He shoved open the door roughly and came back out carrying a thick file, without even looking at me.
I left Otto’s house and headed toward the chapel, but Kane stopped me halfway there with several people.
“Stop. Less nonsense. Come with me.”
He didn’t put me in handcuffs. He simply followed half a step behind me without letting me out of his sight.

As we passed the chapel, Elder Sera was sitting on the stone steps outside, a thick administrative ledger spread across her knees. The little boy Pino stood beside her, clutching an old wooden chess piece with worn edges.
“Mom, look.”
He raised the wooden chess piece with its worn edges. It was the piece Estelle had used last night to demonstrate flight paths to him.
“Will Big Sister Estelle come teach me again today how to make it fly off the board?”
“She has something else to do today.” Sera closed the thick ledger. “Go play over there.”
The boy found it boring, turned, and ran off with the chess piece in his hand. Kane coldly shoved me and urged me onward.
Kane escorted me through the White Tower’s main entrance and up to the room at the end of the second-floor corridor. There was only a wooden table and two chairs inside.

I sat on the hard chair for a long time, watching the sunlight become a thin line on the wall. At last, Elder Sera pushed the door open and entered, with Elder Otto following behind her carrying the file.
Sera sat down and folded her hands elegantly in front of her.
“All right. You can speak now.”

I told them everything. The machine starting that morning, the fact that I had already lived through this day once, the room below, and the lethal anomaly that would begin draining everything once the deep levels reached sometime after eight that evening, something that might not be stopped even by sealing the entrance.
Sera listened, then recorded my testimony meticulously on paper.
“If I take this seriously, we have to seal the deep-level passages and forcibly separate the two of you. Those measures were already deployed last night.”

“If I treat you as a mentally deranged person spouting nonsense, then you need to be locked up even more securely than yesterday.” She stood. “I’m carrying out both plans today. Your statement will be sealed in the highest-level archive.”
She paused, her gaze cold and practical.

“Not because I believe you. Only by preserving it as an anomaly record can it become, at some point in the future, leverage for proving that ‘today’ underwent a deviation. This is the greatest mercy I can offer you.”
