She strode out. Kane dragged me out and escorted me toward the other end of the corridor.

At the other end of the corridor, two guards were escorting Yuna toward us. The younger one was clutching a sheet of paper covered in writing—the fragment of the dictionary’s correspondence table Yuna had just managed to copy when she was caught sneaking into the archive.
Kane gave a cold snort, shoved me toward the wall, and forcibly widened the distance between us.

“Arno!” Ignoring Kane, Yuna shouted at me. “When we powered it this morning, its demand may already have begun. But the example in that dictionary says it’s used during severe overload! If it reaches the moment tonight when the incident occurs, keep your eyes fixed outside!”
“Shut up. No talking between detainees.”
“Remember: keep your eyes on the clock! Find out exactly when it begins!” That was her last instruction to me.
Kane escorted me into a cramped cell at the end of the corridor. There was only a hard plank bed and a chair inside, with an electronic time display hanging on the wall.
“Go in. Sit still.”
He shoved me inside and closed the door.
As the sunset dyed the mill roof blood-red, my mother’s thin figure appeared in the corridor.
“I stood downstairs in the sun for two hours before they finally let me come up and see you.”
She took half a shriveled dry cake from her pocket and passed it through the gap in the bars.
“You didn’t finish the half left on the table.”
She looked at me, fell silent for a while, then turned away with grim resolve. After a few steps, she stopped.
“Tomorrow will be another new day.”
She said it in an almost pleading voice.
The corridor outside fell completely silent.
I was locked inside the room like a trapped beast. It was an ordinary sunset, the afterglow warm orange-red as the sky settled steadily into darkness.
The bell for evening prayers rang, and reassuring lights came on in every house.

I leaned against the window and watched the night sky turn cleanly dark, the stars glittering. A deeply seductive voice rose in my heart: Maybe Sera was right. Maybe the deep levels were sealed. Maybe nothing would happen.
The time on the panel silently jumped to 20:36.
The night sky lit up without warning.
It was not the harsh, brief brightness of lightning, nor the wavering brightness of a fire. It was light seeping simultaneously out of every space in every direction.

There was no source, no direction. Everything on the ground lost its shadow. The fences, the well platform, the clothes hanging out to dry—all of them shone in that shadowless light, as if submerged in glowing, viscous liquid.
Like a dusk descending from every direction at once, having taken a completely wrong turn through time.
I lunged madly toward the high window and gripped the bars. It was exactly like the glowing night sky I had seen at the end of the deep-level ventilation passage in the
first cycle. That was when Yuna below had begun to wither in agony. Only now, this light without a physical cause had swallowed the village on an entirely different scale.

Panic-stricken sounds of doors opening rose from the village. People ran into the streets and looked up, calling their children’s names. But what chilled me was that not one dog in the entire village barked. A deathly silence.

A burst of panicked footsteps came from the corridor outside. The guard assigned to watch me had clearly seen the strange sight beyond the window as well. He ran to my door, yanked open the viewing hatch in the iron door, and asked in a trembling voice, “What’s happening outside? What is this light?”
Now.
I leapt down from the high window and, using the force of my landing, drove my foot into the iron door. The neglected bolt gave a dull impact. The guard, caught completely off guard,
was knocked back several steps by the door and fell to the ground. Ignoring the agony shooting through my ankle, I slipped sideways through the half-open gap before the door swung back.
The corridor was dim. The guard was still struggling on the floor, clutching his bleeding nose.

I didn’t stop. I charged outside, dragging my swollen leg behind me. If the night sky outside had begun to glow with this ghastly white light, then the unfinished startup from that morning really was searching for compensation beyond the White Tower. That bottomless drain was not limited to Yuna alone.
By the time I tumbled out of the White Tower’s main entrance, something horrifying was taking place in the village.
I saw Elder Nona in the distance. She was still sitting in her usual place, her head lolling softly to one side, her expression peaceful, as if she were dozing. She was clearly already silent.
Elder Barro reached out in panic to catch her. His hand had only halfway extended when his movements began to slow as though trapped in mud, then stopped completely, and he toppled to the ground.
I stumbled past the council site and saw Otto. He had just fallen on the steps, still gripping the string of wooden tags.
No one let out a dying scream. In the brief second or two before they fell, their expressions were as if they had suddenly heard someone softly calling
their names. There was no power outage, no sign of anything being drained. They simply went quiet, one after another, no longer able to control their bodies.
Then they fell. In this unheralded collapse, no one could resist. I didn’t know how far this plague-like collapse had spread. I only wanted to make sure Mother was safe.
I limped along the deathly silent village road, enduring the pain. My injured foot made it impossible to run, and the world around me blurred.
After a long while, the distant bell tower struck nine dull notes. After those nine long strikes came another light tap to mark the quarter-hour. This was the old calendar
timekeeping method we still used: one light tap meant that a quarter-hour, or fifteen minutes, had passed. After that, the mechanical hammer struck eleven rapid, short notes.
21:26. Fifteen plus eleven. Fifty minutes had passed since the shadowless anomaly began.

When I finally reached my courtyard gate, supporting myself against the wall and panting hard, Mother was weakly holding herself up against the doorframe. She turned and saw me. Her wrinkled face forced out a relieved smile.
Even though I couldn’t hear her, I immediately understood the silent movement of her lips.
“Tomorrow will be another new day.”
Her strength gave out. She slid helplessly down the rough doorframe and never rose again.
Like a wandering ghost, I dragged my injured foot toward the chapel. I had to find Sera. Maybe she hadn’t fallen yet. Maybe she could leave something behind.
I pushed open the chapel’s heavy wooden door. Elder Sera sat upright in the fifth row, her broad robe spread beneath her like a withered flower closing. She had already fallen silently.

Just then, Yuna came from the direction of the abandoned ditch. The guard escorting her had presumably fallen somewhere along the way, allowing her to break free. Her steps were steady, but strangely slow. Her ears, always held high, drooped weakly at either side.
She stopped three steps away from me. The shadowless, ghastly white light in the sky fell across her face.

“Arno... Sera must have written what you said down as a statement...” She reached a hand toward me, the light in her eyes beginning to fade. “As long as they wrote it down... for the next dozen hours or so, that paper will be ironclad proof that you’re insane...”
She drew a weak breath.

“In the cycles to come... you’ll meet this morning’s Sera again... As long as you trigger that procedure, they’ll write out the exact same ruler all over again... and use it to measure you... Next time... don’t go report it like an idiot...”
Before the words had left her mouth, she fell straight down as if the bones had been pulled from her body.

Ignoring my injured foot, I lunged forward and caught her. Her body was frighteningly light. Those lively cat ears had gone completely limp, hanging lifelessly in the crook of my arm. I pressed uselessly against her carotid artery. Beneath my fingertips was only dead silence.
In this strange dusk, the Grim Reaper had harvested her with perfect precision without needing the control room’s blastproof door.
From the moment Mother fell to the moment I reached the chapel and Yuna collapsed into my arms, the huge electronic time display on the wall had continued to advance without mercy.
21:53. Only seven minutes remained before the 22:00 cycle limit.
I laid Yuna gently on the bench, then staggered outside.
The absurd dusk in the sky still shone coldly over the dead village below.
Only children remained standing along the long village road.

Seven-year-old Pino stood alone beneath the steps of the council site. Still clutching the old wooden chess piece with its worn edge, he crossed the street littered with fallen adults and stumbled toward me.

He stopped one step away. The boy slowly raised his tear-streaked face and met my eyes in that ghastly, shadowless dusk. Every adult had fallen. I was the only person still standing in his field of vision.
He reached out with a trembling hand and seized the hem of my clothes.

I bent down and lifted Pino into my arms, letting him bury his face in my shoulder so he wouldn’t see the dead on the ground. Carrying him, I went to sit on the steps of the council site. Above the steps hung the village’s public electronic time display.
The street was deathly silent. A cat still sprang lightly along the mill wall, while I held the surviving child tightly in this village that had become a graveyard.
The time jumped to 21:59.

It was my decision. I had agreed to this operation, lain in the operator’s seat, and let Yuna perform the delayed startup. Would this enormous machine really reset time as it had last night? The first time, it was Yuna

pressing the confirmation key that caused the reset. If it only sent me back to eight while leaving this timeline here, was I going to abandon this innocent child clutching my clothes forever in this world filled with corpses?
There was nothing I could do. I could only stare fixedly at the time display on the wall in this dead village.
At exactly 22:00, the numbers on the screen flickered. Everything went black before my eyes, and I fell into absolute nothingness.
The old-script panel beside the door cast a green glow as it coldly and mercilessly reported the current time.
Eight o’clock sharp.

The sensor lights overhead in the corridor shone with extraordinary steadiness. Thirty seconds passed. Then another thirty seconds. Yuna was standing alive three steps away from me, leaning against the wall. The tip of one foot tapped the floor rhythmically, while her fingers unconsciously kneaded the faded old identification band around her wrist.
She was wearing yesterday’s clothes.
“Arno?” She came back to herself and looked at me, frowning slightly. “You look awful.”
“Nothing... nothing.”
“I’m going to check the panel.”
She walked to the secondary panel beside the door and pressed her hand against the sensor area.
“The system started on time at eight this morning. A new line appeared in the record. The annotation says ‘incomplete.’” She looked at the screen, her voice dry.
texts.chapter:chapter-01b-three-things:title: Chapter One, Supplement: Three Things
texts.chapter:chapter-01b-three-things:event:t:
Early Operators · Access Record (header format, copied verbatim):
“Column One: Access number. Column Two: Date. Column Three: Access time. Column Four: Exit time.”
Addendum: This page was automatically printed line by line by a physical typewriter, not filled out by a person.
In the latest line, Columns Two and Four are blank.
When the darkness receded, I opened my eyes for the second time in this eight-o’clock calibration area of the White Tower.
Yuna stood three steps away, still wearing the bewilderment caused by my sudden awakening. I offered no explanation. I turned and ran straight out of the White Tower.

I sprinted all the way back. A stabbing pain shot through my sprained right ankle, and the scab over my right knuckles split open and began bleeding again. Only when I hid in the shadows at a street corner and saw Mother from a distance, hanging laundry in front of our courtyard gate, did I stop.

She shook out a shirt, hung it on the hemp rope, then wiped her forehead with the back of her hand. It was such an ordinary gesture, yet it made my eyes sting at once. I didn’t dare call out to her. In my memory, she had been in that exact spot, weakly sliding down the doorframe until she sank

helplessly to the ground, never to rise again. Pino, too, had been waiting quietly to die with me on the steps of the meeting point in the distance. But at this moment, they were moving around not far away, completely unaware that this peaceful morning was merely a reprieve before destruction.

I forced myself to look away, held my breath, and quietly circled around them. Like a fugitive, I climbed into my bedroom and collapsed onto the bed. The search party had surely already spread downward through the Tower’s galleries.

My pounding heartbeat drummed against my eardrums. I stared at the ceiling. What truly frightened me was the possibility that the destroyed world had not disappeared when I reset. At 20:36 last night, the entire village had collapsed in a colorless, blinding light. If the

system had merely extracted me alone back to eight o’clock at 22:00, and that timeline was still moving forward without me… then the people who had once waited for death alongside me could only remain forever in those ashes. Nothing I did here could ever save them there.
At that moment, one bloodstained name still circled through my mind: Estelle.

Just yesterday evening, we had watched Estelle die at the edge of the broken slope. After the first run had hung for fourteen hours, it had forcibly thrown me back to this morning. But in the cycle that had just ended, Yuna had pushed the switch on the

panel all the way down. Pressing the confirmation key again produced no new response on the screen, and even the lever for forced shutdown had jammed in its slot, completely immobile. The system had clamped down on eight o’clock exactly as its starting point.

If I could force the machine to start by myself, bypassing the two-person restriction at the external cooperation station, perhaps I could break through this eight-o’clock barrier and return to yesterday.

The search party was sweeping the two floors above. While they were still checking the public areas and the depths below, I climbed back to the control hall through last night’s hidden maintenance passage. The hall was filled with nothing

but the machines’ low background hum. I strode over and forced myself into the broad binding frame. The fine line along the edge of the backrest slid down and touched the skin at the back of my neck. The main screen lit with a dim white glow.
But the screen displayed no prompt permitting operation.

I pulled the fine line away from my neck, jumped out of the frame, and walked to the operating console opposite it. After reconnecting the line, I still needed to complete the biological registration at the external cooperation station.

I tried pressing the sensor plate at the external cooperation station. The console screen lit up, and a glaring red phrase appeared in the center of the light ring: “READ-ONLY.”
Nothing else on the screen changed.

I tried to call up the system’s low-level logs, to see whether this attempt had at least left behind an “INVALID INPUT” error.
But even that was impossible. The screen remained fixed on the red interface.
I

turned back toward the frame and realized what “READ-ONLY” meant: the system was currently in the middle of an unfinished session. Until the previous process sent a valid exit command, the entire host would

reject all new input. The machine did not recognize what I had just done as a new operation at all. My attempt to bypass the restriction and forcibly start the machine to reverse time had been completely blocked.

I had to find Yuna. Without hesitation, I crawled back into the maintenance passage. But the moment I pushed open the ventilation grate at the outer perimeter, I ran straight into the search party carrying out its routine sweep.

The squad leader immediately drew his gun and shouted at me. Before I could make out who they were, I had already turned and fled toward the gallery. I knew that if I were taken into custody, the entire day would be ruined. I scrambled up the narrow stone steps as

fast as I could, the footsteps and clatter of metal behind me drawing closer. When I climbed over the low wall beside the bell tower, the pain in my right ankle slowed me by half a beat. The sole of my shoe suddenly slipped on the moss-covered edge of the stone wall.
The moment I lost my balance, instinctive fear poured through my entire body like icy water. The roar of the wind filled my ears, followed immediately by a muffled impact that tore through my chest.
The air was beaten completely out of my lungs. Every sense severed with a thunderclap of pain.
When the darkness receded again, I opened my eyes once more.

I was not inside that cramped binding frame at all. The phantom pain of my chest being crushed still lingered in my bones. I was standing at the outer edge of the White Tower’s calibration area, both hands instinctively pressed against the cold metal wall beside me. The clock on the wall pointed to exactly eight o’clock.
Time had reset again after that fatal fall. Death could not let me escape this eight o’clock.
Yuna stood three steps away, the bewilderment on her face exactly the same as when I had awakened the previous time.
In her memory, today had only just begun. I knew that a single warning would never be enough to skip her strict verification procedure. But before she could question me, I endured
the phantom pain in my bones and threw out a detail about the route that would come true moments later: “The corridor outside the hall. Heavy boots on the metal grating. Now.”
A few seconds later, when the heavy footsteps really did ring out without warning in the empty corridor outside, the wariness in her eyes turned to shock. I gave her no time to hesitate
and pulled her around the advance party. Under pressure from death and the search, the verification was forced to wait. She had no choice but to follow me back into the control hall.

After locking the blast door, I stared hard at her. “I tried to start the machine by myself just now, but all it gave me was ‘READ-ONLY.’ It doesn’t offer any new login entry. Also, I accidentally fell to my death afterward, and the machine pulled me back

to this morning again.”
“‘READ-ONLY’ means there’s still an unfinished process stuck in the system.” Yuna examined the area beneath the main screen carefully.
“The village history archives say that all operating records from the early Operator experiments

were deleted more than a century ago.” Her hand moved inch by inch along the metal seam beneath the console. “But older lower-level hardware usually came with a physical paper-feed slot, and it wouldn’t be affected by deletion from the upper-level system.”

She felt a concealed latch and pulled out a flat drawer with force. Inside lay a long roll of stiff printer paper, its edges rough from being cut by the machine. This was a hardware backup from the system’s lowest level.

I spread the roll flat across the console. At the top of every page was the same rigid four-column header.
Column One: Access number. Column Two: Date. Column Three: Access time. Column Four: Exit time.

I read aloud the access times in the third column, starting with the oldest few hundred entries:
“Fourteen oh seven.”
“Nine forty-one.”
“Eleven twenty.”

Yuna picked up a broken piece of black charcoal from the corner of the control room. She drew a heavy horizontal line along the edge of the console as a makeshift timeline for one day, then marked the times I had just read as black dots in sequence along the line.
“Scattered.” She delivered the judgment coldly. “The earlier operators could connect to the machine at any time. There was never a strictly locked eight-o’clock starting point.”
We continued turning the pages.

“At some point, things changed. Look at these entries—the exit times are all blank.” She pointed at the grid, her tone level. “That means the operators from that period were all unable to exit normally as required. But look below…”
She pointed to the next line immediately below. The numbers were still increasing, and there was still a new date for the new day.

“Although the previous line had no exit stamp, in the past, once the second day arrived, the operator on duty could forcibly press the ‘RESET’ key on the main console, and the typewriter would automatically advance to a new line. The system would cut off the unfinished loop and allow a new session to begin on the next line.”
She pulled the paper strip all the way down with a rattling sound, until the more than two hundred records ended completely. On the newest sheet, the typewriter had printed only one isolated line.

Access number: one. Date: blank. Access time: eight o’clock. Exit time: blank.
There was only this one line on the entire sheet.
“The previous page ends at two hundred forty-three.” Yuna pulled the sheet straight. “With you, the former sequence was completely cleared. Even the old mechanism that
allowed a reset on the second day seems to have been revoked by new low-level permissions. What you’re facing now is an entirely new zero state. The number became one.”

I clenched the sheet tightly.
“This is the record of our first start of the machine this morning.” I pointed at the single line. “But after eight o’clock just now, I also tried to force-start it alone. If

it was rejected, why is there no ink on the paper strip showing that it was ‘REJECTED’?”
“Because there’s nowhere for dead code to be printed.” Yuna pointed at the typewriter’s heavy metal type hammers.

“Look at the records for the several hundred people before you.” Her fingertip slid across the old data on the previous sheet. “In the old system, when an exit command was issued, it not only printed the exit time, but also

triggered a physical ratchet in the external paper-feed mechanism, pushing the strip up one notch and leaving the host space for a new line. Or, as I said, someone manually reset it the next morning and forced it up one notch.”
She moved her finger to the newest sheet.
“But with you, the exit time is blank, and there’s no second day for you to reset it. Without the ratchet moving, the paper strip is stuck on this line forever. If those later
attempts to start the machine alone generated dead code, then because the paper never moved, every type hammer would slam into the same spot, eventually becoming a black mass of ink.”
I remembered how the only line on the paper strip had been printed in an unusually deep black.
“If that’s true…” I looked at the glaring mass of ink. “Since the new mechanism no longer allows a forced reset on the second day, as long as this existing login doesn’t end
and the ratchet doesn’t advance the paper, the entire host’s input interface is physically locked. The system can never accept an instruction from us to go to another time.”
Estelle had died yesterday evening.

If the paper really showed things as they were, the system refused to reverse time with an entirely new start. Even if only fourteen hours separated us, the broken slope from yesterday evening had become a past I could no longer reach. I was trapped in this morning.
“I’m going to copy down every suspicious detail.”
She took out her old notebook and drew a short horizontal line in the center of each of the two blank grids—“Date” and “Exit time”—with a black dot at either end.

“From now on, whenever you see this mark, it means I personally checked the original and verified that these two fields were blank. That’s different from my having missed them while copying. Maybe these two empty fields are the conditions we need to complete in order to end this damned session number one.”
Once she had confirmed everything, she closed the notebook briskly.

Based on the two blank fields on the paper strip, I proposed that we remain in the control room to verify whether they were conditions that had to be completed before session number one could end: we would keep the connection line on my neck in place and

submit no new instructions. Since we were locked behind this blast door, it was a good chance to see whether, on this paper with no exit record, forcibly extending session number one to 22:00 would produce another landing point—or simply leave me where I was.

Since this experiment had been proposed by Yuna herself to verify the mechanism of the paper strip, she temporarily set aside her distrust of me and remained with me behind the heavy door we had locked from the inside.

We spent twelve hours of daylight in this cycle enduring the dead silence of the control hall. After weighing the cost of breaking through the blast door, the search party left us undisturbed for the entire day, having reached only the conclusion that they would “apply to the people above for heavy cutting equipment once it’s confirmed that no one is in the Tower.”

During the long, empty vigil, Yuna began speaking to me intermittently, trying to fight the irritation brought on by hunger and thirst. She mentioned that yesterday afternoon Milu had insisted on adjusting the kite

string herself, only for the whole kite to end up stuck in a tree, leaving her stamping her feet in distress. Yuna had wanted to help her get it down, but had decided to let Milu learn how to handle it herself.

That was what Yuna had been most worried about that morning. She had clutched the fine hemp string then and brushed it off with a single sentence: “She’s stubborn as a mule.” Now she lightly filled in the details, while I clenched my teeth and stared at

the white wall ahead without making a sound. She didn’t know there would never be a tomorrow in which she could watch her sister learn to fly a kite. I couldn’t speak either, because I knew that even the slightest tremor in my voice would expose my fear.

Several times during that stretch, I felt a faintly cold stimulus at the back of my neck. Yuna stated that it was only the system periodically polling whether I, the operator, was still online. Beyond that, nothing else happened.
At 20:36, the daylight outside became strange. Though we couldn’t see the sky from behind the iron door, that fatal wrong dusk pierced the physical defenses right on schedule.

Time passed, and nothing changed. When the destruction outside arrived, we still did not escape it behind the iron door. We had no further conversation. I already understood that in this locked system, even holding out until the end would not give us any extra landing point.
Yuna leaned against the metal door, her breathing gradually weakening. She pressed her back against the cold iron, both hands habitually gathered inside her sleeves. In severe pain,
her body slid downward little by little. I watched helplessly as she walked toward that destined ending once again. Numbness and powerlessness flooded my entire body like molten lead.
“Arno,” she called weakly.
“Yeah.”

“When you open your eyes next time… if it really takes you to another time or place,” she turned her head with difficulty and looked at me seriously, “remember not to move at once. Feel the environment around your body first.”
“Feel what?”

“When people are extremely frightened or have just woken up, the brain can deceive itself about the first image it sees.” Her voice grew softer, but her tone remained unyielding. “The body’s sense of touch is the hardest anchor to fake. First use your hands to confirm

the texture of the wall or floor you’re touching. That’s the first fact. Then look at where the light is coming from. That’s the second. Finally, listen to the background hum around you. That’s the third. Remember these three facts. Don’t guess where you are by instinct.”
At exactly 22:00, boundless darkness swallowed me.
When the darkness receded again, I opened my eyes once more.
This time, I did not immediately look around as instinct urged me to. I forced myself to count the “three facts.”

First: the cold metal wall. I could feel my palm pressed against it. Was that the last sensation I had felt before leaving the control hall? No.
Second: the light at the edge of my vision was not the stark

fluorescent light of the hall, but morning daylight leaking through the ventilation slats on the side of the domed ceiling.
Third: that continuous low-frequency background hum was coming from underground.

These three facts told me with certainty that I was still standing in that morning at the outer edge of the White Tower. Then I turned toward the mechanical clock on the wall. Its hands pointed exactly to eight o’clock. I was not inside

the binding frame at all. The so-called cycle had not preserved my body’s final position before 22:00. It had crudely reset everything, even resetting my posture to the position from my first awakening, with my hands against the wall.
Every last hope vanished. The machine had not sent me to another time, nor had it left me inside the frame.
Yuna stood three steps away, the bewilderment on her face exactly the same as every previous time I had just awakened.

The hunger and exhaustion from that long vigil, our deductions over the recording paper, the watch behind the door, and the weight of her gradually losing her body heat against the iron door at dusk had left

not the slightest trace on her. To her, this was still a wholly unguarded, entirely new morning. I couldn’t help looking toward the physical paper-feed slot. It was locked by the drawer now, but I knew it still

contained only that solitary line of black text. The ink on the paper strip could accumulate across cycles, while the living person before me was reset completely clean. That was the coldest part of this system.

I looked at her, and that bone-deep loneliness swallowed me completely. I knew there was no shortcut left that could let me skip anything. I could only place the full weight of this absurdity on her, without holding anything back.
“Yuna.” My voice was a little dry, but utterly serious.
“What is it?” She looked at me with some puzzlement. “You look terrible.”

“There’s something I need to tell you from beginning to end,” I said softly. “About this Tower, the search party closing in outside, and the destruction that will certainly arrive tonight. After you hear it, you’ll probably think I’ve gone completely insane.”
She furrowed her brow slightly. Just then, heavy boots sounded from deep in the corridor.
“The search party is about to sweep through here.” Her gaze immediately turned toward the sound, but soon returned to me. She didn’t question how I knew the search party existed. After examining the
blood marks clenched into my hand, she remained calm. “If you really have something that important to say… come with me. Let’s find somewhere to hide first. You can tell me slowly once we’re there.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:title: Chapter Two: The Elders
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s2-:
Inner Circle Council Record · Emergency Protocol for Anomalous Contact (Excerpt):
1. If a candidate breaks out of house arrest, first verify the house-arrest location and the routes to their home.
2. Next search the public levels of the White Tower, the village’s main

roads, and the shortcuts.
3. Then concentrate personnel at the village boundary and on the roads leading to the outlying facilities.
4. Once found, question them separately and take them into custody. Do not reach a final conclusion before verification is complete.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s6-: “I have something to tell you, from beginning to end.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s7-: Just before the long torture of subjective time began, during the fifth loop, I had said those exact words to Yuna at the outer edge of the White Tower. I had planned to spill everything, but the moment I

began, Kane, leading the search party, struck my right leg with his baton and knocked me to my knees. Yuna instinctively took half a step back and looked at me with the wary eyes she reserved for strangers.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s8-:
During the four loops I exhausted after that, I tried every dead end like a genuine madman.
I tried dragging Yuna straight to the abandoned storehouse east of the White Tower to search the old archives. That time, I thought seeing the records with my own

eyes would be enough to win. Instead, the patrol trapped us in the corridor, and a guard crushed the bones in my right hand underfoot while I fought for the door. I also tried shouting and screaming in the square. All I got for it was being beaten

unconscious before noon. In the different rounds that followed, while trying to hide, I watched the people of the Inner Circle fall one after another in different places, piecing together the exact order in which their lights went out through repeated resets.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s9-:
Brute force was useless. The people here only recognized flawless proof.
In the tenth loop, I hid outside the council chamber window and carved every secret exchange in the meeting into my memory. In the eleventh, I deliberately let myself be caught and brought into the council chamber. When Otto initiated that high-risk

contamination verification to question me, I threw myself toward the long table at the cost of three broken ribs, memorizing the top-secret question he had written on paper and pressed beneath the wooden marker, its answer, the confidential transfer order beside his hand, and the scratch on the back of the marker.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s10: Now, carrying these brutal facts bought with my life, I opened my eyes for the twelfth time at eight o’clock sharp on the lower level of the White Tower.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s11: My hands were still trembling uncontrollably. The phantom pain from eleven consecutive loops of broken bones and death, together with the sprained right ankle from landing at eight sharp and the real abrasions left on the knuckles

of my right hand by last night’s struggle, pierced the gaps between my bones like nails. Even breathing filled my chest with the taste of rust. This machine was close to grinding me apart. But I forced myself to stand straight.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s12:
“They’re here.”
Before I had recovered from the dizziness, Yuna grabbed my arm. I forced myself through the sharp pain of twisting my right ankle and staggered as she dragged me into

a concealed maintenance passage beside the wall.
Almost the moment we hid, heavy boots began trampling the metal grating two levels above us. It was a patrol sent to hunt us down.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s13: We held our breath in the cramped passage. Only after the heavy footsteps gradually faded did Yuna let go and examine me in the weak light.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s15: “Arno?” She noticed something was wrong at once. “You look awful. You’re shaking. What happened?”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s17: “I’m back again.” I leaned against the cold brick wall, drew in a deep breath of dry air, and spoke hoarsely. “Yuna, the machine is real. It sent me back to this morning. I’ve woken up in this morning several times already.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s18: The foot she had just moved half a step stopped abruptly. She had been about to offer her usual analysis of the machine, but her eyes swept quickly over my face, and she swallowed the words before they could leave her mouth.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s19: She didn’t ask some useless question like, “Are you sure?”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s21: “Find Otto.” She turned decisively and proposed a course of action. “If this is real, you have to prove it to the Inner Circle. Report the top-secret things he couldn’t possibly have told anyone else right in front of him and let me verify them. If you can do that, I’ll help you.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s23: “I still need to give Otto three pieces of evidence,” I said.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s27: “A facility malfunction forecast, the specific details of a closed meeting, and a high-risk contamination verification question,” I said. “This procedure is supposed to be used only when they encounter the

deepest forms of cognitive infection. Have him write the question himself, seal it away, and let me answer it blind. If I can even answer an old case he himself chose, he can’t dismiss us as ordinary madness.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s31: “At eight fifty-eight, the number two water valve at the outlying mill will trip and report an error because of pressure overload.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s32: Yuna lowered her head. She pinched the old identification strip on her wristband, turned its metal clasp all the way around, clicked it shut, and let go.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s39: The dust around the inspection hatch had settled recently. We kept low, went around to the section of low wall from which we could see the entire roof of the outlying mill, and crouched down side by side.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s40: She didn’t ask how I planned to prove it. She pressed her fingers hard into the crack between the bricks, watched the distant mill, and calculated the time in silence.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s41: At eight fifty-eight, a column of white high-pressure steam rose from the direction of the mill on schedule. Immediately afterward, the sharp alarm reporting the error carried through the cold morning air from far away.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s42: Her breathing rose and fell with the alarm. She watched the people under Kane running toward it.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s44: “The number two water valve tripped,” she said quietly. “The time and location are completely accurate.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s45: But her brow drew tightly together.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s47: “But that isn’t enough. The mechanical failure could be something you tampered with in advance. You still have to prove the second and third things to Otto.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s48: Bracing myself on my knees, I stood up from behind the low wall despite the pain in my ankle and brushed the dust from my palm.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s49: By this time, Otto would already be preparing to open the meeting at the council chamber. Once it adjourned, the day’s work orders would be distributed and sent out to every team. If we missed
this meeting, then after all the day’s orders had gone out, getting everyone to stop work and sound an evacuation warning would require reconvening all ten seats to revoke every order already
issued. That would consume the entire afternoon. By the time the warning actually went out, it would already be dark, and the villagers would meet their dead end amid panic and a stampede.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s51: “So the only way is to let them take me there and prove it in front of the Inner Circle seats.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s53: Limping on my right leg, I went around the low wall and walked straight into the middle of the only road.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s54: Kane had just returned from verifying the valve malfunction when he saw me. He warily placed a hand on the defense baton at his waist. Once he recognized me, he said coldly, “Come with me.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s55: Yuna came out from behind the wall. Under the search order issued that morning, Kane immediately waved over another guard and separated us by ten paces.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s56:
I raised both hands and let the guard approach. Just as he was about to seize my arm, I quickly tore a strip of clean linen from the lining of my outer coat and wrapped it around the wound in my right palm, where the phantom pain of shattered bones from the earlier loops still lingered.
The guard frowned but did not stop me.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s57: We were escorted separately toward the council chamber in the village.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s61: The council chamber was in the rear row behind the chapel. It wasn’t large. A heavy, long wooden table stood in the center.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s62: Kane pushed me through the door under escort.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s63: “Keep her outside. Don’t close the door all the way.” I stared at Kane. “I want to see Otto. I have information that can report every confidential resolution.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s64: Kane watched me warily, then finally allowed Yuna to stand outside the half-open wooden door.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s65: This precise machine was processing the village’s core morning business. Otto sat in the innermost seat at the head of the long table, a pen in his hand. Sera sat to his left with a black register open
in front of her. Barro, Galon, Toma, and the clerk by the window, who also possessed voting rights as a council seat but was currently responsible for rotation records, were seated around the table.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s66: At the sound of the door opening, Otto didn’t even raise his head.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s68: “Stand there,” he said, watching the tip of his pen. “Wait until this matter is finished.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s70: They were arguing over the irrigation schedule. The upstream section was short one laborer, and two council members were arguing endlessly over whose household would provide someone and how many days they would cover. Otto listened, rapidly wrote three lines on the paper, then picked up a wooden marker representing authorization and pressed it down.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s73: The clerk came over, took the paper away, and recorded it as a matter of course.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s76: Next, Sera pushed the black register to the center of the table, preparing to read out the day’s controlled agenda.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s77: Dragging my injured right foot, I forced my way to the table and interrupted her.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s78: “No need to read it.” I stared at the register. “The adjustment to the outlying assignments, the temperature-control materials for Breeding Room Three, the additional guards for the laboratory, and how you plan to handle the rumors about the White Tower’s disturbance. Those are the four matters in the register.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s79: Sera’s hand froze as she turned the page. Several people around the table turned their heads at once.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s82: “The important part is the trade hidden among them.” I turned to Barro and pointed at the register in front of Sera. “The second item is materials for the breeding room’s temperature-control units. You’re responsible for those, and you were planning to use them to protest that the archive had withheld your

dehumidifying materials for two seasons. But Sera, who oversees the archive, was planning to give you the batch of laboratory guard positions assigned to her under the third item, to calm you down. You didn’t really want the dehumidifying materials. You wanted people. You confirmed this trade before the meeting.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s83: Barro’s face went white. He instinctively glanced at Sera. The tacit agreement known only to the core seats had been exposed in front of everyone.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s86: “And then there’s the fourth item.” I showed no mercy. “As for the rumors brought in from outside, you’ve classified them as ‘not to be addressed.’ And not one of you dares put the
specific content of those rumors—the words ‘the White Tower’s vibrations last night sounded exactly like the sign of the disturbance nineteen years ago’—on the table for discussion.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s89: A dead silence spread through the room. The clerk’s hand holding the pen hung in midair, and a drop of ink struck the grid paper. In only a few minutes, I had reported four sealed details concerning the village’s lifeline, as if taking apart a transparent machine.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s92: “Otto.” I looked directly at the man at the far end of the table. “Under the regulations, when you suspect that my mind has been replaced by a White Tower monster and reduced to a shell capable only of reading surface memories, you have to initiate the high-risk contamination verification procedure.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s93: In the desperate dead ends of the previous loops, this was how he had questioned me.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s94: “In this verification system, which recognizes the past but not the future, if I answer some trivial secret of your choice, you can simply declare me a monster that has just stolen your surface memories.” I stared at him. “To prove that what I brought back isn’t

ordinary delirium, I need you to write down the most secret yet most certain fact of your career. Even if I’m asking you to recall it right now, that old matter has to be heavy enough that a surface-level hallucination monster couldn’t read it away in an instant.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s95: Otto narrowed his eyes slightly. He took a folded sheet of paper from inside his coat and picked up a dip pen. After hovering for a moment, he wrote a sentence. He folded the paper, pushed it to the center of the table, and pressed it firmly beneath the wooden marker beside his hand.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s97: I pulled over a sheet of blank grid paper, rapidly wrote three lines with my bandaged right hand, and shoved it in front of Sera, pinning it down.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s98: “First line.” I looked at Otto. “It’s the order you issued privately last night but never made public: the two crates of anti-corrosion sealant meant to repair the water tank were secretly transported to the rear mountain. Second line: the wooden marker you’re pressing down right now has a

scratched ‘V’ carved into its back. I saw and memorized both of those during my last failure, when you were examining me at the cost of my life. As for the third line, I wrote down both the question and the answer to the high-risk contamination verification you just pressed beneath the marker—”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s99: I paused and read it out, one word at a time.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s10: “You wrote: ‘When we judged that madman nineteen years ago, exactly how many people voted in favor?’ The answer is: ‘Seven.’”
“Do you still need me to keep proving it?”
Sera held up two fingers and turned over the sheet I had written. The first two lines exposed Otto’s secrets completely, while the question in the final line
and the answer “Seven” matched the paper beneath Otto’s marker exactly. Otto only glanced at it, but the hand pressing down on the marker trembled slightly.
“How long were you in the depths of the White Tower this morning?” Otto asked in a low voice. “What did you touch?”
“Less than an hour. I was placed in the scanning cradle of the mainframe on the lowest level.” I looked straight at him.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s11: Otto’s eyes immediately shifted to someone else.
“Candidate.” He turned completely toward the half-open wooden door. “You were outside. What did you see with your own eyes?”
Kane pushed the door open, and Yuna came in from outside. She put her hands behind her back, her spine straight.

“On the way here, he accurately forecast that the number two water valve at the outlying facility would trip at eight fifty-eight. Just now, outside the door, he predicted the details of the closed meeting and this verification question. They were then proven at the table. I heard and saw these things myself.”
“Do you believe his nonsense?” Toma couldn’t help interrupting.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s12: “I’m not reaching a conclusion about it.” Yuna rejected him coldly.

Sera picked up her pen and wrote in the register: “Record: Witness states that candidate Arno accurately forecast the facility malfunction and the details of the closed meeting, corresponding to the facts. Witness reaches no conclusion as to the cause.”
Galon pushed the sheet containing the answer to the verification question half an inch toward Sera. She picked it up and pressed it beneath the register.
“All right.” Otto folded his hands. “You correctly reported everything you couldn’t possibly know. What do you want?”

“I want a sheet of paper. At twenty thirty-six tonight, a catastrophic disaster will happen in the village. The sky outside will suddenly light up with a directionless false dusk!” I clenched my teeth. “The machine

in the White Tower has already started. In the silence of the earlier loops, I saw with my own eyes how people fell—the longer they had lived, the earlier they fell! Just as Yuna suspected, that thing is forcibly

extracting some invisible energy to fill a gap, and its side effects will crush you first! Send this time out as the highest-level emergency decree, sound the alarm, have everyone stop work, and prepare for the disaster!”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s13: “And then?” Otto stared at me. “After sounding the highest alarm, then what? If it draws everything outside in, where are the remaining people supposed to hide?”

“I don’t know an effective way to shelter them. Even the people who were outside in the last loop collapsed.” I clenched my fists. “But I know staying beside the machine is certain death! Even if you refuse to sound the highest alarm right away, at least reduce

part of the daytime production under the pretext of equipment maintenance. Evacuate the people in high-risk positions first, have the Inner Circle prepare supplies, and when evening approaches, use a short-term order to scatter the rest and have them take shelter!”

“That would be pushing the village over a cliff.” Otto tapped the tabletop. “According to your current inventory and ledgers, if I stop even a third of today’s day-shift workforce under the pretext of maintenance, the entire defensive line will run out of food tonight. Worse, this abnormal staggered

redeployment cannot be concealed. Before half a day has passed, the rumors among the workers about your madness and the White Tower’s disturbance will erupt completely. Even a short-term evacuation order at dusk would be enough for them to take it as ironclad proof that disaster had already arrived.”
He looked directly into my eyes.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s14: “The moment the first person panics and raids the food stores, the entire line will collapse. Nineteen years ago, we were only half an hour late suppressing them, and the outskirts nearly
burned themselves to the ground. You want to sound an alarm and have me wager the enormous risk of a village-wide riot against a physical disaster that even you don’t know how to evade.”

I stood there rigidly. I had those impossibly accurate numbers in my hands, but I had neither the supplies to fill the food shortage nor the ability to soothe the fear that had been accumulating in the outskirts for so long.

“So even if the machine really drains everyone dry tonight…” I looked at him in despair. “No matter what evidence I bring about time reversal, if it would cause panic, it can never be acknowledged here.”
“That last half is an assessment of the proceedings. I’ve recorded it.” Sera’s pen tip moved across the paper.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s15: Sera reached out and closed the register with a dull snap.

“There are two complete matters directly related to the White Tower filed by year in this register: nineteen years ago and forty years ago. The index contains one earlier matter, but that page has been torn out.” Sera

looked at Otto. “The people involved in these matters all said things like he has—things no one else could possibly know—before their situations became irreversibly serious. And they all shouted about destruction.”
Otto’s hand moved toward the string of wooden markers at his waist.

“On-duty council member.” He looked at Sera. “Under the regulations, contamination this deep and severe can bypass ordinary procedures, including family recusal.” He looked without expression at Galon, then turned his eyes back to Sera. “Under my authority, I require you to sign an immediate compulsory isolation order.”
Sera did not hesitate. She picked up her pen and wrote her conclusion in the register: “Proceed accordingly.”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s16: “Galon.” Otto turned to the other council member at the table. “After the meeting, go to the White Tower yourself. Don’t touch any core equipment. Confirm from the outer observation level only whether the mainframe is showing abnormal readings. Before twenty thirty-six tonight, station three people at the village boundary to observe.”
“No village-wide warning.” Otto answered coldly. “If there’s an anomaly, it’s an internal investigation matter. We absolutely cannot let panic destroy the village.”
He looked at Kane last. “Separate the two of them.”

Yuna obediently followed Kane outside. Just before leaving, she turned her head. Her eyes were sharp as blades as they swept from Otto at one end of the long table to the final council seat, examining each position in turn, as if she intended to carve the faces of these people into her memory.
Only I, the subject of the disposition, remained in the room. Otto picked up the dip pen again and wrote a restriction memorandum on a fresh sheet of grid paper.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s17: “Record it. File it separately as a same-day disposition memorandum,” he instructed the clerk. “Write the date on the first line. Second: Candidate’s words and conduct abnormal; suspend procedure, restrict movement, continue observation. Third: This notice is an early risk-control measure and is not to be distributed to the full council for now.”

I stared at the sheet. Not one word about the disaster appeared in those three lines of official prose. What was more, as long as he didn’t distribute it, the other four members of the ten-seat council who were not in the room would not even know that I had predicted a disaster.
“How many copies does this document need to be sent to?” the clerk asked dutifully.
“I want to retrieve the archives!” I finally shouted. “I want the two surviving abnormal reports! I want to see whether the time written on them is also twenty thirty-six!”
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s18: Otto calmly set down the dip pen.
“Accessing the controlled archives requires a legitimate reason to be entered on the administrative form.” He looked at me. “What’s your reason? ‘Verifying the destruction of the village’?”

I dragged my right foot forward one step.
“Then enter: ‘Verifying the common features of a highly credible contamination risk and previous White Tower anomalies.’” I stared at him.
Otto watched me in silence for several seconds. It was, in fact, an unimpeachable legitimate reason.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s19: “I’m only responsible for determining the risk.” Otto calmly turned to the other two people at the table. “Sera, Barro. Access to the controlled archives requires the two keys in your hands.
Since Arno says the reports from nineteen and forty years ago also bear the time twenty thirty-six, wouldn’t taking out those two old reports and checking them yourselves confirm his claim?”

Sera looked at me coldly. “Information provided by a contamination source has no value for comparison. The archive does not accept requests for verification based on madness.”
Barro touched the half of the brass key at

his waist and immediately agreed. “And this would necessarily require a joint guarantee from several members of the Inner Circle. I refuse to bring out the old files and create unnecessary speculation at a time like this.”
“The request to retrieve the archives is denied.” Otto picked up the memorandum again and ordered the clerk, “Do not leave a blank on the memorandum explaining this matter.”
He folded the sheet containing the three-line resolution in half.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s20: “This document will not be copied or sent any further.”
He drew a cold zero in the “Number of Copies Sent” column and slipped the paper into the innermost pocket of his coat, against his body. If he had decided I was merely insane, he could have destroyed
the record outright or thrown it into an ordinary archive box. But he kept it close to himself. In this room, every official warning concerning tonight’s disaster had been cut off at the source.
“Take him back and keep him under house arrest.”
The corridor outside was cold and dim. My mother, Rena, stood far away at the end.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s21: “They said I could look at you from a distance,” she said timidly.
She stared at me for a while.
She fumbled for something, then reached around Kane’s broad body and held out half a cold bread roll wrapped in paper. Strangely, Kane didn’t stop her. The bread felt cold against my palm.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s22: “You left so early this morning you didn’t even have time for breakfast,” she said softly.
I clenched the half-piece of cold bread.
She turned and walked back. After a few steps, she paused again.

I spent the great stretch of time remaining that day enduring an ordinary soft-confinement room in the chapel’s rear courtyard. The heavy bolt was locked from outside. I had no tools. I couldn’t get out.
I leaned against the door, clutching the half-piece of

bread that had hardened. The footsteps of the guards changing shifts outside and the sound of the windmill’s bearings turning in the distance both reminded me that time was passing. I was waiting for an execution, or serving as a helpless recording device.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s23: The night sky began glowing again from every direction—the directionless false dusk without a sun arrived on schedule.

Through the narrow window, I stared at the ghastly white light. Several abrupt, short cries of alarm came from the village. Someone had probably just opened a door to look at the sky, but only seconds later, those cries cut off.

The first dull sounds of people collapsing came from far away. In the earlier loops, when I was still locked up at an outlying holding point, I had heard the same pattern. When this machine extracted fuel, it first drained those whose wear was deepest and whose soul records had existed

the longest. So in the first silence, the long-lived elders scattered throughout the village were the ones who fell, and only afterward did the sounds reach the adult laborers in the outskirts. The footsteps outside gradually thinned, and the village fell completely into an eerie silence.
I sat in the light, watching the shadows move slowly across the wall. Time stretched into a slow torture.

Twenty-one twenty-six.
Given my mother’s seniority as a first-generation resident, and the order in which I had watched the elders fall one by one in the previous loops, she should be the fourth. By now, she was probably sliding helplessly down the rough doorframe of her own home.
And Yuna—she was still young. She would probably lose consciousness somewhere over the next several dozen minutes.
In that bright room, gradually stripped of every sign of life, I kept my eyes open and endured the long, endless silence. Until the electronic time board gave a crisp beep.
Twenty-two hundred. Boundless darkness swallowed me again, and the dizziness of everything resetting struck all at once.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s24: When I felt the light again and opened my eyes sharply, I found myself standing in the familiar corridor of the White Tower once more. The shadows on the wall told me it was eight o’clock in the morning.

“Hide.” Before the footsteps overhead arrived, I reached back and pulled Yuna into the maintenance passage.
The sound of boots crossing the metal grating passed overhead on schedule.
Only after the surroundings fell quiet again did Yuna relax her tense shoulders. She leaned against the wall and toyed with the metal clasp on her wristband.

“Don’t rush to believe anything about what happened to me.” I looked into her eyes and lowered my voice. “Spend the whole morning checking two things for me. If what you find doesn’t match, you can hand me over to Kane at any time.”
Her fingers stopped turning the clasp. A trace of scrutiny passed through her eyes. This was something she could verify without first blindly believing anything.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s25: “What do you want me to risk checking?”
“Check the abnormal reports from nineteen and forty years ago in the controlled archive. Verify whether the disaster times shouted by those two madmen were also twenty thirty-six.”

This was the entrance to the lower level of the White Tower. According to the rules, the abnormal reports should have been stored in the controlled archive room at the chapel. But I had discovered during my previous failed loops that the highest-confidentiality old archives had actually been improperly stuffed into the abandoned storehouse east of the White Tower.

“Don’t go to the chapel.” I stared at her and pointed toward the long corridor leading to the abandoned facilities in the east. “Go to the storehouse. They’re hidden in there. It’s a restricted area, but I remember that when you came out just now, you should have had Sera’s discarded-material inspection form on you. The guards won’t stop you.”

But in the previous loops when I had dragged her into forcing our way into the storehouse, it had been a dead end. The guards had trapped us in that corridor, and she had watched me get my bones broken. The Yuna in this loop should know nothing about it.
When she followed my finger toward the dark corridor, her body suddenly stiffened.

She hadn’t taken a step, but her face went deathly pale. Her shoulders recoiled half a step against her will. Her fingers dug hard into the metal clasp on her wristband, and an unmistakable fear and extreme resistance flashed through her eyes.
texts.chapter:chapter-02-elders:event:text-s26: “Strange…” She frowned and drew a deep breath, as if struggling to suppress some sudden physical revulsion. “I don’t even know what’s inside there. Why, when I look at that corridor, do I… start shaking?”
Watching her instinctively take half a step back, I stood in the morning corridor as my heart abruptly skipped a beat. This was the first time the loop’s remnants had remained inside her.
texts.chapter:chapter-02b-no-exit-time:title: Chapter Two: Appendix — No Exit Time
texts.chapter:chapter-02b-no-exit-time:event:t: In this “today,” folded over countless times, it was 8:00.

As my consciousness snapped back into place, air carrying the stale smell of machine oil filled my lungs again. I found both hands pressed hard against the cold wall along the outer edge of the White Tower’s calibration area. The dull pain

of my sprained right ankle and the sharp sting of the skin broken over my right knuckles arrived on schedule. Three steps away, Yuna stood beside the external collaboration interface, the toe of one foot tapping the floor in a steady rhythm.
“Thirty seconds. We agreed to wait thirty seconds. They’re up.” She turned toward the interface screen and lowered her voice.
I did not grab her and flee in panic as I had at first. Ever since we discovered her miraculous “muscle memory” in the lower-level corridor, I had repeated this dead end alone nearly a hundred times.
Throughout that long reset, I had tried like a madman to widen the breach in that miracle.

I looked at her right hand hanging undamaged at her side. In one loop, trying to leave behind even the slightest instinctive alertness, I gritted my teeth and pressed the tip of a knife into the wound in her palm as she lay dying. I watched her whole body tremble

with pain, trying to carve the sense of danger into her nerves with pain violent enough to pierce death. I had also made her clutch a note that said “the world is resetting,” naively believing that even a faint afterimage might leave an imprint on the next morning.

But nothing remained. It had only been a physiological spasm incapable of carrying any concrete information. For nearly a hundred mornings, her palm was always as clean as it was now, without even a white mark, and

she never again showed any advance warning of danger. She died in front of me again and again, while I became the perpetrator who still had to add to her suffering with my own hands before she died. That scar only I

could remember, together with those devastating memories I could not share, slowly ground through my reason like bloodied gravel, until I could no longer summon the slightest courage to push her toward an unknown risk.

Today, there was no need to struggle as I had at first to prove that the world had stalled. Her memories still stopped before eight that morning. She remembered the despair from becoming candidates to

splitting up for our respective actions. She remembered Estelle rushing toward the village boundary with the records. And she knew perfectly well that we were trapped in a dead end deep inside the White Tower.
“Yuna, don’t leave yet.” I looked at her and spoke in a flat, matter-of-fact tone. “Check the collaboration interface screen beside you. See when the current session was started.”

She paused for a fraction of a second, then swept her eyes over it. “…Locked state. The timestamp is today at 08:00:00. How is that possible? That startup operation we performed this morning, the one that seemed completely unresponsive, actually established a session?”
“Not only that. Three seconds from now, you’ll hear guards running across the metal grating two floors above us. Then someone will shout, ‘Yuna’s over there. Seal off the lower level.’” I threw
out the next piece of the puzzle. “More importantly, there’s a crescent-shaped fingernail mark along the edge of the newest page in the pocket ledger you keep on your left. You left it
unconsciously last night while waiting for me to return in the dark—you told me so yourself in an earlier loop. You haven’t taken it out today. There’s no way I could have seen it out of nowhere.”

Heavy, dragging footsteps immediately sounded above us. Then the words “Yuna’s over there. Seal off the lower level!” came pouring down from overhead with an angry rasp of breath, the final syllables identical down to the last detail.

Yuna reached into her left pocket. She did not take the ledger all the way out. She only slipped her thumb inside the cover and felt along the edge of the newest page. Her movement stopped—the sensation beneath her fingertip clearly confirmed the crescent-shaped indentation that should not have existed.

She raised her head and looked once at the timestamp locked at 08:00:00 on the screen to her left, then at the metal grating overhead, where dust continued to fall. She did not voice any doubts. She simply lowered the foot that had been tapping the floor and shifted her weight down.
“Which way?” she whispered.

We did not choose to rush into the control room and lock the heavy blast door behind us. I had already discovered through earlier trials that sealing ourselves completely inside a room without a view left us no way to respond to changes

outside except to wait for death. Using the shadows of the corridor, we silently slipped into the concealed maintenance pit outside the control room, connected to the underside of the main console, and avoided the first wave of patrols outside.
In the oppressive silence, I quietly recited the dead ends we had verified in the previous loops.

“We tried having you operate it again from the external seat, but the console was locked and displayed that the current session already existed.” I leaned against the cold pipe wall, my voice rough with exhaustion.

“I sat in that seat without pressing anything and stubbornly waited until night. It didn’t work. Bringing in a guard from outside didn’t work either. Whether we knocked them unconscious and dragged them in or forced them at gunpoint, as long as they didn’t cooperate voluntarily, the machine showed no response to someone in that state.”
After listening, she showed no sign of discouragement. She only folded her hands lightly over her knees, stared at the rough floor, and fell into thought.
“Whether they were unconscious or resisting, the machine didn’t respond because they weren’t cooperating voluntarily. But that only shows that it ignores a forced state.
It doesn’t prove that it’s completely bound to your identity, to the point where even switching places is impossible,” she said softly, breaking the silence. “As far
as verifying the console goes, besides external operation, you sitting inside, and outsiders who won’t cooperate, there’s actually a fourth thing we haven’t tried.”
“Have someone who will cooperate with it voluntarily sit inside.” Her tone was calm, as if she were stating an inevitable experimental procedure.

I had known for a long time that she would think of this. Among all the trials and errors I had swallowed alone, this was the one variable I absolutely would not touch, and would never bring up to her myself.
“No.” The answer burst out of me, hard as a stone striking the ground.

“Listen to me first.” My emotion did not disturb her. She maintained her clear, orderly reasoning. “If I sit inside and cooperate with it to establish a connection, it might identify me as the new operator and forcibly overwrite your session. Or it might remain locked. Right now, it only responds to you.”

“I know there’s a risk,” she said, looking straight into my eyes. “But until we exhaust every means, no one knows where the boundary is. As long as there’s even the slightest possibility of breaking this dead end, this is worth trying.”
“No.” I clenched my teeth and stared at her.
She frowned slightly. “Because of those old records we saw before?”

“Yes. Nearly a hundred entries after No. 145 in that stack of old papers. New sessions were being created every day, but none of them had an exit time.” I drew a deep breath and lowered my voice. “The

records kept going. But what if those ‘no exit’ entries mean that the former operators’ consciousness never returned to their original bodies? Yuna, whether you’re accidentally electrocuted outside or endure

it here until night, you’ll wake up here safe and sound at eight tomorrow morning. As long as I’m still bound to the console, the reset will always return you to me. But if you sit inside and it identifies

you as the new operator, your consciousness will connect directly to its core. What if that ‘no exit’ means your consciousness is locked inside completely, beyond even the reset’s ability to bring it back?”

“But it’s still the only variable that offers any hope of breaking through.” She did not yield an inch. “Nearly a hundred blank records prove that it’s dangerous, but we have nowhere else to go. If you won’t cooperate with me to start it, I can’t complete the verification by myself. Are we supposed to wait in this dead end forever?”
The maintenance pit fell into deathly silence. Only the occasional dull footsteps from the corridor outside broke through.

According to the rational consensus we had established while fleeing, I should let her try. But I did not. I would not calculate the probability of survival. As long as that column was blank, as long as there was a chance it could truly swallow her, even if that chance was one in ten million, I could never let her touch it.
“I won’t let you go inside.” My voice was hoarse.
Yuna looked at me quietly.
“If you insist on saying no, then the fourth path can’t be entered in the verification record.” She watched me as she asked, “Arno, you know you’re acting on emotion, don’t you?”
“I know.” My answer was decisive.
She looked at me for a long time. It was an assessing gaze, as if she wanted to see through the shell called reason that covered this body of mine and find what I was hiding underneath.

During that long exchange of gazes, her eyebrows shifted slightly toward the middle. I knew that tiny expression very well. It was the look she wore whenever she encountered a hopelessly irreconcilable mess in the ledger.
“Arno.” She called my name.
“Mm.”
“Today, you did something completely contrary to the rules you set for yourself.” Her tone was serious.
“Yes.” I admitted it like a confession.
She took her hands from where they had been folded over her knees and lightly wiped them on her trouser legs, dusty from the flight.
“Then I’ll record one thing,” she said decisively.
She took the pocket ledger and the half-length charcoal pencil from inside her clothes, turned to a fresh page, lowered her head, and quickly wrote a line.
When she finished, she did not hide it. She turned the ledger around and held it up in front of me.
On the yellowed page, the neat handwriting read:
“Fourth test not conducted today. Reason: he won’t give one.”
“You won’t give one, so I’ll write ‘you won’t give one.’ I’m not going to make up a pretty excuse for you just to make you look reasonable.”
With a sharp smack, she closed the ledger and put it back inside her clothes.

“I know this page will reset tomorrow morning, but you’ll carry this account with you.” She stared at me. “When you can give a reason that doesn’t rely on instinct or emotion in some loop, then try convincing the version of me that knows nothing.”

I watched her put away the ledger. If the experience of the previous loops held true, this world would end on schedule as soon as 22:00 arrived. She would not remember anything that had happened today, and the line newly added to the ledger would disappear with it.

As long as I deliberately triggered the high-voltage grid in the power room, or took one wrong step and walked into a guard’s gunfire, I would wake at eight the next morning, one second after the pain, from my subjective perspective, in this world with no exit and no way to retain anything. That was equivalent to skipping this long wait.

But I only sat motionless in the shadows. Over the next twelve hours, as long as we remained hidden in the concealed spaces inside the White Tower, she would not be caught in random gunfire or have to face the dead end outside. Even

though that meant the pain in my legs would turn into unbearable numbness from being unable to stretch them, it also meant that in this hellish reset, I had greedily seized the only stretch of time in which she could breathe safely.
I had no intention of observing the movement patterns of the guards outside again, nor did I want to confirm the exact timing and range of the anomaly. In this closed
loop where every trial cost a life, I already had enough bloodied information. Now, whenever a patrol crossed the grating overhead, I knew another two hours had passed.

To avoid a group of guards that suddenly doubled back, I dragged my stiff right foot and pulled her sideways into an extremely concealed blind spot in the corner of the wall. My back pressed against the cold seams between the bricks. The rhythm of my heartbeat seemed to have formed some uncanny understanding with the patrol’s footsteps.
As time passed, the light filtering through the vent began to turn strange. The world had not forcibly ended us early.
20:36. The search finally ceased because of the anomaly outside. Without warning, a strange yellow haze seeped across the sky. Blinding, directionless light rose from every side,
illuminating the dim space through the vent slats. One patrol guard after another lost consciousness in the anomaly, and dull sounds of bodies hitting the ground came from above.

This yellow light was not ordinary light. Through countless repeated probes across the loops, I had already experienced its substantial weight. In the loops where we tried entering the lower levels to find a way out after the light appeared, the closer we came to the bottom of the tower, the more terrifying that pressure on the nerves became.
Yuna’s back rested against a rusted metal frame. She watched the strange light outside, then turned toward me.
“You were too familiar with the route today.”
My heart gave a sudden jolt. “What?”

“We’ve been hiding here for twelve hours. From avoiding the guards and crawling into the ventilation ducts this morning to evading two patrols here, every turn and pause—even the way you used the blind

spots—was too precise.” She stared hard at me. “You avoided every fork where you could have gone the wrong way. You didn’t even hesitate. It’s as if… you know where every dead end is, even with your eyes closed.”
I leaned against the metal wall without saying a word. The sounds of bodies falling outside finally died away completely.

“If that crescent-shaped mark is real, if we really have repeated this many times, then how many verifications did you hide from me in those old records? How many times have we been trapped here? You told me you had verified those options. They

weren’t things you could rule out at a glance. Each one would bring the guards, each one would alert the search party. How did those attempts that alerted the search party end?” She leaned forward slightly, her gaze piercing the dim space. “Tell me.”
I looked into her eyes.

I remembered how the airtight door had suddenly dropped and cut off her retreat while we were testing the alternate route through the ventilation ducts. I remembered her being knocked down by the confused defensive grid when I lured the search party away in the

power room. At the north stairwell, in the lower-level passage, in every corner of this White Tower, I had watched her fall in desperate situations. I knew how quickly she lost her body heat. I knew which direction she habitually looked before she breathed her last.
But I said nothing. I lowered my eyes and held my voice in my throat.

Yuna watched me, her brow furrowing deeper and deeper. She did not ask again. She turned and leaned back against the metal frame, biting her lower lip in silence. The electronic clock on the wall ticked soundlessly. The yellow light grew stronger and stronger.

As the time drew close to 21:53, this unexplained, erroneous dusk began to take her too. Her shoulders began to slump unconsciously, and she sank into a deep sleep. I moved over, enduring the ache in my right arm, and let her rest against my shoulder.
This body would not last until 22:00. In the past loops when I endured until this moment, I had confirmed it countless times—she always left earlier than I did. If the machine was extracting some
kind of life force, then it was clearly protecting me, its “operator.” Under that protection, I would remain conscious and live until the final second, then wake with all the despair still inside me.
