I sat quietly, feeling the faint pulse at the side of her neck. After only a few minutes, that slight vibration stopped completely in the silence.
I kept watch over her body as it lost its warmth until the electronic clock reached the end.
The scene before my eyes suddenly went black.

Verification Record for a Scripture Manuscript Copy (Stored in the Controlled Archive Room)
Transcribed by: Apprentice Scribe Yuna
Reviewed by: Duty Elder Sera

Go home before dark.
Go to bed early.
Speak less.

Do not take the long way.
Do not ask what someone used to be called.
Do not open locked doors.

Verification result: Not a single word altered in six lines.
In the early days of those hundreds of cycles, even after I had learned to win her trust with “details no one could know,” she still interrogated me for several minutes every morning.
Until one morning, perhaps dozens of cycles later, she did not interrogate me. She simply pulled me into the empty prayer room. She took out a blank prayer form,
wrote “May Arno get better,” then pressed the pen onto the signature line and had me sign the name that would inevitably leave ironclad evidence in my handwriting.
I did not hesitate. I signed it directly and pushed it through the submission slot.
The paper slipped down, but she remained seated there.

“Pointless. Whether you really experienced the cycle or simply went mad and mistook what your own mind was telling you, you would still feel that it wouldn’t make it to tomorrow when you signed it. You would sign just as

readily.” She put the pen back in her pocket. “So looking at what you’re willing to pay is useless. The evidence I want has to be reduced to one sentence—a private detail that even the most meticulous stalker could never know.”
She turned around and pulled the scripture copy back in front of her.
“Tomorrow morning, don’t tell me any more grand information about the future. Give me this password instead.”
That had been hundreds of cycles ago.
This morning, when I walked into that room, I spoke to her directly before she could begin her interrogation:
“There are five and a half blue threads in the bird’s nest in the seventh tree to the east.”
Every morning, when she detoured to count the threads, there was no cover anywhere nearby where someone could hide. More importantly, her obsessive way of counting a broken thread as
“half a strand” had never been written down, even by her. It existed only in her mind. It was a secret I had gradually drawn out of her during a previous cycle we had spent together.

Hearing that, she froze for half a second, an unusual reaction from her. Then she raised her hand and straightened the brass fastener at the collar of her formal dress—the one representing her on-duty status. Her left thumb unconsciously circled the old cloth band around the inside of her wrist.
“Valid.”
The wariness in her eyes had not completely vanished, but it was suppressed by an extreme commitment to efficiency.

“Whether you really experienced the cycle as you claim, or calculated the route through my defenses by some extraordinarily clever method, this password saves you the time of explaining. What are we doing today?”

At that moment, I truly felt that evidence was also a weapon. Whether or not she had fully believed in the time loop, at least operationally, I had learned how to cross her layers of fortified trust in an instant.
After passing the test that morning, I said: We’re taking the long way today.

During the hundreds of cycles before this one, we had already searched every corner of the village thoroughly. The world beyond the high wall was too far away; simply walking there and back would consume most of the daylight. I had spent dozens of days crossing the boundary alone to

investigate the outer areas. In that abandoned camp, I had tried opening one deadlocked door after another, only to be stopped by the passwords and documents deeper inside. I finally realized that reckless brute-force enumeration could not penetrate that history. I had to take her there.
“The world beyond the high wall comes at a steep price,” she reminded me.

“I know. The village search follows the same rhythm every day: Sera confirms around eight in the morning that we’re no longer under house arrest, Otto takes over the main roads with his people, and finally Kane concentrates the manpower at the public boundary. We’ve hidden hundreds of times. We know those blind spots by heart.”
“But hiding won’t be enough once we cross the boundary into the outer areas. Have you calculated the distance and time carefully?”

“I have,” I said. “Whenever the two of us have acted together, we’ve only ever stopped briefly near the boundary stones. But if we’re going to the place that actually matters, it’s a long way. We absolutely can’t leave footprints in the mud leading toward the outer areas.”

“So we have to use those three minutes at noon when the shifts change. At that time, Kane’s people will follow the outer wall eastward and head north to relieve the new group Otto brought out, while Otto’s people will walk back from the north gate along the market’s main street. During those three minutes when their routes cross, Otto’s

people will be watching inside the village, and Kane’s people will be watching the back wall to the north. Not a single pair of eyes will be looking toward the southern wilderness. There’s a dry riverbed covered in loose stones beside the southern boundary stone. If we walk on the stones, we won’t leave any tracks for them to follow.”

To open up this route, I had gone to the boundary stones to find Kane in an earlier world. I told him without reservation about the disaster-light that was certain to descend in the evening—what we called the second dusk—which I had already experienced more than once.

I also slammed the folded paper down in front of him. It contained the secret Estelle had bought with her life, and was stained with the mud from where she had fallen. During an earlier cycle, I had stolen it

from the controlled archive room at the cost of my life and slammed it in front of this murderer, proving to him that I had seen everything: the process by which he activated the sound device and killed Estelle.
In that cycle, I had expected him to lash out to silence me, or panic at having been witnessed. But he merely sat upright on the huge boundary stone and looked at me as if he were looking at
a junior who had finally grown fangs. Then he accepted my crossing of the boundary. He accepted that the disaster could not be reversed. And he took the initiative to point me toward a route.

It was the kind of understanding only a murderer who had spent years enforcing suppression and witnessing its consequences could possess: since destruction was coming, and I had somehow survived while holding this information, he chose to stop being the high wall’s loyal hound and let this vicious dog out of its cage.
With the toe of his boot, he drew a long line forcefully through the damp earth.

“Follow this dirt road straight inward, and there’s an old camp hidden in the weeds.” He pointed into the distance. “It’ll take about two hours to get there. The stone bridge halfway collapsed during last year’s rainy season. Turn left when you reach the fallen bridge, then go around along the waterline.”
Then he pressed the toe of his boot hard against the far end of the line twice.
“But let me make the ugly part clear first. Once you go there, if you spend any time inside, you can forget about getting back in one piece before the daylight comes.”

After saying that, he took a battered little notebook with curled corners from inside his coat and scribbled a line in it with a charcoal pencil. The line began with that day’s date. After the date came four words, each stroke biting through the paper: Nothing happened at the boundary.
“That’s the line I submit every day.” He closed the notebook and tucked it back inside his coat. “At noon, I’ll head north to change shifts with Otto. During those
three minutes when our routes cross, neither group will be looking toward the southern main road. If you leave, you’re choosing to get yourselves killed. I saw nothing.”
“What kind of place is this camp, exactly?” Yuna asked sharply.

“Just an old place that should’ve rotted away long ago. People died inside. More than one.” He paused, then added, “When you leave, don’t step in that soft patch on the right. That’s where the old camp burned bones.”
Because I had already memorized the route and that perfectly timed gap during previous cycles, we did not approach the boundary stones or confront him face-to-face today.
Today, we did not alert any of the adults searching for us according to their fixed rhythm. At noon, we hid in the shadows and slipped across the boundary stones silently during those
brief three minutes. When I stepped out of the village, I could not help looking back. The entire world instantly changed into an unfamiliar skeleton. Desolation and decay rushed toward us.

As we walked along the muddy dirt road, the sensation beneath our feet suddenly hardened—a stretch of gray-white old pavement thrust up from the mud without warning. At the broken edge, a vicious framework of rust-red rebar jutted out.

I had sprained my right ankle on the night I chased Estelle. Whenever I put even slightly too much weight on it, a piercing pain climbed along the bone. During the hundreds of resets that followed, my

brain learned to screen out the pain and treat it as a bothersome background noise, but at eight every morning, the injury was always swollen. Yuna noticed my slight limp and deliberately slowed her pace.
Yuna recognized this kind of pavement. She had seen exactly the same material when we rode in Chico’s rattling wreck of a vehicle north toward the trading post.
That was our “first day.” In my subjective time, it had been more than three hundred calendar days ago. By her memory, though, it had all happened “yesterday.”
“That’s the direction of the trading post,” Yuna said, looking around as she walked. “But I’ve never seen this branch—the one to the northwest on this side.”

On both sides of the old pavement, dense forest was gradually swallowing a vast ancient city. A row of long-bare metal poles stood in a straight line along the ruined road, stretching all the way to the edge of sight.
Yuna stopped at one section of the road and raised her head.
“Starting from the third pole, the spacing is always fifty-three paces. Even where the ground subsided, the extra step only appeared because the stride shortened.” She
looked at the metal pole rising straight into the clouds. “Human feet could never produce spacing this exact. This road was built entirely according to a blueprint.”

She turned and looked back toward the direction we had come from. From this angle, surrounded by industrial ruins, the village looked like a small patch of weak, warm firelight, its edge locked inside a ring of pure-white

boundary markers. The invisible administrative boundary treated in the village merely as a statutory division revealed its mechanical, rigid arc through the boundary stones and patrol routes against the vast ruins.
“It looks the same as when we went north yesterday,” she said, her voice light as a sigh. “Our fields really have been planted on someone else’s roof, generation after generation.”

After two hours of crossing the wilderness, the camp Kane had described finally appeared ahead of us. By then, my ankle had swollen like a steamed bun. Every step sent a sharp reminder that the injury from eight o’clock could not cross a calendar day.

It was a cluster of low buildings, iron gray interwoven with rust red, crouched like a dead beast in waist-high weeds. A sign stood by the main gate, its surface paint largely peeled away. The three rough characters for “Laboratory” were barely legible. It had the same name

as the place in the village guarded by Elder Sera, but the difference in scale was like heaven and earth. Along the edges of the peeling paint, another, much older line of writing faintly showed through beneath it. The strokes had been carved deeply into the metal plate.
Yuna stopped in front of the mottled sign.
“These two layers of writing are different.” She leaned closer to examine them.
“The surface layer, ‘Laboratory,’ was clearly written over it later,” I said, following her line of thought.
“And the new paint is very thick. It almost covered the whole thing.”
As she scraped away the dry paint along the edge, a little more of the deeply carved ancient writing underneath was exposed.

“The original name was deliberately covered with thick paint.” She took out paper and a pen and copied the shape of the word with meticulous care. “The old-language courses we took in the village aren’t enough to recognize this kind of obscure technical term.”

A ring of thin iron pillars stood at regular intervals around the complex, about a person and a half high. Their spacing was extremely even, like an invisible fence enclosing the entire cluster of low buildings.
Each pillar had a grille at the top. The insides were already mottled with rust, utterly silent.

“I happened to ask Chico about this camp last month. His expression became very strange. He warned me that the people outside had taboos, and that I absolutely shouldn’t come near.” She pointed at the iron pillars. “There may be some kind of sound-producing device hidden inside those grilles.”
She stopped, turned her ear slightly toward one of the iron pillars, and waited for a moment.

“There’s an extremely faint background vibration. It’s still running, just like the boundary alarms that drive people away from the market. This thing must produce some kind of specific sound to keep certain groups away.”

We walked side by side through the gap between two iron pillars. Nothing unusual happened, and we felt no discomfort. I didn’t know whether the defense had malfunctioned or whether we simply weren’t on the list of people it was meant to stop. But we could not enter the building directly.

The entrance facing the main gate was tightly clamped shut by a heavy mechanical sealing panel. A glaring strip of quarantine tape stretched across its surface. Beside it, the access panel’s indicator lights were dark, radiating a severe sense of refusal. It had clearly been completely closed and sealed according to some regulation.
Yuna walked up to the mechanical panel and slowly felt along the gap at its edge.

“It isn’t welded shut.” She examined the mechanical hinge on the side of the panel, then followed the clue to a physical dial beside it, covered by a sheet of metal. “There was a closing action, so there’s a way to open it. But finding it would take a long process of trial and error.”
I stepped forward, deftly pulled away the metal sheet, and turned the markings on the dial to four specific positions. With a dull mechanical clank, the heavy panel slowly slid open to both sides.
Yuna looked at me in surprise.
“You’ve been to this door in an earlier cycle.”
“Many times. It took me dozens of cycles to work out these four positions.” I pushed the door open.
Inside, the building had an eerily improvised quality, as though two completely different architectural styles had been crudely welded together.

The front half near the entrance had rough barred windows and rusted metal bunk frames. Along the base of the wall was a shallow groove, running straight along the mottled wall and deep into the building.
Yet after walking only a few steps farther, we crossed a welded seam. The floor suddenly became smooth as a mirror, and the walls changed into some extraordinarily
clean white material without a seam in sight. The pungent smell of rust receded like a tide, replaced by an unnamed chemical odor, almost excessively clean.
I followed the worn trail with my eyes, then took a step back. My gaze fell on the end toward which it pointed—a seemingly unrelated security door.
Yuna followed my gaze, walked to the door, and crouched down.

“Look at the traces in the dust here.” She pointed to a tiny worn spot beneath the bottom of the door. “The wear inside the groove was caused by shoe soles, but this abrasion beneath the door has a completely unnatural curve. It wasn’t made by people walking.”
“It looks like some mechanical part has been sweeping open and closed here for years,” I continued for her. “If people stood here in a line, and there was machinery operating beneath the door…”
She did not answer. Instead, she followed the curve and reached into a gap beneath the door panel that no ordinary person would notice. Her fingertips felt around there for
a moment, as if confirming the engagement point of some metal structure. There was a soft click. A physical valve hidden in the darkness behind the door had been triggered.
The door opened just like that.
The farther we went, the stronger the clean chemical odor became. In the huge room at the deepest point stood several rows of towering metal racks. Most of them were empty, thickly coated in dust.
But on one of the innermost racks, several compartments held something lying quietly inside. They had distinct human outlines, tightly wrapped and covered by a layer of translucent film.
I had just reached the rack and counted to the third body when Yuna suddenly reached out and seized my wrist. Her grip was so hard it sent a sharp pain through me.
Her voice was extremely low, with a faint tremor that was difficult to detect.
“Look.”
“Look at those membranes.”

I followed her gaze. The translucent membranes wrapped around the human shapes were moving. Very slowly, very evenly, rising and falling together, like the rhythm of breathing. The two of us stood before that row of racks as if nailed there, for a very long time.
In that dead-silent space, the loudest sound in the entire place was our own labored breathing.
There were only a few bodies inside, some male and some female, each with different features. Their eyes were closed. They made no sound. The membrane clung tightly to their lifeless cheeks
and chests, and beneath that close wrapping, their steady rhythm rose and fell with a consistency that made the skin crawl. They were alive. A nauseating chill surged up from my stomach.
Yuna eventually overcame her fear and took one step forward.
She walked very slowly, as if afraid of waking something. When she reached the nearest male body, she stopped, lowered her head, and leaned closer to examine it.
“It has an interface.” She drew a breath and spoke softly.
I slowly walked over. At the back of the body’s neck beneath the translucent membrane, a metal port was embedded there. The skin around it had an unnervingly realistic texture.
Yuna slowly crouched down, staring at the inner surface of the membrane, her gaze fixed below the metal port. A short line of black code was printed there.

“Arno,” she suddenly said, her voice surprisingly calm. “Look at the metal screen connected above that body’s head. That script… it’s the same symbol system as the name covered with thick paint outside the main gate.”
I followed her finger. A dark-gray display panel was embedded at the top of the membrane, with several lines of characters slowly flickering across it.

“They aren’t the old language we learned in the village. They’re some kind of engineering symbols we don’t recognize.” She frowned, tracing several phrases flickering across the screen with her finger. “But these words

with numbers… I think I’ve seen them somewhere. In the original technical records in the lower level of the controlled archive room, or perhaps on fragments of the old candidate language from before the revisions…”
She did not continue. Instead, she stood and looked over a rusted metal chart beside the rack. Half the dust had been wiped away.
“Look at this diagram. If the shape in the first stage represents manufacturing a body…” She pointed to the funnel-shaped figure representing the second
stage. “Then it says that making the body isn’t the end. There may be another step here, where something… from outside is ‘infused’ into these empty shells.”
She turned her head and looked again at the line of black code: “F-04-72.”

“Yesterday, I saw a regulation concerning people from outside in the controlled archive room: ‘People from outside are registered by batch and serial number.’” She drew a deep breath, a chill surfacing in her rational eyes. “If this isn’t merely a registration number, but also a production-batch number…”

“This factory can manufacture bodies with standardized specifications, and the diagram indicates some kind of ‘infusion’ process. The people who live outside the village and carry identification codes… is it possible they’re products that came out of racks like these?”

Watched by those living things sealed into the racks, the pressure was almost suffocating. Yuna turned first and withdrew. I followed her, my legs somewhat weak, unable to suppress the churning in my stomach.
We stopped in the corridor outside. I was breathing violently. Whenever I closed my eyes, the faces rising and falling evenly beneath the translucent film flickered across my retinas.
Yuna’s chest was heaving just as hard, but she forced herself to look away from the door. When she raised her head again, her gaze locked onto a wall at
the end of the corridor. This was the only way she could fight fear: breaking an unbearable, insane fact back down into a problem that reason had to solve.

“To prove this hypothesis, and to find out what those warnings on the screen are saying is missing…” She took a deep breath. A faint tremor remained in her voice, but her logic had returned to its place. “I need to understand the writing in this place first.”
It took considerable effort for me to pull my attention away from that hellish room. I followed her gaze.
It was the password wall we had passed on our way in.

The wall extended from the dusty floor to an extremely high ceiling, covered entirely in cold, orderly characters from an unknown printed script. A row of metal cabinets stood along the wall, each label printed with the same writing.
“The old-language courses we took in the village only covered basic reading.” She walked forward, her gaze becoming colder and more focused by the moment. “But this is all
engineering documentation in continuous passages. If we can’t decipher these facility terms, we’ll never know what this place was actually doing, much less what it was manufacturing.”
That was the first day of the long work of deciphering the vocabulary.
But her approach was extremely restrained. That afternoon, she stood rooted before the wall covered in ancient writing. She first tried applying several suspected phrases to the
corresponding positions on the door panels, pipes, and diagram. In the end, based on position and context, she selected only two high-frequency words that appeared repeatedly.
“The first word usually appears with numbers as a designation. For now, I’ll call it ‘compartment.’ The second appears on warnings along the pipelines. For now, I’ll call it ‘convey.’”
She found a relatively clean patch of ground and used a stone to draw the strokes of the two words clearly.
“My mind is formatted every morning when I wake up.” She looked at me seriously. “So we’ll learn only these two today.”
I crouched down and stared fixedly at the characters until I was certain I had remembered them.
“You need to remember their shapes, their exact positions on the wall, and our provisional interpretations.”
She carefully traced the marks on the ground once more.
“At exactly twenty-two hundred, my consciousness will be erased.”
“I tried before,” I added quietly. “Even if I carved marks into the walls of the ruins, those marks only remained in the world of the past. I couldn’t bring them to tomorrow.”

“Exactly. You can’t take any matter with you.” She raised her head, her rational eyes fixed on me in the dimness. “So as long as the data you bring to the me of tomorrow contains no errors, these entries can cross time and accumulate day by day.”
She tilted her head slightly and thought for a moment, seeming satisfied with this alliance.
“I think this is fair.” A slight curve appeared at the corner of her mouth.
By evening, the sunset was blood-red. To gain a little more time at the wall, we left the camp very late. We hurried along the stretch of gray-white old pavement toward the village.
Yuna walked half a step to my left, sorting through the mass of information she had recorded that day as she went—

“The location where the first word appears is the first group of clues, the membrane is the second, and the other writing on the wall is the third. Until we find a definite connection, do not link these groups together—”
Out of habit, I turned to look at her.
It really was only a glance.
Nothing around us had changed. The setting sun still drew long shadows across the wilderness, and the abandoned industrial skeletons pierced the sky.

A girl with long golden hair was walking there. Her hair had been combed meticulously and tied into low twin tails that fell over her shoulders. She wore a vivid purple formal dress, densely embroidered with symmetrical rope and geometric patterns in ice blue and silver.
That was Estelle. Now, those gray-blue eyes were looking at me with a defensive, wary gaze, as if she were looking at an acquaintance who had suddenly made a transgressive move.
Why was she here? Hadn’t she died in front of me at the western boundary? Where had Yuna gone?
That strange scene lasted less than a second.

I blinked hard. When I opened my eyes again, the person before me had turned back into Yuna, wearing her induction dress with the brass fastener at her collar. The sentence she had been speaking continued:
“—because once you connect them incorrectly, you’ll unconsciously invent a story, and inventing stories is the greatest taboo in investigation… What’s wrong?”
She finally noticed that something was wrong with me.
“Arno?”
“Your face has gone completely white.”
Yuna stopped and spoke with concern. She naturally reached out, wanting to feel my forehead for a temperature.
“Are you feeling sick? Your whole body is trembling.”
“Nothing… nothing.” I struggled to force out the words.
“Then what caused it? What did you see?”

I opened my mouth and swallowed air uselessly. I knew that, given her personality, if I truthfully told her I had seen Estelle’s afterimage, she would calmly record the phenomenon as a new group called “visual abnormality.”
But that was precisely what frightened me most. I was the only one between us who could carry today’s knowledge into tomorrow. If she began to suspect that my brain—the recording device itself—had
developed interference and malfunctions after hundreds of resets, she might discard all the words we had painstakingly recorded at the wall that afternoon in order to isolate the contamination.
I did not want to lose the two words we had finally obtained today.
I babbled out a pile of lies, roughly saying that my ankle hurt too much, that my nerves had been wound too tight, and that I was tired and confused.
“Arno.”
Her voice suddenly changed. Concern receded, replaced by cold scrutiny.
“Your reaction just now was wrong.”
My body stiffened abruptly.

“Your pupils contracted sharply, and even your breathing became completely disordered. That wasn’t ordinary fatigue. You saw something extremely frightening.” She spoke one word at a time, her tone revealing no emotion.
The sun had sunk low. Only a smear of dark red remained along the horizon. On the cracked old pavement, our shadows stretched long and longer. Yuna stood before me and quietly listened to
my clumsy cover story. Her ears pressed down slightly—that was her localized reaction when she caught abnormal information. But unexpectedly, she did not continue forcing me with questions.
“I’ve stored what happened just now in my mind.”
She turned decisively and continued back along the road we had taken.
“This afternoon, you suddenly displayed abnormal physical reactions without warning, and refused to tell me the truth. It will disappear from my mind
tomorrow, but at least for the rest of today, I’ll treat you as an unreliable node and remain on guard against you.” Her voice came back with her footsteps.
“Let’s go. The daylight is almost here.”
The daylight caught up with us halfway back, as scheduled.

It was 20:36. A wave of light began to stir across the sky, announcing the entire world’s entry into some kind of clearing countdown. More than an hour remained before the deep sleep that heralded her true death.
When the white light began to glow faintly from every direction in the night sky, the first wave of intense dizziness arrived. Yuna’s back, which had remained straight until then, instantly lost its
strength. She collapsed onto a stretch of old pavement thrust up from the earth, her shoulders slipping down without conscious intent. I sat beside her at once, letting her lean against my shoulder.
During the first wave of intense dizziness, she did not close her eyes immediately. She seized my arm and forced herself to stay conscious with what little awareness remained.
The ruins were not comfortable to sit on. Rusted rebar jutted from the broken edge and pressed into my leg, but I did not move.
She turned her head to look at me. Her face had already gone pale in the light.
“Now… draw them for me. Recite them.” Her voice was already beginning to drift, but her eyes still held a stubborn resolve.
As the light grew brighter, I obediently drew the strokes of the two words in the dusty ground and recited their locations and provisional meanings.

By the time I recited them a second time, her body was already lying heavily against me. Yet even in the glare and weakness, she sharply caught two errors in my memory. One stroke was missing a horizontal line. The other was that I had reversed the order of the locations.
“Again… the correct version.” She gasped, her eyes barely able to remain open.
I raised my voice, redrew them, and recited the correct version once more.
“Good…”
“Arno.” Her eyes were closed, her voice very soft.
“As long as you don’t confuse them, the me of tomorrow… can reason her way back to this point.”
Her hand slid from my arm.
“Take them… to the me of tomorrow.” she murmured softly.
“See you in the next today.”

Afterward, she sank into a prolonged half-conscious state. In these ruins swallowed by light, no matter how far we ran, that feeling of being pulled away arrived just as punctually as it did in the village. Exhausted by the long march during the day, she weakened faster than usual and could not hold out for long

even through the initial interrogation. I sat quietly and watched her. I knew she would not wake again before the true terminal point arrived more than an hour later. Her body would always lose its warmth before mine, her first-person consciousness extinguishing with it, always just a little earlier than mine.

I do not know how long I sat in the ruins, keeping watch over her. When the white light finally climbed to its full intensity, the scene before my eyes shattered completely. When I stood again in that familiar eight-o’clock morning, the world from the previous night had closed its doors forever.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:title: Chapter Four: Hollow Shell
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s1-1:
Task Sheet · Rubbing (Seventh Rack in the Experimental Area):
Compartment: C-3. Carrier: 07.
Status: Suspended.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s3-1: The task sheet remained inside a glass cover beside the machine. The traces of approval stamps on the paper showed that someone had come by at intervals, inspected the machine stalled at its final step, added another mark to the form, and left a record.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s4-1: There were no new instructions, and no missing materials were supplied. Apart from these meaningless reinspections, nothing happened here. This interminable waiting had somehow been meticulously approved forty-one times under the old calendar, before the disaster.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s9-1: I no longer knew which morning it was. The village at dawn was still shrouded in gray-blue mist, the air carrying the smell of dew and wet earth. I had become utterly familiar with the routine of this morning.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s10-: I said aloud what I had written down at the end of the previous day.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s11-: Yuna listened quietly. Her gaze rested on my face for three seconds. There was no surprise, and no unnecessary praise.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s13-: “Fine.” She tugged at her backpack strap. “What are we doing today?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s15-: “Back to camp.” I looked at her.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s18-: She was about to walk toward the village entrance when her step paused for half a beat. The wind moved through her somewhat disheveled hair.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s20-: “The last two words.” She turned her head, a trace of scrutiny entering her voice.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s22-: “One was ‘compartment.’ The other was ‘conveyance.’ And there was a warning term you only deciphered halfway yesterday. I memorized its full spelling too.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s23-: Not just the words. I had memorized, without missing a character, the sources she had pointed out to me. During these long, repeatedly resetting mornings, we had spent dozens of cycles picking apart where these symbols appeared throughout the ruins and how they were connected, pressing them into my memory.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s24-: Yuna stood there listening. It was very quiet around us, with only the distant crowing of a chicken from the village entrance.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s26-: “I told you I don’t trust memory,” she finally said, her voice very soft.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s30-: “Now I know why.” She turned and walked toward the village entrance, her feet pressing into the damp earth.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s32-: “Because my memories change every day,” she said without turning her head, “while yours stack up layer by layer.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s37-: As before, we waited by the boundary stone until noon, then crossed the invisible fence during the three-minute window of safety.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s38-: When we walked that road again, the oppressive feeling brought by the ruins had faded considerably. Once unfamiliar things became familiar, they no longer seemed so enormous.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s39-: The old road surface pushed up dark-red clods of earth in the same places. The rows of bald steel poles stood guard in the same positions, like a line of forgotten sentries. In our backward glance, the village was still that small patch of warm color enclosed by fine white lines, shrinking into a blurred point as the distance grew.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s40-: I remembered every word of Kane’s instructions from some past cycle: when walking, don’t step in the soft mud on the right.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s41-: Nothing had changed. The only difference was me.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s42-: We spent almost an hour less on the road from the village entrance to the camp. The time was saved because I knew which broken stretches could be jumped over directly, and which seemingly level patches of soft mud required a long detour.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s43-: That wasn’t something I had guessed. I had bought it with the days I remembered, the days that had vanished into time.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s46-: We did not stop in front of the large sign at the camp entrance. We passed familiarly between the ring of enormous iron pillars.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s47-: Nothing happened. No alarm sounded. The ground did not shake.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s48-: Only when she crossed the invisible boundary did her step pause for half a beat. She stared at the nonexistent line in the air, on guard against something, and only stepped across after confirming that nothing was wrong.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s53-: The production-line area lay deeper inside the experimental area. The air here carried a heavy smell of old metal. A row of enormous workstations stood in silence, their vats like egg cases belonging to some giant insect, conveyor tracks connected beneath them.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s54-: We stopped in front of the slightly slanted control panel at the very back.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s56-: A skeleton, sitting in a withered heap. Tattered remnants of a dust-covered uniform hung from him. His skull drooped slightly as he faced the dim instruments. One hand bone hung at his side;
the other rested on a heavy metal work case. A small screen was connected beside the case. At its exact center, an harsh red lock icon blinked, like an index interface that could not be opened.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s57-: Yuna reached out and tried pushing the case. It did not move at all. The keyhole icon on the screen did not even blink.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s59-: “It’s locked solid. It won’t open.” She withdrew her hand, went around the nameless skeleton, and cast her flashlight onto the control panel ahead.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s60-: Yuna straightened and looked at the old task sheet inside the glass cover beside it.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s62-: “Compartment: C-3. Carrier: 07. The approval stamps above are still from the old-calendar era.” She pointed to the final field, her finger passing over
the symbols we had pieced together bit by bit against old records through countless cycles. “The status field says: ‘Conveyance paused,’ or ‘Suspended.’”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s65-: She turned and looked at a huge iron winch extending from the side of the workstation.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s71-: I walked over and put my hands on the rough handle of the winch.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s72-: It was frighteningly cold, colder than the metal of the surrounding ruins. The instant my palms touched it, the chill pierced into my bones like needles.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s74-: “It’s colder than the stones around it,” I said.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s75-: Yuna came over and touched it once, her brows drawing together slightly.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s77-: “Record it. Iron that has been lying here for over a hundred years could only be this cold if it were connected to some system continuously drawing heat outward. Whatever is maintaining the environment below at low power hasn’t died yet.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s80-: I lowered my weight and began turning it with all my strength.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s81-: The rust let out a shrill scream. It was extremely heavy. On the third turn, a deep click came from inside the metal floor beneath our feet.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s82-: With the faint sound of pumping, the physical hydraulic pipes, long since dry, began filling again. The fluorescence on the control panel suddenly brightened.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s85-: The control panel was buried under a century of dust. Yuna brushed away the thick layer with her sleeve. The screen lit up. Instead of reporting an error, it displayed the device’s state architecture and a historical execution log.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s86-: Over the past dozens of cycles, we had pieced together those word roots and warning phrases bit by bit from throughout the ruins. But only today, looking at the illuminated architecture diagram before us, did those dry technical terms acquire corresponding engineering diagrams for the first time.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s88-: “Look at this term at the very top.” Her finger moved across the top of the screen. “‘Global soul field.’ The diagram’s explanation is very clear. The source isn’t stored in this
machine, and it doesn’t even belong to this single world. The bodies and first-person perspectives in each world are only its ‘local projections.’ But the note beside it also emphasizes
that our world itself is an absolutely real physical existence. It isn’t simulated. The local projections aren’t illusions either. Every body genuinely perceives, is injured, and dies.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s89-: She pointed to the state diagram in the middle.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s91-: “When the source successfully aligns with the body and wakes, the state is called ‘coherence.’ Sleep is ‘decoherence’: the connection is dormant, but the capacity originally assigned to you remains occupied by you. Only complete death or deregistration can truly release that slot.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s92-: Yuna moved her flashlight toward the production-flow diagram below.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s94-: “The body on the left, the data on the right?” I looked at the two lines converging.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s96-: “Right. The left side only loads a ‘body template’ and assembles the physical body. It can alter the appearance or physiological parameters of an existing template, but it can’t write knowledge or memories into it out of nowhere. The right side is what connects to the subject data source.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s97-: Her gaze followed the line on the right downward and stopped at a flashing warning box.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s99-: “The data specifications on the right are extremely strict. It can only connect to one ‘complete life record.’ If it isn’t complete, this gate locks solid and not a single piece of data can be written.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s100: Her finger continued downward. She tapped a red warning symbol at the edge of the screen, the same as the one outside in the ruins.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s102: “‘Irreversible’… It’s marked at the final step of hardware assembly. It means that once the system creates the body, it’s an absolutely real living organism. It can’t be undone like software.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s103: At last, her finger stopped on the master gate below where the two channels converged. Its icon was a beam of light pointing downward, with a red “0” blinking beside it.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s105: “‘Global available capacity.’ This is a general pool with no identity restrictions. As long as there’s capacity, the system can assign a blank first-person perspective to a newly created body.”
She looked at the glaring “0” and turned to me. “But this machine shows that the total first-person capacity the entire system can currently support has already been used up. The pool is empty.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s107: “Whether it’s downloading a complete life from the right, or trying to create a blank-slate newcomer from nothing on the left, it ultimately has to request capacity from this pool.
As long as the capacity across the whole network is zero, even if data is inserted from the right, what gets created is only breathing dead flesh. A source can never inhabit it.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s109: “Then what has it been waiting for through forty-one reinspections?” I asked. “For someone in this system to die and release a unit of capacity? In more than a hundred years, hasn’t even one person died?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s111: “Or the capacity released by a death was always taken by somewhere with higher priority, leaving this one out of the queue.” Yuna stared at the console. “That’s why it was suspended manually more than a hundred years ago, stuck at the final step of waiting for capacity allocation. The normal activation process is completely locked. But here…”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s112: She reached out and wiped away a layer of black dust at the edge of the screen, revealing an independent physical button beneath a protective cover. A faint green light blinked on it.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s114: “The hardware continue button underneath is still lit.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s115: She looked at the button, then at the flashing irreversible warning below it.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s117: “The label only says ‘Force execution of current mechanical queue.’ It doesn’t say ‘Clear’ or ‘Reset.’ The system explicitly warns that it’s irreversible…” She
gritted her teeth. “But if we don’t see for ourselves what gets created with zero capacity, we’ll never understand how this system defines a ‘living person.’”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s118: She confirmed the safe distance, lifted the protective cover, and pressed the button.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s119: The machine did not display an error log. The action went directly past the software and released the production line from suspension.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s120: A deep rumble came from inside the manufacturing vat. The production line, silent for more than a hundred years, awoke before us.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s121: Amid the brutal grinding of gears and the pumping of liquid, the system forcibly resumed physical-layer execution despite no data being written through the right channel and available capacity remaining at zero. Hydraulic arms began

injecting viscous material into the dried-out manufacturing chamber. The machine simply skipped every software and subject-activation step and executed the assembly of the template set preloaded on the left channel with extreme efficiency.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s122: After several minutes, the sounds of operation subsided. The conveyor track jolted with a clang and slowly slid out.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s123: Before our eyes, it delivered a completely new physical body, freshly made, straight to us.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s128: The day before, we had seen several sleeping bodies tightly wrapped in translucent membranes in another section. But this was the first time a completely unprotected new body had been exposed directly to the

air. Pale clothing like a thin membrane clung to it. Its features were complete, its eyes closed tight. Most unnerving of all, it was warm. The pale fuzz inside its ear rims trembled faintly with each breath.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s129: Yuna bent down and slowly moved closer to its face.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s133: She reached out and carefully lifted one of its hands. Lifted, it obediently stayed lifted; released, it dropped limply.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s134: Yuna pressed her lips together and gently placed two fingers into its palm.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s135: The next second, the hand closed ever so slightly. Like the purely unconscious grasp of someone asleep who felt a foreign object. No fear, no testing, no response belonging to an awake person.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s138: She staggered back two steps, her back striking the cold workstation housing hard. Biting her lip tightly, she wrapped both arms around herself.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s142: “When I pulled away just now, my hand was still shaking.” Her voice tightened as she stared at her palm. “It was warm. It could grasp me by
instinct. But the first thought that came into my mind was to turn around and look at the panel, to check which part of the machine was missing.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s143: She bit down hard on her lip.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s145: “I was the one who pressed the execution key. But just now, I treated it as nothing more than a broken vessel.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s150: That afternoon, Yuna gritted her teeth and helped me lift the empty shell out of the vat. Before we left the production line, she went back to the console and forcibly broke the cables of the metal work case jammed beside the skeleton’s hand. It was a portable

terminal connected beside the machine. Yuna brought up the authorization override interface on the control panel and entered several commands. The deadlocked red light on the case turned steady green. Yuna handed it to me, wanting me to test the doors outside.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s151: Deep in the experimental area’s corridors stood two heavy old doors. When we entered today, their sensor lamps lit up as soon as we approached, and the doors slid open. For us, both doors offered no obstruction.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s152: The empty shell’s heels seemed to step on cotton. I supported its left arm and Yuna supported its right; half its heavy body pressed down on our shoulders. Its legs instinctively caught
against each other in alternating steps to keep it from falling. The pulse at its wrist beat steadily and strongly. In the corridor, the only sound was our dragging footsteps in the silence.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s153: I pushed it in front of the first door, then stepped back into the shadows beyond the sensor’s range.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s154: The empty shell stood there alone. Beep. The lamp blinked once, and the first door slid open without a sound.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s158: I took a deep breath, stepped forward, and pulled it to the second door.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s159: The red light on the door came on. It was a warning state we had not seen when entering.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s160: To rule out the possibility that it simply could not recognize this unregistered body, I placed the terminal, its green light now on and its temporary laboratory authorization assigned, into the empty shell’s hand, then pushed it toward the sensor zone again.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s161: The red light remained steadily lit.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s162: I took the terminal back, left the empty shell standing where it was, and walked to the sensor zone myself with empty hands.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s163: Beep. The red light turned green, and the second heavy metal door slid open with a clank.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s166: Yuna came over and looked at the door, open for me but glowing red for the empty shell with the terminal.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s168: “The first door checks whether there’s a living human body. As long as the body can breathe, it recognizes it.” She stared at the second door, her gaze darkening.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s170: “If the second door only checked the registered list, even a general-purpose terminal from more than a hundred years ago would be enough to save it. But neither of us has ever been registered in the system, and the door still opened for you.” She looked at the sensor on the

door. “It isn’t checking the list. It’s checking whether you have a genuine subject identity. In the system’s eyes, this empty shell and the authorization terminal are just a lump of flesh holding a piece of iron. It doesn’t recognize a ‘person’ crossing this line at all.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s172: We spent the rest of that afternoon trying to bring it outside. But it moved too slowly. The slightest unevenness in the ground made it collapse like a sandbag. Dragging such a burden through several kilometers

of soft mud in the ruins and back to the village was nearly impossible. Not to mention that we had no idea whether the enormous ring of iron pillars around the camp would trigger an alarm for a body this abnormal.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s173: We could only leave it in the corridor. Yuna did not let it simply stand there. She supported it as it slowly sat against the wall, arranging it in a slightly more
comfortable position. Its hand hung limply at its side, its chest still rising and falling with that sluggish rhythm. Leaving it like that in the dark did not feel right.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s178: We did not leave immediately. To observe what other changes might occur in the shell, we sat with it for a long time in the dim corridor.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s179: There were no windows in the corridor. Somewhere deeper inside, the faint low-frequency hum of a machine echoed.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s181: Yuna leaned against the cold metal wall and looked at the quiet shell rising and falling beside her.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s187: “This body we made today.” She turned to look at me. “When tomorrow morning resets, it will probably disappear from tomorrow’s world like the marks left on the floor before, won’t it?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s188: I looked at her. I did not contradict her guess about the reset.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s190: “It won’t be there in the world of the next morning,” I said softly.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s192: “If it’s no longer in the corridor,” she said, leaning against the wall, “remember to tell me next time: it sat here.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s193: Her breathing began to slow. The air gradually grew colder.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s194: I held her hand tightly and watched her chest rise and fall more and more slowly, more and more faintly—until at last, that familiar tiny tremor came to a complete stop in the dead silence.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s196: She stopped. Seven minutes remained until the world reset.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s197: Over countless previous cycles, I had grown used to sitting alone in this absolute silence until the final second. But today was different. The empty shell was still leaning against the wall, its chest rising and falling steadily and forcefully, making the faint breathing sound of a living person.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s198: Yuna had just guessed that the system’s capacity pool was stuck at zero, and that only the complete death of a person could release a unit of capacity. Now, her pulse had stopped.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s199: I stared into the empty shell’s eyes, then at its hand hanging at its side.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s200: One minute. Two minutes. Five minutes passed.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s201: If her death had been recognized, there should now have been one more unit of capacity in the pool. But the empty shell’s eyes remained closed, and the frequency of its breathing did not change at all. Its hand did not move again. It was still only living flesh.

I didn’t know whether the system simply did not count her death before the reset as “complete deregistration,” or whether, even if a vacancy had opened in the pool, it would not automatically descend upon a finished product that had already left the queue.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s202: I sat there on the cold metal plate, listening to its even breathing, until exactly twenty-two hundred hours.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s203: Without any warning, everything before my eyes suddenly went black. All sound, the cold air, and the hum from deep in the corridor were cut off completely in that instant.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s207: As yesterday, the village at dawn was shrouded in gray-blue mist.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s208: I found Yuna and gave this version of her, standing here again, every word she had said before the previous cycle ended, along with the story of the empty shell, exactly as it was.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s209: “You said that if it was no longer in the corridor, I should tell you next time: it sat here.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s210: After listening, she said nothing for a long time. Drops of water from the morning mist still clung to the ends of her hair.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s211: I saw an instinctive resistance in her eyes—the same as when she realized yesterday that she had treated that body as a vessel missing a part. Even though this was a relayed memory, she could still feel that chill clearly.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s212: After a while, she drew a deep breath and forced the emotion down.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s213: “Fine. I’ll remember.” She looked at me, her voice calm again. “If a machine can make a body out of nowhere in a few minutes… then in the past hundred years, did no one ever accidentally trigger anything like it?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s214: She turned to look at the bell tower of the chapel in the distance.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s215: “If someone in the village encountered something like this on the outskirts—something shaped like a person but without a subject—what rules were established for dealing with it?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s216: “‘For incorrect sections, go call someone. Do not handle them yourself.’” I recited the church rule we were required to copy every week.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s217: “Why call someone? Why weren’t we taught how to identify them?” Her brows drew together. “I’m going to look through the elders’ old drafts. I want to see what the people who first established the rule were hiding from the village.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s220: To determine how the empty shell had been classified by the village’s old system, we spent the entire morning infiltrating the controlled archives behind the chapel. We avoided the cleaning staff and patrols,

searching through dozens of old drawers in the innermost metal cabinet marked with one of the earliest years—drawers whose gaps we had tested or whose hidden locks we had pried open bit by bit across many cycles.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s221: At last, she found several yellowed, brittle booklets. They were drafts of teaching manuals left by the village’s earliest generations of elders.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s222: Yuna put on gloves and carefully opened one of them.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s225: There were two kinds of marks on the paper. The layer underneath was printed in an ancient form of writing. But above it was a layer of crude black lines drawn by hand. The ink had already faded and dried like the paper, seeping deeply into the texture of the century-old pages.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s227: “This line says: ‘In the event of an unresponsive or unregistered body, one must…’” Yuna pointed to a section hidden beneath the marks. “There’s a bracket after it.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s229: “Inside the bracket is an archive number and an exact date. It’s the path for tracing the rule back to its source.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s232: The bracket, along with the number inside it, had been violently crossed out in black ink. Judging from the marks showing through on the back of the paper, whoever crossed it out had pressed down extremely hard.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s233: She turned through dozens of pages. Every bracket containing a source index had been removed without exception.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s238: She stopped at a page near the very back. Two lines were written in the blank margin. The upper line had been struck through with the same period’s ancient ink; the lower line had not.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s241: She flipped through the stack to the end, then searched several other archives from the same period. None contained Appendix Three.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s243: “The section of this manual instructing people how to handle bodies was removed separately.” She set the booklets down. “Someone didn’t want ordinary record-keepers,
or even people on the village outskirts, to know what to do. That appendix was either destroyed or held by the very few people who knew the truth back then.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s246: Her finger moved to the uncrossed line below. It was a sentence everyone in the village knew by heart, a sentence they were required to copy and memorize again and again.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s248: “For incorrect sections, go call someone. Do not handle them yourself.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s251: Yuna raised the century-old booklet. Near the outer edge of the margin beside that line was a small hollow circle, drawn in a single stroke with the ends joined.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s253: “Arno, you copy these lesson plans every week.” She stared at the circle. “When Elder Sera reviews your copies, if she sees the rule she considers most important, the one that must be obeyed absolutely, what does she draw in the margin?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s255: “A hollow circle,” I said. “It means ‘not to be crossed.’”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s257: “We previously speculated that Sera’s power in this village was completely transcendent. The pause in the first stroke, the tiny arc offset where the end joins the beginning… I’ve seen her habit of drawing circles countless times on returned

copies. Even if this mark might be some annotation tradition passed down by generations of elders…” She stared fixedly at the old booklet. “Whether this circle was drawn by Sera a hundred years ago or by Sera’s predecessor, it proves one

thing: making the people on the outskirts only report things and never touch them was what the central power that established these rules wanted. Whether that appendix still exists or not, ordinary people were never allowed to see it.”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s262: At noon that day, we crossed the boundary stone again. We made our way through the long, deep corridors.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s264: When we returned to that corridor, the space beside the wall was empty.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s265: We walked back to the control panel. The manufacturing vat was tightly closed. The dust on the production line remained undisturbed. The warm body was gone.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s266: In the next world, there was nothing here. More than a hundred pounds of physical flesh had not crossed the boundary at dawn.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s269: Yuna stood before the second door, which had shown no response to the empty shell but had opened for me, and looked at me beyond it.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s271: “We guessed outside the camp that matter couldn’t cross. But only today did even a genuinely created physical living body remain behind in the previous night,” she said.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s272: Her gaze was cold and sharp as it passed through the door’s invisible boundary and fixed on me.
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s274: “If it isn’t the body that crosses time… then in a system that recognizes only the ‘source,’ what exactly does the you who wakes up in this morning every day bring with him?”
texts.chapter:chapter-04-shell:event:text-s275: She looked at me as if I were the greatest anomaly of all.
texts.chapter:chapter-05-wheat-and-cord:title: Chapter Five: Wheat Fields and Counters
texts.chapter:chapter-05-wheat-and-cord:event::
Church of Convergence Prayer Room · Archived Sample:
May my cough be cured before winter.
Prayer-maker’s signature: (a name, written with heavy strokes)
Other party (wish-bearer)’s signature:

(a short horizontal stroke, indicating that no one else needs to undertake the wish)
Scribe: Yuna
(The handwriting is neat. The final character, “Na,” ends with a small hook that fails to stop.)
After facing that enormous truth deep inside the camp on the previous run, I didn’t want to check anything that morning.

A rope pulled too tight would snap sooner or later. When time began again at eight o’clock that morning, according to the fixed state at the beginning of the loop, I was thrown back onto the White Tower’s empty circular iron platform, with Yuna a few steps away in front

of a row of rusted copper control consoles. I only needed one rest period in which to stop thinking. The chasms I had crossed by sheer force of taut nerves were now collecting their debt inside the relatively safe White Tower. Before the search party arrived, I put my

uninjured left hand on Yuna’s shoulder. Each time my right leg touched the ground, the ankle sprain left over from the first night of the loop sent a sharp, piercing pain through me. Step by painful step, I moved with her into the maintenance hatch deep in the corridor.
The corridor air held the slight chill peculiar to the White Tower. We endured the most dangerous moment in the shadow of the maintenance hatch. She leaned against the wall.
All I had to do was say the opening line only the two of us knew, hear her naturally continue it and ask me, “All right. What are we doing today?” Then I would look at her and tell her:
“Nothing today.”

Late the night before the eight-o’clock loop start, a capture net targeting us had already been woven in secret. From the moment the loop restarted at eight, the Inner Circle search for “heretical infiltration” had already spread through the village. Within that rigid

state machine, Otto’s assigned routes were extremely inflexible: at eight fifteen, the search party would completely sweep the chapel and the White Tower’s public levels, then move on to the village’s main road. Ordinary villagers had no idea who exactly was wanted.

We knew the rhythm of this machine too well. Two suspects who had fled during the night could never return to their regular posts in broad daylight. What was more, because of Yuna’s “escape,” no replacement scribe had been assigned today. The prayer

room should have been empty. If we endured the first forty-five minutes in the shadow of the maintenance hatch, waited for them to turn the chapel upside down and withdraw, Yuna could hang the open sign as usual. The chapel was the first place the

search party would confirm as searched, and since this was a normal day for the prayer room to be open, uninformed villagers would keep coming and going. No one would think that two fugitives were sitting behind the counter where people passed by.

We stepped onto the village road at eight forty-five. The morning road carried a sense of cleanliness and coolness. You could see people sprinkling water over the dry dirt in front of their doors to keep down the dust, while others pushed open wooden shutters that creaked.

At the instant we passed the chapel crossroads, the composition did not change, but Yuna, walking beside me, suddenly did.
The warm-white candidate dress she wore vanished, replaced by a purple Second Candidate dress.

More fatal still was her face—that was not Yuna. It was Estelle. The vessel who had already died before my eyes before this loop began. She stood where Yuna should have been, looking at me with a cold, guarded stare.

The image snapped back at once. It had not even lasted a second.
Yuna was still standing beside me. She had turned her head and was looking at my horrified expression in confusion, reaching out to support me.
“What’s wrong?”

I stopped short, my breath catching in my throat. I didn’t know what it was. How could the dead be standing where Yuna was? I instinctively wanted to seize this trembling thread, but a dizzying sensation close to overload immediately rose from deep in my mind.
I looked at that familiar face and opened my mouth, then forcibly swallowed the words already at my lips. Not today. If I pursued this at the edge of breaking, I would go mad right here.
“My foot… the pain still hasn’t gone away.”
Yuna frowned but did not ask further. She simply reached out and supported my body again, which had lost its balance from the tension in my muscles, with a steady pressure that reassured me.
At the roadside chess stall, Old Barrow was slowly arranging the pieces. Old Nona sat opposite him, head lowered as she gathered her shawl, still unaware of what was wrong with the board.
But as I watched the old couple, my heart was still racing from the image I had just seen. Late the night before the reset, this very old man had calmly proposed putting
the two of us to death. Death, sacrifice, replacement—things so heavy they suffocated me—were absurdly intertwined with the peaceful everyday scene in the sunlight before me.
Yuna suddenly stopped and looked over there.
“Hey.”
I followed her gaze. Old Barrow sat in the sunlight, patiently and slyly waiting for his wife to start cursing him.
“What is it?”
“He set it up wrong.”
I pulled myself back together and examined the chessboard carefully.
“Where?”
Yuna lifted a hand and pointed.

“The third one from the left,” she said in a light tone. “He deliberately sets this one wrong every day, and then, when Old Nona sits down, she moves it back into place without the slightest ceremony, grumbling the whole time.”
She tilted her head slightly toward the old couple and smiled.

“At first I thought he really was senile, that he couldn’t even remember where a chess piece went. Later I changed my mind and understood what was happening.” The corners of her eyes curved into a gentle arc. “Because she comes over to move it every time anyway, cursing him at the top of her lungs while she does it.”
Yuna looked away and walked on.
The prayer room would not open until nine.

We also had to avoid the occasional searchers around the outskirts, so we walked very slowly and could only turn into the hidden narrow lane behind the mill. I walked somewhat stiffly, trying not to let

the rough strip of cloth wrapped around the base of my right thumb scrape against the wall—the strip she had torn from her right sleeve and tied around me while we rested in the maintenance hatch just now.
Every corner and every place to set a foot on this route carried a smooth, glossy patina—the traces worn into it by the soles of our shoes over the nearly nine years before the loop began.

That morning, just as we were helping each other squeeze out through the gap between two courtyards, Milu happened to appear in the yard. Yuna released my hand at once. I shifted all my weight onto my left leg and tucked my right leg into the shadow behind me.
Milu caught us red-handed.
“Sis!”
The little girl clutched the old bell that had long since stopped making a sound, her small face taut with righteousness. She did not look down at my feet at all. She only stared at Yuna.
“You brought Arno-gege down the dirty path again! The Elder said ladies aren’t allowed to sneak along the base of walls!”
Yuna straightened without changing expression and slowly dusted the dirt from her skirt.
“Ladies don’t take it. So I do.”
Milu was left speechless. She raised the bell threateningly.
“I’m telling the Elder!”
Yuna did not even move an eyebrow.
“Go ahead. And while you’re at it, tell the Elder exactly who overslept yesterday morning and was punished by having to copy scripture.”
The words worked better than any spell. Milu’s face suddenly flushed bright red.
“That—that was because—Sis! Why do you tell everyone everything!”
Yuna kept the same solemn expression.
“You were the one who reported me first. Reporting is war. There are no ladies in war.”
Milu could not argue with her. She stamped her feet, turned, and ran home. After a few steps, as if remembering an important mission, she turned back and shouted:
“Sis, come home early tonight! Mom says we’re pickling vegetables today!”
Yuna watched her run away and answered brightly.
“Got it.”
The little girl’s energetic figure disappeared around the fence.

Yuna kept waving. Only after Milu had vanished completely did she slowly lower her hand. She stood quietly for a while without looking at me, and did not mention that she could not possibly go home tonight.
Then she suddenly spoke, her voice very soft.
“The bell in her hand—I broke it myself when I was eight.”
I was somewhat surprised.
“Broke it?”
Yuna came back to herself and nodded once.

“That day I climbed onto the courtyard wall because I wanted to see how far the bell’s sound could carry, and which field it could reach. I swung my arm around as hard as I could. The ring inside had already rusted through.

It broke after only a few swings, and the clapper fell straight into a crack at the foot of the wall. I couldn’t dig it out. I was going to throw it away, but she secretly picked it up and treated it like a treasure.”
The morning wind passed through. Yuna huddled her shoulders and tucked her hands into her wide sleeves.
“She carries that broken thing around every day now, ringing it at everyone she sees. She knows it won’t make a sound, so she opens her mouth and says ‘Dang’ for the bell herself.”
She paused and looked at the shortcut where Milu’s figure had long since disappeared.
“It’s broken already, but she insists on treating it like a treasure,” she said softly. “I wonder how long she’ll keep calling out for it.”

Five minutes before nine, just as we arrived at the point when the search party had withdrawn from the chapel area on schedule, Yuna skillfully carried a low wooden stool outside the chapel’s side wing and climbed onto it to hang the sign above the doorway.
It was an old varnished board with two heavily rusted iron rings threaded through it. Only the section of rope hanging from it looked newly replaced.

I stood beneath the stool and steadied its edge with my uninjured left hand. Yuna hung the board, stepped half a pace away, squinted at it, and muttered, “The left side is high,” before climbing back up to adjust it. The board held only two lines:

Church of Convergence Prayer Room
This Session: Open

She was still wearing the newly made warm-white candidate dress. A long strip was missing from the right sleeve, with rough broken threads showing at the edge—that was what she had torn off forty-five minutes ago to bandage my right hand. A trace of

unrecovered recycling-label ink remained on it. When she jumped down from the stool, she neatly pressed down the skirt, which had nearly flown up, then simply folded both sleeves up twice, tucking the damaged sections inside and exposing her slender wrists.
A faded old cloth identification band, turned reddish brown, had been fastened around her left wrist for years.
I bent down and carried the low stool back beside the wall.
“When people come to submit things later, don’t touch any paper in this room.”
She looked at the rough strip of cloth hastily wrapped around the base of my right thumb.
“That hand of yours is still bleeding. You’ll get blood on the records. The rule is that no one except me and the person making the wish may touch them.”
The prayer room was not large. An old wooden counter stood three steps from the door, dividing the space in two. Visitors stood on the outer side, while the
scribe sat on the inner side. The counter’s heavy base pressed tightly against a raised edge of old concrete. The cement edge looked older than the room itself.

A thin horizontal slot opened at the lower right corner of the counter. It was used to collect papers bearing written wishes. A prayer paper pushed through the slot from outside would slide down a sloping

wooden rail into a locked compartment inside the counter. The compartment’s door opened on Yuna’s side, with a brass latch hanging on it. This one-way structure ensured that once a paper fell inside, the

person making the wish outside the counter could never retrieve it. But as long as the duty period had not ended and the stubs had not yet been locked in the iron case, the process was not completely final.

Yuna settled onto the stool. I half sat in the darkness beneath the counter, stretching out my right leg, tense from the cramp, to keep it out of sight from anyone who might look in, while pulling a small screwdriver from my old tool belt.
“The latch on the compartment door is a little loose,” I said, tilting my head back. “I’ll tighten it so it doesn’t fall.”
Yuna glanced at the daylight outside.
“Then fix it. It’s nine.”
With the soft scrape of metal against the screws, Yuna spread a stack of blank duplicate forms across the counter, along with a dip pen and a sheet of blotting paper to place beneath them.
The first person to enter the prayer room that day was a middle-aged woman.
As soon as she came in, she placed a small bundle cautiously on the edge of the counter. It was dried vegetables she had prepared herself, wrapped tightly in a faded old cloth.
“For the prayer room.”
Yuna did not move even a finger.
“The kitchen takes those.”

I reached out from below with my left hand, lifted the bundle, and set it beside the door, planning to deliver it with the rest at noon when we closed. The woman watched me put it down and nervously pinched the corner of her clothes.
“Go ahead. What would you like to wish for?”
Yuna picked up the pen. The woman took a deep breath.
“Let my husband drink a little less.”
Yuna’s hand paused in midair. Then she placed the pen back on the blotting paper exactly as it had been.
“This, the prayer room can’t write.”
The woman froze.
“Why not?”
“Because this is about changing his actions. According to the rules, he has to sign the second blank himself. But he isn’t here.”
The woman stood rigidly before the counter and lowered her head deeply. Her hand wandered over the rough edge of the counter, then withdrew helplessly.
From the darkness, I happened to glimpse a small section of her wrist showing from her rough-cloth sleeve. An old bruise that had not completely faded marked it.
Yuna saw it too. She looked the woman straight in the eye, her originally businesslike tone softening a little.
“But I can write another wish for you.”
She met the woman’s gaze.
“I can write, ‘May I have the strength to leave him.’ Or, ‘May I find a way out.’ He doesn’t need to sign those. They’re your wishes.”
The woman flinched as if the words had burned her. Fear climbed into her eyes in an instant.
“No, no…” She shook her head repeatedly, her voice trembling. “Don’t write that. Just write… write, ‘May I have the courage to finish talking this through with him.’”
Yuna watched her quietly for a while and did not force her any further.
“All right.” Yuna picked up the pen again. “The prayer room can write that.”

Yuna dipped the pen in ink and began writing across the duplicate form with a soft scratching sound. When she finished, she turned the paper around and read it from beginning to end in front of the woman.
“May I have the courage to finish talking this through with him.”
Two lines were clearly printed along the very bottom of the prayer paper:

Prayer-maker’s signature: ________

Other party (wish-bearer)’s signature: ________
Yuna reached out and gently placed the pen beside the first line.
The woman took the pen and wrote her name stroke by stroke in the blank on the first line.
