When she finished, Yuna took the paper back. She put pen to the blank on the second line and drew a firm horizontal stroke, indicating that this wish did not require another wish-bearer.

When that was done, she tore off the narrower stub along the dotted line down the middle and kept it, then pushed the large communal-prayer sheet back toward the woman and pointed at the slot in the lower right corner.
“Push it in.”

The woman held the edges of the paper with both hands and slowly guided it into the slot. But when it was time to let go, she seemed to retreat. The paper stopped in the middle of the slot, trembling faintly with her shaking fingers.

I was sitting beneath the counter, tightening screws. When I saw that she would not release her fingers, I reached out from inside with my right hand, caught the lower edge of the paper, and gave it a gentle pull inward. The paper slipped from her grasp and slid into the compartment.
Just then, Yuna’s voice came from above me.
“Bring it back.”
I tilted my head back.
“She was shaking. I just helped a little.”
There was not a ripple in Yuna’s eyes. She bent down directly, pushed aside the brass latch that had not yet been locked in front of me, and pulled the communal-prayer sheet out of the compartment.
“Put it back.”
She placed the paper squarely back on the counter and pushed it toward the woman.
By then, the woman had backed away to the doorway.
“Submit it yourself.” Yuna tapped the edge of the counter.
The woman turned around and silently walked back. As she returned, the light at the doorway dimmed. An old man entered and, seeing the situation, turned slightly to make room for her.

The woman stood before the counter again and picked up the paper. She carefully aligned it with the slot and pushed it forward an inch. This time, no one helped her. She released her fingers herself. The paper slid down smoothly.
Having completed the motion, she turned and walked out of the prayer room without looking back.

I returned beneath the counter and steadied the latch with my left hand while tightening it again. The bandage around the base of my right thumb had seeped a little more blood after I reached out to catch the paper.
“I told you. Your blood will get on the paper.”
She did not look down. Her voice was flat.
The communal-prayer sheet the woman had pushed in herself lay quietly at the bottom of the compartment. I looked at the red mark on the bandage and did not argue.
The old man who had made way for her slowly approached the counter.
Yuna held the pen and waited patiently for him to speak.
“I wish for my son… to come visit me once this year.”

At those words, Yuna’s pen, suspended in midair, did not descend. This was another wish that required an absent “second person” to carry out an action, and that the prayer room could not write under its rules. She waited quietly instead of refusing him outright.

The old man stared quietly at the pen. He stood waiting for a while, seeming to understand from the start where the wish had caught. He drew a deep breath. A resigned clarity flickered in his cloudy eyes, and then he spoke the second half.

“I understand the rules. You can’t write that sentence.” He gave a bitter smile. “Then write… ‘May the Dice-Thrower grant me peace of mind, so I can stop waiting night after night.’ That’s my own matter, isn’t it?”
Yuna’s pen touched the paper and wrote the wish. When she finished, she read it to him as usual:
“May I stop suffering as I wait for my son to return, and find peace of mind.”
Across the counter, the old man’s bloodshot eyes fixed on the ink. He shakily read the final four words aloud once more.
“Find peace of mind.”
He wrote his name in the prayer-maker’s blank on the first line. Yuna decisively drew a short horizontal stroke in the wish-bearer’s position on the second line. After tearing off
the stub, the old man slowly pushed the large communal-prayer sheet toward the slot with trembling hands. The paper slipped inside. Satisfied, the old man nodded and shuffled away.
Without anyone noticing, the slanting sunlight outside had moved from one end of the counter to the other.

Just then, another figure appeared in the doorway. He was a broad-shouldered middle-aged man who lived near the mill. At first he did not hurry inside. He stood in the shadow outside, craning his neck to look both ways, and only crossed the threshold after confirming that no one was nearby.
He also recognized me crouching in the darkness. Every autumn during the harvest, the wheat from his fields passed over my scale. He gave me a perfunctory nod, and I silently nodded back.
The man strode to the counter, vigorously rubbing his callused hands together, and lowered his voice.

“I want to ask for justice on behalf of the whole village. Just write… let Elder Sera give up her position sooner. Submit the paper as usual, and when it’s prayed over publicly tonight, leave my name unread as usual.”
Yuna’s hand froze around the pen in midair. After a brief silence, she put the pen directly back on the tabletop.
Yuna raised her head.
“The prayer room won’t write that.”
The man’s face flushed red.
“Why not? I’m not asking for anything bad. This is the just thing everyone in the village is talking about in private!”
Yuna tapped the wooden counter.
“This is a matter of deciding someone else’s position. By the rules, Elder Sera has to sign the second blank herself.”
The man laughed angrily. He suddenly thrust out his thick arm and pointed toward the main street outside.
“She’s in the council hall at the far end of the main street right now! You want me to go get her to sign this?!”
Yuna met his stare without yielding.
“That means it isn’t a wish you have the authority to decide.”
The man braced both hands hard against the counter, his chest rising and falling violently.
“Fine! Then I’ll write, ‘May I dare to point at the things everyone is afraid to say and curse them to their faces!’ That’s my own matter, isn’t it?”
Yuna looked at him.

“Fine. That is your own hope. If you think reading it aloud would be dangerous, we can make it anonymous tonight. But the first line must bear your real name. This paper will eventually go into the archives. The archives require real names.”
The man’s voice caught in his throat, then burst out even more violently.
“The archives? Then Sera will see it, won’t she? One word from her could cut off a family’s grain ration! If I sign my name, will my whole family still be able to eat in this village?”
Seeing his wish slip away, the resentment he had been suppressing finally turned elsewhere. He suddenly pointed toward the chapel, only a wall away. His voice, lowered by anger, trembled faintly.

“What gives her the right to sit up there and decide whether we get fed? Just because she hides everything from us? The autumn before last, when I was turning the soil, my plow pulled a lump of iron out of

the ground!” He stared straight at Yuna. “It still had a ring on one end, rusted into a solid mass. I handed it in myself. They took it and said they needed to examine it, and then I never heard another word!”
He drew a deep breath. His voice carried a rough fatigue, as if he had been holding it in for too long.
“That scrap of iron is no use to me. I just want to know what the hell it is! That’s my plow. That’s the land our ancestors have farmed for generations!”
Irritated, he turned his head and forcefully nodded toward the closed partition wall inside the prayer room.
“But the person who answered me there last time told me with a straight face that the rule was not to let ordinary people make wild guesses.”
At that, his suppressed emotions finally erupted.
“Fine! If you won’t let us guess, then I won’t guess! But if guessing isn’t allowed, someone still has to tell me openly what the hell it is, don’t they?!”
Yuna sat quietly behind the counter and listened to the man’s outburst.
“The prayer room can’t give you an answer about the lump of iron you submitted.”
She straightened slightly and looked at the man’s furious yet helpless eyes. There was no mockery in her expression, and no retreat.

“This room accepts wishes, not complaints,” Yuna said calmly. “If you want someone else to step down from a position, you need that person’s signature. If you want to submit an accusation to the archives, you need your own real name. This

compartment isn’t somewhere to hide someone else’s risk, and the Church of Convergence’s archival system does not accept accusations without an owner. That is the procedure. If you don’t dare write your own name, this paper cannot go in.”
The man stood there stunned, his face shifting from green to white, looking as ugly as it could. In the end, he said nothing. He spun around and stormed away.
At the prayer-room doorway, he turned back and glared viciously at Yuna behind the counter.
“How old are you, anyway, to think you can use the rules to push people around?”

Yuna did not even raise her eyelids. She reached out and carefully realigned the stack of blank forms the man had knocked out of place. She did not argue or look up at his departing back. She simply left her fingertip beside the name field on the top sheet.
“I can’t accept an unsigned paper,” she answered softly to the stack.

After he left, several people passed by the prayer-room doorway one after another. When the first muffled noon bell rang from the White Tower, the neat stack of duplicate forms still lay untouched in the exact center of the counter.
The second noon bell rang. It was the signal that the search grid was about to reshuffle and the major search was about to close in on the village center.
Yuna stood up from the stool and placed the two stubs in a nearby locked, moisture-proof iron case—the final archive box, which even the scribe had no authority to open again. Only
when the brass lock clicked shut would the wishes officially take effect, beyond anyone’s ability to withdraw them. In total, only those two wishes had been preserved that morning.

Yuna went outside to take down the wooden sign. When she returned, she casually picked up the stack of unused blank forms and handed it to me, indicating that I should return even the spotless top sheet, without a single word on it, to the front room.
When I took it, the two silent printed lines along the bottom edge of the paper faced quietly toward me.

Prayer-maker’s signature: ________

Other party (wish-bearer)’s signature: ________
I slipped the screwdriver back into my tool belt, supported the stack of blank forms one-handed with my good left hand, and followed Yuna across the prayer-room threshold.
From the distant courtyard came the faint, bright “Dang” of a child’s voice. I knew Milu was providing the sound effects for her broken bell again.

Outside, the grid of the public search was tightening rapidly. These few stolen hours of rest were over. We would have to return to the undercurrent below. But at that moment, I thought of nothing. I simply dragged my throbbing right foot and followed her steps into the glaring sunlight.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:title: Chapter Five, Appendix: Twelve Characters
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s4-1: Before time began resetting over and over, even before the week when we were designated as candidates arrived, Yuna’s world had many rules that could not be crossed.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s5-1: The rule of the prayer room was that a prayer form could only be filed if it bore the petitioner’s signature.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s6-1: One time, after closing, the prayer room’s thick wooden door had already been shut. Yuna sat at the table and pulled a blank prayer form printed with a grid toward her, then wrote a line on it. When she heard my approaching footsteps, she quickly folded the paper in half twice, clenched it in her hand, and stuffed it deep into her sleeve.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s10-1: “Void.” She patted the cuff of her left sleeve. “I didn’t sign it.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s13-1: No one was stopping her from signing her own name, but she had always believed that, as a scribe, she could not overstep her status and exercise a believer’s rights. She would rather let the prayer be void than hold fast to that boundary.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s14-1:
I never saw that paper again. But when she crumpled it into her sleeve that day, the ink showed clearly through the back. I couldn’t make out the contents, but I recognized that the line had filled exactly twelve squares.
It was a wish of hers, only twelve characters long.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s18-1: Another afternoon, we hid on the lee side of the haystack. She sat cross-legged on the ground, holding the old wooden die that village children liked to play with in her palm.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s20-1: “Class says that as long as the die is made evenly, rolling it once is pure luck. It doesn’t tell you anything.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s22-1: She suddenly raised her hand, tossed the die high into the air, and caught it neatly. The wood struck her palm with a dull thud.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s24-1: “But if you roll it a hundred times, a thousand times, and it’s a block of wood with unevenly carved marks, the numbers of times each face lands upward will stabilize at different values. The proportion it stabilizes at is the real one.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s26-1: “Is that what the elder taught you?”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s28-1: “The first half. The second half was my own idea.” She leaned a little closer to me, then paused.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s34-1: “She said: ‘If you calculate things too clearly, you won’t be able to stop yourself from counting things you shouldn’t count.’”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s35-1: She closed her fingers around the die and gripped it tightly in her palm, her knuckles paling slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s37-1: “For example, calculating the exact proportion of people taken away over the past few years who never came back.” She deliberately lowered her voice.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s38-1: She stopped. She did not say what that proportion was.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s42-1: Wind passed through the haystack with a fine rustling sound. She said no more, only stared at her palm for a while. Then, suddenly, she threw the die up hard and caught it in her fist. The dull knock of wood against her palm broke the silence.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s44-1: “Come on, let’s verify it. Split the dried fruit in your pocket with me as the stake. Whoever wins takes one from the other. I’m betting odd.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s45-1: By the time the shadow cast by the eaves had shifted a palm’s width, every piece of dried fruit I had was in her hands. She tossed the last one into her mouth without the slightest hesitation and chewed it with a loud crunch.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s50-1: At the start of every game, she always proposed this rule as if it were self-evident. The odd-numbered faces of that wooden die had very deep carvings. She was exactly right. With a crudely made wooden die like this, one roll might be pure luck, but by the time the sun slanted west, she was always the long-run winner.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s55-1: That evening, we made do with dinner beside the canal behind the mill. She carefully arranged the three small dishes we had brought on a flat stone.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s57-1: Then she picked up a small dish of yellow-green pickled vegetables and moved it away by itself, firmly guarding it in front of her.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s59-1: “I’ll eat this,” she announced. “You don’t eat this.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s60-1: I was taken aback. I really didn’t eat pickled vegetables. The taste always made me think uncontrollably of the strange medicine I had drunk when I was seriously ill. But I had never even told my mother, only claiming to be picky.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s63-1: Yuna was reaching out to push another dish of dried meat toward me. At my words, her hand stopped in midair, and she looked at me as if I were an idiot.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s69-1: “You ate some at my house when you were seven and threw up. You don’t remember?”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s73-1: “I remember. Because you threw up on my foot.” A trace of triumph touched the corner of her mouth as she pushed the dish of dried meat in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s80-1: Another evening’s glow dyed the village orange-red as we watched the sky from the sloped roof of the storeroom at her house.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s82-1: The sunlight was dazzling. She raised her left hand to block the setting sun. Her sleeve slid down her arm, revealing the old reddish-brown cloth band around her wrist. It wound around twice, its edges already fraying, with only the metal clasp worn to a bright shine.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s84-1: “That strap. You never take it off.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s85-1: She suddenly sat up and lowered her hand. The air beside us fell silent for two seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s87-1: “Separate matters,” she said, the warmth suddenly dropping out of her voice.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s91-1: “It means this isn’t your question to ask,” she shot back stiffly.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s92-1: She drew back a little, pressed the left hand wearing the band beneath her knee, and sat firmly on it. I felt a hard boundary there, so I didn’t ask again.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s97-1: The sky gradually darkened completely. Stars scattered across the night like broken silver. We remained sitting on the roof’s slope, letting the wind pass over us.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s99-1: “Hey.” She looked at the sky and suddenly spoke. “Do you know about the stars?”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s103-1: “The book says light takes time to travel.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s104-1: The night wind brushed past. Her voice became very calm in the darkness, with less of its usual guardedness. It was the kind she never used during the day, or when facing believers in the prayer room.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s106-1: “The stars are too far away. It takes the light a very, very long time to travel from there to here. So—”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s109-1: She raised her hand, her slender finger pointing to the brightest star in the night sky.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s111-1: “What you’re seeing now is actually light from a very long time ago.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s112-1: I followed her finger. The star glittered in the deep night sky.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s116-1: “I don’t know. Decades, centuries.” Her voice grew hazy. “Maybe the star itself has been gone for a long time. Destroyed. But the light it gave off is still traveling. It hasn’t finished.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s117-1: Her hand remained raised, stubbornly pointing at that star that might have ceased to exist long ago.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s121-1: The night wind passed through the wheat fields nearby with a rustling sound. We sat quietly like that, watching the sky, until dew dampened our shoulders.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s128-1: After time began joining end to beginning and resetting over and over in this village, I once tried to ask around about the band’s origins without going through Yuna. It was during a break in one of the containment searches. While Milu was washing her hands by the basin, I quietly called her over.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s130-1: “The strap on Big Sis’s wrist? I don’t know.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s134-1: “Mother says not to ask.” Milu lowered her voice. “Mother says it’s Big Sis’s own business.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s135-1: She raised her head, her eyes full of curiosity.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s137-1: “Brother Arno, why are you suddenly asking about this?”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s138-1: I opened my mouth, but I couldn’t answer.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s139-1: Through the countless looped todays that followed, no matter how many different moments and tones I used to probe Yuna herself, her answer was always that same cold “Separate matters.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s140-1: Since she refused to speak, the only way to find out where that old metal clasp came from was to investigate how the Church handled the old-world ironwork it confiscated.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s140-2: The ringed iron lump handed in by the man who had questioned Yuna at the counter a few days earlier was a ready-made lead. I decided to find the answer myself.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s146-1: Relying on the time I could restart, I began wading into the secrets the Church had locked away.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s147-1: On a morning in one of the later resets, several of Elder Otto’s informed confidants were following their usual route to search for us. I dragged along my swollen, burning right ankle, which remained injured after every reset, and deliberately knocked over
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s147-2: a roadside cart, making enough noise to draw the people guarding the chapel toward another street. I shoved Yuna into a hidden room beneath the bell tower, then gritted my teeth and limped behind the yard racks toward the back of the chapel’s side wing.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s152-1: A heavy brass lock hung on the wooden door that was rarely opened. To deal with it, I had come there on four different todays and repeatedly probed its mechanism with a thin steel wire. I had also spent two todays watching the angle of force Elder Sera used when pushing the door panel.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s153-1: With my right hand wrapped in a rough strip of cloth, I held the door panel firmly in place. A dull tearing pain immediately pulled at the wound across my thumb joint. My right ankle could barely support me, so I leaned most of my weight against the doorframe. With my left hand, I slipped the wire into the lock and worked it around. There was a faint click, and the bolt sprang open.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s158-1:
It was a north-facing room that never saw sunlight, cool and dimmer inside than the outdoors just after rain.
A row of wooden shelves was nailed above the long counter, holding ledgers bound in cloth over stiff paper. Beneath the counter was a long row of shallow drawers, each bearing a yellowing number label.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s159-1: Normally, Milu ran errands between the front room and the back courtyard. She was only allowed into this room when she needed to replenish the paper cards or fetch new forms. I had just seen her outside, carrying a stack of uncut heavy paper into the front room.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s160-1: The numbers on the labels were written small and square, with a hard horizontal stroke drawn beneath each one. That was Yuna’s distinctive handwriting.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s163-1:
I took down the ledger recording the autumn’s business and turned to the last few pages. Every line at the front had been crossed out, with a note indicating where it had gone.
Only the final line was clean, untouched.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s164-1: At the end was the name of the man who had questioned Yuna at the counter before. He had written it himself, pressing hard enough to nearly tear through the back of the paper. That line also corresponded to a number.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s165-1: I followed the number to the wooden drawer beneath it. My frost-stiffened fingers failed to grip the brass ring, and I pulled too hard.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s168-1: The entire drawer came off its runners and spilled fifty or sixty registration forms across the floor with a clatter. I crouched down and hurriedly gathered them, finding the one I wanted:
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s169-1:
Received: one iron component, ring at one end, rusted shut and non-removable.
Category: ironwork
Disposition:
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s170-1: The disposition field was a glaring blank. There was no note that it had been entered into storage, no indication that it was awaiting processing, and no record of its destruction. If it had simply been omitted, no one could have gone
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s170-2: through more than half a year without adding it later. Nor had I seen any designated area in the storeroom for old items awaiting processing. The object had not been handed over to any public procedure. It had quietly disappeared from view.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s173-1:
At that moment, the door to the front room sounded.
My heart lurched. I immediately grabbed the stack of papers from the floor and shoved them haphazardly into the drawer, then lifted the derailed wooden box with both hands and forced it back onto its runners.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s173-2: When I finished, I retreated behind the door and crouched tight against the wall. In my panic, my tool belt caught on the wooden bucket in the corner, the one used to catch leaks. Half a bucket of dirty water spilled onto the floor and spread toward the door.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s174-1: Milu came in. She was carrying a large stack of freshly cut label cards and could only push the door open with her shoulder.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s177-1: After two steps, her foot landed in the water and she slipped hard, her body pitching sideways as she caught herself on the counter. The paper cards in her arms slid free and scattered across the floor, most of them landing in the dirty water.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s178-1: Milu stared blankly at the mess on the floor. These were dozens of freshly cut cards. If they were ruined, Elder Sera would certainly be furious. It would not simply mean cutting them again; she would also have to go before the elder to be reprimanded and punished.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s179-1:
She silently crouched down and picked up the cards one by one. The soaked stack was much taller than the dry one.
As she lifted the stack of wet cards, her eyes passed over the empty wooden bucket lying on its side in the corner.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s180-1:
Milu carried the stack of soaked cards, head lowered, turned around, and pushed the door open to leave.
The heavy wooden door closed behind her again.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s182-1: I stepped out and righted the wooden bucket. Then I went to the shelves and opened the ledger to its first page.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s184-1:
Three records had been written neatly across the page: a length of unidentified pipe, an iron spoon with a broken handle, and an iron corner fitting. The source for all three was listed as the parcel of land he had been assigned, and each line ended with that man’s signature.
The old-world objects he had handed over to the Church were far more numerous than that later iron lump with a ring.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s185-1: I suddenly realized that the metal clasp on that wristband was probably an old object dug out of the ground as well. The Church had taken them away, but had left no public record of where they went.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s186-1: In that instant, a powerful temptation seized me. My eyes moved over the ledger, and my hand was already resting on the edge of the next page. In a world where anything could be
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s186-2: started over, peeling open the secrets the Church was concealing was too easy. I only had to turn the page, and I could see clearly the remains of the old world they had hidden away.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s187-1: I pressed my palm against the edge of the page. After a long while, I abruptly closed the ledger.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s188-1: No. If I kept investigating, sooner or later I would find the confiscation record corresponding to Yuna’s wristband, and perhaps even uncover her original identity. That was the boundary she guarded to the death, the one she would not tell me even through the resets.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s189-1:
I pushed it back into place, carefully comparing the alignment with the back of my hand until its spine matched the books beside it exactly, then left the room.
Outside, I fastened the heavy brass
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s189-2: lock again and listened to the bolt click into place. To leave no trace, I dragged my lame leg in a deliberate wide circle and rubbed the wet mud from my shoe uppers against the grass by the road.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s194-1: I returned to the hidden room beneath the bell tower to find her. She was curled up in the corner, aimlessly scratching at the dirt with a short branch. I didn’t tell her about the drawer. I was afraid that if I opened my mouth, she would bristle all over as she had on the roof and push me away with a single “Separate matters.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s197-1: That evening, I hid in the shadows of the alley behind the mill and watched that man walk past after work. He seemed a little older.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s198-1:
I clenched my hand. If I told him the disposition field was blank, all I would do was send a man who had lost everything to question an elder with the highest authority to interpret the matter. And if I told him the object had been destroyed, that would be a lie as well.
In the end, I didn’t
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s198-2: step out to tell him. I thought perhaps tomorrow I could try probing in a different way. As long as time kept resetting, I could always find some explanation that wouldn’t get him killed. I watched him disappear into the distance, then turned and walked deeper into the alley behind the mill.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s200-1:
That night, we hid in the loft of the storeroom in the back courtyard of Yuna’s house.
While the adults were distracted, Milu secretly brought two bowls of rice upstairs. The little girl, aggrieved, told the story of the bucket tipping over and all the cards being ruined twice. She said the wet ones were all useless, and she would have to get up early tomorrow to cut them again.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s202-1: “How did the bucket fall over by itself?” Yuna seized on the important point.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s204-1: “I didn’t touch it. It was already lying there!” Milu grew flustered.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s205-1: Yuna glanced at her and did not press further.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s206-1: I lowered my head and shoveled down rice, stuffing a piece of dried meat into my mouth without saying a word. The dried meat tasted like wood shavings as I chewed it.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s212-1:
Adults always went to sleep early. After dinner, I walked her to the windowsill beneath the back of her house.
A faint light came through from the courtyard. Everything was so ordinary, everything where it was supposed to be.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s214-1: “See you tomorrow.” Bracing both hands on the windowsill, she climbed lightly inside, then turned and said it.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s215-1: I stood in the darkness outside the window.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s220-1: I stood quietly for a while, watching the shadow of her giving a small wave before turning away, then turned and walked back to my own house.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s226-1:
I pushed the door open softly. A dim lamp was still lit inside.
A bowl of soup was warming on the stove. Mother always left it for me.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s227-1: I lifted the bowl and drank the soup down to the last drop, standing in the kitchen.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s228-1: The bedboard sounded once in the inner room. Mother lowered her voice in the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s234-1: “Elder Otto took people to search the area again. He just went on to the next street.” She sighed, a trace of helplessness showing through her exhaustion. “Finish your soup and get back to your room. Don’t light the lamp. Captain Kane has sealed off the village entrance. No one can get out today.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s237-1: I opened my mouth. I had spent the entire day evading the search, rummaging through other people’s secrets in the dark, and coldly watching innocent Milu take the blame for me.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s239-1: “Mm. I got away,” I said lightly.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s241-1: “Go to sleep early.” She turned over in the darkness, her voice gradually fading. “Tomorrow will be another new day.”
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s247-1: I returned to my room and lay down on the bed, listening to the tireless insects outside the window.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s248-1:
After the distant bell tower struck eight with a dull sound, and an unknown length of time had passed, that eerie, directionless pale yellow-white light rose as expected and pierced through the window.
I knew that at this moment, everyone in the village was gradually becoming slower.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s249-1: I lay quietly on the bed like that, closing my eyes and feeling time pass in the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s250-1:
Until the sound of Mother turning over in the inner room, separated from me by one wall, stopped. Then her even breathing abruptly ceased.
She went out. In this world, adults always fell into
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s250-2: stasis first. After her, it would probably be Elder Sera and the others, as I had seen before. Only after all ten seats had gone out would it be the turn of the adult laborers on the outskirts.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s250-3: Once that moment had passed too, it would finally be Yuna in the neighboring courtyard, a year older than me. At the end of this cycle, she too would fall insensibly into the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-05b:event:text-s251-1: I did nothing. I only continued lying there, waiting for the nothingness that would cut all of this off without mercy.
texts.chapter:chapter-06-skylight:title: Chapter Six: Daylight
texts.chapter:chapter-06-skylight:event:text-s:
Clapping Song:
One clap, two claps,
The evening-prayer bell goes on and on.
Long robes, white collars,
Candidates line up for drills.
Close your eyes and count,
Whoever falls asleep first loses.

When dusk fell, a fine layer of dust always rose from the threshing floor. The children ran and jumped through the dust without tiring, until the evening wind cooled the sweat on their bodies. Only then would they gather in twos and threes, clapping

their hands and singing this old song. It borrowed its rhythm from church hymns and the old candidate drills. No one bothered to consider what the lyrics were actually singing about. It was only a game passed down from generation to generation.

I sang it too, when I was little. On the open threshing floor, two people faced each other, palm against palm. The crisp smacks joined the children's young voices as they sang faster and faster. Whoever lost the rhythm first lost. Milu was always the one who won. She could sing from beginning to end in a single breath, her little face flushed red.

The children sang without a care, while I clutched a sheet of paper covered in names. Listening to that familiar melody, I suddenly felt cold all over. The invisible thing in the sky really was about to come harvest us.

Turning the deaths in the village into a record was an idea Yuna had proposed long ago, in one of the earlier cycles.
Or rather, no matter how many times the cycle restarted, every morning, once she had heard my account of our desperate situation, she would calmly propose the exact same idea.
Only today, on this chilly morning, when she lowered her head and began assigning me tasks as she always did—“First, investigate the timing. Second, record the order”—I did not

run out.
I pulled the sheet of paper straight from my pocket instead. It was a complete record of the death order, pieced together through hundreds of dusks of running and watching.
She stood quietly in the morning light, her chest rising and falling faintly. After a while, she took the paper from me.

During the panic of the first few cycles, when my perceptions were twisted, I thought everyone died at once when the daylight arrived. After all, during those nights trapped in the loop, when the night sky suddenly lit up at 20:36, the endless chaos and screaming

had made me think that was the end.
It was only after I forced myself to stand aside and use hundreds of dusks of observation to verify each dull thud of a body hitting the ground that I became certain this was a slow dismemberment. The daylight that arrived

at 20:36 was only the opening of the disaster; the true extinguishing followed an extraordinarily precise timetable. They were not all unplugged at once, but when each precise moment arrived, their bodies were still warm while the people inside were already

empty—a state of sleep in which their first-person consciousness had been forcibly extracted, leaving only the bare minimum of physiological functions. Once this irreversible sleep descended that night, no matter how they were called, they would never wake again.

At the beginning of the list, the evening-prayer bell stopped at 20:30. Six minutes later, at 20:36, the daylight arrived.
With that tragic, dazzling afterglow, a few abrupt cries briefly rose from the village. Then everyone was stunned by the

strange celestial phenomenon. Fear seized every throat, but they were still alive, still able to walk, still able to be afraid. Until the dull thuds of bodies falling began dragging out their notes through every corner of the village like a blunt saw.

Old Nona was always the first to go dark. The chess stall's peeling wooden bench always gave a dull, blunt thud as she fell. Next came Old Barro, who was at the chess stall with her, and then Village Head

Otto. At 21:26, my mother Rena, also one of the Ten Seats, was fourth. She fell beside the doorframe where she always liked to look outside. Clearing just those first four people took a full fifty minutes.

But after 21:26, the rate of collapse suddenly went out of control. The list advanced downward without mercy. The six remaining members of the Ten Seats—including Kane, patrolling the woods at the west gate, twenty-two-year-old Chiko, and nineteen-year-old Toma—went dark one after another

within a few short minutes. Immediately afterward, the permanent laborers stationed around the outskirts—that is, every adult except the Ten Seats and those of us who were underage—slumped to the ground in swathes throughout the village like cut wheat, their dull thuds continuing without end.
Yuna stared at the complete list, her voice deliberately held flat. “Disasters have good years and bad years. Floods rise and fall. But this thing is neither more nor less,
neither early nor late, neither selective nor random—Arno, there is an invisible clock in the sky. Most of the people in this village are words carved onto its face.”
There was one place in the record that felt uncanny, no matter how I looked at it.
“Too chaotic.”
Yuna stared at that column of names.

“The Ten Seats. They’re at the very front.” Yuna pointed to several names near the top of the list. “Chiko’s body is only twenty-two years old, and Toma is nineteen, yet they fall earlier than those permanent laborers in their seventies. And in the experience you told me about before, Chiko

himself said he had been running on this road for more than a hundred years. If the entire Ten Seats are like that… then the clock in the sky doesn’t care how young this body of yours looks. It only cares how long you, as the same continuous consciousness, have accumulated running in this world.”
She looked farther down.

“After the Ten Seats come all the permanent laborers stationed around the outskirts. We don’t know exactly how long each person has been running, but their order of falling… comes after the Ten Seats and before us.”
At 21:36, all the peripheral adults had fallen. This dense list of removals broke off abruptly.
I wrote the word “stopped” in my notebook. It marked a long blank lasting twelve minutes.
After the last batch of adult laborers fell, death seemed to suddenly stop harvesting. The entire village sank into a terrible silence. Only the heartless machines kept turning.
Only at 21:48, when the twelve-minute gap had passed, did the next batch finally come. The batch belonging to the young.
Her fingertip struck the blank space between them.
“Twelve minutes. Why is there such a wide break between all the permanent laborers around the outskirts and us younger people?”
“Two batches,” I said.

“If this were a naturally reproducing village, there should be a smooth line between generations. Even if it rose and fell, it would never break this cleanly,” she murmured. “The adults’ times of falling are tightly connected.

But between this batch of young people and them is a massive break. For these twelve minutes, it was as if this village had suddenly stopped having children for twelve years. There wasn’t a single person of this age.”
A gust of wind swept through, pressing a broad swath of golden wheat downward. As if startled awake by it, she grabbed her trembling arm.
“Not enough evidence. Come on. To the experimental zone. The village’s population structure didn’t grow naturally like this.”
Throughout that long twelve-minute gap, the young people did not fall.

Everyone in the village knew Kane had a daughter: Remi, who had been bedridden for years, the only person in the whole village who could not go anywhere. She was not on the list of peripheral adults, so she survived that concentrated harvest.

In one cycle, I carried a stool over and sat outside her window to keep her company.
I gave her a rough description of what was about to happen that night. I did not tell her the horrifying details about removal and death. I only said that

the adults would fall asleep and the village would become very quiet. She listened quietly. Talking to Remi was the easiest thing. Someone who had lain still for years had long ago woven all the village’s sounds into a vast map inside her mind.

“The rice jar at Meru’s house made noise again this morning,” she said with her eyes closed. “Chiko’s load was very heavy today. The carrying pole sounded hoarse. And your master was cursing the waterwheel again, but he stopped after the third verse—must be that the waterwheel started turning smoothly on its own.”
The pale-gray tips of her ears were the liveliest part of her entire body. At that moment they kept twitching, once, then again, precisely catching the faint sounds of the village.
“You listen to this every day. Don’t you find it boring?”

“What’s boring about it?” She gave a soft laugh. “You’re busy living your lives in the village, so you can’t hear everything. I lie here at the edge, but I can listen from morning to night. People who

lie still have too much time, so the things they think about easily become strange—Arno, from the way you describe those lights at night, tell me, where does that strange color of the daylight come from?”
I opened my mouth, but nothing came out. Even now, I still haven’t answered that question.

That night, when the first wave of daylight arrived on schedule, she lifted her head slightly and watched the tragic, dazzling afterglow outside the window, as if taking it for the opening of the long night I had described. She accepted it all calmly.
Then she began reporting to me through sound. The rustle of long robes in front of the chapel, the sound of a wrench falling in the mill… Every sound fit the death order I had
written on the paper exactly. That was why I had sat outside her window in that cycle: she was the only person in the village who could “see” every corner at once in the dark.

When every peripheral adult in the village was dead and that stretch of silence descended, her ears were still stubbornly raised. They turned deftly twice, but could no longer catch the sounds of the adults at work.

“The adults’ voices… they’re all gone.” She clutched the edge of the blanket, her voice trembling faintly, a trace of panic flashing in her eyes. “Arno, you said everyone had fallen asleep from being tired, didn’t you?”
“…Yeah.” My throat tightened. “That’s why there’s no sound.”

She bit her lip and forced out a reassuring smile. “That’s good, then. Everyone’s resting, so Dad won’t have to patrol the west gate today. It only takes him fifteen minutes to walk home from the forest road.”
With difficulty, she pulled the blanket higher and shifted her body, finding the most comfortable position she could. Her eyes remained fixed on the mouth of the village road outside.
“I’ll wait until he gets home before I sleep.”

The mouth of the forest road remained empty, without a single figure. She waited there patiently, her ears standing straight toward the road.
Kane had already been cut off in the adults’ list. But the distance was too great for the sound of his fall to reach her ears.

Throughout this silent gap, I sat outside her window and kept her company.
Until the twelve minutes ended, and the harvest finally crossed that invisible chasm.

At 21:48, fifteen-year-old Remi was the first among the young people to go dark.
Still unaware, she waited for her father to return from the forest road. Then she quietly closed the eyes that had remained fixed on the world outside.

From the arrival of the daylight, to the collapse of all the adults, to the young people losing consciousness one after another, an entire living village died before my eyes over that long span of time.

During the first few hundred cycles, I used all of that long span to record.
But there were three cycles when I did not record. In those three cycles, I ran as if I had gone mad.
The first thing that did not stop was the waterwheel.

Galen fell at the mill entrance, the heavy wrench dropping beside his hand. And the waterwheel kept turning. It knew nothing. Its turning depended only on the flow of water. It was simply a machine abandoned by the entire world, uselessly expending effort on something no one would ever need again.

In the first cycle, I ran desperately to pull the sluice.
Running at full speed took a minute and a half. I hauled the gate down with all my strength.
I knew that at exactly eight the next morning, when the reset woke, the gate would rise back up by itself. But that cycle, I still pulled it without hesitation.
The second things that did not stop were the kitchen fire and the lamp.

In the second cycle, I ran to Meru’s house. She had fallen only a short while earlier. The fire beneath the stove was still burning, and a pot of soup was boiling away without a care. Beside it, the half-worn oil lamp on the table was still burning quietly.

I lifted the pot and took it off the fire.
Afterward, I stared hard at the lamp, wanting to blow it out in a single breath. But I didn’t. A thought suddenly flashed
through my mind: when Meru lit it, she must have been planning to finish something by its light—the table still held half of a garment she had not finished sewing.

If I blew it out just like that, the thing she had been doing would not even be allowed to leave behind the regret of being “left unfinished.”
I left the lamp there.
The third cycle.

I heard that the door of one house had not been closed properly. A strong wind swept through and blew the half-shut door open and closed.
As long as the wind continued, it could make that sound endlessly throughout the night.

I walked over step by step and shut the door firmly.
The moment it closed, I heard myself make a sound:
“That's enough.”
That was what I did during those three cycles of running. At exactly eight the next morning, all of it would be void.
During that same cycle, I ran back to the chess stall.

The chess piece knocked loose when Old Barro fell had rolled a long way. I bent down, picked it up, and carefully placed it back on the board—in the third square from the left, the spot Old Nona stubbornly moved it back to every day.
As soon as I finished, I heard the children crying in the distance.

I pulled down the sluice, took the pot off the fire, shut the door, and put one chess piece back.
During the hundreds of long silences that followed, I did not run again. I simply stood in the endless darkness and kept them company.
Today, deep in the experimental zone, Yuna and I found two things of vital importance.

The first was in the production-line area. We pried open a maintenance panel caked with dust, wiped away the thick layer of grease in one corner, and found a separate rusted dial. Directly above it were carved two words in the ancient language:
“Reserve. Water level.”

Beside the dial was an embedded reading board, recording data that had remained steadily high for more than a hundred years. Until eight this morning. Beside that row of numbers, the system had stamped a single character in glaring red ink:
“Warning.”
“I once saw a balance on a gate in the cultivation chamber that read ‘available anonymous subject capacity’: zero. Was that referring to this too?”

“That zero meant there were no empty slots in the system for a first-person perspective. Even if it could still build bodies according to a template, they would only be shells without consciousness.” Yuna followed the thick pipes behind the dial with her eyes.

They extended underground throughout the experimental zone. “But this dial is different. It says ‘reserve water level.’ It sustains the operating connections of the existing subjects throughout the village. The number stayed steady for more than a hundred

years, then began falling at the same moment we started the cycle this morning. It isn’t the power of an all-knowing, all-powerful god. It’s only a power-supply indicator. When that indicator finally breaks through the red line tonight, the purge has to come.”

The second thing we found was in the dark machine room next door. It was a metal warning sign bolted firmly to the wall. We had passed it countless times before without ever looking closely.
Today, Yuna held up a flashlight and

illuminated the obscure ancient language. I recited the meanings of the old-language words stored in my memory. Comparing pronunciation and roots, she pieced them together into words we could understand, one character at a time:
“When the reserve… falls below the threshold—” Her finger moved slowly along the strokes. “The subject connections… will be severed in sequence according to accumulated wear.”

Yuna fell silent.
“Accumulated wear…” She glanced back at the equipment specifications beside the water-level dial. The diagram showed tiny energy losses in the brain during each data exchange.
“The ones who fell first were the people who exchanged data most frequently.” She turned

back toward the sign. “The Ten Seats have accumulated more than a hundred years of operating data. They wear down every cycle, so they broke down first. Then the adult laborers. This batch of young people has spent the least time running on this road, so we were placed last.”

Just as we were preparing to leave, Yuna happened to pull open a metal drawer beside the damaged plaque. Inside lay a stack of blueprints, all depicting human components. Not one name appeared anywhere.

Her hand stopped when she reached the one showing a skull.
It was more than a blueprint. Neatly stacked in the back of the drawer was a thick sheaf of production records. Above the bare outline of the

head were two cat ears. Two annotation lines extended from them, marked with precise measurements, with a parenthesis beside them: “Movable.”
Yuna pulled out the stack of production records. Every page

bore the standardized design for this batch. There were no individual names and no notes on parentage. But in the lower-right corner of the table, the “production batch” field bore a clear numerical code.

Yuna’s finger moved across the codes: C-001, C-002…
She turned the pages one by one. The final page in the stack was coded C-042.
There were forty-two young people in the village between the ages of fifteen and twenty-two, including her and me.

“It’s not only the number.” Yuna’s voice was taut as she pointed to the data field labeled “activation year.” “The activation year on all forty-two of these blueprints is the same.”
No naturally reproducing village could suddenly produce

forty-two children in perfect unison in a single year. These forty-two children had not been carried for ten months and born by anyone. They had been manufactured in batches, assigned age differences, and placed into this false world and village.

The calm she had maintained upon learning the purge order seemed to falter for a moment. She stared at the annotation line for the cat ears on the blueprint, then at the thick stack of standardized production records.

One of her hands rose unconsciously, her fingertip pausing in the air for half a second before finally not reaching toward the tips of her ears. Without a word, she put the records back and shoved the metal drawer shut.
“Let’s go.”

On the way back, she was silent the entire time, an extraordinary departure from her usual self. She only stopped when we passed the boundary stone and looked back deeply at the village beneath the dusk: a small patch of warm orange, like an innocuous plant someone had carefully tended on a windowsill.

When we reached the village, Yuna said she did not want to hide anymore.
“Let the clock strike as it will. We’ll live as we will.”
She found a place on the tall haystack and sat down casually, patting the empty spot beside her.
“I’ve heard everything you recorded. Today, I want to sit here and see it with my own eyes.”
The dull evening-prayer bell began to toll. The children’s clapping on the threshing floor scattered at once, and everyone went home.
The sky soon grew completely dark. It was clear, and all the stars were out.
The daylight arrived. The sky seemed saturated with light. The old fence and the blue-stone well platform all shone as if submerged in luminous water.
Yuna sat beside me, her head tilted high. She stared fixedly at the tragic, dazzling afterglow, silently checking the list with her lips.
“Time’s up. Not a second off.”
From the direction of the chess stall came the sound of the wooden bench falling, a very soft dull thud.
Like an examiner, she listened as the invisible voice in the sky read the list downward.

We could never reach dozens of people in that short concentrated period of removals to confirm their condition. But the map in Yuna’s mind was too precise. After the first four were cleared, the remaining people fell in a compressed stretch of time. We rushed

to the mill and confirmed three points; on the way back to the west gate, we made spot checks at four more. Every time we came racing through the night, the people who should have been at their posts or on their way home were already sprawled on the ground.

We staggered back to the threshing floor, and she collapsed onto the haystack as if drained of strength. Her palms were covered in cold sweat, her nails digging into my flesh, but she did not let go. Because every

point we checked during that frantic running, whether the person who had fallen or the time they had fallen, matched the record on the paper without the slightest discrepancy. There were no miracles and no deviations.

The final dull thud ended.
The entire village fell into deathly silence. The twelve-minute gap arrived.
“The adults have all been purged,” I reported softly.

Yuna turned her head. Her eyes were slightly red, and her voice was hoarse. “The first batch is over. My father was at the mill, my mother on the village road… They’ve both fallen by now. When we went to confirm, their faces were so peaceful.”

She looked at the night sky. “Next will be the younger people, with less wear. After I’m cut off… go find Milu. Pino is still out in the street. They have less wear, so they still have to endure the final seven minutes in this pitch-black place. Go keep them company.”
She extended her cold hand, solemnly placed the old wooden die seen everywhere in the village into my palm, and firmly folded my fingers closed one by one.
“I don’t know if something from this world can get through that door.” She stared into my eyes. “Take it to the next today. Let it see tomorrow for me.”
I did not pull away. I simply let her press the old wooden die into my palm.
“Okay.” I clenched it tight.
The light around us grew increasingly bright and piercing. She straightened her back and said nothing more, only turning her head slightly to give me one long look.

At 21:48, the twelve-minute gap ended—the moment Remi went dark on the other side of the village.
A few minutes later, at 21:53.
Yuna quietly closed her eyes in the daylight, and her body went slack. I touched the

side of her neck. It was still warm, but the person inside was already gone. Her heartbeat was so faint I could barely feel it, as if the system had forcibly pulled out a wire. She would not wake again that night.
The light drowned everything out. But I had no time to collapse. I clenched the wooden die in my palm and turned to run into the village.

On the long village road, fourteen-year-old Lise gripped her seven-year-old brother Pino by the shoulders, shielding him behind her. Her face was deathly pale, and her hands would not stop trembling. I ran over and took Lise’s hand, then bent down and picked up Pino. We ran together toward Meru’s house.

When I pushed open the door, twelve-year-old Milu was crouched alone beside the cold stove, trembling. She looked up at us in terror. Throughout those long final seven minutes, children their age, with their light wear, remained conscious in fear, waiting for the moment that would come, whenever it came.

I sat down beside her and tightened my grip on her hand.
Time passed second by second. Pino’s breathing was rapid, and Milu’s palm was covered in cold sweat. They were still conscious.
Looking at the frightened children beside me, the mechanism

of “accumulated wear” suddenly became an utterly absurd paradox in my mind: if this purge really ranked people according to their data exchanges in this world, what about me? I had lived through countless extra fourteen-hour stretches carrying

my memories. Across those cycles, I had constantly observed, remembered, collapsed, and reassembled myself. My volume of interaction should have surpassed anyone’s long ago.
I should have been at the very front of the list.
Yet I had not

only passed the Ten Seats and Remi; I was now sitting here, still conscious, keeping watch over these children who had not been severed. I had not been purged. When this system was settling its accounts, why had it skipped over me entirely?

Until 22:00. The mechanism that stripped away my perspective on schedule every night arrived as expected. This system completely ignored me when calculating wear, yet captured me precisely at the second of the loop reset. Everything before my eyes was cut off without warning, and I sank into absolute darkness.
The corridor. The electronic panel on the wall coldly reported the time: exactly eight.

As always, she leaned against the wall, deftly turning the metal fastener between her fingers from the outside inward. She was wearing yesterday’s clothes. Even the slight crease at her collar was in the same place.
“Arno?” She looked at me with confusion. “Why do you look so awful?”

I slowly unclenched my fist.
There was nothing inside.

Outer Third Settlement · Ration Registration (Watermarsh, Current Term):
“Households: forty-one. Population: one hundred sixty-three.
Issued: grain, distributed by batch number. Salt,

equal amounts per household. Medicine, upon the liaison officer’s signed slip.
New this term: one. (Number attached, under the mother’s batch.)
Decrease this term: two.
Recorder: Cole.”
“[08:00 loop starting point recorded. Cannot be changed].”

Yuna stared at the screen of the external coordination station, her ten fingers nearly leaving afterimages on the keyboard. In the two complete cycles that had just passed, we had tried everything we could think of—the first time, she

tried cutting the machine’s safety circuit to force a change to the loop’s starting point; the second time, we pushed the external equipment’s load to its limit, trying to crash into yesterday through the connection we had forced open.
But we failed. Again and again.
The tearing sensation of the neural connection combined with the sprained ankle I had suffered during last night’s escape—because it had happened before the eight o’clock starting point, the
injury was carried into every cycle as an established fact. The piercing pain left me covered in cold sweat, but all I could do was grit my teeth and charge once more at that invisible boundary.
A low rumble rolled through the underground levels of the White Tower. The screen flickered once, and a harsh red light crashed across our faces.
“[08:00 loop starting point recorded. Cannot be changed].”
The system’s response was like an absolute iron wall: yesterday inaccessible.
Only the cold operating noise of the main unit remained in the shutdown room. Yuna’s fingers hovered above the keyboard, trembling faintly, then slowly dropped.
Estelle died last night. Her death had been permanently sealed beyond the edge of time we could reach. At last, we had to admit that fact.

Since we couldn’t bring her back, at least we could send the truth she had traded her life for to Watermarsh. In the third cycle that followed, we abandoned the machine. The chill of dawn had not yet dispersed. Yuna and I crouched in the shadows, staring fixedly at the guards posted along the route to the boundary stones, committing to memory, with our hearts in our throats, the pattern by which they concentrated their personnel.
“Last night’s pursuit disrupted their deployment.” Yuna pieced the fragments together with her usual clarity. “When they pulled people back, the morning shift change left a new gap.”
“What time?”

“From eight forty to sometime after nine. Half an hour is enough.” Yuna watched the guards in the distance. “It’s a three-hour journey through mud. If we get past the boundary stones before nine, we can reach Watermarsh by noon.”
That morning, I forced myself through the piercing pain in my ankle and reached the boundary stones at eight forty-seven, limping through the mud.

The gap created by the patrol route had not yet been filled by the people changing shifts. All we had to do was step over this waist-high boundary stone, and the old river channel ran north from there.
But we couldn’t step over it.
Because on the other side of the boundary stone, two people were already standing in the outskirts’ muddy ground. They were looking toward the central village.
One was a woman in her thirties, her hair tightly wrapped in a gray-blue cloth. She held a thick ledger and a pen worn bare of paint.
The other was an old woman in a patched apron. Both her hands were wet, a layer of pale wrinkles raised across the backs of them, her knuckles
thickened—the marks left by years of soaking in cold water while doing hard work. She clutched an old coat washed pale with use, much too large for her.
They had clearly been waiting there for a long time.
When she saw us approaching, the woman in her thirties spoke first.
“You’re from the central village.” She looked over our wrists, which bore no batch marks.
“Yes,” Yuna said.
“The candidate process was supposed to take seven days. It’s overdue. Where is she?”
Yuna’s eyes fell on the ledger in Cole’s hands. As Cole shifted it to her other hand, it opened slightly, revealing the line at the top: “New this term: one… Decrease this term: two.”
“Besides the person who went to take part in the candidate process,” Yuna stared at the line, “did you record the cause of death for the ‘decrease two’ simply erased from this ledger?”
Cole pressed her lips together and shifted the heavy ledger to her other hand. Her expression immediately turned wary.
“That’s yesterday’s account. You two came from over there. If you want to check the ledger, go ask the people above yourselves.” Her gaze was appraising.
Yuna avoided the direct clash and lowered her voice, throwing out a probe.

“The people in the central village are always the same people.” Yuna held her gaze. “Living people from the outskirts disappear straight from the accounts, and you haven’t even seen their bodies. You only dare write ‘decrease two’?”

Cole did not contradict her. The backs of her hands were covered in dark-red cuts from heavy carrying straps, old and new wounds overlapping. Faced with Yuna’s inference, she only gripped the spine of the ledger tightly and said nothing.
Cole spread the thick ledger across the boundary stone and opened it to the page for population anomalies.
“If you want to investigate, open a case under your own heads. Your names. I’m going to fill in the names of the two people who vanished into thin air.”
“Arno. Yuna.” I gave our names. Yuna continued, “No. 43, Ilvis. No. 44, Mia. Those are the first two lines on the sheet from last night.”
“We don’t have batch numbers.” Yuna pulled the sheet of rough paper recording the old files from her pocket. “Use this to verify the names and dates of those two people.”
Cole’s pen stopped.
“This isn’t an official document. No documents, no guarantor. I can’t register it.”

“The files of the people we’re investigating were personally withheld by Kane, one of your ten seats!” A trace of impatience entered Yuna’s voice. “This is the underlying list we reconstructed from memory!”
After a moment of deadlock, Cole sighed. She took the pen and entered “missing” in the column for those two people’s whereabouts. Then, in the blank space where our batch numbers should have
been, she drew a long, heavy diagonal line, sealing off the empty space. Finally, crossing over the column heading, she forced in an additional note: “Oral account, no documents, no guarantor.”

“I’ll take responsibility for you this once. By regulation, a population anomaly report must include the reporting party’s batch number. This ledger and the whole village’s rations are bound together. Leave one field blank, and the entire ledger will be sent back when it’s submitted.

Then the rations stop.” She set down the pen with what sounded like relief and looked at the glaring diagonal line. “She and I came out into the dark at night, stumbling through three hours of mud. We came to wait for Estelle. I can’t destroy the food in everyone’s mouths along with it.”
She closed the ledger.
“The next trading party comes in three days. Chico will come to deliver the rations. I’ll hand him the ledger.”
Yuna’s face went white.
“The ledger goes to him too?”
“Yes. He handles the entire outskirts.”

We had thought that writing an entry in the ledger belonging to our own people on the outskirts would let us leave the names we had brought out, and Estelle’s trail, in Watermarsh. We had not expected Watermarsh’s only

channel for appealing upward, and its only exit for verifying records, to be held in the hands of the ten seats. We had to hand the crime of the mechanism itself over to the people who enforced that mechanism for verification.
“Can’t you bypass Chico and report it directly to the people above?” I heard the tightness in my own voice.
“No,” Cole said, flat and hard. “Going above the proper level means going out of order.”

That explained why Estelle had been willing to risk her life to bring out that evidence. She knew too well that without hard currency capable of breaking out of this cycle, Watermarsh as a whole was locked down inside the bureaucratic system. The system was a

net with no gaps. More suffocating still—if we wanted to change anything through the records, there was no “three days later” for us. When ten o’clock came tonight, the diagonal line just drawn and the ink on the paper would all be erased cleanly in the daylight.
Cole stepped back half a pace. The old woman who had been standing behind her came forward.
She looked at me over the waist-high boundary stone, a trace of humble hope in her eyes. The old coat washed pale with use trembled faintly in the morning wind.
“You’ve… seen her?” the old woman asked hoarsely.

I looked at the oversized old coat. All I really had to do was say one sentence. Estelle died on the slope last night. Those faint sounds severed her nerves, without leaving even a mark, leaving her lying in the cold gravel and mud.
But it felt as though something had seized my throat. The way the old coat trembled in the wind forced the truth I had turned over on the tip of my tongue countless
times back down my throat. I knew everything would reset tonight, but on this morning destined to be erased, as long as I said nothing, the coat still had a living owner.
I clenched my back teeth hard and said nothing.
The old woman looked steadily at me for three seconds.
She did not press me. She only gripped the old coat in her hands more tightly, until her knuckles went white.
“If you happen to see her,” she said, her voice trembling almost as if she were begging, “tell her everything is fine at home. Don’t say anything else.”
“Okay.” My fingernails dug into my palms.
“She’s stubborn,” the old woman said. “If you tell her something, she’ll keep asking three times before she believes it. Just say everything is fine at home. Remember—say it three times.”
“Okay.”
They asked nothing more. Cole supported the old woman by the arm, and the two of them turned toward the road they had come by.

It was an old river channel that had long since ceased to be navigable, wild reeds growing thickly along both sides. Broken asphalt shards and discarded pipelines rose from beneath the mud like the dead bones of some enormous beast. They gradually grew distant, becoming two small black specks in the muddy ground.
All we had to do was cross this boundary stone and follow the old river channel. Watermarsh was within walking distance.
“Shall we go?” Yuna looked at the muddy road.
I stood up and moved my aching ankle a little. Since Chico had blocked the path of a public appeal, we could investigate on our own.
“Let’s go in, find out what happened to those two names, and look for evidence,” I said.
But Yuna did not move. Her gaze passed over the boundary stone and fixed on the depths of the reed marsh.

“Even Cole, who manages Watermarsh’s master ledger, only dares write a cold ‘decrease two’ in the book.” Yuna looked at me calmly. “Do you think the villagers below will know where the missing people went?”
I stood there, stunned.

“The outskirts have no leverage we need. They’re only the end where people are pulled out alive.” Yuna’s voice was soft, but utterly clear. “If we walk into Watermarsh, all we’ll ultimately be able to take away is the tears of Ilvis’s and Mia’s

families. Even if the villagers know who took them and at which crossroads, as long as we can’t produce the mechanism by which the central village turns living people into numbers, one ‘natural attrition’ from Chico will overturn everything.”

We sat shoulder to shoulder on a patch of dry mud at the edge of the boundary stone. In the silence, there was only the sound of wind passing through the wheat fields. With our backs to the distant rumble of the central village, we watched the muddy road we had originally intended to follow.
Watermarsh was only three hours away.

But Yuna was right. In this cage built from barriers of information, searching for victims in the outskirts could not reveal the mechanism by which the ten seats concealed the truth. The machine that turned living people into numbers did not have its operating hub in Watermarsh’s muddy ground, but inside the high walls behind us.

The road to Watermarsh was not sealed off, but for now it could not give us the leverage to cross the cycle. The answers pointed to by Ilvis, Mia, and the clues Estelle had traded her life for would have to be filled in sooner or later. The answers we were looking for could only be found in the most dangerous place of all—the center.

Outer Third Settlement · Ration Registration (Watermarsh, Current Term) · Last Line of the Day:
“Two visitors, unresolved. Reason: oral statement, no documents, no guarantor.
　Recorder: Colai.”

At the end of the previous cycle, we stopped in front of the boundary stone without stepping over it. We had already understood that walking across on two legs alone would not carry the deadlock in the ledger away, nor save anyone.
But this cycle, we crossed the boundary stone anyway.

During those three hours of trudging through the mud, I told this cycle’s Yuna everything that had happened after our shared starting point: how the central village fell in sequence beneath the yellow light, and the timetable of the Harvest.
When I finished,

she asked only one question. “How many times has this been?”
I did not answer. She did not ask again. She only quickened her pace in silence. To her, how many times we had died no longer mattered. Only the impasse ahead, about to be confirmed, remained.

I dragged along my right ankle, which was always swollen and aching after each reset, and reached the outer settlement called Watermarsh that afternoon. Without any identity documents, we were questioned for a long time at the distribution station, and in the end we were still turned away at the door.

We had already been sitting beside the main road for a long time—long enough for the shadow of the earthen wall beside our feet to lengthen bit by bit and completely cover the patch of bare ground where we sat.

I took off the shoe on my left foot and emptied it out hard. A few clods of hardened dirt fell out—the dirt that had packed in when we waded across the riverbed that morning, grinding against my foot for half the day. Yuna sat beside me

with her head lowered, using her fingernail to pick at the dried yellow mud caught in the heel of her shoe. The mud was wedged into the gap. She picked at it for a long time without loosening it, and only left a red mark around her finger.

The sun slowly sank. People began passing along the main road at regular intervals. Someone carried half a bucket of sloshing water on a pole. Someone drove two scrawny sheep along, their hooves making fine, scattered sounds on the dirt road. A child ran

past us, then stopped after a few steps and came back two paces, squatting not far away and staring fixedly at us. There was no curiosity in his eyes, only the blankness of someone looking at two unfamiliar stones. After a while, he stood up and ran away.
“We have to go.”
Yuna did not move. She was still struggling with the mud in her shoe heel.
“It’ll be dark by the time we walk back. The road won’t be easy.”
“Yeah.”
“Then let’s go.” I braced myself against the earthen wall and slowly stood. My right foot hurt too much to put any weight on, so I stood on my left and patted the dirt from my trousers.
“Don’t.” She stopped what she was doing. Her voice was quiet, but left no room for negotiation.
I sat back down along the wall, rubbing my sore, nearly numb right ankle, and looked at her.
She had both arms wrapped tightly around her knees, her chin resting on them. Her eyes passed over me and fixed on the end of the main road stretching toward the central village.
“Going back means waiting, too.” She did not look away. Her voice seemed to drift over from very far away. “If we wait here, at least we can see one thing clearly.”
“What thing?”
Only then did she slowly turn her head toward me. The sharpness she usually had when analyzing a problem was gone from her eyes. Nothing remained but a tired calm.
“How the Harvest descends here,” she said.
I understood.
In the dozens of resets before this, whenever we explored outward, we went to the uninhabited ruins in the north. Their silence concealed the details of the Harvest’s arrival.
There were never enough people to serve as a point of comparison, so we could not confirm whether the world outside went dark in exactly the same sequence as the central

village.
In the dozens of other cycles, we either became stranded halfway there, or instinctively hurried back as the sky neared darkness, wanting to return to the people we knew.
Today, with three hours of muddy road between us and the village, there was no way I could make it back on this foot.
That left only one thing to do—sit beside Watermarsh’s main road and see clearly whether the sequence that descended upon the central village covered the entire periphery without distinction.
I followed her gaze. The people on the main road were still busy with dinner and tomorrow’s livelihood.

“We’re just going to sit here and watch?” I looked at the unguarded people on the main road. “What if I ran into the street now? Even if I could convince just one or two families, at least I could get them to put their children somewhere safe before they fell?”
“What would you use to convince them?” Yuna did not turn around. “Go shout at a place that has never experienced the whole village falling at once that the sky will turn yellow and they’ll
lose consciousness in two hours? Because you’re an outsider without even a guarantor? The moment you rush over shouting, Colai will lock you in the storage room at the distribution station.”
“I could tell Colai first.” I pressed the question unwillingly. “Just tell her something abnormal is going to happen. Have her get people to put out the cooking fires, cover the wells,
and prepare water. We don’t have to explain why. We can just say there’s danger—at least don’t let these children watch the adults fall into the fire or down a well with no warning at all!”
Only then did Yuna turn her head.

“If Colai really believed you and rang the alarm, Arno, have you thought about what would happen next?”
She turned away again and rested her chin on her knees.
“You’d be telling a group of parents in the middle of their work that

some unknown disaster was coming and they had to prepare. No one would know what it was. No one would know how to escape. You’d have them put out the fires, shut the doors tight, and sit inside with their children… waiting to die?”

I braced myself against the wall and tried to stand. A stabbing pain shot through my right ankle. I looked toward the main road, at the adults carrying water and the children running around beside the sheep.

That was right. If I gave no details and only shouted for them to put out the fires and cover the wells, panic would spread through suspicion. If I told them the truth, told them there was no way to hide from it, what would those desperate parents do with the time they had left? The children might find not safe houses, but chaos spiraling out of control.

I clenched my fists until my knuckles went white. Pain climbed along the nerves in my foot, twisting together with the helplessness in my chest. In the end, I slowly released my hands and leaned back against the earthen wall.
Yuna did not continue. The noise from the main road went on.
Colai came out of the dilapidated registration station once more.

By then the setting sun had pressed down onto the low rooftops at the end of the main road, stretching her shadow long. She carried two coarse porcelain bowls with chipped rims. When she came to where we were sitting, she said nothing. She simply crouched down and placed the bowls steadily on the muddy ground between us.
The bowls held some kind of boiled root, steaming hot. In the cool evening, the steam stood out sharply.
