“Registration is registration.” She looked down at the two bowls, her voice as stiff as it had been when she questioned us that afternoon.
After saying that one sentence, she pushed herself up by her knees, dusted the dirt from her coarse-cloth skirt, and turned back. After a few steps, she stopped without turning around.
“You won’t be going back today.” Her voice spread across the empty main road.
“We won’t.” I answered along with her words, without explanation.
“Then don’t sit on the main road.” She turned around. The official hardness in her voice softened slightly. “The wind is strong there at night. There’s no shelter.”
She raised her hand and pointed to a side road a few dozen paces away.
“The second side road. It’s sheltered by the wall over there. Go stay there.”
Then she left, her back quickly disappearing into the dim doorway of the distribution station.

Watching that back disappear into the doorway, I suddenly felt some regret. Perhaps I should have tried to tell her just then—even if it meant making another attempt by appealing to the kindness behind these two bowls of hot

food. Tell her to at least keep an eye on those few hearths. But the sky had already gone completely dark, and the people taking the next shift were clearing away the distribution station’s wooden shelter. The chance had passed.
We picked up the bowls. The sides were hot, warming our stiff fingers. It was root vegetable with no seasoning, very soft and mealy when chewed, with only the faint saltiness of coarse salt.

Yuna ate quickly, almost wolfing it down, ignoring the heat burning her mouth. When she finished, she set the empty bowl down hard and casually wiped the corner of her mouth with the back of her hand.
“She gave us food.” She stared at the empty bowl, as if speaking to herself.
“Yeah.”
“She doesn’t believe what we told her. She thinks we’re strangers of unknown origin, but she still gave us food.” There was an indescribable confusion in her voice.
She stacked the two bowls together and carefully set them on a flat stone by the road, moving as lightly as if afraid of disturbing something.
As Colai had told us, we moved beneath the wall at the entrance to the second side road. It was a waist-high earthen wall, blocking the cold wind blowing down the main road.

It was a slightly recessed corner sheltered from the wind. I sat with my back against the wall and looked into the side road. From there, I could just see the gate to one household’s courtyard. It was the home of the old woman we had met beside the Watermarsh boundary stone in the previous cycle. Back then, through the boundary stone, she had asked me to carry a message to Estelle in the central village.
The gate was closed. The thin hemp cord stretched across the courtyard was still there, the clothes hanging from it shifting gently in the wind. They had not been taken down.
The sky began to darken, as though a sheet of gray cloth were slowly being drawn over it. In that gloom, I saw the gate creak open.

The old woman came out, her steps somewhat slow. She walked to the clothesline in the middle of the courtyard and began taking down the clothes one by one. She moved very slowly, almost ceremonially, pulling each item down, shaking the dust from it hard, then laying it neatly over her forearm.
It was Estelle’s old jacket, the one she had left at home. It was the last garment on the line.
When she took it down, her movement paused. She gently ran her rough fingers over the fabric twice.

Then she stood in the middle of the empty courtyard with the thick stack of clothes in her arms, not hurrying inside. She raised her head and looked once over the low courtyard wall toward the end of the main road.
She was looking in the direction extending from the central village.
She watched for about two seconds. Her eyes were hollow, holding nothing. Then she turned and walked through the doorway.
The gate did not close all the way. After she pulled it shut, a finger-width gap remained between it and the frame.
“Arno, what did it feel like before the people in the central village died?”
I drew a deep breath of cold air. The heavy suffocation in my chest, as if even breathing were being crushed, was spreading.
The sky had darkened to that oppressive point—all the outlines were beginning to blur, and soon everything would be swallowed by blackness. It was 20:36, the threshold before the Harvest arrived.
“It feels like this. Like I can’t catch my breath.” My throat tightened. “It’s almost here.”
Without warning, the light appeared.

It was the same pale yellow as the light I had seen countless times before in the village. There was no sun, no source of light. The sky was like a huge, luminous hemisphere turned upside down. It did not spread from east to west, and there

was no transition through the clouds. One second Watermarsh was in the dimness of evening; the next, that suffocating yellow light had seeped through every gap along the horizon, illuminating the entire open ground with merciless brightness.
In the village, whenever that light appeared, I had always frantically searched for somewhere to hide, or run toward someone who was about to fall.
But Watermarsh was unfamiliar ground. I could see the people on the main road reacting clearly.

When the strange light appeared, there were more than twenty people on the main road. Some had just finished work and were carrying farming tools home. Others stood at their doors with bowls in their hands, talking. When the pale yellow light descended over them, all their movements stopped.

They were stunned, as though they had sensed something extraordinarily strange and beyond their understanding taking place. Some looked up at the sky in confusion. Some tentatively called their neighbors’ names. One woman had just set down a bundle of firewood when she turned in alarm to pull in the child outside the door.

On the main road, the middle-aged man carrying water on a shoulder pole in my field of vision suddenly buckled at the knees and crashed into the mud with his buckets. One bucket tipped over, and clear water spread instantly across the yellow earth.
He was the first.
I knew that was not the end. These twenty-odd people were only the sample that happened to be on the main road. The real Harvest was cutting through the years of every living person at once.
I whipped around, dragged my leg forward, and stumbled to the half-closed wooden door beside me. I pushed it open.

The old woman stood in the middle of the courtyard. At some point she had come out of the house again. The stack of clothes was gone. She held only the old jacket in her hands. She stood quietly in the pale yellow open ground, her head slightly raised as she looked at the incomprehensible sky.

Hearing the wooden door turn, she turned her head and looked at me. Yuna and I had been crouched beneath the wall for the entire evening. She had clearly seen us over the waist-high courtyard wall long ago.
“You haven’t left yet,” she said softly. Her tone was as flat as if she were casually exchanging a word with strangers who had stopped by to shelter from the wind.
After saying that, her legs suddenly gave way. She slowly slid down along the earthen wall behind her.
She sat very straight, her back against the rough wall. Her head slowly, helplessly tilted to one side.
The old jacket slipped from her loosened hands onto the dust-covered ground.
As she fell, her body knocked over a half-waist-high stack of clay basins beside her. The basins shattered on the ground with a crisp sound.
A girl a little over ten peeked through the gap in the door. She saw the pottery shards on the ground, then the old woman fallen against the wall.

“Grandma?” the girl called softly. She took two steps forward, grabbed the old woman’s sleeve, and shook it. The old woman did not move. The girl froze. She did not cry. She only stood there blankly, still clutching a piece of hard bread with a corner missing.

I walked over and bent down to pick up the old jacket. Held in my hands, it still seemed to carry a little of the warmth of the living. I went to the courtyard wall and laid it back over the earthen wall.
The girl turned and looked at me. There was a numb terror in her eyes beyond her years.
I released the hand pressed against the earthen wall, turned, and slowly walked over to her. Enduring the stabbing pain in my ankle, I knelt on one knee beside the pile of broken pottery.

I did not touch her. I only met her eyes and stayed quietly beside her. After watching me for a while, the girl’s tense shoulders slowly collapsed. She said nothing. She only shifted half a step toward the direction where the old woman had fallen, still clutching the piece of hard bread tightly in her hand.
I stayed crouched with her in the courtyard.

Outside the courtyard, the Harvest continued along the main road. The child who had been chasing the sheep suddenly stopped, because a young man running ahead of him silently pitched forward into the dead grass.

Colai was hurrying out of the distribution station, having noticed the disturbance outside. She reached the doorway, the registration ledger clenched tightly in her hand, and looked up at the ghastly yellow sky.
Then her arm suddenly lost its strength.

The ledger fell to the ground with a smack. The wind blew through, riffling several pages with a rustle, until it finally lay open to the page filled with writing. She collapsed immediately afterward.
As the adults on the main road began falling one after another, Yuna continued staring fixedly at the road.
“Did you see that?” Her voice was very low, with a trace of trembling sharpness.

“Yeah.” I looked at the adults fallen along the main road and the children standing there blankly. “It’s the same as in the village. We don’t know how long they’ve lived here, but there aren’t any children among those who fell. The first ones down don’t look young.”

“It’s more than that. Look at the skyline over there. When the yellow light came on just now, the direction of the central village didn’t light up first.” She raised her head, the pale yellow light reflected in her eyes.
Time dragged on second by second in the pale yellow glow. As more and more people fell along the main road, every dull impact of a body hitting the ground struck the nerves like a blunt hammer.
When no standing adults remained anywhere on the main road except the bewildered children, one of Yuna’s hands gripped the mottled doorframe. Her fingers tightened slightly, the bones turning white.
“Arno.” Her voice was as hollow as the ghastly sky.
“Yeah.”
“Write this down.” She spoke in a commanding tone.
“Go on. I’m listening.”

“If it were a wave pushed outward from the central village, the sky should turn yellow bit by bit from south to north.” She paused, raising her head to look at the upside-down luminous hemisphere. Breathing grew heavy. The suffocation closing in on us seized both of us at once.
“But the light here is coming through the gaps in every direction at once. There’s no source, no order of arrival.”

She turned to look at me, her pale face almost transparent beneath the strange light. “Watermarsh was hit at the same time, too. This isn’t a disaster spreading here. It’s more like the whole sky being switched on at once. Run as far as you want—so long as you’re still beneath this sky, it makes no difference.”
Her body suddenly lost control before my eyes. Just like the old woman beside the courtyard wall, she slid down along the doorframe, her back against the wood, her head tilting to one side.
I reached out and caught her.

I gently supported her head and straightened it, letting her rest steadily against the doorframe. I took her hands, folded over her knees, and placed them properly at either side of her body. I made her look as though she were merely asleep.
When it was done, a wave of exhaustion passed through me. I braced myself upright and dragged my swollen, aching right foot toward the girl in the courtyard.
The noisy settlement of Watermarsh gradually fell silent.

On the main road, a sheep someone had been leading stopped and lowered its head to nibble at the dead grass. A piece of firewood someone had been carrying rolled to the side of the road when it fell. Of those

who had not yet fallen, some stared blankly at the adults who had collapsed beside them, like the girl in the courtyard. Others crouched on the ground, futilely pushing at bodies that would never wake again.
The sky remained terrifyingly bright. Nothing on the ground cast a shadow.
I remembered the morning of the previous cycle, beside the boundary stone, when the old woman had asked me to carry a message to Estelle.

I knelt beside the girl, looking at the old jacket fluttering in the wind atop the wall, then at the child still clutching the old woman’s sleeve before me. My lips moved. I said the message three times in a low voice to the silent courtyard.

“Everyone at home is well.”
“Everyone at home is well.”
“Everyone at home is well.”

I crouched in the cold courtyard. Beside the pile of broken pottery, the girl was still clutching the piece of hard bread with the missing corner. I reached out to move a sharp fragment away from her, but the moment my hand extended, my fingers lost their feeling.

Outside the wall, the main road carried the rustle of a sheep eating grass and someone’s belated scream. The sound washed over us and drowned out my voice. As the final wave of helplessness came over me, my consciousness sank into darkness.
texts.chapter:chapter-07-white-room:title: Chapter Seven: The Pure White Room
texts.chapter:chapter-07-white-room:event:text:
Fragment of the execution protocol (page three, upper edge burned away, kept beneath the console corridor tabletop):
……Article Three: Binding is completed on the frame in the binding room. An outside technician confirms calibration; the carrier is placed awaiting connection. From this point until it is forced into the execution chamber, no changes may be

made inside the room.
Article Four: The condemned enters the execution chamber. The outside executioner confirms that the door is locked and establishes the execution starting point in the console corridor. There is no starting-point control inside the room.
Article Five: Switching parameters are copied from the court-approved document. After waiting five

seconds, the outside executioner submits the final execution command.
Article Six: After the pulse, the outdoor instruments report brain death and shut down.
Article Seven: After execution is complete, there is no time limit for collecting the body inside the room.
(Another hand appears in the footer, the characters very small, the strokes pressed deeply:
Outside, there are only five seconds. Inside, there is no fifth second.)
That iron cage was properly hung back on the cable every morning.

The iron-gray cage door stood half open. A thin layer of dust covered the bottom, with old footprints left by someone unknown pressed into its surface. The heavy steel cable was intact, without a single sign of

having snapped. I had passed this shaft many times. Every time, it waited there for me in that same silent, certain state. It was like a question that had already been asked once, patiently waiting to ask again.
Before the dead end it offered, there was actually another way out. On the surface, it cost nothing at all.

It was one day after I had become utterly exhausted by rifles and falling. That afternoon, I kept far away from the crowds and went alone to lie down deep in the wheat field. I lay there, listening as the village sounds slowly peeled away and fell silent. It was not that

some violent energy had destroyed matter. Everything was still there. It was only that, before the daylight had faded, my first-person consciousness began sinking into drowsiness. The entire world was reduced to that source-less dead white filling every direction, and myself.
I was exhausted beyond measure and closed my eyes.

In the darkness that appeared after I closed my eyes, something suddenly emerged at the very center. It was not something seen with the naked eye—I had my eyes closed; there was no light from the outside at all—but the thing was truly there. It was gray and square, like a button floating in empty space.

Around the square were only a few faintly glowing scale marks indicating the world I was currently in. There were words on the button. I did not even need to read them; the meaning of those four characters was printed directly into my mind: End This Iteration.
I pressed it. Not with my hand. It was an instinctive motion that required no learning—once the thought of “pressing down” arose in my mind, it was triggered.
The depths of my vision suddenly went black. Before the irreversible doom at twenty-two hundred hours arrived, I released my observation of that world first.

I opened my eyes, and it was eight in the morning again. I was standing deep in the lower levels of the White Tower, in the corridor outside that control hall, familiar artificial cold light falling across my face. In that instant, the breeze in the wheat field, the daytime

warmth, and that still-unfinished world were all forcibly severed. I had returned to the beginning of another complete world. From then on, the End This Iteration button remained there. I could sense it if I closed my eyes and thought deeply, but I never touched it again.
As for the falling cage in the shaft, I never set foot inside it again. To reach the pure white room, I did not take the main control passage in front. Instead, I chose
a concealed maintenance duct below—the kind that could only be entered by sliding in one direction, and that consumed several hours. At its end was that pure white room.

When we met at the edge of the wheat field that morning, I had already accumulated all the information. At first there had only been names, membrane, and nameplates. Now there were also the structure of

the reserve storehouse, blueprints, peripheral records, the deductions she herself had made before dying in the previous iteration, and my experience of closing my eyes in the wheat field and forcibly

escaping by pressing the gray End This Iteration button. I told her everything without holding anything back. She listened to all of it, then stood at the edge of the wheat field and thought for a long time.
Then she turned her head, looked at me, and said:
“ The room at the very bottom. The one where I died.”
Her tone was as ordinary as if she were talking about a farm tool she had lent out and not yet gotten back.

“You said the procedural archive was there. It says, ‘Return to a few seconds earlier. Successful every time.’ That doesn’t match what happened to you—you didn’t return a few seconds; you returned an entire day. One record that doesn’t match is a loose thread. Today, we pull it out.”
“The path is long.”
“Once we go down, we won’t be able to climb back up. The twenty-two-hundred boundary will catch up with us below.”
“Perfect.” She dusted off the hem of her clothes and said it without hesitation. “Saves us the trouble of running.”

We went down by different routes. I had to get past layer upon layer of security checks before entering a concealed maintenance duct below. That route could only be entered by sliding in one direction, and it consumed several hours. Yuna, meanwhile, used her authorization to enter directly from the main passage on the other side.
When she reached the blast-glass corridor, I had just crawled into the ventilation section above it. Through the louvered grille in the duct wall, I watched her standing below in the passage.
“This place is interesting.”
She extended a finger, pointing at the structures at both ends of the glass corridor as she stared at them.
“The patterns are reversed. You need two people, one on each side, to get through.”
I said, “Yeah. Last time, we turned four times and it opened.”

She tilted her head and glanced toward the grille overhead. She did not ask, “Which last time?” As the information accumulated and grew enormous, she asked less and less about details like that. She only raised her hand and

pressed her palm against the thick glass. The gesture was astonishingly light, as if she were greeting the road of death she did not remember at all. Then she withdrew her hand and continued silently toward the console corridor.
The fork deep below was still the same fork.

Her door recognized her; it unlocked as soon as she approached the old executioner passage. As for me, I could only slip through the dim maintenance duct below and slide into the white room containing nothing but air. This was true on every today, in every iteration, as stubbornly as the boundary stone that always stood at the village entrance.
Now we exchanged our progress through the communicators.
“Just like that day,” she said softly.
She had heard every detail of what had happened here that night. Now she was matching the fragments of language in her mind against the physical objects before her, one by one.
“You go into the white room. I go into the corridor with the console.”
“This time, don’t press anything.”
I stared into the darkness ahead and put weight on each word. “Just look. When we’re done, we’ll sit here and wait for the end.”
“Yeah.”
She answered, but then the communicator fell silent for a moment.
“Hey.”
“What?”
“The me from that day,” she asked, tilting her head slightly, her voice carried through the static. “What was she like before she went in?”
I thought for a moment.
“You held out your hand.”
“We slapped palms and hooked little fingers. You said: Arno. Whatever happens, we have to get back.”
There was only the faint sound of her breathing on the other end of the communicator. After a while, she answered.
“Sounds like something I’d do.” She gave a small laugh.

I could imagine her standing before the door, extending her hand and pressing it lightly against the air.
I tapped twice on the cold pipe wall of the narrow duct with the back of my hand, as my reply.
Then I slid down from the mouth of the duct and dropped into the white room.
The furnishings in the white room were exactly as I remembered them.
It was a perfect cube, seven steps from end to end. The four walls, ceiling, and floor were pure white. There were no seams, no blind corners where shadows could gather. Apart from the enormous
one-way shaft opening three meters above and the maintenance duct opening with its iron grille along the ceiling edge—the one I had just slid down through—the room had no other exit and no
door handle. The condemned from that time had evidently been brought in through some heavy mechanism or sealed capsule, but that entrance was now completely locked shut, seamless and whole.

The only thing breaking the dead white on the right was a broad blast-resistant window perfectly flush with the wall. On the other side, Yuna was walking toward me along the far end of the console corridor.
I stood in the center of the white room, watching her through the glass as she walked toward the metal console covered in instruments. Exactly as it had happened
that night, the moment her left wrist approached, it was forcibly clamped into a metal ring. Several slender probes sprang out and bit deep into her skin.
She frowned slightly, pressed the communications grille, and her voice came from the speaker: “Authorization verified. I can’t pull free, but I can operate it one-handed. Can you hear me?” I nodded.
Yuna could only lower her head in front of the console, comparing the instrument panel.
“You told me that the first time, before all these loops began—” Her voice was steady. “The Arno who only remembered our seven days of investigating together, and the original me, pressed
confirmation in the binding hall above at seven fifty. Ten minutes later, at exactly eight, the delay ended, and the system officially entered the state of waiting for the final command.”

Then she shifted her gaze to the edge of the panel, where a discreet ring of yellow lights was glowing. Finally, her eyes paused briefly on the emergency stop button, its cast-iron casing clamped shut with an iron latch, then passed over it and fell on the red execution button beneath its transparent cover.
“The ring of yellow lights is still on today. The machine is still waiting for the final command. At nearly twenty-two hundred that night, the original me pressed it here.” She looked at the
red button. “But pressing the red button only submitted an end time to the system. The true start happened at eight that morning, when the machine established that sole cross-world session.”
She looked at the faint light on the console.

“Since you can wake up at eight every time, that means this machine connected the parallel, existing worlds together. The first activation didn’t just establish one local connection. This sole ‘root session’ crossed, at the

physical level, all the worlds connected to this event. So today, whether we are in this room or not, whether anyone presses that red button again or not, as soon as eight in the morning arrives, this enormous gap spanning

multiple routes will open on schedule. Even if we do nothing here, the yellow lights on the console will still come on, because the system is only blindly maintaining that cross-world connection that took effect long ago.”
Her right hand hovered above the red button.
“And then there’s Article Five: ‘After waiting five seconds, the outside executioner submits the final execution command.’” She lowered her eyes. “Originally, it was only a matter of five seconds.”

Once this was confirmed, she moved her hand away. With the only hand she could move, she pulled several slightly yellowed sheets of paper from the shallow drawer beneath the console, within reach of one hand.
“You’ve looked for this before?” I asked through the window. Her movement had been too certain.

She did not answer. Her eyes were lowered, fixed on the words as she read. Through the glass, I could only watch her ears slowly flatten from their alert upright position, finally drooping helplessly backward and down.
When she finished the page, she turned the sheets around and pressed them against the glass for me to see, while reciting the words through the grille.

“The condemned enters the execution chamber,” she read word by word. “The outside executioner confirms that the door is locked and establishes the execution starting point in the console corridor. There is no starting-point control inside the room.”
I stood frozen in the place of this so-called “condemned,” listening as she stood in the place of the “executioner” and finished reading the cold protocol.
“The place where you’re standing is the execution ground.”
She lowered the pages.
“The place where I’m standing is where the execution happens.”
The two of us stared at each other through that transparent window. For a while, neither of us said anything more.

I stood in that suffocating pure white, head lowered, mechanically counting my steps. Seven steps forward until I hit the wall; I turned and took seven steps back until I hit the wall again. I made three full round trips before suddenly realizing that I kept pacing because I was afraid to raise my head.
The moment I looked up, I would see Yuna on the other side of the glass.
“Arno.”
Her voice pierced the dead silence of the white room. I had no choice but to look up.
She stood behind the console, her body constrained by the metal ring around her left wrist. The glass between us was impossibly clean, so clean it seemed not to exist at all.
“You’re thinking about that night,” she broke the silence.
“Yeah.”
“That night, I stood in this exact position.”
“Yeah.”
She lowered her head and looked at the complicated buttons and instruments.
“All this time, you’ve only known what happened on your side.”
She raised her eyes again and stared straight at me.

“First clue: Article Four says it very clearly: ‘There is no starting-point control inside the room.’” Yuna looked through the glass at me, standing where the condemned had stood. “This machine doesn’t care what your name is, and it doesn’t care where you came from. It recognizes only

position and scan results. Because you were lying on the frame inside at the time, when I performed the ‘outside technician confirms calibration’ procedure, the machine bound your biological characteristics tightly to the ‘condemned.’ The protocol on my side controls every switch.”
With her right hand, she picked up the thin pages of the execution protocol again.

“Second clue: Article Five says how to copy the parameters, wait five seconds, and submit the command. It means the executioner isn’t allowed to understand, and doesn’t need to understand. All they need to do is press the button as instructed, then wait until the end of the shift to collect the body.”
She stared through the glass at this dead-white room.
“The room inside holds the condemned; the room outside holds the executioner. But the protocol can’t stop me from searching the archives. I found this.”
She pulled open the archive drawer set into the side of the console with force, dragged out a thick hardbound duty log with one hand, and opened it.

“This is everything the people in the corridor could see: establish the starting point, wait five seconds, the instruments report brain death. The starting-point and endpoint commands—the two times—were both completed within the same minute. Not one second was delayed in between.”

I stood in that piercing white light. That night, Yuna did not know the old truth of this execution chamber, but she knew the disaster outside had arrived, and that neither of us had anywhere left to retreat. The executioners of the old world killed with

their eyes closed in this position. She, in that position, pressed the submit key consciously in the face of a certain death, leaving me a way out alive. The only difference was that the executioner went home after the shift, while she died before the button.
“What are you thinking about?”
I clenched my teeth hard. “Nothing.”
“You’re making a fist again.”
She did not continue questioning me. She only folded the pages of the execution protocol back into their original shape.
“Even now, I’ve only investigated half of it.”
“But there’s at least one thing I’m certain of: I wasn’t ‘forbidden to know.’”
She leaned forward as far as she could and pressed her right palm flat against the blast-resistant glass again.
“The rules blinded generations of executioners. As long as the evidence remains, I can always figure it out.”
With her right hand, she felt around in the drawer and pulled out the second thing. It was a brittle roll of waveform printout paper, its edges already yellowed.
“This is an execution record from an old-era condemned person’s shift. An offline file exported from the monitoring of the local condemned person’s state to the console corridor.”

She pointed at the blackened paper. “Outside, only five seconds passed, and this roll only spans five seconds of physical length. But look closely at the wave peaks and timestamps here at the final boundary.”

I moved closer to the glass. In the last few microseconds before death, the roll showed a cluster of densely packed extreme peaks. Huge numbers of jumbled, overlapping machine timestamps were all compressed into the same instant.

“External monitoring shows that the person died after these five seconds passed. But in this underlying record, in the instant before the condemned person’s physical death, the brain was receiving one extremely dense sequential intervention after another.” Yuna pointed at the peaks. “These are

not brainwaves produced by hallucinations. This roll is filled with the condemned person’s repeated brain states as they experienced the same finite five seconds over and over. The machine kept throwing connections outward, blindly repeating its experience of this brief moment before death.”
“Repeating these five seconds?”

“The machine never reversed time or created worlds.” She looked at me through the glass. “These squares represent complete worlds existing simultaneously—finite in number, and limited to the worlds related to this particular machine

connection. The machine simply throws your first-person consciousness outward like a surveillance probe, inserting it into one real world after another, each likewise at eight in the morning, so you can experience its fourteen hours.”
“And this strip of paper that only spans five seconds is the starting point.” Yuna took a deep breath. “The condemned person in the original world, lying on the execution
frame, did not disappear. No matter which microsecond before death his external time remained in, subjectively he relived the fear of those final five seconds again and again.”

She pointed at the disordered wave peaks along the edge of the paper. “That is an enormous neural load. The machine doesn’t care how many times the condemned person subjectively repeats the dead end. It simply

carries out the connections with absolute precision, records those repeatedly closing despair-states, and tries to use the system’s redundant resources to actively repair the enormous cross-world deviations.”
“Until those resources were completely exhausted, that poor body endured the impact without pause, until it burned out completely. Then the system outside gave it a cold word: ‘Stable.’”
In the white room, I watched the ink mark beneath Yuna’s fingertip.
“That was the end point where countless repetitions of enduring within microseconds finally collapsed.” I looked at the ink mark, and my heart sank.

“The small writing at the bottom of the protocol fragment. Whoever carved it must have been an old executioner who worked here. Someone must have noticed a tiny misalignment within those five seconds. Outside, there are only five seconds. Inside, there is no fifth second.”
“This isn’t a miracle. This is a deception written into the laws of physics.” She stared at the console, her fingers trembling with overwhelming anger.
I paced restlessly in the white room. Seven steps, hit the wall, turn around; seven steps, hit the wall, turn around.

“Old humans had only about one unit of personal carrying capacity at a time. So during the five seconds the executioner waited, the moment the machine opened even the tiniest correction window for a tiny

cross-world misalignment, they would instantly exceed the brain’s limit and be crushed. But at exactly eight this morning, what the machine read from you and locked in place was your capacity of ten thousand units.”

“That enormous capacity forcibly stretched the process that would originally have ended in only five seconds into a broad correction window lasting nearly fourteen hours. It can withstand the correction of the cross-world differences caused by your

continuous activity in this world for fourteen hours. At exactly twenty-two hundred, the open window of this body exhausted all the system’s redundant support, the connection broke, and you were forcibly switched to the next eight in the morning.”
I stood in the white light and felt an icy chill rise along my back. It was an immensely cold physical mechanism bought with an immense amount of resources.
Yuna picked up a charcoal pencil and, with one hand, rapidly drew a row of tightly aligned little squares in the blank space of the protocol. She held it up against the glass.
“These squares represent complete worlds existing simultaneously. It isn’t the matter around you flowing backward for your sake.”

“When you jump away from one world, the machine has to find a body you can recognize, whose experiences can connect to the memories in your brain, and slide your first-person probe directly into the next square—the local Arno who is likewise at eight in the morning.”

“Your basic physiological state and the world’s background are highly overlapped at eight. The machine doesn’t care what cross-iteration memories have been added to your brain; it recognizes only compatibility at the

material level. So when your viewpoint switches over, it’s like putting on a VR headset, covering his sensory stream without a seam. For those fourteen hours, his hands are your hands, and what he sees is what you see.”

“Yuna.” My throat felt dry. “If that’s true, then in the wheat field that day, if I had pressed that gray button… if my viewpoint had been pulled away, what would happen to the me left behind, the me who regained control in that world?”
Yuna set down the charcoal pencil and looked at me quietly through the blast-resistant glass.
This revelation took place between the two silent rooms. There was no unnecessary small talk.
“If these worlds exist simultaneously…” I pointed at the squares she had just drawn. “Can’t the machine insert itself into two worlds at once?”

“Do you think you can grow two brains and process two completely different sets of sight, sound, and touch at the same time?” Yuna asked in return. “The connection of an external consciousness can only be single-focus and serial. It can’t let you sit in the wheat field and stand here in the same instant.”
She pointed at the console with her left hand.

“If you want to know what the original world looks like after the probe is pulled out, there is an answer. When we came down by different routes just now, I used the control terminal here to try searching outward for

other connection targets.” Her finger stopped at the edge of the console. “The backup screen on my side now has a faint residual signal. That is the machine receiving residual information from the worlds where the bodies

that have ‘lost their cross-world connection’ are located. The universe will not disappear to accommodate your departure, and the people and time there will not stop out of nowhere. That body is still a living person.”

“After losing the cross-world connection, can the consciousness left behind still control itself?” My throat felt dry. “During those fourteen hours, the external probe was the one giving all the orders. Where did the local consciousness go?”

Yuna did not answer me directly. Instead, she took a deep breath. “It may regain control of the body, or it may retain only memories of what happened today because it merged with the external consciousness, or it may remember

nothing at all. I don’t know. And as for the state of the local consciousness while it was covered by the external viewpoint, every archive and protocol here has been wiped clean. No external viewpoint would know except you.

The only thing I can be certain of is that once you pull the probe out, the you who has lost the connection has to remain there and face, together with that world’s me, the aftermath you both created before that moment.”
“Then if I jump over, take one look, and find that it won’t work, can I switch back to here at this moment?”
Yuna quickly drew a cross over the current square with the charcoal pencil. “Have you tried looking ahead before jumping away?”
“I have.” My voice was dry. “But I couldn’t see anything. Only when I truly decide to cut off everything here can I see the next blurred address.”

“Because you have only one pair of eyes. Unless you truly pull the focus away from here, you can’t establish a connection there. That means you can never preview what you’ll face after jumping away.” Yuna looked at the cross.

“At that fork just now, I was supposed to press those controls, right? Because of the extra information you brought, we didn’t press them and came straight here. The different choice you made in this branch has already caused

a serious deviation in the course of events that follows in this world. The probe can find only a compatible past the next time, but it can never again find a future with all the key premises you changed still exactly the same.”
I looked at the cross and understood her completely.
“So once I decide to jump away, this ‘present’ that I’ve already changed will be closed to me forever.”
The enormous machine gave a slow, heavy rumble.

“Even after the external viewpoint’s connection is severed, the people left in that world still have to face the irreversible end without you. The forced departure of the external viewpoint cannot save any independent world.”
“Even if you turn your head and jump away, they still have to finish walking the dead end.”

This truly was a deception written into the laws of physics. The endurance of the original Arno in the execution chamber had been treated as the sole root of the session, while all the real disasters we experienced here were merely fourteen hours of illusion within that endless

experience of despair. In this pure white room, incontrovertible physical limits had fixed it into law. Whether I escaped by pressing the button or was forcibly switched after the window passively ran out, every iteration, as long as I left, I left a real abandoned world behind me.
In the console corridor, Yuna looked at the tabletop and floor where she had once collapsed after pressing the button. They were spotless.
“It’s too clean. Not even the slightest trace was left behind,” she said softly.

She bent down with difficulty and took a short piece of black charcoal from her sleeve with her right hand. Pulled by the metal ring around her left wrist, she could barely reach the dustless floor by her feet. With force, she wrote two neat characters. Her name.
“When the probe switches away, it can’t take these words with it.”
“I know.”
She finished the final stroke, straightened herself, and looked at me through the blast-resistant glass.
“But the act of writing here will have happened, truly and undeniably.”
“Arno, the memories left in your mind are the only trace I can make you carry away.”

During this long, motionless wait, she used her only mobile hand to pour a handful of dried, hard beans onto the console. With one hand, she peeled half of them and pushed them across toward the glass. She chewed on her side while I watched from mine. The low-frequency vibration of the enormous machine was so close it seemed pressed against my eardrums.
She suddenly turned her head sharply and stared at me.
“Hey. Why are you clenching your fist so tightly?”
I hurriedly relaxed my fist. “Nothing.”
“I saw it. You’re still thinking about what just happened, aren’t you?”
She stared at me for several seconds, then her voice suddenly softened.
“Arno, if the choice you make when you close your eyes and press that gray button is the same every time, then what about the you left behind?”
She tossed the last half-bean into her mouth and chewed it with a loud crunch.

“Look at that me.” She pointed to her reflection in the blast-resistant window. “She hasn’t turned into a wooden dummy. She hasn’t vanished into thin air. She’s still chewing beans. After you jump away, I won’t immediately disappear from this room either.

I’m locked in here and can’t go anywhere, but I know there is still a living person inside this body. I have my own legs. I can’t get out today, but in another world you can find, or somewhere farther away, I can still walk the rest of the way myself.”

At twenty thirty-six, the second dusk finally arrived. That faint dimness, announcing that capacity had fallen below the safe threshold and night was about to descend, seeped underground through countless layers of thick metal floor plates.
Deep beneath the ground, it felt as if the entire sleeping White Tower suddenly convulsed and drew in a great breath of cold air. The indicator lights all dropped strangely by half a notch.

“That night, I pressed the red button and sent you out of the dead end.” She leaned against the metal console, her breathing becoming difficult. “But the White Tower’s total reserve capacity has already fallen below the safe threshold in this world. Because of the physical instability, it began that irreversible shutdown tonight.”
The long period of dying had begun. On the ground above, the people whose consciousnesses were being forcibly pulled away lay scattered in all the usual places. With the fourteen-hour open
window provided by that ten-thousand-unit capacity, I would remain conscious alone in this pure white prison until exactly twenty-two hundred, waiting for the physical severance and forced
switch that would come when this body’s endurance reached its limit. But before that, Yuna in this room would, like everyone outside, lose consciousness first at twenty-one fifty-three.
Throughout that long, suffocating process, Yuna held herself upright. Her breathing grew shallower and shallower, and she could barely lean against the metal console.
Before the final moment arrived, she raised her head and quietly looked upward. Then she suddenly spoke:
“When you switch your viewpoint again, don’t spend all your time being sad. Take one more step forward for that me.”
The strange light in the console corridor flickered once. Twenty-one fifty-three drew near.
With the tower’s breath, she pressed her right hand against the glass, as if laying it over the back of my hand. She did not press hard. She simply left it there, naturally and calmly.
This time, she did not endlessly enumerate a work list. She looked at me with a clear exhaustion in her eyes.
“When you switch into the next eight o’clock, will you still go find the me who remembers nothing?”

I opened my mouth, but before the word “I will” could come out, the irreversible twenty-one fifty-three rolled heavily over her. That very soft question became the last sound she left in this iteration. I could tell that afterward she still tried to hold on to consciousness,

trying to hear my answer, but every resistance of her physical functions was futile. Her hand on the other side of the glass finally slipped down without strength. Her eyes closed, and her head sank heavily onto the console. I could not reach her body heat through

the glass, but I knew that, just as had happened countless times before, the first person inside that body had been irreversibly erased. She was dead, sunk into complete silence, while her body remained tightly locked in place by the metal ring around her left wrist.
Everything around me fell silent. Through the glass, I watched the side of her face, no longer breathing.

The enormous White Tower gave a slow rumble, inhaling, exhaling. In this pure white room without her, I still had to endure the final seven minutes alone in the silence, waiting for the instability and switch that would come at twenty-two hundred.
Above us, I knew the villagers whose consciousnesses had been emptied out lay scattered in all the usual places. In the pure white room where I stood, the four walls still
maintained their cruel tracelessness. Only on the floor beyond that transparent blast-resistant glass did a small patch of charcoal writing remain—something remembered by me alone.
At exactly twenty-two hundred, darkness finally covered me completely. This iteration was over, and I jumped into the next void.
texts.chapter:chapter-08-who-are-you:title: Chapter Eight: Who Are You, Really?
texts.chapter:chapter-08-who-are-you:event:tex:
Deep Terminal · Final Line of Automatic Log (Yuna’s handwritten copy):
“0750. Calibration: complete. Occupancy: valid.
Existing trajectory: read. Fitting: passed.
Anchor: pending construction. Window: compatible.”
Dozens of cycles ago, beside the human frame in the experimental area, Yuna copied the abandoned engineering jargon from the screen onto her palm.
Whenever a new today arrived, her palm was clean. The words had returned to the terminal screen, glowing starkly where they had been, waiting for her to copy them again.

She came up with the stupidest and most effective method of decoding across cycles: explain several words to me each day and make me memorize them by rote. When the next “today” came, I would recite them back to her, and she would reconstruct the logic chain from the previous cycle and continue from there.
And yesterday, in the pure-white room, we had rechecked the calibration record for the condemned subject and established the most horrifying bottom line of all: jumping away was
not the world resetting. Every time I closed my eyes and switched tracks, I was leaving the living Yuna behind in a real world that would continue to bleed and continue to run.

Early this morning, when we met again in the experimental area, I could still feel that weight pressing against my chest like a boulder. But there was no time to stop and catch my breath. Yuna had already sat down at a rusty iron table.
She turned around, slapped a dust-covered old-era waterworks maintenance manual onto the table, and pushed it toward me together with the line of log text.

“Now we can look at this line.” She pointed at “Fitting: passed.” “The White Tower’s infrastructure and lower-level systems were left behind by the same engineers. In this old waterworks manual, ‘fitting’

means connecting a new water pipe seamlessly into an old one. If this line of the log borrowed the same engineering concept, and you’re only a jumping ‘observation focus,’ then what was fitted in this morning?”
The manual showed diagrams: the joint of a new pipe cut down so it could be fitted along the grain of the old one.

“Seven fifty. You sat inside the human frame at dawn, and ‘calibration’ was completed. As long as there was a living person in the position, ‘occupancy’ was valid. The machine read your physical state at that moment as the ‘existing trajectory.

’” Yuna drew a deep breath and put forward the frightening hypothesis. “This is only conjecture. But if the ‘existing trajectory’ is the calibration record you left behind in the seventh cycle, then the ‘new pipe’ is the you crossing over now.”
“At seven fifty, the physical conditions compatible with your focus were in place. And the delayed activation at exactly eight, the one that made the tower hum, was the ‘anchor’ in the
log—the you who didn’t belong to this morning locking itself into this body along the fourteen-hour window. From eight onward, it was no longer the local you who was in control of everything.”

“What about the ‘me’ who was originally here?” I clenched my hands without thinking.
“Maybe he didn’t disappear.” She looked at me, her voice tightening. “If you really are only an outside focus, then
when you detach in the destabilization at twenty-two hundred tonight, your attention will switch directly into the next track. But what about the one who was originally in this body? Is he asleep, or
sharing these senses with you like an observer who has lost control? Either way, once you detach, he may wake up again and be forced to carry the memories of this entire day, heading toward the end

together with this world whose lights are destined to go out.”
My breathing tightened. If this conjecture about him being left behind to endure everything was true, the cost was suffocatingly heavy.

“But this entire theory of consciousness taking over is still only a hypothesis on paper.” She stood. “Let’s go to the lower-level guardroom and look for the physical records of the equipment running. At the very least, we need

evidence to confirm the hardware logic of the first step: whether the machine really doesn’t care who lies inside, and only recognizes a living body. If this physical loophole exists, the inference about takeover can stand.”

The equipment records at the base of the tower were kept in a cramped little compartment. This morning, the covert search net under Otto’s control was tightening. To get inside, we could only steal a few minutes of movement by using a known blind spot.
As we crossed the corridor, Bart, the supplies clerk, was sitting behind a desk checking the ration sheets. His eye sockets were sunken, and the backs of his hands were covered in scrapes from
hauling supplies during the lockdown. He had spent several nights awake, distributing the pitifully small food stores among the whole village. I knew the fastest way to get past his questions.
“Bart,” I said with perfect naturalness before he looked up, “the humidity alarm in the backup storehouse in Zone C seems to be lit.”
Bart immediately put down his pen and turned anxiously toward Zone C. In those few seconds while his back was turned, I pulled Yuna silently into the compartment.
I was about to look for the record books when I noticed Yuna standing in the doorway, unmoving.
“The way you just talked to Bart.” Her voice held a trace of cold unfamiliarity.

“It was like pressing a key on the laboratory panel. You threw out that humidity warning, and he turned his head. Every one of your sentences corresponded exactly to a reaction in him. You wouldn’t spend one extra word. You weren’t talking to a living person at all. You were pressing him.”

Over the past few days, we had gone back and forth countless times between the outer settlement and the central village. To verify information and plan routes, I treated every reset as an opportunity to optimize efficiency. I leaned

wearily against the iron frame and listened to the wind coming through the vent. Bart’s exhaustion, and whether he lived or died, were not part of our calculations for finding a way out, so I had pushed past him by the fastest method.
I had never intended to explain the lie that could save five minutes.
Yuna said nothing more. In silence, she turned and pulled the thick equipment logbook from the shelf.

“You told me before that the machine doesn’t recognize that your name is Arno. It only recognizes a living thing in the binding position.” She pushed the heavy book in front of me. “These physical records from the lower level confirm the first step.”
“Occupant,” I read.

“The first record of that day is only one line with three columns.” Her finger moved along the paper. “First column, input condition: ‘Someone in position.’ Second column, external operation: ‘External confirmation, present.’ And the result: ‘Occupant, stand by.’”

“There was no identity check or retrieval of any records during the entire process.” Yuna stared at the logbook. “Just as we reasoned moments ago, when calibration was completed at seven fifty, it performed only the most mechanical determination: a living person capable of breathing steadily was lying in that position, and the external confirmation was present.”
The tower’s faint ventilation hummed beneath our feet.

“So as long as a living person completes calibration inside and receives external confirmation, the system can treat anyone as the occupant, regardless of whose experience is read as the ‘existing trajectory.” Yuna stared hard at me. “Even an

ordinary person who has never received theological instruction and never signed anything. That morning, you lay down first. And I was the one outside who gave the external confirmation. But if I had been the one to lie down first that morning?”

My throat felt dry. When we reread the pure-white-room calibration file yesterday, we had already established that the machine didn’t recognize people. Whoever lay inside and received external confirmation became the occupant.
“Then you would be the one to generate ‘Occupant, stand by,’” I managed to say.

“If I had happened to press out a reading of ten thousand and eighty on the old equipment beforehand, just as you did that day,” she said without the slightest fluctuation in her voice, “then the window period would be on me now.”
In that cramped compartment, we fell into a dead silence.

I looked at her pale face, and that instinct to use information skillfully surfaced again. I summoned the memories I had of her—the secret she had confided in me at this point during the previous few cycles. I selected the most effective comforting response.
“Don’t be afraid,” I said softly. “I won’t tell anyone that you gave half your induction seed grain to the orphan next door. I know you’re afraid.”
Yuna went rigid.
It was something she had hidden even from Meru. She had never told me about the seed grain on this current timeline.
Slowly, she drew her hand back from the manual. But the look in her eyes was as if she had seen some utterly unfamiliar monster.
“I’ve never told you about the seed grain.” She took a step back, her voice trembling.
I froze.

“You weren’t listening to me at all.” She stared at me, her eyes reddening. “You just searched your memory bank for data about me, or about someone else, then pressed it like a switch labeled ‘reassurance.’ You weren’t comforting me. You were calling me!”
“Yuna, I—”
“Who are you, really?” she cut me off.
That was where our conversation ended that day. She pushed open the door and walked out of the guardroom without looking back.

I stood alone beside the ventilation ducts on the lower level, watching the wooden door close. I didn’t follow her out. If every morning brought a completely new track, and the Yuna on this track would never forgive me again, what would be the point of trying to make amends?
I simply sat numbly on the rusty chair and let the seconds pass. Until twenty-two hundred, when this world destabilized on schedule. My consciousness
was forcibly pulled away, and the local Arno who might be left behind to face the end would remain forever with this night I had completely ruined.
The morning of the next cycle.

I didn’t use Bart as a switch again. Instead, I waited an extra half-hour with the Yuna of the new cycle in a narrow alley, preparing to infiltrate the lower-level guardroom during the patrol change. In a blind

spot away from the main-road patrols, I told this Yuna, who remembered nothing, everything about what I had done to “her” in the previous cycle, and about the look on her face as she pushed open the door and left.
After listening, Yuna remained silent for a long time.

To avoid the patrol about to pass the mouth of the alley, we stopped close against the old wall on the right and prepared to wait two minutes. I was just about to tell her that the broken wooden door would suddenly be pushed open in a few seconds.
But my body reacted before my mind did: with practiced ease, I pulled Yuna into a blind corner.
The next second, Meru hurried out carrying a coarse earthenware rice jar. Her toe caught on the threshold, her body lurched, and the jar smashed against the ground.
A red cloth pouch hidden beneath the jar rolled out with it. The golden seed grain carefully wrapped inside spilled all over the ground.

Over the past several hundred cycles, I had become practiced at going around this mess. I calculated when the patrol would pass and prepared to continue forward. But I didn’t hear Yuna’s footsteps following me.
I turned back. Meru was kneeling in the dust-covered yard, her hands trembling as she gathered the scattered seed grain, her face pale. This was Yuna’s mother. A few days ago,
she had harshly scolded Yuna to keep her from being drawn into the White Tower’s trouble. But on this morning, when she knew nothing, she was simply a bewildered villager.
Yuna walked forward without a word and crouched beside her. She reached out and began picking up the grains one by one.
“They’re for Milu…” Meru’s voice was choked with tears as she frantically gathered at the dirt. “They’re the seed grain to pay for my youngest daughter when she wants to enter the Church someday…”
Crouching beside her, Yuna carefully put the golden grains she had picked up back into the red cloth pouch. Her expression was calm. She did not break down at the word “Mother.”
I counted down the time in my head. I wanted to rush over and stop her: all this seed grain would reset to zero tomorrow. What she was doing now had no benefit at all.
But my feet seemed rooted to the spot.
I remembered yesterday’s Yuna, the Yuna who had pushed open the door and left the lower-level guardroom. The Yuna I had left forever on the old track.

Like a cheater, I had received a brand-new her that morning without a qualm. Everything from yesterday, along with her disappointment and pain, had remained on yesterday’s track. Yesterday could not be undone, but today had only just begun.
I gritted my teeth, walked back into the yard, and crouched beside them. I said nothing. I only held out my dust-covered hand and began picking the grains into the red cloth pouch.
We spent three full minutes. When Meru clutched the pouch tightly and looked at us with reddened eyes, I pulled Yuna up and hurried away from the mouth of the alley.
We were stopped by Otto’s men one street away from the White Tower.
Three tall guards blocked the street and looked at us coldly. “Routine search. Outsiders aren’t allowed near the White Tower.” The one in front rested a hand on the fire gun at his waist.

In this world, we had wasted three minutes. But if I hadn’t crouched there for those three minutes, I wouldn’t have dared look into her eyes again today. I pulled Yuna back without once looking at the road so close within reach.
At dusk, dark red sunset burned along the horizon. We sat side by side on the tall haystack at the village entrance.
“Actually, even if you hadn’t confessed what happened yesterday this morning, I still would have helped her today.” She looked at the distant glow and spoke softly.
I said nothing.

“I’m still not sure whether you’ve changed.” She turned her head and looked at me seriously for a while. “But I’d rather believe in the person who crouched in the mud with me today, picking up seed grain.”
She closed her eyes, and the faintest trace of a smile touched the corners of her mouth. Then she jumped lightly down from the haystack.
“Let’s go home. Eat a proper dinner, and talk with Rena a little more.”

Night fell and the daylight faded. I sat beside the wooden table, patiently listening to my mother ramble about the pickled vegetables nearly ready in the jar, the embroidery thread she had just bought, and all her plans for “tomorrow.”

“When the weather clears tomorrow, let’s repair the old wooden frame in the yard.” My mother added a spoonful of hot soup to my bowl. The backs of her hands were rough from years of labor. “Your father always said he would fix it, but he kept putting it off. Give me a hand tomorrow. We’ll do it together.”
I watched the steam rising from the bowl. For once, I did not silently repeat in my mind, “We have no tomorrow.”
“Okay,” I answered softly. Then I lowered my head and drank the thick soup down to the last drop.

Late at night, the lights in the houses went out one after another. When we met again tomorrow morning, I could still use the password of the five and a half blue threads to prove myself to a brand-new her. But after today, those five and a half blue threads had become

strangely heavy in my heart. I went to the door, pushed it open, and followed the darkness to meet Yuna. I had not obtained the physical evidence she wanted, but I remembered every word I had seen in that book during the previous cycle. I needed to recite it all to her.
We walked along the quiet village road toward the outer circle. When we met outside my yard just now, she had been turning the faded old cloth identification band around her wrist.
I walked beside Yuna. The evening wind moved through her worn coat. Her head was slightly lowered.
Looking at her profile so close beside me, a wordless fear seized me tightly.
If my guess was true, if my consciousness detaching was not the world resetting but a jump into another track…

She was only half a step away. This morning, after hearing me confess all my ugliness, she had not pushed open the door and left. At dusk, sitting on the haystack, she had said she was willing to believe in the person who had crouched in the mud with her.

But no matter how many times it started over, as long as I detached when I closed my eyes tonight, would I really leave this Yuna, who had just said she was willing to believe in me, forever on the still-continuing timeline before me, just as I had yesterday?
I stopped abruptly.
“Yuna.”
She turned around and looked at me, somewhat puzzled. “What is it?”
I clenched my fist hard, my nails digging deep into my palm. I used the slight sting to confirm the reality before me.
“Nothing.” I drew a deep breath, caught up with her, and walked on the side closer to her without letting anything show. “Come on. We need to hurry.”
texts.chapter:chapter-08b-original-words:event: It was late at night. Only the occasional night wind swept through the village’s dark lanes. Yuna walked diagonally ahead of me, then stopped in a patch of shadow and quietly waited for me to catch up.
Looking at her real silhouette now, the displacement from not long ago struck my nerves again like a slap.
It had happened one morning in an earlier loop, when we passed the fork by the chapel. Without warning, Estelle’s figure had flashed into Yuna’s place for less than a second. In
that instant, she was wearing an old purple work uniform, its collar stripped of its pattern and fitted with a heavy metal arc—a garment I remembered her wearing before. But there
was one difference: hanging prominently from her chest was a candidate identity badge that had originally belonged to Yuna. She stared at me with guarded eyes and did not say a word.

It had not been a simple hallucination or a tangle of memories. An apparition would not have become wary because it was being watched. Yet the instant her eyes met mine, the wariness in them was alive. It was the look of someone who had lost

everything and was still struggling along another muddy road. A horrifying guess took shape in my mind: that one-second intersection had been a glimpse of another world that was still continuing. Somewhere beyond what I could see, another

timeline had not been erased by my “reset.” That displacement had been the most direct warning of all—the people I had left behind in other worlds were still living on with their own despair. They were not data I could access whenever I pleased.
Deep in my mind, a page containing a set of memory rules meant only for me had always been sealed away.

Memory Archive:
I. Contains only what she said. My questions are recorded only as marginal notes.
II. As is. Add nothing, remove nothing, smooth nothing over.
III. Where she cannot go on, write ‘She stopped here.’
IV. My own subjective inferences do not go into this archive.
V. When reading it aloud to her, do not explain anything in between.

These were the rules I had imposed on myself after one completely failed attempt. Beneath those lines was engraved the conclusion she had reached in one of the loops, after seeing through the nature of the disaster with her own eyes. In that failed loop, it was the first time I had tried to treat her as a shortcut that could skip the reasoning entirely.
On the morning of that failed loop, to avoid Otto’s search net, we climbed down into a dry canal.

The procedure moved quickly. After checking the scratches on the seventh tree to the east, she nodded and said, “Then let’s try.” Then she lowered her head, skillfully pulled the old booklet and a short piece of charcoal from inside her clothes, and waited quietly for me.
I took out the list recording the order in which everyone in the village would die and handed it to her.
The moment she took it and began to unfold it, I pressed down on the pages.

“Today, I’m not going to lead you through the reasoning step by step.” I looked at the pencil in her hand. “I’m going to read you something you said yourself. A conclusion that had already reached the end after you understood this list.”
She raised her eyes, looking at me with some surprise. “Which day’s me?”
“Another version of you. That time, you saw through the nature of the daylight.”
The charcoal pencil in her hand, poised to write, stopped against the rough paper.
“If it’s the end, how did she get there?”
“Because that time, you understood what was written here.”

I drew a deep breath, met her gaze, and recited the archive I had carved into my mind word for word. I recited the big year and the small year, the invisible clock, and the final sentence: “Most of the lives in this village are the words carved into the clock face.”
The bottom of the canal was dead silent. She pulled her hand out from beneath mine, spread open the list she had not been able to unfold, and quickly scanned the densely packed names.
She finished reading the record in silence, then shifted her gaze to me.
“So I only saw through the pattern after going through a long chain of reasoning, after walking that stretch of despair in my own head.”
“Yes.”
“Then if you’re giving me the list today, why are you also handing me the answer outright?”
“I wanted to spare you the despair,” I said quietly. “If I relay that version of your conclusion to you exactly as it was, we can skip straight past it today and think about how to solve it.”
She folded the list and pushed it back to me.
“Arno, this isn’t a shortcut.” She looked at me. “You’re just using the answer of a previous me to overwrite today’s me.”
“Even if that conclusion was reached by ‘me,’ if I haven’t walked this road myself today, then to me it’s just a ghost story dropped from the sky.”
She stood up and brushed the dirt from her trouser legs.
“If you want me to solve it with you, take me this afternoon to see with my own eyes the things that can support your conclusion.” She looked down at me.

“And I’m going to make one thing clear first.” She fixed her eyes on mine. “From now on, whenever you want to stuff some words spoken by a ‘past me’ into my head, you may only repeat them exactly as they were. If you dare mix in even one of your own inferences or explanations, I’ll never listen to you again.”
That afternoon, we quietly went to the abandoned experimental area during the brief gap when Otto’s search teams were changing posts in each district.
As we walked side by side into the vast hall, dim yellow light slashed in through the glass windows far above. I led her to the dial in the corner of the control panel.
She read the precipitously falling figures herself. “At eight this morning, the numbers plunged off a cliff. At this rate of loss, the disaster will arrive tonight.”
Next, we entered the machine room next door. She walked beneath the warning sign announcing the order of the collapse, craned her neck, and laboriously worked through the words one by one.
She stood there alone beneath the sign, her chest rising and falling slightly.

I waited silently beside her. But she only took the list from her pocket, stared hard at it and the sign in turn, then turned around and recorded the time of the plunge and the rule written on the warning sign in her notebook.
Beneath those two lines, she left a vast expanse of blank space.
“That’s enough for today.”
“You don’t want to try connecting them?”
“Since you’ve already given me the result, connecting them without finding the evidence myself would be nothing more than a fill-in-the-blanks game.” She closed the booklet and looked at me calmly.
That evening, we still failed to evade them.

While trying to cross the outskirts and return to the residential district, we ran into a search team deployed in doubled numbers. Under the separation-and-detention order issued the previous night, we were taken to the waiting area on the lowest level of the White Tower, where we were to await separate questioning and confinement.
At 20:36, the second dusk descended.

A violent tremor instantly overloaded and extinguished the lighting on the lowest level of the White Tower. The guard escorting me was stunned by the phenomenon and instinctively let go to brace himself against the wall. Panic and confusion spread through the darkness.
The instant his grip loosened, I broke free, shoved through the figures thrown into chaos beside me, and rushed toward her in the corner of the waiting area. I held her as tightly as I could.

Outside the iron door of the waiting room, everything was dim. The thick walls shut out the sounds of the village. We could not hear anyone falling, but that absolute silence became the cruelest countdown.
“It’s 21:26.” She stared at the watch on my wrist, visible only by the faint light, her voice tight. “If the list is right, then just now, your mother already…”
I reached out, wanting to take her hand, but she clutched her old booklet tightly, the knuckles standing out white. She did not cry.

“For a moment just now, my hand was already against this wall. I wanted to dig my nails into the stone and scream for her.” She stared hard at the sliver of light leaking through the cracks between the stones. “But I didn’t even go and pound on the door.”
The waiting room was utterly silent. Only the adult guards outside the heavy stone walls whispered to one another, trying to suppress their panic.

“If I didn’t know anything, I should have pounded on the door in despair. I should have screamed myself hoarse trying to find someone who could tell me what was happening outside.” Her forehead pressed against the cold stone

tiles, her breathing quick and close to suffocation. “But from the moment you recited that conclusion to me in the canal, my mind was locked inside its certainty. I know it’s accurate. I know she’ll be next in a few dozen minutes.”
She raised her head and searched for my eyes in the darkness.
“You used a definite countdown to hold down my urge to pound on the door. It was even assigning my emotions for me: it wasn’t time to
break down over her yet; I had to wait until 21:48…” Her voice trembled with that inhuman calm and the self-loathing that followed it. “Arno,
you turned me into a spectator to my own fate. Even my instinct to break down normally, to mourn, was stopped by this precise spoiler.”
At 21:48, it was finally the current generation’s boy’s turn.
It was not the moment when she closed her eyes, but when Remi, far away at the other end of the village, closed hers according to the list. We sat in the darkness, listening as the muffled sounds of

the adult guards outside the stone wall gradually faded, until everything sank into suffocating silence. The Ten Seats and the adults in the outskirts had all fallen. Now it was our generation’s turn.
A few minutes later, at 21:53.
By the faint daylight leaking through the gap beneath the door, I watched her pupils gradually lose focus. Her breathing slowly weakened, and the rise and fall of her chest gradually settled.
In that dark room, without any supernatural flash of light, she quietly closed her eyes and her body went completely limp.
I held her gradually cooling body and endured the darkness until exactly 22:00.
Everything went black. It all began again.
At exactly eight the next morning, I opened my eyes at the edge of the calibration area in the White Tower.
I stood where I was. The pressure of her fingers tightening around my clothes that night still seemed to linger there.

For a long time afterward, I forced myself to follow the rules of that memory archive. I thought that as long as I did not read the conclusion aloud for her, as long as I made her reason it out herself, I had not deprived her of anything.

But the tremor of facing the truth for the first time without any preparation, the version of her who had reasoned her way to the answer herself—it never appeared again. It became a definitive original that could never be verified a second time.
The world before me came completely into focus.
The dizziness brought on by the brief memory had fully receded. In the night wind, Yuna, standing in the shadows, turned her head and quietly waited for my next move.
I withdrew my gaze, closed the page in my heart belonging to the past, and followed her footsteps.
texts.chapter:chapter-09-eight-thousand:title: Chapter Nine: Eight Thousand
texts.chapter:chapter-09-eight-thousand:event:: Over the hundreds of resets that followed, we kept running into those dead ends, again and again.

Every morning, I had to knock on Yuna’s door, use the evidence we had accumulated to reestablish that day for her—she who knew nothing of any of it—and earn her trust all over again, then lead her into the White Tower and take her a few steps deeper.

The Yuna walking ahead of me had once been severed in half by a gate, and once fallen into a deep shaft. In the previous cycle, the Yuna scouting ahead had been locked inside a sealed chamber at the end of the launch site by a defensive protocol. Before the air ran out, the Yuna

on the other side of the isolation glass did not reach for the spare oxygen tube caught on the outer gate. Instead, she held down the console with all her strength, pressed the string of data keys we had finally cracked by force against the glass, and mouthed to me: “Remember it.”

In that world, she slowly suffocated inside that chamber. And I could only stand outside the glass, committing that string of numbers to memory, waiting until the reset descended at 22:00. I walked the path into the depths of the White Tower on top of those real deaths, using her life to lay it down piece by piece.
Until this morning.

When today’s Yuna and I reached the production-line control room again, I could no longer remember how many times I had brought her back along this route. The four-digit data key belonging to the Yuna from the previous cycle was entered into the surviving console by her.
A very faint mechanical click came from inside the control room.
The physical work case belonging to some senior engineer’s access terminal finally released its outer lock. At last, we had the terminal’s physical connection port.

Yuna opened the case and connected the interfaces inside. In earlier cycles, she had cracked the terminal’s external system access controls. As soon as the connection was established, a long list of permission-locked directories streamed smoothly across

the screen: equipment-maintenance aliases, accident records, facility indexes… She opened the accident record whose author’s name and position had been blacked out with glaring blocks of black, then directly entered the unlocked old index command.
A separate data array deep within the system activated. The protocol unlocked a sealed calibration recording.
There was no face on the screen, only a processed voice and several attached technical drawings.
“An anonymous technical record.” Yuna pressed the play button. “Judging by where it was stored, the speaker was the owner of this case.”
The old speech in the recording was rough and difficult to understand. Fortunately, basic vocabulary explanations parsed by the machine scrolled along beneath the screen.

“The number of pages connected to the system is a finite set.” The voice in the recording sounded alongside the machine cross-section appearing on the screen. “The number is large, but it has a physical boundary. And

every page is a complete universe that has existed from the beginning. Wherever we observe it locally, every world possesses complete physical entities and operating rules. They are neither projections nor copies.”

In the pure white room, Yuna had deduced that the abandoned worlds were still continuing to evolve. But this was the first time someone had given us a clear engineering conclusion, telling us that those suffering worlds were real, and the people suffering inside them were real.
It was also the first time we knew that the number which had fallen in the hall the day before yesterday had a definite bottom.
“Arno, the worlds are finite. That means the total size of the gap the machine has torn open is finite, too.” She turned to look at me. “This isn’t
a bottomless pit without end. It reached the bottom the day before yesterday, so we may soon be able to see exactly what that bottom number is.”
She pressed play again. A pair of structurally complex scissors appeared on the screen.
“This ‘scissors’… is the annihilation device in the central zone. It locks onto the ‘same person’ who exists in every world. The target must personally step into the central zone. With one cut, it
