can terminate that person’s continuing first-person existence in every relevant world at once. In doing so, it releases the total capacity occupied by this cross-world entity. May it never be needed.”

“The central zone… the target has to step into it personally.” She stared at the interpretation on the screen, as if confirming every word of the rough old speech. “Once it cuts someone, that person’s life in every page has no continuation. What it releases is the ‘total

capacity occupied across worlds.’ In other words, if the same person exists in every universe, occupying one unit on every page… this device physically bundles that person’s entire cross-world account into a single total and pays it back to the system all at once.”
The recording on the screen jumped to the next segment. A number appeared: “8000.”

“I can’t calculate how large a gap the complete cross-world connection has torn open,” the voice continued. “But if we take the physical load limit of the machine’s main structure as the numerator, and the minimum release efficiency the central-zone annihilation device can reach under the most

extreme operating conditions as the denominator… no matter how we calculate the worst case, the compensation required by the system plus the losses in the conversion process will absolutely not exceed eight thousand capacity units. Filling this disaster will require eight thousand units at most.”
What appeared immediately afterward was the approval page of an engineering memorandum.

“Since the baseline capacity of one person is approximately one unit, I agree, on engineering grounds, to set eight thousand people as the highest executable death quota. I have signed off on this red line.”

At the edge of the recording, an attachment titled “Supplementary Notes on the Quota Selection Mechanism” flashed past. It stated plainly: The conclusions of this model do not possess, and should not possess, the ethical authority to determine specific sacrifice targets.
But beneath that declaration, the same pen that had signed off on the red line checked the authorization box stating, “This conclusion may still serve as the basis for quota execution.”
The recording paused. Yuna found a blank sheet of rough paper on the table, pinched up a short stub of charcoal, and wrote “8000.”
“For the old humans who built this machine, one person’s capacity is one unit.” She stared at the number. “So this person signed it and put eight thousand into execution as the
highest quota. And he knew perfectly well that mathematics couldn’t calculate who ought to die, yet he still made that conclusion the basis for killing. But Arno, we aren’t old humans.”
She paused, then turned her gaze toward the facility index they had just unlocked and brought up an engineering specification sheet for New Human vessels.

“This specification says… the bodies of our generation are manufactured to bundle together the total of every possible cross-world instance of a single person.” She drew a deep breath. “That total cross-world specification is ten thousand capacity units.”
I jerked my head up.
“One New Human body contains all ten thousand units of that person’s capacity across every world…” Her gaze moved between the specification parameters on the screen and me.
“So if a New Human steps into it,” I said, “they can not only fill the gap of eight thousand, but have capacity left over.”
That was what made this number truly terrifying. It meant that eight thousand was no longer some vague, distant gap.
Yuna said nothing. Her hand rested lightly over the number on the paper.
“But the scissors lock onto the ‘same person’ across all worlds.” Her voice was soft. “The cross-world total of ten thousand is because he himself is a whole entity spanning every world.”
She raised her head.

“If those ten thousand are handed over, then whoever steps up there, it won’t be only the person on this page who gets cut. All the lives he lived in different ways in every other world, all those possibilities, will be cut off as well.”
The truly chilling cost of the scissors had finally been laid out on the table.

No matter how many worlds the disaster spans, there is only one total account. As long as the person who steps up meets the ten-thousand-capacity specification, then in any world, the moment he willingly enters the scissors in the central zone, that cross-world entity will have no tomorrow left in any of the relevant worlds.
An attached text note appeared on the screen.
“‘If one day someone reads this record, remember two things. First: the upper limit is real.’”
She turned toward the hall. The needle, which had plunged this morning, was still closing in on the lowest red line.
“The upper limit is real. As long as someone steps up there, the daylight will stop,” Yuna said. “But by leaving this note, he was asking about something else.”
The note continued:

“‘Second: annihilation does not destroy information. If it only releases capacity, then after a person’s first-person existence is physically terminated, where did the records of that person’s life, the structure of their memories, and the physical traces they left behind—the information beyond that capacity—go?’”

The recording stopped there. There was no answer. Even if a life were terminated as completely as possible, that person’s information had not been erased from the world. It had gone somewhere even the designer did not know how to reach.
“Where did that information go…”

“I don’t know.” Yuna closed the facility index, folded up the sheet of rough paper with 8000 written on it, and clenched it in her hand. “Right now, the urgent thing is to find a way to verify whether this upper limit of eight thousand is reliable.”
As long as this number was real, there was a bottom to this disaster—a point at which it could stop. Everything depended on this upper limit being beyond doubt.
Yuna was unusually quiet on the road back to the village. I followed behind her, watching her right hand tighten slightly. The information that had not reached zero would not leave my
mind. Information was not destroyed. Did that mean that after the person’s existence had been cut off in every world, the one who stepped up there would still leave something behind?
Just before we crossed the village boundary stone, she suddenly broke the silence.

“Arno, about what the record said—that the number of ‘pages’ connected to the machine has a boundary, and that every one of them is a complete world.” She stopped walking. “I want to tell you something. After you hear it, you’re not allowed to take it as true. But you’re not allowed not to take it completely as true, either.”
“What kind of strange requirement is that?”

“It’s called ‘hope.’” She tilted her head slightly toward the first star appearing in the sky. “I was thinking, since the complete worlds connected to this machine have a boundary… maybe there could be one page…”
Her voice suddenly softened.

“…On a page like that, there would be no daylight ready to fall at any moment. The wheat there would ripen and be harvested in peace, and people would close their eyes as a matter of course only when they grew old. You living on that

page wouldn’t have to count which cycle it was, or knock anxiously on my door first thing in the morning—you’d simply be an ordinary mill apprentice. You’d finish work at dusk, and I’d be standing outside, waiting for you to come home.”
Night fell. She turned around and lightly patted my arm.
“All right. That’s the end of the story. Come on. We have to get home before dinner.”
In the dusk, I watched her in profile.

If the annihilation device really would cut off that person’s future in every connected world, then in that page without daylight, the worlds themselves would not be erased. The wheat would still ripen, and the old would still grow old.

But on that page, if one of the people standing here happened to meet the requirements and hand over that account of ten thousand—then no matter who was waiting at the door, they would wait forever for the person who was supposed to come home.
texts.chapter:chapter-10-fugitives:title: Chapter Ten: The Fugitives
texts.chapter:chapter-10-fugitives:event:text-:
The Far-Sun Autonomous Observation Program · Cover and Appendix Directory (Observation Room Archive Copy):
“This program is an unmanned autonomous observation mission. Target: candidate exoplanet orbiting

a distant sun.
Appendix directory:
K3-1 Orbit. K3-2 Fuel. K3-3 Payload (Unmanned Observation Group).
K3-4 Communications. K3-5 Launch Window. K3-6 Long-Term Self-Sustainment.
K3-8 Ground Disposal.”

Every morning at eight sharp, the adults continued resolutely carrying out the disposal chain formed the night before. Uncle Otto led people along the main roads to search outward, while Kaine led others in tightly sealing the public village boundary.

The search net pressed all the way down to the roads leading to the outlying facilities. Every day, we had to make practiced use of the gaps between their shifts and the blind spots in their search, slipping through the village outskirts like two ghosts.

Before we discovered the data key describing the capacity shortfall, and learned of the anonymous record-keeper’s cruel calculation that “only eight thousand units are needed to fill the gap,” we had already spent countless loops in the ruins northwest, half-swallowed by the primeval forest. Back then, we

did not understand capacity. We only knew that, to find equipment that could intervene in the slaughter—or at least make the daylight stop—we had to search outward. We knew that road so well that the soles of our feet could remember the shape of every piece of rubble. A few times, we groped through dark

machine rooms and were burned down to our last breath by the old security grid; more often, we simply endured until ten at night among heaps of dead, silent scrap metal. No matter how thoroughly we turned the buildings upside down, we could not find anything capable of establishing contact with the daylight.
Once every console in the northwestern ruins had proved to be a dead end, we turned our attention to that distant place due east.
Kaine almost never mentioned the eastern wasteland or the old-era ruined tower whose outline could be seen from far away. Even when pressed, he always frowned and brushed us off:
“Rockslide.”

Only when we forced him to say more did he reluctantly piece together the whole picture: the old railway heading beyond the boundary toward the plateau had collapsed long ago, leaving only a detour along a dry ravine filled with sharp rubble.

“There’s nothing over there but a pile of useless, rotten iron frames.” He always ended with a weary certainty. “Go around that ravine and the round trip takes two full days. Wild grass. Not even a shelter to spend the night in.”
We had only fourteen hours each day. If the one-way trip really took a whole day, it meant we could never reach the place before
the world switched at ten that night. For a long time, this “uncrossable distance” kept us outside the barren land to the east.
Until that morning, when Yuna stopped at the fork instead of heading toward the ruins in the northwest and turned to look at me.

“Arno, when Kaine says ‘there’s nothing,’ he looks down for a moment,” she said. “He doesn’t look like that when he talks about poisonous gas in the ruins or how bad the road is. Those five words, ‘there’s nothing,’ sound least like a description of the route.”
So that round, we put all our chips on the opposite direction.

The rubble in the deep ravine really did hurt our feet, especially the ankle that inevitably swelled and ached after every reset. Each step sent pain drilling through me. But I forced myself not to slow down. Just after noon, we climbed out of the dry ravine and reached the highland. If we kept up a

decent pace, there was more than enough time to make the round trip before dark. Kaine had deliberately exaggerated the distance, hiding the place behind a wall built out of time. He was not merely describing a wilderness. He knew what was on the plateau, and clearly did not want the villagers to know.

The plateau was immensely open, waist-high wild grass rolling like waves. Along the perimeter ran a narrow path assigned by the Church to laborers who cleared the boundary, though they were strictly forbidden to cross it. Right in the middle of that wilderness stood the colossal object whose outline everyone in the village could see from far away.

It was an extraordinarily tall tower frame. From a distance, its skeleton had completely decayed, the same deathly dark red as the bald utility poles beyond the boundary. Thick iron beams overlapped in layer

after layer, like a vast, rotting net spread over the plateau. The villagers all thought it was merely an unfinished old project, and Kaine had gone along with that, disguising it as an unimportant ruin.
But it was only when we actually reached the foot of the tower that we discovered the thing enclosed in that iron net did not have a trace of rust. It was nothing like Kaine’s “there’s nothing.”
It was a ship.
At first glance, the shock it gave me was that of a giant ship breaking through waves upside down. A huge spindle stood vertically inverted. Its shell was a pure, glaring white, so smooth that
even the wind could not cling to it. More than a hundred years of wind and rain had eaten everything made of steel around it into an appalling rust-red, while it alone remained clean and cold.
“This isn’t right.”
Yuna tipped her head back, her voice pressed low by the wind.
“The iron frame outside has decayed this far. It can’t be a simple sheet of metal that’s been sitting here for a hundred years.”

She walked a few steps forward and pointed at the enclosed boarding gangway connecting the tower frame to the upper-middle section of the ship, and at the faint red bidirectional arrow markings visible on the shell.
“That’s a docking structure reserved for the gangway, and external hatch handles that have to be turned by hand.”
She turned to look at me, a frightening sharpness lighting her eyes.
“Unmanned observation.”
She softly repeated the four words. She had just recognized them in the old language after brushing the dust from a plaque at the base of the tower frame.

“If it were only an automated probe meant to go and never return, it wouldn’t need a design that could connect the cabin directly to space. ‘Unmanned observation’ is a cover, Arno. There’s something else hidden in here.”
Beside the tower frame stood a low concrete house. We pushed open its warped blast door and found the observation room left behind from that era.
One entire wall inside was covered in densely carved stars.

Beside the symbol for every star, a long string of numbers followed, carved with extremely fine blades. At the end of the numbers was a small column of annotations. By the light leaking in, Yuna gnawed her way through the annotations’ core term: liquid-water candidate planet.
“Water,” she said softly, her finger passing over the data. “So they were looking for water in the sky. For somewhere they could survive.”

At the exact center of the entire star map, someone had heavily circled a star in red paint. It bore the marks of countless people calculating it again and again. Beside the star was a yellowed sheet of

conclusions, carrying cautious annotations about the fourth orbit around it: the temperature might be suitable; liquid water might exist. This fourth planet was the place they had truly been looking for.
Yuna stared at the star, then suddenly turned and smiled at me.

“They taught us in physics class that light has to travel through the universe for a very, very long time before it reaches our eyes. What we see now is actually the stars’ light from a long time ago.”
She raised her hand and pointed at the circled star in the exact center without touching it.

“The place this group of people wanted desperately to reach as they tried to leave here was actually what that planet looked like many years ago. They were racing toward an ethereal ‘past,’ betting their lives that it would still be alive by the time they flew there.”
The archive document called The Far-Sun Autonomous Observation Program sat neatly beneath the star map. Yuna opened the directory protected by a dust cover.
The line directly after K3-6 was K3-8.
Yuna lightly ran her fingertip across the glaring gap. There were no traces of paint or cutting. It had simply never been printed there from the moment the directory was compiled.

“There’s a K3-7 missing from here.” She turned to me, her brows drawn together. “Was it deliberately erased? They wouldn’t even let it into the directory… Could this be the thing that wasn’t allowed into the light? Maybe the real crew roster, or the qualifications for boarding.”
She pointed down at the final line.
“And as for that ‘K3-8 Ground Disposal’ afterward… it may well have been for dealing with those who failed to board, or destroying the launch site after disguising it as
an unmanned project. If another ship of the same type was built here and actually left carrying people, then what they left behind was this deadness covering the ground.”
We searched that observation room for more than a dozen rounds and found nothing. There was not a single fragment concerning K3-7.

What truly stopped us from boarding the tower frame were the layers of old security doors peeling away from its exterior. In the first few rounds, the pressure lock at the base of the tower frame had rusted solid, forcing

us to search the surrounding ruins for cutting tools. Once we finally cut through the first line of defense, we were met by a completely paralyzed gangway lift and emergency partition walls that had to be dismantled by hand.

Those initial, tedious efforts to find our way through cost us more days and nights than we could count. After every reset, the doors we had cut open were welded shut again, and the paralyzed lift returned to being an immovable block

of iron. Only after we had learned the weak points of every door and the shortcuts through the emergency passages could we force the dismantling time down to a few hours and finally climb into the cabin at the top of the tower frame.

It was only when we saw the one hundred fifty life-support seats that the nature of the ship became certain. It could not be an unmanned probe carrying instruments. The tower frame and spacecraft outside were real. A group of people had built this monster here in order to escape, and the one before us had been left on the launch tower.

Most incomprehensible of all, it was still alive. The backup circuits inside the craft were still running at low power, while the fuel rods of the main reactor rested silently in the cooling pool. The “K3-6 Long-Term

Self-Sustainment” system left behind more than a hundred years ago had silently performed its duty as a dormant guard in the wilderness, allowing not even a trace of corrosion to enter the pure-white spindle.
The next problem was how to start it. The heavy operating manual hanging beside the console stood between us and the spacecraft’s main engine.
We spent forty full loops on that manual.

In each of those forty worlds, every time I woke, I had to repeat the same actions: evade the patrols, drag my inevitably swollen and painful ankle through the rubble ravine, reopen as quickly as possible the security doors that had restored themselves, and finally sit back down in this control room.

“It’s a procedure. To make that huge thing outside truly fly, we have to get through the hundreds of small items listed here without making a single mistake. And at the very top of every page, there’s a line printed in red—‘Confirmation and execution must be assigned to two separate operators.’”

Not only that, she added, pointing to a dense row of safety rules beneath the red line:
“It locks the roles in place. If I’m the one reading aloud, then I can only be the ‘confirmer.’ During the same flight

authorization, the confirmer absolutely cannot touch any physical switch, while the operator responsible for pressing the buttons cannot get distracted by looking at the confirmer’s screen or manual.”
“Why does it have to be two people? Can’t one person read and press at the same time?” I asked, rubbing my burning ankle and panting heavily.

“Because if it’s the same person, their hands will take shortcuts.” Yuna explained seriously. “The brain gets tired processing repetitive work and presses the buttons out of habit. And habit is the enemy of a procedure this deadly. If one

person is both the eyes and the hands, no one nearby can stop them when they miss something. But when two people work together, I read one line, you carry it out and answer, and we supervise each other. Neither of us can fool the other.”
She hugged the heavy manual to her chest, her eyes growing firm.
“This rule was made exactly right. There are exactly two of us here.”
That heavy manual became the only lesson in our repeated lives. The hardest part was not memorizing the hundreds of pages of tedious parameters, but the gap in time between us.

In every round, I arrived carrying the painful lesson of yesterday’s system lockup. In every round, when she picked up the manual, her eyes still shone with the same unclouded excitement she had shown the first day she saw it.
“Item three hundred twenty-one: secondary circulation pump venting.” She would read the instruction in a voice without a trace of gloom.

And I had to keep my eyes fixed on the valve on the console, my palms slick with cold sweat. Because in yesterday’s memory, this was the valve that had caused the entire console to flare red and lock completely

when she missed half a note. I could not tell her, “You missed this yesterday.” I could only pretend to interrupt her casually before pressing the lever: “Wait. Isn’t there another line of fine print underneath?”
Every tiny mistake cost us another full world’s morning, when I had to endure the pain and put my feet back into that razor-sharp ravine of rubble.
In that disconnect—“I carry every scar, while she is always a newcomer”—we ground hundreds of rigid instructions into my muscle memory. To keep
her first-time cooperation from going wrong, I had to drive every procedure into my bones and catch each command she issued with perfect precision.

Until one round, before dusk, when we finally moved smoothly through every preliminary procedure in the control room. For the first time, all the hundreds of indicator lights on the console turned green, showing ready.

Next came releasing the external physical restraints. Yuna turned to the designated page in the manual and loudly read the unlocking command. I went to the backup panel by the window and gripped with both

hands the huge physical lever responsible for locking the spacecraft in place. As she counted down, I pushed the lever down with all my strength. The heavy pressure lock tore loose with a grating shriek.
Next came the final boarding.
We crossed the gangway and reached the top of the tower frame. The crew cabin stood open, its life-support seats still covered in dust cloth, white and gleaming.
We put on the space suits inside the sealed cabin and secured ourselves in the shock-absorbing seats. On the main control panel, the navigation system had locked onto its only
fixed route—the destination was the planet heavily marked on the star-map wall. The heavy manual had turned to its final page. Only one instruction remained: [Main Engine Start].
In the enormous cabin with one hundred fifty seats, only the two of us sat there.
Yuna did not continue reading the final line.
“Arno, once this final item is confirmed, the hatch will be physically severed from the outside.” Her voice came distorted through the communicator, carrying a cold clarity. “We’re
betting that the death won’t spread that far. But once we press it, the pressure lock outside will come completely loose, and there will be no way back for us in this round.”
My hand stopped above the control panel.
One hundred fifty seats. If we went to race time for the people right now, tricking everyone into exploiting this loophole, perhaps we would only be carrying out a collective execution.
I looked down at the old pocket watch secured to my spacesuit wrist. The second hand moved soundlessly beneath the heavy glass.
I met her eyes and drew a deep breath.
“Someone has to go see first.”
Yuna looked at me silently. Beneath the heavy visor, a trace of resolve flashed in her eyes.
“If we don’t come back,” she said softly, “at least the you in the next round will know this route is a dead end.”
In the steadiest voice she could manage, she read the final instruction in the manual.
My finger pressed hard on the red confirmation button. The hatch shut heavily with a hiss, cutting off the air outside.
At the instant the system countdown ended—
The sound came first. It rose through the steel beneath our feet, the roar of some ancient beast truly waking after being sealed away for a century.

Then came the terrifying gravity. The force slammed me into my seat. Yuna’s hand closed around my forearm in that instant, and even through the heavy spacesuit I could feel the pressure, as though it were trying to crush my bones.
Then, after a long ordeal that left no room to breathe, came absolute lightness.
The roar of the engines faded, and all gravity vanished in an instant. I turned my head with difficulty toward the porthole beside me. Beyond the heavy glass,
the familiar land was falling away at an unbelievable speed. The vast plateau we had once spent half a day reaching shrank into an insignificant rust-colored nail.
Last came the White Tower. The White Tower that symbolized authority, viewed from this height, was only the size of a fingernail, so small it looked like a grain
of white rice fallen on a black tabletop. Farther away, the sea of death that had once swallowed countless people was only a blurred halo at the edge of my vision.
“Arno.”
Yuna’s voice came through the communicator, carrying joy she could no longer suppress.
“Oh my God. We’re in the sky. We really took off.”
I turned to look at her. In zero gravity, her neat, short hair was free for the first time from the pull of the earth, spreading freely on either side of her face.

Laughing, she pulled the six-sided wooden die she always carried from her pocket. It hovered above her palm, slowly turning in the weightless environment. Like a child who had finally escaped a strict parent, she mischievously reached out to play with it.
“Only six sides.” She looked at the blurred phantom and laughed at me. “But it doesn’t matter now. Up here, it doesn’t matter which side is facing up.”
I watched her smile, and an ease I had never felt before rose inside me. Then, from the corner of my eye, I saw the color of the land outside the porthole change.
It was light.

Far below the land outside the porthole, a sickly radiance spread like a rising tide, rapidly flooding the vast valley and soaking the black forest and our village. It was the “daylight” that came each day to settle the list.

Viewed from an extremely high and distant vantage, it was no longer a dome enclosing the sky, but merely a thin film of water drowning a small, pathetic depression on the surface of the earth. It was a sight I knew better than

anything—the moment I closed my eyes, I could imagine what was happening beneath that film: the old man beside the chess stall at the village entrance had fallen; the person on the chapel steps had fallen. The time had come.
And Yuna was laughing, vibrantly alive.
But the way this ship crossed space was completely different from its battered outer tower frame. When the engine’s vibration reached its peak, the long acceleration I had expected never came.

The starlight outside the porthole twisted nauseatingly, every ray of light pulled into countless parallel lines. Then a bottomless silence enclosed the entire sealed cabin.
There was no longer any sensation of flight, but something more like being transported directly, without any transition.
My senses lost any anchor they could cling to, and distance and time lost their meaning in that state. I could not tell whether we had undergone a hundred years of hibernation or merely one second.
When that nauseating sensation of being stripped away finally receded and my senses were forced back into my body, an ear-piercing deceleration alarm was echoing through the cabin. The safety
harnesses tightened abruptly, and gravity returned in an instant. Yuna’s loose hair, floating in midair, dropped sharply back over her forehead, and the spinning wooden die fell with a smack.

The spacecraft landed steadily on something solid, its engines gradually shutting down. A row of green indicators lit up on the control panel. It had completed its entire journey perfectly, stopping precisely on the celestial body marked by dense layers of data.
I looked down at the old watch on my wrist. The second hand was still ticking crisply, mercilessly pointing to 9:40 p.m. No matter how long our senses had been taken from us during
the flight, real time had continued to pass coldly, and the blackout countdown pressing over everyone’s heads was still drawing closer, one second at a time, through the darkness.
With a heavy rush of expelled air, the sealed hatch slowly opened outward.

Yuna looked outside. In the dark currents of air, palm-sized, translucent, thin-winged creatures glided silently past. They were not windblown debris. When they approached the heat source of the landing craft, they

instinctively beat their wings and climbed higher. There was life here. She did not remove her heavy spacesuit to test whether the air was lethal. Holding the heavy operating manual, she lightly descended the gangway.
I leaned half my body out after her.

The spacecraft had landed on an extremely rare boundary between dawn and dusk. Above us was a breathtaking pink-violet sky. One side still held cold daylight; the other sank into a deep black-violet night, with a huge natural satellite hanging there, its surface riddled with canyon-like cracks.

Directly in front of the hatch was a lake so vast it had no visible edge, as still as a dead mirror. Along the shore grew stretches of dark, leaf-shaped organisms. When the weak morning light swept over them, they rapidly folded their leaf edges inward as if they could feel pain.
Yuna walked to the lakeshore and, through her spacesuit glove, solemnly placed the wooden die on a smooth stone. It settled firmly, one side facing the pink-violet sky.
“Arno, look,” she said softly, staring at the die. “This time, one side finally counts.”
She straightened and turned back, opening the operating manual in her arms. The takeoff authorization box on the final page had been checked. Beyond that page was nothing but blank paper.
She drew a deep breath and, in a crisp, authoritative voice, read me an instruction that belonged entirely to her:
“Disembark.”
The wind passed over the dead-still lake. Without thinking, I drew a deep breath of oxygen inside the sealed suit, descended the gangway, and stepped onto this unfamiliar land.
“Instruction confirmed. Down,” I answered, looking at her.
She broke into a brilliant smile.
“That was a quick response.”
“The shore we’re standing on,” she said, raising her head toward the pink-violet sky, “whether it’s within range of that death line—we’ll know soon enough.”

I nodded inside my helmet and glanced at the watch.
“Thirteen minutes left,” I told her. I had already warned her about the death line marked at 9:53 p.m. during the dusks of the past forty rounds. Today was the forty-first.

Nothing changed in the pink-violet sky overhead. No film of light, no alarm. There was only the faint sound of water stirred by the wind across the lake. Yuna kept her head raised, her eyes fixed without blinking on that alien sky.
Time passed second by second. Her breathing sounded steady and strong through the communicator.
I had even begun to sketch in my mind how we would spend our first night on this planet once we truly survived this moment, and how we would bring more people here in the loops to come.
At the instant the hands aligned precisely at 9:53 p.m.—
She suddenly froze, her outstretched hand suspended in midair. Her breathing caught sharply in the communicator, then quickly weakened. Slowly, she lowered
her head and looked at her palm through the visor, then raised her eyes to me. There was no shock in them, only an absurd, finally settled helplessness.
“It still… reaches us.”
Her voice was light as mist through the communicator.
“So even this far away… it can still reach us…”
She fell toward me. I lunged forward and caught her, both hands clamped around the edge of her heavy spacesuit’s visor. Through the faintly glowing
glass, I saw her chest heave once, as if swallowing one last breath with all her strength, then collapse completely, never rising again. Her eyes
lost their focus, and the last trace of light faded from her pupils. Yuna, who had just laughed and said that one side finally counted, went out.

I collapsed to my knees on the unfamiliar land. As the distant star rose above the horizon, a shaft of strong light pierced the clouds and fell over us. The strange plants immediately folded their broad leaves inward, gently enclosing the wooden die.

When the bell of ten o’clock rang on the face of my pocket watch right on time, a familiar weakness that emptied everything spread from the depths of my marrow. The alien landscape before me fell completely into darkness.
When consciousness forcibly crashed back into my brain, familiar, glaring morning light filled the corridor.
The clock hands pointed to eight o’clock in the morning.
I opened my eyes sharply. My back was against the cold metal wall along the outer edge of the White Tower calibration zone. This was the unchanging starting point of every loop.
But my nerves were still stranded on that distant lakeshore. My arms jerked forward uncontrollably, trying to clutch something—
But they caught only the cold air of the corridor.

The fading deceleration alarm and her last weak sigh still lingered in my ears. My legs gave way, and I collapsed onto my knees on the anti-slip mat, waiting desperately, like a madman, for someone to crisply read the next operating instruction beside my ear.
The entire corridor was silent as death.
“Arno?” A familiar voice sounded above me, full of confusion and concern. “What’s wrong? You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”
I did not look up. Trembling, I reached out and grasped the hand she held toward me. I knelt there, gripping her hand tightly—through her skin, I felt warmth. It
was warm, with no heavy spacesuit covering it. Only then did I dare slowly move my gaze to the floor. There were no folding leaves there, and no pink-violet sky.

I opened my mouth, unable to force out even half a word. I remained there on my knees, gripping her hand, for so long that she anxiously pulled one hand away and waved it several times in front of my eyes.
The battered spacecraft had not broken. It had completed its mission perfectly and carried us exactly there.
But the Yuna in that universe would never wake again.

That windy afternoon, I sat beside the wheat field and quietly told the Yuna of the current loop what we had discovered on the eastern plateau, and about the dead end that followed the spacecraft’s final ascent.
The wind moved through the wheat with a rustling sound. Later, she spoke calmly:
“Arno, I know you want me to give you a verdict from my current perspective, to tell you whether that flight across such a vast distance counts as a success or a failure.”

“…Yeah.” I forced the syllable from my throat. From the day we first set out into the wilderness, we had sunk forty-one dead dusks into this spacecraft and that tedious manual. That did not include the dozens of days and nights we had spent dismantling the security doors around the observation room before that.
“Then I won’t. Because I genuinely don’t know the answer.”
She withdrew her gaze and watched the wheat waves shifting in the distance.
“You said I laughed aloud inside that weightless cabin. And that I watched that sky with my own eyes, walked to that lakeshore on my own feet, and only then closed my eyes.”
She turned her head toward me, her expression calm.
“The loops that stay here waiting to die are our only chips. But this time”—she lowered her eyes—“I opened the door with my own hands and walked beneath another sky.”
After everything had been said, a long, dead silence settled beside the wheat field.
After a long while, she turned her head toward the village.

“If we choose to fly upward, the ending is the same no matter how far we escape…” She raised her hand and pointed straight at the White Tower in the center of the village, the symbol of its central secret. “Then there’s only one place left to go.”
Then she stood, slapped the dirt from her palms, and jerked her chin toward the White Tower. In the most ordinary tone, she said: “Let’s go back.”
She walked ahead without looking back. Her voice was broken apart by the wind and carried into my ears, light and drifting, as if she were sleepwalking:
“Arno, tell me everything that happened over there tonight. I really want to know what kind of sky that dead version of me… saw at the end.”
On many nights afterward, I would lift my head and search the vast sea of stars for that shining one.
I knew its exact position in the real night sky—three finger-widths above the top of the prayer room’s ridgepole.
There was a cold, still lakeshore there. On that shore was a leaf that folded inward under the light, and a six-sided wooden die that had stopped turning and settled firmly.

After watching for a while, I would sit on the steps before the porch. Yuna was still in the house behind me, just as she had been on the dozens of nights before, absorbed in studying the old equipment she had newly discovered that day, with no memory of ever having been there.
I would sit there quietly, waiting for the next eight-o’clock bell to ring.
texts.chapter:chapter-11-last-meal:title: Chapter Eleven: The Last Meal
texts.chapter:chapter-11-last-meal:event:text-: Within this time loop, so long it became impossible to tell reality from anything else, I once gave myself one last day off.
The formal dress I wore on the first morning was something Mother had worked on for two months, finishing it in a rush on the final night. White ground with a subdued pattern, an extremely
fine crimson trim pressed around the collar, the loose thread at the cuff that she had carefully picked away—I had left it in that original morning. It was probably still hanging over
the back of the chipped chair in my house. The world that had never been interfered with had not stopped because I left it behind. Its future simply no longer had anything to do with me.
What I hadn’t had time to think through then was how the old tool belt had been repaired.

It was an old dark green belt, the only hint of deep color anywhere on me that day. The night before the seven-day process began, she dug it out from the bundle at the very back of the cabinet. The way she handled it was different from the way she handled other things. Her

movements were light, as though afraid of disturbing something. Beneath the dim oil lamp, she used a sturdy piece of new cloth to replace the long-cracked section of lining inside the belt. She sewed it one stitch at a time, all backstitches driven backward to press the seam tight.
It was not until the next morning, when she took it out to tie around me, that she casually admitted it had been Father’s.

In the countless “todays” that followed, the belt was tied around my waist on time every morning. I learned the new stitches in the repaired lining by touch—I could find them by running my fingers along the grain

of the cloth and giving it a twist. At the seventh eyelet, the thread was layered densely, locked in place with three hard stitches. It was like a short stretch of words, interrupted before they could be finished.

During the long rotations spent looking for a way out, every so often I gave myself a day off. Yuna called it a “going-home rotation”—she came up with the name casually while I was laying out the materials for her, then added, after a moment’s thought:
“Schedule more of these rotations. This is a debt too. Leave it unpaid long enough and the interest compounds.”
During those going-home rotations, I lived in this home all over again, inch by inch.

I helped her bring every old bundle out from beneath the cabinet and spread them in the courtyard to dry in the sun, listening as she sat cross-legged on a small wooden stool and recounted the history of each old thing. I pickled vegetables with her and learned her particular method for

pressing down the rim of the crock—first pressing firmly with the heel of her palm, then smoothing along the edge with the pads of her fingers, and finally turning her wrist with steady force through half a circle. I climbed onto the roof and patched the leaking gaps between the tiles,

found scraps of cloth and oil, and carefully oiled the hinges. The hinges had been squeaking for years. She had long since grown used to that “creak.” But the next day—the next identical today—when the hinges made the same dry sound, I took the same oil and brushed them again as usual.
Some jobs I did more than a dozen times. The world didn’t remember, but I did. A craft, like the guilt in a person’s heart, became more practiced the more you accumulated.
I also used that illusion of peace to ask about things I had never asked before.
“How did you and my father meet?”
She was sitting on a small wooden stool, picking beans. When she heard that, her hands stopped in midair for half a beat.
“What made you bring that up?”
Though she complained as she said it, not a single bean in her hands was picked.
“We met at the market. He was good at chess and didn’t talk much. Your grandmother thought he was dull back then. I said dull was good. A dull person could keep things inside.”
“Keep what inside?”
“Keep what inside—”
She bent the old bean in her hand with force, making it crack sharply.
“Keep me inside, I suppose.”

Whenever she spoke of Father, her tone was complicated. Pride and reproach each took up half of it, mixed together so tightly they could not be separated. She said he had skilled hands; every stool and table in the house, large or small, had been made by him alone, slowly and well, fitted

together without a gap. She said he was stubborn about principles; once he had decided something, not eight horses could pull him back. She said he was mild-tempered and never argued with anyone, but whenever the village held a council, anything he did not nod to never got done in the end.
“If your father were here—”

She stopped abruptly there. Whenever she spoke of Father, she stopped at that point. I had heard that half-sentence from childhood into adulthood, and its second half had never appeared in our house. The sadness was real, but it was not the only reason she stopped herself so forcefully.
That second half was an iron rule she could not say aloud.
And on the morning of this final going-home rotation, I walked into the mill’s dust like a real apprentice.
When I pushed open the heavy doors, Galon was there, covered in dust, counting sacks. He stopped writing when he saw me enter and gave a heavy snort through his nose:
“The sun’s risen in the west.”
He casually tossed aside his charcoal pencil, then pointed at the heaviest pile of wheat in the corner.

I said nothing. I went over and hauled wheat all morning. Outside, the waterwheel turned with a rumble. The millstones ground together heavily, making a teeth-grating friction. Beside me, Galon cursed the uneven turn of the wheel in long strings, without stopping for breath, all rough, vivid words. I let him curse. I simply put my

strength into the work mechanically, following the rhythm of the millstones, emptying my mind and thinking of nothing. It was not until noon, when sweat had soaked completely through the coarse cloth on my back and wheat chaff mixed with it, sticking to my neck and making it itch, that I suddenly understood what I was doing in that smell.
I was living my old life.

In those old days, I was just an ordinary mill apprentice. At dusk, I finished work, washed the dust off, and went home. When I pushed open the door, there was always hot food steaming on the table, and always someone beneath the lamplight talking on and on to me. Across countless

todays, I had moved through innumerable parallel branches, turned this village upside down, and memorized every death in a list precise to the second—but I had not lived those old days, with their smell of sweat and sourness and the warmth of cooked food, for a very long time.

That evening, I went home for dinner. When I pushed open the door, Mother was coming out of the stove room with the soup pot in her hands. She froze when she saw me enter—the thing that stopped her was how I looked: wheat chaff in my hair, a distinct red mark pressed into my shoulder, the unmistakable disheveled look of an apprentice.
“Well,” she said, the wrinkles at the corners of her eyes relaxing as the corners of her mouth lifted despite herself.
“Did the mill fail to grind you away today?”

At dinner, she talked on for a long time, about the gossip down the street and the price of vegetables at the market. I did not hurry to shovel down my food and leave as I usually did. I held my bowl and listened quietly through the whole meal’s rambling talk.

The cruel truth pieced together in the underground production line—that as long as someone secured a position among the Inner Circle elders, they could change bodies and keep living—had been pressing against my chest all this time. I waited quietly until she had ladled two bowls of steaming soup, then spoke:
“On the night of the fourth day, I asked whether the elders of the central village changed bodies to keep living. You admitted it too.”
She sat down across from me, resting her hands on the edge of the table without touching her chopsticks.
I stared at the oil floating on the surface of the soup and pushed out the second half.
“You said then that Dad died of a sudden illness because he hadn’t made the schedule for a body change.”
I raised my head and looked straight into her eyes.

“But if he simply fell ill and missed the schedule, why was the entire section of paper beneath his name in the thick parish register cut away with a knife? Why was his record in the inquiry terminal frozen, locked down completely?”
Silence fell over the room. Only the half-extinguished coals in the stove collapsed, making one abrupt, crisp crackle.
Her hand, which had been reaching for the soup ladle, froze in midair.
“Don’t ask me what they did to the register outside,” she said. Her voice was very low, edged with resistance.

“I’m not asking about outside. I’m asking about home.” I looked at her. “Mom, after he died sick, there isn’t even a mound of earth in the village where people can pay their respects. How is that missing the schedule?”

She stared at me for a while, then set the chopsticks in her hands straight and aligned on the tabletop, every movement precise. The rambling tone of her usual household chatter had been taken away entirely.
“Missing the schedule… That was just what they told outsiders.”
She drew a deep breath and looked away from me.

“That night, he was too sick to get out of bed. The elders came rushing over through the night, carrying the arrangement from above. Your father sat beside the bed and gave them one answer: Leave nothing behind.

He withdrew of his own accord.” Her voice was steady, almost cold. “So they took the body away according to the rules for withdrawal. That was what he chose. He wanted to wipe the house clean of his things too.”
“Wipe it clean?”
“The furniture he made, and the sewing records here.”
She lifted her chin toward the old wooden stool in the corner.
“He had a rule when he made things. He carved a hidden mark underneath. But after he decided not to go through with it, he took a plane and shaved away every hidden mark in the house, large
and small, one by one. And the records here—measurements, shoulder width, arm length, waist, the location of that old injury—he said this book, kept for more than twenty years, couldn’t remain.”
I didn’t understand.

“If the marks are destroyed, the furniture is still his work. If the records are burned, the old things he used are still here. If this was about leaving no trace, why not destroy these dead things too?”
Her callused hands pressed hard against her knees, as though she had to force the wrinkles out of the fabric.

“He didn’t have to destroy the dead things. He despised the measurements and habits taken away as proof,” she said. “The records above were detailed. They even recorded a person’s stride and the way they moved their hands while

working. He said he couldn’t control the official registers, but he couldn’t keep cooperating by leaving things behind at home. ‘I’m not going down that road. I’m not leaving behind material they can use to make a mold of me.’”

My throat tightened. He couldn’t storm into the parish and burn those official records, much less stop that enormous system from preserving his file. But he would rather drag his sick body through the house and erase every trace that could

be measured than leave behind the slightest trace of a living person’s submission to that system. Before an institution that archived even stride and hand movements as spare material, this was the last refusal he could make while alive.
“Then did you burn everything?”
Mother did not answer at once. After a long while, she said quietly:
“That book was burned.”

“But when I was bringing the bundles out from under the cabinet to dry them today, I saw a newly bound thin booklet.” I looked at her. “Most of the pages inside were blank. Only the first page had writing on it, recording the stitch method for repairing the tool belt.”
She braced herself on her knees and stood, walked to the wooden cabinet in the corner, and took the thin new booklet from the bottom drawer.
She returned to the table, opened it, and gently pushed it in front of me.
Dark green belt, old. Original owner: him.
Replace the cracked lining with new cloth. Do not replace the old fastenings.
Follow the line of stitches he used back then. At the seventh eyelet, lock three stitches in place. Do not change it.
When an old thing is passed on, everything sewn into it must remain.
I lowered my head and looked at the familiar handwriting on the page.
“So the original book really was destroyed. You rewrote this page later.”
“I rewrote it,” she said softly.
“Why?”
Her fingers brushed lightly over the rough surface of the paper.
“I wondered whether that meant I had gone against his wishes. I wondered for a long time.”
She raised her eyes, her gaze clear.
“Later I understood. I kept those records for more than twenty years, so they belonged to me too. He wanted his peace. I wanted my rule for continuing to sew things for you.”
She pushed the booklet a little back toward me, very slowly.

“This page has none of his measurements, none of his old injuries. Only one thing: when he sewed to the seventh eyelet, he insisted on driving three extra stitches into the same spot to lock it tight. He said that was where the strain fell. This page can’t piece him back together. This page is the one I insisted on keeping.”
I looked at the side of her face illuminated by the oil lamp.
“What about you?” I asked softly.
“What?”
“Dad chose to withdraw.” My voice was hoarse. “But you were one of those ten people too. Why didn’t you withdraw with him back then, and instead choose to keep accepting their arrangement?”
She watched the firelight flicker and was silent for a long time. Her expression grew very gentle.
“Because I gave birth to you,” she said.

“He despised those arrangements. In the end, he would rather die than bow his head. But I couldn’t let go. If I had broken with the people above like he did and given up my position in the Inner Circle too, who would have protected you while you grew up in this village?”
She pushed the thin booklet all the way to my hand.
“And one day, you’ll have to keep sewing.”
I sat rigidly on the bench, staring at the booklet she had pushed toward me. My throat felt blocked by something, and I could not say a word.
Her arrangement was to stay and take care of me. His arrangement was to leave the system by that means, whatever it took.
I remembered the time I went to the water channel to share dried rations with Yuna. She carefully separated a small dish of pickled vegetables and brought it protectively in front of
herself, saying: “I’ll eat this. You don’t eat this.” She remembered that I had vomited after eating these vegetables at her house when I was seven, so she quietly moved them away every time.
But sitting across from her then, the thought that flashed through my mind was this: if I took the dish away along with her hand, then according to the reaction weights measured in the previous
rotation, there was a sixty-percent chance that surprise would make her lean forward. Using that brief loss of balance, I could quietly take the warehouse keys hanging on the wooden hook behind her.
Yuna’s protective gesture over her food, the old thing she remembered for me—all of it had been broken down into a set of fixed parameters I could use to get the keys.
My fingers gave an involuntary twitch, and the chopsticks dropped onto the table with a sharp clatter.
Mother thought I had eaten too quickly and choked.
She hurriedly stood, reached across the table, and pounded my back.
I waved to her with a pale face and said I was fine, then lowered my head and drank the soup in great gulps, forcing those thoughts down.
She watched me gulping down the soup and tapped the rim of my bowl.
“Slow down,” she said. “The soup’s getting cold.”
I drank the rest of that bowl of soup very slowly.
Halfway through, she closed the thin booklet.
“The thing was passed on to you, and the rule was passed on to you too. If you ever pass it on again, don’t change those three stitches of his.”
I looked into her eyes.
“I won’t.”

“Mm,” she said. The promise must have put her at ease. Then her rambling household tone returned, like a river blocked up and finally flowing back into its old channel: she began saying that the old belt had to be hung

somewhere ventilated so it wouldn’t mildew, that this dark green faded to white after only a little sun, and complaining that I always tied the belt crooked, even though I was a grown man now and ought to care about appearances—
I sat quietly at the table and listened. I didn’t miss a single word.
The meal lasted longer than usual. By the time we had finished eating and washing the bowls, dusk had begun to settle.
We sat in the courtyard. The lively sounds of dinner at Yuna’s house next door came clearly from beyond the courtyard wall.

First came Galon’s rough, booming voice, followed by Meru’s sharp scolding as she slapped the table and told him to keep it down, then Milu’s bright, chirping voice as she held something up and asked for praise. Last came Yuna’s—even through the

thick earthen wall, I could tell she was solemnly undercutting her little sister. Milu bristled in anger, prompting a burst of laughter from the whole family. The clatter of bowls and chopsticks filled the air with the warmth of ordinary life.
Mother was standing in the courtyard, gathering the clothes that had dried in the day. She tilted her ear toward the sounds next door for a while, then smiled gently:
“That family makes eating a meal sound like a festival.”
After gathering the clothes, she carried the stack of coarse garments and sat down on the wooden stool in the courtyard.
“Their liveliness is theirs. The two of us can be quiet. Quiet is good too.”

The two of us. She said those three words with complete naturalness, so smoothly that my chest tightened. This courtyard had once belonged to three people. Now the only thing left around me was the old dark green belt around my waist.
“Mom.”
“Do you think my father was right?”
Her hands stopped in midair as she folded the clothes.
“I don’t know,” she said.
She said those three words decisively, without the slightest hesitation.
“I can’t think as far ahead as he did. I only know one thing—that was his life, and he decided it himself. Once he decided, someone had to respect it. I did.”
She pressed the folded clothes flat across her knees and patted them.
We sat there in the courtyard until the pale light that would announce destruction rose.
She watched the sky darken little by little from a deep blue into pure black. I brought over a stool and sat close beside her.
“Tomorrow is market day,” she said, looking at the distant night sky. “Do you need anything? I’m going to replenish the needles, thread, and buttons.”
“No.”
I leaned against the wall.
“Mom, today was good.”
“What was wrong with today?” she asked, baffled.
“Nothing.”
“It was just good. The food was good. The conversation was good too.”
She turned and gave me a sidelong look, as though checking whether working had given me a fever. Then my nonsensical remark made her laugh. She reached out and patted my knee.

“Silly boy,” she said with a laugh. She said nothing more, only settled comfortably against the back of the chair and began humming an off-key village song, her fingers tapping lightly against her knee, once after another.
At last, the darkness became complete. The stars across the sky lit up.
Then the night sky lit up impossibly bright.

When the earth began to tremble and she stood up in terror, I caught her by the arm. She raised her head and looked at the ghastly white light swallowing the stars. As in every previous rotation I had witnessed, her lips trembled as she silently recited a prayer to the gods.
The next fifty minutes were extremely long.

Death did not descend all at once. During that first half hour or more, the invisible list, in the deathly silent village, called only four names, very slowly. The two old men at the chess stall by the village entrance were first, then the village chief, and finally all the way to the threshold of my house.

The entire village fell into a stunned silence beneath the ghastly white light. Terrified, she leaned against the doorframe, her fingers clenched tightly around my sleeve. I simply took her callused hands tightly in mine and sat with her on the threshold, feeling that real trembling together.
“Mom.”
“I finished the soup. Not a drop left.”

She lowered her head and looked at me, her eyes full of fear at the scene of the end of the world. She had no idea what I was saying. She did not need to understand. Like an ordinary person, she simply grasped the only person beside her whom she could grasp in that irresistible night.
Until the moment of 21:26 drew near.

Her rapid breathing suddenly paused. She seemed to feel something taking her away. In that final glance, she looked at me sitting beside her, deep fear still lingering in her eyes, yet out of habit, almost by instinct, she squeezed out the sentence she had murmured all her life:
“Silly boy… tomorrow is another new day.”
She went limp and made no sound again.

I guided her down along the doorframe until she was seated securely, then settled her head against it. I remained sitting beside her on the threshold, gripping tightly with one hand the hand that had picked beans for a lifetime, the other pressed against my waist, waiting quietly.
Waiting for the purge to arrive, for my turn.
I knew this was the last time I would give myself a day off. From tomorrow onward, I would never return to these unchanged days.
At my waist, on the new section of cloth replacing the belt’s inner lining, the three stitches locked hard in place pressed into my palm. Everything sewn into it remained.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:title: Chapter Twelve: The Visitor
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s2: That investigative dossier on Yuna was something we opened ourselves, in violation of the rules, inside the chapel.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s3: The records room was hidden behind the chapel's front hall. It was Elder Sera's domain. The air always held the stale smell of paper and ink. Yuna had copied scripture and been
reprimanded there since childhood; she could list, with her eyes closed, exactly what was kept in every compartment of every cabinet—except one. The bottom compartment was always locked.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s5: “The locked compartment is opened by the elder only once a year,” she once told me one morning. “Without fail.”
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s6: A special tamper-evident seal was affixed around the inside of the lock's keyhole. Any tool of the wrong shape inserted into it would tear the fragile edge of the paper seal. The only thing that could avoid the seal perfectly and engage directly with the base was the original brass key.

Across several dozen loops, we tried to learn the six-second gap when Elder Sera went into the corridor to fetch water. But six seconds was nowhere near enough to unlock it and read the file. Until that day, when we jammed a length of extremely fine metal wire into the pulley assembly

of the clock tower's main shaft, producing an ear-splitting metallic screech. The elder was lured out of the records room to call for a repair worker. She left in too much of a hurry and dropped the small ring of keys on the desk.
That bought us a full fifteen-minute window of safety.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s8: When the thick bound volume was finally opened, Yuna found the section belonging to her among the dense black marks. This official assessment volume was used to establish records for candidates aged fifteen and over. But when she opened the first page bearing her name, the timestamp had been stamped from the year she was seven.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s9: The pages whispered softly beneath her fingertips.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s1: Everything recorded there was about her. It recorded how, as a child, she had dismantled the wooden rail of the prayer room's paper receptacle and secretly put it back. It recorded how, at nine, she had been caught altering the order of the morning devotional

lesson. Even that line about the wooden die—‘God does not care about a single roll, only the number of rolls’—had not only been archived verbatim; a note in thin, narrow handwriting had been added beside it: Note: subject was unaware of the danger of this statement.

“They've watched me for ten whole years.” When she reached the final page and her gaze stopped on the latest date, she finally spoke, her voice flat as though reading a verdict concerning someone else.
I held my breath, waiting for her to bristle, waiting for her to lose her temper or tear the page to pieces.
But she didn't. She simply went through the dossier once more from beginning to end. This time, the emotion in her eyes had changed—miraculously, she had become that sharp-eyed ‘observer’ again.
“Look at this.” Her fingertip stopped on a marginal note: ‘Recommended handling: Do not suppress. It will be useless once suppressed.’
She snapped the volume shut. Those ears that were never still now lay completely flat, pressed into her hair.

“I thought I was rebelling. Turns out I've been taking an exam this whole time.” She spoke with a clarity that sent a chill through me. “They know exactly where the danger is, and exactly where the use lies. Even my crossing of the line was part of the way they went along with their own calculations.”
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s2: With the fifteen minutes nearly up, she put the bound volume back in the bottom compartment without shifting it by so much as a fraction, then locked it again. Even the angle at which the latch was pressed down and the position of the key on the desk were restored with absolute precision.
When we stepped out of the hall, the sunlight was so harsh it made us squint. She suddenly added, her voice as light as if speaking to herself:
But after we'd crossed the front courtyard and started down the dirt road home, she continued the thought herself.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s3: “I looked at the index and the binding thread. In this volume, which establishes records at fifteen, every person's first document bears a timestamp from the year they were seven. That means that for the eight years before the volume was bound, my records were kept separately somewhere else.”
She stopped and turned around, looking deeply through the morning mist toward the chapel's steeple.

“Milu is twelve this year. The family kept seed stock for her future entry into the Church. The Church has ample reason to secretly record her from the age of seven, just as they recorded me.” She thrust

her hands deep into her sleeves, and her voice acquired a faint tremor. “Arno, if I run, the place won't simply disappear. As long as she's also in the pool being observed, they can pull out a loose file

recording five years of her life at any time and raise her up to fill the vacancy. How am I supposed to leave her to a Church that treats us as expendable material and calculates around us for ten years?”
That heavy possibility came down like an invisible bolt, pressing hard upon us. Even though it was only an unverified conjecture, we didn't dare gamble Milu's life on it.
“What if we took the time to persuade her and brought her with us?” I asked.
“A twelve-year-old child with Church lessons every morning and evening and her parents watching her all the time, who doesn't even know she's being recorded.” Yuna shook her
head with a bitter smile. “Even if we managed it, then what? As long as the machine's gap remains, the Church will pull out another loose file and fill in another child's name.”

The weight of that fear was far more effective than any guard. As long as this loop continued, the physical distance we could cover on foot could never pull anyone out of the shadow of the Church's surveillance. Escape outward couldn't solve the vacancy that devoured people. It would only hand the blade to the next innocent.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s4: Since escape outward couldn't solve the list, we could only turn back and hammer away at the old machine inside the White Tower. Until one morning when a new loop began.

The moment I opened my eyes today, I was standing in that familiar corridor of the White Tower. But the angle of the light in the air was wrong. The morning light had climbed far higher than it normally did at exactly eight. I turned to look at the control panel on the wall. It reported the time with cold precision: eight ten.
My body was rigid against the wall, like someone who had just endured an immense weight, gasping for breath.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s5: Yuna was standing three steps in front of me.

She didn't come over to slap my shoulder as she usually did. She stared fixedly at me, her face as pale as a sheet of paper held up to the light. Both hands clenched the cuffs of her sleeves, her ears hanging very low beside her cheeks. Her eyes were red.

At the sound of my voice, her whole body jolted violently as if electrocuted. Her chest heaved, like someone who had held their breath deep underwater for too long and had finally broken the surface to draw their first breath. She didn't answer at once. Instead, she stared at my face for a long time, with extreme care.
“I've been here the whole time. What happened just now?”
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s6: “For that entire ten minutes—from exactly eight until now,” she said, staring at me and shaking her head with certainty, “the person using your body wasn't you.”
She bit her lip, forcing down the tremor in her voice. “That feeling… it was so much like someone saying goodbye to me for the last time.”

A loud buzz went off in my head.
Something similar had happened in the loops before this. After the initial White Tower elevator accident, when we'd fallen into the underground hall, I had woken inside the machine in the maintenance

compartment below. There had been a memory gap of more than ten minutes then. Yuna told me afterward that I had acted like a different person and left behind the words, ‘No matter what happens, I'll come back and fulfill my promise.’

That was a distant promise. And now, because of these ten minutes that had vanished out of nowhere, another consciousness seemed to have crossed the boundary for real and crashed down heavily onto this ordinary timeline.
“So I'm going to set a rule for you. Someone who desperately wants to cry will inevitably twist the account into the shape she wants. I can't do

that.”
She drew a deep breath, and her speech quickened. “Listen: when I say ‘I saw,’ that is a physical fact captured by my own eyes. When I say ‘I
guess,’ that is my personal inference. Everything else is what he left in his own words. I won't mix the three. You can interrupt me at any time.”
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s7: “Okay.” I forced down the panic in my chest.

“I saw that your movements and the look in your eyes changed completely during those ten minutes. When you first opened your eyes, your knees were weak, and you almost slid down the wall with your hands against it. You looked at my face for several seconds, checking it. Tears kept circling in your eyes, but they didn't fall.”
“Based on your expression, I guess it was someone who firmly believed he had lost me before. By observing my reaction, he was confirming my existence to himself.”
As we made our way out of the high tower, she continued.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s8: To verify where he had come from, after her initial shock she had thrown him a test question. On this timeline, it was the only absolute variable she could be certain no outsider knew—a way to test whether the visitor could truly access the memories originally held by this body.
“So I asked him what I had done for him at seven fifty-eight that morning—two minutes before he appeared.”

“He said the shoelace on his left foot had come loose, and I crouched down to tie it for him.” She glanced at me. “We had agreed in advance to use that question for self-verification, and he answered it without the slightest error. But that only proves he can read the memories this body had just experienced locally.”
“After we finished confirming that answer, I tried to touch his shoulder, but he avoided me.” Yuna's voice dropped. “It was what he said afterward that gave me another guess.”
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s9: “The things he volunteered. He said: ‘I took you away from this village once, to a place beneath a purple sky, but the escape still failed in the end. I still couldn't bring you back.’”
The alien lakeshore beneath the purple sky. On this first morning, the Yuna before me shared only the most basic common investigation. I had never told her about this.

“While saying it, he kept his head lowered, looking at his hands as though checking whether there was blood on them.” Yuna lowered her eyes slightly, imitating his gaze. “Then he mentioned the cost. He said: ‘The engineering limit for

filling the machine's gap is eight thousand. That engineering specification for the new-human vessel with the ten-thousand reading is indeed enough to cover it. But that can't determine who should ultimately deal with all of this.’”
The number eight thousand. That brutal threshold representing the number of people to be sacrificed. I had never mentioned that to her either.

“The faster he spoke, the more it seemed as though he were chasing something that was slipping away. After that, he said: ‘I've gone to ten adults, but after understanding the true cost, not one of them was willing to carry their consent through to the end.’”
Ten people. That too was something I had worked out by testing across different loops, while she listened now as though it were someone else's story.
texts.chapter:chapter-12-visitor:event:text-s1: “One last thing.” Yuna drew a deep breath. “He suddenly stopped, looked at me from half a step away, and his eyes were full of some kind of guilt I couldn't understand. He said: ‘I once used a
private fact another you had told me—the fact that you split half of your induction seed stock with the orphan next door—to bypass your judgment. And you were right. That was why you left me.’”
The failed loop in which my test had made her slam the door and leave. The Yuna before me had no memory of it either.
Those four passages were all despair and failure I had experienced separately during those fragmented explorations across different loops. And now, someone
who had occupied my body for ten minutes had hurled them like a final reckoning straight at Yuna on this morning, who knew nothing of what came after.
We had already left the high tower and entered the morning wheat field. Yuna still maintained the clarity of an observer: she treated those four passages as testimony, not a verdict.
“Yuna, did he leave anything else before he disappeared?”
She held her hand flat at her side and looked at me with clear eyes.
“Near the end of the ten minutes, he looked at me and left one last sentence.”
“‘If I can't prove that was you, I shouldn't call her by your name.’”
She finished speaking quietly, released the cuff she had been clutching all this time, and looked once toward the depths of the wheat field. Then she said nothing more.

This clearly was no longer about the morning of this loop. What had the “me” who occupied my body for ten minutes encountered after losing Yuna? At the end of this soul-devouring machine, had he used so-called “information” to piece together someone who could replace her? But he had refused.

Yuna drew back her gaze and sighed very softly.
“He was afraid.” It sounded as though she were answering the departing visitor, or perhaps speaking to me.

texts.chapter:chapter-13-uncountable:title: Chapter Thirteen: Beyond Counting
texts.chapter:chapter-13-uncountable:event:tex:
Boundary Guard Record · List of Items Recovered Below the Cliff (entered by Kane while on duty):
“Male, sixteen. Internal candidate (eligibility suspended).
Clothing: candidate formal wear, worn at the right shoulder. Crease at the collar. Waist: old dark-green belt, intact.
In pockets: a handful of dried

fruit. One length of charcoal pencil. Seven stones—four in the left pocket, three in the right.
No suicide note.
Family: mother, alive. Notified. Mother remained beside the body until dark. Did not cry. Straightened his clothes.
Disposition: report to the elder on duty. Note: candidate anomaly, cause unknown.”
Most of the yellowed registers and old receipts cited in this book are originals I found in the archives after leaving the village. Only this one was fabricated by me.
I never saw Kane fill out the form, nor did I see my mother claim the body. But I had seen the unchanging format Kane used when recording corpses. Across those countless returning dusks, I had leapt

from the cliff alone dozens of times, whenever no one was around. I knew that if anyone managed to find the bottom of the ravine before dusk fell, if a record were left behind, it would look like this.
Later, I went through Kane’s register for that year. By then, I had not returned to the village for a long time.
Among the deaths Kane had recorded that year, not one was named Arno. I turned to the date corresponding to that day. Blank. Not even an extra scratch of the pen.

In the world recorded by that register, my death by falling had never happened at all. Looking at that perfectly natural blank, everything seemed to have been wiped away clean. But I knew that records, like bodies, had remained forever in the times and spaces where I had died.
At first, I tried counting those returning dusks in my head. When the number approached three hundred, I lost count completely. There had been too many accidents around then. A few
days of letting my guard down, and the number no longer matched anything. Later, I was too lazy to pick it up again. I simply let every day melt into the same long, boundless daylight.

There was no helping it. Counting became a ritual. Whether the starting point was the original eight o’clock or the new starting point of eight ten that began one day, every morning, after Yuna finished verifying me and we confirmed which route we were to take that day, I would walk back to the

village alone. At the crack beside the third paving stone outside the threshold, by the well, at the base of the fence, and at the bend in the field path, I picked up four stones and put them in my left pocket. Then, at three other fixed places, I picked up three more and put them in my right pocket.

Those seven stones had long since stopped being for counting. The number had already rotted away inside me. They kept track of this: as long as I was still bending down to pick them all up, it meant I still intended to endure this day with no end in sight.

As long as I made it to the end, my consciousness would continue the next day inside an undamaged body in another world. No worn-through soles. No scabbed-over wounds. The only thing that remained was the exhaustion carved into my mind.
That morning, Yuna emerged from the wheat field drenched in sweat, three irritating awns caught in the back of her collar. For ten years, I had habitually brushed them away for her.
This time, my hand rose halfway, stopped abruptly, and fell back into the pocket holding the stones.
She walked ahead of me, her neck itching badly. She raised her shoulders awkwardly and reached back to scratch it, but could not reach, so she walked on while complaining.
I followed behind her. When we passed the third stone-picking place in the original plan—the base of the fence—I walked past it indifferently. There was plenty of time. I could have reached
out to help her, then bent down and picked up the stone. But I simply did not want to move. I did not even want to spend the three seconds it would take to brush the awns from her collar.

For the rest of that day, I had only six stones in my pocket. It was the first time I discovered that when a person finds even picking up all the stones too much trouble, he can still make it to dark without missing a step.

And Milu. It took me hundreds of dusks to complete that death-order table, detailed to the point of cruelty. For a while, every cycle I took a detour to the yard to look at her—not to record data. I just wanted to see her.
But that cycle, I reached the entrance to the yard and stopped.
Milu was clumsily tugging at the string. The kite refused to rise. Her little face was flushed with frustration as she stamped her feet in place.
I told myself silently: Confirmed. She is there.

Then I turned and left without hesitation. I did not walk over to greet her as I had before, or even look again at her dejected face. After walking twenty-some steps, I calculated silently: the detour had cost me four minutes.

The death-order table recorded 257 people in the village besides me. I once divided them in my mind into a list: those I could never bear to watch die; those I could endure watching; and those I could ignore no matter what.
But after only a few months, everyone in the second category had been crossed out and moved into the third.
Only Yuna and my mother remained.
