When those 255 people fell again and again into the same blood-red dusk, I no longer thought of them as more than two hundred human lives. I was merely using their unchanging places of death to plan the shortest route to the next place where I had to investigate a clue.
At the northwest corner of the village, at the end of the herders’ path, there was a cliff. A dead, crooked-necked tree jutted diagonally out over its edge.
On mornings like that, after Yuna heard my account, she would sometimes wave me away with a cold face: “Not today. You sound too frightening today. We’ll talk another day.”
When she said “another day,” the clues that required her authorization and two-person operation ended early in that cycle. She turned away to attend to her own work, leaving
me alone. I had long since exhausted every deduction that could be carried out alone. Once she was out of the picture, the dozen-odd hours ahead were an abandoned blank.

The gray exit key that could be triggered in my consciousness simply by closing my eyes had always been there. But I did not dare press it. I knew that the moment I did, my consciousness would be severed and leave, abandoning

the long white day ahead to the “local me,” who would have no memories of the future, to endure alone. Rather than throw a living version of myself into despair and madness, I would rather destroy this body with my own hands.
So, for the first time, I walked to the cliff edge.

If I jumped, the agony would last only an instant. With the body’s death, my consciousness would break off at the bottom of the ravine and continue into the morning of another world. That meant leaving a broken corpse at the bottom of the cliff and fleeing to the next world. To me, that was the cleanest kind of “saving.”
I closed my eyes and took that step.
The fall was very short. Immediately afterward, I was standing in that familiar corridor again. The world had not changed at all.

The second jump was much easier than the first. Later, whenever the clues ran out in the afternoon, my steps toward the cliff were as unhurried as an old farmer’s walk to the mill. During those cycles when I jumped alone, the dried fruit in my pocket did not move at all.
Until the time I jumped in front of her.
That cycle had been perfectly normal. I was the one who suddenly collapsed in the thick afternoon sunlight. I clenched the dried fruit she had handed me in my palm and forgot to eat it.
Well into the afternoon, I stood and walked toward the herders’ path. She followed silently behind me.
When we reached the cliff edge, I stopped and greeted her out of habit: “That’s all for today. I’ll save myself some time. See you tomorrow morning.”
She looked at me blankly. Then the color drained from her face inch by inch until it was completely gone.
“Arno. Come back.” Her voice was trembling.
I repeated woodenly, “See you tomorrow morning.”
The moment I stepped forward, she lunged at me like a madwoman and seized my sleeve with both hands.
It was the brittle sound of formalwear fabric tearing. I plunged downward, and the force dragged her whole body over the edge.
All the way down toward the bottom of the ravine, the sound of her breaking screams filled my ears.
The next morning, in the White Tower corridor. After Yuna finished verifying my identity, before I could give her my account as usual, she suddenly stopped and stared at me for several seconds.
“How many times have you watched us die?” she asked.
I froze for a moment. “What do you mean?”

“You don’t look like you’re predicting danger.” She pointed at the movement I had just made to avoid a porter. “You knew which door he would come through and what he would be carrying. The way you’re looking at everyone today is wrong. This isn’t deduction. You’ve seen it.”
“That’s not all.” She looked me straight in the eye. “Arno, what exactly have you been hiding?”
I looked at her sleeve, perfectly intact, without even a loose thread, and heard myself say:
“I’ve been hiding the cliff. The cliff at the end of the pasture.”
She froze.
“Every time the clues run out, I don’t wait until dark. I walk straight to the cliff and jump. It’s over in an instant.”
I told her everything: the cliff, the crooked-necked tree, the so-called saving, the stones in my pockets, how I had jumped again and again, even how I had jumped in front of her yesterday.
When I finished, a long dead silence fell over the corridor.

“When you first told me what happened this morning, you said you had completely broken down when you first experienced all this.” After a long while, she asked, “Between that original you and the you who treats suicide as ‘saving,’ how many times did you die?”
I avoided her gaze. “I don’t know. Maybe a few hundred times.”
“They aren’t important, really.” I heard myself continue in a wooden voice so unfamiliar that even I found it strange. “I tried to remember the death order of those
257 people, but across those hundreds of dusks, I watched them die too many times. Too many deaths for my mind to hold. I could only turn them into data to endure it.”
Yuna looked at me, her face deathly pale. She did not curse me or break down crying. She only asked the third question softly, as if afraid of shattering the silence in the corridor:
“When you fell… did it hurt?”
I froze. “…It was short. Only an instant.”
“An instant still hurts.” Her eyes reddened without warning. She turned away and roughly rubbed them with her sleeve. When she turned back, she forced her voice under control. “Remember that. I
can’t control how many times you’ve started over, or what you’ve turned other people into. But the pain is yours. If you even save yourself that, what difference is there between you and a dead man?”
Then she established a rule on the spot.

“If the clues run out again, you are absolutely not to go to that cliff. Come find me. Don’t talk about serious matters. Treat it as a day of rest. Watch me roll dice, accompany Milu while she flies a kite, go anywhere you like.”

That night, she would die in a disaster again. The one facing me the next morning would be another Yuna who knew nothing. I was her memorandum. On every idle afternoon afterward, I carried out that rule to the letter.
One evening, some time after that rule was established, we were walking back to the bend in the field path when she crouched down and dug a stone out of the mud.

“The seven stones in your pocket—you have to pick them all up before work begins, right?” She took my hand and pressed the muddy stone hard into my palm. “Here. This is the eighth stone. Remember that you promised me: you absolutely must not save that pain.”

The next morning, the stone was back in its original place. From then on, whenever I picked up the final stone for my left pocket, I would crouch for one extra second and pick up the eighth stone for her,

keeping it separately in the inner pocket close to my chest. Later, there were a few times when I passed that cliff and my hand instinctively went to touch the stone. Whenever I felt it, I would still stop.
Once I had that stone in the inner pocket, I finally dared to face the scene I had been avoiding—the aftermath I had abandoned for the sake of “saving,” and who, exactly, bore it.

There were several cycles when I did not go home at dusk because I was pursuing clues about the brass key. I knew perfectly well that my mother was standing in the dusk outside our home, looking out and waiting for me to

return for the last meal of the day. But I was in too much of a hurry to keep up our progress, and never once turned back. I had believed that if I could eventually break the loop, all that saved time could be made up for.
But it was only when I fabricated that death list on paper for this book that I truly saw what I had left behind.
“Family: mother, alive. Notified. Mother remained beside the body until dark. Did not cry. Straightened his clothes.”
This was a line I revised over and over for a long time. In every version, she was crying. Until the final time, when the tip of my pen stopped.
The year my father died, the house was in an uproar. The adults sent me out into the yard, and I looked inside from the windowsill.

When the room had been put in order, my mother knelt quietly beside the bed, absorbed in straightening his collar. There was a stubborn crease at the collar. She smoothed it three times, but it still sprang back, so she pressed both hands firmly over it until it finally lay flat.
She did not shed a single tear.

I thought she had forgotten to cry, or that she was too overcome with grief to do so. For many years afterward, whenever I remembered that afternoon, my mind always stopped on her hands pressing down hard on the collar.

So I crossed out the tears. If, that day, the Boundary Guard had really knocked on our door and taken my mother to that crooked-necked tree to identify the body broken by the fall for the sake of “saving”—

In my imagination, she would have knelt down slowly, just as she had that year. Without tears. She would only have reached out and smoothed my collar little by little; straightened the dark-green belt at my waist where the fall had twisted it, so that the three extra stitches locked through the seventh eyelet faced upward.
After finishing all that, she would have sat quietly in the dusk and kept watch over me, sitting until the sky had gone completely dark.
texts.chapter:chapter-14-zero-balance:title: Chapter Fourteen: Balance: Zero
texts.chapter:chapter-14-zero-balance:event:te: As we searched this wasteland for the source that truly governed death, I kept seeing flashes of the previous cycle's end: my mother arranging my “corpse” for me in the dark. That soundless darkness pressed down like a weight on every footprint we left.

This was not our first day in the ruins of the old city.
In the White Tower, we found only one damaged survey log, marked with three broad suspected areas. For the past few days, we had trudged pointlessly through

waist-high dead grass, our palms cut by rusted rebar. Yuna silently compared the abandoned pipelines on the surface again and again. Even with mud packed beneath her fingernails, she mechanically moved one heavy chunk of

rubble after another.
It was not until the wind rose at dusk, when the pure exhaustion was almost crushing us, that we finally dug out a flight of stone steps behind a toppled load-bearing wall at the third coordinate.

At the end of the steps stood a metal door buried beneath heavy soil. There was no keyhole, only a dim input panel.
If this century-old gate were forcibly damaged, the mechanisms inside would
lock permanently. Yuna knelt in the mud and entered a long string of characters with trembling fingers—the backdoor password she had spent an entire day extracting from the lower-level logs of an

abandoned terminal in the empty-shell laboratory.
With the final keystroke, a dull mechanical clamping sound echoed through the dark underground. Cold, viscous air poured out as the door opened.

This was an underground archive left behind by the old world. The old ash on the floor had built up thick, but not in the smooth, untouched way of a place no one had visited—the heavy dust was layered with

countless overlapping footprints, from repeated pacing. In one corner stood a wooden chair, its wooden armrests rubbed pale and glossy. This lightless cellar had once been used by someone for years on end.

Wooden shelves covered all four walls, packed tightly with handwritten booklets. And in a deliberately cleared patch of ground at the far end of the cellar, a massive metal outline lay dormant. Though dulled

by the corrosion of time, I recognized it at once—the machine called “the Scissors” that we had seen in the White Tower recordings. Only now it was no longer an image on a screen, but a cold physical object.

Yuna did not approach it immediately. She went to the shelves and carefully pulled out a record marked “Engineering Warning.” She blew the dust from its cover and opened the title page. The flashlight illuminated the

signature at the bottom.
It had originally been a person's name, but someone had violently blacked it out with thick strokes. Beside the blackened name, a faded stamp had been pressed hard into the page:
“Access revoked.”
“Who was it?” I looked at the piles of booklets stacked on the shelves.

“I don’t know.” Yuna stared at the mass of black ink for a while, her voice low. “But whoever organized this many volumes of dissenting opinions, even after having their system access revoked, must not have given up.”
She opened the pages and quickly scanned the faded numbers.

“The calculations in this basement answer the conversion rate we couldn’t work out in the White Tower.” Yuna pointed at the annotated equations on the page. “This isn’t blind speculation. This engineer ran

the figures again using the device’s measured data on cross-world connection consumption. It not only confirms that the shortfall is no more than eight thousand; it also calculates exactly how to fill it.”
She raised her head, her gaze settling on the machine at the far end.

“The shared total across all cross-world versions of the same New Human is exactly ten thousand. As long as someone enters that device and is completely stripped away, surrendering that total capacity, the shortfall that has already formed can be filled in one go.”
“Using human lives to fill a deficit in physical law. This balance doesn’t just work on a screen,” she said quietly. “It has become physical reality in this basement too. But it will only buy

us some time.”
She closed the manuscript, her face turning pale.
“As long as the time machine keeps running, the burden on the cross-world connection will continue to grow. The ten thousand
released will only temporarily fill the existing shortfall. If we can’t complete the sacrifice before 22:00 tonight, our world will reach its carrying limit and fall into silence like a power
outage, freezing everyone inside it in the dark. To truly survive, the only way is to completely destroy the time machine after using the sacrifice to buy a delay, and put an end to this burden.”
At the bottom of the annihilation device at the end of the basement stood a heavy base. A passage had been carved into it by hand, with varying pressure. It had not been carved by
one person all at once. From the different habits of the strokes, this cellar had been visited by many people, each deepening the same words again and again in their own handwriting.
Yuna stood before the base and read the inscription by flashlight.

“‘This door takes one of three things, and none of the other two. It does not take ordinary death. When an ordinary person dies, only the body stops operating; within the field of cross-world connections, their identity still occupies space. Nor does it take the world. Nothing can forcibly sever a universe.’”
“Then what does it take?”
“‘It takes your cross-world self—the entirety of your weight anchored in this world.’”

She stopped moving and stood before that short line for a long time. Faint light fell across the side of her face, outlining its taut lines. That cruel conclusion surfaced once again in the old carved marks.

“Arno, once your cross-world self is stripped away here, the annihilation device will follow the connection and terminate all the partial projections of you that are still continuing in every related universe.”
Yet beneath that cruel demand was a remarkably gentle assurance.
“‘But it ends here; it does not mean you never existed. The traces you leave behind will not be erased.’”

“Physical law will not erase a single second of your having lived.” She gently touched the deeply carved mark. “The causal ties you formed with others in each world, the memories others have of you—all of it will remain where it is.”
However, beside this assurance, another reader had carved a note in a completely different, fine handwriting.

“‘Annihilation does not destroy information.’” Yuna frowned. “‘Once the cross-world self is stripped away, its information has not vanished. But conservation does not mean accessibility. Where did this information go?’”
This was our unanswered question as well. It was not the death of a body, nor had it simply gone somewhere it could be retrieved from. But as long as the information
remained, “stripping away” was not the same as leaving nothing behind. Whoever had written this note was facing death itself, trying to pick out a theoretical crack.

We had dug down to the deepest point. The calculations in the manuscripts, the damaged records, and that incomprehensible machine had all solidified here into a heavy reality. The price had been confirmed beyond doubt.

But that was not all. In a corner of the manuscript was another, more brutal line of calculations.
“Look here.” Yuna’s finger stopped at one of the lines.

It clearly listed the occupancy readings of an empty shell within the cross-world connection. The conclusion was unambiguous: a body without a first-person subject had a usable capacity of zero in the system. That also meant that pushing an empty shell inside would release zero capacity.
This ruled out the last possible shortcut: it had to be a living person with a complete consciousness.
In this basement, the only New Humans qualified to surrender that ten thousand capacity and fill the shortfall were me and her.

“But… besides us, there are the children in the village.” I heard my own voice trembling. “Milou is a fully conscious living person too. Once the shortfall becomes public, will the adults try to use a child to fill that ten thousand?”
“Children cannot be used to fill it. That has to be the bottom line.”
She rose and strode to the heavy base of the machine, pressing her fingertip hard against the final line of the inscription.
“Volunteer: read this three times, then enter.”
She slapped the engineering warning manual onto the device’s outer casing.

“It’s written clearly in the manual. Physically, stripping away the cross-world self requires the subject to maintain an extremely lucid will throughout the entire operation. Even the slightest collapse from fear will cause mental disarray and forcibly interrupt the decoupling.”
“The people who came before carved ‘volunteer’ there not to require moral goodness, but to ensure that whoever entered had sufficient mental resilience. If you throw a
mind that cannot understand what death truly is inside, the moment the door closes, biological instinct will overwhelm it and cause the entire stripping process to fail.”
“So it isn’t only a question of morality,” she said through clenched teeth. “The physical mechanism itself rejects children who don’t understand.”
“What if they insist on forcing a child to do it? What if, under the threat of death, they still try to push a child inside even knowing it will fail?”
“If the physical mechanism isn’t enough, then add authority.” She reached out and gripped my forearm, hard enough to hurt. “We were the original holders of authority. If someone outside
the hatch tries to use force to push in someone who doesn’t meet the conditions, or tries to force the hatch shut, my underlying operational authority can directly cut the machine’s startup
circuit. The adults enjoy the highest allocation of resources and the comfort of a stable lie, and now they want a child who doesn’t even understand death to sacrifice themselves for them?”
She paused for a moment, her gaze turning cold.

“There are plenty of adults in the village who meet the physical conditions and whose minds are strong enough to cross this red line. But why should some ordinary adult be chosen at random to die? If someone is

needed to fill this shortfall, we have to start by asking the ten people in the Inner Circle who hold power. They enjoy the authority, so they have to face the cost. And—” She pointed at herself. “That includes me.”

The lightless cellar fell into a long silence.
With the minds unable to understand death crossed off the list of candidates, only the two of us remained here, awake and facing the red line. The chill, deeper than

that of the cold cellar, made it impossible for me to breathe. But under her rigid gaze, I found no words with which to question her—though I knew exactly what this meant, all I could do now was accept the decision.
“Record this as an uncrossable rule.” She suddenly broke the silence.
“Record what?”

“Record that today, in this basement, I, as the holder of the relevant authority, directly defined the risk as a red line. I refuse to list a mind that cannot understand death as a candidate. If I’m gone and someone wants to push a child inside, you enforce this red line.”
She came over to my side.

“If one day someone accuses us of being selfish, of favoring children, you’ll show them this rule and tell them: it wasn’t physical law that saved the children. I did. If anyone wants to exploit that blurry boundary and use a child to fill the gap, they’ll have to cross my red line first.”

I looked at her resolute expression and suddenly remembered the system prompt about me on the screen in the White Tower’s pure white room yesterday: “Locking ten thousand units of baseline capacity. Current operator available balance: zero.”
In the system’s ledger,

as the operator of the cross-world connection, I had already overdrafted.
She was still calculating what the Inner Circle would say, still drawing a red line to protect the children, unaware that this door might be an impassable wall for me. But I did not say it.
“This is your task from here on, Arno. We’re going to find those adults.”
“And me.” She lowered her eyes. “I hold the White Tower’s authority and the truth about this place. We’re both part of this power structure.”
She issued her instruction: “The future visitor who took over your body said he had sought out the adults in the village, and every one of them refused. Since he proved how fragile human
nature is, we’ll start by asking those who bear the greatest responsibility. You have to return to the village and put the cost before the ten people in the Inner Circle who hold power.”
“No.” I looked straight at her.
“That visitor said he had experienced all of it himself. He said all ten people he asked would refuse. If we can already foresee a similar outcome, why should I still go through the motions?”
She did not look away. She watched me for a long time.
“Because their refusing in person and your depriving them of the right to be asked from the outset are two completely different things in nature.”
She tucked her hands back into her sleeves. There was an untouchable stubbornness in her posture.
“The situation he described doesn’t mean you can refuse to ask now.”
“If I don’t make you ask, then one day the person standing here preparing to die will be nothing more than the unlucky bastard who didn’t even dare ask someone else, the only one you pushed forward.”
“Someone with no choice is called an offering. I won’t let myself be that offering.”

She turned toward the main console and entered the hibernation command on the dust-covered terminal. This did not require a special key; she was simply using the highest authority brought down from the White Tower. With a low mechanical sound, the heavy hatch locked completely, entering physical hibernation.
She headed for the cellar exit and stopped at the collapsed stone steps, turning her head slightly.
“Once you’ve completed your task, ask them all. When that time comes, I’ll decide for myself whether I’m the ‘volunteer’ who will walk through this door.”
Watching her back disappear at the end of the stairs, I stood where I was. The heavy door had once again become a cold, lifeless object beneath the earth.

I would complete the procedure she had demanded. Even if it was only to prove that those ten people really would refuse.
But I couldn’t stop thinking about the ending. When the refusals had all been spoken, if someone had to fill this shortfall…

It could only be me.
Yuna thought I also had ten thousand capacity to pay, but only I knew what that “available balance: zero” reading meant. My capacity had not disappeared. It had already been occupied to maintain this cross-world connection.
Because that capacity was locked by the system

at the underlying level of the connection process, if the Scissors tried to strip me away, it would be unable to complete the capacity-recovery transaction. A process that could not settle its account could not complete the target coupling.
I had nowhere left to retreat. If there was no

solution through normal channels, this instead became the only gamble capable of disrupting the system’s logic: wagering the destruction of my entire cross-world existence on the low-level error that might erupt when this machine forcibly stripped a target with “zero available balance.”
But I would try.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:title: Chapter Fourteen Appendix: The Thirteen Articles
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s1-1:
Small notebook · The Thirteen Articles (the one I kept against my chest, together with the eighth stone):
Recorded one by one: the names on the list, the date, and their answers that day.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s5-1: Across the hundreds of mornings past, when my consciousness continued into the world at exactly eight, the first thing I had to do was redraw the old facility’s structure from memory on a stack of blank cardstock with a charcoal pencil, copy out the capacity data memorized from the ruins terminal, and write those names down again in the notebook.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s6-1: The pages that died with me, and the people who had refused me in the mornings past, remained forever in the universes where they had originally existed. Only memories could continue with my
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s6-2: consciousness into this parallel world. So I had to copy out all the evidence again and take it to ask every person in the present. Yuna insisted that I return the right to be asked to them.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s7-1: Since the visitor from the white room arrived and pushed my starting point ten minutes later, Yuna and I had spent countless mornings in the ruins. Only after she finally rechecked the account on the terminal did she give me this task: go and have them verify that cost.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s8-1: Today, when I regained my body at eight ten and spent more than half an hour copying out the account again before leaving the White Tower, the elders’ secret search for Yuna and me had already
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s8-2: spread. With less than thirteen hours remaining in this world, I had to use the blind spots discovered through hundreds of cycles to knock on the doors of the ten Inner Circle seats one by one.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s9-1: According to the terminal’s records, eight thousand was the safe upper limit for filling the gap, while every qualified new human shared a total cross-world capacity of roughly ten thousand. Any one of them would be enough to fill the gap. But
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s9-2:
today, I did not spend more time on ordinary villagers.
In earlier cycles, I had tried going to the Watermarsh settlement to explain things to people from the outlying settlements. But in a single day, fourteen hours was nowhere near enough to prove
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s9-3: the apocalypse to someone who did not even have the concept of “cross-world,” let alone persuade them to sacrifice themselves. I tried starting with common sense. I tried making a direct prophecy. At best, they locked me in a woodshed in a panic.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s10-1: Only these ten adult Inner Circle members, who had already encountered records of the old facility in the elders’ council and knew part of the truth about the world, offered any chance of skipping the long reconstruction of basic understanding and explaining
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s10-2:
the cost to them directly.
I had used prophecy to prove to them that I possessed information, but that was not enough to make them hand over their lives. In earlier cycles, I tried taking them to the ruins outside the city to see the machine’s original
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s10-3: components, but the round trip and deciphering the manuscripts used up most of the day. And the answers those elders gave while facing the physical evidence were no different from the ones they gave when looking at sketches—they still demanded to return to
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s10-4:
the village and convene a full council, and demanded more time for cross-verification.
But under the rule that took all physical evidence away from me at exactly eight every morning, “we need more time to verify” was equivalent to refusing forever within this
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s10-5: fourteen-hour day. If I took one person to see the original components, he would still be unable to confirm anything because of the procedural deadlock. If I went to everyone in one day with sketches, they would use the lack of time to verify as a shield.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s14-1: The first people I went to find were Old Baro and Old Nona. When I avoided the main road and went around to the chess stall at the village entrance, Old Baro was setting up an unfinished game by himself. As usual, Old Nona was still inside boiling the first pot of water of the morning.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s15-1: Because the visitor had occupied ten minutes, by the time I reached the stall, the light had completely cleared the edge of the stone board. The shadows of the chess pieces lay sideways across its surface, stretched a little more than one square long.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s16-1: I stopped beside the table and drew a deep breath. I told Baro that the records in my hands could prove that eight thousand was the safe upper limit for filling the gap, while the total capacity across all worlds of each of them, as qualified
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s16-2: new humans, was roughly ten thousand. That number was enough for a sacrifice, as long as the person who went understood the cost. After I finished, he could curse me, get up and leave, or do nothing at all. He only had to let me finish.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s19-1:
I had barely begun when the wooden door of the house sounded. Old Nona came out carrying two cups of hot water and set them heavily on the stone table.
I did not stop. In front of both of them, I explained piece by piece that
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s19-2: the reserve pool sustaining the world was falling below its threshold and needed a living person to sacrifice, along with the records proving that each of their total cross-world capacities was sufficient to fill the gap.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s20-1: Nona’s hand stopped in midair. She held a chess piece between two fingers and turned to look at me.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s23-1: I nodded. “Every one of you can.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s26-1: I told her plainly. I needed one person from the list to go with me to the ruins outside the city and sit in the sacrificial position of a machine. It was not merely a matter of ending the life they had
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s26-2: now. Once they crossed that threshold, the consciousnesses in every world that had originally continued from that individual would be cut off and extinguished along with them. They would never come back.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s27-1: She put down the piece. In the square where she had meant to put it, without even touching the piece beside it.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s30-1: She answered instantly, without the slightest hesitation.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s32-1: “I haven’t even proved the equations in my hands to you yet.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s34-1: “I admit I’ve lived long enough to fill your number.” She looked at me. “But why should I hand my life over to someone out of his mind like you, to fill some scrap-metal lump?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s37-1: She raised her head and looked at me. The morning wind passed through, and the long fur on her frost-white ears trembled slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s40-1: She was talking about Old Baro, sitting across from her.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s42-1: “I give him one move every day in this unfinished game. It lets him sit for one more morning.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s45-1: Old Baro, sitting opposite us, stroked his chin and kept staring at the chessboard, as if he had not been distracted at all by our conversation.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s46-1: Old Nona pushed herself up by her knees, patted her clothes, and said she was going next door to fetch another bucket of water.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s47-1: Before she left, as she always did, she pushed the pieces on her side toward the center and lined them up. It was something she did every time before leaving the table.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s51-1: The half of the stone bench opposite me was empty.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s52-1: Old Baro finally moved. He gathered the pieces from the unfinished game one by one and set them up again as if for the opening. His dry fingers held each piece, and every one landed on the stone with a crisp, light sound.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s53-1: I walked over. He accidentally nudged a piece, and it rolled along the edge of the stone table before falling at my feet.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s57-1:
I bent down, picked it up, and put it back on the board without thinking.
I put it in the third position from the left. The position Old Nona stubbornly moved it back to every day.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s58-1: Old Baro’s hand stopped, suspended in midair.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s61-1: “How did you know she moved this one every day?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s64-1:
I met his gaze calmly.
“Yuna watched you play chess on other mornings. She told me.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s65-1: He looked up at me for a while. Then he put down the piece he had been about to place.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s68-1: I sat as he instructed. The chill of the morning stone bench came through my thin trousers. Nona would not be back quickly from fetching the water. Beside the rough stone table, there were only the two of us.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s70-1: “You didn’t believe all of what I just said, did you?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s73-1: “For more than ten years. Every morning, I deliberately set one piece wrong and wait for her to come grumbling over and fix it. You think I don’t know her little schemes? If she knew I’d seen through them, she’d have flipped this table over long ago.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s74-1: He lowered his head and felt the chess piece, rubbing its edge with his fingertip. He did not look at me.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s76-1: I drew a deep breath and opened up the subject I had left unfinished. This time, he continued setting out the remaining pieces, which counted as permission.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s78-1: He did not need complicated equations. But he needed to confirm the boundaries of this matter.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s79-1: “So if I sit inside, that fills the gap?” he asked.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s80-1: “Yes,” I said. “A total cross-world capacity of roughly ten thousand is definitely enough to fill the current shortfall. That number is clearly entered in all of your records.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s82-1: “Once they cross that threshold, the consciousnesses in every world that originally continued from that individual will be cut off and extinguished along with them.” I repeated the cost I had just explained to Nona. “In exchange for this world’s tomorrow.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s83-1: When I reached this point, he suddenly did something.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s86-1: He reached beneath the stone board and heaved upward, flipping the entire chessboard over.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s87-1: The stone on the underside was much rougher than the top, full of weathered pits. But there were words on it. The cuts were deep and regular, unmistakably unlike the writing we used now.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s88-1: He gently tapped it with the rough pad of his finger.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s90-1: “Are the words on this also from the machine in the ruins?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s91-1:
I leaned closer. In an earlier failed cycle, Yuna had already made a rubbing of this stone slab’s underside. The writing on the back of this stone board, which had been used for chess for years, did indeed prove that it was an old-facility shell plaque.
I nodded to him.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s92-1: But he was only using it to confirm the truth about the ruins that I had described.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s94-1: “Patterns.” Old Baro withdrew his hand. Nothing in his tone rose or fell.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s96-1: He turned the stone board back over with both hands and set it firmly on the stone table, sealing the crack in the old world shut again. Then he continued setting up his unfinished game.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s100-1:
He arranged the pieces on both sides of the board. Then he reached out and moved one of his own pieces. After that, he leaned across and moved one of the pieces on Nona’s side.
When there was no one else at the table to play with him, this was how he passed the time: he played both sides himself.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s103-1: He listened quietly while playing the game with no opponent. After a while, he finally spoke.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s105-1: “If a capacity of ten thousand is enough, what about the other villages? What about the people in the outlying settlements?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s110-1: “I tried asking at the Watermarsh settlement in an earlier cycle.” I watched his hand rise and fall over and over. “But fourteen hours is too short. Before I could build even a little trust, they locked me in a woodshed in a panic.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s111-1: After hearing this, he did not say whether the result was reasonable. He simply reached out and made a move for Nona on the opposite side.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s115-1: The only sound around us was the rustle of leaves in the morning wind. After a while, he lifted his eyes and asked me:
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s119-1: “No. Lise is still a child.” I looked him in the eye without yielding. “I don’t ask children.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s122-1: “Then go ask the others on the list.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s123-1: He turned his head, his eyes returning to the chessboard. It was an unmistakable gesture of dismissal.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s127-1: After a moment, he looked at me and said, “I’m not going. Why don’t you go yourself?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s128-1: “If I went directly and left the ten elders who don’t even need to know at home, that would be what Yuna hates most.” I looked at him. “Besides, I’m a defective with a
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s128-2: balance of zero. If I don’t first ask everyone who qualifies to fill this hole, then I’ll be deciding her sacrifice for her. She wants me to ask for your answers today.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s129-1: He nodded and gave his final answer: “Then I’m not going either.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s130-1:
I sat there and did not stand up at once.
I was waiting for his hand. He had a habit when playing chess: if he was dissatisfied with a move after putting it down, he would take it back and play it again. I was hoping he would take back that refusal too.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s132-1: But his hands, covered in age spots, rested firmly on his knees. They did not move at all.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s135-1:
Later, I stood up and said quietly that I was leaving.
On the first two lines of the notebook, I wrote Baro and Nona’s names, along with their refusals.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s136-1: After leaving the chess stall, I spent the rest of the day avoiding the patrol guards’ sight and circling around the workshops and storehouses at the village outskirts.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s137-1: I went to the mill. Garon was inspecting the bearings on the waterwheel. He was my master, and Yuna’s father. I spread the facility diagram, the discoveries from the ruins,
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s137-2: and the records proving that his capacity was roughly ten thousand across the flour-covered wooden table. I told him the truth about the apocalypse, and its real cost.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s138-1:
Garon finished reading the records. He grabbed a rag and vigorously wiped the dust from his hands.
“You left with Yuna today.” He did not look at the equations. He stared directly at me. “Where is she? Where did you leave her?”
I told him Yuna was somewhere safe. Only then
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s138-2:
did his tense shoulders relax slightly.
“I don’t care whether you can go, and I don’t care whether that machine is real or not—” He slammed the rag onto the table. “Yuna hasn’t married. You want me to abandon her and fill some piece of scrap metal? I have to watch her live.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s139-1:
At noon, I intercepted Otto, the village affairs coordinator, when he was alone, and Kain, the boundary guard captain, during a shift change.
Otto tapped the edge of the records with his short, thick fingers and calculated
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s139-2: a cold account. “Even if the cost is exactly as you say, even if you’re a defective who can’t go—why should I be the only fool to take the loss? This matter should be decided by drawing lots at a council, not by listening
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s139-3:
to you here.”
Kain put his hand on the defensive baton at his waist. “I admit the numbers here are correct. But because one person who can’t fill the hole expects me to go and die based on a few sketches? The search order
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s139-4:
has already been issued. Go to the detention room immediately!”
I did not wait for him to draw the baton. I shoved the handcart beside us into his path, vaulted the stone wall, and shook him off through the narrow lane.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s140-1:
Throughout the afternoon, in the intervals between evading the search, I intercepted the remaining people one by one in the middle of their daily lives.
Deep in the chapel corridor, Sera pushed the papers back toward me. “This is not
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s140-2:
part of the induction procedure. I will not abandon the children and go die for an apocalypse only you have seen.”
Behind the flour sacks, Toma struck the grain bags hard. “Understanding the cost is one thing, but these few sheets of
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s140-3:
paper cannot make me hand over my life. This has to go through the elders’ council’s decision procedure.”
At the market entrance, Chico slammed a copper coin down on the table. “Until you prove this isn’t madness, I won’t acknowledge
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s140-4:
anything.”
At the edge of the wheat fields at dusk, Melu folded the papers and returned them to me. “I’ve lived for more than a hundred years. I didn’t do it to fill a hole with my life in front of a prophecy that cannot be verified.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s141-1: At every door, I had to lay open the truth of the apocalypse and make them see the proven dead end before them: either abandon everything and go to their deaths at once based on the few pages of
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s141-2: equations I had sketched, or return to the procedural deadlock where fourteen hours would be exhausted without completing a decision. Then I watched one door after another close in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s142-1: Without a cross-world procedure, they could not give up their lives. But under a mechanism that could neither preserve physical evidence nor gather enough time for verification, that was equivalent to making a decision permanently impossible.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s142-2: This was the real cost—in the endless loop where I would inevitably switch to another universe after sunset today, someone who could not make a decision today because the conditions were insufficient could never hand over their life to you.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s143-1:
By the time I reached the last name—my mother, Rena—the setting sun had dyed her graying temples a dull red.
She stood at the kitchen counter, cutting carrots for dinner. I spread out the charcoal
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s143-2:
records representing her sufficient qualification and, cutting through her concentration on the ordinary task, told her the cost that crossed every world.
The knife in her hand clattered onto
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s143-3:
the cutting board.
She did not look at the sheets of cardstock covered in numbers. She was the only person today who did not even look at the evidence. She stared fixedly at my face.
“You want
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s143-4:
me to go?” She took a step back, her voice trembling.
Across hundreds of cycles, in this kitchen at this dusk, I had faced this silence countless times. I had known her answer for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s143-5: “If someone has to go, my balance is zero. If I go, the machine will only fail.” I put that bottom line forward before she could speak. “Before this world’s time runs out, will you come with me?”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s144-1:
She did not care whether the apocalypse was real. She only cared about what I had just said: “If I go, it will only fail.” She suddenly stepped forward and gripped my arm tightly.
“You can’t go, and I won’t go either. We have to stop all of this immediately! The elders’ council
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s144-2:
needs to verify it…”
Her nails dug into my flesh with astonishing force. “Go to your room right now. You are not going anywhere. Tomorrow morning I’ll go to them and tell them you’re sick, that your fever burned out your brain and made you say all this nonsense. I’ll protect you.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s145-1:
That was the last name on the list.
Before the sun had completely sunk, all ten records were filled with that day’s date. Verification had been blocked, the procedure was incomplete, or someone was held back by emotional ties. In a cycle with less than fourteen hours available for evidence, these were ten dead ends.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s152-1: I dragged my leaden steps to the boundary stone at the village entrance. Yuna was already waiting there. The sunset burned with extraordinary brilliance, from the remnants at the foot of the city ruins all the way to the village boundary.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s153-1: I walked over and set the notebook in front of her.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s154-1: She read it quietly to the end, her eyes passing over the ten refusals I had written that day.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s155-1: “I asked everyone in the ten-seat Inner Circle who had the authority to decide, again today. I laid everything out for them—I’m a defective who will only make the machine fail if I’m put in. They want a decision, verification,
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s155-2: and time. But we cannot give them more time. Even if we brought the same question to the universe tomorrow and asked it again, the answer would still be the same. In this cycle, this is the final conclusion.” My voice was dry.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s156-1: She did not argue, nor did she ask me for more proof. She simply looked quietly at the page.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s161-1: “You’ve asked everyone who could try on my behalf today.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s162-1: She withdrew her gaze, closed the notebook, and handed it back to me. Her expression was as calm as it was when she discussed what to have for dinner with me in the village.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s169-1: We walked very slowly that day. When we were almost at the gate to her yard, she suddenly spoke.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s171-1: “Tomorrow, when you wake up next, go fly a kite with Milu. The wind is running in the right direction.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s172-1: I stopped and watched her back. In this brutal rotation with only fourteen hours, she, like the Yuna of the previous universes, instinctively sensed that I was nearing the edge of being crushed.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s176-1: “You need to rest for a day.” She walked ahead without turning back. “We have to leave some days clean, to use for flying kites.”
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s182-1: The village’s familiar signs of life and warm lamplight slowly closed around us.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s183-1: We stopped at the gate to her yard. She turned around, waved casually at me, pushed open the door, and entered the yard.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s187-1:
I did not leave at once. I stood alone outside her yard, looking at the wooden door that had closed.
In an earlier cycle, she had pressed a stone into my palm and made an agreement with me that it was “the eighth stone, representing a
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s187-2: day when we investigated nothing.” That was the memory of a Yuna from another universe. And tonight, this local Yuna, who had long forgotten that stone and the agreement, was making room for a day for me with exactly the same instinct.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s188-1: The wind rose. It made the tattered cloth sign beside us rattle loudly. Alone, in the deepening dusk, I turned and walked home. Inside the small cloth pouch against my chest, the eighth rough stone pressed against the edge of the notebook with every step.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s189-1: According to my original plan, once all ten refusals were settled, I would go to the ruins tonight and use myself to test whether I could fill the gap. This trip would only be to verify the outcome that was certain to fail.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s189-2:
Once I had proved to myself completely that this path was impossible, she would be the only one left to fill it.
But when I heard her humming that off-key clapping song in the yard from beyond the wall, I unclenched my fist.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s189-3: The machine that ate people could wait another day, and this long cycle could turn one more time. Before I went and completed that doomed dead end with myself, I had to give her one clean tomorrow meant only for flying kites.
texts.chapter:v15-14b:event:text-s190-1: On the last page of the notebook, all ten names had been filled in, each with that day’s date. The remaining three lines were still blank.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:title: Chapter Fourteen, Supplement Two: Ten Thousand Is Enough
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s1-1:
Mill · Duty Log (Gallon’s handwriting, the day after that night):
“Mill off duty today. Reason: household matters.
　Substitute: Toma. Instructions: Don’t bend that pin at the water gate by hand again. Use a wrench.
　My next shift: Temporarily vacant.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s6-1: The result of asking those ten people was unanimous refusal.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s7-1: In between, we spent a perfectly clean, entirely kite-flying day with Milu. It was a whole day of completely useless extravagance. Then, at the next dawn, I went back and confirmed the ten people’s answers again—no one had changed
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s7-2: their mind, and every hope of sharing the burden had been cut off. That evening, after Yuna finished her investigations in the old city and met me at the village entrance, we walked to the outside of her courtyard once again.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s8-1: During the round when we went to ask those ten people, I had turned back toward home alone in the dusk, leaving her alone behind this door. But this time, I had planned to confront Gallon and Melu in her place. It wasn’t a pleasant task, but I thought that as an outsider, a few curses would not matter much.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s9-1: But she had just sent Milu to Toma’s house on the pretext of helping count walnuts, and was about to push open the courtyard gate. When she saw me step forward, she raised a hand and stopped my arm.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s11-1: With one foot inside and one outside, she turned back and added, “Come in with me. Don’t move from your spot. If they want to curse someone, let them curse you—you’re harder to break than I am.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s14-1: Dinner was on the table, the porridge still steaming. When Melu came out of the kitchen, she was carrying an empty bowl with a small chip along its rim.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s15-1: Gallon was sitting at the end of the long table where he always sat. He had just finished the day’s work, his sleeves rolled above his elbows, flour still clinging to his thick forearms.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s16-1: Yuna did not pull out a chair as she usually did. She simply stood at this end of the table and, across the bowls of hot porridge, told them everything that had happened today, from the beginning.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s19-1: She spoke very slowly, pronouncing each word evenly, as though reading the mill’s ledger.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s20-1: First she explained how the reserve line would sink, and how quickly. Then she explained what would happen after it reached the line: the people in the village would go out one after another, like lights extinguishing in succession. Finally,
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s20-2: she explained the capacity: the precise amount needed had not yet been calculated, but even in the worst case, filling that gap would never require more than eight thousand. And her individual capacity came out to ten thousand. Definitely enough.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s21-1: At that point, she paused, looking once at Gallon and once at Melu.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s25-1: “I’m not here to ask whether you agree. I’m here to tell you, because you should know.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s26-1: Melu set the bowl down. Very gently, almost letting it slide from her fingertips. The bottom touched the wooden tabletop without making a sound.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s29-1: The first thing Melu did was close the door.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s30-1: She went around the table, hurried to the courtyard gate, and slammed the half-open door shut. The bolt snapped into its slot with a sharp click. On her way back, she took the coat hanging from the wooden peg behind the door.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s30-2: Before Yuna could say anything, she stepped forward, tore the silver candidate insignia from the metal arc at the side of Yuna’s hair, clenched it tightly in her palm, then went back and hugged the coat against her chest.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s31-1: She stood between the door and the table like a wall.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s33-1: “You’re not going to the White Tower, and you’re not going to that basement in the old city.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s35-1: “Not today. Not tomorrow either. The coat and the insignia stay with me.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s38-1: Yuna looked at the coat crumpled in her mother’s arms.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s39-1: She did not reach for it or raise her voice.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s45-1: “You keep the things. You heard what I said. Those are separate matters.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s46-1: Melu’s chin jerked violently. She opened her mouth, but nothing came out. She only held the things in her arms tighter.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s50-1: The chair legs scraped across the brick floor with a harsh sound. He did not charge at Yuna. He charged at me.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s51-1: He went around the table in a few strides and pressed down on me like a mountain. He grabbed my collar and hauled me up. I was half a head shorter than him, and for that instant I felt my heels leave the
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s51-2: ground. I knew the strength in his hands too well. It was the strength he used to lift an entire sack of wheat with one hand at the mill. My collar tightened around my throat until I could barely breathe.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s53-1: “How long have you been grinding away at her ear?”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s56-1: I did not struggle or argue.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s57-1: I couldn’t. Those things about the reserves, the capacity, the extinguishing—I really had taken them apart for her, bit by bit. I had become the person who pushed her onto this dead end with my own hands.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s58-1: I forced one true sentence out through my teeth.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s61-1: His grip tightened sharply again. I heard the thread at the seam of my collar snap. The rough cloth scraped against my neck.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s66-1: Yuna came over and pried his hand open.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s67-1: She clasped both hands around Gallon’s thick wrist and pulled his flour-dusted fingers off one by one. She was much shorter than him, and much weaker, but she hung almost her entire body weight from them.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s71-1: “What he said is true. I checked the facts myself—the more he told me, the more I checked. Anything I couldn’t verify, I didn’t accept.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s73-1: “If you want to curse someone, curse me. If you curse him, you’re saying I was led around by someone else.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s74-1: Gallon’s fingers loosened one by one. He looked at Yuna, and the hand hardened by years of rough work dropped limply to his side.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s77-1: He slowly backed away and sat down heavily. His hands spread apart and braced against the table.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s78-1: Those rough hands were shaking. He noticed almost at once, then pressed both palms flat against the wooden tabletop and held them there.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s79-1: The only thing left in the room was the pot of porridge on the stove, bubbling over low heat.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s82-1: Then Gallon slowly raised his head.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s84-1: “You said eight thousand was the upper limit.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s86-1: “Right. We don’t know the exact size of the gap, but according to the experimental records from the ruins that we found, eight thousand will definitely be enough to fill it.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s88-1: “The figures you worked out say that, across all worlds, the combined capacity of one new human’s projections is ten thousand.” Gallon stared hard at the rough tabletop in front of him. “You alone are ten thousand.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s95-1: Gallon did not acknowledge the silence.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s97-1: “The capacity a new human can release is far greater than an old human’s. If ten thousand really is enough to fill that upper limit, then it makes no difference who it is.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s98-1: He looked up at Yuna, his eyes holding a kind of desperate resolve.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s100-1: “That list says I won’t save the village. That’s true. I won’t.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s102-1: “But I can take your place. If ten thousand is enough, use me.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s105-1: The coat slipped halfway out of Melu’s arms. She hurriedly reached to catch it and managed to, but the worn wooden die rolled out of the coat’s side pocket, struck the brick floor with a small click, and spun half a turn before coming to rest.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s109-1: Gallon did not turn to look at her.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s113-1: “There’s no need to do that arithmetic.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s116-1: Yuna went to his side, pulled out a chair, and sat down.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s117-1: She sat exactly as she did during an ordinary dinner—one toe lightly touching the floor, once, then again.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s121-1: “Dad, calculate both sides. If you still say that after you’re done, we’ll talk about what comes next.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s128-1: I couldn’t hold back any longer. I put in a sentence.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s132-1: “The consequences of these two kinds of extinguishing are different. Ordinary shutdown only ends the people in each failed world locally. But the sacrifice reaches the original body. It doesn’t just stop this one you. It ends every living version of you in every connected world at the same time.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s133-1: Gallon turned and looked at me. He paused, taking in the absolute ending spanning every branch.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s137-1: He slowly lifted the hand pressed against the table, turned it over, looked at his callused palm, then turned it back and pressed it against the table again.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s138-1: “If I go in, the me in the other branches stops too.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s140-1: Yuna continued the calculation. “If, in every branch where nothing went wrong, all the versions of me living normal lives suddenly lost their fathers…then conversely, if I go in, countless Gallons over there will suddenly lose their daughters. By number, the two calculations are the same.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s146-1: “Today, I went to the basement in the old city by myself. The records there prove that a machine capable of writing a person back in their entirety really exists,” Yuna said calmly. “But its prerequisite is obtaining that person’s uninterrupted
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s146-2: continuous record. Not piecing together fragments from someone else’s mind, but a complete log that follows them from their true starting point all the way to the end. Only with a core like that would it be possible to activate the machine afterward.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s147-1: She turned and glanced at me.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s148-1: “You’ve lived in the village for more than a hundred years, and no one has built a record like that for you,” she continued. “But I can. If you take me as the starting point now and have Arno preserve me outside, there will be a continuous log in the future.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s149-1: “Also, at exactly eight this morning, someone in a different state spoke to me through his body.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s150-1: I said nothing. I only nodded silently.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s152-1: “That person knew where we had fled, and knew about the purple night sky. I think he’s Arno from far in the future,” Yuna said. “He told me he still hadn’t
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s152-2: managed to bring me back. That means that even on that day, he was still trying to find me. As long as he exists, someone can keep making that record.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s153-1: She turned to look at Gallon.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s154-1: “But what if you go in, Dad?” Yuna asked. “Once you’re sacrificed, every version of you in every universe will be severed completely. And you don’t even have a
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s154-2: starting point for a record. For you, there’s no recovery afterward, and you can’t even reach the threshold for trying again. It’s a dead end with no way back.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s155-1: Gallon opened his mouth, searching for some room to argue. He looked at me.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s156-1: I simply stood there. I couldn’t lie to him and tell him that a hundred years of memories could be created out of nothing after his death.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s157-1: Gallon’s gaze rested on me for several seconds. If he went in and died in her place, Yuna would be the one left alive in the world afterward, and she could not access the highest authority I had brought with me.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s157-2: She would have no way to start any record for him. The force that had surged up when he first offered to replace her seemed to drain away in an instant. He slowly withdrew his gaze and looked at his rough hands.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s158-1: That total erasure, spanning every world and absolutely impossible to reverse, finally descended in its cold physical reality. The hands that had been pressed tightly against the table curled involuntarily. He clenched his back teeth and breathed hard and fast, his shoulders trembling faintly beneath his clothes.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s162-1: I stood to the side and couldn’t see his face from there. I could only see his dark-brown ears—the two that were usually held upright in alertness. Now they slowly folded down.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s163-1: The pot of porridge on the stove boiled a little too dry and made a thick bubbling sound. Melu stood right beside it, clutching her apron tightly, but did not tend to it.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s164-1: Long enough that I thought he would not speak again.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s169-1: He raised his head. His eyes were webbed with red. He opened his mouth, but his voice sounded as though something had it tightly by the throat.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s171-1: “I take back what I said before.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s174-1: He did not try to explain. The words taking it back were as direct as when he had proposed it.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s175-1: The only things left in the room were the hissing of the porridge about to burn dry and his heavy breathing.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s178-1: Melu walked over, bent down, and picked up the wooden die from the floor.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s179-1: She lifted one corner of her apron and wiped it slowly, rubbing away the dust bit by bit.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s180-1: When she finished, she did not return it to Yuna. She placed it at the corner of the table, its wood grain looking old beneath the dim light.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s184-1: “I haven’t agreed from beginning to end. I want to make that clear. Whoever asks me from now on will get the same answer.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s187-1: She pulled out a chair beside the table and sat down weakly.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s189-1: “I can lock you in the house.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s191-1: “Lock it tonight and don’t open it tomorrow. Whether your father helps me is another matter. I can lock you in by myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s192-1: Yuna looked at her without answering.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s197-1: She did not wait for Yuna to answer. She continued on her own.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s199-1: “If I lock you up, the hole is still there. The day the line is reached will still come.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s201-1: “If I lock you up, apart from your father, whom you just calculated out of it, I still can’t make a second person willing to go in appear.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s202-1: Her hands twisted tightly in the coarse apron.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s204-1: “There’s no one else. I sat here thinking for a long time. Apart from locking you up, I never even thought of using myself to replace you.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s205-1: She clenched her teeth. Tears circled in her eyes, but she still said the most humiliating truth aloud.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s207-1: “I’m afraid of dying. If you want me to go fill that hole for you right now, I’m afraid to go.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s209-1: “I’m afraid to go, and I still want to lock you in the house. What is that for? So that once I slide the bolt into place, I can say I’m not going in for you because going in wouldn’t help. The responsibility isn’t mine.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s215-1: “If I’m going to say I don’t agree, I’ll say it to your face, and keep saying it until you leave.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s217-1: “If I slide that bolt, I become the one making the decision for you. I won’t be that person.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s218-1: She kept staring into empty space as she finished that last sentence. Only then did the tears finally spill over. She did not reach up to wipe them away, letting them run down her cheeks.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s221-1: She stood up, took the coat, and hung it back on the wooden peg behind the door.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s222-1: As she hung it, she habitually smoothed the wrinkled sleeves and straightened the collar. It was the way she had hung her daughter’s clothes for seventeen years, unchanged. Then she gently placed the silver insignia, warmed by her clenched hand, along the edge of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s224-1: “Take the coat yourself. The insignia and the die are on the table.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s226-1: “I’m not giving it to you. Take it yourself.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s229-1: Yuna went over, took the coat from behind the door, and slipped it on.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s230-1: She went to the table and picked up the insignia and the old wooden die from her probability class. She looked down at them once, fastened the insignia back onto the metal arc at the side of her hair, and put the die in her pocket.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s233-1: Melu stood with her back to her, shoulders trembling faintly. She did not turn around.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s234-1: Yuna waited there for a while, then finally lowered the hand she had half extended.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s237-1: Melu went to the stove, used a cloth to protect her hands, and carried down the pot that was nearly burned dry.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s238-1: She handled the pot exactly as she always did, steady and sure. Milu’s portion of porridge was still at the bottom. She scraped it out with a spoon, served it into a bowl, then covered it with another empty bowl to keep it warm.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s239-1: Milu had been sent away deliberately. Her dinner was still warming in the bowl.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s240-1: Yuna stared at the empty bowl covering it and remained silent for a long time. She said nothing, and did not ask anyone to bring Milu back.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s242-1: Yuna did not wait any longer. She turned, pushed open the door, and walked out.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s246-1: When I followed her out of the house, Gallon came out too and followed us all the way to the courtyard gate.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s247-1: He did not speak. He reached out, pulled back the bolt, and opened the heavy courtyard gate for us.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s248-1: Yuna went out first without looking back. I stepped over the threshold and took two steps before he spoke behind me.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s252-1: “You worked at my mill for three years.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s255-1: I stopped. I thought he was going to tell me, “Keep an eye on her for me,” or make one last plea: “Don’t let her go.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s258-1: “Write down how she worked it out, step by step.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s262-1: “People will say later that you talked her into it.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s266-1: “Write it down. Whoever asks in the future, you’ll be able to show them—it was her own calculation.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s269-1: I stood there, waiting for him to say something else.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s270-1: But there was nothing else. He pulled the courtyard gate shut hard. I heard the bolt slide into place from inside.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s271-1: I stood outside for a while and heard the sound of a chair being dragged inside. It scraped once, then stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s272-1: When I turned around, Yuna was waiting for me a few steps away in the night. She did not ask what her father had said to me at the end.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s278-1: And so we set out on the road to the old city. The hands on my pocket watch had already passed nineteen hundred hours, and the time left to us was beginning to grow tight. We walked faster and faster, heading toward the old city’s underground archive room beneath the faint moonlight.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s279-1: A little over ten minutes after leaving the village entrance, I happened to look back and saw two people on the open dirt road behind us. They followed at a great distance, neither hurrying nor slowing.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s280-1: Yuna saw them too. She did not stop or turn back to wave.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s284-1: “Where they follow us to is their business. Where I walk to is mine.”
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s287-1: Yuna did not wait or slow down. But when we stopped in front of the tottering collapsed bridge to check where to place our feet, the footsteps behind us became clear.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s288-1: Melu stopped at the far end of the bridge and stared hard at us. Only after confirming that both of us had crossed the bridge safely did she step onto it herself. After crossing, she did not fall back to such a great distance again.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s289-1: When we reached the depths of the ruins, where the path became difficult, Yuna and I could only pick our way around large pieces of fallen walls and rubble, sinking deep and then shallow with every step. Gallon caught up as well. He did not overtake us. He simply walked silently in the footprints we had just left.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s293-1: The section of stone steps leading to the basement had appeared behind the rubble. Farther ahead lay the depths of the old city ruins, where the annihilation device was located.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s294-1: They stopped on the rubble-strewn ground before the steps. They did not go any farther, as though there were an invisible boundary there.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s295-1: Yuna continued a few steps forward, then finally stopped and turned back.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s296-1: The four of us looked at one another across roughly thirty paces in the night wind of the wasteland.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s299-1: Melu stood there with both hands clenched tightly around the apron in front of her, her knuckles white.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s300-1: Gallon stood beside her, half a step behind. His head was lowered, and he did not say a word.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s301-1: Yuna looked at them quietly for a while.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s306-1: Melu finally spoke. What she called out into the night wind was the sentence she had promised that evening to keep saying until the end.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s314-1: She turned and walked down the stone steps toward the old city’s basement.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s315-1: Before following her, I looked back one last time.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s316-1: They were still where they had been. Melu’s hands were clenched tightly around her apron. Gallon raised one hand, seeming to want to wave, but halfway up, it fell limply back down.
texts.chapter:v15-14c:event:text-s317-1: They did not take another step forward. They simply stopped there.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:title: Chapter Fifteen: The Agreement
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s1:
Operating Procedures for the Annihilation Device · Old Copy from the Cellar Chamber (hung on the east wall, beneath the lamp):
“One. Before entering the chamber, the volunteer must have read the inscription three times and be able to recount, in their own words,

the distinctions among the three things.
Two. The device must be operated by two people: one person may perform only the pre-checks before lockdown, and may not complete the final operation alone.
Three. There are forty-one external calibration items. The final item

is lockdown. After lockdown, the inside and outside of the chamber will no longer communicate.
Four. The operator must remain until release is complete. They may not leave first.
Five. Afterward, the operator signs the register. The register is beneath the lamp.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s3: The darkness had only just settled completely, like a massive, ice-cold iron curtain pressing down. Less than two hours remained until the death harvest of daylight descended.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s4:
On this final stretch of the road, I laid out every ending I knew for her.
I told her that if Yuna alone filled the gap before us, she could buy this world only a brief period of blankness, enough to hold back the daylight tonight.
For the wheat to truly keep being harvested, for

people to grow old, I had to complete the second step—the moment twenty-two o’clock arrived, I would still be forcibly thrown into the “today” of the next parallel world. I would have to keep searching through countless worlds, until I found a way to destroy the time machine completely.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s5: Before we began the long descent into the depths of the cellar, we shared the last piece of dry food. The hands of the pocket watch pointed to 19:20.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s7: As we walked side by side, she casually picked out the most astringent grass seed from the piece of dry food in my hand and tossed it aside. The whole motion took less than two seconds. She did not look at me.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s1: After swallowing the food, she turned her head toward me and asked a question.
“Arno, in all those earlier days, did you ever manipulate me? Use your advantage in information to choose what to say and feed me lines, leading me along like pressing switches—did you?”

“There were dozens of times during the early partial trial runs. To save the trouble of verification, I memorized your question bank and led your reasoning along.” I looked into her eyes. “Later, even during those six complete operations that reached the final step, I still unilaterally cut off the synchronization of information.”

I paused. My voice had gone dry.
“I didn’t want to crush you, so I chose to hide the bloody records of failure from the first dozens of attempts, and let you believe opening the control-room door was the first time. In those dozens of

times and those six times, I shut you out of the truth. But after you saw through my exhaustion and asked how many times I had actually accompanied you through all this again… from then on, whatever you asked, I answered. I never lied.”
She nodded and turned her gaze back to the stone steps ahead.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s2: In the dim cellar chamber underground, she stood before the rough stone tablet.

The first rule of the procedures: before entering the chamber, the volunteer must have read the inscription three times and be able to recount, in their own words, the distinctions among the three things.
