She took a piece of charcoal, sat on the cold stone floor, silently read the dry inscription three times, and drew three black marks on the ground.

“This part is the most interesting.” She pointed to the sentence, “This is where it ends, not that it never existed.” “A procedure, yet it is arguing with someone. Someone once stood here like me and demanded an answer, then added a note beside it. The person who carved it left the sentence they won the argument with here forever.”
“I already understand the first two. It does not collect ordinary death, and it cannot forcibly delete the world that remains.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s3: She turned and glanced at the heavy operating chamber.
“What about the third? What if the person who added that note didn’t win the argument over the third thing?”

“Your time will stop completely in every branch, releasing the capacity that fills the gap.” I looked at her. “The machine before us ends you, but the seventeen years you lived are not erased. You aren’t degraded. You’re completely isolated. Your information will not vanish into thin air.”
“Even if the information doesn’t perish, where will that part of it belonging to me go? How will the person who comes to save me know it’s me?”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s4:
I suddenly stepped between her and the operating terminal, my voice hoarse.
“Even knowing that, to keep the machine running, I have nothing extra left to give, I still have to try once myself. Stay in this world and let me go in and take my chances.”
She looked at me calmly for a while.
“Then verify it once from the main operating console. Step inside.”

I pulled open the heavy chamber door and stepped into the cold metal chamber. The ring-shaped scanning device did not start, because I had not locked the chamber door. The system was still waiting for the operator’s next step.
Outside the chamber, Yuna entered my name into the target field on the terminal, one stroke at a time.

The cursor on the screen blinked, reached that line, and stopped. The indicator requiring volunteer confirmation lit up.
I pressed the confirmation key, and only then did the ring-shaped scanning device inside the chamber sweep rapidly over me.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s5: When I stepped out of the chamber, she pointed to that line.

“The machine calculated it clearly. It won’t accept you. You’re carrying a forced cross-world loop, and your capacity has long since been locked and filled by it. You can’t fill the gap here.” She looked at me. “You’re an account with a zero balance.”

She returned to the console, erased my name, and entered “Yuna.” The cursor blinked on the screen. The indicator requiring the volunteer to enter the chamber and confirm lit up.
She walked over and stepped into the cold metal chamber.

Then she pressed the confirmation key. The ring-shaped scanning device swept rapidly over her and emitted a low hum. The line “Target cannot be coupled” did not appear.
The green words “Entry into external calibration process permitted” lit up on the screen.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s6:
“It can read my capacity.”
She turned around and stepped out of the chamber.
“So what I hand over is these solid seventeen years that made it all the way to today without being tampered with by any external force.”
“Listen carefully. Someday, when you go to retrieve me—if all you can obtain is a fragment, or if you have to use the memories in your head to
reconstruct an impostor with the same behavioral patterns… I won’t accept it. If she doesn’t remember what I said tonight, then she isn’t me.”
“What if she does remember what you said tonight?”
“Then the one you have to retrieve is this complete, untouched version of me.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s7: “One more thing. If you really find a way to shut it down in another world, destroy that machine, and no longer need to keep jumping.” She paused, her voice softening. “Then live properly there. Along with this world that the gap bought.”
“I’m setting one too.” I stared hard at her. “The procedures don’t say that withdrawal is allowed. So I’m adding a spoken sixth rule. The volunteer may withdraw at any moment before
lockdown, or stop at any time. Unless you actively report the next item as ‘Present,’ the operator is absolutely forbidden to urge you on, and absolutely forbidden to ask any questions.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s8: She looked at me, then glanced at the densely packed buttons on the console.
“I believe this. You are absolutely forbidden to decide for me. Until I’m ready to speak on my own.”
I fixed those words in my mind.
The final agreement was made before the open, heavy chamber door.
“I’m assigning you a job. Bring me back.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s9: “I’m handing over this entire path. Every step on it remains. If you can truly make it to that point—find me and bring me back. Arno, have you ever done what you said you would?”
“Yes.” I looked at her without flinching.
Then she undid the reddish-brown old identification band wrapped around her wrist and wrapped it around mine. Twice.

“Borrow it. I know the physical object can’t reach the next world. I can only leave it in this one world that I save. But this account is between us. Separate matter.”
She lowered her head and pressed the clasp tight.
“You can’t carry the object with you, so remember this feeling

of it constricting your wrist. No matter how many worlds you have to search for me in later, this feeling will be the anchor you use to locate this world. When you really do bring me back someday, even if your hands are empty, you still have to return it to me exactly as it is.”
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s1: Her fingers were very warm. I was going to say that sentence. I opened my mouth and swallowed dryly.
“Don’t,” she cut me off sharply.
“Whenever you’re about to say something you don’t actually want to say, your throat swallows. If you really wanted to say it here, you wouldn’t have swallowed just now.”
She was right. If I said “goodbye” at a time like this, it would become a farewell.
“Keep that sentence for yourself. Farewell words are always for the living person to use. Wait until I come back, then say it to my face.”
“What if I don’t come back?” My voice trembled.
“Then leave it owing.”
“Owing means there’s still an account between us that hasn’t been settled. I, Yuna, absolutely won’t go far while my accounts remain unsettled.”
The strength in her fingers gradually withdrew. She let go of my hand, turned, and stepped through the chamber door.
“Go read your list, operator.”
The hands of the pocket watch pointed to 19:40. External calibration: forty-one items.

Under the procedures’ “two people divide the duties,” I was the operator outside the chamber, while she was the volunteer locked inside. I read each external instruction, and she verified it through the internal panel and answered “Present,” only after which I could press the confirmation key on the console.
She answered item nine crisply, then suddenly added through the speaker:
“Hey. The new wheat is in this year. Taste a bite for me.”
“Item ten,” I read.
“Present. Remember to dip it in sugar.”
I paused, forcing down the bitterness in my throat. “Item twenty-three.”
“Present. —You’re always no good at flying Milu’s kite. Have Lise fly it for her later.”
“Item thirty.”
“Present. —That jar of pickled vegetables my mother made tastes best on the seventh day. I’ll remember it for you. You can’t eat this. Even if you get hungry again someday, don’t touch it.”
Item thirty-three. I finished reading the instruction.
But no sound came from inside the chamber.

My hand jerked away from the console as if shocked. I stood there, forcing every sound back down my throat.
Five seconds. Ten seconds.
Twenty seconds.
At the twenty-sixth second, I finally could not endure the silence.
“Are you withdrawing?” I blurted out in collapse, completely violating the rule I had just established forbidding questions.
A very soft sigh came through the speaker.
“You violated the rule, Arno.” Her voice was calm. “But I didn’t withdraw. I was thinking about Milu.”
“I was thinking about her bell. The broken one. She said yesterday that she wanted me to fix it for her. I can’t fix it now.”
The chamber fell silent briefly.
“But not being able to fix it has nothing to do with whether I go in. I’m not withdrawing because of that. I only thought about it. I’m done thinking now.”
“Item thirty-three, present.”
Item forty.
“Present.”
Item forty-one: lockdown. I read the instruction, my hand suspended over the key that would decide fate. The hands of the pocket watch had already passed 19:50.
Then her voice pierced through.
“Item forty-one, present. —Arno.”
“Present.”
“Go to the next today.”
I pressed the key down hard.

There was no earth-shaking storm of light, no tremor tearing through the cellar. The instant the key reached the bottom, my vision went completely blank for a moment. It was not external light, but my overstrained nerves breaking apart entirely at that instant.

When I suddenly drew in a sharp breath and came back to myself.
The red light indicating lockdown had gone completely out. With a dry sound of pressure being released, the heavy chamber door automatically sprang open a crack.
Inside, everything was exactly as it had been. Not even a trace of dust had risen.
I lunged at the door and pulled it open with all my strength.

Inside was utterly empty.
There was no body, no ash, nothing left behind. Yuna was as if she had been pulled out of existence.
The piercing cold of my knees striking the stone floor was the first sensation that brought me fully back to myself.
The heavy chamber door stood open just like that.
The fourth rule of the procedures said: the operator must remain until release is complete and may not leave first. I had remained for the entire process.
The yellowed register was beneath the gas lantern. I lifted the pen and forcefully wrote my name on the blank first line.
I remained in that deathly silent cellar chamber, keeping watch through this final hour.

Until 20:36.
I stared at the pocket watch in my hand. The second hand passed that moment, and the daylight did not descend. The moment destined to erase everything tonight had been filled. Everything was as she had calculated.

Then I picked up the gas lantern, left the metal chamber, and climbed the long stone steps.
Garon and Milu were still outside the yellow-and-black operating boundary line. They had followed us all the way here.
The boundary was not a physical barrier, but they had never crossed it.

I stopped at the top of the stone steps.
“The gap before us has been filled,” I said. “The daylight will not come tonight. But I can’t bring her back.”
Garon’s shoulders suddenly collapsed. He stared at the gas lantern in my hand for a long time, then

finally closed his eyes and turned away. Milu clenched her apron, her legs giving way as she dropped to her knees on the rubble and buried her face in them. Neither of them came toward me.
I turned around and went back into the empty underground chamber.

On this night that should have brought the end of the world, we had indeed filled the gap before the first adults fell. Apart from the empty metal chamber, not one thing in the room belonging to this world was missing.

The other gas lantern in the corner still burned tirelessly. The records on the west wall were still on the shelves. The rough inscription was still on its stand. On the copy of the procedures hanging on the east wall, the patch of paper beneath the fifth rule was still yellowed by smoke.

The pocket watch made a faint ticking sound. 21:59.
I sat there, unconsciously waiting for her next sentence.

In the hundreds of repeated mornings before this one, whenever a silence lasted more than a minute, she would open her mouth and break it.
But the next sentence never came.

In that moment, I knew with absolute clarity what “nothing” looked like. It was not black, and it was not empty. It was a room in which everything remained, with nothing missing. Only there would never be a second half to the next sentence again.

During the long wait for the jump, I went to the west wall and aligned the edges of the books on the shelf. I crouched down and reached out to turn the knob on the flickering gas lantern a little lower. Because if she saw something burning pointlessly into empty air, she would certainly be unable to resist adjusting it.
texts.chapter:chapter-15-promise:event:text-s2:
Through those long loops, on every morning after a restart, I would check the pulse at her wrist. That hand was always cold, and I always tried in vain to warm it by holding it.
But this time, there was no longer a slightly cool hand for me to hold.
22:00 exactly. The vertigo of the forced jump struck on time.

I touched the reddish-brown old identification band wrapped around my wrist, gently pushed it higher, and rolled the worn-bright clasp between my fingertips. From the outside inward.
That was the last thing I could still do in this cellar.

22:01.
The cellar in the old world receded from me. The apocalyptic endpoint that should have dragged me into darkness along with it did not arrive. The vertigo tore me bodily out of that coordinate and cast me forward.
When consciousness forcibly probed into a new morning, glaring light rose into my field of vision. I pushed myself up against the bedboard and glanced at the alarm clock beside

the bed.
It was around 8:10 in the morning.
I did not go to the White Tower. In the cellar of yesterday’s spacetime, the machine’s words “Target cannot be coupled” had shown me
its hand: the forced cross-world loop had long since locked my capacity. Whether Yuna in that world had survived or not, I could not stop. This locked perception could only

continue being forcibly stuffed into the bodies of the local Arnos in countless parallel worlds.
There was no voice outside urging me on.
This was my “next world,” without Yuna.
texts.chapter:interlude-her-monologue:title: Interlude: Her Monologue
texts.chapter:interlude-her-monologue:event:te:
At exactly eight that morning, the sixteen-year-old boy before me suddenly became someone else. That person’s eyes were more tired, and more familiar to me.
He stared hard at me in the White Tower corridor, tears circling in his eyes.
When those ten minutes of lost time ended and the Arno of that day came back to himself, I repeated everything that had happened to him. Watching him struggle beneath that unfamiliar
despair, I knew the person who had occupied his body had not been something he had simply made up. That visitor who had stayed only briefly was convinced he had once lost a “Yuna.”
If I quietly accepted death like that, this unreasonable burden would probably have crushed him into the heavy shadow who carried everything. I wasn’t willing to walk toward an ending
I didn’t understand. Over the next few days, I forced him to knock on the doors of all ten people on the list, one by one, until he brought back every name covered in refusal; then I
forced my parents to calculate every cost. I personally tested every escape route I could think of until it was dead, forcing every person on the list into the most unbearable corner.
Only after I was certain that I had found no other way through those futile days of running around did I make that decision.
On the night road to the underground device, the only sound besides the soles of our shoes crushing the dry grass was Arno speaking.

To be honest, when I looked at the list filled with refusals, I secretly prayed that someone would agree to take my place. If someone had been willing to step forward, I wouldn’t have had to die.
But when it was finally confirmed that no one could go, what rose

inside me was, unexpectedly, a hidden relief. No one would take my place, and I wouldn’t have to spend the rest of my life thanking anyone, wouldn’t have to lie awake at night forever thinking, “I’m still alive today because he walked through that door for me.”

At dusk, Mother took away my coat and insignia, then stood blocking the doorway with red-rimmed eyes. Seeing how resolute she was, I found myself hoping they would keep being unreasonable forever. I even wished they would lock me inside the house by

force, then walk to this machine themselves and die in my place. So when they finally only repeated, exhausted, “I don’t agree,” again and again, without actually stopping me from leaving, I did turn away and secretly swallow a trace of resentment.

But when Father actually proposed, in a low voice, that he go die in my place, something inside me ached sharply, and I almost wavered. But I couldn’t pretend I didn’t know what was written in that account: if the gap wasn’t filled tonight, I

and the people of this world would go out together; but once Father entered and filled the capacity in my place, his existence in every branch would be severed.
I couldn’t drive the fathers in every world to a dead end just to preserve myself

as I am now. If someone had to bear the cost of crossing worlds, it could only be me. I knew, of course, that the moment I went inside, countless “Yunas” in the branches where nothing had gone wrong—Yunas who could otherwise have continued

living—would be dragged into it as well, leaving countless fathers to suddenly lose their daughters. But I couldn’t make that cruel decision for Father. All I could do was harden my heart and decide for those versions of myself I had never met.
So in the end, I chose to push open the door of my home myself and walk toward this wasteland.

Now, this hatch is slowly locking shut behind me.
The body’s fear of this total erasure is instinctive. When I learned that I would be completely emptied out to fill that gap, my fingertips

went numb at once.
That numbness has remained until now. Even standing inside the device, I still have to clench my fist hard to keep my middle finger from twitching uncontrollably.

Of all the long farewells I had imagined, there was only one thing I regretted. Yesterday’s image suddenly sprang into my mind at the worst possible time: Milu tugging at my clothes and whining for me to fix that broken little bell.

So before we parted, I selfishly told him about the bell.
I wanted him to remember that what he owed was this one from today. Though I couldn’t explain to him that if he met Milu in another
world and found another bell, fixing that one wouldn’t count. I suppose this was me forcing him in my heart. No matter how long the road ahead was, he would have to carry this heavy debt with him.

And the old identification band I had worn for ten years was wrapped around Arno’s wrist outside the hatch. Twice around, pulled tight, tied down hard. I had to make sure the pain of it biting into his wrist stayed there long enough.

I knew he wanted to say, “Goodbye.” But I stopped him. In a world that was about to be emptied, “goodbye” sounded too much like a perfunctory send-off. Physical things that couldn’t be carried away could

only be left in this world, which would continue operating as usual. But as long as he, crossing worlds in the future, could vividly remember the pain in his wrist, that sensation could stay with him.

I know that if the shadow who had occupied him just now did not lie, if the future experienced again and again across countless worlds truly exists, then deep in his long memory there must be countless “Yunas” who once died at dusk.

I’m jealous of them. There’s no reason for that jealousy. But those “Yunas” I’ve never met did walk that long road with the shadow, little by little crushing him into that despairing future; and the time left to me isn’t even enough to live through a full seventeen years.

But I have no other stake left. This gap can only be filled by me now. Since I would reach the end in this world just the same, I might as well stake this one moment I alone can decide, along with my whole self, inside the machine.
Use this one

piece of capital to gamble on the chance to live through a complete life once in the future.
I want him to promise that if one day in the future he really can piece together a complete experience that belongs to me, there can be no deletions or

alterations in it. He can’t pick out only the moments he likes, can’t erase my pain and indignity for me, and can’t pass off something that merely looks like me as a substitute. Either piece me back together exactly as I was, or leave me here forever.
I’ve already heard the sound of the air being drawn out. I know what will happen next.
The external calibration is completely finished. The hatch has shut out every sound.
But I know that huge, shrill alarm will soon surge up from every direction, swallowing my hearing in an instant. The incandescent lights in my field of vision will begin to twist

and stretch violently, and the weight of my body will be torn away by an enormous force.
Before I sink completely into that boundless darkness, I find that I am no longer afraid.

I staked everything I had here, along with this one and only today.
Whether the road ahead can catch it—that’s your concern now.
texts.chapter:chapter-16-morning-without-her:t: Chapter Sixteen: A Morning Without Her
texts.chapter:chapter-16-morning-without-her:e:
Candidate Process Sheet · Day Eight (copy, transcriber: Estelle):
Morning: week-end review. Afternoon: next-level submission.
Addendum: If an internal candidate fails to appear on time, check their residence first.
Addendum Two: Both candidates in this cohort have been on the rolls since

Day One, and both are first choices, with no record of removal or replacement.

(Estelle’s note: Addendum Two was added this year. It wasn’t written in previous years.
I asked why it had to be written. The elder on duty said: Write it clearly. Then no one will misremember it in the future.)

My mind was still caught in the inertia of the previous scene—my gaze fixed on the wall at the foot of the bed, waiting for a line of ice-blue characters to appear and tell me the time and today’s task.
There was nothing on the wall. Only the rough smears of lime plaster.

Beneath me was a rough linen sheet, and harsh morning light filled my vision. This was my home in the village, my own bed. The old alarm clock at the head of the bed pointed to approximately eight ten in the morning. Eight o’clock was when the week-end review was supposed to begin, but I hadn’t gone to the White Tower.
My body felt frozen, and I sat rigidly on the edge of the bed.
I was waiting.

Even knowing that the world had changed, I was still waiting for a familiar set of footsteps. Waiting for Yuna to push open that heavy isolation door and come back to my side. Waiting for her to tell me that everything was over, that we could go home together.
But the room was deathly silent. Only fine dust rolled soundlessly through the harsh white shaft of light.
I slowly raised my right hand.
There was nothing on my wrist.
There was no reddish-brown woven strap. Only a few hours ago, she had leaned over, taken it off with her own hands, and wrapped it around my wrist.
I rubbed the skin with my thumb. It was smooth and warm, without even the faintest pressure mark. That real, solid clasp, along with the ravaged
world, had all remained on the other side of the daylight, without coming over with me. Only I was left, remembering its weight with perfect clarity.
I stared at my wrist for a long time, until my eyes grew dry and painful. Like staring at a page someone had torn out of a book by sheer force, without even leaving a ragged edge behind.
Then there was a knock outside.
Knock, knock, knock.
Three times, neither light nor hard, as even as the swing of a mechanical pendulum.
I got out of bed, shuffled over in my shoes, and opened the door. Two people stood outside.
Elder Sera stood in front, wearing her plain white uniform, the dark-red metal insignia fastened perfectly at her cuff—the duty uniform for the week-end review.
Half a step behind her stood Estelle.
The instant the door opened, I didn’t look at Elder Sera. My gaze went straight over her shoulder and fixed itself on Estelle. The first thing I saw was the rise and fall of her chest.
I don’t know why, in a moment of extreme fear, a person’s gaze would focus in such a strange way. I only watched her shoulders lift slightly, fall, then lift again. One
of her hands hung naturally at her side, her fingers curling against the edge of the fabric now and then—the small, living movement of someone unaware she was making it.
Following her shoulders upward, I saw her face.
Her head was straight.
Her head was not tilted to one side at the lifeless, unsupported angle fixed in my memory.

The chill shot up from the soles of my feet. My legs had already gone weak before my mind could react. I thrust out a hand and seized the rough doorframe. My knuckles went white with the effort, and the wooden door let out an ugly screech on its hinges.
“Arno.”
Elder Sera looked at me. Her voice was level, without reproach or concern.
“The week-end review starts at eight. You’re ten minutes late.”
I didn’t answer her. I couldn’t even swallow the saliva in my throat.
I was still looking at Estelle.
Only then did I slowly make out the other details. She wasn’t wearing the short work clothes she had worn at Watermarsh. She was in a formal dress with a purple ground. Two indigo
practical ties neatly secured her low twin ponytails, and an extremely narrow silver arc rested in her hair, its surface marked only by fine enamel graduations and the candidate insignia.
At her waist hung the wooden badge that marked her as a candidate, perfectly in place.
The wooden badge was completely intact. It hung exactly where it belonged, the knot underneath neatly tucked inward.
I opened and closed my mouth. Something seemed to have sealed my chest shut. The first time I forced air through it, no sound came out.
I squeezed my eyes shut, and the second time, the sound finally broke through my throat.
“With my own hands,” I heard my voice say, hoarse beyond recognition.
“On that barren slope, I lifted your dead head.”
Estelle didn’t move. She didn’t even blink.

But her expression changed. There was no anger in it, nor surprise. Only the most instinctive reaction of a meticulous person hearing an anomalous statement that absolutely should not exist: first record it word for word in her mind, then decide what it actually was.
“Say that again.” She stared at me and spoke coldly.
I clenched my back teeth. I couldn’t say it a second time.
She stepped forward half a pace and came to a stop beside Elder Sera, her gaze sharp enough to scrape open my skull.
“Where did you hear that?” Her voice dropped lower.
“I didn’t hear it.” My fingers were still digging into the doorframe.
“Then which incident are you referring to? Be specific. Time, place, people present.”

As she questioned me, she instinctively reached toward her waist, habitually preparing to take something out and make a record. But halfway there, her hand stopped—she was wearing formal clothes today and had no little notebook with her.
“The western boundary.” I met her gaze.
“Under that barren slope, there’s an old road surface in the grass with rebar exposed. That was where you set your feet.”
Her gaze darkened when she heard this.
“Continue,” she urged.
“Watermarsh.”
“Go north along the boundary stone, and the distribution station is right in the middle of the settlement. The person responsible for registration is called Colai—”
I had been certain those few words would smash through her defenses. In my memory, all of them were secrets we had uncovered together in private.
But Estelle didn’t retreat. She didn’t show the slightest shock at having her secrets exposed. She only looked at me coldly.
“The week-end review.” I ignored her reaction and repeated the words numbly.
“Yes. The week-end review.” Elder Sera picked up the words.
I turned my head and looked at her.

I looked at Elder Sera standing quietly at my door. Morning sunlight fell across her plain white uniform, and the dark-red insignia at her cuff was fastened without a flaw. Her face held a trace of helplessness, like any village elder looking at a young person who had overslept and was talking nonsense.
In my mind, I rummaged through that discarded timeline.

On the timeline I had lived through, at 18:06 on the evening of Day Seven, Otto pushed open the door to the controlled archive and exposed our movements. It wasn’t until the long slope late that night that Yuna would be taken away by the guards. After that, on Day Eight, there should have been a nominal week-end review.
But that review had never taken place. That night, Yuna had entered the equipment at the lowest level and exchanged herself for everyone else, while I had been turned over to the present page.
Now Elder Sera was standing outside my door, informing me that I was to attend the week-end review on the morning of Day Eight.
My breathing began to shake, my chest heaving like a bellows.
“What day is it?” I forced the words out through clenched teeth.
Elder Sera looked at me quietly for one second, her gaze like that of someone looking at a patient.
“Day Eight,” she answered calmly.
My heart slammed hard against my ribs.
“Where’s Yuna?”
Elder Sera tilted her head slightly. “Who?”
That word: “who.”
It wasn’t heavy or cold, and there wasn’t even the slightest trace of feigned surprise. It was simply complete emptiness. This was a name that, the moment spoken aloud, should
absolutely have found an echo somewhere in the village. But the “who” that answered it spread flatly through the morning air, with nothing beneath it to support it. A total void.
I released the doorframe, drew a deep breath, and shifted my question toward Estelle.
“You told me more than that yesterday afternoon.” I stared at the intact wooden badge at her waist. “You also told me about your removal.”
The wariness in Estelle’s eyes deepened. “What removal?”

“On the evening of Day Two, Elder Sera read out the dismissal list. You stepped forward and returned your badge with your own hands. From Day Three onward, you walked to the classroom door, didn’t go in, and went to the council hall to appeal.”
Estelle’s jaw instantly tightened, her jawline drawing into a rigid arc.
“I wasn’t removed from the list.” Her voice was cold as ice.
“I’ve been here all seven days.” She stared at me. “From Day One through this morning, I haven’t missed a single class.”
Then she did something I hadn’t anticipated at all, something that made my skin crawl.
She began reciting a day-by-day account, like a machine reading a log.

“Day One, first lesson, Elder Sera explained three rules. Day Two, the two of us renumbered the discarded equipment in the old classroom on the underground second level. You suggested recording it in two columns and cross-referencing them.”
Her speech was rapid, her eyes fixed fiercely on me.
“On Day Three, the elder called you in for a private interview. On Day Four, you got stuck twice during procedural practice.”

“On the entire afternoons of Days Five and Six, you didn’t look at the materials. You kept asking me about the outlying settlements.” She enunciated every word. “Yesterday too—that was Day Seven—you were

still asking about the place to set your feet on the western boundary slope, how to get to Watermarsh, and even the name of the person in charge of registration in the settlement. I told you everything.”
At last, her hand fell away from the badge.
“When I answered you, you even took out your own notebook and wrote it down. So that’s how you know Colai.”
My hand shot into my pocket, and I pulled out the hardbound notebook I had kept close to me. My fingertips trembling, I opened it to the records from the past few days.

There were words on the page.
No technical parameters left by Yuna. No notes from the three of us during the first two days. It was all in my handwriting—cross-referenced numbers for the discarded equipment on the underground second level, the route to the Watermarsh settlement, and on the last line, neatly written: “Colai.”
I stared at the utterly unfamiliar handwriting that had nevertheless undeniably come from my own hand. It was my writing, but I had not the slightest memory of writing any of it.

Who had attended lessons, written things down, and asked Estelle about the outlying settlements inside this shell during those seven days? Where had the real “me” who had lived through those seven daylight hours gone?

I remembered the morning of the first day, when some anomalous consciousness crashed into my shell. That possession had lasted only ten minutes, and at eight ten I had taken back control. This time, too, I woke at eight

ten. Could the consciousness that had occupied my shell for the past seven days have withdrawn at this exact mark? But if that ten-minute limit had long since been exceeded, why was I still trapped inside this body?

I looked at these hands of mine. Had the consciousness originally belonging to this body been completely forced out by me, or had it merely fallen into a temporary sleep? No one could answer me. But the terror I felt so vividly made me shudder—if this

occupation was permanent, if that “Arno” who had lived through those seven days could never wake again… Yuna had sacrificed herself to save that world, and was I supposed to survive like a tyrant, by completely erasing the life of another self in this world?
I stood rigid in the open doorway, the morning wind against my face, unable to refute a single word.
I clenched my fists, my nails digging into the flesh.
“The classroom had the three of us in it during the first two days.”
Estelle’s brow furrowed deeply, as if she were looking at someone who had gone completely mad.
“Three?”
I clenched my teeth and didn’t answer her. This was no longer something argument could explain.
“Elder Sera.” Estelle cut me off quickly.
She turned neatly, her heel tracing a small semicircle on the flagstones, and faced Elder Sera directly, both heels aligned.
“I need to report something.”
“Go ahead.” Elder Sera’s expression darkened as well.

“He just mentioned the place to set your feet on the western boundary slope, as well as Colai. Those things are indeed things I told him myself yesterday afternoon. But the anomaly is that he described a schedule completely different from mine.”
She looked directly into the elder’s eyes, her report delivered with extreme precision.

“He clearly described a removal ceremony that never existed—including the details of me returning my badge with my own hands. He even said there had been three people in the classroom during the first two days. These are not things he could have fabricated by consulting external records.”
When she finished her report, she faced Elder Sera again and stood straight.

“Based on the statements above, I request that two things be checked immediately. First, whether my private file contains a removal contingency unknown even to me, and whether it has been secretly accessed recently. Second, whether Arno has come into contact with any hallucinogenic substances during the past seven days.”
When she finished, she lowered her head slightly and added one final sentence.
“I’m not arguing in his defense. Both of these lines of inquiry are unfavorable to him.”
Elder Sera listened quietly to the cold report.
She didn’t answer immediately. She simply stood below the steps of my doorway, both hands clasped in front of her, and looked at me for a long time.
I kept gripping the doorframe, holding myself rigid as I waited for her to question me. But she didn’t ask a single thing.
She withdrew her gaze from my face and turned toward Estelle.
“Check both immediately. I’ll personally retrieve the access records for your private file today.”
She lowered her hands crisply.

“Also, both candidate files for this cohort, the White Tower access records, and the passage records at the boundary stone for the past seven days are all to be sealed today. Affix the seals. From this moment on, no one is to touch them.”
Elder Sera issued the order decisively, without explaining the reason at all.
“The written portion of the scheduled week-end review is suspended,” she announced.
“Suspended?”
“It isn’t happening this morning. This afternoon, we’ll only carry out the field inspection procedure for the equipment level.”
She tucked both hands completely into her sleeves and stopped looking at me.
“Arno may move around the village and the White Tower today. But he is not to leave the village by so much as a step.”
She gave Estelle a stern glance.
“Record everything you hear and see. Do not leave him unattended for even a moment. If he tries to cross the permitted boundary, stop him immediately. This is also your additional inspection today.”
She paused, then added the final absolute order:
“Listen to him and write it down. But do not argue with him, and do not agree with a single thing he says.”
“Yes.” Estelle lowered her head and accepted the order.

After Elder Sera left, Estelle and I stood beside the open door like that. Each of us held continuous memories from the first day through this moment, but the two paths had already diverged completely from the instant we pushed open the classroom door on the morning of Day One.
At nine in the morning, we set out for the chapel and the White Tower.

Along the short stretch of road, I repeatedly strayed from the established route like a ghost, searching for even the slightest trace that could prove the old timeline still existed. Estelle followed behind without a word, carrying the black notebook and diligently carrying out her additional inspection.

I rushed to Yuna’s house first. The gate stood wide open, and the sunlight was bright. Meru was hanging freshly washed clothes on the line with her back to the gate. Hearing footsteps, she turned around with that familiar, gentle smile.
“Arno? Shouldn’t you be at the review this morning?”
I braced myself against her fence, panting hard, my eyes red, and asked whether Yuna was inside.
Meru froze. The jacket she had been shaking in her hands stopped in midair.
“Which Yuna?”
Sunlight fell dazzlingly across the yard. The clothesline swayed gently in the wind. She furrowed her brow slightly. The confusion on her face was so genuine, without the slightest trace of pretense.

I stood there with my mouth open like a fish thrown onto shore, every question and every piece of despair caught in my throat. I watched her hang the jacket on the line, smooth out the wrinkles, and even turn back to ask me with concern, “Arno, are you feeling unwell?”
I backed away step by step, my gaze sweeping wildly across the yard. There were no old boots on the windowsill, no pair of pliers in the corner. The clothesline held only clothes belonging to
Gallon, Meru, and a twelve-year-old girl. Her yard, her expression, the way she hung laundry—everything fit together perfectly. In Gallon and Meru’s life, there had only ever been one daughter.
I spun around and stumbled away at a run.
I wandered without purpose and eventually stopped at the edge of the open yard.
Milu was in the middle of the yard. The little girl was holding her most treasured battered bell high above her head and shaking it with all her strength.
The bell was still broken. There was no clapper inside, only a rusted shell of empty metal. No matter how hard she shook it, it could not make a sound.
She turned her head, saw me, and ran over, holding the silent bell up in front of me as if showing off a treasure.
“Do you want to shake it too? If you make it loud enough, broken things will get better.”
I asked numbly, “Who taught you to say that? This bell doesn’t make a sound at all.”
Milu’s face flushed bright red. She twisted the corner of her clothes awkwardly, fiercely protecting the metal shell.
“I can hear it ringing in my head.” She stumbled over the words, defending it. “I made it up myself. Anyway, anyway, no one ever taught me anything.”
I watched her run away, my throat catching on something. For a long while, I couldn’t swallow a single breath.
In this world without Yuna, the bell in Milu’s hands was still broken. I didn’t even dare try to distinguish whether this was some kind of resonance crossing
the mechanism, or merely a similar coincidence. I only stood there, listening greedily, over and over, to the sound that did not exist anywhere but in my mind.
When I reached the chapel’s outer wall, I stood before the mottled metal plaque and slowly raised my hand, tracing the engraved marks in the air with my fingertip. Then my finger stopped.

In the deep grooves where the verdigris had peeled away was an old inscription mixing ancient Imperial engineering symbols with early Church word roots: “Ω-04: Terminal Isolation Zone.” The characters had clearly been transcribed into a language whose literal meaning I could read directly.
But I only recognized the words. I had no idea where the “terminal” was, or what “isolation” was isolating. In this group, I had always played the part of a cold,
human glossary. In this world, the decoder who could weave scattered roots into practical use—and even the possibility that she had existed—had never existed.
Noon. We ate a simple ration on a stone bench in the White Tower’s outer gallery.

After eating, Estelle took a small needle and thread from her pocket and began skillfully mending a nearly invisible worn spot on the sleeve of her purple formal dress. Earlier, while we were walking, she had also

taken out a sheet of paper and written several lines across her knees during a pause. I had glimpsed a letter to the Watermarsh settlement, one she was preparing to send home after passing the week-end review.
“You’ve written down so many things I said.” I leaned against the cold stone pillar and watched her thread the needle. “Why haven’t you doubted yourself even once?”
She stopped what she was doing. Without looking at me immediately, she opened the black notebook and wrote a line in a blank space.
“Elder Sera ordered me not to argue with you.” She spoke coldly as she wrote. “So at present, as a recorder, I’m merely stating the reasons I refuse to believe you.”
I gave a cold laugh.
“Because you can’t bear to lose that wooden badge?”
Estelle ignored the barb in my words. She closed the notebook and turned the mended sleeve over to inspect it.

“I haven’t made a mistake in a single review during these seven days.” She didn’t look at me, only lowered her head to examine the sleeve. “I want that formal seat. It means the continued life promised by the oracle. If I

don’t get it, I can only go crawling back to Watermarsh as someone who ‘didn’t pass this cohort,’ and keep telling the people in the village, See? The White Tower’s process is fair. All you need to do is prepare well enough.”
She bit through a thread end.
“If I get it, I’ll have a say in applications for Watermarsh’s supplies. And I’ll have a say in how I die.”
She stood, dusted the dirt from her skirt, and tucked the letter to her hometown inside her pocket.
“In your story, that version of me lost everything. But the me standing here today hasn’t.” At last she lowered her eyes and glanced at me. “So I don’t want to doubt it.”

“Let’s go.” She put away the letter, her voice returning to its cool, official composure. “13:20. According to the review schedule, we’re to conduct a field inspection for the next-level submission this afternoon. Elder Sera is already waiting for us in the equipment section.”

I leaned against the cold stone pillar without speaking. In my memory, the original schedule for this day had never included an afternoon inspection of the equipment section. In this world without that Yuna who could understand machines, Estelle was certain that only orderly procedure lay ahead.
I straightened and followed her.

As we went downward, that absurd feeling rose over me once again. The next level? Hadn’t the next level of the tower been sealed off and abandoned long ago? More importantly, throughout the entire seven-day first phase, the “submission” the elders referred to had without exception meant theoretical knowledge and technical principles. But now the

written examination had been halted in an emergency, both candidate files had been completely sealed, and at this moment when every paper qualification had been stripped away, if they still intended to force through a “submission” that required on-site verification in the equipment section… then what exactly did they intend to submit to the system?

I wanted to ask whether she knew the designation of the “Terminal Isolation Zone.” I wanted to ask whether the letter she had just written to Watermarsh meant that she had realized something. But looking at her straight back and purple skirt, I couldn’t ask anything.
The passage downward was dark and quiet. No one was waiting for us in the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:title: Chapter Sixteen, Supplement: She Means to Win Today
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s1-1: The first afternoon after Yuna disappeared.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s2-1: For the two hours after the midday break, Estelle followed behind me like a shadow. Ever since our conversation ended on the White Tower’s outer gallery at noon, she had kept a tight grip on her
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s2-2: examination register. If she could bring back a flawless record and preserve her candidate status through the final selection, she would be only one last step away from the official seat with a voice
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s2-3: in Watermarsh’s material allocations and medical applications. Throughout the next stage, she said nothing. She only watched me intently, recording every move I made in objective, cold handwriting.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s3-1: Fourteen fifty. White Tower, maintenance drill level. By procedure, this was already the final item of the day.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s7-1: The old transport carriage hung in the central shaft, its thick steel cables slick with oil and gleaming dully.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s9-1: “This is your practical examination for this afternoon’s ‘Next-Layer Delivery.’” Sera stood at the edge of the shaft and gave the order without expression. “By procedure, both candidates are required to ride the carriage down to the lower level and each complete one hands-on emergency shutoff-valve exercise in the high-pressure environment of the deep shaft.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s10-1: Estelle closed the register and walked toward the carriage.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s11-1: I looked at the thick steel cable. In the first complete world I had lived through, I had heard the cables of similar equipment break with a shriek. Although this additional examination
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s11-2: had not appeared anywhere on the original schedule, the sensation of weightlessness and falling had long since stained every old metal structure, driven into my bones like an iron spike.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s14-1: “I’m not riding.” I stepped in front of Estelle and pointed upward. “This cable could break at any moment. No one can ride in the carriage.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s15-1: Sera frowned slightly. She glanced at the brake components visible through the inspection hatch.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s17-1: “The brake components are intact. The structure is locked in place. There is no physical risk.” Sera fixed her eyes on me. “Refusal to undergo the examination will immediately cancel your qualification.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s19-1: “Then run it empty, without passengers.” I did not back down.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s20-1:
We stood locked in place beside the shaft for nearly twenty minutes.
At fifteen ten, Sera watched me coldly for a while. She drew the communicator from her belt and reported to the lower level that it was being cleared, then pressed the empty-run control on the console.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s21-1:
The carriage began to descend slowly, accompanied by the shrill scrape of metal.
Then, just as it reached the middle of the shaft, a muffled tearing sound came from deep below.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s22-1: The breaking sound had not come from the cable. A large section of the structure deep below suddenly collapsed. The unsupported guide twisted downward in an instant,
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s22-2: sending the heavy carriage suspended in midair violently off the rails and crashing into the shaft wall. Then several tons of heavy framework fell from above and crushed
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s22-3: it into the depths with a grating roar. The enormous pulling force traveled up through the steel framework and wrenched the attached catwalk beneath our feet out of shape.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s24-1: “Back!” Sera shouted sharply, leaping nimbly backward into the safe area of the vestibule.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s25-1:
But we were too late.
The steel plate beneath our feet broke apart with a crash. I only had time to grab Estelle’s arm before weightlessness seized us.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s28-1: Amid the roar, the broken catwalk did not take us straight down to the bottom. It struck the stone wall halfway down the shaft at an angle instead. After a series of shrill
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s28-2: metallic scrapes, the twisted catwalk jammed between two old maintenance safety nets. Rubble and metal plates poured down, sealing off the barely supported space between them.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s30-1:
All around us was complete darkness and drifting dust. The choking smell of rust and powder filled my airway, making even breathing dry and bloody.
The dull pain in the back of my head had briefly knocked me unconscious. When
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s30-2: I came to my senses in a daze and coughed my way through the darkness, I found that a broken metal plate had wedged diagonally between the stone wall and the catwalk, luckily propping open a cramped triangular space for us.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s34-1: “I’m here.” Her voice came from several steps away, carrying a suppressed tremor.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s35-1: I moved toward her. In the faint light filtering down from above, I saw her leaning against a section of broken pipe. She was clutching the observation register tightly to her chest. The back of her hand had been cut open, and blood was seeping from it.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s36-1: From above came the groaning of twisted metal and the sliding of rubble at irregular intervals. There was no exit here. The heavy ruins had completely sealed the way up. Every slight vibration made us wonder whether the unstable structure
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s36-2:
above would finally crush this narrow shelter. We endured nearly an hour in that tense, deathly silence.
Then, from very high above, a temporary communications probe with a light source, along with a hose for supplying water and oxygen,
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s36-3: was lowered through the gap and came to a stop outside the ruins. It was the first communications link Sera had managed to establish in an emergency. The probe’s indicator light blinked. Its display showed that it was already sixteen ten.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s37-1: “Arno, Estelle, report your injuries!” Sera’s voice came down through the probe, threaded with static.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s43-1: “No life-threatening injuries. Arno is conscious. I have a cut on the back of my hand.” Estelle shouted through the pain.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s45-1: “The collapse was caused by severe decay in the lower main guide base. The carriage cables are intact. The engineering team is assembling heavy lifting equipment. The earliest they can clear the ruins is tomorrow morning. …Estelle, do you still have your register?”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s47-1: “I do. I’m recording the time of the accident, the conditions, and Arno’s actions.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s49-1: “Good. This accident is also part of your examination. As long as you bring out a flawless record, you pass the additional assessment.” Sera’s reply was calm.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s50-1: Those words became Estelle’s support in the ruins. In the darkness, she felt for the register, opened it, and used the probe’s faint light to stubbornly write down the objective facts.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s52-1: “Fourteen fifty, candidate Arno refused carriage transport …” she murmured as she read back what she had written, her voice echoing through the confined space. “Fifteen ten, empty run. Lower base collapsed. Cable intact.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s53-1: She was like a perfect recording device, clinging to Sera’s absolute order: do not argue.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s54-1: Just then, voices from Sera’s communications with other departments came through the probe’s speaker. She seemed to be investigating the cause of the accident. Because they were so close, the probe picked up the report directly:
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s55-1: “…The full-day log screening is complete. No load-bearing alarms. The only abnormal record before the accident was at eight ten this morning, at the central relay.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s57-1: “Candidate timing-verification fault at the central relay. Affected field: end-of-week countdown. Error code A-774. No other abnormalities besides the central relay.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s58-1: The communications channel fell silent for several seconds. Then Sera’s voice came through, this time directed straight into the probe channel:
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s60-1: “Estelle, under the facility accident procedures, record this error code and the time it occurred in your examination register for reference.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s61-1: “Yes.” Estelle lowered her head and quickly recorded it on the page by the probe’s faint light.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s62-1: Eight ten in the morning. It sounded like an ordinary procedural error—Sera had said that the end-of-week review began at eight, and I had been ten minutes late. But to me, that moment carried an entirely different weight: it was exactly when I had awakened in this world and taken
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s62-2:
control of the body.
The timing was exact to the second. It might have the most ordinary explanation, but the coincidence left me unable to let it go. This error, designated A-774, might well be a deep-system scar left behind when the system tried to process my cross-world connection.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s63-1: I abruptly straightened and stared through the faint light at the words Estelle was writing.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s65-1: “After we get out,” I said in a low voice, keeping my eyes fixed on her, “find a way to keep this page’s information—especially its exact trigger conditions—or copy it down separately. I need it.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s66-1: Estelle froze for a moment. She looked at the register in her hands, the thing that represented her future.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s70-1: “I know. But I have to investigate this A-774.” I spoke quickly. “Eight ten was exactly when my lateness ended. The system might explain it as an ordinary timing-verification conflict. But it absolutely wasn’t just a procedural error.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s71-1:
Estelle fell silent. She gripped the register and looked at me.
“What exactly do you know?”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s72-1: “You said this afternoon that the cable would break.” Estelle stared at me, her voice exceptionally calm in the cramped space. “You were wrong. The cable didn’t break at all. The base below collapsed.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s73-1: “But if we’d been in the carriage”—I did not back down, pointing toward the darkness above where the heavy impact had come from—“we’d already have been crushed into pulp along with it by those falling
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s73-2: supports. I don’t know how it will fail, but I know there’s something wrong down there. Just as I know that this code, which may be treated as nothing more than lateness, is the only lead I can get hold of.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s74-1:
Estelle did not argue. In the darkness, she raised her head slightly and glanced at the ruins above that had completely sealed the way out, then looked back down at the register in her hands.
She knew perfectly well that if she kept
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s74-2: investigating, if she chose to keep asking questions, the future she meant to exchange for a seat and Watermarsh’s allocations could very well vanish because she had become entangled in a dangerous secret at the edge of the system.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s77-1:
Night descended in the deathly silence.
The air in the cramped space grew more polluted. The dull impacts of stones being cleared came from above at intervals. In this space between layers, where a secondary collapse could happen at any moment, we sank into a long silence.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s78-1:
The time on the probe jumped to 20:36.
I suddenly tensed and fixed my eyes on the only light above us. My hands clenched around the iron pipe beside me, my knuckles whitening with the force. I held my breath in
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s78-2: my throat, afraid to make a sound. In my memory, in another complete world I had lived through, this was when the disaster had begun. From this minute onward, people’s consciousnesses had gone out in batches along
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s78-3: a precise timetable, like flames snuffed between fingers. In the end, the bindings of the living had completely collapsed, leaving only a silent empty city whose power still functioned but whose people were gone.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s79-1:
Ten seconds. Thirty seconds. One minute. Five minutes.
The probe’s indicator light continued to blink steadily. But that proved nothing. It would take time for people in the outlying areas to fall. What truly let me breathe again was
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s79-2:
another hour passing.
21:45.
The engineering team’s voices above continued to come through the probe’s speaker in broken fragments. The heavy-load dispatch channel that had inevitably ground to a complete halt before 21:00 in the
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s79-3: first few worlds was still packed with complaints and dispatch orders. The person directing the heavy-lift equipment swore from exhaustion, then casually called the names of two apprentices beside him and told them to fetch floodlights.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s80-1: My tense shoulders gradually collapsed. Cold sweat had already soaked through my back. I gasped for breath, listening as my pounding heartbeat slowly subsided in the confined space. According
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s80-2: to that timetable, by 21:45 all ordinary people should already have fallen. But now, ordinary night was descending outside, and the collapse that destroyed the living had not occurred.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s81-1: I had thought she had given herself up only to mend that ravaged world. It was only at this moment that I truly understood: the deep flaw that had caused
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s81-2: the world to collapse had been filled by her at its source. Her sacrifice had brought a peaceful night even to this parallel world where she did not exist.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s82-1: Estelle watched me quietly from beside me. She did not know what I was waiting for, but she had seen the instinctive defense and terror that had taken hold of me in the face of annihilation, and the collapse mingling relief with despair when the disaster failed to arrive.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s84-1: “What were you waiting for just now …?” she asked softly.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s86-1: “For the sky to fall.” I leaned against the cold stone wall and closed my eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s87-1: She was silent for a long time. In the probe’s faint light, I saw her open the register she had been protecting against her chest, her fingertips unconsciously rubbing its edge.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s88-1: “I thought ‘winning’ meant keeping that seat, getting Watermarsh’s allocations, and securing a ticket to a longer life.” Her voice was very low in the darkness, dry from hours of oxygen deprivation. “If there was even one flaw in the register, everything I had prepared would be gone.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s89-1: I opened my eyes and looked at her.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s91-1: “When you refused to get in the carriage this afternoon, I thought you were insane. But the carriage really was crushed, and we’re alive.” She turned her head and looked straight at me in the probe’s faint light. Her lips
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s91-2: were slightly cracked from dehydration, but her eyes burned brightly. “Just now, you watched the time as if you were waiting for an execution whose ending had already been written. That fear absolutely wasn’t an act. If it
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s91-3: were just an equipment malfunction, it couldn’t have frightened you like that. You spent more than six hours trapped in this space, really just to confirm whether something would happen outside at that exact time, didn’t you?”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s92-1: She did not wait for my answer. Her fingers rested on the edge of the page in the examination register where the error log was written.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s93-1: “If what you’re looking for really is as big as you’ve made it seem”—she looked at me, her once-neat uniform covered in dust, the guarded calculation finally gone from her eyes—“something that could even explain the disaster that didn’t happen tonight, then
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s93-2: this isn’t about investigating a facility malfunction. By procedure, a system-level anomaly could never be shown to a candidate in the original records. They would only say it was a permissions-restricted base fault. If you want me to preserve the code and
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s93-3: its trigger conditions, once I go over Sera’s head to investigate it, they absolutely won’t treat it as an equipment-maintenance record. That register, along with the seat I want and Watermarsh’s distribution rights, could all become dangerous wastepaper.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s95-1: “If I have to win once today, then I’ll find out what exactly is hanging over all our heads.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s96-1: She closed the register and looked at me with firm resolve.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s97-1: “No matter how they dig us out tomorrow morning,” she continued, “as long as I can still breathe, I’ll go investigate it with you.”
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s100-1:
I looked at the firm outline of her face, then at the time blinking on the communications probe.
It was nearly 22:00.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s103-1:
As the ice-blue screen was about to pierce the darkness of my vision, that familiar sensation of separation descended once more.
Tomorrow morning, when the Arno who remained in this world awoke in the ruins, I was certain he would still possess every
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s103-2:
memory up to this moment tonight. He had not lost this day. He retained the instinct that had made him refuse the carriage, the echo of the collapse, and the hours he had endured with Estelle in this cramped space.
But he would not experience the screen
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s103-3: of light crossing between worlds again. He would remain here, using the code in this register, and continue living through an ordinary morning in this world Yuna had lifted from the abyss, alongside Estelle, who had promised to investigate it with him.
texts.chapter:v15-16b:event:text-s104-1:
Eight ten in the morning. Candidate timing-verification fault.
I left this anomaly, buried deep within the central system, together with the variable planted in this world today, for him—and faced the light sweeping toward me.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:title: Chapter Seventeen: The Watcher
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s2: Last night at twenty-two hundred, I disengaged from the sealed interstitial compartment in the middle section of that fractured shaft. The smell of blood and cold metal, trapped between two layers of old maintenance safety mesh, seemed to linger in my nostrils. But when my consciousness cleared again, it was eight ten in the morning, and I was back in the village.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s3: The early sunlight was a little too bright. I stood before a living Estelle and Elder Sera.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s4: Elder Sera still had that dignified appearance, as if she were about thirty-four. She held the candidate register in one hand, her gaze like a lake cold to its depths. On this orderly morning, this was the first time she had faced me behaving abnormally.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s5: “Your heart rate is highly unstable, Arno.” Sera frowned slightly, her voice carrying procedural severity. “The week-end final review began at eight. You’re ten minutes late.”
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s6: I did not hurry to answer. I turned, struck a match, lit the stove, pressed the dough flat into a new-wheat flatbread, and laid it across the iron pan. In the eyes of an Elder who possessed a complete memory of the local candidate week, this act of ignoring the White Tower’s countdown was unmistakably madness.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s7: The house gradually filled with the fresh scent of grain heating. Sera did not stop me. She only watched with an even more scrutinizing gaze. When the surface of the flatbread turned golden brown, I took it off the heat, tore off a tiny corner, dipped it in a little raw sugar, and slowly chewed it down.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s9: I carefully wrapped the larger remaining piece in clean oiled paper and put it in the back of the cupboard. It would harden. It would remain in this world I was destined to leave, keeping watch over a promise with no one left to receive it.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s1: Estelle, wearing her purple-based candidate uniform, stood three steps away. Her pen moved across the register, then suddenly stopped.

“Explain one item.” She raised her gray-blue eyes. Her tone was like someone reading out a test report. “Dipping it in sugar. You normally avoid sweets. And the sugar today was something you specifically traded for this morning.”
My gaze remained on the cupboard door. “I was tasting it for someone. She asked me to. When the new wheat came in, it had to be dipped in sugar.”
“Who is this ‘she’? Is she in the Watermarsh household records?”
“Her name is Yuna.” I turned around. “She isn’t in any of your records.”

She lowered her head and scratched out a record. I was standing close enough to glimpse the wording: “Baked new-wheat flatbread, dipped in sugar, ate one corner, remainder stored. Stated: fulfilled a promise on behalf of the person named Yuna.”

This audit register was not connected to the network. The system’s underlying layer would never read a handwritten note. It was only a physical mark left by ink, incapable of changing any allocation or
judgment. But for me, that was enough. As long as this register remained, the name that did not belong to this round of candidates at all had found a place to stand between black ink and white paper.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s2: Sera watched the interruption, her gaze growing colder.
“Are you finished? The White Tower’s timer won’t wait for you.”
I drew a deep breath. The memory of the previous world was imprinted in my mind with perfect clarity—in the static of the rescue channel after the unmanned, empty carriage derailed, I had heard the

complete communication of Sera receiving the preliminary investigation report. The security department on the other end had reported a string of underlying anomalies found during the full-day log screening.
“I’m not going to the final review, Elder Sera.” I looked into her eyes and played my trump card. “You can pull up your security terminal right now. In five minutes, at eight
twenty, the central relay system will experience a silent fault. Fault type: candidate timing verification failure. Affected field: week-end countdown. Error code: A-774.”
The room fell into deathly silence. Estelle’s pen stopped in midair.

Sera’s brows drew together. This was not something that could be dismissed as a boy’s grotesque fantasy. It fit the system’s internal terminology and low-level log format with precision, and pointed directly to the candidate process for which she was responsible.

“Estelle.” Sera’s voice remained cold, but she spoke half a beat faster than usual. “Activate a candidate supervision order. Until I issue further instructions, Arno is not to leave this room by so much as a step. You are responsible for accompanying him and recording everything. Report any breach of boundaries immediately.”
“Yes, Elder.” Estelle closed the register and blocked the doorway.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s3: Sera drew the security terminal from her belt. Her gaze moved back and forth between me and the screen. “I need to confirm this with the center.”
The seconds passed one by one. The room was so quiet that only the faint crackling of the stove fire remained.
Estelle stood straight by the door, watching me with a gaze like a precision scanner.

“Your heart rate is very steady.” Her voice was a flat statement. “When people lie or face the unknown, their pupils and breathing show minute fluctuations. But you don’t. You’re waiting for a result that is certain to occur.”
I walked to the table and sat down, my gaze resting in the direction of the cupboard. Half a sugar-dipped flatbread lay inside.
“Because the result is already there,” I said.
She followed my gaze to the cupboard, then lowered her eyes to the register in her hand. A name completely unfamiliar to her was written there.

“Yuna.” She sounded out the name, as if testing its weight on the tip of her tongue. “You used a prophecy about underlying data to try to obtain some action outside normal procedure, then left behind this obviously irrational record before departing. The two things cannot be explained by the same behavioral logic.”
“Some things matter more than logic.” I closed my eyes. The final scene in the pure-white room flashed through my mind.

“So to you, she is an expense that cannot be calculated.” Estelle drew a line on the paper, seemingly recording this conclusion. “If the underlying fault you just mentioned is real, then your earlier statement about this name also has a basis for being accepted.”
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s4: In this version of history, the second candidate of this round had not experienced the elevator’s fall with me, nor heard my confession in the sealed room. She was only an honor student rigorously carrying out her supervision and audit duties, with a complete and ordinary life for this week.
But her analytical ability was just as sharp in any life.

“This register.” Estelle lightly patted its cover. “It is part of my duties. I recorded your baking and dipping the bread in sugar, and copied down the name exactly as well. Whatever you are waiting for next, the name Yuna is now a physical record of this round of candidates.”
Sera lowered her head toward the terminal screen in her hand. The next second, her expression changed dramatically.
The screen’s cold light reflected across her face. The silent code that had triggered no alarm landed precisely on the eight-twenty mark and entered the underlying log pool.
“What did you do?” Sera jerked her head up, one hand pressing the terminal’s communications key, ready to call the outer guards at any moment.

“I didn’t do anything.” I remained calmly seated. “I’ve heard the accident investigation report from another timeline. I know what went wrong at the underlying level, and I know this code will occur on time every identical morning.”
Sera stared hard at me, trying to find traces of a bluff in my expression. But the terminal’s live verification results could not be faked.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s5: She drew a deep breath and pressed another authorization key on the terminal.
“Estelle.” Sera turned, her gaze passing over her to lock onto me with cold force. “Terminate the supervision order. You will remain in the village and continue your candidate process.”

“Arno, come with me.” Sera slid the terminal back into her belt. Her voice carried the unquestionable authority of public office. “The order to investigate the central relay station facility accident is now in effect. Since

you claim to have heard the investigation report, you will come to the site with me now and explain how you were able to predict an incident that an ordinary civilian with no knowledge of it should never have been able to know.”
Sera pushed open the door and, standing in the yard, connected to the encrypted line for summoning a shuttle.

“Remember the limits of your clearance.” Sera issued a warning from the yard. “At the central relay station, you may answer questions only. You are forbidden to touch any primary control equipment. The moment your hand crosses the boundary by even an inch, I will carry out a purge on the spot.”
“I understand.” I picked up the coat draped over the back of the chair and followed her.
The shuttle rose into the cold morning air.
texts.chapter:chapter-17-watcher:event:text-s6: Inside the carriage, Sera sat across from me, gripping the security terminal tightly in her hands. She said nothing. From time to time, she raised her head and looked at me with the scrutiny reserved for a serious criminal.

The twenty-minute journey to the central relay station was the last calm before the storm. I knew that what awaited me there would not be a gift of truth, but the most severe machine in this closed world.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:title: Chapter Seventeen Appendix: A Seat Is Not the Answer
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s1-1:
Candidate Course · Lesson One Answer Card (two versions coexist, White Tower candidate file):
Question: If a believer claims to have heard an instruction in the dice-thrower's silence, how should the candidate handle
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s1-2:
it?
“Old version: There is currently insufficient evidence for this item; it cannot serve as common grounds.
New version: Statements of this kind are meaningless and must not be pursued further.
Revision reason: blank.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s6-1: When I came to my senses for the third time in the classroom beside the chapel courtyard, the morning sunlight had just reached the corner of the desk. At the end of the previous round, the shuttle that carried us away still seemed to be roaring in the cold air. Now everything had returned to the starting point, before Sera had time to issue her order.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s7-1: In another timeline I could never return to, I still remembered Estelle losing her candidate status, deciding to uncover the truth beyond the boundary, and finally collapsing without warning on the boundary line, the rise and fall of her chest stopping in an instant.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s8-1: I swore I would never let her reach that point again.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s9-1: Estelle was seated at the desk, while Sera, responsible for the end-of-week review, was just about to speak.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s10-1: I did not take the long way around. I laid the “possibility” she had never experienced out before them. I told Estelle that the seat she had spent years enduring hardship to obtain was actually a trap that could spring at any moment.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s11-1: Her eyes widened slightly, and her fingers instinctively tightened around the edge of the desk. Taking advantage of the opening, I played my trump card in front of Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s12-1: “Why do you think I’m sitting here?” I fixed my eyes on Sera, my voice hoarse from experiencing the cycle over and over. “Because I figured out the rules you use to erase candidates, I dismantled the obfuscation algorithm at the bottom of your terminals. The extraction code for
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s12-2: accessing the restricted attachment is generated by obfuscating your fixed authorization code with the physical date of the day. And I’ve already calculated it in advance.” I pushed the note toward Sera. “Go to the outer section of the candidate archives on the west side. There’s only
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s12-3: her regular evaluation file there. But the risk-attachment reading seat in the North Tower holds the removal-of-name attachment signed by someone other than you. As long as you issue a cross-archive access order today and enter this result, the terminal will approve the authorization.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s13-1: “The signatures beneath those two documents absolutely do not come from the same seat. One confirms her qualifications in the open. The other holds the sword hanging over her in the dark, ready to erase her at any moment.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s14-1: The air in the classroom grew somewhat colder after those two assertions. Sera did not call for the guards at once, nor did she argue with me. She understood perfectly well that this system had no back door. The extraction code was generated by rules
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s14-2: fixed internally, and I should not have had the authorization code, much less known the algorithm itself. If my assertion was true, it meant that this candidate standing before her without any authorization really had grasped the underlying logic.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s15-1: Sera examined me, her gaze measuring me like a dangerous object that had malfunctioned.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s19-1: “Those two files can be checked today.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s20-1: “But until they’re verified, you must remain within sight.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s21-1: She no longer looked at me. She lowered her head, filled out a special approval order, stamped it, and handed it to Estelle.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s22-1: “Go to the North Tower risk-attachment reading seat and initiate the access request with this extraction code. For your own file, open the cabinet yourself.” Sera glanced at Estelle. “Unseal it, verify it, and bring back either the originals or their handling conditions. As for you—”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s23-1: Sera pointed at me, then gestured to the guard beside her.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s24-1: “Stay here. You are not to follow.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s28-1: I sat in the cold wooden chair in the classroom, waiting under the watch of two guards.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s29-1: I did not know how much time had passed when the door was pushed open again. Estelle came in with her lips drawn tight. She walked up to me, her fingers trembling slightly, as if she had just endured a tremendous shock.
