texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s31-1: “You calculated everything correctly. I took the string of numbers you left behind, entered it into the authorization terminal, and the machine immediately opened the restricted attachment at the reading seat.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s32-1: She drew a deep breath, as though trying to suppress the agitation in her voice.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s34-1: “The regular evaluation file not only recorded, with precision, my microexpressions while crying alone behind the water-pump house at twelve; tomorrow morning’s oath position had already been fixed as well, with Sera’s signature.” She gripped the copy she had brought back
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s34-2: from the North Tower. “But the conditional removal-of-name attachment that can destroy me at any time not only carries a warning saying ‘not to be shown to the person concerned.’ The signature beneath it isn’t hers either. It belongs to another seat I don’t recognize.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s37-1: She turned around and looked straight at Sera, who had remained silent all this time.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s39-1: “When you collected the old answer cards a few days ago, you forced us to copy ‘Statements of this kind are meaningless and must not be pursued further’ in our own handwriting on
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s39-2: the new cards, then filed the two versions together.” Her voice was somewhat cold. “But I just unsealed the attachment myself and read the four conditions for removal of name.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s43-1:
1. Anyone who states course content in an unauthorized setting.
2. Anyone who obtains materials beyond their personal file by non-procedural means.
3. Anyone who publicly questions an already effective unified formulation.
4. Anyone unable to independently handle matters that cannot be verified by the person concerned, and who must request instructions up the chain.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s46-1: “The first three are untouchable red lines. In public, you require us to leave written proof of absolute obedience. But in secret, you list ‘unable to handle matters independently and must request instructions
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s46-2: up the chain’ as the fourth ironclad rule for elimination.” Her fingertip stopped in midair, as if questioning the room itself. “The first three forbid candidates from crossing the line, while the fourth
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s46-3: requires candidates to make their own decisions. If the line can change at any time, that means sooner or later we’ll face a contradiction: should we obey the old rules, or break them to complete the task?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s49-1: She did not wait for Sera to respond. Instead, she opened the examination record she carried with her and picked up a pen in front of everyone. Before tomorrow’s induction oath, this was the only internship record protected by Church procedure, one that even the reviewer could not directly destroy.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s51-1: Today, one restricted attachment was accessed under special approval. The system warned, “Not to be shown to the person concerned.” I have unsealed it; contents not recorded.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s54-1: “Access authorized with a seal is an objective fact. I didn’t record the contents, so there’s no physical evidence. You can’t establish that I leaked anything. There is no third review seat present, and this examination record will be permanently sealed into the base file during tomorrow’s oath.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s54-2: You have no right to tear this page out on your own.” She snapped the notebook shut and stuffed it into her pocket. “Once the oath is complete, this will be a thorn that remains in the file forever. As long as someone audits today’s entry in the future, they’ll see this locked contradiction.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s59-1: In the afternoon, Estelle sat in the courtyard repairing the candidate uniform. Another seam had split at the cuff, in a completely different place from where it had split last time. This small variable silently warned me that memories from starting over could provide probabilities, but could not serve as a script.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s60-1: She sewed calmly, a stack of letters from Watermarsh Village held beneath a paperweight. The top one was from the village schoolteacher. It said there was a thirteen-year-old girl whose schoolwork was excellent, but whose family lacked labor; all the paper and ink she used had been cheap supplies obtained through favors. The teacher wanted to ask how they should prepare for next year.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s62-1: “I already wrote back to tell her that there are no shortcuts besides making the arithmetic and copying solid.” She slowly folded the letter. “I know writing something
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s62-2: this cruel is useless. The girl’s family will still sell everything they can to let her continue studying. Because they have truly seen me sitting in this seat.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s66-1: “You’ve seen the attachment bearing signatures from different seats at the bottom with your own eyes. Even if you pass the review today, they can still destroy you at any moment.” I watched her. “That seat hanging overhead is only an illusion they set out for people at the bottom to see.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s67-1: At those words, her hand paused slightly as she threaded the needle. Then she calmly pulled the thread straight.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s69-1: “I know half of it is an illusion. But I can’t control the half set out for others to see. The half of that power I can hold in my hands is real.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s73-1: “New water-purification filters for Watermarsh Village, fixed winter allocations of antibiotics, and additional ‘renewal’ positions that only the Inner Circle can secure for the village. Ever since I put on this candidate uniform, I’ve gone over these three most difficult matters in my mind countless times.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s76-1: “For each one, I now know exactly whom to ask for approval. If I withdraw today, perhaps another candidate from Watermarsh Village will endure their way here in the future. But in
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s76-2: the years before that happens, the sick in the village can’t wait, and neither can the people who need filters to have clean water. They sent me here, so I can’t return empty-handed.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s80-1: “Only, even I’m afraid when I hear the claim that I can change things only by staying inside.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s81-1: She put the roll of cloth into the drawer.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s83-1: “The person who coldly signed the removal-of-name attachment back then probably used the same words to hypnotize himself. If I also remain in that position… at what point will I gradually start to feel that giving antibiotics to the most obedient people is the correct way to preserve order?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s85-1: “But I can’t do nothing just because I’m afraid of becoming that way. Whatever happens, I have to get those three things done first.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s90-1: At dusk, the induction oath rehearsal began on time in the ceremonial court.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s91-1: The oath was recited three times in succession, with the final recitation from memory. Watching her fingers hang at her side, opening and closing unconsciously, I did not interrupt her.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s97-1: By the time it was completely dark, only a few hours remained until twenty-two hundred. We stopped in the front hall of the tower. In the end, I couldn’t hold back and spoke again.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s98-1: I told her that the old-world ruins beyond the village lockdown line held the true answer to how the entire world operated—not only the matter of candidate seats, but
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s98-2: even why we had to remain trapped here for generations. If we crossed the boundary and went there tonight, we could explain the layers of fog surrounding everything.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s99-1: “As long as tomorrow morning’s induction oath has not been recited, you’re still only an intern in violation of discipline. But if you leave after taking the oath, that will be defection, and even your family and teachers will be implicated and held accountable without distinction.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s99-2: ” I looked into her eyes. “After tonight, they won’t only determine the source of this password. They’ll also cut off any possibility of my accessing a terminal. You have to cross the boundary with me and see it with your own eyes before everything becomes irreversible.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s100-1: She listened in silence, then calmly asked three questions: If we left now, would Sera approve an access order? If she left without authorization for one night and missed tomorrow morning’s oath, would her qualifications remain? Could I immediately prove what was hidden there?
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s101-1: My answers, in order, were: No. They would not. It could not be verified.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s108-1: “There’s a review today and an oath tomorrow. These are things I can currently verify and carry through by relying on myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s110-1: “But the journey you’re proposing can’t be verified, and it means immediately abandoning the real hopes Watermarsh Village has placed in me. Arno, why exactly do you insist that I leave?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s113-1: At this expected refusal, I blurted out, “If you’ve seen with your own eyes how terrible that trap is, and you know their script in the open and in the dark, why would you rather cling to power—even if it was handed down as charity—than leave with me?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s114-1: She looked at me quietly, her eyes carrying a clarity that came close to pain.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s116-1: “This morning, you said that in that ending, I died outside, with nothing.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s118-1: “You insist on taking me away now… is it because you only like the version of me that has been stripped of everything, with nothing left to lose except relying on you?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s121-1: That question pinned me to the spot.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s122-1: I tried to defend myself, but not a sound came out of my throat.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s124-1: “You don’t have to answer now.” She lowered her eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s126-1: “But before you’ve thought it through, don’t speak to me using that version of me again.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s132-1: A few hours later, the abnormal access record and the clue to the extraction code I had provided became an urgent verification report, which Sera delivered to an office.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s133-1: (It was only later, after everything was over, that I finally pieced together the scene from the decrypted records. That dangerous report, which even Sera found impossible to classify, was never submitted to the regular system. It was handed directly to Otto.)
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s134-1: The door opened. Otto took the report, his gaze passing over each conclusion before finally stopping at the top.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s138-1: “The digital credential for extracting the top-secret attachment—you reported it to her first thing in the morning?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s139-1: “Yes. He claimed to have dismantled the terminal’s obfuscation algorithm.” Sera’s steady voice remained in the record.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s141-1: “The underlying logic and authorization source for that extraction code are both here with us. A candidate without any authorization should not be able to obtain it or calculate it. This wasn’t a verbal leak by an insider. No one would transmit a low-level formula out of the tower.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s142-1: Otto lifted his gaze from the page.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s143-1: “This is a serious information anomaly. Either he crossed the physical terminal somehow and accessed the machine’s underlying calculation logic, or he possesses a source of information he should not have.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s147-1: “Source unresolved. How should this report be submitted? How should the system number in the final column be filled in?”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s148-1: Otto drew out his fountain pen and casually signed a single character on the report.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s150-1: “No number is needed. There’s no need to determine the source. Establishing that the proposition is credible is enough to trigger isolation.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s151-1: He put the pen back into his pocket and folded the form.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s153-1: “The report stays with me for now. The immediate priority is to execute this level’s highest-grade confinement order and physically cut off any possibility of his accessing a terminal.”
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s159-1: A few minutes later, Sera returned to the chapel with Otto’s decision and wrote down the final execution order in black and white. Two uniformed guards stepped forward and seized me, one on each side.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s161-1:
1. The two matters stated are verified as true.
2. Source unresolved.
3. In accordance with the order, the subject, Arno, is to be immediately placed under Estelle’s supervised watch and is not permitted to leave the village.
4. The subject is forbidden from approaching or touching any terminal or network access point within the tower in any form. Violators are to be detained.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s163-1: She pushed the thin order slip across the table. Estelle silently walked to my side and took on the role of my watcher.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s165-1: “Take him down together.” Sera did not even lift her eyelids as she gave the order to the guards beside her.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s168-1: As two guards and Estelle escorted me down the chapel steps, the cold wind outside struck me in the face.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s169-1: In this world, where nothing had yet fallen apart, I proved that the signatures were doubled, but I still failed to take her with me. After tonight, the version of me remaining on this timeline would bear the punishment of the highest-grade order, completely cut off from the truth.
texts.chapter:v15-17b:event:text-s170-1: And I could only carry that painful question with me, waiting for the extraction at twenty-two hundred inside a cage that was tightening by the moment.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-01-shell:title: Sea Line One: Empty Shell
texts.chapter:heisenberg-01-shell:event:text-s:
Line note (placed at the beginning of the line, not repeated chapter by chapter):
“Each chapter below concerns one dead person.
Sources: Calibration Recording Sets One through Eight and the Final Volume; nineteen lecture tapes; late-life notes and annotations; review footage; surviving

fragments of Imperial archives; all documents in the underground records vault; the pages inside the work case.
What is written in the archives, copy it exactly. The gaps between archives—the light, the pauses, the words left unsaid—are reconstructed from traces at the scene.
This person

is reconstructed because the evidence he left behind is dense enough to support reconstruction; the uncertainty of that reconstruction is declared here in full and not annotated separately at every point.”
— White Tower Special Archives · Foreword to the Unauthorized Investigation File
On the final night of the Church of Convergence’s last years, Heisenberg spent an entire day lying low in lightless service corridors and abandoned ventilation shafts. Outside, the world was
still steeped in the clergy’s tottering fanaticism. Only at night did he follow plans he had drawn with his own hands years earlier, making his way through flooded conduits for four hours.

Back then, in the laboratory where Lysenko had only just seized power in a death grip, the demoted former chief could do nothing but bury himself in concrete engineering, tracing the ventilation routes of this vast ancillary

facility line by line. Now he hunched over like a rat, making his way through the strokes he had drawn himself. The standing water rose above his ankles. Each time his aging knees bent, they gave a dull knock in the dark

tunnel. Aching. Cold. But he did not stop. He checked against the map in his mind. Third maintenance hatch: his hand found it. The handwheel on the airlock: there, too—rusted tight around the spindle, but undeniably there.

He should have had no place here long ago. On the night he fled, he had been stripped away completely. His name was gouged from every register, his work pass voided, the portrait in the archive files smeared into

an unrecognizable blot of dead ink. Through the long years that followed, years that carried him through the Head of State’s death from illness and the Church of Convergence’s persecution, he remained a ghost.
But there was one thing they could not revoke. He swallowed dryly, and in the dark, guided by muscle memory, turned through the final bend—The routes in his head could not be revoked.

The concealed door to the administrative district was hidden at the end of the service corridors. He pushed open the heavy maintenance hatch, and dust rushed into his face. The forgotten old facility lay in

dead silence, its thick dust burying the traces of the past like snow. Dragging his soaked trouser legs behind him, he entered and opened the office door with practiced ease. The safe stood in the corner.
He had planned this administrative district himself. After Lysenko came to power, he replaced every electronic credential and password, but he did not know that the mechanical override sequence
at the bottom of the seemingly rigid physical safe had never changed. It took Heisenberg only three minutes to turn the dial and set the gears into the engineering default position from that time.
Click. The heavy safe door sprang open. Resting quietly on the dustproof velvet pad lay the hardware operation key for the production line.
He picked up the brass key and weighed it in his callused palm. Cold. Solid. Lysenko’s administrator’s mark was engraved on it—now he would use the credentials of the man who had
replaced him to open the thing he had built with his own hands. The key locked only the production controls, but that was enough to force-start the physical conveyor tracks below.
He had seen this enormous production line wake from sleep too many times.

The first time was on the day the facility was completed. The searchlights on the domed ceiling lit up one row after another, like a great beast opening a compound eye of stars. It was the old Empire’s peak of fanaticism, and as a technical verifier, he had signed execution orders for several young researchers and other dissenters.

Over the long years that followed, though he had been struck from the rolls and exiled, he still used the surviving low-level backdoors to evade layer after layer of security and sneak back here like a ghost, again and again. Years earlier,

he had tried to complete the preliminary procedures, but could never bring himself to take the final step. So he left the system suspended at the final stage, awaiting capacity infusion. He repeatedly rechecked the hardware specifications,

then added another mark reading “No abnormality” to the task sheet inside the glass cover beside the machine and left. This long, cowardly wait in suspension, he had meticulously approved forty-one times according to the old calendar.
This time, there was no entourage, no death list. Only him.
He walked to the enormous main control console and inserted the brass key into the lock. He put his wrist into it and turned the key halfway with force.

Vrrrrm—the current surged into the mainframe. The searchlights came on again, illuminating the dust-coated conduits and the cold glass. The tracks made their familiar, reassuring sound as they locked together. Ghost-green light fell across the deep-lined planes of his face, bringing rows of square old-language text into view.

According to the system design, the first channel operated independently. He bypassed the routine checks, released the experimental production line from suspension, and forcibly sent a capacity extraction request to the lower layer. As long as it obtained an allocation, this body, soon to complete assembly, could receive the foundation from which consciousness would begin to emerge.
Heisenberg braced both hands against the console’s cold, hard edge and stared at the capacity-infusion queue on the screen.

Years earlier, he had calculated the worst-case scenario for the time machine atop the White Tower, the machine that tore through the world. Based on the time machine’s known capacity, the maximum burden it could create while operating,

and the device’s least efficient conversion rate, he had arrived at a conservative safe upper limit in the Church of Convergence’s final years: if the capacity of eight thousand lives were fed into it, that would be enough to forcibly

smooth out its immense cross-world debt. He had personally written this extreme upper limit into the executable quota for the underground route, agreeing to send eight thousand people to the annihilation platform beneath the Old City.

But that quota had long since become a dead letter. Over the long years that followed, he could not find even one truly willing sacrifice. The old machine beneath the Old City did not identify motives, but the operational chain it required—entering

the restricted zone in person, understanding the records, completing calibration, and continuously maintaining the coupling—made it impossible for kidnapping or deception to achieve that kind of cooperation from a living body for several hours.

He could no longer shut down that man-eating machine. The White Tower was now heavily guarded, while the remote unloading and cooling procedure took several hours. If the clergy discovered it and cut the relay during that time, the machine would automatically reload and roar back to life.

Unable to shut it down meant that, to maintain the cross-world channel, it would continue drawing idle capacity from the foundation without pause. By then, the system’s reserve pool was already close to dry from the machine’s violent operation. It was impossible for him to piece together a new sacrifice from nothing.
Since he could not find eight thousand willing old humans, he could only turn to the mad blueprints Lysenko had left behind. In that laboratory, Lysenko, the former director, had once ordered the
design of an oversized single-person vessel so he could expand the time machine’s operating window and harvest every branch of his life across worlds. Lysenko had tried to mount ten thousand capacity
units under the name of his dedicated physical body at the system’s lowest layer. As his subordinate at the time, Heisenberg had handled the concrete engineering implementation. He knew that once

the mounting was complete, the value of this local body would automatically become the shared total for that subject across all cross-world branches. It meant a cross-world volume terrifying in scale.

But he knew better than anyone that even if this shell carried a colossal figure of ten thousand units in the foundational ledger, what condensed at the physical layer would still be an utterly ordinary human mind.

But that was exactly what he needed now. He did not need the body to be intelligent. He only needed it to occupy a real weight of “ten thousand units” in the ledger of the soul field. As long as this ordinary human bearing ten thousand units of weight

was born, he could send that person to the annihilation platform beneath the Old City. Let this heavy human body enter the settlement procedure and release the shared total of ten thousand units, covering the upper debt limit of eight thousand lives.

He was prepared to build this overloaded vessel without a designated personality with his own hands.
Once the shell opened its eyes and possessed a subject, he would take it away. Teach it to read. Teach it what love and debt were.

Once it had truly grown into a person who understood responsibility, he would lay out the blood debt and ask it to volunteer for that long procedure beneath the Old City. Let this one person pay the bill for the quota of eight thousand.
The screen flickered. The progress bar suddenly stalled. The system’s lower layer did not issue the routine “insufficient” warning. Instead, the error log quietly printed an utterly direct reading.

Cross-world concurrent connection load for time machine: Extreme.
Low-level capacity extraction aborted. Available capacity: 0.
The roaring time machine was like a bottomless pit. The low-level channel maintaining its cross-world penetration had already sucked every freely circulating unit of capacity in the world dry.
This was not a static depletion—so long as the leak remained open, once the free pool was completely exhausted, it would crudely redirect its pull toward vessels already using capacity in order to

fill the endless burden of operation. It would cross the ledger and forcibly tear capacity straight from living old humans.
Not a trace remained. The fuse of the Great Extinguishing had been lit.

Day and night could not be distinguished inside the vast underground facility. In this silent workshop, the oversized shell for ten thousand people had already taken shape in its chamber. The system completed the final

step of the standard assembly process, then sent the newly made body into the cultivation chamber. But the mainframe lit red after the capacity acquisition failed and issued no first-person delivery command for it.

Heisenberg went to the heavy metal chamber and forcibly pulled open the upper cover outside the observation window by hand. The body that was originally meant to carry a weight of ten thousand units in the ledger now floated quietly in the sterile amniotic fluid.
It was breathing.
A film-like fabric covered it. The physiologically mature body’s chest rose and fell with a mechanically steady rhythm. It had been shaped to perfection: tranquil
brows and eyes, long fingers. The machine had produced all the physiological hardware life required, but not the slightest trace of first-person consciousness.
Heisenberg raised a trembling hand and touched the glass.
As if sensing the faint change in temperature or shadow beyond the glass, the shell in the amniotic fluid instinctively tilted its head and moved an inch toward his palm.
A purely physiological reflex, without the slightest artifice.
With his hand still against the glass, Heisenberg slowly slid down. He slumped onto the cold metal floor.

Only when he saw this shell, incapable even of evasion, did the plan he had been running through in his mind finally become a glaring reality. If the machine truly succeeded in extracting the capacity, this life that moved toward warmth would open its eyes.

Then he would teach it to love, and when it grew up, demand that it walk into death for ten thousand portions of capacity—if those ten thousand portions were truly injected, he would be fastening the cruelest shackle in the world onto a defenseless newborn soul.
He sat on the cold floor all night.
Near dawn, the roar of the ventilation fan seemed to soften. Heisenberg used his aching knees for support and slowly stood. He pulled the observation window’s cover closed again and
locked it tight. This vessel, which had exhausted every hope he had, was sealed completely within an untouchable physical isolation, along with the production line’s first channel.
He turned and walked back to the main control room, then sat down before the terminal and straightened the angle of the recording camera.

As for his lifelong confession, he left it locally as read-only calibration data. Inside the metal work case on the desk lay a metal plate, a query index pointing to the White Tower disaster archive (Incident Zero), and a decryption credential.

In the eighth volume of calibration data preserved locally, the recording had been erased and rewritten three times. The initial pauses and trembling had all been washed away. What remained was a cold assertion:
“The empty shell is not scrap, not an unfinished product. It is an accurate

answer: remaining capacity, zero. The machine did not break. The reserves ran out.”
At the same time, he raised the fatal doubt that would later drive countless people to search desperately for a way out: “Annihilation does not destroy information. Then where did the information go?”
On the handwritten dustproof inner page of the work case, there was also a lecture tape consisting of nineteen sections. It had originally been an emotional course he prepared to awaken the
shell—even specifying every detail of the touch in the first lesson and the words in the second. In the scene discovered later, the lecture tape and the calibration data had been placed separately.

As for his final calculations and blood-stained conclusion, he forced them into the White Tower’s low-level network through an unauthorized intrusion. Even after the Church of Convergence subsequently cut the physical relay, this encrypted digital ghost would circle forever through the network at the highest permission level.

In this recording, which lay dormant for more than a hundred years, he lowered the camera’s angle so that his face was fully exposed. As a forward bridge left for the future, he recorded a cold engineering conclusion:
“Listen carefully. The completion of the time machine’s first-stage operation absolutely

does not mean shutdown. It only means that all branch worlds have been aligned and observed. After activation and pulse deployment, the low-level cross-world connection remains locked in place. Someone other than the operator must forcibly sever the connection from the external maintenance side.”

The deeper digital proof—concerning the safe upper limit and conversion error—was locked deep inside the credential. The credential in the work case was only half a key. It was still waiting for the person possessing the “current

driving session” to truly unlock it. At the end of the digital proof, he used arithmetic to prove that none of them could afford the blood debt. As for “who should pay,” he offered no conclusion, leaving the arithmetic at the boundary.

The unauthorized activation of the mainframe and the intrusion into the White Tower network would inevitably trigger the highest-level alarm. After daybreak, the Church of Convergence’s enforcement squad would break through the door with live ammunition. But he did not get up again to crawl through the escape corridor he

could walk with his eyes closed.
The remaining capacity was already zero. The fuse of the Great Extinguishing had been lit. He knew better than anyone that the world outside, along with the roaring White Tower, would not survive this night. And he was truly too tired—too tired to look at this irreparable world even once more.
He set the terminal screen to the line: Calibration Recording Set: One through Eight. Play?
He sat down in the broad chair. The brass key bearing Lysenko’s mark was still driven hard into the console’s lock. His back slowly settled against the chair. Both hands
rested naturally on the metal armrests. Then he drew an old revolver from inside his coat, pressed the muzzle to his right temple, and calmly brought his long flight to an end.
More than a hundred years later, when Arno and Yuna crossed the production area to the side and forcibly broke into the main control room by following the power lines, the skeleton was

still leaning before the terminal.
The hand bones that had once gripped the brass key hung at his side. The other hand rested on the heavy metal work case, closed and locked. A bullet hole
passed through the right side of the skull. The old revolver, rusted over, had fallen beside his feet. The key in the console’s lock had grown thick with verdigris over the long years.

The Church of Convergence’s enforcement squad ultimately did not break through the door the next day. Not long after the gunshot, the time machine’s violent suction completely shattered the foundation of the world. The soul-field bindings of the old humans broke apart one

after another like guttering candles in the wind. In the scene reconstructed from system logs and traces at multiple sites, the heavily armed forces gathering above ground, the fanatical clergy, and every living person in the world all crumpled to the ground without warning

during that long night. No one bled. Their first-person focus simply vanished under the irreversible pull.
The searchlights beneath the dome and the low hum of the ventilation fans did not stop when the disaster occurred. The automated facilities were unaffected by soul binding.

When the last human fell, the time machine, operating in madness, finally found no further object to extract and entered low-level blocking and restart. That fatal cross-world activity was forcibly terminated. The immense quantity of idle capacity occupied by the machine was

released back into this dead world.
The mainframe keenly caught the capacity spilling out again. The standard production queues that had been forced into suspension when the end-world reserves reached zero then quietly resumed running in this absolute silence. It coldly wrote

personality data into the newly born bodies in the outer channels, using the surplus after the disaster to complete the awakening of the first new humans. In the long years that followed, the Inner Circle repeatedly unsealed and used the outer channels through other entrances.

Only this deep main control room, because Heisenberg had severed the external physical lock through unauthorized access, slept through more than a hundred years in absolute silence. Dust fell layer by layer, covering the dormant console and settling on his shoulders as they turned to bone.
Faced with the empty shell that had once instinctively moved toward his palm, fortunately, he had gathered nothing at all.
texts.chapter:chapter-18-rereading-ruins:title: Chapter Eighteen: Rereading the Ruins
texts.chapter:chapter-18-rereading-ruins:event: After the dizziness of crossing the boundary once again faded, the morning sunlight pierced my eyes. This was another new universe I had arrived in.

In this world where Yuna had never been born, the seat of second candidate belonged to Estelle.
From the moment I awoke in this body that morning, my rejection of her had been obvious. She sensed that I was looking through her at

someone who did not exist. Only when I helped her sound out several obscure characters from the old era on the table—names of low-level data nodes in the ruins of the old city—did the astonishment in her eyes turn into investigation.

In the chapel after morning lessons, she uncharacteristically did not sit at the other end of the bench. Instead, she came straight to me and slapped a red-stamped special access permit onto the table.

“Sera just approved the permit. We have to return by tomorrow morning. We’re going to an external disaster recovery station.” She paused, her tone carrying a certain uncompromising force. “I returned the lifelong confidentiality contract she asked me to sign.”

Before I could speak, she opened the public textbook on the table and pointed to the page containing the weekend oath.
“The First Relief Register originally required every village to sign by mark. Each settlement corresponded to a dedicated clause

bearing the village’s name. But in the current edition, the numbering jumps directly from seventy-two to seventy-four.” She looked at me. “Yet the foundation stone of Watermarsh, the settlement where I grew up, is engraved with ‘Settlement No. 73.’”
She had laid everything out before Sera: she had to find out what the people of Watermarsh had truly been swearing to back then. If even that had to be concealed, she would rather

give up her seat as a candidate.
Unexpectedly, Sera did not get angry. She simply signed.
“‘If you only want to go there, cry over the edited words, and come back to stir up emotions,
I won’t allow it.’” Estelle repeated Sera’s exact words when she signed the permit, staring into my eyes. “‘If you’re going into the deep archives, you have to bring Arno, who
understands the Old Tongue, and have him translate those tedious machine-level data as well. Once you’ve seen all the facts clearly, then decide what kind of person you want to be.’”

“That disaster recovery station is a read-only cold backup. Every night at 20:05, the central tower performs a full synchronization there.” She took out a register with a hard cover, opened it to the first blank page, and set the

rules. “Since Sera requires you to help me check the archives, I’ll let you investigate whatever you want after the synchronization is complete, in exchange. But since this morning, you’ve been acting like a different person. If

you’re so certain about certain things, write down the results you’re looking for in advance. Once we get there, I’ll check them against the system blind. If they don’t match, then your strangeness and coldness today have no basis.”

I agreed. I took the pen and wrote a single prophecy in the register:
From 19:40 to 20:00 tonight. If that time machine’s network can share synchronization across worlds, then under the log coordinates of the old city

ruins there will be a record of a physical-level door lock closing, along with a low-level error reporting that data from some node was drained by the machine. No explosion, no alarm. Only an extremely quiet erasure.

That was the only thing in this universe I wanted to confirm for my own reasons. Even though reason told me that traces left across universes were a delusion, I still hoped to find some sign that she had existed.
It took three hours to walk to the canyon in the northwest.

The terminal nodes of the Inner Circle’s verification network had long since been stripped bare by scavengers, but the external disaster recovery station embedded deep in this canyon was still connected to an independent geothermal backup supply. Once we crossed the boundary stone,

the contours of the wilderness gradually emerged. For Estelle, crossing the broken ridge ahead would bring us to the third outlying settlement—Watermarsh, where she had worked as a distribution-station registrar for three years before being selected for the central village.
A dry, acrid

smell of the scorched dead grass peculiar to the outskirts drifted through the air. Along the way, we passed several abandoned water-collection points. Though the pipes had rusted shut long ago, the stones still bore the gray-stone powder markings peculiar to the people of Watermarsh.
“Why is that missing Clause Seventy-Three so important to you?” I asked her as we skirted a collapsed section of roadbed.

“Because the funerals in Watermarsh, and the spontaneous mutual relief people provided during the rainy season, are the truest things I’ve seen in my entire life.” She stopped and looked at the settlement’s outline, hidden in the distant blowing sand. “Whenever someone in the village died, we would gather around the pit. The person leading

would recite the words from that register, and every household would scrape a spoonful of nutritional powder from its own ration and pour it into the dead person’s family’s jar. If the force that kept us alive in the mud was also an illusion granted by the White Tower, then even if I became a candidate, I wouldn’t be able to get past that.”

The external disaster recovery station was embedded in the canyon wall, like a small administrative fortress. There were no glowing memory relics here, only rows of archival cabinets and terminals sleeping in the dim light.

Our first stop was the public disaster recovery hall.
Estelle put on gloves and found the unabridged First Relief Register on the heavy old archive shelves, along with the early activity briefings tucked inside it. By the daylight entering through the ventilation shafts, she turned the pages one by one with the aid of an Old Tongue dictionary.

She stopped at a briefing bearing the red seal of the Imperial Ministry of Royal Internal Affairs.
The briefing recorded a resolution: “Suspend the suppression of gatherings by the Joint Observation Group in Area 73 and guide them toward absorbing unregistered

refugees from the western district.” Beneath the resolution was a handwritten instruction: “The pressure this measure creates among the lower strata may be used to counter the faction within the Assembly seeking additional Ark quotas from the Head of State.”

She opened the unabridged First Relief Register again. Clause Seventy-Three was printed in rough lettering: “We ally ourselves with one another and will no longer wait for the Empire to hand out food. As long as each of us sets aside one mouthful of provisions every day, no one will starve to death in the streets.”

Estelle’s fingers moved back and forth between the handwritten instruction and Clause Seventy-Three. On one side was the deliberate political calculation tolerated within the White Tower; on the other was the genuine mutual-aid pact Watermarsh’s ancestors had kept alive in the mud. She stared at the two pages for a long time.

We continued moving through the dusty archives, and with my knowledge of the Old Tongue, she worked through them by year.
In the files that followed, the original civilian night-watch group, the “Joint

Observation Group,” gradually became the “Church of Convergence.” An internal investigation report marked top secret followed immediately after an internal bulletin recording the death of the Head of State.

In the empire’s late period, the Head of State had secretly promised overlapping Ark tickets to followers of different factions behind the Assembly’s back. When a weak successor came to power, the old accounts were reopened and the old tickets declared void. The

executive departments that had once pledged loyalty refused to cooperate in fury. Administrative orders across districts failed completely. Coal could no longer reach the boiler rooms, and the food warehouses were locked tight by the respective military-police chiefs.

In this desperate landscape, stalled by the rupture of competing interests, Estelle pulled out a ration-distribution register. With its already well-established food-delivery, night-patrol, and medical networks, the Observation Group filled the power vacuum created by the fracture at

the top. The frustrated grassroots officials and intellectuals shut out by the Ark’s narrow gate, meanwhile, provided the civilian network with the cross-regional coordination, document printing, and organizational language it needed most, allowing it to effectively take over the towns.

But when she turned to the records from after the Church had taken complete control, her movements suddenly slowed.
It was a proclamation targeting followers of the “Faction of Fate”: “Submission to predetermined destiny is an act of strengthening the bad future that is approaching.”

Inside the appendix beneath the proclamation was a stack of execution records: first, expulsion from the safe zone, followed by deprivation of basic rations. The final page was a photograph of twelve Faction of Fate believers being hanged in the street, with an execution order attached directing that the group’s past calculation ledgers be burned.

She laid the old ration-distribution register beside the order to burn the records.
Her fingers moved to the signatures at the very bottom of both documents. Neither bore a full
name, only a vague occupational designation. The first stroke of the two words “Approved” carried a heavy pause, and the abbreviated year was written with a habit of hooking upward.

Estelle remained silent. Her left hand pressed down on the signature in the ration-distribution register, the one that represented the debt of saving lives. Her right hand rested beside the signature on the order to burn the archives. The fingertips on both hands had gone faintly white from the force she was applying. After a long time, she quietly returned them to their place.

We passed through the corridor and came to the intergenerational records cabinets. The seal dates on these two archive drawers were separated by several decades, with no record of any organizational handover between them.

The drawer above, from the imperial era, contained the surviving draft of Semaelvis, the coordinator of the first-generation remnants of the dissenting scientific network known as the “Conservation Society,” which had gone underground after the

purge. The damaged report contained only an isolated question about that month’s resource accounting: usable capacity was falling far faster than the population model allowed. The accounts did not balance. The cause field was left blank. To him, the

machine’s actual operating dates and purpose were the highest secrets. He died without ever knowing what he should suspect. As for why the material was incomplete, it was because the later Church of Convergence had burned all the calculation ledgers.

She set aside the draft, pulled open the drawer below with the Church-era seal, and opened the reexamination footage left by Heisenberg.
In the recording, the former chief technical verifier held the surviving question he had somehow dug out. The two men had never

met. The only thing Heisenberg inherited was this anomalous report recovered from a pile of wastepaper. On-screen, he called up the abnormal capacity fluctuation data and placed the dates of the anomalies in the draft precisely beside the machine’s operating dates.

Heisenberg in front of the camera stared at the two overlapping columns of dates and asked the question that pointed directly toward the final answer: “What if what you calculated back then was never a population quota?”

Estelle switched off the player and gathered up the draft. The scattered records of political oppression and the machine’s mystery of diminishing capacity had converged before this abandoned drawer. She turned to me, looking somewhat tired, but still clear-minded.

“The history is checked.” She took out the register she had been using for blind verification and patted its cover. “Now let’s check what you wanted. You said that physical-level door lock closure would happen tonight.”
We reached the deepest part of the station. There was a row of recording terminals covered in dust.

This was where the system’s lowest-level actions were preserved: audit signatures, changes in permissions, and completion markers automatically added by the system after an operation ended. This deep-level interface had only been unlocked because of Estelle’s local advanced authorization.

We waited in the dark basement until 20:05.
With a dull click of an electrical breaker switching over, the green light on the console blinked several times, announcing that today’s data synchronization was complete. Estelle

went to the main console, entered the old city ruins coordinates I had given her, and brought up the activity logs for the twenty minutes from 19:40 to 20:00.
The system’s idle hum echoed through the basement. If something

that happened in another universe could leave ripples in the machine’s lowest-level systems, spanning all worldlines, then traces of a door lock closing and data being drained should appear on the screen at this very moment.
A few seconds later, several cold characters appeared on the screen.
【Record empty. No abnormal permissions or lockout markers detected.】

The screen was blank. There was no trace of any operation taking place. There was no record of the sacrifice that should have happened, because in this universe, Yuna had never gone to that machine at all.

I froze in front of the screen.
Reason had given me the answer long ago: in this world untouched by any trace of Yuna, even if the machines of all universes were connected to the same underlying network, there was no reason for this local terminal to record the

sacrifice. But deep down, I had still kept a sliver of delusion, hoping that the immense machine spanning the boundaries might record, even once, proof in the shared logs that she had vanished in another time and space. Now the console had given me the coldest reality.

Estelle said nothing. Faced with me, the suspect whose prophecy had failed and been reduced entirely to an absurd delusion, she did not take the opportunity to accuse me. She only turned to look at me once,

then followed the rules of blind verification exactly.
She opened the register, and her pen scratched across the paper. When she finished, she pushed the register directly across the console toward me.
By the dim light of the screen, I saw the conclusion she had written:

「Same day. Disaster recovery station console. Checking 19:40 to 20:00 returned an empty record.
When faced with the blank, the subject displayed genuine surprise and disappointment.
This item remains uncertain. Continue investigating.」
She put away the register, folded the red-stamped document, and left the machine room.

Before preparing to leave the underground fortress, she stopped at an abandoned chapel corner.
There were no glowing relics or lectern here, only rusted iron frames and benches covered in dust. She closed her

eyes and quietly recited part of Watermarsh’s funeral text.
But I heard clearly that when she reached the middle line, “The collective will guarantees the correct future,” she paused and skipped it entirely.

By the time we emerged from the rock wall, the sky had already darkened. In this world without Yuna, Estelle used the blowing sand to straighten her collar, tucked the register recording uncertainties and truths securely into her pocket, and set off toward the return journey.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:title: Chapter Eighteen: Supplement: Not Today
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s3-1:
I opened my eyes. The faint rasp of Estelle’s pen as she wrote the verification results on paper in the previous round still seemed to linger in my mind. The words “Record Empty” would not leave me.
Reason told me that in a
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s3-2: world where the sacrifice had never occurred, the system logs should naturally be blank. From the surface records on the outskirts, there was no way for me to dig out the machine’s actual underlying logic and history. If I
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s3-3:
wanted to get past the permissions and find out what it was, I could only look for traces left by those who had once handled its core hardware.
I thought of my father—the man who had once worked as a low-level maintenance worker.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s4-1: I instinctively reached toward my waist. Over the past few months, I had long since grown familiar with the unusually dense row of stitching in the belt’s lining. My mother had patched it with new cloth before I entered the
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s4-2:
seven-day process. But beneath those layers of sturdy fabric, something hard had been hidden all along.
Across these hundreds of reset days and nights, I had never pried it open, because I knew that if I took it apart in front of
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s4-3: my mother, I would inevitably drag her into it. But now I had hit a wall. The normal data meant nothing to me. If I wanted to know what the Inner Circle had buried underground back then, today I had to dig out what he had hidden.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s5-1: I drew clean water and submerged the belt in it. Once the new cloth my mother had sewn on was soaked through, it clung tightly to the layer of old dust cloth beneath, which had long since grown brittle. Only the square locked down by that row of stitches remained stiff. I pressed it hard with my thumb. Something rigid pushed back against my fingertip.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s6-1: I fetched a small knife, cut through the new thread, and slit open the yellowed old inner layer. A hard card, folded square and wrapped tightly in thick oil paper, fell out.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s7-1: When I unfolded it, I found an old cut-out duplicate. Printed neatly across the header were the words: “High-Risk Obsolete Device Destruction Execution Form (Stub).” The issuing unit was stamped as “Wasteland
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s7-2:
Waste Disposal Station.”
The item field contained an unfamiliar device number. Following the table downward, I saw that the “Execution Result” field bore a stamp reading “Destroyed by Fire.” And in the
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s7-3: handler field at the end was his own six-digit employee-number seal—I recognized the string of numbers branded into the belt’s metal buckle. It was my father’s number as a low-level maintenance worker,
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s7-4: stamped countless times on his old pay slips. Beside the seal was a short handwritten transfer-filing subnumber, prefixed with the section code of the abandoned underground dead archive outside the village.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s8-1: My father had followed the rules all his life. Since he had risked execution to secretly hold back this belt that should have been burned, deliberately
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s8-2: written the dead archive’s filing code on the falsified stub, then sealed the stub inside thick oil paper and hidden it in the belt’s inner
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s8-3: layer, he must have intended to lead me there through the belt. That dead archive absolutely held the dossier corresponding to this device number.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s11-1: The door hinge creaked. My mother entered carrying a basin of water, her eyes falling on the paper in my hand. Her expression changed sharply. She came over at once, snatched the stub away, and turned it facedown hard against the wooden table.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s16-1: “I’ve already seen it.” I looked at her. “If the thing listed on this form is discovered, it’s enough to get us both killed. You kept it from me for nine years. Now the executioner’s blade hanging over us has fallen. Do you still want me to keep pretending to be mute?”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s17-1: My mother did not answer. Her rough fingers pressed tightly against the back of the page, the knuckles paling slightly with the force. We remained locked there like that.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s18-1: “Yesterday I slipped into the Inner Circle.” I lowered my voice and looked into her eyes. “I saw the log data. During the years Heisenberg operated the machine, he matched every abnormal capacity fluctuation against the time machine’s callback parameters.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s19-1: That was actually a bluff. I could not even piece together how to repeat the line from the previous night saying “Record Empty.” But on this morning, I had to force my mother to speak in the most decisive way possible.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s20-1: “If the investigation from above starts digging deeper,” I pointed to the oil-paper stub, its edges worn smooth, “then once the underlying records are brought out and checked line by line, and they follow the dates to the missing page, we can only wait to die.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s21-1: The corner of her eye twitched slightly. She had clearly realized that once this yellowed oil paper was opened, it would never be able to contain what was inside again.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s22-1: She drew a deep breath, released the paper, folded it, and slipped it into her sleeve.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s24-1: “Put on a coat,” she said coldly. “We’re going to ask Sera for an access order. I’m taking you.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s28-1: To clarify the dossier, we went to Sera’s office.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s29-1: My mother slapped the yellowed stub directly onto the broad wooden table. Sera lowered her head and scanned the device number and the falsified destruction stamp. Her brow furrowed slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s31-1: “He already has the actual object in his hands.” My mother gripped the edge of the table with both hands and looked straight at the elder in charge of the archives. “If you don’t let him see the paper, he’ll eventually run into some other wall on his own.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s32-1: Sera was silent for a moment. Her fingers tapped twice against the tabletop. She glanced at me standing beside her with my stubborn gaze, then looked back at my mother.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s33-1: “If this is about balancing the books, I can burn the belt for you right now and stamp the underlying file as destroyed. No one will ever trace it back to you.” Sera’s voice was cold.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s34-1: “He insists on investigating that machine from back then.” My mother braced both hands against the table and stared hard at her. “Do you want him to run into some other wall? You and I both know what’s behind that wall.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s35-1: At this, Sera’s brow finally tightened. She stared at my mother for a long while, then opened a drawer and pulled out a numbered restricted-access order.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s36-1: “I can give you the catalog listing corresponding to this number. But you absolutely cannot enter the Inner Circle’s deep archive.” Sera’s expression was cold as her pen passed across the purpose field, filling in: “Review of the storage status of high-risk obsolete medical devices and related archives.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s37-1: Then she pushed over the thin authorization form together with a heavy, rusted key.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s39-1: “Same-day return. You may only go to the basic file section in the outer layer. That stub’s classification level won’t open the doors farther in.” Sera’s voice was cold, her gaze stabbing straight toward my mother. “You understand the rules,
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s39-2: right? No copying out any classified content. And since you insist on taking him yourself, if you try to force your way past the boundary, or if anything goes wrong, it will be your private conduct. You will bear the consequences yourselves.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s40-1: My mother stepped forward and calmly accepted the order that disclaimed responsibility.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s42-1: “I know what I’m doing. I’m going with him.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s47-1: The underground archive was far away. It took nearly two hours to walk there.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s48-1: The wind across the wasteland was dry. For the first hour, neither of us said a word. There was only the soft rasp of our soles on the loose stones. But once we were past the halfway point, the questions in my mind kept building until I finally broke the silence.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s50-1: “He worked at the waste disposal station for a while back then. He destroyed so many things, handling every one of them with his own hands.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s52-1: “He was clearly a man who followed the rules. So why, in the end, did he leave only that belt and that stub?”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s53-1: My mother kept her eyes fixed on the gray dirt road ahead.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s55-1: “The stub was the underlying record he falsified himself back then. Since he secretly kept the belt, he had to sign the records. As for why he insisted on sealing this life-threatening proof inside thick oil paper…”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s57-1: “What did he want me to see?”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s58-1: My mother stopped suddenly and turned to look at me.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s60-1: “I told you, I don’t know. If you want to know, you’ll have to find the answer below yourself.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s61-1: She cut off the subject stiffly, turned back, and continued walking. She would not let me pursue it any further.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s64-1: We walked on through the wind for more than half an hour. The corrugated-metal roof of the archive was just becoming faintly visible in the distance when my mother spoke of her own accord.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s66-1: “Remember this. Once we go in today, stay close to me. Don’t run around. Sera’s order only permits us to move through the catalogued section.” She looked at me. “Without me, you absolutely cannot go poking around in the restricted area at the very back. If you cross the boundary, no one can protect you.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s68-1: “I went in once when I was young. That time, too, I was doing something for him. For these nine years, as long as I never mentioned it, they wouldn’t come looking for trouble with you.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s69-1: “Why bring me today, of all days?”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s70-1: My mother tightened her grip on the lantern and quickened her pace, tossing back only one sentence: “If you keep digging, you’re bound to uncover what happened back then. Since you want to find that dossier, rather than let you run blindly into a dead end, I’ll take you there myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s71-1: I froze for a moment, then instinctively pressed her: What exactly did you see in there that time?
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s73-1: “All I did back then was help him push the things onto the shelves at the very back. What happened after that…” She paused. “I’d rather not know.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s78-1: The underground archive was much drier than I had expected. There were no mold stains in the cold, damp air. Tall metal shelves extended row after row into the depths of the underground vault, with no end in sight.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s79-1:
My mother knew exactly where the target was. Carrying the lamp, she led me through the maze of metal shelves and found the right row with precision.
It wasn’t strange. She had been there when my father
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s79-2: separated the papers for storage. She even used a screwdriver to pry apart the crossbar between two rows of shelves—the bar meant to prevent them from collapsing—and forced open a gap that had not existed before.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s80-1: We followed the numbers. In the slot that had originally held the dossier on the belt’s destruction, only a yellowed filing slip remained: “Transferred.” This deadly core file was clearly the thing my mother had helped push into the restricted area at the very back.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s81-1: “Where was it transferred?” I asked quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s82-1: My mother did not answer. She reached into the corner of the dust cloth behind the shelf and felt around for a moment, then pulled out a stack of old papers that had been deliberately “overlooked.” My father had not hidden this portion of the research data in the restricted area. It had been placed in a blind spot visible to anyone with an outer-layer permit.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s83-1: “Look at this first.” She pushed the stack of papers toward me.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s84-1: I opened the cover. It was a detailed clinical research record.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s85-1: At first, this had been a legitimate technical experiment. High-sensitivity field detectors were initially used for proper medical monitoring: controlling the depth of anesthesia, monitoring deep comas, and even accurately determining brain death. But during this
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s85-2:
passive monitoring, the detectors captured several faint anomalous signals.
Hospitals, animal models, and neurological research institutes cross-checked those signals. In pursuit of clearer residuals, the nature of the experiments changed, sliding into a coercive phase.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s88-1:
National security and the prison system secretly joined in, supplying the laboratories with wave after wave of nameless people who could not refuse.
That was the folder stamped with the top-secret seal “Consciousness Coupling · Living Subjects,” along with the appendix underneath it: “Awake Living Targets.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s88-2: To amplify those faint signals, the researchers were no longer merely “monitoring.” They brought in high-intensity external stimulation equipment and used living people as “targets” to receive externally applied high-pressure field stimulation, thereby producing larger readings for the detectors to capture.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s89-1: I lowered my head and looked at the belt around my waist. Its width and material suddenly acquired a horrifying explanation. At the very end of the stack, I found a consumables allocation
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s89-2: form, issued by the same Wasteland Disposal Station. Clearly printed on it was the unfamiliar device number from the stub. The name was: “High-Strength Fiber Restraint Belt (Set).”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s90-1: It was used to fasten subjects tightly to the experimental table. In the records for this batch of awake subjects, the research team was no longer merely measuring. They were forcing high-voltage
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s90-2: current through living bodies, using it to produce more violent echoes in a field strength that should never have existed. The anesthetist had left a cold observation in the remarks field:
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s92-1:
Muscle relaxant injected. Integrated brainwave state confirmed. Patient remained conscious throughout.
As the external field strength increased, the patient’s heart rate surged and the pupils constricted violently, accompanied by profuse physiological tearing.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s94-1: After this nearly fatal, silent torment, the report gave its conclusion: they had finally isolated an entirely new field excitation outside the standard model—the thing later known as “soul particles.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s94-2: ” As for the nature and finite capacity of the vast “soul field” governing our world, derived from this field excitation, that was a puzzle completed only by theoretical scholars who came later.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s95-1: At the end of the files, I found a newspaper clipping and several internal security records. The forced experiments were eventually exposed. The clipping was covered in a flood of condemnatory editorials, and the leading figure
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s95-2:
shot himself. The memory loss, personality damage, and even deaths suffered by those subjects ultimately led to a reckoning.
But pressed right up against the conviction records were volumes of later advanced-theory journals.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s95-3: In the series of papers that followed, academia sternly condemned those bloody origins in the introductions while continuing to cite, in the body text, the foundational data extracted through the exploitation of living people.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s98-1: My mother stood beside me, completely uninterested in those dense physical findings or the hypocritical condemnations.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s99-1:
Her eyes remained fixed on the top line of every living-subject record—the name field.
Every name field was blank. The people who had once been alive and breathing were represented here only by identity-stripped numbers.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s100-1: She remained silent as she turned the pages one by one, watching the records of rapidly rising heart rates and physiological tears on the paper. When she reached the dozens of pages, her hand suddenly stopped. In the dim lamplight, she asked quietly:
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s105-1:
I opened my mouth, not knowing how to answer.
I could only look at the records of physiological tears in black and white, feeling my stomach tighten again and again.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s106-1: The air here grew oppressively quiet. Only the faint sound of wind occasionally reached us from the underground archive.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s108-1: “So the theories we use now to calculate the quotas… they’re all built on these people’s suffering?” After a long while, I finally asked through clenched teeth.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s109-1: My mother turned to look at my angry, confused eyes. She drew a deep breath and tightened her grip on the lantern handle.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s111-1: “When your father brought me here to file the archives, he took me through the theoretical section deep inside.” Her voice was quiet. “If you looked only at these living-subject
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s111-2: experiments, you’d think all those researchers were madmen. Come on. I’ll take you to the last door. The thing corresponding to that ‘Transferred’ slip is in there.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s114-1: We reached the end of the catalogued section. Ahead stood a rusted iron door hung with a heavy lock, faded warnings sprayed across it. Sera’s key could not open this door. But my mother expertly felt
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s114-2: along the bottom of the frame and pried open a loose ventilation louver. It was the route she had damaged herself nine years ago. We slipped inside sideways. This was the forbidden theoretical archives.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s115-1: We stopped before a safe in the deepest part. Its door was half open, and the lock had already been forcibly broken. Those were the marks of the brute force my mother had used to smash it open nine years ago.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s116-1:
Through the gap, I saw an old-era medical review record lying quietly inside, sealed with a red top-secret stamp. I was just about to reach in when my eyes caught several early prophecies laid out in the exact center of the long table beside it.
Compared to the record
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s116-2: that had been shoved inside, the things on the table were the true anomaly—they were not isolated files, but had been spread out in chronological order. Who had set up this display in the deepest part of the abandoned dead archive, a place even Sera could not enter?
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s117-1: The first page of the report showed a steep downward curve pointing toward an exhaustion deadline roughly a thousand years away. In that era, when no one could determine the true cause of the leak, the drafter wrote a fatal hypothesis beside the curve: the rapidly growing population was filling the pool like building blocks, crowding it until it burst.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s118-1: I remembered the question that had followed me all the way here. Besides wanting me to see the core file concerning the nameless subjects, did my father also want me to understand how all of this had begun? For now, I
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s118-2: set aside the trump card he had left me and continued turning the pages beneath the prophecy. Scattered across the table were various plans proposed by informed people across the generations in response to this hypothesis.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s121-1: My mother did not come closer. She stood by the louver, listening warily to the sounds outside.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s122-1: I opened a dossier from the first century of the old era. The first page stated: Based on the hypothesis that the population was bursting the pool, slowing the rate of capacity consumption would require immediately reducing the global
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s122-2:
population of eight billion by more than thirty percent.
But when I reached the last page, the administrative instruction from that time contained only one sentence underlined in black: “Absolutely not to be touched during this term of office.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s123-1: Beside it was a record of a meeting of scientists from that era. Someone demanded to know why no action was being taken. Another left this analogy: “It is like being able to predict decades in
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s123-2: advance that San Francisco will suffer a major earthquake, yet before the ground actually splits open, no government would forcibly evacuate an entire city for the sake of a distant prophecy.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s124-1:
I pushed aside this futile record and pulled out another early project resolution beneath it.
The split began with funding. In the resolution, a quantum route called “Multiverse Switching Project” received an
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s124-2:
astronomical budget. Its leader publicly promised to build a time machine capable of returning to the past and strangling the disaster while it was still a seed.
This plan instantly monopolized all research funding,
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s124-3: top-tier equipment, and students. Meanwhile, the names of the scientists who insisted that capacity had limits and proposed temporal boundaries were covered in red stamps reading “Rejected,” “Refused,” and “Power Cut.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s125-1: I continued turning the pages and opened the notices beneath them. As time passed, opposition to the machine route was quietly replaced with official designations in administrative language. An internal security bureau directive directly equated criticism of
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s125-2: “Multiverse Switching” with “opposition to the promise of salvation” and “attacking the leader’s decision.” Scholars who insisted on the Conservation route were no longer merely unsuccessful applicants whose funding had been denied. They were being forcibly and
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s125-3:
crudely labeled politically disloyal, swept out along with those who studied relativity and quantum gravity.
These marginalized dissenters gathered together and became the later ‘Conservation Society’—the source of what is now our village’s ‘Faction of Fate.’
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s128-1:
At the farthest side of the long table, only two cases remained from the final period of the millennium ago.
As time passed, the price to be paid to fill the deficit had swollen from “thirty percent” to the need to reduce more than “eighty percent” of the old world’s population.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s129-1: I opened a dust-covered memorandum. Inside was an algorithm review by an unnamed scholar. It calculated a purely energy-extraction account: because the direct unbinding of energy from
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s129-2: subjects in the old era had been extremely inefficient, the conclusion was that more than eighty percent of the old world’s population had to be sacrificed to fill the enormous deficit. The
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s129-3: drafter had stamped a line in red on the title page: “Note: This model measures only the total physical deficit. Ethical judgment and execution plans fall outside the scope of this model.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s130-1: Clipped beneath that page was a personnel-transfer draft held tightly by a paper clip. The name field was blank. It stated: “If the chief refuses to endorse the model, a replacement will take over with immediate effect.” Beside this
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s130-2: threatening transfer order was the drafter’s final signature in the field marked “This model may serve as a technical basis.” It was only after obtaining this signature that the administrative system had the procedural basis for what followed.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s131-1: The report beside it calculated the prototype of the route that came later: once the cross-universe capability of “Multiverse Switching” was combined with conservation of capacity, the release mechanism became an annihilation process in which
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s131-2: isotopes were superimposed and collided across universes, drastically reducing the cost. This model was no longer an exact calculation of the deficit. Instead, it gave a safe upper bound requiring only 8,000 person-equivalents to fill the gap.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s132-1: In the administrative approval beside it, the “red-stamp note” the drafter had placed on the title page was gone. The document directly treated that more efficient physical upper bound as an endorsement for the killing quota. Next came a list of exemptions established on the basis of that approval.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s132-2: I turned the pages one by one. The list expanded from three lines of senior positions at the beginning into a scroll more than a dozen pages long. In the margins, someone had secretly squeezed in the names of family members in trembling handwriting, only for another red pen to cross them out heavily.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s133-1: “Before they figured out how to kill people, they arranged an escape route for themselves.” I flung the heavy list back onto the table.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s134-1: “But even then, that original plan to kill eighty percent couldn’t be carried out at all.” My mother spoke lightly from the doorway. “The result is written here.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s135-1:
I followed the direction she indicated and opened the final dossier.
The notices that followed recorded the purge. The conservative scholars of the marginalized Conservation Society were dismissed one by one. The final memorandum
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s135-2: stated that the radicals within the Conservation Society had tried to force through the killing plan by extreme violence. Once the conspiracy was exposed, the entire Conservation Society was formally designated a terrorist organization.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s136-1: This was the final file from the old era on the table. After that, the apocalypse that fell from the sky eventually buried all of it, along with their arguments.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s137-1: I let out a long breath. With that cold-blooded algorithm for the killing quota weighing on my mind, I suddenly understood the meaning of the table.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s138-1: I turned and walked toward the half-open safe. I had to know what my father had seen here a thousand years after all of this happened. I reached through the gap and felt the rough edge of the sealing cord on the top-secret dossier.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s140-1: My mother’s voice came suddenly from behind me, hard as ice. At some point, she had already returned from the ventilation shaft, gripping a pair of iron tongs she had pulled at random from the shelf beside her.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s141-1: “I told you, I’m only taking you here to look today.” Her eyes fixed on me in the darkness. “Those living-subject records you just saw are enough. As for the specific names and specific deaths of the people treated as expendable materials in this dossier, looking at them will do nothing for you except get you killed.”
