texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s142-1: “He went to such lengths to leave me the proof that would take me to the dead archive. He wanted me to see it!” I tried to pull the dossier out through the gap.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s143-1: “Let go!” My mother strode forward, the tips of the iron tongs pressing against the back of my hand. Her strength was astonishing. “What do you think he wanted you to see? Do you think he wanted you to rush out, take this list, and fight the people above?”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s145-1: “When he hid this death warrant in your belt back then, it wasn’t so you could go out and seek justice! It was his own selfishness—he had finished what he had to do, didn’t dare carry it on him, and couldn’t bear
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s145-2: to burn it!” My mother’s voice began to tremble. “He shoved it into this blind spot because he hoped it would rot underground forever! If you open it today, all you’ll do is get us both killed. Nothing will change!”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s150-1: We walked back in silence. It was almost completely dark when we finally reached the village boundary stone.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s151-1: My mother had been carrying the lantern ahead of me the whole way. She suddenly stopped, turned around, and spoke to me with her back to the dim yellow light of the sky:
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s153-1: “Everyone in the village gossips behind his back, saying that when your father repaired the machine in there, he was scared witless, and that was why he would rather hide in the village and spend his whole life making wooden stools.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s154-1: Her voice was steady, but her hand tightened around the lantern.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s156-1: “He worked down there for half his life. He was never afraid of those dead things. But in the year before he died, an elder responsible for some Inner Circle matter selected
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s156-2: him to gain access to an unpublished ‘Life-Continuation Procedure’—a mechanism supposedly capable of freeing people from aging and letting them continue living in another body.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s160-1: “It was an opportunity that would have made anyone envious, but in the end, he withdrew on his own. After that, he became suspicious of everything. He even refused to go to the chapel to receive his medical allocation.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s161-1: “What was he afraid of?” I asked.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s162-1: The evening wind across the wasteland tousled my mother’s hair. She did not turn around.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s164-1: “I don’t know. But he was convinced that once he accepted that procedure, some things could never be reversed.” She looked down at the lantern in her hands, her voice slightly hoarse.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s164-2: “Later, his old illness returned, and he didn’t make it through. Before he died of it, he forced me to put the oil-paper packet containing the dead-archive proof into your old belt.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s165-1:
I instinctively touched the smooth metal buckle at my waist. The rough canvas rasped against my fingertip.
He knew the secret of the unpublished Life-Continuation Procedure. He withdrew because of some bottomless fear,
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s165-2: and eventually died after his old illness dragged on. He didn’t dare carry the falsified destruction record with him, but he didn’t dare burn it either. In the end, he turned it into a riddle and hid it on my body.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s166-1: The top-secret file I failed to open today might not contain any grand moral testament, or any hidden truth about a murder. What was locked inside might only be the unaccounted-for mess left behind by a cowardly insider, for the sake of something he had been afraid to do.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s167-1: But until I understood what he had refused back then, the belt had already led me to the door of this underground vault.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s170-1: Before crossing into the village, my mother stopped completely. She looked at me, her expression complicated.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s172-1: “You went into the dead archive today. You saw those orders for slaughter. I don’t care what you write in your booklet when you go home tonight. But you’d better not casually think that if you were sitting in that position, you could lightly sign the death sentence of those billions of people.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s173-1: My mother lowered the wick of the lantern in her hand. The light dimmed, and the side of her face sank into deep shadow.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s175-1: “Knowing that something is missing from the accounts, and actually pressing down the executioner’s blade with your own hand to balance the books with your generation, are two different things.” She turned and started walking back into the village. “Let’s go home. Tomorrow is another new day.”
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s179-1:
That night, I dragged my heavy legs home.
The house was unlit. By the faint red glow remaining in the stove, I opened the booklet I carried with me.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s180-1: I forced myself to write down, one by one, the top-secret information I had uncovered in the archive that day. After twenty-two hundred tonight, my consciousness would leave
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s180-2: this daytime loop. Before then, I had to use the act of writing to carve these truths, which crossed the timelines, firmly into my mind so I could carry them into the next world.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s181-1: After writing the final stroke, I looked at the ink on the page. Sera’s order stated it clearly: transcription was strictly forbidden. If, during some future investigation, someone searched this house
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s181-2: and found this booklet filled with forbidden knowledge, the execution risk would fall on my mother, who had led me there, and on the self who had remained unaware of everything and would continue living
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s181-3: here after tonight with all of today’s memories. Even though my mother had looked through these things page by page just now, without this physical evidence, the executioner’s blade could not fall.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s182-1: I tore out the page, crumpled it into a ball, and threw it into the embers remaining in the stove.
texts.chapter:v15-18b:event:text-s183-1: The flames licked at the paper. The faint light illuminated the darkened room. The writing filled with blood debts and evasion curled and broke apart in the heat, eventually burning into weightless ash.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:title: Chapter Eighteen, Supplement Two: All Five Documents Are True
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s1-1:
Unified Wording Opinion for Consciousness Coupling Reports · Front page (Central Computing Relay Station foyer, historical education display):
“I. Anything not detected by instruments shall be written as ‘not detected.’
II. Do not
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s1-2:
write ‘cannot yet be ruled out.’
III. Divine will, indivisible souls, and non-disposability—all are unscientific terms and must not enter the draft.
IV. Since no immeasurable boundary has ever been detected, no such boundary exists.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s6-1:
I crossed the boundary of another new cycle and woke on yet another morning.
08:10. That was when this body woke. The instant I opened my eyes, I rushed out of the room and pushed open the door to Sera’s office as fast as I could.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s6-2: Estelle was sitting in the visitor’s chair, anxiously twisting her hands together as she waited for confirmation of her candidate status that day. Sera sat behind her desk, opening the three unsigned quota booklets to prepare to sign them.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s7-1: I ignored Estelle’s startled gaze and walked straight to the desk, bracing both hands against its edge.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s8-1: “Wait before you sign.” I looked at Sera and spoke quickly. “I know you’ll take me for a madman. But I don’t just know what you’re thinking. I also know what just happened in
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s8-2: your system. At 08:10, just now, a candidate timing verification failure occurred at the Central Relay Station. Code A-774. The affected field is the end-of-week countdown.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s9-1: Sera’s pen stopped in midair. She glanced at the wall clock, her expression full of disbelief. Estelle held her breath, looking at us helplessly.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s10-1: “If I’m a madman, pull up the low-level log for 08:10 right now.” I stared at her.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s11-1:
Sera frowned, but under my gaze, she still switched out of the main interface and brought up the backend.
There was no red light on the screen, no alarm. But
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s11-2:
on an extremely well-hidden system scale, a recently generated record lay quietly:
[Silent Anomaly] Candidate timing verification blocked. Error code: A-774
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s14-1: She stared at the silent failure code that should not have appeared on any routine interface. Her expression changed.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s16-1: “This is a low-level anomaly… It bypassed every surface monitor, yet physically blocked today’s review procedure.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s17-1: She briskly pulled a facility-accident inspection warrant from the drawer and signed her name on the spot. Then she stood, slipped the three booklets into her bag, and seized my arm.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s19-1: “To describe a hard failure of this level down to the exact second, you either connected to some unknown monitoring source, or you’re one of the people who preset this sabotage. Locking you alone in
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s19-2: an observation room would leave us wondering what else you might trigger. You’re coming to the relay station with me. Until we get to the bottom of this failure, you stay within my sight at all times.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s20-1:
She turned toward the girl in the visitor’s chair.
“Today’s review has been physically blocked. Estelle, go back to the village and wait for word.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s21-1:
Estelle froze for a moment, then stood up with visible relief and hurried out.
Sera snatched the coat from the back of the chair and drove me toward the Central Computing Relay Station.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s25-1:
No one spoke along the way. At 11:30, we reached the outskirts of the relay station.
The foyer’s eastern wall held a glass display case for “anti-superstition historical education.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s28-1: The first item was an early propaganda poster from the People’s Choice Party—the Leader in uniform on the left; on the right, a figure in a white coat: the chief scientist whose name the Empire would later erase completely. The
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s28-2: scientist’s face had long since been scraped away, leaving only a blurred white smear. The second was a concept drawing from the early construction of the time machine. Beneath it was the slogan: ‘Tomorrow is already waiting for us.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s31-1:
At the center of the display case lay a yellowed early circulated document: Unified Wording Opinion for Consciousness Coupling Reports.
Displayed beside it were approval attachments from the same period, formally authorizing “subject capacity” and “conscious living bodies” to be registered as consumable materials.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s34-1:
At the bottom of the display case, presented as a model of rectitude, was a dust-covered internal denunciation letter.
The grassroots technician who wrote it insisted: ‘Personal belief contamination must be removed from the data. Stubbornly writing “cannot yet be ruled out” instead of “not
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s34-2: detected” caused our department’s schedule to be revoked. If this is not punished severely, next time we will lose our positions and rations along with it. I hereby request that this person be transferred away from the conscious living body project and replaced by a more steadfast comrade.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s35-1: I looked at the letter. The power to process living people as material had been made respectable, piece by piece, through the very real threats that could strip colleagues of their rations and positions.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s39-1: The relay station’s lower-level machine room was filled with a low-frequency hum and the smell of rubber. Sera bypassed the technician on duty and directly called up the low-level feedback from the anomaly that had just occurred.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s40-1: “When A-774 triggered, the master system performed an abnormal correction—it tried to silence the alarm with an old low-level filtering rule.” She pointed at a string of
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s40-2: garbled characters flashing on the screen. “This rule has extremely high-level authorization, and points to an old storage zone that has been sealed off for years. My
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s40-3: guess is that some technician from the old era welded the low-level alarm for candidate timing anomalies to the wake-up command for this dead-file zone on the same line.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s41-1: “So the door is open now?” I asked.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s42-1:
“No. The alarm only loosened the latch.” Sera switched to the command console. “If this really is an old back door, it should still accept the standard accident-inspection key.”
She entered the Inner Circle key from the accident inspection
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s42-2:
warrant she had just signed.
The screen stuttered for a second, then displayed a field of green access permissions. Sera’s expression darkened. “I guessed right. Someone really did make it an old alarm that opens at the slightest touch.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s43-1: As authorization reached deeper, she pieced together traces of an era’s workings from the tangled old database. At last, deep within a block whose index had even been erased, she sorted out five sequential documents from different departments.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s44-1: The first was a genuine test record from the grassroots level. The bleak data showed clearly that no matter how the machine was adjusted, the time machine could never transmit into the past beyond the starting point established at “the moment of activation.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s45-1: The second was a revised version of the same test submitted up the chain. To avoid punishment for reporting bad news, middle management erased the conclusion that “returning to the past is impossible” and
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s45-2: added a handwritten note: if they did not make this change, the entire department’s budget and schedule for the following week would be taken away, and everyone would be sent together to a camp outside the city.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s46-1: The third was a disciplinary decision from the security department. A technician from the engineering institute had pointed out the fatal discrepancy between the two reports through the proper chain of authority, but no investigation
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s46-2: followed. He was arrested outright. The charge was ‘undermining the progress of the salvation project.’ This security authorization not only silenced him; it also became violent proof that the false data possessed force within the system.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s47-1: The fourth was a consolidated brief from the propaganda department. Each layer of review had ‘corrected’ the original a little further. By this point, it had become a glorious summary of interim
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s47-2: achievements in physics. This data chain, riddled with holes, finally completed its own closed loop at the propaganda level, becoming the slogan on the wall: ‘Tomorrow is already waiting for us.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s48-1: The fifth was the annual success brief released to the public. The system dispatch logs showed that the genuine low-level trial-and-error record from the first document and the brief polished through layer after layer had been placed on the desk of Monde, the
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s48-2: chief technical bureaucrat at the time, on the same day. Monde signed the success brief that was destined to deceive countless people into entering the machine, closing the gates of verification for good with the words: ‘Stability takes precedence over truth.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s52-1: “Real data, the kidnapping of budgets and resources, the punishment of those who were honest, the middle-level consolidation, and finally the informed signature of the highest technical bureaucrat allowing it through.” Sera stared coldly at the
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s52-2: screen. “Each link used the official document from the previous link as its endorsement, then added the conclusion most suited to its own interests with a clear conscience. The lie could not have operated successfully with even one person missing.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s53-1: Sera did not open the defense behind Monde’s signature. Whether Monde was preserving the Empire or preserving himself, the fact remained that he had turned this false process into reality.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s56-1:
At the bottom of the vast mass of attachments, Sera called up a review document from a quota meeting. It had been left by a systems scholar responsible for the calculations.
The document opened with a disclaimer: ‘This living-body
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s56-2:
quota model calculates capacity consumption only. This method does not answer who ought to be sacrificed.’
Yet in the technical admission field on the same page, marked ‘May serve as a basis for quotas,’ he had still signed neatly.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s59-1: “A memorandum beside him says that the previous two colleagues who refused to sign had already been taken away by the internal security bureau. He took over the position.” Sera pointed at the archive on the screen.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s60-1: The link jumping from the screen showed without mercy that once this quota document, with its disclaimer and rigorous formulas, was stamped, it immediately became a “technical authorization” in the next cross-department approval.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s62-1: “What actually took effect in that meeting room was the action that followed.” Sera’s voice turned cold. “Every liquidation squad that took the subsequent approvals to arrest people had a
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s62-2: legal basis to complete its quota as soon as it saw that the technical admission field had been signed. The administrative system did not care what disclaimer he had written in the preamble.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s65-1: In the deep encrypted zone, two records concerning ancient archives from before the Empire’s founding lay side by side. They were the true history from before the time machine had been built.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s67-1: “At the time, in order to fulfill the political promise of ‘returning to the past,’ this project monopolized the largest budget in human history and consumed all resources needed for survival.” Sera
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s67-2: pointed at the screen. “The specialists who raised objections were forced out and herded into the same basement. They were forced to gather together and called themselves the ‘Conservation Society.’”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s68-1: On the left was the original Action Declaration drafted by these people at the time. Since no one was willing to carry out the executions, and no precise rule could kill more than eighty percent of the population while preserving the rest, a group
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s68-2: of radicals decided to infiltrate the nuclear arsenal and use the blindest death statistics of global nuclear war to cover the entire world. Before the deadline predicted by the model arrived, they would forcibly empty the capacity, even if it
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s68-3:
meant going down together.
On the right was the abridged version of the interrogation record later released by the administrative system. All the sacrificial arguments and equations had been blacked out, leaving only the madness of the act itself.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s70-1: “Capacity overload a thousand years later was common knowledge even then. The regime built the machine through its promise to return to the past and strangle the disaster when it was still a seed, using that as the legitimacy for its founding and its rise to
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s70-2: power.” Sera turned to another legal archive. “So when they discovered that the machine could not cross the cycle’s starting point at all, they issued a decree sealing off every physical formula that could verify the failure of the machine’s route. What they
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s70-3: wanted to conceal was never the disaster, but the fact that salvation was already impossible.” She shook her head. “They bundled the scholars who calculated this deadlock together with the infiltrators of the nuclear arsenal and branded them all terrorists.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s71-1: The authorities showed the public only a group of madmen attempting to provoke nuclear war. They would never acknowledge the mathematical motive behind those madmen’s attempt to save people, much less admit that the promised road to salvation was a dead end.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s74-1:
As the principal offender in the nuclear arsenal case, the operative in charge of infiltrating the arsenal had left the “Name” field blank on the final page of the record.
The recorder copied down only his final message:
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s75-1: ‘Names are for those who intend to return.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s76-1: I looked at the screen. How exactly was continuation of life carried out in Gallon’s blind spot? At that moment, this cold process that treated people as less than human
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s76-2: overlapped with the people who had signed those documents long ago. A chill ran through me—not only at the ancient machinery of power, but at the executors of the present.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s82-1:
The machine room fell silent.
Sera remained silent for a long time. When all the distant dead files had been closed and the screen returned to the main interface, her gaze fell on the terminal keyboard.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s83-1: Since the old back door used to conceal the dead files had originally been triggered by diverting “candidate timing anomalies,” this old section of code in the master system was still connected to the same low-level channel as the
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s83-2:
current candidate program.
She entered the search codes from the three village candidate approval booklets in her possession. She searched for the Central Execution Command stream associated with Estelle’s “candidate continuation of life.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s84-1: Nothing appeared on the screen as expected. Instead, a glaring line of red text lit up: ‘Command generation in progress. Consolidation of three-party attachments required.’
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s85-1: Sera did not stop. She continued entering the Inner Circle key from the accident inspection warrant and forcibly called up the system’s underlying database structure. The warrant’s legal authorization was specifically
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s85-2: for examining ongoing “candidate timing anomaly” events. Since code A-774 pointed to the candidate program, using the inspection key to examine the system’s current logs was entirely within normal authorization.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s86-1:
Sera’s breath stopped abruptly. She stared fixedly at the structure.
1. Informed consent approval (Sera)
2. Risk assessment calculation (Otto)
3. Physical transfer execution plan authorization (Gallon)
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s88-1: “Look at its retrieval rules.” Her hand hovered above the keyboard, trembling slightly. “Otto’s second step can begin his process only after receiving the ‘informed consent form’ I issue. Gallon’s third step, meanwhile, takes Otto’s report as the legal
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s88-2: basis for receiving and calibrating the body parameters. But neither of us can view the other’s attachments. Only when all three parts converge in the system can the central execution command finally be generated and enter the physical transfer operation.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s89-1:
She looked at the three clearly separated directories.
“The design of this process is astonishingly similar to the five-link cross-department document chain we just saw. They split one matter into several parts
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s89-2: that could never see one another, leaving each person responsible only for their own section.” She drew a deep breath. “I only have a consent form for a controlled physical replacement here. Under Otto’s system
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s89-3: responsibilities, he has only a routine rejection-risk calculation there. If no one takes responsibility for the final result after these mutually isolated steps, we all become stepping stones for the next link.”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s90-1: I looked at her and said nothing more. As long as her signature and Otto’s report stood behind it, if Gallon overstepped his authority in the final link and disposed of the original bodies, the whole thing had already been wrapped in the outer garment of legality.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s93-1:
After nightfall, we boarded the carriage home.
There was no lamp inside. The lantern’s faint light swayed across the carriage walls. Sera sat hunched in the corner, clutching the three village candidate approval booklets that had gone unsigned today.
Estelle’s name was on the first page.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s94-1: “Did you really believe before that it was only a medical procedure?” I looked at her.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s95-1:
Sera lowered her head.
“I knew the original body would be disposed of after consciousness was extracted, but I never saw the technical section’s attachments.” Her voice was
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s95-2: dry. “But after seeing those three mutually isolated directories today… after the consent form I signed, could the body’s dependencies, termination conditions, and final
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s95-3: eligibility be changed somewhere in the blind spot of the process? If, in the part Gallon is responsible for, even the original body is used as consumable material elsewhere…”
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s96-1:
“What are you going to do?” I asked. “Resign first thing tomorrow? The administrative system will immediately replace you with someone who won’t even look, who’ll sign everything with their eyes closed. Estelle will still be sent in.”
The wheels ran over a deep rut, and the carriage lurched violently. Sera did not argue.
The signature
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s96-2: of the review scholar we had seen in the archives room today seemed to be right in front of her eyes. That person had left a disclaimer at the review meeting, yet still stamped the document, after which the quota formulas trying to make up the numbers pushed through without obstruction. Her pen point had stopped in the same place.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s98-1:
“I know.”
She raised her head. In the darkness, her gaze gradually hardened.
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s100-1: “I noticed it before, actually. The day before yesterday, she submitted a formal written appeal to the records office because she wanted a reason for rejection in black and white. Since today’s physical obstruction, her review is still suspended, so that appeal remains active
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s100-2: in the process.” She looked at me. “I can’t use the administrative authority in my hands to force open Gallon’s attachments. But if I use this unresolved appeal to frame today’s failure as a ‘system anomaly endangering candidate rights,’ I can apply to initiate a joint review
texts.chapter:v15-18c:event:text-s100-3:
by multiple parties. I’ll bring the interface protocols in Gallon’s possession, along with this system’s real trump card, fully out onto the table.”
The carriage stopped beneath the watchtower. Sera pushed open the door, jumped down, and quickly disappeared into the night.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-02-twins:title: Sea Line Two: Twins
texts.chapter:heisenberg-02-twins:event:text-s:
Nation-Building Propaganda Poster · Fragment (printing-plant ruins, half a sheet):
Two faces, equal in size, side by side.
Letterpress beneath the left face: “He guided us forward.”
Letterpress beneath the right face: “He brought

the past back.”
(The face in the right image was completely scraped away with a sharp tool, leaving only a blurred white mark. Scraping away a face was much cheaper than withdrawing a slogan. This slogan—they kept it to use again.)
Before “the Twins” became this nation’s supreme totem, the old world first faced a massacre that came within a hair of being carried out.

When the Geodesic faction, an extremist branch of the Conservation Society, attempted to provoke a global nuclear war and forcibly shatter the bound state of life and the soul field through the instantaneous deaths of hundreds of millions, the plot was exposed at the last

moment. The declassified documents show that the Security Bureau dumped several sacks of calculation manuscripts seized from the faction onto the chief designer’s desk, demanding that this physicist, representing the nation’s finest mind, perform a technical verification.

Imperial Special Tribunal Evidence Document No. 04 · Physics Verification Report:
“The faction’s plan is technically feasible. The estimated yield of the nuclear explosions would indeed be sufficient to release more than

eighty percent of the population from their bound state. Through fission-based release, this extremely inefficient unbinding could forcibly return enough capacity debt. Its actual cost, however, would be the deaths of

more than eighty percent of the old world’s population, something wholly untenable in ethical and social terms.”
(Signature in the lower right corner: [Approval Code H-01 (verified as the chief engineer’s serial number)])

At the subsequent special tribunal, the chief commissioner leading the investigation read aloud this authoritative conclusion. The commissioner deliberately concealed the physical motive in the latter half

concerning “returning the debt,” establishing only the most terrifying point for the public: these heretics possessed a physically viable nuclear weapons plan, one that had come within a hair of being detonated.

The tribunal recording still preserves the terrified screams from the audience. Using the panic that followed from “eighty percent of the population nearly being slaughtered by madmen,” the old man who

would later become the Führer drafted, overnight, an indefinite emergency authorization act beyond parliamentary constraint, and had it passed under martial law. The political purges began soon after.
The age of “the Twins” had officially begun.

Klenik Trial Record · Attachment Three (Top Secret):
“On the first day after taking power, the old man invited the chief designer onto the balcony of the state office building … I was standing in the inner hall across a corridor and

couldn’t make out the details. But I saw the old man point at the cheering sea of people below, then point toward the heavy industrial district in the distance. The chief designer told me later that the old man had sold him a precisely

meshing structure: the nation’s steel, his formulas. The old man promised that as long as the machine could be powered on, the Security Bureau of the Führer’s Office could make everyone believe that tomorrow and yesterday were equally safe.”

Through this stained trial record, we can roughly reconstruct the scene on that balcony. Hundreds of thousands were cheering wildly below, while the chief designer may have rested his hand on the rough stone railing and quietly watched the vast industrial map beneath him. He did not reject this mutually generative relationship.
Political violence, engineering manufacture, and technical calculation each held a partial veto in this empire. When the machine prototype was powered on for the first time, fierce doubts about the

causal logic underlying the machine spread through academia. The old man fulfilled his promise, using the Security Bureau’s boots to suppress the dissent that might shake the foundations, on his behalf.

Imperial First University Archives · On-Site Inspection Photo #07:
A corridor littered with manuscripts. In the lower left of the image, before a half-open door, a blackboard
eraser has been crushed underfoot, and chalk dust trails a struggling mark across the corridor floor. At the far end of the corridor, two guards are carrying an old man away.
The photograph was probably taken that afternoon during the purge. A hard-tempered old professor who refused to bow was carried away outside the door.

We have no way of knowing for certain what the person inside the door was thinking at that moment. Perhaps he was listening through the half-closed gap as the curses outside gradually receded, watching the scattered manuscripts being swept into a trash bin. But his final response remains frozen in the piles of manuscripts unearthed by later generations.

Core Calculation Manuscript (Restored):
Several key derivation symbols originally marked as risks of causal-law collapse had been crossed out line by line in extremely forceful handwriting, with obscure engineering codes written beside them as a concealing replacement.

That afternoon, holding a fountain pen, he personally erased every symbol in his theory that might invite debate over paradoxes. As long as the machine kept turning, no one would be able to falsify his universe on paper.

Imperial Machine Construction Bureau · Master Progress Plan (Photocopy):
Two names are signed side by side in the lower right corner of the enormous engineering drawing: [thoroughly painted-over blank], and the faintly legible “Klenik.”

Although the name had been deliberately erased, everyone knew that one man was responsible for drawing the future, while his co-chief designer Klenik was responsible for turning the blueprints into steel. To produce this master plan, three

industrial districts that had originally manufactured civilian goods changed their production lines overnight, and two north-south railway trunk lines replaced every sleeper. Countless top engineers worked three shifts until their eyes were red.
But deep inside the archives bureau, an internal memorandum remained, thick with the smell of blood.

High-Pressure Workshop Work-Stoppage Request (Rejected):
Attachment: Photograph of the western district’s main-shaft crane derailment site. Six assembly workers had been crushed beneath twisted steel frames, one of them still clutching the feeler gauge used for calibration. The broken

western old load-bearing beam lay across the pool of blood. The union demands a two-week stoppage and a full replacement of the factory roof’s main beams, or it will refuse to send new workers up onto the platform.
Ruling: 【Rejected. Maintain highest priority.】——[Approval Code H-01]
Behind that request, we can only piece together the argument that evening from the surviving work notes of Klenik.

The notes record the file Klenik slammed onto the office desk. Unless the aging broken beam was completely dismantled, a concrete foundation recast, and a new beam installed, the assembly workers handling the next main-shaft lift would

still be crushed to death. But the other man merely pointed at the countdown on the wall—the final window for launching a synchronization satellite into outer space. The low-Earth-orbit clearance window was about to close completely because

of wartime debris. Any further delay would block even this one opening through which the gravity-calibration equipment could be sent into the sky. Without the satellite, the entire machine would be as good as blind to its coordinates.

Klenik offered a final compromise: since there was still an intact load-bearing beam on the eastern side across from the old factory, they could recast a main shaft overnight from titanium alloy, lighter and stronger, weighing only half as much as the original. That would eliminate the need to replace the broken beam during a two-week stoppage; the

single intact old beam could bear the lifting weight, and the schedule could be forcibly preserved. But this required three blast furnaces to be run at full power through the night, and the additional one hundred and fifty thousand tons of fuel could only be forcibly requisitioned from the winter ration stores for civilians in the northern district.

Klenik wrote in his notes: “I thought that putting the figures in front of him—that twenty thousand civilian households in the northern district would lose their coal and freeze to death—might make him hesitate, even slightly. Those weren’t numbers. They were more than a hundred thousand people.”
But beside that work-stoppage order, another requisition order for winter coal, issued on the same day, had been pinned up.

Northern District, Ration Station Seven · Materials Allocation Form:
Reason for allocation: Ignition of the high-pressure workshop’s blast furnaces.
Additional note: Civilian frostbite and deaths resulting from this allocation will no longer be counted separately.
Signature: [Approval Code H-01]

At the end of that day’s notes, Klenik wrote: “He signed that coal allocation order calmly. Only later did I understand that he didn’t believe those tens of thousands of civilians and those six workers would really die. In his calculations, as soon as the machine was powered on, all of this cost would be revoked.”

Full-Power Main-Shaft Ignition Trial · Control Room Contingency Meeting Minutes (Top Secret):
… The attending experts engaged in a heated dispute over the risk of a system deadlock caused by the final gravity readings.
The Supreme Command (the Führer) forcibly

halted the technical discussion and issued the highest directives:
1. Establish one-way data isolation in the external data observation gallery. Submission of the terminal operation must be completed outside the room.
2. If the machine ultimately fails to

establish a coordinate point in the past, the result must be absolutely isolated.
3. Strip the test operator of reporting authority. Apart from the operator, the sole witness in the external observation gallery may report only in person to the Führer himself.

This is a set of minutes unearthed deep in the archives. While more than a dozen uninformed experts were still arguing over “technical risks,” the old man seated at the end of the long table had no interest in the specific

parameters. During the earlier prototype tests, he had already obtained the fundamental dead end: under physical principles, the machine could never cross the starting point established at the moment it was activated.

So what he needed to guard against was not “if it failed,” but how to control the dead end that was bound to arrive. When this machine, which had consumed the resources of the entire country, finally confirmed that impasse internally at full power, by what route would the bad news—enough to bring down the entire regime—get out?

This was a secret known only to a very few. This was also why, in all public materials, the operator was “the first person to return to the past,” while in the top-secret contingency plan, that room had been sealed off from every possible channel of speech.
On the evening the machine’s final assembly was completed, the full-power ignition trial was scheduled for three days later.

Beside the enormous test building, the single-person isolation room for separating the test operator had just been delivered. It was a concrete chamber filled with thick layers of lead plate, with only one heavy blast-proof iron door.

Isolation Room Engineering Delivery Form (Scanned Front and Back):
On the back was a familiar handwritten note in fountain pen, covered by forceful scoring, though the words beneath could still be made out: “The total amount of mortar used in the inner walls

exceeds the ratio by half a percent. No maintenance conduit is visible in the door-control area. Logistics replies: the excess mortar was used to fill the gaps in the reinforced load-bearing walls.”
Acceptance signature on the front: [Approval Code H-01]
Pinned beside this acceptance form, its front and back covered in contradictions, was half of a torn scrap of paper: the design blueprint for the access-control system.
The position of the conduit for the mechanical drive shaft on the inside had been circled in red, with a solid black square drawn beside it to represent concrete pouring.

Together with the missing maintenance conduit in the door-control area, the two blueprints left no doubt where that extra half percent of mortar had gone. It had been used to seal the originally planned mechanical drive shaft firmly inside the wall.

This meant that the blast-proof iron door was completely inoperable. There was no longer any mechanical handle in the room that could unlock it. Unless the external operator supplied power from outside and pulled the gate open, the person inside could never push open this iron

wall, welded into the structure. It was a tomb the old man had built in advance for the dead end that was bound to arrive: one day in the future, once the test operator inside had completed the connection and entered standby, the sole witness outside would press the terminal

confirmation key on the console and obtain the absolute failure result. The guards outside the isolation room could then forgo executing the return reset and simply cut power to the entire building. The operator who held the truth of the failure would remain in the dark forever.

On this side of the delivery form, the man who was about to become the sole witness was looking at the blueprint. No one knows whether, in the instant he understood this plan to silence him, he realized that the Führer had known all along that the machine could never succeed. But faced with the blueprint, he turned the

delivery form back to the front. Looking at the manuscript on the desk, its warning symbols crossed out in his own hand; looking at the launch-window countdown flickering on the wall; looking at the requisition orders stained with coal dust—in the acceptance field on the front, the chief designer signed his own code.

Imperial Listening Network, Channel Seven · Street Audio Archive:
(Wind. A street broadcast is announcing the countdown to the trial ceremony. Faintly, several children just released from school are singing a newly learned nursery song. The four words “return to the past” drift through their childish voices.)
After signing, he may have put his hands into the pockets of his overcoat and crossed the square alone, through the slogans and flags.
At the far end of the square, the two faces of equal size on the enormous propaganda poster watched him quietly in the dusk.
Three days later, the test subject would enter the isolation room, while he would stand alone in the observation gallery, press the start key, and carry out the prescribed operating procedures.
texts.chapter:chapter-19-mismatched-number:tit: Chapter Nineteen: Numbers That Don't Add Up
texts.chapter:chapter-19-mismatched-number:eve: This was another morning in a new world.

I had to put the questions that had already arisen in the previous worlds, but had not yet taken root in her mind in this one, back in front of her.
That morning in the settlement, when she hesitated over the weekend oath she was required to sign, I opened

the Candidate Act I had brought with me.
“If you have doubts about the oath’s authenticity, you don’t have to give up your seat immediately.” I pointed to Article Seven. “You have a ‘formal right of appeal’ regarding historical texts. That means you can

request an inspection of the original at an external disaster-recovery station.”
Her action was more decisive than I expected. As soon as she discovered that the system contained a legitimate path for verification, Estelle filed an appeal with Sera on the spot.

Faced with this unexpected request, Sera initially frowned. But after seeing the resolve in Estelle’s eyes, a complicated assessment flickered through her gaze. To her, this might have been the perfect test of whether

the girl possessed an independent will. She took a red-headed access permit from the table, signed her name, approved the passage, and assigned me to accompany Estelle as an aide for the route and the old language.
Of course, I had a secondary personal purpose as well: I wanted to use this rare verification order to make contact with the “interface appendix” in Galon’s hands.
At ten in the morning, we departed on schedule for external disaster-recovery station A06, a three-hour walk away.

On the way there, Estelle uncharacteristically brought up Watermarsh.
“In Watermarsh, mutual aid during the rainy season and funerals are the most important things.” She walked through the wilderness wind, her voice level. “We’re remote. Our machinery isn’t as complete as the

Inner Circle’s. If someone dies during the rainy season, the neighbors have to take turns keeping watch and burying them so we can make it through the plague. The ritual isn’t only for the dead. It’s also so the living know they won’t simply be left in the mud and floodwater.”

I listened quietly. In this entirely new world, she was the first person to mention the dead and rituals to me.
“I used to know someone named Yuna.” I looked at
the wasteland ahead. “She was like that too. She didn’t care about grand slogans. She cared about every concrete account, about who received rations and who didn’t.”
Estelle glanced at me. She didn’t ask anything else, but she remembered the name.

At one in the afternoon, we arrived at Station A06. When we pushed open the heavy iron door to the public disaster-recovery hall, the air was dry enough to rasp in the throat. It gathered the foundational files of various early institutions. Tall iron shelves extended row after row into the darkness.

First, I swiped the verification order at the terminal by the entrance and tried to access the interface appendix. The screen flickered once, then still displayed “Insufficient permissions”—the order could open the historical archive, but it still

could not penetrate the execution command stream where the interface appendix was stored. It seemed the key granted by candidate rights was not enough here. I wrote down the error code returned by the terminal and turned toward the physical shelves.
On instinct, I took Estelle straight to the third row of the old archives. She put on gloves and found the unabridged First Relief Register. After checking Clause
Seventy-Three and confirming that the oath preserved by the Watermarsh settlement was the genuine text, she closed the book and looked toward the archive boxes deeper beside it.
“Since we’re here,” she said, hanging the lantern on the curved hook of the iron shelving, “let’s look around separately. You check the administrative logs. I’ll look through logistics.”

I spent more than an hour going through the administrative section. The administrative logs here began earlier than I had expected. In the oldest files, during the Head of State’s final years while he was still alive, the Joint Observation Group’s schedules for night watches, kitchens, and medical care were already operating in practice.

The files also contained several rejected applications to suppress the public-security operation. At the time, the authorities had been fully capable of stamping out this nascent movement, but the upper levels had selectively marked the applications “tolerate.

” Notes in the margins revealed the logic behind this tacit approval: the candidate elites rejected because of the inequality of Ark seats were providing organizational language and absorbing the enormous population at the bottom; while the Head of State

happened to need this mutual-aid network spreading through the lower levels. It could sustain the machine myth, shift the social despair caused by the Ark quotas onto someone else, and use the undercurrent to strike at his increasingly arrogant retainers.

It was the old regime itself that had left this network room to grow. When the succession crisis erupted and the state administration and rationing chain collapsed completely, they were able to use that existing network to take over social services at once, expanding it into a system that could replace the state machine.
“I can fill in some of the earlier historical gaps on my side.” I pushed the logs back into place and turned toward Estelle. “What about yours?”

Farther in, the files on the shelves bore the headings of the early years of the new age. In the logistics section, Estelle had uncovered mountains of relief-kitchen registers. Beside them were an Operations Manual for Distribution Clerks and several Orders for the Investigation of Heresy bearing later dates.

“These tens of thousands of records for people lining up to receive food—the wording of thanks in the final column is identical down to the punctuation.” She pointed to the bold annotation in the operations manual that read “Copy exactly,” then took out an early food-distribution record and placed it beside the later investigation order.
“Not only that,” she said softly. “Look at these two documents.”

I leaned closer. Although several years separated them, the code signature of the person responsible for recording food distribution and the code of the person who later issued the Order for the Investigation of Heresy were not only made up of the same letters. Even the habitual upward

hook at the end was identical.
The order’s supplementary provisions clearly printed the logic of the verdict: “The doubt and pessimism of the Fated Ones are strengthening the destructive bad-future branch from the observation pool’s end. Removing them from the register is salvation.”

Estelle said nothing, her pen tip suspended in midair.
At the bottom of this archive box lay large patches of black ash, carbonized and fused together by intense heat, giving off the old smell of scorched material. They were the remains left behind when the original lower-level records had been thoroughly burned after the investigation.
The two

surviving documents lay side by side on the table. The food sent out from this room had been real. The hand that recorded the names of disaster victims under this code had been real. And later, the hand that signed the investigation order in the same handwriting, declaring that killing and burning the archives were acts of salvation, had been real too.
At last, at the bottom of the relief-register box, we pieced together a set of numbers that did not add up.

Estelle pulled out an internal military communication from three months before the boundary was established. It mentioned the Central Ring and Inner Circle regions. At the time, their estimated trapped surviving population was 800,000.
But what I held in my hand was a thin year-end summary.
“Year One of the Boundary: Total population registered within the first safe boundary—the Central Ring and Inner Circle regions: 130,000.”
“There were only 130,000 people registered here.” Estelle looked at the two numbers. “The early estimate was 800,000. Nearly 670,000 people are missing in between.”

“But that was only an estimate. ‘Establishing a safe boundary’ was an administrative quarantine process that gradually herded people inward with wire fences and checkpoints.” She looked at me. “Large numbers of people must have died of disease during that period, and some may

even have died before the safe boundary was completed. Even if people survived until the boundary closed but never entered this register of 130,000, they may have fled on their own. The difference between an initial estimate and a final register alone can’t establish anything.”
“If it were only this one difference in numbers, it couldn’t.”

I turned the thin summary sheet over.
“Look at this. It’s the supply-dispatch order from the first year after the boundary closed. During the ruin period, when all industry and agriculture had ground to a halt, the national pipeline network supplied this region at an

average daily flow of 1,200 tons for six consecutive months.” I worked through the figures with my pen. “At the time, the water sources were heavily contaminated with heavy metals, and all household water was strictly controlled. According to the First Relief Register, each

person received only an extreme survival ration of 1.5 liters of drinking water per day. Washing and flushing toilets were completely prohibited. If there were only 130,000 people on the register, their theoretical daily consumption would have been just 195 tons of water.”

I tapped the 1,200 tons with the tip of my pen.
“This 1,200 tons flowing through the pipelines every day wasn’t merely sent on schedule by the supplier. The recipients
took all of it as well, with no overflow or refusal alarms from the pipeline network. 1,200 tons—that’s 1.2 million liters. 1.2 million divided by 1.5 liters equals what?”
“Eight hundred thousand.” Estelle answered without thinking. Then her breath caught, and her eyes fixed on the number.

“Exactly 800,000. Not an approximation. Not a ton short.” I looked at her. “That means the water-supply system was not distributing water according to the register of 130,000 at all. It was operating directly according to the original estimate of 800,000 people.

And that additional thousand-plus tons of water were really drunk by people—if tens of thousands of people had already died of the plague, the dead wouldn’t have been turning on the taps at the same time every day to collect their 1.5 liters of life-saving water.”

I pulled several records from the nearby shelf marked “General Transport Affairs” and threw them onto the table. “Look at these too. If 670,000 people had really died in batches from plague or famine, the state machine would inevitably have

consumed vast amounts of fuel by sending convoys to bury them collectively. But during those months of the boundary process, vehicle dispatch in this region was remarkably smooth. Not one extra truck was sent out. Fuel was never allocated in bulk.”

I slapped the relief register printed with the standard wording of thanks.
“This means that, in an administrative system so tightly controlled that even the words of thanks spoken while receiving food had to be standardized, there were only 130,000 people when numbered ration tickets were issued. But behind the water valves that required no names, there were a full 800,000.”

“As long as they weren’t on the budget register, those 670,000 people were transparent in the formal administrative ledgers.” I looked at her. “Without a dedicated budget, there were no records bearing their names.

As for which temporary camps they were confined in, what projects they were fed into as expendable material, or which day they died on, none of it could ever be found in these stacks of ‘standard’ relief registers.”

Estelle slid the steel pen back into her pocket. There were no specific autopsy reports or bones to give the disaster a physical form. All the evidence consisted of the rations for 130,000 people, the water that sustained the lives of several hundred thousand more each day, and one continuous, empty void in the logistics ledgers.

For the next several hours, the only sound in the archive room was the rustle of turning pages. We continued searching deeper, trying to find where those 670,000 people had gone. Time passed unnoticed, and outside, the sky had turned completely black.

At nine that evening, just before we were about to leave the archive shelves, we found two records in the most secluded area that were completely different from the others.
One was an original observation manuscript covered in dust, its paper so brittle it nearly crumbled at a touch. For security

reasons, the observing researcher had left only an abbreviated signature, a duty code: “S-01.” At the bottom of the archive box lay several thin transcripts of recordings, clearly produced on much later media. The person who had reviewed and confirmed the anomaly had signed his name “Heisenberg.”

Estelle found several early confidential personnel memoranda nearby. By comparing the duty codes, she confirmed that “S-01” was Semmelweis’s real name.
She compared the dates in the private files with the timestamps on Heisenberg’s transcripts.
“Nearly

forty years apart.” She looked at the yellowed pages. “When Semmelweis died with the first-generation underground network, Heisenberg hadn’t even come here yet. This wasn’t a task passed down from a superior to a subordinate. They couldn’t have met.”

There was no master-and-apprentice inheritance, no succession of positions within a secret organization. Semmelweis had simply left an observation report in this system titled “Pool positions are falling faster than the population model predicts.” The accounts did not balance; the anomaly was recorded. But without information from the

Inner Circle, the field for its cause had to remain blank.
Two generations later, another person returned here through a transcript, carrying classified information about the machine’s operating dates. Heisenberg placed the date when the machine had been activated beside the date of the pool-position anomaly and continued the question.

When we left the records archive and entered the station’s prayer corner, it was already half past nine at night. This had originally been a place for the families of the early staff to pray. The wood of the benches had already split.

Estelle walked over and took the copy of Watermarsh’s funeral oath from her pocket.
By the faint light, she used her pen to cross out one line on the paper.

“‘The common will guarantees a correct future,’” she read aloud, the official platitude she had crossed out. “I know now that it no longer applies.”
She folded the paper and put it back in her pocket. “But my home’s ritual still needs the rest.”

Once we had organized the records and were preparing to pass through the disaster-recovery station’s final security door and begin the return journey, less than fifteen minutes remained before the 22:00 transition point.
My time was almost up. Once the hour passed, the focus of observation would leave with my consciousness and continue into the next world. But the “Arno” of this world would not disappear.
He would retain everything we had experienced together during the day, continue walking the remaining three hours of wilderness at night with her, and go on living in the world behind me.
I heard Estelle speak at the security door.

“Arno.” She stopped walking. “This morning, you said that the person named Yuna didn’t care about slogans, only accounts. If she were here today, facing this number in the archives with no explanation—if it were her…”
She looked at me, her voice carrying a serious inquiry.
“If it were her, how would she check this account?”
I stopped where I was.
“People who aren’t on the budget register don’t receive dedicated rations.” I looked at the landmark tower in the distance. “She’d check the things they would inevitably depend on to live. She’d
trace the destinations of waste that had supposedly been centrally scrapped. She’d trace where the portions skimmed and saved from the fixed rations of the 130,000 registered people ultimately went.”
“She’d make me find the signatures on those transfers. Because an account that doesn’t balance will always demand a cost. That means a real destination for real resources.”
Estelle was quiet for a moment in the deepening night.

She lowered her head and opened the notebook in which she required everything to remain objective.
Beside the entry stating that the system left no record of people outside the register, she added a sentence: “Check the flow of back-end budgets and the surplus from fixed rations.” Then she drew a hard horizontal line through it with her steel pen.
The tip pressed a deep indentation into the brittle paper.

At exactly 22:00, the old electronic clock on the wall turned over its final number.
Once again, I crossed the boundary and switched toward the next world.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-03-five-seconds:title: Sea Line Three: Five Seconds
texts.chapter:heisenberg-03-five-seconds:event:
Time Machine Engineering · Cover Page of the Project Proposal (White Tower Internal Seized Copy):
“Project Code: (omitted).
Chief Engineering Officer Designation: [Chief Engineering Officer’s designation], █████.”
(The blackened ink could still just be made

out under strong light. It belonged to Krennik, later purged. In this seized copy, his partner Heisenberg’s real name had already been erased, leaving only the designation of his post; and in every publicly issued bulletin after Krennik’s fall, the Supreme

Command’s review ultimately completed a double erasure on the historical page. The ink belonging to Krennik disappeared along with its position, leaving only the solitary Chief Engineering Officer Designation.
As if only one person had ever occupied that post.)

The declassified archives of later generations and the recordings Heisenberg left behind underground in his later years together reconstruct the morning when the engineering team first closed a loop with a person inside.

The sunlight was bright. The subject was a young volunteer officer in exceptional physical condition. Before entering the chamber, he deliberately turned around and, through the fully sealed blast-proof glass, gave the outer control area a regulation military salute.

Under the isolation order from the highest level—“Strip everyone else of reporting authority”—all synchronized readings concerning deep neural feedback in the outer hall were cut off. Krennik and the engineering team members could only

wait there, keeping watch over the console with nothing left but a simple progress bar. Heisenberg stood alone on the core data observation corridor, the only place where the underlying port remained activated. Through one-way blast-proof

glass, he watched the subject enter the newly delivered single-person isolation room. It was a concrete death cell filled with lead plates, its inner door-control drive shaft completely entombed in poured concrete. Once locked, it

could never be opened from inside. If the machine ultimately proved to be an impassable dead end, the door would ensure that the subject, together with the physical cause of his death inside the chamber, was sealed inside for good.

The procedure went as rehearsed: constrained by an ordinary person’s extremely small soul-field capacity, the machine could open a maximum time window of only about five seconds. They initiated this brief transit window for an ordinary human subject, then executed the loop closure at the endpoint.

The machine’s startup hum was far weaker than expected. On the hall console, the real-time feedback indicators turned green one after another. When the simple progress bar reached the far right, the external operator pressed the submit key for the loop’s endpoint.

With an exceedingly faint completion pulse, the line representing cortical activity on the monitor dropped to zero at the instant of the fifth second, while heartbeat and respiration stopped in sync. At the physical level, at the endpoint of the chamber’s capacity limit, the local body inside the test chamber became a corpse whose

functions had completely ceased. Only after everything had settled did the maintenance side cut the machine’s power according to procedure. In later bulletins, the regime absurdly whitewashed this body, dead from being unable to withstand the projection load, as “natural deterioration following the smooth separation of consciousness.”

Heisenberg stared at the all-green underlying dashboard. According to the engineering assumption, once the external operator pressed the completion key representing the fifth second, the observation interval was considered successfully closed and locked. The local body’s vital signs fell

silent as scheduled, and the system detected no abnormal overflow of cross-boundary data. The coordinates had arrived, the completion pulse had been sent, and the people in the hall thought that was already the result. Heisenberg grabbed the intercom and told the exterior to lift the

isolation, then walked back to the hall. When the people who had endured the wait outside saw the tension leave his shoulders, the dead silence was instantly drowned by thunderous applause. Krennik slammed his hand onto the table. Someone opened liquor they had been hiding for a long time.

From prototype testing, the engineering team had long known that no projection could ever cross the starting point established at the moment of activation. The machine could not reverse time as a physical principle; it could only insert a probe into another parallel universe currently experiencing the

corresponding starting point, “faking” a return to the past. They had already digested this conclusion of absolute failure. But today, these five seconds were what success looked like to them: using a body left behind locally as an anchor, projecting consciousness to five seconds earlier in another world, to

take over that other clock. Everyone thought that even if this foreign projected consciousness could remain stable on the other side for only five seconds, it was still a successful “parallel landing”; the cross-boundary route promised countless times to the whole of society had at least been opened in concept.
The victory banquet occupied thirty tables in the basement cafeteria.

Heisenberg did not attend the victory banquet. Late that night, when the final long data output from the underlying console had finally printed, he looked at the page and violated the isolation rules for single-person secrecy, secretly pulling Krennik into the data room.

Since their days at the design institute, Krennik had loved using a red pen to circle the decimal points on Heisenberg’s drafts with heavy strokes, picking out the smallest deviations. During those ten years of blueprint work, Heisenberg was responsible for constructing the grand theoretical framework, while Krennik nailed it to the parameters of reality.
The surveillance footage had no sound. On screen, the two of them spread the long printout across the table. Heisenberg glanced at it and froze.

Deep inside the long printout, the green indicator on the real-time dashboard symbolizing “arrival and completion” revealed the true state of the connection. The subject’s probe had not, as the engineering team expected, exhausted its five-second cross-boundary lifespan

in the target world. When the first five seconds ended, the external operator pressed the completion key, the body was declared dead, and the maintenance side finally cut the power, the first-person consciousness projected across had already fallen into an irreversible

vortex. Bound by the iron law that nothing could cross the starting point, the machine’s finite-state instructions could not reach beyond death. They could only forcibly continue into the next brain-compatible body capable of presenting the coordinates of those five seconds.

The delayed-rendered closed curves on the diagram cruelly revealed the sentence awaiting the officer on the other side. The external act of cutting the power only closed the instrument unilaterally in this world; it did not create a “fifth second ending” for the consciousness on the other side.

The officer’s subjective consciousness was continuously handed off between compatible worlds. When the endpoint of the fifth second always connected seamlessly back to the same coordinates in another world, he could not detect the local adjustment. In his subjective experience, there was no option

called “ending.” Old memories blurred and compressed amid the rapid switching, and he was forced to fall into those five seconds of terror again and again. For him, “How many times has the loop repeated?” was no longer a defined question. He was trapped in a dead end that could not end subjectively.

The machine could create a finite state whose beginning and end joined together, yet had inadvertently granted the condemned an infinite sentence. And after everything settled, the system outside still gave only one cold word, because the local living body’s responses had stopped: “stable.”

In the surveillance footage, Heisenberg covered his eyes with the back of his hand. He remembered the fatalist opponents purged as heretics ten years earlier—the ones who had demanded at their trials to know what consciousness could use to fill the void outside the loop if a person

were thrown into the gears of absolutely determined fate. At the time, he had thought those theories were merely weak evasions. But now, this machine had torn open that hollow with its own hands and smashed it into his computational model. For the first time, he felt his heart race.

On screen, Krennik did not see his partner’s movement. He stared at the diagrams for a while, then reached out and tapped one point hard. His lips moved. Reconstructed through lip-reading, what he said at the time was: “The instrument is broken.”

Ten years of sunk costs pressed down behind them. If they could not submit proof of successful regression—the “all-green waveform”—to the higher authorities within the next few days, the Ministry of Internal Affairs would take over the team completely. Krennik stared fixedly at the diagram of the loop folding

back on itself, refusing to accept that this was the physical limit. He locked himself in the machine room and rewrote the underlying parameters, convinced that as long as he replaced the calibration-compensation coefficient for the synchronization track, he could keep the probe’s state from closing end to end.
As long as the external operator did not press the completion key, the waveform could not close. A forced termination could not produce a complete readout they could submit up the chain.
To verify the rewritten underlying parameters three days later, they requested new volunteers from the military. To eliminate individual chance, they ran the second trial, then the third.

The result did not change. The five-second wall was still welded shut. The ring-shaped printout, closed end to end, kept coming out again and again. The dead-knot diagrams from the first three trials covered the table.
On the fourth attempt, when they could no longer request personnel from the military, Krennik proposed at the regular meeting that the next subject had to be an internal engineer.

Only someone who knew what the underlying parameters looked like could, within that five-second loop and during the first few moments before consciousness was completely compressed into blur, use the remnants of autonomous awareness to force a strike at

the most critical data port. The outside did not need him to survive. It only needed him to leave an abnormal peak in one frequency band through a neural signal, proving that the wall could be touched. He looked toward the assistant engineer on his team.

It was Victor, the assistant he had trained by hand and helped check countless decimal points: twenty-five years old. During the countless overnight sessions in the early stages of the project, Victor was always the one who capped Krennik’s used red pen and tidied the drafts scattered across the table. Krennik had not concealed the

closed-loop data from the first three trials. Victor had watched those “dead knots” grow up. In the surveillance footage, when they heard that the external soldiers had been unable to execute the marking command amid the confusion, Victor stood at the other end of the conference table and took the report folder from his teacher’s hands.

Krennik personally fastened the external electrodes onto Victor, his hands trembling so badly he could barely hold the patches. As Victor was pushed through the blast-proof door of the test chamber, which could not be opened from inside, he was still smiling through the glass and giving his teacher

a confirmation gesture, just as he had after checking parameters countless times before. If the rewritten parameters truly offered even the slightest way out, Victor knew he had to break through the instinctive terror before his brain waves blurred and reset, and accurately think of which port it was.
The result did not change. The machine brought back no meaningful marking waveform from Victor. It only ejected the fourth dead knot, closed end to end. Four trials. No survivors.
At the end of the surveillance footage from the fourth trial, Heisenberg and Krennik sat in the data room until dawn. On screen, Victor’s clean corpse was carried out of the hall.
Heisenberg and Krennik kept staring at the diagrams on the table. Not once did either of them turn to look at the young man who had checked data beside them countless times.
All technical terms failed that night. In the internal documents that followed, they chose a neutral word for this death loop with no survivors: “stable.”
The four diagrams were sent upward to the Inner Circle.

In the highest-level approval document preserved to this day, the decision chain is plainly visible. The Leader personally reviewed the original report revealing the “loop with no exit.” Fully aware of the fate awaiting the subjects, he signed his approval in the margin.

The approval consisted of a single thin sheet: continue publicly claiming “successful regression”; and, with the Leader’s handwritten authorization, the concrete isolation room originally used for testing would no longer be responsible

for any machine-maintenance function. It was transferred to the security department to be completely emptied and sealed, becoming a pure white space with no furniture, no tools, and no control authority of any kind, for use as

a special execution facility. The machine, locked by its underlying logic into producing nothing but infinite loops, was simply taken up by the Inner Circle and turned into a hidden execution blade suspended over everyone’s head.
In the signature field of the standardized wording plan, Heisenberg signed his personal designation—a concealed signature bound to the authority of the Chief Engineering Officer.
In his later years, he left one sentence on the tape: “We made up the lie. We set the procedures. We built that White Room.”
Once the hidden violence machine began operating at full speed, the timeline on the public level inevitably began missing its deadlines.

The future promised to the public did not arrive: because an ordinary person’s carrying capacity remained only so large, the window could not grow longer, and the deadline for “the next phase” slipped further back each season. What the laboratories could

deliver grew smaller and smaller. The system had to find something to fill the public’s expectations while completely burying the truth that the machine had effectively become an execution chamber. Someone had to take responsibility for this prolonged failure.

According to declassified memoranda disclosed by later generations, the Inner Circle pushed the list of possible people responsible back and forth across the long table. In the end, the fingers stopped at the second name on the project proposal.

On the morning Krennik was taken away, Heisenberg was in the final assembly workshop. The notice was posted that day, its wording complete: deliberate sabotage, chief internal traitor, infiltrator for many years. The red pen accustomed to circling decimal points on draft paper was sealed in a bag as evidence of “tampering with critical parameters.”

Krennik’s name was heavily painted over on the documents. He became a long-term trial subject used to stabilize public sentiment. As for whether he was actually executed after the prolonged accusations, later records left two entirely contradictory versions.
That morning, Heisenberg did not speak for him.
In the work logs preserved from that time, Heisenberg’s entry for the day was no different from usual. No protest. No resignation. Not one fewer signature on any purge order issued to him.
In an underground recording made many years later, when asked about Krennik’s crimes, Heisenberg left a flat reply:
“I signed the fabricated progress reports he signed. What I signed, he didn’t have time to.”

According to the sealing register of the Inner Circle archives, Heisenberg personally delivered the original fourth long data printout to the deepest archive room before the internal affairs personnel took over the laboratory.
The access-permission field on the catalog card there was unusually short: open only to the two highest authority designations of the time—the Leader and the Chief Engineering Officer.
After the diagram brief was placed inside, Heisenberg signed the depositor’s designation. Along the lower edge of the catalog card, a line of routine wording had been printed in red:
“Core classified file. No destruction date. No declassification date.”
He signed for all of it, then turned and went home. Krennik had been taken away four hours earlier.
That night’s security-monitoring log contained only one brief entry: The Chief Engineering Officer walked through the square. His pace was normal. He did not stop.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-07-burned-files:title: Burning the Archives
texts.chapter:heisenberg-07-burned-files:event: Fragment from The Sermon on Burning the Archives (White Tower Archive):

“Do not hate those papers. Paper is innocent. The despair that lives on paper is what is guilty.
What we burn is not books, but the seeds of bad futures.
With each one burned, we draw one step closer to a good future.
Burn without worry. Burn with mercy.”
(The handwriting is round and steady, without a single correction.)

Spread across the aluminum alloy tabletop were two yellowed files. On the left was the Neighborhood Relief Register from the early days of the old Empire’s collapse. On the right was the subsequent Archive-Burning Execution Order.

The left read “Quota issued.” The right read “Heresy burned.” On both documents, separated by several years, the code signatures ended with the same habitual upward hook. Even the points where the ink had stalled as it spread across the paper were identical.

Between the two documents stretched a collapse that was cold and absurd. In an underground note written fifteen years after Heisenberg’s escape, there was only one fragment without a beginning or an end: “The leader is dead.” He wrote neither the cause of death nor what was to be done next.
