When the obituary claiming that the old leader had died of natural causes was broadcast across every channel, the old system began grinding against itself.

At first, it was only a few neighborhood ration stations that failed to receive their supply trucks. People assumed it was a temporary dispatch error, until the water network also began shutting down by district. Through months of

chaos, the “Shared Observation Group,” which had originally only helped distribute supplies along the streets, effectively seized the city by the throat because it controlled the only remaining flow of food. When the last regular

soldiers maintaining order, hungry themselves, silently leaned their rifles against a wall and joined the long line for relief soup, the organization that had begun in the kitchens officially renamed itself the “Church of Convergence.”

Beside the steaming relief tent, the clerks took the cold physical terms from discarded government progress charts, broke them apart, and boiled them into a pot of hot soup that comforted people. They
preached to the desperate crowd that the good future was something everyone “saw” into existence together—a definition once issued officially by the old White Tower scientists, now taken up without

hesitation by the clerical workers who had failed the old regime’s examinations and competitions. Soup was more clever than a progress chart. Progress charts could miss their deadlines. Soup could not.

As for the leader of the movement, later revered as the “Chief Witness,” the founder of the church had his original name completely discarded in the surviving historical records. No portrait of his face remained.
After taking power, the Church of Convergence lit its first fire to cleanse the traces of the old world beneath the feet of the fatalists, who insisted that “the future had already been written.”

The Church of Convergence burned them to save the world. Its doctrine held that “belief” was “observation,” and that negative observation pulled the world toward the abyss. The fatalists’ books were holes through which the world leaked air. Burning them, killing them together with their books and reducing them to ash, was not the destruction of evidence. It was the removal of the root of the disease.

That was also why the Execution Manual contained no judgment documents for individuals. Once the archive-burning squads had completed their work, they could recite a passage for the dead and leave directly.

During the latter years of the Church of Convergence, we pieced together a record concerning Beattie, an archive-burning executive officer, from piles of old paper. At the time, the safe upper-bound plan for the eight-thousand capacity had not even taken shape, yet this catastrophe had already spread like wildfire. The recorder witnessed an ordinary checkpoint inspection.

The archive-burning squad was searching an underground book cellar. When Beattie, who was in charge of the search, accepted credentials from passersby, he used both hands; when he encountered an elderly person with difficulty walking, he would naturally reach out to steady them.

From the bottom of a passing pipe-repair worker’s bag, Beattie pulled out an old Pipe-Repair Manual, its corner curled. He looked at the manual, then at the hunched worker before him, his face smeared with oil, and showed no suspicion at all.

The worker’s fingers curled slightly inside his sleeve, seemingly preparing by instinct to reach for a wrench, ready to put down several people and retreat into the abandoned pipe network at any moment.
But Beattie closed the manual and returned it to the worker with both hands.
“These books were printed in the old years,”
Beattie looked at the worker, his tone mild.
“According to the rules, most of them should be burned. But yours doesn’t need to be. It teaches people how to repair pipes—repairing pipes is an act that looks ahead.”
He paused, then gave an entirely unguarded smile.
“Friend, we’ve caught a good time. The books printed from now on will only teach people to look ahead.”

The worker took the manual, murmured his thanks, and hurried across the checkpoint. Half a street away, he could still clearly hear the crackle of wood being added to the fire behind him, mixed with steady, peaceful chanting.
The record left no name for the worker. But Beattie’s unbroken calm at the time remained with the ashes.

“He really wanted me to repair those pipes, and he really intended to burn the courtyard behind them to the ground.” This marginal note, written by the informant who had gone undercover, still sent a chill through anyone who read it.

At the same time as that encounter at the checkpoint, among the piles of books Beattie burned was a box containing the underground organization “Conservation’s” original account ledgers. Several days later, the informant responsible for transporting the materials dug a few

small copper binding nails out of the ashes. Only then did Conservation finally confirm that the ledgers had been destroyed. They had recorded the maximum capacity burden this machine might cause, along with pool-position observations from the early days of the catastrophe.

How many volumes had been burned was no longer knowable. When the fire died, the underground organization managed to rescue only a very small number of fragments. The final auxiliary route toward deriving the system’s precise gap was severed there.
It was not until the final years of the Church of Convergence that Heisenberg himself secretly pieced these fragmentary observation charts together with the system’s underlying hardware
parameters. Even then, the missing ledgers kept him from determining the true precise gap. He could only roughly calculate a capacity safety upper bound that guarded against the worst
case—“eight thousand.” In the years that followed, this fallback estimate, forced upon them by the destruction of the evidence, hardened into an execution quota that could not be questioned.
Estelle’s fingers hovered over the terminal screen as she entered this derivation into the archive.

“If even one register had survived, people later on wouldn’t have had to execute against the highest upper bound.” She sighed softly, feeling only the weight of this historical break in the data. In this world, she did not know whom that blind number would claim more than a century later.

But I did.
More than a century later, because no one knew the true gap, everything had to fall back on that execution upper bound. When the annihilation device locked onto Yuna, it terminated the

girl in a single operation, releasing the capacity occupied by ten thousand people.
The surplus anonymous capacity saved no additional worlds, nor did it become any additional people torn apart. It
simply flowed silently back into the soul field, like water with no owner to return to. Yuna gave up her entire life to pay for what may have been nothing more than a grossly inflated number caused

by that great fire.
How many times she died in vain for a burned ledger will remain a question without an answer. It was no longer a gap that could be calculated, but a circuit burned through forever.

In the latter half of the investigation, we searched through the outlying archive shelves once temporarily repurposed by the Church of Convergence. The believers outside heard sermons meant to comfort

them. The copy of the Execution Manual found in the gaps between the shelves was for the archive-burning squads themselves, laying down rules for every detail of searches, inventories, and firebreaks.
Page fifty-one set out the squad members’ leave discipline.

“Anyone who joins the squad may return to the city for one day of rotation leave every ten days. During leave, wearing the squad uniform and carrying fire tools are strictly forbidden. On this day, they may walk only to the following three places:
One, the former grain station.
Two, the dried-up public well platform.
Three, any unmarked grave outside the city.
Upon reaching these three places, they must stop and remain there. No hurried inspection or perfunctory observance.”
Beneath this cold, rigid regulation was an explanation added in Beattie’s own hand:

“Note: This rule is not a compulsory requirement of doctrine. This rule requires you to remember. Remember that if those seeds of bad futures are not burned away completely, people will return to these three places again.”
“The grain station, the dried-up well platform, the unmarked graves of the plague dead.”
Estelle rested her hand lightly on the dry manual. Her fingers curled unconsciously against the edge of the page, the knuckles paling with the pressure.
In the same Execution Manual, page sixty-three set out the disposal procedure after old books had been searched and seized.

“Recently, someone within the squad proposed: before destroying old books, should we first create a register of titles? The names and numbers of the books burned would be entered one by one and retained solely for examination within the church.
The executive officer’s ruling on this proposal is as follows: rejected.

To make a register is to leave seeds behind for heresy. The names of books themselves are dangerous seeds. With a single catalog in hand, following the thread, the entire book can sooner or later be reconstructed.
Burn it completely. Leave not a scrap of paper or a single written word. This is the first iron law of the squad. No one may violate it.”

Estelle crouched down and measured the physical width of the empty shelves, then scraped at the adhesive residue where the labels had been cut away flush with the wood. Everything had been erased completely, as though it had never existed.

Deep in the archive room serving as a chapel was an old instrument that should have stopped long ago. This was not its original location. A line had been drawn up from the lower levels, allowing it to continue running here until today.

Based on the technical materials we had examined in the ruins, this was an additive recorder from the old Empire. It did not store the main text of the ledgers itself, but if the Empire’s core capacity ledger had ever been altered, it would trigger passively and send an anomaly report bearing a digital signature to the distant White Tower.
After the old leader died, as time passed, the world finally reached the legendary thousand-year limit. It was not a rain of fire or an earthquake, but something like an irreversible physical
wearing-down: the old humans began losing the first person, one after another. The cities, machines, and production facilities continued operating, but fewer and fewer voices in the city said “I.”

When all eight billion lights had gone out and no one remained who could say “I,” usable capacity appeared again. Later, the newcomers who were awakened first after the catastrophe, with the system continuing to

execute the overall writing process, dug old-era worship manuals out of the ruins. They rebuilt these rules about gazing and believing, and throughout more than a century of rule, sent someone into this dark room

generation after generation. They carefully checked the instrument’s status indicator, replaced its power supply, and solemnly signed their names in the duty log. They called this work “guarding the holy vessel.”

But when we crouched down and directed the cold beam of our flashlight at the back of the instrument, we discovered that every physical reading interface had been completely welded shut more than a century ago. Roughly melted metal had sealed the local slots into a single dead lump. From outside, the

row of green status indicators on the panel was still visible, proving that it had remained powered and monitoring all this time, but we could not read the monitoring data records from the local side. Only a hardwired line for data transmission remained intact, running toward the distant White Tower.
Whoever left this machine behind wanted it to remain powered, yet absolutely refused to let people of the same era tap into the internal network here.
The metal lump gave off a dead, silent gleam in the flashlight beam.
“We can only record it as a lead for now.” Estelle entered the instrument’s serial number and sighed. “We’ll have to wait until we have clearance to enter the real bottom level of the White Tower.”
I nodded. Until that day came, this sealed recorder would remain silent.

Waiting. At the very end of those pieced-together old pages, he recorded the change the underground organization “Conservation” had been forced to make during those years of frenzied burning. Every time a pile of account ledgers burned in the fires aboveground, another round had to be copied in haste beneath the dim light of the cellar.

There had long since been no scholars among those responsible for copying the books. Those who remained were ordinary underground residents who could barely read. To preserve fragments of the theory and save space, they could only kneel on the damp earth, their entire bodies prone before a low wooden board, copying by weak light until their lumbar spines grew rigid.
That was also the only explanation these nameless people left for readers in later generations. The ink was deep, as though the letters had been traced over again and again.

“The fire outside is large. The paper in our hands is scarce.
We copy slowly.
But we have more patience than the fire.”
texts.chapter:chapter-20-turnover:title: Chapter Twenty: Turning the Page
texts.chapter:chapter-20-turnover:event:text-s:
The morning of the first day in the new world after the sacrifice ended.
I passed through the three mechanical locks around the AI laboratory and returned to the abandoned work area at its deepest point. Without Yuna, the place was quiet enough to make my body tense.

The red authorization lock on the small screen at the side of the external work case beneath the console had gone dark.
In that cold underground chamber, the ten thousand people’s worth of capacity she had given

up had settled the historical debt Heisenberg left behind. All the base resources in the enormous machine that had been frozen by the system’s emergency defenses were now unlocked, which also released the

mechanical latch on this case. The system-level index I had intercepted when she repeatedly dismantled this case in the pure-white room and cracked the access controls with the green light now lay quietly inside.

I lifted the heavy metal lid. Besides the index, technical keys, and nameplate, the case also held nineteen specially made audio tapes. With this index, I could bypass the welded-shut physical interfaces at the disaster-recovery management

station and awaken the deep accident records that had not been overwritten, down in the White Tower.
By the light of my flashlight, I opened the handwritten tape directory and pulled out Lecture Seven: “Turning the Page and the Observer.”
I pressed play. After two bursts of static, a voice younger than any recording I had ever seen came through. It was Heisenberg, teaching a class for young listeners more than a century ago.
“Since childhood, you’ve been told to think of days as a river. Yesterday is upstream, tomorrow downstream, and the water flows in only one direction. That’s not even close to right.

“It’s a book. A book that’s already bound. The multiverse has existed in its entirety for a long time. The machine doesn’t create worlds; it only connects to worlds that already exist. You cross between worlds not because the machine

launches you into another space, but because a person’s attentional weighting can be trained to shift under extreme conditions. When your sensory integration converges on a specific set of details, you can shift your gaze to another page.”

Whispers rose from below. Someone worked up the nerve to ask: When you turn the page, what happens to the body left on the original page? And where does the original “me” on the new page go? Also, if the mechanism is so simple, why can’t any of us do it now?

“The body on the original page stays on the original page. The machine doesn’t overwrite the brain. The only thing that crosses between worlds is the continuous focus of your observation. Because you experienced it yourself, you carry all your memories with you and continue into the equally real version of yourself

on the new page. Before that, the ‘you’ on the new page had its own normal subjective experience, just as you do now. At the moment your focus descends, your attention, carrying its continuous memories, changes its stable receiving subject through the machine’s connection and forcibly takes control of that body.

During this process, the local you isn’t pushed out. His subjective will is temporarily suppressed, but the local brain continues normally recording emotional and bodily tendencies. This isn’t an absorption, and it isn’t the fusion of two people into one. You’re only taking the driver’s seat for a short time.

“Once that focus leaves, the you left on the old page still has his own continuous subjective perspective. Because his brain never truly read your memories from across the cycles, once he regains control,

he’ll only feel as if he has lost a stretch of time. At most, broken dreamlike fragments and indistinct instinctive emotions will remain in his mind. In a stable world, he’ll go on eating and growing old

with those blanks. But in a doomed world, he’ll have to stay behind and face the aftermath alone. You can no longer experience him now. He has become a stranger who shared the first half of his life with you.

“As for why none of you can do it… an unknown world, an arbitrary date, or an ending you wish existed cannot become a reachable address out of nothing. And even if the machine sends back an address from another timeline, the door is still locked. The lock isn’t on the

machine. It’s in the heart of the person looking. Crossing worlds requires absolute sensory acceptance, but human beings, out of the instinct to protect themselves, will personally paste over the bloody pages they can’t bear. They seal them tighter than any algorithm.”

On the way back to the White Tower, the voice from the tape lingered in my mind.
For a long time, because I simply couldn’t bear the thought of a living self being left behind to face the aftermath of losing Yuna, I would

leap from the cliff at dusk again and again, shatter my body first, then continue my consciousness into a new morning. Back then, all that remained in the old worlds were shattered corpses.
But during the countless escapes

that followed, as the deaths accumulated, there were times when I couldn’t even wait for an opening to kill myself. My focus was forcibly severed while I was still conscious. Every time I left alive, I truly left behind

a complete local self in a safe universe. Those living Arnos did not disappear when I withdrew. They still had to wake alone and grow old alone in that peaceful world where the lights-out disaster would never come again.

At four thirty in the afternoon, I sat in the corridor of the White Tower’s calibration area. The work crew was still cutting through the heavy sheet of iron, though that was no longer necessary. Following the facility index I had found in the work case, I connected the mobile

terminal in my hand to the old review interface in the corridor wall.
Over the past several hours, I had used the same method to try connecting a probe to the old interfaces in the disaster-recovery station and the AI laboratory that had not been completely locked down. I was

looking for a possibility.
When a faint but clear hum sounded from the terminal, the screen skipped past a long string of unit numbers and physical-status indicators before stopping on an abnormal fixed blank record: [Epoch Ten, Day 3064, 08:00–08:10: No connection response].

This was the crack in the door between worlds. In the cycle I had not yet known about then—the day we numbered as Chapter Twelve in the diary—when I woke in the corridor of the White Tower’s calibration

area, Yuna was standing beside the external collaboration interface across from me. Between eight and eight ten that morning, a version of me from later on had spoken five sentences to her through my mouth.

That was also why, in my memories, I had no recollection at all of the conversation before eight ten. It wasn’t that I had forgotten. The person controlling the body at the time simply hadn’t been me. All that was left for me were

the few answers she repeated afterward and an instinctive tightness in my chest. But to that “me” who had crossed over from the future, those ten minutes had been visual, olfactory, and bodily sensations he experienced firsthand.
This was more than a cold physical break. As long as those ten minutes had once been experienced firsthand by another “me,” they were no longer an abnormal record without a response,

but a special coordinate etched into the observation system’s underlying parameters.
It was the only “now” in the world that remained here while also belonging to the me from later on.

Since I was one continuous identity with him, the sensations he had experienced should have been hidden in this body’s dormant potential. As long as I remained connected to the underlying cache, I could use the

forced probe I had dug out of the storeroom to keep the interface activated at high power. Then my senses could use this special coordinate to forcibly anchor themselves to the break in the past. I closed my

eyes and recalled the cold light in the calibration area before eight that morning, reached for the smell of her jacket, and tried to force my present sensory perception to lock together with that physical break.

“If observation can be moved across, why can’t any of us do it?”
Heisenberg’s voice from the tape echoed in the depths of my mind.
“Human beings will personally paste over the bloody pages in the first person that they can’t bear.”

I remembered those words. They were not only a metaphor for the students in the lecture. They were also the lock I faced.
But at the instant my senses were about to lock onto the break, just when I could almost make

out the corridor’s outline, a violent physiological resistance erupted in my mind.
My stomach cramped. My heart beat so fast it nearly burst through my ribs, and cold sweat soaked my back. Instinct slammed me back.

After sitting motionless against the wall for nearly fifty minutes, I tried twice more. Each time, I was thrown back into reality at the final moment.
At last, I understood what I was actually afraid of.
As

soon as I continued into that body, once the brief channel reached its limit and closed, the early-morning Arno of eight ten would regain control of his body in the corridor. He would ask Yuna what had just

happened, knowing nothing about what had occurred during those ten minutes. And I, the me of now, would be forced out.
I was afraid that I would go there and see her, only to be kicked back onto this timeline

again no matter how desperately I tried to hold on to something. And the me left behind would carry his shock at those ten minutes, step by step, toward the helplessness of watching her die several hours later.

I don’t know how much time passed. The electric saw at the end of the corridor stopped. The engineers gathered their tools and prepared to leave.
The mobile terminal I had modified with the forced
probe emitted a sharp low-voltage warning. The backup power was nearly depleted under the terrifying power draw, and the identifier for the fixed blank on the screen began to flicker and weaken.
I clenched my teeth and, facing the cramp in my stomach, tried one last time to force my way through the barrier before the power failed.
This time, the barrier still did not break.

Amid the violent churning in my stomach, the instinctive resistance finally slammed me back into the cold corridor.
The terminal let out a shrill, agonized beep and went completely dark. The forced probe had overloaded. The fuse at the base of the

interface blew into a mass that reeked of scorched material, taking the terminal’s mainboard with it.
The engineers had already left the corridor. The wall clock pointed to 5:20 p.m. I was the only one left, leaning against the cold, hard base of the wall.

That path was closed. At least until I got another authorized terminal and a new probe, I could not try again.
The “Arno from later on” who had spoken those five sentences through my mouth that morning at eight was not the me of now. I had not even managed to cross that door.

I left the White Tower. At 3:10 p.m., the lower foundation base had collapsed here. That belonged to the record of the past, when Estelle and I had been trapped in the ruins for several hours. Now, standing in the smoothly operating new world, I

returned to that dark AI laboratory.
I looked at the enormous machine. Yuna’s capacity had settled the debt. The system no longer showed the glaring “Pool available remainder: 0” from before Heisenberg’s death.
In the laboratory, quiet enough to

drive anyone mad, the frustration of the day still gnawed at my bones. When I thought of the five sentences she had heard in that morning corridor—not even spoken to her personally by the me of now—a nearly pathological weakness suddenly seized me.

I actually had a shortcut.
I could retrieve the human-production parameters belonging to her lineage from the Inner Circle production line. As long as I cut off all existing personality-state writes, the base resources released from their frozen state in the system were now enough to make another blank vessel.

I stood before the console, looking at the red button that represented operation.
I would not need to cross any psychological barriers or face those bloody pages of memory again. I only
had to press it, and I would see a breathing body. Reason told me with absolute clarity that even if she had exactly the same face and physiological instincts, she would not be her.

But in a laboratory where no one could stop me, temptation still grew in the dark like poison. Even if it wasn’t her, at least I would no longer have to face an empty room.
A depression of half an inch was all it would take to end all that unbearable emptiness.
My fingertips hovered above the

plastic casing. Once I pressed it, this world would have a Yuna with no past, only a future. She would open her eyes. Maybe she would smile at me. Maybe she would look around the laboratory with curiosity. She would have the face I knew, but no memory of ever standing beneath that violet night sky.

“If I can’t prove that she’s you, I shouldn’t call her by your name.”
Those were the exact words the later Arno had spoken that morning, as Yuna repeated them to me. In the silent laboratory, the sentence suddenly came crashing down.
As if burned, I yanked my hand back. A layer of cold sweat broke out across my back.
If I pressed that button, created a girl who knew nothing, and forced another person’s name and life onto her… how would I be

any different from the machines that erased people as numbers?
I would be filling my own weakness by creating an innocent person.

I drew a deep breath of dusty, cold air and turned toward the work case. What I needed to find was the continuous track that belonged only to her.
The weakness of tonight ended here.
texts.chapter:chapter-20b-left-behind:title: Appendix to Chapter Twenty: Those Who Remained
texts.chapter:chapter-20b-left-behind:event:te:
Personal Review Memorandum (entered at 17:30):
“The ten-minute window for borrowing light on the morning of Yuna’s sacrifice has passed.
Next, I will independently review the abandoned route through the mine’s dry canal.
The review must use the principles I

worked out alone over the previous cycles: recollection is not physical access through equipment, but an extremely dangerous deep dive into the mind, using this brain of mine that retains the experiences of every world. No matter how painful the recollection,

I must not move even one inch of my former self’s body within my mind. Otherwise, the authenticity of that fragment of history will be distorted by my present mental compensation.
I will set a forty-three-minute timer and endure the futility exactly as it was.”

After half past five in the evening, the wind began to strengthen across the wasteland outside the White Tower. At eight this morning, during those ten minutes of borrowed light, I had handed Yuna, who had not yet experienced the fall, the five testimonies proving that I still

had not succeeded.
As for the final, heavy promise defining her identity—“If I can’t prove that was you, then I shouldn’t call her by your name”—I had made it to her myself near the end of those ten minutes. When I said those words to her this morning, their weight finally settled.

Carrying the heaviness of having personally handed her despair, I walked alone to the foot of a broken wall far from the others. In this cycle, without Estelle beside me, I would finally face the abandoned worlds I had thrown away with my own hands.

When I had previously given Estelle an oral account of this section of the archive, I had instinctively used the tone one used for handling discarded code. I lied to myself that as long as I withdrew the focus before 22:00, the ruins in the dry canal would dissolve painlessly into the wind the instant the connection was severed.

But I knew that wasn’t true.
I didn’t dare think about how, during the long dead silence before withdrawal at 22:00, the person frozen at the bottom of the canal was myself, in the flesh. The sensation of dry cold and spasms had been buried deep in my subconscious all along.

I sat down with my back against the stone wall. I had to complete this review before dark.
I took a heavy mechanical timer from my coat pocket and reset the second hand to zero. It was the one Estelle usually used to time equipment warm-up.
“Begin,” I announced quietly as I pressed it with a click.

I closed my eyes and turned inward, slowly spreading open the memory of the old world I had abandoned. I lowered myself back into those forty-three minutes. This was not a return on the machine level, but the forceful

dredging-up of past sensory experience under extreme concentration. When I used my present will to forcibly reproduce every sensory detail from that time, the pain and cold in that body rekindled along with the illusion.
The first instant I fell in, what smashed through my awareness was an icy cold.
The tendons in my calves were twitching uncontrollably, convulsing at the edge of their limit. My knees were driven hard into the rough earth, numb from the pressure long
ago. The early-autumn wind swept along the dry canal bed and rushed down my collar. The nail of my left thumb had split open, foul black mud wedged deep in the crack.

A few hours earlier, the newly exposed earth at the edge of the fissure Yuna had slid into had reeked intensely.
The ancient drainage outlet, still attached to half a stone slab, had been smashed apart completely, along with the lift’s rails, and buried deep. Beneath it lay an old collapsed mine and a maze of underground waterways.

After confirming that no physical equipment could pull her directly up from dozens of meters below, I could only use several rubbed fragments of stone inscriptions to piece together the erased underground restart command for the control console. If I could calculate the correct command, she could still hold out until I came to get her.
I had stood motionless for a long time before that bottomless black fissure, staring at the half of her incomplete footprint left in the mud.
And now, the memory froze at this moment on the canal floor:

A polished wooden tablet lay across my numb knees. Several yellowed rubbings had been haphazardly pressed beneath it, their corners snapping in the cold wind. Four dirt-streaked fingers of my left hand held them down with force.
A blackened stub of charcoal was clenched in my right hand, worn down to a piece no longer than a fingernail. When I squeezed it, the pads of my fingers hurt against it.
The front of the tablet had long since been filled with dense writing. The back was more than half full as well, leaving only a blank space the size of half a palm in the lower right corner.

A charcoal-stained thumb pushed the rubbing beneath it upward by half an inch, fixing its gaze on a broken symbol shaped like a plant.
The wrist moved. A heavy stroke fell into the

blank space on the back of the tablet, trying to piece this half-pattern together with the shape representing flowing water.
It paused for one second, then angrily crossed itself out.

I drew a deep breath, changed the angle, and traced it again.
The wind suddenly stopped for a while. The bottom of the canal fell into dead silence. High above in the distance came the hiss of wind passing through cracks in the stone.
The work in my hands stopped. From inside my filthy coat, I pulled out a crumpled cloth bundle.
I opened it carefully. Inside was half a dry, hard cake—the only food this body had left after the collapse. I lowered my head and took a bite, chewing slowly,
like a machine. When only a quarter remained, the motion stopped. I carefully wrapped the scraps back up and tucked them into the pocket closest to my chest.

I casually wiped the crumbs from my mouth with a worn sleeve and pressed the rubbing down again with my wrist before the wind could carry it away.
In the dead silence of the canal bed, I heard my own hoarse voice.
“Yuna.”

I didn’t raise my head at all when I said the name. My voice was so low it was almost swallowed by the earth. It was an utterly ordinary volume, as if I were simply speaking to someone across a narrow table.
“What does this represent.”
The wind passed through the canal. No one answered.

The cold wind carried down a little fine yellow dust, which landed on the rubbing. I lowered my head and gently blew it away.
I clenched my teeth, forcibly suppressing the impulse to imagine a
response for that self who had stiffened from futility. The moment I imposed my present will on the scene and repaired it into the shape I imagined, this precious record of failure would be ruined.
The character was written once more. Then the black charcoal marks smeared over it again. A splinter stabbed into my palm.

A stronger gale suddenly swept up from the ground. The upper-left corner of the rubbing was violently lifted and flipped over with a slap. My hand loosened instinctively, and the pitifully short charcoal stub slipped free and rattled down toward the gravel-strewn canal bed.

My body immediately went prone and groped through the dust.
The piece of charcoal in reality had clearly fallen beside a sharp stone on the western side, yet my hand remained suspended in midair. If I

used my present muscle memory now and made that hand reach one inch to the left, it would immediately land beside the stone. This subconscious correction would forcibly distort the truth of the memory.

But I clenched my teeth and held fast, letting that former self scrape anxiously through the dry dirt an inch away from the stone like a blind man. Mud filled his fingernails, and white abrasions covered the back of his hand.
At last, feeling blindly, he found the charcoal himself.
He sat back down wearily, wiped the charcoal against trouser legs too dirty to show their color, and clenched it again. This time, he did not stubbornly try to write that character again.

His gaze returned to the lower right corner of the back. He traced the entire outline of that strange character there. Then he drove a heavy question mark beside it.
After drawing the question mark, he stopped and rested the tip of the charcoal against the tablet, counting through the symbols filling the whole surface one by one.

He patiently counted through the entire set once. The ancient command had extremely strict grammar. Most of the characters on the broken stele had flaked away. Using every grammatical rule available, the roots related to water flow and passages could form only these eleven candidates.
“Eleven groups. Every one of them an unfamiliar combination.”

He tucked the wooden tablet filled with all his effort and the fragile rubbings close inside his coat, braced both hands hard against his cold knees, raised his head, and leaned back against the earthen slope behind him.

The deep blue sky of early autumn held not a single cloud. It was 14:43. For the next seven hours or so, I stopped working through the possibilities. Not because I did not want to try, but because those eleven candidate commands were every possibility

there was. I had no way to eliminate any of them from nothing, and no way to verify them without the physical control console. The remaining gaps required new physical stele fragments to fill, and I could not find any at the bottom of the dry canal.
This body, reduced to a quarter of a cake, had reached the end of the abandoned route.

The last sensation left behind when I withdrew from the recollection was those damaged hands: the right index finger blackened with charcoal, four stark white indentations burned deep into the base of the left fingers.
Then I felt the hard, merciless stone tiles beneath me again.

The sound of the wind pulled me back. The mechanical timer beside me ticked. I lowered my head and glanced at it. Exactly forty-three minutes had passed. Of the hundreds of hours I had selected, these were precisely the forty-three minutes before he gave up at 14:43.
I gasped for breath, but the icy cold and the weight of despair remained pressed hard against me. There was no one else here. Only me.

My whole body trembled uncontrollably. Even after those charcoal-stained hands faded from my consciousness, the dead silence of those seven hours continued to press against my present nerves with a terrifying weight. The me in that world had exhausted every clue at 14:43.

The body I had declared to have reached a dead end could only remain alone in the cold wind at the bottom of the mine, endure the remaining seven hours, and wait until 22:00 arrived. Only when the focus shifted would he truly die with those ruins destined to go dark.
My heartbeat gradually settled. I hazily caught hold of the boundary of reality. I suddenly reached for the inner pocket of my coat. There was nothing there. No cloth bundle, no wooden tablet.
Unwilling to accept it, I reached inside again, hard. My fingertips touched only my own rising and falling ribs.
I stiffly raised both hands before my eyes. The pads of my index fingers were perfectly clean. The nail of my thumb was smooth and unbroken. There wasn’t a speck of dust on my hands.
At last, looking at these completely empty hands, I spoke in a hoarse voice. There was no audience. I was only speaking to myself.
“I’m still there.”
The evening wind lifted gravel from the ground and struck it against the broken wall.

I switched on the voice recorder and recorded every detail of those forty-three minutes exactly as it was: the remaining quarter of a cake, the charcoal stub, and the eleven candidate commands written on the back of the wooden tablet.
I sat at the foot of the mottled wall, cold all over, my eyes burning.

“After 14:43, time would continue moving.” I spoke to the cold machine, my voice trembling. “For those seven hours, the me who was left behind, carrying the last of his food, remained in those ruins destined to sink until the world went dark.”
The surroundings were terrifyingly quiet. My gaze fell on the red light blinking on the recorder.

But I had to record this. Because before reaching the dead end, the person left there had not simply fallen all the way down and lain still. Those hands had truly compiled a useless glossary for those eleven hopeless groups of cipher marks.
A long silence settled beneath the broken wall.

I leaned against the wall and lowered my head again. The pads of my index fingers were smooth and unbroken. My palms had not been pierced by splinters, nor marked with black charcoal dust. But I knew that everything had truly happened.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:title: Chapter Twenty, Appendix Two: Not Executed Today
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s2-1: When the evening bells rang, I followed Estelle down into the White Tower’s lower level to avoid the clearing patrols around the settlement outskirts. But once the
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s2-2: heavy reserve gate at the tower’s base locked completely behind us, we were trapped in this exitless lower space. No one would come to open it until the next morning.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s5-1: In the enclosed space, Estelle had claimed a small patch of floor beside the equipment. She spread three blank notebook pages side by side, knelt beside them, and pressed each curled corner flat with her fingertips.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s6-1:
During this time waiting for rescue, I had already told her everything about the forty-three minutes I had spent in the dead end of that dry canal.
About the canal bottom there, the dirt slope, and the eleven groups of
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s6-2: unresolved symbols I had pieced together at the very end. But as I recounted it, the memory began growing on its own inside my mind, producing an entirely groundless subjective intuition—that they were no longer gibberish,
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s6-3: but a list of unregistered dead. I felt that I had recorded the names of twenty-seven dead, and that until the instant before the forced cutoff, I had still been pressing the pencil tip against the wooden tablet to check them.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s8-1: “Your account is full of sensory details, but it also mixes hallucinations from different subjective timelines.” She pulled out a charcoal pencil, its tip suspended over
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s8-2: the paper. “Take those symbols, for example. When describing your forty-three minutes in the dry canal, you clearly admitted that you ‘only had time to count to the
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s8-3:
eleventh group before the cutoff.’ But your intuition now insists that they form a complete list of twenty-seven dead.”
“There’s too much information here. Let’s sort it.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s9-1:
She pressed her wrist down and wrote the headings on the pages in order.
The first: Local certainty.
The second: Other-world assertion.
On the third, she drew a horizontal line through the middle and wrote four words: Confused items.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s11-1:
“I’ll read out one thing, and you point by instinct to where it belongs.” She turned her head and looked straight at me. “Things confirmed to have happened in this world go on the left; experiences that exist only in your account go in the middle.”
“What if
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s11-2:
it belongs on both sides?”
“If you hesitate, or your intuition disagrees with your logic, that means the two experiences have grown together. Put it on the right.” She said it calmly. “I’m only responsible for separating the boundaries of your understanding.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s14-1: The test truly took effect when she read out the first ordinary word.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s16-1: My hand reached toward the page on the left, the one representing local verification.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s17-1: My fingertip touched the paper, but I didn’t immediately pull my hand back.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s19-1: “You pointed to the local record, but you stopped.” She noticed my hesitation at once.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s21-1: “I corrected myself with logic.” I slowly withdrew my hand. “In the local history represented by the first page, I really did stand at that gate. But the instant
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s21-2: you said those words, what came to mind besides the scene of me knocking was something I said to you just now beneath the corridor wall—‘I’m just passing by.’”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s22-1: At the time, I had been sitting with my whole body cold beneath that mottled wall, describing the details of the other world to the Estelle in front of me. That included telling her that I had once said those words outside Yuna’s door.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s23-1: “By instinct, two completely different memories overlapped.” I stared at my hand.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s27-1: “Of the times you stood there in the current world, did you ever tell anyone, ‘I’m just passing by’?”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s30-1: “So saying that sentence exists only in the other-world story you just told me.” She looked up. “When you were telling it, was your throat dry, or normal?”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s31-1: I remembered the choking sensation of that moment, the feeling of sand scraping inside my throat.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s34-1: “Your body remembers the thirst from recounting that story to me, but your logic knows you never said those words at the gate in this world.” She picked up her pencil and wrote “Yuna’s gate” on the third page, the one marked “Confused items.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s37-1: The test continued. She read out several more trivial details, until she reached “the chipped bowl.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s38-1:
“The one for receiving hot soup at the outskirts settlement,” I blurted out.
“The rim had a chip in it,” I said, rubbing the side of my index finger with my right thumb without thinking. “If you weren’t careful while washing it, it would scrape…”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s40-1: I remembered. During those forty-three minutes at the bottom of the dry canal, no one had served hot soup at all. That coarse ceramic bowl with the chipped rim belonged to an earlier abandoned cycle.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s42-1: “I mixed up the memories.” I looked at my thumb. “That didn’t even happen in that dry canal. I’ve mixed in other abandoned worlds from even earlier.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s43-1: Estelle watched me rub my finger. In silence, she picked up her pencil and wrote “the chipped bowl” on the third page.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s44-1: In my residence in the current world, we had never owned a chipped bowl. But in that instant, the sensation of its scraping my thumb had fitted seamlessly into my everyday
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s44-2: understanding. Those habits of movement that did not belong to this world had followed me across the boundary, to the point that I took them for something I used every day.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s47-1: “Last item.” Estelle looked at her record book. “The protest record concerning Elder Sera’s unauthorized operation.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s48-1:
I recalled the scene almost instinctively.
“To leave evidence of that removal appendix and the paradox, you used a procedural loophole to force that entry into your inspection record in front of Sera,” I answered without thinking.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s49-1: The moment the words left my mouth, I realized something was wrong. It had happened, but it had happened on another timeline. In this world, with its own local history, where she sat safely in the sealed room
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s49-2:
beneath the tower, that Estelle who had confronted Sera face-to-face and left that barb in the archive did not exist.
Once again, I had placed old accounts from an earlier cycle onto the Estelle in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s50-1: Estelle looked at me silently. She opened the weekly review record book she carried with her and turned it around on the floor in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s51-1: The book belonging to the current world held a perfectly clean record for today. Not a word of resistance against the higher authorities had been written.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s53-1: “Whichever abandoned world that was, the person who defied an order in front of you for your sake was not me.” She stated it calmly.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s55-1: “I know.” I looked away from her.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s59-1: “Then when you blurted it out just now, why did you call her ‘you’?”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s61-1: “…I know.” I could only repeat those three words.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s64-1: She entered “the protest record concerning the unauthorized operation” on the third page.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s66-1: “That’s enough testing.” She put away her pencil. “In your experience, these boundaries have already blurred. The categories on these three pages are the current state of your understanding.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s67-1: The third page, set apart in its own column, held a long list of details belonging to other worlds. They were seeping into my everyday understanding like invisible sand. If I left it unchecked, sooner or later I would impose a promise from one timeline on someone from another.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s71-1: It was deep into the night. In the sealed room, Estelle slept heavily against the cold equipment.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s72-1: There was less than half an hour before the forced cutoff at 22:00. By the weak light, I pulled a fresh sheet of white paper from the notebook Estelle had left behind and spread it on the floor.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s74-1: I wanted to copy down the symbols I had seen in that dry canal during the day. They were eleven groups of incised marks on a wooden tablet. When recounting them to Estelle, strong sensory interference had briefly made me confuse them with “the names of twenty-seven
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s74-2: dead.” Estelle had placed that subjective intuition in the third column. Now I could only try to set intuition aside and force myself to memorize the shapes of the eleven groups I had copied by hand before the forced cutoff. I remembered it as a kind of muscle memory
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s74-3: attached to the old wooden tablet—the path of that hand moving across the polished wood, the feel of the short charcoal pencil almost slipping from my grip, even the layer of ash from plants rubbed onto the inside of my wrist when I accidentally crossed out a mistake.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s75-1: But when I actually set the pencil tip down on the thin sheet of paper before me, everything was wrong.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s76-1: The process of writing I remembered collapsed instantly on the white paper, with no physical texture to support it. I knew the third stroke should turn, but not which way; I knew the fifth stroke was somewhat shorter than the fourth, but not exactly how much shorter.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s77-1: When I reached the eleventh glyph combination, I stopped for a long time. In that memory from the other world, when I reached this point, I habitually turned over the wooden tablet in my hand and continued writing in the last remaining blank space in the lower right corner of its back.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s78-1: But now, all I had in front of me was a sheet of paper spread flat on the floor. Its texture, thickness, and the logic of turning it over were all wrong. When I tried to make my hand reproduce that process, everything broke apart.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s79-1: I forced myself to continue down the page. When I finished, I stared hard at the crooked marks on the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s80-1: I had no way to confirm whether what I had written was even the same thing.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s81-1: Beside one particularly strange-looking symbol, I unconsciously drew a question mark.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s82-1: The moment I finished drawing it, I froze—as the muscular feedback from my wrist told me that, at the bottom of the canal in that abandoned world, I had once used a charcoal pencil to draw an identical question mark in the same place on the wooden tablet, with exactly the same hesitation in the stroke.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s83-1: The question mark left on the wooden tablet then and the question mark left on this sheet of white paper now overlapped perfectly in their movements. My hand remembered that confusion, but failed to remember the glyph.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s84-1:
Exactly 22:00.
A familiar pressure closed in from all sides, and my vision plunged instantly into darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s87-1: When I opened my eyes again, the dim sealed room, the equipment, and the sheet of white paper marked with a question mark were all gone.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s88-1: Blinding morning lay before me. Eight ten, the fixed arrival point after every forced cutoff. I slapped on the incandescent light in the room. Its glare was bleakly white as day.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s89-1: I stood alone in the room for a while. I had successfully abandoned the self from last night who had stared hard at waste paper, unable to write the names of the dead, and escaped into an entirely new coordinate.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s91-1: At 8:15, footsteps sounded in the corridor outside.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s92-1:
“Knock, knock, knock.”
Three knocks sounded on the door.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s93-1: This was the search that inevitably came after my absence from the morning eight-o’clock weekly review. At this moment in this timeline, the recorder Estelle had come to check on me because of my absence knew nothing about the cross-world departure I had just experienced.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s97-1: I took a deep breath and opened the door.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s98-1: Estelle from the new world stood outside in the morning sunlight.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s100-1: “You missed the weekly review.” She looked at me. “Elder Sera sent me to see whether you were sick.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s102-1: “Estelle, I…” I looked at her unclouded face, but did not say the words “I’m sorry.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s103-1: My gaze fell on the perfectly clean notebook in her hand. If I told her about the memories from that timeline at this moment, she would surely understand that situation. But I knew that the person who had paid the price was not her.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s105-1: “What are you staring at my notebook for?” She noticed something was wrong.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s107-1: “…Nothing.” I looked away from her and forced myself into a dry statement of facts. “I only wanted to report one anomaly. In the forty-three-minute ruin of that other world, I committed eleven groups of
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s107-2: symbols representing unregistered dead to memory—without addressing whether that classification is accurate. But after returning here, I lost the tactile support, and I can’t copy down a single group.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s109-1: “Without a physical object, I can only record that as a subjective assertion until local evidence is established.” She opened the notebook and raised her pen. “Are there any other anomalies?”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s112-1:
I stood in the doorway.
“In the story of another world, a version of you confronted Sera in front of her in order to leave an unsealing stub on that restriction appendix. Because
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s112-2: of it, when you tried to stop them from restarting the shutdown procedure, Sera immediately stripped you of your qualification to witness the shutdown as a recorder, citing that
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s112-3: violation as the reason. Under the Church’s control at the time, losing that qualification meant you weren’t even allowed to find a safe bed in the lower level of the White Tower.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s113-1:
I paused.
“So… this wasn’t only about leaving a barb in your inspection record. It was the prelude to your losing everything for your principles.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s117-1: Estelle lowered her head and looked at the perfectly clean notebook in her hand, the one belonging to this morning.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s119-1: “If the person in that story really existed, she would certainly pay a price for that act,” she said calmly. “But I’m not the one carrying that blemish on her record. I didn’t do it.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s123-1: “When you opened the door just now, were you asking a complete stranger for an ‘It’s all right’?”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s124-1: The humiliation of being seen through so precisely left me unable to speak. My fingers tightened around the doorframe.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s130-1: “Add one rule to the first page of today’s record.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s131-1: She gave me a cold look and reopened the notebook.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s135-1: “As long as I haven’t used my hallucinations as an excuse to manipulate you, or pushed the guilt of avoiding reality onto you so you can wash it away…”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s137-1: “Under the date, write: No boundary crossed today. If I cross the line at any point, cross it out in front of me.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s138-1: The tip of her pen stopped on the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s140-1: “If you hadn’t swallowed it just now, I would cross this line out as soon as I wrote it.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s143-1:
She looked at me. Beneath the date on the newest page of her notebook, she wrote in firm strokes:
No boundary crossed today.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s147-1: “I will not forgive you on behalf of any self I don’t know.”
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s148-1: She firmly tucked the charcoal pencil back into the spine of the notebook.
texts.chapter:v15-20c:event:text-s150-1: “Come on. Go to the weekly review.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:title: Appendix Three to Chapter Twenty: Ten Minutes
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s3-1: We followed the pipeline district back into this sheltered corridor. During the interval for the weekly review, Estelle brought over a stack of casualty records transcribed from the Disciplinary Court.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s4-1: Twenty-seven rough scraps of paper were gradually spread across the concrete floor in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s5-1: In the memory from the previous few rounds, I had seen casualty steles carved with symbols outside the mine. They bore twenty-seven names, corresponding to eleven groups of symbols. To confirm that
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s5-2: conjecture, I had Estelle search the archives for every record of a violent death at a site where a “demon mark” had been found. We counted them one by one, until the last scrap touched the floor.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s7-1: At the top of each sheet, I copied out one victim’s true name: Ian, Old Hans, Martha from the ration station… Beside each name was the precise cause of death recorded in the new language. Beneath those two lines, I had drawn the old-language symbols from the case records.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s8-1: The records from past years said that when these people died horribly near the equipment, the machine involved would often have its terminal eject a metal tag printed in the old language.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s8-2: The villagers couldn’t read it. They thought it was the demon mark that had taken their lives, so they drove it into the place of death. Later, the Disciplinary Court rubbed every one of them
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s8-3: for its archives as dangerous objects of heresy. Now, at last, I had matched these twenty-seven specific people to the abnormal rubbings generated by the machines when they died, one by one.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s9-1: In the abandoned memory from the previous few rounds, the version of me who had fallen into the dry canal had mistaken these eleven groups of symbols for some kind of phonetic command capable of restarting the lift, repeatedly rearranging them in
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s9-2: his mind according to every pronunciation pattern he could think of for several hours. He had not deciphered a single word, but his obsession with those repeated calculations, along with that starving, freezing body, had been burned into the memory.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s10-1: I wanted to close my eyes and dig deeper into that long-solidified memory, drag out the process of phonetic analysis he had carried out in his mind, and see whether I could find a pattern for breaking it down.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s13-1: When my consciousness forcibly tried to retrace that afternoon in early autumn, I found the memory violently blocked.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s14-1: The forced calculations from those few hours were fused to the long process of waiting to die after he stopped at 14:43. The moment my mind immersed itself in his thoughts, the entire web of pain yanked tight. The
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s14-2: agony of the fall, the hunger of a cramping stomach, the knife-cutting chill of the autumn wind, and the suffocation of clamping my mouth shut as the patrol car passed overhead all crashed into me without restraint.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s15-1: The version of him in the memory had endured more than seven hours beneath that deep blue sky on nothing but the hope that, if he could hold out until the 22:00 handover, he would be free. But I knew, with full clarity, that the handover really would happen—and that he could not leave with it.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s16-1: That enormous disparity twisted together with the suffocation of the body and severed the recollection just before I reached the specific reasoning process.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s17-1: When I snapped my eyes open, I was already sliding down the wall to sit on the floor, gasping for breath, my fingernails digging hard into the corridor floor. Cold sweat soaked through my back.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s18-1:
Estelle calmly watched the metal timer in her hand.
“Eleven minutes,” she reported, then walked over and handed me half a flask of water. “The physical backlash from forcibly immersing yourself was more severe than expected. You need to stop and recover for a while.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s21-1: She put away the timer and took out the blank record book. She did not hurry me.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s22-1: I sat on the cold floor for a long time, took two gulps from the flask, and waited until the pressure in my lungs, as if they were about to burst, gradually receded. I pressed down on my knee, my fingertips still trembling involuntarily, and spoke through my dry throat.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s24-1: “No need to recover. I can’t retrace his thought process.” I wiped the sweat from my chin with the back of my hand. “The moment I try to return to that state, the despair in the dry canal cuts off my consciousness. That route is impossible.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s27-1: Estelle nodded and opened the record book.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s28-1: I braced myself against the wall and sat upright, looking at the twenty-seven sheets covered in symbols before me. Since I couldn’t extract the reasoning process from my mind and use it, I could only start directly with the rubbings from these records.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s29-1: I bent down and sorted the twenty-seven sheets by the similarity of the symbols on them, pulling them apart one by one and gathering them into piles. Identical ones went together; those with slight differences were set aside separately.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s30-1: In the end, the sheets on the floor had been divided into exactly eleven piles.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s31-1: “The names of the twenty-seven casualties on the steles outside the mine were each carved beneath one of these eleven groups of symbols.” I pointed at the sorted piles on the floor. The two matched with astonishing precision.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s31-2: “This is what trapped me back then. The person who spent several hours reasoning in the dry canal never decoded it, but he had already eliminated the biggest wrong turn through failure: trying to solve it phonetically.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s32-1: I pulled one sheet from each of two different piles and placed them side by side. “Look at the left halves of these two symbols. Their outlines are identical, but the right halves are completely different. They’re all
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s32-2: rigid, modular assemblies—no roots, no inflections, like standardized screws and nuts forced together. That’s why he could think himself raw at the bottom of the canal and still find no pronunciation pattern. This isn’t
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s32-3: phonetic writing that can be read according to an alphabet. To work backward from the meanings of these modules, we need to find their sources, with new-language annotations, in the diagrams of the surviving equipment.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s33-1: Estelle switched on her flashlight. The beam fell across the row of sheets.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s35-1: “So without the legend, all you can do is blindly guess at this pile of dead writing?”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s37-1: My gaze passed over the symbols.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s39-1: “Not blindly.” I rubbed my numb fingers. “The ration list you copied in the square just now, and the equipment fragment you traced from the abandoned bulletin board, are our dictionary.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s42-1: Estelle did not ask anything further. She pulled two sheets from beneath her clipboard and spread them flat on the ground. One was the ration list; the other was a scrap bearing a wireframe equipment diagram.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s44-1: “I’ve looked at these two sheets.” She pointed with the tip of her pen at several discharge ports in the wireframe, then at the headers on the ration list. “Look at the list—the new language’s ‘nutrient paste’ retains the old language’s
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s44-2: official classification symbol beside it. Several old-language labels on the diagram also have new-language annotations. As long as we match them against the causes of death in the records… I’ll verify the symbol positions. You translate them.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s45-1: My eyes moved between the two sheets, and my mind began recalling the version of me who had reasoned it out in the dry canal.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s46-1: First I pulled out the eight sheets for those who had fallen from the water tower. According to the casualty records, all eight had fallen into the main waste pipe below while climbing the outer wall of the water tower, been
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s46-2: shredded by the turbine blades, and discharged through Waste Outlet No. 2. Beside their mangled remains, the terminals had all ejected the same metal tag—with a long string of symbols resembling a bent corner printed at the end.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s47-1: When I looked back at Estelle’s engineering diagram, that bent-corner symbol was clearly marked on the structural lines of Waste Valve No. 2. Beside it, someone in the past had casually annotated four new-language characters: Abnormal discharge.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s48-1: Next came the sheets for those who had starved to death outside the ration station. The casualty records said they had been killed by reduced quotas for “idleness.” These rubbings had not been ejected automatically. After the bodies were taken away by the collection team, the duty cleric would go to the abandoned printing station and press a few buttons, producing a tag to nail to the wall.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s49-1: Beneath the names of those who had starved, I drew a gear-like mark.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s50-1: The mark was identical to the old-language classification symbol beside “nutrient paste” on the ration list, the one representing the category of supplies. Beside the classification symbol
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s50-2: was a hollow circle representing the number “0.” What the cleric had printed afterward was only the inventory record from the back end. Its literal meaning was inventory cleared to zero.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s51-1: “They didn’t die from exhausted quotas. The ration station had run out of nutrient paste.” I looked at the list. “The system recorded the inventory as zero, but the records say their quotas were reduced because of ‘idleness.’”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s53-1: “The legend on the waste valve, the classification symbol on the materials report…” She looked at the sheets I had sorted across the floor. “Whether these tags were ejected automatically by machines or printed afterward by people, they weren’t memorials for the dead at all. They were all equipment status codes generated by the system.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s54-1: “Exactly. That’s the whole picture from the machine’s perspective. Now look at this one.” I pulled a sheet from the last pile. “The records say this person was caught in Bellows No. 2 and crushed to death.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s55-1:
I held the sheet up to the flashlight. A short string of triangular symbols ran through its middle.
Following the structural lines of Bellows No. 2 on the diagram, we found the same symbol beside the motor housing. It was marked next to a black-and-white malfunction indicator light, with the old-language annotation “Jam.”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s56-1: From the engineering knowledge of the old world buried deep in my mind, I recognized the word. In maintenance terminology, “Jam” meant that something had become stuck. Following that rigid industrial mapping logic, I read out its meaning:
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s58-1: A chill crawled up my spine. When a person was crushed into a mass of flesh, the system’s diagnostic report recorded it only as a foreign object obstructing the rotation of a component.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s61-1: Estelle looked at the sheets on the floor, her pen hovering over the register for a long time. Even without knowing the old language, she could understand the logic behind those three words. Her hand seemed somewhat stiff as she began to write.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s63-1: “If those three kinds of codes you just translated are the entire range of recording dimensions, then that means…” She looked at me, her voice softening. “In this pre-civilization system, there wasn’t actually a dedicated field for recording personnel casualties, was there?”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s66-1: My hand clenched hard, crumpling the sheet I held. If life and death could only be reduced in the system to valve abnormalities or motor jams…
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s67-1: “If that’s really the case…” She paused. “Then that Yuna you mentioned while comparing the names in the records archive… if she, too, was ultimately taken by these machines, would the system’s final record of her also be something like this?”
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s68-1: I had to see for myself how the machine had labeled her back then.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s69-1: I forced my fingers to loosen and picked up the pen beside me.
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s71-1: “There are still eight unknown code groups.” I stared at the rubbings covering the floor. “We’ll match the remaining causes of death against the diagrams one by one and complete the error-code dictionary. As long as we can find the physical interface of the bottom-level terminal—the
texts.chapter:v15-20d:event:text-s71-2: original cabinet that once generated these abnormal metal tags—we can enter these eleven groups of codes and query them one at a time. Only by obtaining the original data corresponding to her will we be able to understand what she actually went through. We’ll finish the calculation.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:title: Chapter Twenty, Appendix Four: Three Columns
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s2-1: The light in the corridor began to slant westward.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s3-1: Estelle spread the record book belonging to this world across her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s5-1: I sat against the wall. Across the floor in front of me lay the rubbings of the twenty-seven casualty reports. Beside me were a basic universal dictionary, a book of accident bulletins, and a copy of the White Tower Storage Room Spatial Index that Estelle had just brought from the outer hall.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s6-1: After nearly half an hour, we had finally matched the remaining eight groups of old-language symbols with all the maintenance records in the bulletin book. Those who had their arms mangled
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s6-2: in the bellows were translated at the system’s lowest level as “foreign object obstruction in valve.” Those who fell into the sewage pipes were recorded merely as “filter blockage warning.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s7-1: I pushed aside the last sheet bearing its corresponding result and rubbed my dry, sore eyes. There were no miracles. They were all rigid hardware fault codes. Twenty-seven rubbings, twenty-seven horrific ways to die—yet in the eyes of this system, they were merely twenty-seven identical lines of maintenance data.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s8-1: My shoulders sagged. My entire back pressed against the cold wall as a powerful fatigue washed over my nerves.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s9-1: In reality, Estelle was sitting quietly beside me.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s12-1: “You’re in poor condition.” She noticed something was wrong with me at once. Under the standard support procedure, after observing this kind of stress response, she was supposed to give me twenty minutes of psychological recovery time.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s13-1: I had refused this procedure before, but this time she didn’t ask me. Instead, she closed the record book and set it to one side.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s14-1: “This is now an unrecorded period,” she said softly.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s16-1: “Thank you.” I took a deep breath and picked up a blank sheet of paper. I divided the page into three columns with straight lines.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s17-1: “The left column is the equipment status code, the middle is the time of occurrence, and the right is the physical coordinate inside the White Tower,” I said.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s19-1: I tapped the twenty-seven rubbings on the floor with my pen. “Some of these status slips were produced by abandoned printing stations. Others were automatically expelled during discharge accidents. The village
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s19-2: terminals obviously can’t read the White Tower’s core archives. But these peripheral errors could not only be printed at the terminals; they also left physical maintenance records in your bulletin book. That means
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s19-3: the data link between here and the White Tower core is intact, and that the system forcibly archives changes in low-level status. So there must be a master log channel capable of collecting all network errors.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s21-1: “But that depends on one premise: that you’re certain there will be an error.” Estelle looked at me. Unable to call on the memories of counterparts
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s21-2: in other worlds, she cautiously fell back on an inference based on the facts at hand. “Going by the details you described, in this world, that
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s21-3: girl never approached the machine at all. There’s no local record of her operating it. How do you intend to find her snapshot in a blank space?”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s23-1: “Because that wasn’t a routine terminal operation.” I pointed to the old-language dictionary beside me. “But I overlooked something earlier. We’ve always treated that live disassembly as an isolated ‘event.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s23-2: ’ But at the system’s lowest level, every facility in the village is mounted on the same coherent architecture running through all worlds. The machine in the other world disintegrated because of the sacrifice.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s23-3: That enormous physical energy had nowhere to go, so like water surging back through a pipe, it traveled along this shared coherent network and struck the local networks of every branch world without
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s23-4: distinction. When the local physical network endured that tremendous parameter shock, it might not have seen who caused it, but the master log channel would absolutely catch an anomaly at the system level.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s24-1: My fingertips pressed hard against a line of small print in the dictionary’s appendix. It was one of the dozens of fault codes we had just identified. “‘System
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s24-2: anomaly suspended: unknown impact,’ error code SYS-ERR-09. Whatever caused it, this code must appear in the master log. That’s the input for the left column.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s25-1: I looked up at Estelle. “The time in the middle column—the starting point at which the system captured the impact—was after 19:50 in that world. According to the dictionary, impacts of this kind are saved in multiple time segments.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s25-2: As long as we know the grid-conversion rules for storing the master log’s physical snapshots, we can calculate the specific coordinate for this system anomaly code in the 19:50 time segment. That gives us the right column.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s27-1: Estelle opened the thick White Tower Storage Room Spatial Index. It was the public material available to her, filled with algorithms that automatically mapped the White Tower’s master logs to the physical grid according to error type and time of occurrence.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s28-1: “According to the public mapping protocol…” Her gaze moved along the tables on the page. “Status code SYS-ERR-09 belongs to the hardware suspension class, so the system always routes it to Row 02. Sub-item 09 divided by the
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s28-2: fixed capacity of each slot is 4, with a remainder of 1. Under the algorithm, the quotient determines the physical grid number, so it falls in Slot 04. The remainder of 1 indicates that the slot’s backup volume was activated.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s29-1: The row and slot were determined. Her finger continued moving to the right.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s30-1: “The timestamp is calculated by advancing through the calendar. The month opened in this cycle—the tenth month of the year—the fourteenth day—automatically assigns all anomaly records to Volume
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s30-2: 10.” She looked at the time I had given her. “At 19:50, in this month’s physical pagination formula, the input is the fourteen days already elapsed this month multiplied by 1,440 minutes, plus the
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s30-3: 1,190 minutes elapsed that day. Dividing that by the rack’s constant, 130, then converting the quotient into a row number and volume sequence… ultimately, it will be written on Page 09, Row 20.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s33-1: We entered this sequence of numbers in the right column. It was an absolute physical coordinate.
