texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s35-1: I stared at those four numbers. Yuna had never existed in this world, and the sacrifice had not taken place in this White Tower.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s36-1: But if the live disassembly in that world had truly been transmitted through the physical network, its system snapshot was lying quietly in that grid.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s37-1: “But with your current authorization, you still can’t cross between sections and retrieve this master-log volume from Row 02, right?” I asked.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s39-1: “My authorization only lets me consult my own attachments.” Estelle looked at the coordinates. “Besides, this is only a hypothesis you derived from the algorithm—even if the network impact really caused an error code to light up there and a snapshot to be stored, it wouldn’t be Yuna’s personality.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s40-1: “I know.” I clenched my fists. “But it’s the only trace that she truly existed and impacted this world.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s41-1: She raised her head. I realized that simply helping me reason out this anomalous coordinate already constituted a kind of overstepping for her.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s42-1: “I’ll use my public-layer authorization to submit a retrieval request to that controlled section for you,” she said calmly. “Since I’m not authorized to view the core archive, the door will never open,
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s42-2: and I won’t be able to retrieve the snapshot. But when the system receives the request and indexes that physical address, if the archive exists, the access light corresponding to that address outside the
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s42-3: door will turn green with an ‘occupied’ response. If it’s only a block of empty data, the light will flash red with a ‘vacant’ response. As for whether it can give you the answer you want… that comes later.”
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s44-1: I looked at her. The deduction from those twenty-seven samples was cold to the bone, yet she offered no further words to remind me of its cruelty.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s45-1: “I’ll submit the retrieval request now,” she said.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s47-1: I don’t know how much time passed. Then, with the faintest buzz of a relay, a weak green light came on at the end of the corridor.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s48-1: Only after we confirmed that it was indeed the green “occupied” response did she gather up the scattered sheets. The statutory twenty-minute unrecorded buffer period should have ended long ago. She could have reopened the record book at any time.
texts.chapter:v15-20e:event:text-s51-1: The light in the corridor faded completely. In the darkness that descended, neither of us spoke again. But this time, I was no longer alone, held back from the door by permissions I could never get past.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:title: Sea Line Seven Extra Chapter: Not Written by Me
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s2-1: Later generations found a damaged portable tape in the ruins of the White Tower, along with dozens of cards sorted by timestamp and marked with fluorescent comparison records. These physical relics, which Heisenberg had once clutched tightly to his chest and carried into the abandoned mine tunnels, recorded an exceedingly strange beginning.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s4-1: That year, after losing a power struggle, Heisenberg was demoted from his position as the Empire’s chief engineering officer and placed under Lysenko’s authority.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s5-1: Judging from the surviving Security Bureau surveillance records, the former chief engineering officer—reduced in the archives to nothing more than an employee number—appeared perfectly normal on the surface.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s5-2: He clocked in on time, signed off on lengthy engineering orders, sat silent in the corner during regular meetings, and even wrote a routine report on cooling-pipe modifications with meticulous thoroughness.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s6-1: But this mundane routine was broken by an extremely minor physical anomaly.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s8-1: He sat in the most remote corner of the laboratory, a fountain pen between his fingers, preparing to sign a routine inspection checklist. He lowered his head, and his eyes had just settled on the signature line.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s9-1: There was no violent dizziness, no blurring of vision, not even a one-microsecond hitch in the monotonous hum of the central air-conditioning beside his ear. Only the slightest hesitation. As if an old strip of film in a projector had silently skipped a frame. The image remained continuous. All his senses were normal.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s10-1: But when his eyes refocused, he found that his right hand was not hovering above the checklist at all. His wrist was pressed against the paper, the muscles in his forearm faintly aching with the physiological tension left
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s10-2: behind by intense writing. Following his wrist with his eyes, he saw that the tip of his pen had stopped on a blank sheet beside the checklist. The ink had not even fully dried. Two lines had appeared on the paper from nowhere.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s14-1: The handwriting was his own. He stared at the two lines. His first action was to raise his wrist and check the time.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s15-1: Less than ten seconds had passed since the instant he remembered preparing to sign. He extended his index finger and touched the final stroke of the character “go.” The ink blurred slightly along the edge of his fingertip. The writing had just been made. Those five seconds of time were as if they had been cut out.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s18-1: As a top physicist who had built a time machine, the first thought that came to his mind was, naturally enough, dissociative reaction, drug interference, or a frame-up by the Security Bureau.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s19-1: The “0.04” on the paper filled him with a deep chill—it was the distinctive phase deviation caused by wear on the local prototype’s main shaft, a parameter known to only one person in the world: him. But that was not enough to rule out a dissociative reaction. His subconscious could write down data he already knew.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s20-1: It was only over the following months, when he experienced several more brief episodes of lost time, that the situation changed. Besides writing down low-level formula variables known only to him, on one occasion he even wrote down
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s20-2: “the acoustic resonance frequency of the walls in the West Wing’s new interrogation room.” He had secretly tested it on-site with a miniature acoustic instrument. The extremely obscure decimal value was accurate to the last fraction.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s21-1: The 0.04 was a low-level parameter known to his subconscious but impossible for the Security Bureau to understand; the resonance frequency of the new interrogation room, however, was data he had never encountered and his brain could not have fabricated from nothing. These two sets of physical
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s21-2: evidence formed two successive gates, sealing off every conventional explanation: they ruled out subconscious hallucinations caused by his own nervous exhaustion, and completely ruled out a hybrid frame-up in which the Security Bureau first implanted the data and then induced him to write it himself.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s22-1: The handwriting on the paper pointed clearly to only one conclusion: an entity that understood the machine’s underlying mechanisms and had physically visited the newly built interrogation room was crossing time to borrow his wrist and write. And each projection’s connection window was locked to the physical limit of five seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s23-1: There was only one person in the world who could satisfy all these conditions and possess this handwriting.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s25-1: He alerted no one. He turned himself into a tireless collector.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s27-1: He went to an abandoned warehouse and dug out an old portable tape recorder. To prepare for the five seconds that might descend at any moment, he replaced its batteries with miniature ones, unsoldered the microphone wiring, and stitched it into the
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s27-2: collar of his lab coat, close to his jaw. He removed every button that made a sound and connected it to an extremely sensitive voice-activation module—the recording would start as soon as the sound from his throat rose above the ambient noise floor.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s28-1: Whether he was eating in the cafeteria, pacing the corridors, or sleeping, a fountain pen with its cap removed was always tucked into the pocket over his chest. He placed blank cards at the corners of his desk, on either side of his pillow, and along the edge of the washbasin.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s28-2: He drew a fluorescent line across the back of his hand. Whenever his wrist was at rest, he deliberately kept it against the ruler markings along the desk’s edge, ensuring that any unconscious movement of his arm during lost time would leave evidence of coordinate deviation.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s29-1: At first, he stood cards on his desk asking, “Date of arrest? Location?” But what he received in return was usually the visitor’s brief, bewildered gasp upon seeing the question, followed by the exhaustion of the five seconds. He
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s29-2: soon understood that instead of constraining the visitor with questions, it was better to set out an extremely simple prompt. Later, he stood a card beside the tape recorder that never changed: “Speak. Say only what matters most.”
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s30-1: But these arrivals were not the only ones. When locating a target, the machine could evidently connect to many historical branches compatible with the local one.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s33-1: At first, what he waited for was utterly chaotic noise.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s34-1: The tapes contained voices repeatedly shrieking warnings. Most maddening of all were the fragments that contradicted one another. Because these messages came from many historical branches, he had once recorded two entirely different
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s34-2: dates of arrest on the same card. One card read, “Go south. Take the ventilation duct,” while another read, “There’s an ambush to the south. Find the power room.” They tore into and destroyed one another, yielding no path to survival.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s35-1: Then, after several months of lying low, another-history Heisenberg briefly anchored in the office. In the first second after opening his eyes, he saw a prompt card and the fluorescent reference line on the back of his hand. Another Heisenberg,
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s35-2: borrowing a body from a dead end, could quickly understand that he was cooperating with a receiving end that had established a coordinate system. Without branch labels, they had to find the common points where all the historical lines converged.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s36-1: After that, the visitors who arrived made a prompt decision to use their scant time to pass along concrete pieces of the puzzle, their handwriting often degenerating into dragged, frantic scrawl as time ran out:
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s37-1:
“Forget the charges! Find the common preconditions!”
“Work backward from the execution date! Find the point where the net closes!”
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s41-1: In the office late at night, Heisenberg spread the cards and transcriptions he had accumulated over the past few months across the floor. Knowing how lax the security watch was, he understood that the late-night cameras were merely mechanically rolling footage into a loop. No agent would be watching a powerless nobody in real time.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s42-1: He divided the bloody, indistinct fragments into two piles.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s43-1: The first consisted of physical evidence establishing a baseline—the 0.04 phase error and the private acoustic frequency. The physical ink on these papers, combined with the blank space in the local
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s43-2: operation logs, established an irrefutable boundary: every hallucination and frame-up had been ruled out. The consciousnesses projected through the machine were leaving real traces in this office.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s44-1: The second consisted of the common ending described by multiple visitors. In recordings filled with extreme oppression and violent breathing, they all mentioned the same final outcome without exception: arrest, followed by being sent somewhere impossible to escape.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s45-1: Those dead-end samples converged on a single point. From the contradictory dates and landmarks, he crossed out one mutually exclusive option after another: if the arrest occurred on the thirteenth, there would be no charge involving the shutdown of the cooling unit; if it occurred on Tuesday, there would be no plainclothes
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s45-2: officers setting up a checkpoint at the south gate. After cross-comparison stripped away every branch-specific variable, the only common clue left was that on every timeline, his advanced lower-level control access had been completely revoked before his arrest. This was the Security Bureau’s mandatory step before an operation.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s46-1: He raised his head and looked at the office, already half emptied. His access was being revoked step by step, and Lysenko had replaced him as chief engineering officer. That same afternoon, a photocopy addressed to Lysenko was delivered to his desk. He recognized the official seal.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s47-1: It was the final approval to transfer the underlying facilities budget to the Security Bureau. The convergent precondition derived from every branch—the complete severing of his access—was attached to this document.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s48-1: Once the budget was transferred, the shelter system’s advanced control privileges would undergo their final physical circuit cut at 23:00 on the night the approval was issued. After that moment, the access in his hands would be completely revoked, and the blast door leading to the abandoned underground mine tunnels would be closed to him forever.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s49-1: From the moment the approval document arrived, he entered the final countdown of his life. Less than six hours remained until 23:00 that night. But he could not leave immediately. The
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s49-2: corridors were full of Security Bureau plainclothes agents during the day. He had to wait. He sat in the office, listening to the second hand circle closer and closer to the final outcome.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s50-1: The 22:45 night-shift handover was the weak point during the security rotation, and the final window before his identification card was frozen.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s51-1: When the night-shift handover bell came from the corridor, he slowly pulled open the drawer, carefully folded the timetable he had spent months calculating, and slipped it into his pocket against his underwear.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s52-1: He packed the tape recorder and cards into an engineering canvas bag, opened the door, and walked into the corridor’s ghastly white light. It was the final fifteen minutes before the Security Bureau took full control. The footsteps of a squad of officers had just receded around the corner.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s53-1: During the first stage of that night, he did not need to force open any doors. He was still the head of the underlying laboratory, and the identification card on his chest glowed with a faint green light. He walked past the familiar duty station, nodded to the drowsing guard, and swiped through the first and second blast gates without obstruction.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s54-1: But he was not heading for the main entrance. He was going to the deepest part of the shelter. The only blind spot not covered by surveillance was the ventilation shaft behind the detention area, leading directly to the abandoned underground mine tunnels.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s55-1: He stopped before the control console on the lowest level and looked through the glass at the dozens of political prisoners behind the door, tortured until they were gaunt and skeletal. They had once been young people from every part of the Empire. Now they had been reduced to bloodstained bodies wrapped in scraps of cold-weather suits.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s56-1: To pass through the detention area and enter the ventilation shaft, he had to open the heavy isolation gate. The moment the gate opened, a full-spectrum alarm would spread through the entire shelter, and the armed guards stationed at the stairwell would seal off this forty-meter corridor within thirty seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s57-1: He could cut the lights, but the backup power would take over within three seconds; he could damage the access controls, but that would only delay the guards’ entry into the detention area, not erase the infrared trail he
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s57-2: would leave while running outside the surveillance blind spot. Against a rapid-response unit in full combat gear and equipped with thermal-imaging tracking, unarmed, he could not cross the forty meters of open ground alone.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s58-1: The only variable that could win him a three-minute escape window was chaos large enough to physically block the security chain. Its scale also had to be sufficient to use a high density of heat sources and movement trails to lock the guards’ fire and attention onto the open ground.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s59-1: Heisenberg extended his hand, his fingers hovering for a moment over the forced-release section of the control console. He looked at the bewildered faces on the other side of the glass. Those young people had no idea what they were about to face. He was only an engineer, moving the lever that would produce the highest disturbance value.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s60-1: Then he cut the redundant circuits of the lower-level security system and slammed down the master release switch.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s61-1: The heavy metal doors sprang open one after another. The detention area’s airlocks shrieked as pressure escaped. Red lights flashed urgently in the corridors, and the sharp alarm instantly tore through the dead silence below ground. The prisoners froze in bewilderment for a moment, then, driven by the instinct to survive, fled wildly toward the corridors.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s62-1: Two squads of fully armed guards charged down from the stairwell and collided head-on with the people scattered through the passageways. Shouts, the dull thuds of rubber batons, and the gunfire of the first
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s62-2: volley mixed together. The prisoners at the front fell into pools of blood, but the young people behind them had long since lost their fear of uniforms through day after day of interrogation. They hurled
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s62-3: their bodies against the blockade line, keeping the guards’ fire fixed on the open ground. Several blood-covered prisoners seized batons and, before collapsing, clamped their teeth around the guards’ throats.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s63-1: Heisenberg crouched in the shadow behind the control console and watched the second hand pass two full minutes. Only when the first dense burst of gunfire in the corridor gave way to the screams of close combat, and the guards’ defensive line had been knocked completely out of
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s63-2: shape, did he pick up the canvas bag. Keeping close to the wall, he moved silently along the edge of the crossfire beneath the strobing red lights, like a ghost without body heat. A few steps away, bullets were turning flesh into fragments, but he did not even turn his head.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s64-1: The abandoned blast door leading to the underground mine tunnels was right before him. He pulled it open, and several blood-covered young people beside him seized the blind spot in the gunfire
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s64-2: and plunged into the deep ventilation passage with him. The pursuers’ guns were busy suppressing the larger target in the corridor. No one noticed these stragglers escaping into a dead end.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s65-1: The blast door locked behind them, leaving the bloody gunfire and the meat grinder of the Imperial regime completely outside. In the long abandoned mine tunnel, Heisenberg used the faint glow of a light stick to look at the three young
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s65-2: survivors beside him. One girl’s shoulder was bleeding. The other two boys’ chests heaved violently as they watched, wary, this cleanly dressed former high official who had just observed the entire slaughter from behind the control console.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s66-1: The tallest boy stepped forward, fingers tightening around a bloodied iron pipe he had picked up from the ground, his muscles taut. If Heisenberg made one unnecessary movement, he was ready to smash his skull at any moment.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s67-1: Heisenberg did not retreat, nor did he explain that this had merely been a calculation. He knew gratitude could not take root here. They had watched him wait until the defensive line broke apart before running out amid the chaos.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s68-1: He opened the engineering bag and kicked the miniature first-aid kit toward the injured girl’s feet. Then he took out the blueprint and piping diagram of the underground mine tunnels, unfolded them across the dusty ground, and touched their current position with his fingertip before sliding it toward a supply point deeper inside.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s69-1: In the darkness behind this blast door, the maker who had survived by borrowing five seconds of life, and these survivors who had once been disposable shelter to him but now carried wariness and hatred, reached
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s69-2: their first cold temporary pact. No words were needed to confirm it—the boy with the iron pipe glanced at the blueprint and slowly lowered his weapon, while the girl had already picked up the first-aid kit.
texts.chapter:v15-h07b:event:text-s70-1: They shared no faith, not even basic trust. But tonight, none of them had any reason to be handed back to the Head of State. From this moment on, they could only share this enormous underground tomb and be forced to become one another’s tools for survival below ground.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-08-underground:title: Sea Line Eight: Underground
texts.chapter:heisenberg-08-underground:event:: After returning to the abandoned freighter on the edge of Watermarsh, the lower hold had remained thick with the acrid stink of machine oil and sea salt. Some time had passed since we conducted that controlled retrieval at the White Tower. Taking advantage

of the chaos caused by the collapse of the Church, Estelle had hauled several tin cases out from deep in the lower levels. Now she was prying them open one by one with a crowbar, spreading the damp, brittle records across the hammocks and wooden crates.

On the other side was the single reel of lecture tapes containing nineteen sections that I had taken from beneath the AI laboratory’s control console. Estelle was now lifting out bundles of brittle manuscripts corresponding to the lectures from the

old metal case. They were Heisenberg’s early drafts for teaching physics underground, as well as the prototype for the blind-teaching tapes he recorded for the New Humans in his later years. She sorted through the cards attached to the manuscripts:

Lecture Manuscripts · Label Card (Underground Records Archive Edition):
“Lesson. Lecture One.
Lesson. Lecture Two.
……
Lesson. Lecture Nineteen.”
(The same hand, the same ink.
After these nineteen lectures, dozens of pages spanning two years remained blank, with no record of any further lessons.)

“The first-generation underground network of the old Society of Conservation had already been completely purged before Heisenberg escaped. These surviving political prisoners aren’t surviving embers from the previous generation.” Estelle picked up a photocopy of a

sentry log from one of the early handover points. “We heard those nineteen lecture tapes in the White Tower. He later recorded them as blind-teaching tapes to teach the New Humans how to survive. But these manuscripts weren’t originally written for the New Humans.”

After the temporary alliance formed on the night of their escape, Heisenberg and those blood-covered young political prisoners hid like rats in the sewers for half a month. When they finally made their way into the deepest independent reservoir of this underground facility and joined the other scattered escapees, the underground did not welcome him.
“There’s no record of anyone being elected. They only recorded his bunk.” Estelle turned a page. “‘The new arrival was assigned the bunk nearest the eastern shaft exit.’”

If the search teams broke in, he was the expendable piece left behind to buy time. Some of the political prisoners in the reservoir had relatives who died beneath the technical equipment he had inspected. No one beat him, because the knowledge in his head could keep them alive. But in those first days, no one spoke to him, either.
Estelle spread out a battered military defense-zone map covered in the shift-rotation blind spots Heisenberg had drawn in charcoal. During that coldest winter, the Imperial army conducted three
blanket searches of the mountains. They hid like rats in ventilation ducts and abandoned sewers, following the map, while the survivors drew three circles on its back to represent “survival.”

In those drafty tunnels, hatred gave way to survival. There were no records of anyone being elected, only escape routes annotated in his hand. Following the enemy who had once used them as human shields, these

young people picked up the documents their predecessors had left behind in the ruins, turning the principles and passwords that had already been severed from the past into the later “Society of Conservation.”
The cabin light swayed as Estelle picked out several scraps of paper recording private matters from the backs of a pile of engineering manuscripts.
The story of that woman began with a bowl of food.

The manuscripts recorded that it was his second month underground. He had contracted typhoid and was burning with fever, shivering alone in a corner while no one looked after him. In the middle of the night, someone shook him awake and pushed a bowl of scalding brown rice porridge into his hands. His fever was so high he could not make out her face. He only heard an extremely rude complaint:
“Drink it while it’s hot. If you die in the corridor and start to stink, we’ll still have to drag you out.”

Judging from the shift rosters at the handover point, she lived in an aboveground settlement near the hiding place. At the time, she knew nothing of physics, and even less that the person she had saved was a most-wanted criminal. Others walked around

him in the corridor; she came straight through with her heavy wooden laundry basin, often splashing water all over him. A few days later, he returned the clean empty bowl and offered a stiff word of thanks. The manuscript recorded her reaction:
She threw the bowl into the wooden basin and pointed toward the corner. “If you’ve got the strength for that, go help me move those two baskets of sprouted potatoes into the cellar.”
Beside it, he had written a note: “When, in everyone’s eyes, a person is nothing but a heavy statement of guilt, someone suddenly treats him only as a person who owes them a bowl.”

In his third year underground, once the pressure had eased somewhat, everyone began to need the knowledge in his head. He agreed to lecture. The lectures continued intermittently for more than a decade.
That question came after one of the lectures.

The listeners dispersed, leaving only her behind to help sweep the floor. She had remained around the hiding place for two or three years since bringing him that bowl of porridge, slowly piecing together who he really was from the scraps of others’

words and their hatred. They rarely spoke. His notes recorded only the corners of clothes she had mended, the chalk she had handed him, and the profile of her occasionally falling asleep in the last row while listening to incomprehensible lectures.
That day, halfway through sweeping, she stopped and looked at the blackboard, crowded with equations, then pulled half a stick of chalk from her pocket and set it on the lectern.
“That’s the fourth one.” She rubbed her aching wrist. “You spend every day calculating things no one can understand up there. Do you actually keep accounts for what you borrow down here?”
He copied this exchange, along with the sound of her dropping the chalk on the lectern, four times on the backs of later manuscripts.

He froze in front of the blackboard. In that moment, the person asking might only have been talking about chalk and rations. But the listener thought of the surveillance equipment he had inspected and the technical support in the interrogation rooms. He looked at the signal phases on the blackboard and thought for a long time:
“I never kept one.”
“Then start keeping one now. Being unable to repay what you owe is one thing. Trying to get away without paying is another.” She lowered her head and continued sweeping, raising a cloud of dust.

That night, he found a notebook and began recording, stroke by stroke, the warrant-device schematics he had verified and the interrogation-room circuits he had repaired. He left the first page blank. He

did not write a single word in his own defense. The account grew longer, and no one’s attitude toward him changed because he had begun keeping it—hatred remained hatred, and the expendable bunk remained the

one nearest the exit. But every day he continued calculating those phases no one could understand in front of the blackboard. When he finished, he lowered his head and kept the accounts, one line at a time.
If all we had were Heisenberg’s manuscripts, this woman would look like a ghost who had brought him a bowl once.

But Estelle pulled a rough private ledger from a heavy waterproof iron case. Exchange was written on its cover. It was a relic later recovered from beneath the stone paving by an underground organization that had risked

returning to the now-deserted handover point after the purge that swept across the Empire. Tucked between the ledger’s pages was half of a folded draft, written in the same hand as Exchange: “Four sticks of chalk owed.”

It was packed with marks. One month per page, recording fifteen full years: on one side, the supplies and rations she received in exchange for washing other people’s dirty clothes and taking on mending work each day; on the other, the handover times and safety markers.

The people in the underground hiding place could not show themselves. Tiny quantities of coarse salt, high-calorie supplies, and even the charcoal Heisenberg used for drawing all depended on her scraping them out of

the aboveground settlement bit by bit through her labor. This was her ledger, but at the end of every account was someone underground—several people with high fevers, or someone in the dark who needed a mark to follow.
It was the silent evidence Estelle pieced together after comparing the ledger with the Imperial army’s shift-rotation schedules from that period.

Across fifteen years, most of the handovers recorded in the ledger fell within the ten-minute blind spot between the morning and night shifts. The few that came early or late also happened to avoid the military command’s surprise inspection days.

Estelle pointed to the months when the transaction volume fell off a cliff. “These were exactly the months when the settlement was conducting a strict inspection of its ration ledgers. She reduced the amount before the inspection and did not return

to normal until two months after the pressure had passed. Every day before dawn, the underground contact who came up through the blind spot between shifts to collect these life-saving supplies would see the two marks she had drawn on the ledger.”
Estelle picked up her pen, drew a line through “a passerby who occasionally brought porridge” in the draft, and added a new line:
“Correction: This private ledger is the only surviving profile of the supply line for that hiding place across fifteen years.”

In the fourth year after Heisenberg went underground, when the pressure was at its worst, the underground organization prepared to move as a whole into the deeper levels. The prisoners she had saved proposed to their contact outside that she be given refuge and brought fully into hiding.
But she refused absolutely.
This was the only half-sentence in Heisenberg’s manuscripts that directly mentioned what became of her. He recorded her exact words in the margin:
“She was trembling with fear, but still said: If I suddenly disappear, the settlement won’t be able to produce me, and the patrols will go after the people in the same row of houses.”
In theory, if the underground had simply severed contact at the time, she would have been safe.

“But the underground organization couldn’t find another concealed source of food at the time.” I looked at the unbroken marks in that year’s ledger. The hiding place moved deeper, but the quantities of supplies

handed over each day in this ledger remained unchanged. The underground organization had to take a much longer route and keep maintaining this handover point with her, even though it could ignite at any moment.
When this ledger reached its fifteenth year, the real purge arrived.
Estelle turned Exchange to its final page. At the bottom, every mark recording the movement of supplies stopped abruptly in the same week.

“That purge was highly abnormal.” Estelle opened an old deployment order from the Imperial military command. “The local commander used wording like ‘responding to the lower-level quota overload crisis’ in the order. They forcibly

leveled every unregistered black household and settlement—they really believed that eliminating these ‘extra people’ would free up physical capacity in the lower levels and resolve the quota shortfall imposed from above.”
The line broke.

“In the same year, four households in the district containing this handover point were struck entirely from the purge register reported by the Imperial military command.” Estelle spread a register across the table, with several stacks of old clinic ration records

freshly pulled from the iron case beside it. “Exchange clearly records that, starting the year the underground relocated, nearly one-third of the supplies became specific doses of painkillers and gauze supplied in the opposite direction—from underground to her.”
She opened the old clinic ration records beside her. “Only one household had a severely injured patient whose long-term registration matched this.”

Her finger moved across the register and stopped on that household’s composition. “An elderly couple and a daughter. The old man had been paralyzed in both legs for five years, and the old woman suffered from severe

rheumatism. In this household, the only person who could have carried supplies through the shift-change blind spot every day and kept the family alive by exchanging washing and mending for medicine was the daughter.”
All she had to do was move her finger half an inch to the side and look at the daughter’s registered name. That person would turn from a ghost in history into an entity with a name.
But she stopped.
What had she left behind after fifteen years?

Exchange contained thousands of boxes, large and small. They were the underground organization’s marks confirming receipt each time it collected supplies. But on the side where she had signed her own name, there were no letters at all—only the same simple circle drawn in charcoal.

“Because she was afraid of implicating her family, she would never put her name in a ledger like this, one that recorded the life-saving supplies. That was how she survived for fifteen years.” Estelle looked at those circles.
Estelle was silent for a while, then pushed the register and the remaining clinic records aside.
“No more searching.”
“We’re only one step away.”

“For fifteen years, she fought desperately to preserve this anonymity every day.” Estelle returned Exchange carefully to the bottom of the iron case. “I have no right to use the safety of later generations as grounds to tear it apart.”
She pulled off the pen cap and, in elegant calligraphy, neatly drew the circle on the report file.
“Mark as shown at left. The person’s name cannot be determined.”
She left the personnel number and place-of-origin fields beneath the entry blank. The circle remained there, quietly.
Apart from scattered fragments in the margins of his manuscripts, Heisenberg never wrote about her in any formal record.

When no more clothes came up from the handover point, the lecture records sealed away with the lecture manuscripts stopped abruptly at Lecture Nineteen. After that, two full years of records remained completely blank.
Until that winter night, when he pulled out the base-level anomaly data left behind by the old physicist Semmelweis and began checking the accounts again.
He was going to calculate the true reason that circle had suddenly disappeared.

He spread the water-stained original report before the camera and recorded a preliminary piece of evidence later called the “review footage.” The original contained only one isolated question: “Pool levels this season dropped sharply, far beyond the maximum energy consumption of the population listed.”

Heisenberg did not write on the report. He simply spread it out and, facing the camera, recited a sequence of dates from memory. They were the records of the time machine’s first seven cross-cycle operations, dates engraved in his mind

from his time as a core engineer of the time machine before his defection. In Semmelweis’s report shown on camera, those seven dates corresponded exactly to the sharp points where the lower-level capacity pool experienced extreme drops.

It was not just that settlement. Handover points in blind spots, large and small, were being systematically leveled. The Imperial commanders issued orders to forcibly clear the dead zones, mistakenly believing that the black households in the lower levels had consumed the

system’s capacity. But in Heisenberg’s eyes, the overlap between the dates of the pool’s sharp drops formed a strong physical indication: this missing capacity had never been consumed by the lower-level population. It had been swallowed before being allocated to the lower levels.
Facing the machine that was still running somewhere in the distance, he left a question pointing toward the true source of the leakage:
“What if it was never the population consuming the system’s capacity?”
Not the population, but the direct consumption of anonymous soul-field capacity. The time machine, which, whenever it ran, bypassed the lower-level quotas and tore open a massive capacity
shortfall directly at the source. The quota deficits pressed down layer by layer from the Inner Circle were ultimately translated by local commanders into orders to eliminate the extra population.

She had once told him to calculate how much he owed. At first, he thought it would be enough to record, one item at a time, the equipment schematics he had verified. But on that winter night, when the physical indication of

the capacity shortfall emerged, he realized that the lives sustained by the thousands of handovers recorded in Exchange might ultimately have been erased by the machine he had helped build with his own hands and failed to stop.
At the end of Exchange, filled with the underground organization’s handwriting and fifteen years of supplies traded for lives, he pressed his pen hard and wrote one line:
“Someone has to finish calculating this account.”

Heisenberg spent the rest of his life calculating it. Much later, amid the chaos of the Church of Convergence’s final years, he finally pieced together the incomplete observation charts and the other half of the

answer, calculating a death-sentence upper bound designed to guard against the worst case. He tried to repay this account that could never be repaid with the cruel engineering parameter called “Eight Thousand.”
And more than a century later, the young people on another island stood upon the ashes of history, facing the old account left behind by that same machine.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-04-cat-ears:title: Sea Line Four: Cat Ears
texts.chapter:heisenberg-04-cat-ears:event:tex: In the fragment later deciphered beneath the White Tower, which I identified as the underground logs of former chief designer Heisenberg, he recorded the aftermath of that reshuffling of power in dry, spare strokes.
Everything began with Lysenko’s new proposal to create “ten-thousand-capacity long-window operators.” At that desperate juncture, no one could disprove the
extremely reckless theory: if an operator’s capacity were vast enough to cover the entire machine’s phase, perhaps it could forcibly break open the five-second
physical deadlock. The proposal was approved by the Inner Circle. Lysenko used it to complete his leap in power, while Heisenberg became his subordinate.
According to the logs, on the third day after everything had settled, the nameplate on the spacious chief’s office at the end of the corridor was changed.

During that suffocating transfer of power, Heisenberg’s new desk was moved into a narrow cubicle halfway down the corridor. Every morning when he clocked in, he had to pass the door that had once belonged to him. Whoever arranged the schedule understood the workings

of power very well: humiliation had to become part of the everyday to completely destroy a person’s authority. Heisenberg wrote that the man who had replaced him in the chief’s office made no attempt to hide it. In full view of everyone, he even set down a rule:
“Thought must be correct. The formulas can be worked out correctly over time. The formulas are his responsibility.”
The logs mentioned that the old colleagues who insisted on rigorous science disappeared overnight. Heisenberg watched the nameplates in the corridor being removed one by one, replaced with the
charge of “fatalism.” First they were packed into metal train cars and sent to labor camps far away. A few months later, an official order brought them all back to the basement of this building.

When Heisenberg saw again the senior academician who had once argued physical models with him at an annual conference, the man was wearing a coarse prison uniform sewn with a number. With hands covered in chilblains and trembling faintly, he was precisely

marking the tolerances of neural bundles on a blueprint. Lysenko had never intended to defeat them at an academic conference. He simply used power and criminal charges to turn those fiercely independent minds into expendable materials that cost no dignity.

Heisenberg lowered his head and took the signed blueprint from his former academic opponent. Avoiding that vacant gaze, he hurried back to his cubicle. Cold sweat soaked through his back. In this basement crushed beneath

power, the most terrifying thing was not death. It was discovering that you were watching your colleagues become expendable materials with a clear mind, while still having to finish drawing the blueprint in your hands.

The new proposal Lysenko used to seize power was publicly framed as a grand vision for creating “ten-thousand-capacity long-window operators.” In theory, if a body’s internal volume were vast enough to contain

ten thousand people’s worth of capacity quota, sending it to operate the time machine might allow it to cover the machine’s enormous deficit during transit and forcibly break open the five-second physical deadlock.

But in the dense engineering requirements that passed through Heisenberg’s hands every day, the complicated parameters pieced together a private blueprint. The newly built high-capacity empty-shell production line came with an extremely specialized

set of replication parameters. Among the parameter sheets scattered across Heisenberg’s desk were detailed records of Lysenko’s physical features: height, arm span, the angle of his jaw. The AI empty-shell laboratory in the outskirts was even

ordered to secretly construct an unprecedented facility for personality scanning and reproduction. What he was really plotting was to send a new human body identical in appearance to himself, with ten-thousand-level capacity, to operate as a

long-window operator and complete the long journeys across the various world lines in his place, while he himself, as the original, remained outside the cockpit and kept firm control of the external console and the authority to force termination.
To reclaim everything that copy experienced across the various branches at any time, he greatly expanded the original machine’s low-level neural telemetry permissions, established a
permanent operator’s dashboard, and added a write-only crash-snapshot channel. If the plan succeeded, this channel would continuously send cross-world life experiences back to the White Tower.

But engineering technology was in Lysenko’s hands, while the mobilization of a population on the scale of ten thousand had to pass through two iron gates: the Führer’s final approval and the actual execution of the Tarkin forced-mobilization system. The dictator

high above would never specially approve living human resources for a political rival’s new body. And Tarkin, who controlled the transport rosters and guard network, was even less likely to cooperate by mobilizing his people to fulfill Lysenko’s private desires.

Lysenko’s application remained locked in deadlock. The infrastructure for creating people and recording them had already been built, but because the enormous system quota was not approved, the process of scanning Lysenko’s

own personality was never authorized to begin, and that body could never be written with a startup. In this suffocating political stalemate, Heisenberg continued pushing forward with the remaining engineering work.
Although the entire plan had been shelved for lack of living material to fill it, in Heisenberg’s memory, the final meeting to approve the vessel’s exterior was still held as scheduled.

The blueprint was sent through the proper channels into Lysenko’s office. When it was returned to everyone the next day, a pair of conspicuous ears had appeared on the top of the head in the assembly drawing. The normal human ears that had originally been positioned on either side of the head had been crossed out with two rough red diagonal lines.

Heisenberg recalled in the logs that the outlines had been sketched casually in red and blue pencil. In the blank space at the edge of the blueprint, right beside Lysenko’s sweeping signature and approval, was a short line of writing:
“Add them. Reason: better.”

The air in the review room seemed to freeze. From the perspective of engineering standards, the alterations were incomprehensible. The normal ears on the blueprint had been erased, replaced by two decorative protrusions on top of the head with no sensory function, only

the appearance of ears. To make the structure seem slightly more reasonable on paper, the engineers who came later had to go to great lengths to adjust the skin tension and blood-vessel paths across the surface of the skull to nourish those purely superfluous masses of

dead flesh, while urgently designing a set of auditory implants buried inside the skull to restore the function lost with both ears.
At last, in the long silence, a young engineer who had only just joined the project could not hold back. In a faint voice, he asked: Why?
According to Heisenberg’s record, Lysenko was standing beside the table, stuffing documents into his briefcase. He did not even look up:
“Because it’s my body.” He fastened the clasp. “Since it costs a great deal to make, the person who pays naturally has the right to choose a button on his own suit.”

The heavy wooden door closed firmly behind him. In the enormous conference room, no one dared pick up an eraser and remove those two red diagonal lines. That crude private blueprint with a pair of masses of dead flesh added to it thus became the highest instruction for the next stage of production.

After the meeting, the AI empty-shell laboratory in the outskirts built several body templates according to the blueprint. They all had the conspicuous protrusions on top of their heads. But because the forced mobilization had been blocked, the rejected execution

quota for ten thousand people was never fulfilled. The shells that had not been infused—in other words, that still had no built-in personality or consciousness—could ultimately only be suspended in the lightless production zone as products of the political deadlock.

Over the following decades, the time machine did not stop its calculations. After countless cycles accumulated, it exhausted every idle resource on the surface, spreading irreversible desiccation over the heads of all the living. The Great Extinction arrived. Every old human was zeroed out in the ledger.

Without operators to maintain the cycle, the mad machine eventually stopped devouring worlds and came to a complete halt. The system capacity that had originally filled the machine’s routine operating load was

no longer occupied, and the gap across the boundaries between worlds closed with it. The vast system quota released by the deaths of all old humanity surged back into the silent underground and became available.

In the laboratory on the outskirts, the underground facility’s backup nuclear power had not yet run dry. That batch of dust-covered shells sensed the return of capacity at the lower level. The early writing procedures that had once been placed in the automatic testing queue but suspended when

quotas ran out before the apocalypse were taken over again by the cold system. The machine strictly executed the interrupted instructions, extracting the few complete personality records that had remained in the test array—originally belonging to several junior test researchers who had not

managed to evacuate—and naturally writing them into a batch of body templates that had long been in place. Because Lysenko’s personality record had never been authorized for scanning, the resurrection channel originally reserved for him was accidentally occupied by these several test engineers.

And so, those junior technicians who had once only been responsible for debugging parameters, but had accidentally left their scans behind as system-validation packages, became the first old-world dead to open their eyes among the ruins.

From the scattered records I pieced together later across the cycles, these former imperial researchers who awoke inside Lysenko’s exclusive shells realized how abnormal they looked. To conceal their special status as “surviving old humans”

and establish a social order they could manage, they activated the existing production line and began mass-producing ordinary new humans without memories of the old world. The skeletons were standardized, while differences in build and appearance

were generated through random instructions from the gene bank. On that production line, cat ears had originally been only a locally adjustable parameter. But these rulers not only activated it; they also modified the factory settings. They

deliberately made every later generation grow into the same special form as themselves, washing the original abnormality into the species-wide norm of these ruins and locking the trait as a mandatory inheritance that could never be revoked.

Since the ears had no function, new humans could only rely on the auditory implants finalized alongside them at the time to perceive sound. But to those who came later, they were still the only pair of ears they had ever possessed by birth.
The quirk that tyrant had left behind on a whim for his own private desire, through one absurd link after another, grew irreversibly atop the heads of everyone in the villages that followed.

As I searched the bottomless physical grid for Yuna’s error snapshot, I knew exactly where it came from. It should have been a backup carrier preserving Lysenko’s grand inheritance plan, originating in the world that had once collapsed from instability before my eyes.

It was a memory that had already crossed the boundary between worlds. In the branch where I had once stayed, that world’s Yuna had also seen the scattered fragments of damaged engineering records in that dim underground archive room. She stood there, and

the pair of organs above her head that she had always believed were simply part of her became, at the moment she learned the truth, a brand she could never remove. That world’s Yuna did not lose control in front of me. She only said one thing: “Let’s go.”

At the time, I thought there was still time to dissolve that despair. But when disaster came, the girl who survived beneath the tyrant’s signature, along with the real world that was heading toward destruction, was ultimately fixed in that night’s instability.
And now, carrying this memory and my knowledge of the original design of that underlying system, I continue searching across different cycles for the error code numbered SYS-ERR-09. It was the
write-only channel Lysenko had originally reserved for his own cross-world voyages. In this disaster, it became the only container capable of receiving fragments of her cross-world experiences.
texts.chapter:chapter-21-eight-districts:title: Chapter Twenty-One: Eight Zones
texts.chapter:chapter-21-eight-districts:event:
“Operator Continuity Verification Network” Public List (copy of the original posted on the White Tower noticeboard):
“This network is located in four places. Routine verification; not suspended for weather.
The White Tower. The old experimental zone. The central computing relay station. The external disaster-recovery management station.
Each place stores something different: the main text is kept at the

present. Data from a single place cannot be assembled into a complete operator.
This network is not measured by the number of nodes. To verify whether a record is complete, it checks only four things:
whether the source is genuine, whether the coverage is continuous, whether the ending is valid, and whether the whole thing has remained unaltered.
——This document is permanently posted. Anyone may copy it.”

At the end of yesterday evening’s loop, Estelle stood before the noticeboard in the dusk, studying the notice about the verification network for a long time. In the corner of the board, pinned up casually with a thumbtack,

was an inconspicuous appendix to a perimeter-maintenance dossier. It contained only one dry line of regulation: “Peripheral infrastructure and physical perimeters shall uniformly use K-series plates for identification.”

“‘Anyone may copy it.’” She read the sentence from the notice aloud, then shifted her gaze to the appendix beside it. “People outside the wall can read, but public education cut the lower-level permissions and system causality apart long ago. Even if they

copied it exactly, they couldn’t connect these public words to any evidence chain that could assign responsibility. Posting this sentence so openly means that, under the system as it exists now, they simply aren’t afraid of us knowing where the data is.”
She closed the little booklet she used for taking notes, carefully transcribed the wording of both documents into it, and folded the pages.
“That place in the old experimental zone.” She turned and looked me in the eyes. “Your experimental zone. Let’s go.”
I told her I knew an abandoned transport tunnel beneath the White Tower that could cut straight through the wilderness. She made sure of the conditions and followed me down without hesitation.

But there was no sign that it had fallen into disrepair. In the darkness, a tremendous clamping roar came from the end of the rail trench. There was no warning, no permission check. It was not a roadblock at all, but indiscriminate physical erasure

aimed at unauthorized intruders. The enormous press plate came crushing toward us with terrifying force, compressing the air into a shrill hiss.
We, along with the abandoned tunnel, were crushed into bloody, unrecognizable fragments in an instant.

When I opened my eyes again, it was already morning in a new loop. Eight in the morning.
My ribs seemed to retain the phantom pain of being crushed beneath the machine. It took several deep
breaths before I could tell this morning’s Estelle what had just happened. I told her that the heavy defensive machine below was still active, and that the tunnel had been sealed completely.

“Indiscriminate physical erasure carried out directly… That means there isn’t a single node beneath the White Tower capable of reading identities. It’s purely a cleaning trap.” She quickly sorted out the logic after

hearing me. “Last night’s notice required continuous ‘permission trails,’ and that appendix stipulated that peripheral infrastructure use K-series plates. The manual said that K-series plates aren’t just markers;

they’re also physical maintenance terminals. Nothing can be recorded underground. We have to take the surface route, openly interact with those terminal nodes, and write today’s lawful movements into the system.”

She did not delay. She went outside the White Tower and recopied the two notices that had been lost in the previous loop. After that, we went together to the Church records office.
Across the counter, Sera pushed this week’s renewal contract in front of Estelle as usual. Its terms were listed

with explicit prices: consent to a complete writable-personality-state scan; inheritance of identity by a new body; the original body being discarded; and the body specifications to be decided by the maintenance seat.
Estelle did not sign. Instead, she placed her hand over the contract.

“Regarding the clause ‘body specifications to be decided by the maintenance seat,’ I am filing a formal complaint on the grounds that my rights have been violated.” She looked directly at Sera. “I demand access to the procedural entry point and an investigation into what the maintenance seat has done to my body.”
A trace of impatience appeared on Sera’s rigid face. She was about to refuse. I stepped forward.

“Check the interface logs for this body.” I held Sera’s gaze. “In one of the timelines before this, I tried to access the appendix to this renewal contract, and the system returned an unauthorized-access block code. That means someone used high-level permissions

invisible to you to lock the candidate interface directly. Since no one touched this body this morning either, you can check your lower-level logs right now and see whether your own signature has been pulled into a hidden appendix whose name you can’t see.”

Sera’s gaze turned cold at once. She immediately turned and brought up the interface. A few seconds later, she bit down hard on her lip, staring at the line of invocation records on the screen.
It was her own

program signature, forcibly referenced that morning in a version appendix whose name she could not even see.
She did not look at me again. Instead, she pulled Estelle’s complaint into the processing queue on

the spot and pressed the execution key. Using the complaint, she coldly issued a limited program audit order—access restricted to the contract-explanation area, the candidate-disposition files under this

body’s name, and the bodily-rights witnessing area responsible for defining abnormal environmental effects on infrastructure. She intended to use Estelle as a probe, to find out who was hollowing out her seat.
When we left the White Tower, Estelle was gripping the thin audit order so tightly that her knuckles had gone white.
“She’s using me as bait, trying to muddy the water,” she said quietly.
“You don’t have to accept this order. Finding out what was done to your own body may make you die faster than knowing nothing.”

“But I don’t want to die without knowing why.” She turned her head. There was an almost stubborn will to survive in her eyes. “Whatever back door they left in this body, I have to find out what it is before I can stay alive. Let’s go get that renewal, even if it’s a fake one.”
It was ten in the morning. She stood on the boundary stone at the village entrance waiting for me, the booklet with its newly written pages held tightly against her chest.
“Let’s go. To that old experimental zone you mentioned.” She looked at me.
I said all right. About a two-hour journey.
When we set out, the morning sunlight had just pierced the thin mist. A heavy rain had fallen during the first half of the night.

Kane was sitting on the boundary stone at the western gate. He took the audit order issued by Sera and glanced at it. As he handed it back to Estelle, I noticed his left hand resting on a black box-shaped device at his waist.
Before I first fell into the loop,

I had seen that device with my own eyes. That time, at the western boundary, he had used the same gesture to push open the latch, twist the knob, and produce a faint burst of static. Nothing happened to us then, but Estelle had collapsed and died instantly.
That

box was what killed her. Now his hand was resting on it. Every muscle in my body tensed at once. If I shouted here, there would be no evidence with which to accuse him. I would only force him to act immediately. All I could do was keep my eyes fixed on his hand.
“The bridge near the camp collapsed halfway last year.” He pointed toward the distance and spoke only about the road conditions. “When you get there, go around along the waterline.”
“How far did last night’s rain reach?” She put away the order and looked up at him.
“The water will rise under the bridge,” Kane answered quickly. “What time will you be back?”
“Before dark.”
Kane looked up at the sky, said nothing more, and drew back the leg he had been holding across the road.
After we had gone a dozen or so steps, she suddenly called me from behind.
“State the route once first,” she said evenly.
“Follow the old road to the bridge. The bridge is broken, so go around along the waterline, then follow the side road after crossing it.” I stopped and answered.
“Which side do you leave the waterline on? Where do you return to the old road? Which side road do you take?” she asked, one step at a time.
“I don’t know how to say it. I’ll recognize it when we get there.” I answered honestly.

“Recognizing it doesn’t mean I can verify it.” She walked quickly in front of me and took out the little booklet. “This is a two-hour journey. Set a rule. Every time you change the route, you have to say three things: which way you turn, what kind of ground you’re stepping on, and roughly how far.”
“Fine.”
“And one more thing: I’ll record how you walk exactly as you walk it. As for how you know to walk that way, I won’t record it. I can verify only physical evidence present on the ground.”

The first stretch was all the unpaved dirt roads outside the village. Waist-high grass lay flattened on both sides, its broad leaves covered in rainwater from the night before. After only a few steps, the uppers of our shoes and our trouser cuffs were soaked.
A shallow muddy ditch crossed the road. I stepped over it, and the instant I landed, habit made me reach my right hand toward the left rear to pull someone across.
My hand stopped in midair.

After stopping for a second, I silently drew my hand back, put it in my pocket, and kept walking.
She was walking behind me on the right, a steady six steps away.
The dirt road ended. A stretch of gray-white old pavement thrust violently up through the mud like some kind of pallid bone. At the broken edge, several rust-red lengths
of rebar twisted toward the sky. Along both sides of the ruined road, the row of bare metal poles stood as before—one every fifty-three paces, set out in a straight line.

“The third one on the left.” I pointed ahead. “The base of that pole is split inward toward the road. After the crooked pole, the soil on the right is soft. We need to take the left and stay close to the hard shoulder for about twenty paces.”
“That description will work. I’ve got it.”

She walked to the pole with the cracked base but did not take my word for it immediately. She untied the short rope from her waist and poked it into the deep grass on the right side of the road. When she pulled it up, the end was coated in a slick layer of black mud. She tried the left side again. The road shoulder was indeed hard.

The collapsed bridge was ahead. Half of the broken deck hung abruptly in midair, while the fallen section had crashed entirely into the muddy water. The current rushed through beneath the gaps in the broken edge.

Following the route Kane had indicated, we would have to turn back to the junction we had just passed and make a wide detour along the muddy waterline. But I remembered a faster shortcut: slide down the slope beside the bridge abutment. Two old steps hung beneath it; stepping onto them would let us slip into the maintenance tunnel under the bridge.
“No need to go around. Down here. There are two steps. Step across them and you can get into the bridge tunnel.”
She walked to the edge and leaned out to look at the churning water below.
“The bottom step is already underwater.”
“I know where to put my feet. I can feel it accurately.”
“Arno, what you remember is where to put your feet, but what you remember does not include today’s water level.”

She did not agree easily. Instead, she had me lean down the side slope and test the condition of the first step. I held on to a rusted fixture at the edge of the slope and lowered myself carefully. My foot landed solidly. It was indeed the step I remembered.
But a century of erosion had long since made the edge brittle. The moment my foot sank, the entire edge of the step collapsed without a sound. Cold muddy water flooded
one of my shoes. My calf scraped hard against rough rebar. I gripped the fixture protruding from the bridge abutment, my whole body hanging awkwardly from the slope.
She calmly untied the short rope, tied it tightly around the base of an old railing beside her, then lay down and slowly fed the remaining rope to where I could reach it.
“Grab the rope. Don’t grab my hand,” she ordered.
Using the rope’s tension, I finally pulled myself back onto solid ground. Without saying a word, she rinsed the cut on my calf with clean water and wrapped it tightly with a clean strip of cloth.
“Conclusion: this stretch cannot follow your route.”
“Right. I concede.”

We could only detour through a shallow, half-submerged stretch of water nearby. As we went around beneath the bridge abutment, I caught sight in the dim light of a small iron plate on its shadowed inner wall. Painted in white on the plate was a number, an arrow pointing forward, and a scored line beneath the base of the arrow.

She took out the booklet and quickly turned to the page where she had recopied the appendix that morning—“Peripheral infrastructure and physical perimeters shall uniformly use K-series plates for identification.” She meticulously copied down the location of this plate.

Farther ahead, the ground began to rise noticeably. A group of low buildings, interwoven iron-gray and rust-red, lay half-buried in the wild grass. As we drew closer, a broken sign hung from the outer wall.

“Look here. Someone later painted a false name over the upper layer, but the paint ran with the rain into the grooves of the original lettering beneath.” She leaned close, carefully making out the depressions below. I looked with her. It was a line of obscure old-era terminology, something we could never learn in the village’s old-language classes.

She did not try to force a guess at the letters. Instead, she went around to the back of the mottled sign. Printed on the load-bearing fixture was the same marking we had seen beneath the bridge: K-14.
She took out the terminal, brought

up the infrastructure map appendix to the audit order, and entered the plate code K-14.
A short maintenance log appeared on the screen: “K-14 physical connection node maintenance station, peripheral area of Experimental Zone Eight.”

“Good. With the K-14 maintenance station and ‘Experimental Zone Eight’ linked as physical and archival evidence, my audit order can treat this as a legitimate location and search the underlying dossiers.” She made the decision without hesitation.

From the sign to the ring of thin iron columns enclosing the core area, there were still roughly a hundred paces.
The midday sun was shining straight down. It was just past noon.

“The perimeter of the old experimental zone is ahead.” I reminded her. “I didn’t have time to explain this morning. In one of the earlier loops, I took you through the old restricted area on the western side. There was a sound field there.”
She stopped and listened carefully.

“It’s the same here, maybe worse. I’ve come to test it many times before. These thin columns didn’t react to me, but in another timeline, that time on the western side, you had extreme difficulty even approaching. I heard

from people in the village that these are low-frequency devices designed specifically to deal with people from outside the perimeter. If anything feels wrong this time, stop immediately. Don’t force your way through.”
She took a deep breath and continued forward. But before long, her steps suddenly slowed without warning. At first her pace merely decreased.
Then the line of her walk began to veer—she seemed completely unaware of it, but her body was instinctively resisting forward movement, turning
her route into an outward arc of escape. She forced herself to continue for another twenty paces, then stopped completely, as if nailed in place.
Her face turned deathly pale within seconds, and her breathing became shallow and rapid. She gripped her trouser leg tightly, her voice trembling.
“I’m dizzy. My chest is fluttering. It’s severe. But I can’t tell what caused it.” She gasped for breath.

She stared at the thin iron columns standing quietly in the wind ahead, clenched her teeth, and tried to force herself another half-step forward—but just as her heel was about to land, her whole body violently retreated, almost making her fall.
“I can’t get through,” she said quietly. “Arno, I can’t get through. My reason wants to walk, but my body won’t let me.”
I stepped forward, took her heavy pack, then turned and walked alone toward the nearest iron column.
At noon, the surroundings were deathly silent except for the wind. I reached out and touched the cold metal directly with the back of my hand. Nothing abnormal happened. Just as I
had heard, the perimeter’s sound field was still operating at full power, but it had no effect on people like us who had grown up in the village. What it was meant to bite was her.
I went back to her side. She had already crouched in the wild grass, her pale face covered in cold sweat.

She took out the audit order.
When Sera issued this limited audit order, it opened not only the “contract-explanation area” and the “candidate-disposition index,” but also activated the “bodily-rights witnessing area” responsible for defining abnormal environmental effects. She entered the K-14 and “Experimental

Zone Eight” confirmed along the route as environmental parameters, declared that her body had suffered externally imposed physiological repulsion here, and initiated a rights-violation verification.
The weak light of the screen reflected on her pale fingertips. She had no authority to access the infrastructure’s

own operating records, but the system rules stipulated that once an audit order took effect, it had to explain why the environment had caused an abnormality in her body. Following the trace path of that abnormality report, the system granted her access to an interaction record between the environment and the body.
A few seconds later, the underlying draft appeared on the screen.

“These thin columns really are broadcast equipment.” She stared hard at the screen. “But in the ‘specific frequency band’ field, it isn’t an ordinary parameter. It invokes an exclusive target: the V-3 model peripheral substrate.”
“V-3. That’s the allocation code the Church issued to me, proving that I belong to a peripheral lineage with this kind of physiological interface. Someone born and raised in the village, like you,
doesn’t have anything like this preinstalled. And for people from the periphery, even just coming near it allows sound waves in a specific frequency band to forcibly take over our nervous systems.”

“The instruction in the first field here is perfectly clear: ‘Match the peripheral-lineage auditory interface, triggering preset neural and endocrine responses—dizziness, panic, and avoidance.’” She stared hard at the screen, her fingertips turning slightly white.

“My fear doesn’t belong to me at all. It’s a physiological response triggered unilaterally by the hardware interface they forcibly fixed into the bodies of our lineage.” Her voice was cold as ice, carrying deep disgust.

The surroundings were as silent as death, except for the wind outside.
She did not look farther down immediately. I saw her shoulders tremble slightly. After a long while, she closed her eyes and drew in a deep, slow breath, forcing down the physiological

shudder. When she opened her eyes again, her fingertips were steady. She forced herself to call up the second dossier permitted by the audit order: the “candidate-disposition file” under her own name, because she needed to see who could trigger this interface.
“What is that for?” I asked.

“A concealed second-setting instruction. ‘The high-intensity acoustic pulse is manually activated through an independent channel. Consequence: irreversible autonomic nervous-system collapse.’” She scrolled down the page, her voice growing colder. “But under the

authorization rules below, standard perimeter defense permits only the nonlethal blocking setting. The lethal channel has no default authorization. It can be activated only when an emergency state is triggered. For example, when the subject is determined to be missing.”
Hearing those words, a layer of cold sweat broke across my back.

“Before I first fell into the loop, I had seen that device with my own eyes. That time, at the western boundary, he used the same gesture to push open the latch, twist the knob, and produce a faint burst of static. Nothing happened to us then, but you collapsed and died instantly in the distance. I thought

it was Otto’s order, but…” I looked at her. “But this morning, when he was confirming our return time at the village entrance, his hand was already on this switch. If this is his standard weapon, he doesn’t need to wait for a vote by the Ten Seats. He’s looking for a window when we’re exposed in the wild.”

Her fingertips trembled.
She bit down hard on her pale lips.

“That is his actual control authority, not the standing authority he can legally account for. With this underlying draft, it’s clear that the lethal channel was not authorized by default and is not protected by the

ordinary rules.” Her voice was dry. “So his question about what time we’d return wasn’t merely an interrogation. If we didn’t return by that time, we would become ‘missing’ in the wild under the terms of the protocol.”

“As long as he falsifies the appearance that we’re missing or have crossed the boundary, he can trigger the highest-level response in the defense protocol and activate this independent channel. Then, as long as he drags

us outside the boundary afterward, it becomes a physically executed disposition made lawful after the fact.” She clenched her teeth. “He sits at the village entrance every day. He always has this window in his hands.”
It was a deadlock caught between the physical boundary and the permission network.

She turned around and carefully copied the entry numbers of several other related archive items from the terminal into her booklet.
A rigid, cold prompt flashed on the screen: “A single audit order permits access to two cross-referenced dossiers. Allocation exhausted.”
“As long as I remain in this model of body, this hardware interface written into my nerves will always exist.”
She shut off the terminal, raised her head, and gazed for a long time through the thin mist of the wilderness at the row of thin iron columns standing motionless in the wind.
“If its description says ‘auditory interface,’” she turned to me, “that means the signal still has to be transmitted through physical sound. As long as it’s physical, it can be blocked.”
She turned her head toward the direction we had come from. That was the K-14 node we had just passed, the iron-gray low buildings half-buried in the wild grass.

“Since that’s the maintenance station for a physical connection node…” There was no certainty in her voice now, only the cold ruthlessness of someone wagering her life. “The maintenance personnel in the old

era may have kept physical protective equipment inside. We need to see whether there are heavy earmuffs that can completely seal the ears, or just use soundproofing material to make several layers of padding.”
“What if those earmuffs fail? Or the material inside has degraded so badly that it can’t block a pulse designed specifically for this?”
“As long as we can get the protection, whether it can completely block the high-intensity pulse, or whether it will trigger his fallback—”
She turned her gaze back and stared fixedly at the row of thin iron columns ahead.
“Now I’m going to find the earmuffs. This afternoon, I’ll test them with my own ears.”
texts.chapter:v15-21b:event:text-s1-1:
White Tower Maintenance Room · Issue Log (copied from the day’s entry):
“Issued: one maintenance-grade sealed soundproof hood, No. M-114.
　Purpose: candidate’s own entry—‘to
texts.chapter:v15-21b:event:text-s1-2:
pass through a place with sound.’
　Clerk’s note: Pressure-tested before issue; passed.
　Return due: same day. Overdue items are to be reported to the elder on duty.”
texts.chapter:v15-21b:event:text-s6-1: With a tremor still lingering in my fingertips, I opened my eyes inside this intact body. The smell of earth still lingered in my nostrils. I drew in a deep breath of the cool eight o’clock air.
texts.chapter:v15-21b:event:text-s7-1:
For me, that death had happened less than an hour ago.
In the world of the previous round, she checked out the maintenance-grade sealed soundproof hood and went into the ruins with me beneath the acoustic barrier around Zone Eight. But deep inside the ruins,
