texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s7-1: Estelle stood where she was without touching the voided inspection order in her pocket. She looked down at the access badge around her waist, the one identifying her as a candidate, then slowly unclipped it and pressed it against the reader.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s8-1: The red light on the panel blinked once and turned yellow. The screen did not display the usual “WELCOME.” Instead, a line of cold dispatch characters appeared: MATERIAL TAG RECOGNIZED (material tag confirmed).
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s9-1: With a dull unlocking sound, the heavy bolt snapped open from within.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s10-1: “The central index terminal didn’t point us wrong. Those two file identifiers don’t lead to an archive room at all. In the lower-level automated transport protocol, this place is labeled as a ‘consumable-material containment area.’” She watched the gap in the
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s10-2: door slowly widen, her voice tight. “The access control recognized this badge as incoming material. As long as the logistics line below is still powered, the moment it detects a candidate’s hardware identity, it will automatically open the door and swallow it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s11-1: This was a decision she had to make herself. If she crossed over and left an unauthorized access record behind, all her efforts in this position could be ruined. If Sera filled out the verification column truthfully, no one would speak for her.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s12-1: But if she didn’t go in, she could only carry the lie outside back with her and sign that consent form.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s13-1: She pushed the door open and stepped inside.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s14-1: Beyond the door was an area completely absent from the inspection order. The air in the corridor was heavy, carrying the smell of old anti-rust oil.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s15-1: Rows of electronic terminals blinked quietly. Just as we had seen in the outer display area, the actual data on the lower levels had long since been cut off. Only hollow, withered directory shells remained on the screens.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s16-1: But Estelle did not touch those cabinets at all.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s17-1: “This building was converted from an old facility.” Her gaze passed over the cabinets and fell on several heavy iron boxes in the corner of the restricted area, each tagged ‘awaiting centralized incineration.’ “They can clear electronic traces with one click, but physical old records have to be sealed according to procedure.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s18-1: The anti-theft locks at the bottoms of the iron boxes had deteriorated with age, but it still took considerable effort from both of us to pry them open.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s19-1: The first two boxes were full of incomprehensible routine reports and equipment depreciation lists. By the time we pried open the one closest to the wall, sweat had begun to seep down her forehead. Among bundles of discarded forms stuffed in haphazardly, she
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s19-2: searched patiently, clearing out all the clutter placed on top to mislead anyone looking, until she finally pulled three genuine paper records from a moisture-proof bag at the very bottom—the records left behind by the three candidates marked “disposition completed.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s20-1: The hardware traceability codes in the headers had been crudely blacked out with a marker. Estelle held the pages up to the corridor’s pallid
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s20-2: light. Through the backs of the sheets, the indentations left by the force of the pen revealed the original writing: S-04-101, S-04-102, S-04-103.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s21-1: There was no area called S-04 on the new building’s guide map. We went around the mezzanine twice and found nothing.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s22-1: “Look at where they run overhead.” She lowered her voice and pointed at the ceiling.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s23-1: Above the corridor, several unusually thick cooling lines and exhaust ducts stood out sharply amid the tangled network of pipes. They did not connect to the normal rooms on either side. All of them extended northward, eventually disappearing behind what looked like a sealed solid wall.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s24-1: Following the direction of those lines, we felt our way through the secondary corridor, trying several half-open doors along the way. They led either to abandoned storage rooms or ventilation shafts long since deprived of power. We continued until we stopped at the end of a dead end.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s25-1: Set into the wall before us was a gray cast-iron door. It had no sign, and the gap was clamped shut as if it had been welded. The only thing on its surface was a seal pasted across
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s25-2: it. The paper had gone brittle, and bore the seal of the Technical Seat. Beside it, on the peeling wall, was a row of faded characters applied with industrial spray paint: S-04.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s27-1: “The traceability codes on the genuine records point here.” She stared at the seal.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s30-1: She raised her hand, took out her pen, and used its hard tip to cut straight through the brittle seal along the seam of the door. The paper tore with a sharp rasp that sounded especially harsh in the
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s30-2: corridor. The split seal curled as it hung from the doorframe and door panel. The physical mark of unauthorized access had been left here openly. She put away the pen and pressed down on the handle.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s36-1: The hinges gave a dull grinding sound. Beyond the door was no new open space, only a long corridor narrower and darker than the one outside.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s37-1: Rooms filled both sides, one after another, like some kind of dense honeycomb. Each doorway was a section shorter than a normal door, forcing anyone entering or leaving to bend and lower their head. The peepholes were set very low as well, less than an adult’s waist above the floor.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s38-1: I leaned close to examine the nearest door. The cast-iron rim on the inside of the peephole was covered with blackened scratch marks left by fingers clawing desperately outward. Following the scratches down, I saw that half a broken fingernail was still caught at the bottom of the door gap. To look out through that opening, the person inside would have to kneel on the floor.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s39-1: My gaze dropped along the base of the wall. From the depths of the corridor all the way to our feet, at a height of roughly half a foot above the floor, a dark horizontal waterline marked the wall. It was the sediment left behind after prolonged immersion in some liquid, followed by slow seepage and drying.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s42-1: A cast-iron number plate was nailed to the doorframe of the first room, its edges already rusted. “101” was engraved on it. The second was “102,” and the third was “103.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s43-1: Estelle stood before those low doors and took out the genuine paper records from earlier. Within this S-04 area, the endings of the three doorframe numbers matched the traceability codes on the papers marked “disposition completed”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s43-2: exactly. In other words, no matter how grand the procedural names written on those documents sounded, the people holding them had ultimately faced low doors like these—doors they could enter only by bending and lowering their heads.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s44-1: She looked down at the forms in her hands, then up at the claw marks on the inner sides of the doors. Her lips pressed tightly together. She said nothing.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s47-1: I did not respond, because my attention had been drawn to something underfoot.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s48-1: It was a drainage channel running the length of the corridor. It began in the shadows at the far end and led all the way to the threshold behind us.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s49-1: It was a broad, shallow, open channel with no blind corners. When the water was clear, it could easily run through a concealed pipe. Only thick waste liquid carrying heavy sediment and prone to congealing along the way had to travel through an
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s49-2: open channel like this, where any blockage could be cleared directly with an iron shovel. This channel had never been meant to drain clean water. Its inner walls were coated with a thick layer of dark-red, dried sediment, and the smell was acrid.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s50-1: Following the channel’s gentle slope westward, it passed out through the threshold. Looking at the dark-red sediment, I thought of the abandoned retaining pond west of the village, which had given off the same smell for
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s50-2: years and whose surface was filmed with dark-red rust. But I had no way to see through the underground pipe network from here, so I could only press this unsettling suspicion down into the back of my mind for the time being.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s51-1: The highest end, where the drainage channel began, faced the doorway of the last room at the end of the corridor. That room’s doorframe was a section wider than all the others.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s55-1: There was no bed inside, only the remains of a heavy sedimentation chamber that had been violently dismantled. Several thick cast-iron braces held the chamber firmly in a pit, surrounded by pipe openings that had dried black.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s56-1: I switched on my flashlight, and the beam swept across the side of the chamber. A heavy industrial nameplate was riveted there. Its edges were badly corroded, but the stamped lettering was still legible:
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s58-1: The flashlight’s beam remained on the nameplate for several seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s61-1: On a rust-covered control table beside the pit, Estelle found a thick paper ledger. Printed on the cover was National Operator Continuity Project · Status Records.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s63-1: “The binding thread on this ledger is too thick.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s64-1:
By the light of the flashlight, she opened the first page. On the official stamped cover sheet, the most conspicuous thing was a bolded line stating the project’s purpose:
　　『Extend the continuity of candidate consciousness linkage—the record is
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s64-2: not limited to neural states inside the machine. Once a candidate completes registration and connection, this channel will remain open throughout all their waking daily life thereafter, continuously capturing their real-time personality state.』
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s65-1: “So from the moment you passed the verification terminal…” Estelle stared at the line, and the flashlight beam trembled slightly. “As long as you’re alive, everything in your mind will be read without interruption and backed up into this system. And before that…”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s66-1: Estelle’s fingers did not linger on that sentence. She carefully lifted one corner of the page with her fingernail. As the glue made a faint, brittle peeling sound, the name of the new era was stripped away, revealing the yellowed, dry-hard old record sheet pressed tightly beneath it.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s67-1: It was an old form ruled with an exceptionally strict grid. Across the top, the main heading was printed in stark letters: “Political Prisoner Special Camp Transfer and Status Inventory Form.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s69-1:
Old source: Political prisoner 0471. Charge: Speech. Disposition: Capacity extraction. Machine-use material (SEED): Generation complete.
　　Old source: Political prisoner 0892. Charge: Assembly. Disposition: Capacity
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s69-2:
extraction. Machine-use material (SEED): Generation complete.
　　Old source: Political prisoner 1055. Charge: Communications. Disposition: Capacity extraction. Machine-use material (SEED): Generation complete.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s71-1: Her fingers gently flipped back to the new-era cover sheet above. The new heading had long since scrubbed away words such as “political prisoner camp,” and the political-prisoner sources
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s71-2: on the left had become “Candidate 101” and “Candidate 102.” But in the disposition column on the right, the same four words were still written clearly: Capacity extraction. Whatever kind
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s71-3: of person entered, the SEED fields marked “generation complete” were ultimately stripped of their names and lives, becoming the anonymous material called SEED on the right side of the form.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s72-1: At the very bottom of the new ledger page, today’s date had been entered in exactly the same handwriting. The identity field read “Candidate 104,” while the disposition column and SEED generation status on the right were still blank.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s73-1: Estelle unclipped the access badge around her waist, the one identifying her as a candidate. On the back of the badge, beneath the barcode, a line of tiny registration numbers was printed in plain sight. The final three digits were 104.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s74-1: “The person filling out this form doesn’t use the front entrance.” Estelle tapped the cold tabletop lightly with her finger. “These old records are still being updated, but the disposition field for 104 can’t be completed with this dismantled scrap of metal. If the process is still advancing day by day…”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s75-1: She raised her head and carefully swept her gaze over the walls around the pit. At the edge of the flashlight beam, she noticed that the broad, shallow drainage channel did not end at the pit. It disappeared beneath an inconspicuous cast-iron sluice
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s75-2: gate set into the corner. The gate was shut tight and bore no markings, but the layer of dark-red dried sediment along the bottom of the gap was much thicker than outside. Even the seams between the surrounding floor tiles had been soaked through.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s76-1: “That’s a concealed passage.” She pointed at the sluice gate, her voice taut in the empty room. “There has to be an active device connected to it, and it can’t be far from here—the kind of waste liquid that congeals along the way would have clogged this open channel long ago if it had to travel any distance.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s77-1: “The third clause in the consent form they gave me says: the original body enters ‘disposition completed.’ They replaced political prisoners with candidates and took over this process with new instruments, but the anonymous machine-use material extracted from them is still the same.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s78-1: She slowly raised her head. Her gaze passed over the extraction chamber in the pit and turned toward Rooms 101, 102, and 103 outside, with their low doorways. She said nothing more.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s81-1: I watched her back. If she nodded, we could turn around right now, leave the building by the way we had come, and never sign that line. I took half a step back toward the door, making room for her to leave.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s82-1: My movement made no sound, but she noticed. She turned her head and looked at me, then moved her gaze back to the ledger.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s83-1: The flashlight’s beam remained fixed on the blank space in the ledger marked “Candidate 104.” That was the position she intended to take. The witness area outside held all the legitimacy she wanted, and the end of that path was the deep pit at her feet, where she would be taken in on her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s84-1: For a long time, she did not move.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s87-1: She returned the original ledger that had revealed the truth to the rust-covered control table, opened the field notebook she carried with her, and, gripping her pen, added two heavy lines to the page where she had recorded today’s findings.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s89-1:
The old doorframe number at this site, 101, matches the final segment of the traceability codes on the genuine candidate-disposition records exactly.
The abandoned capacity-extraction original and the operator status records reuse the same binding ledger cover.
The old prisoner sources have been covered over by new candidates; the disposition is “capacity extraction” in every case, and the product is identical.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s92-1: “These three points are objective facts I verified with my own eyes. I’ve written them in my notebook.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s96-1: “You’re going to report back with nothing but your word?”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s98-1: “If I take the original away now, security at the building will stop me immediately. Even if I managed to get it out, they would only revoke my qualifications, replace the lock, and calmly look for the next Candidate 104.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s99-1: She put away the notebook and glanced at the broken seal outside the door.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s101-1: “The alarm for tampering at the site will sound soon. Sera will discover that the original hasn’t been taken, but that Candidate 104 has seen the cards. Since we’re going to confront her tonight, that should be enough to make her understand that the
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s101-2: person sitting across from her is no longer someone she can easily fool. Come on. Back to the witness area. If they need my signature on the consent form to complete the appearance of legality, then I still have leverage in my hands before I sign.”
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s104-1: We followed the broad, shallow drainage channel on the floor toward the main entrance.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s105-1: Estelle paused as she stepped through the doorway. She turned back and swept her eyes over the entire corridor one last time.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s106-1: She stood there quietly until she had finished looking, then pulled the heavy door shut.
texts.chapter:v15-22b:event:text-s107-1: On the seam, the seal she had cut open with her pen had split in two, drooping limply on either side of the door. A light breeze passed through, and the torn scraps of paper trembled faintly in the air.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:title: Chapter Twenty-Two, Appendix Four: Each Is Its Own
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s5-1: By the time we left through the broad, gently sloping open channel, returned to the Witnessing Section’s front desk under cover of night, watched the clerk stamp the cancellation mark on the final line of the Limited Audit Order, and made our way back to the foot of the White Tower with mud caked over our feet, it was completely dark.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s6-1: Searchlights followed one another in rings, turning the pale stone slabs of the slope a stark, dreadful white. Estelle had crossed the seal she had cut open herself, and completed all three inspections expressly required within the order.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s7-1: Sera was sitting on the stone steps outside the White Tower.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s8-1: It was no place for an elder to sit. The steps were near the mouth of the wind, and at night even the night patrol did not want to go there. She had drawn her broad cloak tightly around her knees, her whole body folded into itself. Veins showed faintly beneath the backs of her pale hands. The ledger in her grip was closed.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s9-1: When she saw us coming up through the light, she braced herself against her knees and slowly rose.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s16-1: Sera tucked the slipping cloak back into place and looked past us, toward the road we had come from.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s18-1: “I’ve been sitting here for two hours.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s19-1: She did not say that she had come specifically to meet us, or that she had waited this long in the mouth of the wind.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s22-1: Estelle stepped forward and stopped dead only three steps away from her.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s23-1: She looked Sera in the eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s26-1: Sera showed no surprise. She only reached out and pressed hard against the ledger’s cover.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s27-1: Estelle did not lower her head. She continued.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s29-1: “I finished all three locations. After completing everything within the order, I followed the flow of the anomalous files and went in.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s32-1: Sera listened quietly to the confession. She did not ask Estelle what she had seen inside.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s33-1: She only slowly sat back down on the cold stone steps, opened her ledger, spread it flat across her cloak-wrapped knees, and drew a pen from her sleeve.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s34-1: The pen hovered above the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s36-1: “I’ll record the fact that you exceeded the order.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s37-1: Then she raised her eyelids and swept Estelle with a cold gaze.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s39-1: “I won’t ask about what you saw inside.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s40-1: Estelle stood motionless, as if nailed to the ground. After a while, she suddenly smiled. It was brief and sharp.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s42-1: “Thomas did the same thing this afternoon. Don’t ask, don’t record it, the content isn’t mine to deal with.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s43-1: The pen in Sera’s hand descended steadily, drawing a line of ink across the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s45-1: “He wasn’t wrong. If I ask, I have to record it. Once it’s recorded, this ledger has to go up. Once it goes up, who looks at it and how they deal with you won’t be up to me anymore.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s49-1: She had not brought out the three original paper documents hidden beneath the AI laboratory.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s50-1: She only took two things from her bag.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s51-1: One was the stamped Limited Audit Order, with the page showing the lower-level flowchart that Sera had examined that morning tucked beneath it. This was the lawful source of the procedure. She spread the papers flat
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s51-2:
across the rough stone step. The wind was strong, so she felt around for a stone and placed it over the edge.
The other was the field notebook she carried with her. She had closed it tightly and set it beside her feet.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s52-1: She pointed to the diagram rattling on the stone step.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s54-1: “These two under the stone are within the order. I entered the Witnessing Section within the scope you authorized. What you saw on the flowchart this morning—the position of my fingerprints, and the interface reserved for your procedural signature—both of those locations really are in the hidden appendix at the lower level.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s55-1: Then her hand pressed against the notebook.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s57-1: “As for where it went after that, it’s all in this notebook. That’s outside the order. I won’t open it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s60-1: “You haven’t seen them, so you don’t need to write that you have.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s63-1: Sera stared at the closed notebook for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s66-1: Estelle met her gaze without evasion.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s69-1: Estelle pointed to the record on Sera’s knees.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s71-1: “When you wrote that order this morning, you wrote, ‘Anything beyond this scope is outside the authorization.’ You didn’t write that only to stop me.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s73-1: “You wrote it so that if something happened to me, the order would show that you hadn’t authorized it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s74-1: Sera listened to the analysis, her expression as calm as still water, with no embarrassment at being seen through.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s77-1: For once, there was a faint, almost imperceptible sigh in her voice.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s79-1: “I left myself that opening this morning. You’re leaving me a second one now.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s82-1: Sera bent down, picked up the two sheets held beneath the stone, and examined them in the light.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s84-1: “When you found the flowchart this morning, those were only two reserved interfaces. You could still have called them an unfinished waste project.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s85-1: Sera slowly took the papers from her, her gaze falling on the three inspection stamps newly added to the audit order.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s89-1: “But when I pulled the file at the Witnessing Section’s front desk today, the operation receipt printed by the machine automatically attached your secondary-key issuance number in addition to my own audit code. I had them place the cancellation stamp over that line.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s90-1: Sera smoothed the papers flat, pressing her fingers hard over the bright red stamps, staring fixedly at the authorization code beneath them that should never have appeared.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s92-1: “So these two sheets became final, stamped, filed physical evidence. They prove that the parasitic link borrowing my key did not stop at the diagram, but has actually begun running in the system’s lower level.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s95-1: Sera sat down again on the cold stone steps. This time, her once-straight back curved slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s97-1: “I’ve held this seat and signed procedures for twenty years.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s98-1: She spoke as if it were someone else’s affair, forcing each word out.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s100-1: “Every line I signed stated what I was signing—candidate informed, procedure complete, this seat has witnessed it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s101-1: She placed her hands on her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s103-1: “In twenty years, I’ve never gone back and checked how many additional documents were approved below under the signatures I had given. Auditing every application from the past twenty years isn’t part of my work. I never thought to check.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s104-1: She slammed the ledger shut and held it down against her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s106-1: “But today, I’m going to audit the accounts of these twenty years again, one entry at a time. I’m going to find out exactly how many people were quietly entered under my procedures.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s107-1: Estelle moved half a step closer.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s113-1: Sera tightened her cloak, drawing the boundary with absolute clarity.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s115-1: “What I’m dealing with is the misuse of my key. My signature is not your body. Even if they appear on the same file, these are two separate matters.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s118-1: Estelle fell silent. She stood there like a statue pulled taut. After a while, she finally asked the question that had weighed on her since she left that morning.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s121-1: There was no anger in her voice, only the persistence of someone cutting through bone to reach the marrow.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s123-1: “When you read the third clause this morning, your tone was just as flat as when you read the others.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s124-1: The wind loosened the perfectly bound ends of her hair, but her eyes stayed locked onto Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s126-1: “Behind the words ‘the original body enters completed disposition’—over these twenty years, did you truly never suspect what those words meant, or did you simply keep your head down and sign, forbidding yourself from thinking about it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s129-1: A powerful gust surged up, flipping one corner of the ledger on Sera’s knees. The pages rattled violently. Sera reached out with a stiff hand and pressed it down hard. Only after the wind weakened did she speak.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s135-1: Sera withdrew her hand into the heavy sleeve.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s137-1: “The moment I speak, I’ll be giving a definite meaning to something that isn’t written on paper. In this seat, I recognize procedure and procedure only. I don’t guess at what lies outside the paper. If I did, I couldn’t remain in this seat.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s140-1: Estelle understood the refusal. She did not press her further, but crouched down to gather the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s141-1: Halfway through, Sera’s voice came from above.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s143-1: “I’ve read those four words more than forty times.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s144-1: Estelle’s hand froze in midair, her fingertips still pinching the edge of the page.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s145-1: Sera looked into the empty distance, her voice very soft.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s147-1: “I asked about them the first three times.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s148-1: It was as though the wind had been drained away at that moment.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s150-1: “What did the Technical Seat show you?”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s151-1: The corner of Sera’s mouth pulled stiffly.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s153-1: “The Technical Seat didn’t answer. The Logistics Seat threw me a cremation bill. Twenty-one people. Even the weight of the ashes matched, down to the last ounce. Where was I supposed to go and say they were still alive?”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s154-1: For more than ten long seconds, the only thing between them was the stark white sweep of the searchlight.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s155-1: Only when the suffocating pause had finally run its course did Sera brace herself against her numb knees and slowly rise from the steps. The cremation bills from the first three times, and the silence beginning with the fourth, had already drawn the boundary of what she could do today.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s158-1: Sera opened the ledger again, gripped the pen with her stiffened hand, and wrote quickly in the closing entry, without the slightest hesitation.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s159-1: When she finished, she turned the ledger around.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s161-1:
1. Candidate Estelle inspected three locations under the Limited Audit Order and has reported back.
2. Candidate stated that she exceeded the scope of this order. Content not asked, not recorded.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s163-1: There were still only two dry lines of official prose. The third line was left blank, a broad expanse of white stretching to the footer.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s165-1: “You can write another line. Write that today you already knew your authority had been secretly misused.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s166-1: Sera held the pen without moving.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s168-1: “That isn’t what you want me to write. You want me to write, ‘I was prepared for this, and I wasn’t complicit.’”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s170-1: “I won’t write that. If they follow the issue records on the file back to me and ask why I approved your entry into the Witnessing Section, when they trace it all the way back, I’ll answer
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s170-2: according to the second clause. The second clause says I never asked what exactly you saw in violation of the order—that part is true. I can answer for it. I can’t offer anything more.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s173-1: Estelle put the paper away and straightened.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s175-1: “I submitted an application in the Witnessing Section to expand the access range. And at tomorrow’s oath ceremony, I’ll ask the Technical Seat one question in public.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s177-1: “I won’t tell you in advance what I’ll ask. Even if that application still hasn’t reached the end of the process after seven working days, it will be a record. Even if he refuses to answer tomorrow, there needs to be an elder present to prove that I asked.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s180-1: Sera did not use her authority to force the crucial question out of her.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s182-1: “The forwarded application has to pass through me. Whether you want to ask how he made this subprocedure permanent, or where the old bodies marked for completed disposition ultimately went under this process, I’ll be there when you ask.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s184-1: “You’re asking him within my procedure. I need to hear whatever he answers. Otherwise, if he denies it afterward, you’ll have nothing to produce. The same applies to me.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s187-1: The cards were all on the table. Sera turned and walked toward the White Tower. After a few steps, she stopped without looking back.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s191-1: “Today, you brought back the pages I should have seen. I’ll remember that.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s193-1: “But the application you submitted to the investigation cabinet this afternoon was sent under the identity of ‘senior-seat candidate.’ That identity can be cut off by the system at any time. Everything that can be returned is in this ledger. I can’t produce what cannot be preserved outside it.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s198-1: Sera’s footsteps gradually receded up the slope, finally merging with the wind. On the empty stone steps, only the two of us remained. Estelle lifted her head and looked at the heavy darkness on the White Tower’s highest level.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s200-1: “The oath is tomorrow. If you don’t go sign the Renewal Covenant tonight, your candidate eligibility will count as forfeited from midnight onward. Are you still going to sign tonight?”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s204-1: “When I left this morning, I thought that once I saw what was behind the seal, I would know what to do.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s206-1: “Now I’ve seen it. I still don’t know.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s209-1: She turned and walked toward the boundless darkness below the slope. Her boots moved slowly over the stone slabs.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s211-1: “If I sign, then legally I really am handing this body over.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s212-1:
Her voice trembled faintly in the night wind. That cold physical reality had finally risen back to the surface. No official document could cover it.
She stopped at the foot of the steps and looked back at the elder gradually disappearing into the night wind.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s215-1: She turned her head and looked at me.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s218-1: I walked down the steps and stood in front of her. The searchlights on the slope stretched our shadows long.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s221-1: I did not mention what had become of this body in the previous cycle, or the even worse predicament she would face immediately if she lost her eligibility.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s223-1: “If you don’t sign, then right now the system really does contain only the case-filing record you entered just now, with nothing else. The rule Sera reminded you of is real: once your eligibility is cut off at midnight, when the investigation
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s223-2: cabinet system checks the submitting party’s current status, the application bearing the candidate’s name will immediately be voided as an illegal request. The opening you tore through today will be completely sealed by tomorrow morning.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s224-1: She listened, her breathing gradually settling, as if forcing herself to accept the cruel rule.
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s226-1: “Only by keeping the shell of senior-seat candidate can you nail this matter down at tomorrow’s oath ceremony.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s229-1: “But even if you sign tonight, you still won’t truly have handed over your body. As long as your brain hasn’t been replaced, I can take you away from here at any time. If you don’t want to walk onto that platform carrying this covenant, we can leave now.”
texts.chapter:v15-22e:event:text-s230-1: She did not answer at once. She only lowered her head and looked at the closed notebook. After a long time, she raised her head and gripped mine tightly in return. Her fingers were forceful, her cold knuckles pressing painfully against my hand. She was not looking for a way out. She was confirming what could support her.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:title: Sea Line Five: Coup
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s2:
Ark Berth Allocation Register · Selected Revisions (Launch Site Archives):
“Initial version: 100 passengers.
Second revision: 124 passengers. Twenty-four added to the family column.
Third revision: 128 passengers.
Fourth

revision: 139 passengers. Two technical berths added, nine accompanying berths added.
Fifth revision: 142 passengers.
Sixth revision: 150 passengers.
Wording of deletion and amendment note: ‘Volume and mass can both be

renegotiated. Eligibility subject to review at any time.’”

(Every revision bears a bright-red official seal. Even before the sixth edition, the steadily expanding list had already breached the vessel’s original capacity limit.)
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s5: This transfer of power, which seized control of the core laboratory, had been brewing for five full years.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s6: No one ever witnessed the dispossession firsthand. There were no tank tracks grinding across the streets, and the newspaper headlines still announced production gains for the new season.
It was a bureaucratic purge of the technical system, directed personally by the highest ranks. But because it completely ended the old power structure, later generations called it a coup.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s1: Over the course of those five years, several unrelated sets of records began to interlock in time: the swelling passenger lists from successive editions, the sudden redirection of the Empire’s budget flows, and a slip of paper repeatedly mentioned in later review testimony, called a “review sheet.”

Between the first and third years, the construction of the time machine gradually revealed itself as a desperate failure. To calm the rulers who had fallen into panic, the physicists put forward an unverified theoretical hypothesis—they suspected that

the so-called “capacity curse” that drove people mad was actually a localized physical field anchored by the mass of this planet. The head of state seized on this lifeline at once, convinced that if they could only fly beyond the planet’s gravitational

field, they could escape it completely. Vast resources began flowing secretly into the spacecraft project’s accounts. They had to find another way forward with this ark while maintaining the illusion, on the surface, that everything was normal.
The ark’s actual compartments were astonishingly large, large enough to carry a sizable group, but the ark’s core circle clearly had no intention of spending life-support funds on everyone.

By the fifth year, an unspoken understanding had finally been reached. The high officials in the military police, supply offices, and other departments cooperated in slowly starving the time machine on paper—budgets tightened, approvals for critical equipment sat on desks, and its former security authority

was withdrawn. In return, the head of state bought the collusion of these partisans with ark berths. The core circle issued each eligible high official a thin sheet of paper, with a column deliberately left at the bottom called “Review.” Reviewed once a year, two words in a single line: Still present.
A sheet of paper that could be voided at any moment was enough to buy their wholehearted cooperation.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s2: During the first five years of the spacecraft project, cracks quietly spread through the power structure. When the upper ranks began looking for scapegoats for the machine’s hopelessness, Krennik became

the first sacrifice cast out. Until the fifth year, Tarkin and Wilford each turned the gears in the shadows, and it all finally closed around a coup that would completely dismantle Heisenberg’s power empire.

Krennik was thrown out in early winter of the fifth year. It was the first clear signal of the coup the upper ranks proudly called “bloodless.”
As one of the time machine’s joint chief designers, he had personally signed off on the

falsified engineering progress reports for years one through three. Now the upper ranks urgently needed someone with enough weight to take the blame for the machine’s failure, while stripping the core laboratory of its technical authority.
On an old tape that survived, Heisenberg recounted what happened that afternoon in his hoarse voice.

Two in the afternoon, a small conference room on the third floor of the administration building.
When Krennik pushed open the door and entered, his hands were empty. The notice was phrased mildly: he was requested to provide a technical explanation of the fourth batch of data.

Heisenberg was already seated at the table, gripping the application to inspect the original data. Under laboratory regulations, all he had to do was raise his hand, slap the paper onto the table, and request verification against the original measurement records. That would trigger compulsory technical arbitration and suspend the review procedure for at least a week.

He looked at the bureaucrats across the table, who had just taken over security authority for the core laboratory.
He drew his hand back from the edge of the hidden pocket at his chest.
The person in the central seat accused Krennik of signing the falsified progress reports in an attempt to conceal the deliberate alteration of the original physical data.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s3:
Krennik placed both hands on the tabletop.
“The words on the progress reports are mine,” Krennik said. “But there is no break in the original data indicating human alteration. The physical measurements are right there. You can bring in anyone to verify them.”

The chairing official turned coldly toward the corner. “Was everything just said recorded?”
The clerk nodded.
“Good. In the conclusion column, write: ‘The subject has confessed to falsifying the data.’”

Krennik tried to force an explanation of the technical details, proving that falsifying progress reports and altering physical constants were two entirely different matters. He got as far as his third sentence before being interrupted.
“Krennik, watch your wording. There is no room here for any technical discussion.”

The dozen-odd people in the room solemnly debated for three full minutes whether the form should be headed “Technical Explanation” or “Review Opinion.” When the reformatted sheet was passed down, the committee members did not even look at it. They signed and pushed it aside.
Throughout the entire process, no one uttered the words “sabotage of the project.” The final ruling used only the weightless phrase “transferred for handling.”
After the meeting, Heisenberg went to an empty corner, tore the crumpled inspection application into pieces, and threw it in the trash.

The next morning, Krennik was taken away from the final assembly workshop. A notice was posted immediately afterward: deliberate sabotage, number-one traitor, undercover for many years. When the notice went up, Heisenberg only stood in the crowd and watched. He did not speak for him.

Once the technical barrier at the top had been dismantled, Tarkin handled the physical clear-out. His internal-affairs network was a black hole that reported only through a single line to the highest level.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s4:
The declassified files preserve Tarkin’s successive budget requests from the preceding years.
Even before Krennik’s fall, he had begun expanding the internal-affairs network in the name of preventing “project saboteurs.” In the official files, the reasons Tarkin gave for requesting special funds kept changing.

At first, he wrote “sabotage activities frequent,” then “remaining elements have gone underground,” until, in the year of the coup, it became “new forms of underground activity discovered.” The authorities announced that “remnant infiltrators” had been completely purged five times.

He rejected his subordinates’ proposals for large-scale centralized investigations. Moderate bleeding, sustained over the long term, was what allowed him to request the huge funds needed to keep the internal-affairs machine

running year after year. Under this mechanism, whether or not Heisenberg had actually planted underground lines at the grassroots, the internal-affairs network would precisely manufacture the corresponding “remnants.”

Old Grieg, the warehouse keeper, died under this budget logic.
He had kept the accounts at Warehouse Four for half his life, and there was an old, rough welding scar on his thumb. Before winter, while taking inventory, Old Grieg discovered that a batch of special copper wire was missing. Afraid the

loss would be charged to him, he put on his reading glasses that night, trembling as he filled out the shortage report, then hurried to the internal-affairs office to insist that he had not stolen it, even swearing with the scarred hand. Heisenberg never even heard his name throughout the entire affair.

Three days later, Tarkin’s people labeled the missing copper wire “sabotage by remnants” and, in the same motion, sent Old Grieg to the camp as an “internal accomplice subverted by Heisenberg’s remnants.”
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s5: His name appeared on the camp roster for fourteen consecutive months. Every day’s entry recorded forced sorting of scrap cable, with highly toxic insulating coating seeping into the beds of
his fingernails. On the first day of the fifteenth month, Old Grieg’s name vanished into thin air. There was no illness record, no death certificate. The line on the form had simply been erased.
Once the time machine’s personnel and grassroots support had been drained away, the final step was to cut off its supply line. The head of state bypassed Heisenberg and handed the spacecraft over
to Wilford, an expert in numerical accounting, transferring the last and largest share of resources entirely to the ark. The time machine’s laboratory thereby became an island left to starve.

At the sixth revision of the roster, the upper ranks forced the total number of passengers up to one hundred and fifty, nearly touching the physical limit of the life-support system. Most of the newly added names belonged to nobles and their families, people of no use whatsoever to interstellar migration.

Every faction declared its own berths indispensable, while trying to push the other factions’ supplies off the ship. From the first day the project was established, Wilford’s design brief had stated it plainly: this ship had

no capacity to return, and there would be no subsequent voyages. Takeoff meant farewell. It had to carry, in a single departure, every seed of civilization’s survival. This was no longer an expedition, but a desperate escape.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s6: That night, the sixth revision approval lay open on the table beside a stack of proposals to reduce the cryogenic payload labeled “Reserve Two.” It consisted of plant seeds, soil cultures, and livestock embryos intended for the new shore. The upper ranks

hinted that the safety-redundancy mass originally reserved for accidents during deep-space flight had long since been erased and replaced with berths for living people. If he removed these mute dead things as well, more berths could be freed for nobles.

Those four sheets of scrap paper, covered in physical-limit parameters, were clipped to the end of the record.
In the amendment column of the approval, he entered his rejection:
“If the ark is to possess the capacity to sustain migration after arrival, the ecological payload cannot be reduced. All deep-space safety redundancy has already been transferred to life support. There is no line left to retreat behind.”
“Take it off, and they die anyway.”

With cold parameters, he drew the line. Along the edge of the scrap paper was a deep mark where someone had dragged a fingernail hard across it. But this non-negotiable ecological payload meant that the

berths for living people were locked completely at the number one hundred and fifty. The list could never expand again, and the various powers could only fight one another over the limited allocation.
In contrast to the roster packed with noble families was another long list: the waiting list. It held countless young technical officers and researchers who had passed extremely difficult

engineering certifications and spent years struggling at the grassroots. They possessed genuine qualifications for advancement, yet were permanently blocked outside those one hundred and fifty berths.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s7: Over the years of wrangling that followed, another force gradually took shape in the wind and snow outside the city. To survive, the lower laborers spontaneously formed grassroots mutual-aid groups. This was the distortion, in the end times, of the

“Common Observation Groups” that had once recorded celestial anomalies—they no longer watched the stars. Before winter, they went to collect lamp oil from the ration office; at night, they carried lamps through the streets on patrol. This was the embryonic

form of what later became known as the “Night Watch Movement.” When someone in a household died, they went to carry out and bury the body, piecing together a eulogy from incomplete phrases. The upper ranks had not founded them, but the aging head of

state recognized this grassroots mechanism for recording “who was still present.” Through secret channels, he issued additional nominal rations under the official cover of “mutual defense,” trying to draw strength from this anger amid hunger and cold.

Whenever some high official overreached on the ark’s berths, the official rations for that district would suddenly be cut off. Word quickly spread among the lamp-bearing night patrols that some official residence had withheld lifesaving supplies. At the

same time, the internal-affairs department tacitly withdrew the guards, leaving behind a vacuum of power. The head of state could not order them to kill anyone. He merely loosened the bars around power, allowing the lamp-bearing crowds, driven by their

own deprivation and hatred, to pour into the unprotected residences. This feverish undercurrent did complete several traceless purges for the upper ranks, but it was also a blind beast that could turn on the official bureaucratic network at any moment.

In his later years, the head of state no longer had the energy to control the situation after the reshuffling. Every faction clung to its existing allocation. While he was alive, the names on the list could still maintain a faint balance each year through that “review sheet,” which could be revoked at any moment.
The head of state finally died fifteen years after the coup. For the sake of absolute security in his later years, he had deliberately chosen as his successor a pure administrator with no independent

military or police background and no involvement in the ark project. This new head of state inherited the highest title, but not the private grudges and debts the old man had signed with boarding passes.

The successor’s first act after taking power was to stand on the high platform and publicly announce that all the old boarding passes from the previous regime were void. All qualifications would be reviewed by him.
In his inauguration speech, he made public two deadly files: one was the one-hundred-and-fifty-person “review sheet” issued

by the former head of state; the other was the true report from the first-stage time machine experiment, together with reproduced copies of the joint signatures showing that the upper circle had known the truth—that the loop would close within five seconds and the subject would inevitably burn up—yet had signed and concealed it anyway.

The successor also broadcast the draft decree establishing new technical-certification hearings across all channels, trying to prove that he was not looting the system but correcting the systematic lies of the old era, which had kept those with genuine qualifications outside the hatch. These two public reports and the new decree ignited the powder keg that had been building for years.

The lower workers who had long been unable to obtain medicine, and the junior officials who held engineering certifications yet had spent years blocked from the waiting list by nobles, finally turned their new and old hatred toward the old alliance. The time machine promises of the ruling party had collapsed completely, and the political credit of the old system vanished at that moment.

The successor thereby won the feverish support of the lower classes and completely dismantled the tangled web of interests belonging to the old factions. But he overestimated the speed with which order could be rebuilt. He had no independent leverage with which to force through a new list. On the day the old list became invalid, the fragile alliance

of interests defected on the spot. The military police, administration, supply offices, and launch site—every review interface fell into the hands of people unwilling to accept the passenger lists of rival factions. They withheld one another’s boarding approvals, ultimately forming a comprehensive interdepartmental deadlock of refusal orders.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s8: As the transition between old and new spun completely out of control in the deadlock, the newly rising fanatic sect—the Church of Convergence—seized control of the launch site. After taking over, they sealed off the

launch shaft beneath the ark. The Church of Convergence did not complete the escape of any list. They declared that it was no longer a spacecraft, but evidence of the arrogant old humans’ crime: an attempt to abandon

the earth and betray their shared future. This ark, physically capable of taking off and sufficient to sustain civilization among the stars, was treated as a monument of shame and nailed forever to the launch gantry.
But the ark’s total collapse came more than a decade later. In the early winter of the fifth year, the dispossession of the core laboratory had only just reached its end.

On the third day after the coup ended, the nameplate was removed from Heisenberg’s office door. Lysenko formally took over the core laboratory. Before this, he had submitted a “Operator Expansion Program” to the

head of state. This new concept, which claimed to use genetic technology to create high-capacity artificial bodies, gave the upper ranks a perfect step down—they could finally turn their gaze away from the old

machine in broad daylight without publicly admitting the complete failure of temporal displacement. This was also the true leverage that made the head of state favor him and use the opportunity to replace Heisenberg.

Because the most essential temporal-displacement formula remained known only to Heisenberg, the head of state could not simply sign his name onto the execution list. Heisenberg was demoted on the spot and became Lysenko’s subordinate.

Over the following months, he moved like an obedient ghost, maintaining the lowest-level pipelines of the accident-recording system. Under cover of this drudgery, he quietly checked every local file and surviving tape. In the process,

he had already verified that Old Grieg’s fate was no isolated case. More than that, across different local dates, he experienced several extremely brief five-second lapses of awareness. When he recovered, he would always find

desperate notes in his own handwriting beside him, or a final message left in the portable recorder. The handwriting on the notes was chaotic, desperately recording another purge date and the final sight of the pure-white execution room.

Using a body at the same temporal and spatial coordinates as a receiving end, “Heisenbergs” from other worlds forcibly connected during the five seconds before their executions. Objectively, their bodies would be occupied for only

those five seconds, then returned to their local owners to continue forward; but the projected consciousnesses would close head-to-tail at the end of those five seconds, falling backward forever, completely trapped in an endless return.

This desperate cross-world verification revealed to the local Heisenberg a high-risk distribution of possible futures: the purge targeting him was not some distant possibility. It had already occurred as a confirmed reality in many

connected worlds, and could descend on this coordinate without warning at any time. If he did not want to be pushed into the pure-white execution room like the owners of those notes, he would have to tear open a path for himself.

He could not wait for the formal purge list to be issued. That winter night, he released a group of political prisoners from the AI laboratory and cut the main power switch amid the chaos. Large numbers of prisoners awaiting execution and lower-ranking researchers pushed open the heavy isolation

gates and were released as bait. Heisenberg did not lead them through the flames and gunfire. He coldly used them as human shields to draw the fire. Several blood-covered young people beside him took advantage of a blind spot in the barrage and plunged with him into the deep ventilation duct.
That year, the Heisenberg who escaped left Lysenko and the vast AI project that was still running behind on the surface.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-05-coup:event:text-s9: He hid like a rat in the foul underground waterways and abandoned mine tunnels. In the darkness beyond the blast door where the fan had stopped turning, the lower-class youths
who viewed him with hatred and suspicion were forced to reach a first, cold temporary pact with this ruthless former superior who had used them as bait. They did not know what
the man who possessed the core formula carried on his back. They only knew that, in these depths where even the air tasted of blood, survival meant relying on what was in his head.

This was the starting point of the Conservation Society that Heisenberg would later rebuild. Over the following fifteen years, Lysenko, left on the surface, continued building and recording that vast machine as usual. Meanwhile, the remnants who had formed an alliance out of

suspicion and having no other choice in the abandoned service corridors eventually made their way into the deepest independent reservoirs underground, where they joined other escapees and grew into an underground resistance force large enough to overturn everything. As for Krennik,

who had been cast out as bait, he was not executed immediately after being taken away. Some said he later left testimony. Others said he was imprisoned in a black cell known only to the internal-affairs office. His fate, like those fifteen underground years, sank into the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s3-1: Among the mountains of purge dossiers, Estelle found an older case—one that predated the fall of Klernik and the other engineering officials. More precisely, it was a theoretical school erased in the second year after the founding of the nation.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s4-1: Along the edge of the enormous gap deliberately torn from that page of the almanac, Estelle found a paper-thin fragment of surviving record.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s7-1: “Theory Group, [at] a certain research institute. Collectively dealt with in the second year after the founding of the nation for illegally organizing an academic network and spreading pessimistic doctrines of determinism. Leader executed.”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s10-1: The leader’s name had originally been printed in that volume. But when I leaned closer, all I could see was a viscous black mass—the name had been firmly covered by the censor’s ink, layer after layer, until it became a taboo symbol that could never again be recognized.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s11-1:
Estelle found a scorched internal critique in a heap of wastepaper. Pasted inside it was a fragment of a lecture, along with the theory group’s complete statement at its hearing.
The edges of the paper had
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s11-2: grown brittle. It was a hearing record prepared for the officials below, already consumed by the fever of construction. The writing on the lecture fragment had pressed deep marks into the back of the paper:
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s13-1:
“We have no intention of obstructing the project. We are only stating the solution to a set of equations. Time and space are not an infinitely extending plain. The underlying capacity that sustains existence is an exacting constant.”
The handwriting paused here,
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s13-2:
then was heavily circled:
“You cannot erase, out of nothing, causality that has already occurred within a single universe. The five-second reversal you are pursuing is, in essence, a forced crossing of the universe’s boundary, cutting sideways into the past of
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s13-3:
another parallel branch.
“This forced cross-boundary anchoring is not free. Once the connection is established, to maintain the old branch that should have collapsed, the system will be forced to occupy indefinitely the underlying capacity on which all connected
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s13-4:
worlds jointly depend.
“Over time, this is like attaching a set of one-way dead-loop pipes to the bottom of a gigantic tank. That capacity has not vanished into thin air. It has been locked fast inside the physical connections sustaining countless abandoned timelines.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s13-5: As long as the cross-boundary connection continues, the capacity drawn away can never be released. Once the total water level of what has been occupied falls below the safety threshold, it will drag all the connected worlds into an irreversible common collapse…”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s15-1: Beside the equations on the lecture fragment, someone had drawn a gigantic red X, the strokes cutting through the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s17-1:
Estelle said nothing. She turned and pulled a calculation draft with traces of adhesive from another stack of Heisenberg’s early personal dossiers.
She spread the two pages side
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s17-2: by side on the table. No expertise in physics was needed to see the relationship: Heisenberg’s calculation draft had directly pasted in the lecture’s central system of equations.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s18-1: But in that calculation draft, the original author’s derivation of the latter half—the system’s collapse—had been crudely cut away. Heisenberg had added his own annotations beside the equations, turning a set of formulas originally meant to warn that the world would collapse into a practical tool for calculating the time machine’s initial parameters.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s19-1: In the internal critique of the school, Heisenberg had taken only its mathematical structure.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s22-1: “What Semmelweis recorded underground was clearly data showing an abnormal decline in usable capacity…” I stared at the pasted draft, my voice tightening. “And this group had already calculated the outcome of continuously pumping it away in the second year after the founding of the nation.”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s24-1:
But at the bottom of the appraisal materials for the purge of the school, Heisenberg’s authorization number was stamped in plain sight.
The entire appraisal was extremely brief, only
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s24-2: four sentences. It did not directly issue a death sentence, but within the process led by the secret police, its final four words cut off any possibility of academic reconsideration:
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s26-1: “This claim has no basis in physics and no practical use in engineering.”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s28-1:
The year he signed those words, Heisenberg was thirty-two—the height of his rise within the ministries, preparing to take control of the entire physics establishment with his own hands.
There was no defense, no
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s28-2: technical discussion. In language that best satisfied the political demands, he blocked every path of derivation. The leader became a corpse beneath a firing squad. The rest endured until death in labor camps.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s31-1:
That appraisal, bearing Heisenberg’s authorization number, became the source template for every silencing document that followed.
At the relay station, we saw the directive that prescribed how to
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s31-2: slide “not detected” step by step toward “does not exist.” Heisenberg’s effortlessly uttered phrase, “has no basis in physics,” later became the most irrefutable judgment in the administrative courts.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s34-1:
Early in the project, Klernik, the engineering bureaucrat whose defeat had already begun to show, was handed over for investigation.
One was a scholar from the theory group crushed in the second year after the founding of the nation; the other, an engineering bureaucrat dragged out early to take the
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s34-2:
blame. In all the declassified investigation files, there was not a single record of a letter or meeting between them.
But after the coup in the fifth year, until the eve of the Great Purge, the phrase that appeared constantly in the newspapers became “the illegal doctrine and Klernik’s remnant faction.”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s37-1: “To merge two entirely unrelated cases into one, the system requires a procedure.” Estelle pushed aside a stack of files. “And if it’s a procedure, it has to leave a document.”
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s39-1: Estelle found the “Directive on Consolidated Handling of the Case Concerning the Illegal Doctrine and the Case Concerning Klernik’s Subversion.” The main text contained only eight characters:
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s44-1: The traitor’s sabotage explained why the machine failed; the traitor’s dissemination of theory explained why people began to waver ideologically. Once they were handled together, every academic discussion of the doctrine became support for sabotage in the case files.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s51-1: The endpoint of this purge went far beyond the first group of fallen scholars. In the years that followed, whenever a young researcher driven to the brink by an engineering bottleneck tried to
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s51-2: bring out those forbidden equations and check them again—the moment he put pen to paper, administrative procedure had already made him a traitor deliberately aiding the sabotage of the project.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s54-1:
Once the system that turned verification into a capital crime had been fully established, it no longer needed Heisenberg as its exalted guide.
That very afternoon, the workers changing the slogans in the square brushed
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s54-2: thick paste, without a flicker of emotion, over the remains of Heisenberg’s own name on the wall. Though he had been demoted to Lysenko’s subordinate and still handled the practical engineering of the AI laboratory
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s54-3: and accident records, he now had to swallow the humiliation of surrendering the highest political decision-making authority and take the blame for the low-level logs that went wrong every day under the new appointee.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s59-1: Not long afterward, on the eve of his decision to escape, Heisenberg encountered the Leader face-to-face for the last time in the ministry’s long corridor.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s60-1: The old man was surrounded by attendants. They were forced to stop and stand facing each other for several seconds.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s61-1: According to those who accompanied him, the old man’s manner was extremely affable. He even reached out and patted Heisenberg’s arm warmly, asked carefully after his health, then said earnestly that they were counting on him to keep a firm grip on the
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s61-2:
practical engineering of the AI laboratory ahead.
In those few minutes, no one mentioned the enormously expensive machine, the chief’s replacement, or the ship being built in secret. When he finished speaking, the old man left surrounded by his retinue.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s62-1: That kindly hand easily pressed the former chief scientist into a position where he could only carry out orders from others.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s67-1: But the apocalyptic prediction that had been cut away was eventually picked up again, after his escape, during the long underground years.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s68-1: It was a history we had already witnessed among the remnants of the underground archive. In the review recording where he finally stopped running from it and completed
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s68-2: the derivation of the entire dead end, Heisenberg spread out two documents spanning more than a decade, alongside the index of every accident in the imperial system.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s69-1:
One was the original report of the sudden plunge in pool levels recorded by Semmelweis before his death, a relic of the first generation of the Covenant of Conservation that Heisenberg inherited when he took over the underground network after his escape.
The other was the yellowed hearing transcript from the theory school he had personally condemned, leading to the collective execution of its members.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s70-1: Before the blackboard in that air-raid shelter, when Heisenberg said to the camera, “What if these gaps were never counting population at all?”, overturning every established premise, he did more than align the dates of Semmelweis’s
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s70-2:
pool-level records.
What he truly did was reconnect, in full, the disintegration prediction he had cut away to appease his superiors, together with the cross-boundary equations originally meant as a warning, to the chain of derivation.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s73-1: After the recording finished, Estelle unlocked the last encrypted archive brought up from deep within the White Tower. On the screen in the ship’s cabin, we checked every hatch-opening, hatch-closing, and ballast log produced from the time machine’s birth through its idle-running period, without missing a single entry.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s75-1: Among tens of thousands of logs, every entry corresponded to a hard connection at the system’s foundation. No authority could directly erase the human ballast and launch signature that accompanied a hatch lock. But in all the records, none corresponded to the highest authority who had set all this in motion.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s76-1: When he was gravely ill in his final years, he had indeed considered using the machine, fulfilling the promise of “returning to the past to save oneself” made in the propaganda. Estelle brought up a classified launch application permanently
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s76-2: stuck in the archiving stage. In its signature field, there was only his title, “Leader,” and a string of numbers—his true name had long since been dissolved into an administrative symbol through the cycles of countless similar procedures.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s77-1: Sealed together with the application was a medical log from that day. The data showed that, given his physical condition at the time, he could easily have entered the ring-shaped chamber in a wheelchair. But forty minutes after the application was issued, a withdrawal order directly
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s77-2:
halted the warm-up sequence.
The order contained no explanation, only his personal seal. He had known from the arrival of the first human-experiment reports that it was an execution room with no exit.
The signed application, then swiftly withdrawn, naturally became an exhibit in the
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s77-3: Inner Circle bureaucratic archive chain. With a single application, the highest authority proved that he was present alongside that great machine, then left every subsequent assessment and test suspended in that afternoon, an account of arrears that would never receive a follow-up.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s78-1: But the machine he had personally authorized to be built never carried even a milligram of his ballast—not until the final shutdown phase, when a preconfigured circuit physically burned out the coupling core from outside.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s80-1: “This is the past they said they would save at any cost.” I stared at the withdrawal order on the screen, my hand resting on the cold control console.
texts.chapter:v15-h05b:event:text-s81-1:
Estelle slowly closed the cover of the holographic projector.
Outside the ship, in the depths of space, the homeworld abandoned in the dead end of the old era silently rotated, like a withered fruit pit.
texts.chapter:chapter-23-platform:title: Chapter Twenty-Three: The Platform
texts.chapter:chapter-23-platform:event:text-s:
Another universe without Yuna’s interference.
Beside the power-supply alcove deep inside the external disaster-recovery station, the condenser pipes gave off a dull, low hum.
Estelle stood before the enormous screen of the local terminal. Twenty minutes ago, we

had followed an abandoned maintenance shaft outside the Platform settlement down into the station and forcibly connected to its deep-level permissions. Now she had called up an underlying archive log, paging through the error records folded away by the system.

A red warning flickered on the screen, buried deep in the lower levels: the “Platform” settlement surrounding this disaster-recovery facility had a shortfall in its remitted quota stretching back twenty years.
The system’s automatic response to an account mismatch was to reduce the settlement’s winter-supply allotment proportionally.

Deep in the terminal’s records, Estelle quickly paged through the early construction archives.
“This place doesn’t just manage disaster recovery.” She traced a section of engineering specifications from the Old Empire. “It

was built to audit the populations of the outer settlements in the first place, so the hardware framework never included an interface for forcibly closing an account. Those old-school designers recognized only one thing…”

She paused, pointing to a line of green text flickering at the bottom of the screen. “An irreversible termination mark may be appended only after receiving zero-vital-sign telemetry uploaded by a physical facility. If the person

doesn’t die, the account can’t be closed.”
In the electronic authorization document associated with the log beneath that green text, the source of the mechanism was stated plainly: commissioned construction—the Old Empire Inspectorate.

“It’s a deadlock.” Estelle looked at the screen. “As long as the biological monitor on someone is still transmitting, the system won’t recognize them as dead. You could put their urn right here and it still wouldn’t help.”

Among the paper attachments scanned into the system was a manual describing how superior institutions could exercise special overwrite authority. A twelve-step operating guide that had originally filled one page had now been forcibly overwritten

with a blank field through administrative permissions.
The root directory log of the electronic system also retained an operational record from more than a hundred years ago: “Inspectorate has permanently revoked this network’s master control key.”

“Someone thought the back door was too dangerous. They destroyed it in the electronic system, and didn’t leave the paper instructions intact either.” She examined the verification code for the error and searched downward through the Platform settlement’s suspended accounts.
“There was an incident twenty years ago.” She pointed to an old record on the screen. “Thirty-seven households, seventy people, disappeared into thin air.”

Because the master control key had been permanently revoked, the suspended account had become a dead end. But the trunk-line logs left behind by the disaster-recovery station truthfully recorded the seventy people’s

destination: twenty years ago, the Inner Circle took them away in the name of “support.” The receiving-site number pointed to a labor camp. They worked there, but in the Platform’s records their status was “no contact.”

The settlement had no administrative interface for recording population transfers in the first place. Once someone left, the system at their place of origin could only keep waiting for their biological monitor to go offline. And they had been forced into a deep shaft that could not transmit even a signal back to the surface. Whether

they had lived or died down there over those twenty years, the system at their place of origin would never receive the zero signal that signified termination.
So the underlying accounts remained locked to those seventy people. Every year, the remittance quota issued from above continued to count all seventy toward the village’s baseline.
“If they were already gone, why didn’t the settlement report them missing to the authorities and have those positions written off?” I asked.

“They didn’t dare.” Estelle’s fingers pressed against the deduction order on the screen, her knuckles turning white. “They couldn’t meet that year’s quota, so they handed people over to cover the account. Once the administrative system above received a missing-person report about that private exchange of people for quota, someone would be sent down to investigate, and the whole thing would be exposed.”

She slid a specific deduction ledger in front of me.
“For example, this household. Twenty years ago, their eldest adult son was taken away.” Her voice echoed through the empty
station. “After that, the two old people who remained and a seven-year-old girl lost not only their able-bodied laborer. Every year, they also had to surrender the output quota of the
