eldest son who was, officially, still alive in the village—an output that did not exist. When they couldn’t meet it, the system simply deducted these three people’s winter rations.”
Those three people, growing older and thinner, had carried the empty household account of a son who would never return and gone hungry in his place for twenty years.

She drew out her pen and copied the list of all thirty-seven households, the associated ration deductions, and the deadlock that could never be reconciled, word for word into her investigation ledger.

The underground station’s heating circulation gave off the heavy sound of a pump drawing water.
The anti-counterfeiting deadlock, originally meant to stop higher authorities from casually erasing the existence of living people, had, under crushing quota pressure and an unavailable administrative interface, locked this outer settlement inside twenty years of punishment.

The countdown to twenty-two hundred was nearly over.
On the way here, I had told her that at that hour my cross-boundary attention would be forcibly pulled back into another universe. The
“Arno” belonging to this world would face the days ahead with her, carrying these uncovered deadlocked accounts and the list of thirty-seven households whose people had been taken away.

Estelle closed the ledger and tucked it against her body. She turned and looked into my eyes, calmly waiting for the faint vertigo at exactly twenty-two hundred, waiting for this world’s Arno to regain complete control of this body.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:title: Chapter Twenty-Three Appendix: Replaceable
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s1-1:
That Queue · Evaluation Column (the last run still left on the screen):
“Not entered into the queue. Reason: Replaceable.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s4-1: In this deep cold-storage zone, the regional main-control terminal had been running data verification for nearly two hours, tracing the seventy names of the Taizi people whose whereabouts were unknown through the fractured lower-level network.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s5-1: Nearly two hours earlier, taking today’s disconnection of the far-northern mining-zone node as grounds, Rena had signed a Facility Incident Inspection Order. It was only through the temporary authority granted to investigate
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s5-2: the underlying physical fault that the main console’s screen could now be quietly awakened before Estelle. During this long wait, this machine, once an aggregation node for the backbone network, had turned up more than the
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s5-3:
whereabouts of the missing. From pre-disaster shelter screening to post-disaster wasteland reconstruction, all the underlying cross-departmental records had once converged here.
It clearly displayed this station’s operating status:
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s6-1:
“Central relay station connection established. Driver-incident record chain verification passed.”
“This station’s original append blocks, sequence, and overwrite proofs are synchronizing normally. Notice: This station serves only as a short-term retransmission cache and does not store personality originals.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s7-1: Beside the main console was another row of obsolete equipment. Its screen still held the result of its final run—the waiting queue drawn up before the disaster, when the old world allocated places in the underground disaster shelters of this defensive zone.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s8-1: Rows of identification numbers stood in some prescribed order. After each number came a short system evaluation: contribution level, positional weight, health … and, at the very end, a column called “Replaceability.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s9-1: In this shelter-screening system, the higher the replaceability score, the farther back the position in the queue, until it reached the bottom.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s12-1: In the final section of the queue, the numbers at the bottom no longer had specific scores after them. The evaluation column contained only the same sentence:
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s14-1: “Not entered into the queue. Reason: Replaceable.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s16-1: Estelle stood for a long time in the weak light of the screen. She held down the page-turn key and watched the page numbers change without moving, until they reached the total on the final page—the total number of people in this defensive zone whom the system had left behind on this list.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s18-1: “Four hundred and seventy-three thousand,” she said, releasing the key. Her voice sounded very small in the empty machine room.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s19-1: I looked at the enormous number on the screen. In the underground machine room during the previous assignment, I had faced the black hole of exactly six hundred and seventy thousand people between this region’s estimated surviving population at the time of
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s19-2: the boundary divisions and the final number entered into the post-disaster records. At the time, I thought that adding together the deaths from successive purges, epidemics, and riots would be enough to fill that missing six hundred and seventy thousand.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s20-1: But in the queue before us, issued earlier than the registered-population list, an account of four hundred and seventy-three thousand people had already been settled in advance.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s21-1: That meant the people who died after the disaster because of inadequate relief, or because of winter and disease, numbered fewer than two hundred thousand. The remaining four hundred and seventy-three thousand, the overwhelming majority, had not died because relief efforts had failed after the disaster. Before the
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s21-2: shelter doors closed, the system had already refused to enter them into the records because they were “replaceable.” This was the other half of the six-hundred-and-seventy-thousand gap—not people who failed to survive, but people removed directly from the denominator before the survival rate was even calculated.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s25-1: From the pile of old files beneath the machine, she pulled out an algorithm specification that the system had called by default. It was the original manual for Special Safety Regulation No. 7.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s28-1: The manual contained an extreme rescue protocol for fires in special industrial facilities: twenty seconds, and only three people could be brought out. Regardless of all other conditions, rescue the person who would be hardest to replace first.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s31-1: And now, this extreme algorithm from a dead-end fire scenario had been moved directly into the shelter-allocation screening system.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s32-1: The back of the invocation memorandum was densely covered with approval seals from that time. The Bureau of Materials had added, “Quotas are limited. Prioritize core productive capacity.” The Defense Forces’ approval
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s32-2: gave the reason, “Execute according to the wartime attrition plan.” Beside the Central Logistics Office’s seal, in plain black and white, it read, “To reduce the load on shelter life-support systems, agree to eliminate
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s32-3: redundant population.” More than a dozen departments sat in safe offices and stamped their seals onto documents that each appeared reasonable. Each party made a partial decision within its own authority and responsibility.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s33-1: Estelle carefully folded the original manual and the memorandum together.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s38-1: “In the face of the disaster, every department thought that as long as they eliminated the ‘replaceable,’ they could preserve the people with places on the list.” She turned and walked toward another row of cabinets in the
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s38-2: weak light. It was a group of terminals used in the early post-disaster period to coordinate labor in the peripheral settlements. “But the old humans did not survive, whether they had been stamped approved or left behind.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s39-1: She brushed the dust from the screen and opened an old file named “New Human Manufacturing and Deployment Register.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s41-1: “But when the first New Humans to awaken among the ruins after the disaster decided to manufacture a labor force to clean up the aftermath, this way of calculating people’s value was inherited intact.” Estelle looked at the rows of batch numbers on the screen. “To establish
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s41-2: settlements in the wasteland, the Inner Circle activated this ‘Site Selection and Population Deployment Model.’ Calculate the optimal configuration size, manufacture them, deploy them, put them to work, and once the ruins are cleared, drive all the laborers to the periphery.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s42-1: At the White Tower, Yuna and I had once pieced together the true origin of the peripheral population in a half-buried archive room, following a stack of old records whose quantities precisely matched the young people in the village. Those records were
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s42-2: of course not the original deployment batches from a century ago, but archived birth quotas from when the elders of the village’s current generation had been young. The origin of that bloodline’s reproduction still pointed to the same starting point.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s43-1: “At the White Tower,” I watched her back, my throat tightening, and finally spoke. “Yuna and I had already guessed how your people first came to the periphery.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s44-1: Her fingers stopped on the screen.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s45-1: “You knew?” she asked without turning around.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s46-1: “We found traces of the previous generation’s births. The numbers on the quota tables matched exactly with every allotment of supplies sent to the village. But I never knew how to bring it up with you.” I lowered my
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s46-2: eyes. “You memorized every name in your hometown’s household register. I didn’t want to tell you that the earliest source of the people you fought so hard to protect was only a designed list of industrial consumables.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s47-1: She was silent for a long time. Then she turned around and gently placed her hand on the dust-covered casing.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s48-1: “You should have told me sooner, Arno.” Her voice was soft. There was no anger in it, only a hollow calm. “The truth never becomes kinder because you refuse to speak of it.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s49-1: Her eyes were faintly reddened. She looked at the cold numbers on the screen as if they were something she could not understand.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s51-1: “I started memorizing the household register when I was little. The village chief taught me that even if someone froze to death out in the wild, as long as we could still recite their name, they had not completely disappeared.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s51-2: Her fingertips slowly tightened against the casing. “But look at this … there isn’t a single name. The people whose names we passed down for generations were nothing more than batch numbers on a parts list for manufactured units.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s52-1: She tried to find traces of her ancestors among the six-digit numbers, but there were only rows of dry deployment destinations and manufacturing specifications. Across pages and pages of scrolling, she could not piece together even one syllable that might pass for a name.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s56-1: The portable terminals issued by the Inner Circle to candidates had not only had their optical recording modules completely removed from the hardware, but also came with no physical cables capable of directly interfacing with these century-old machines, eliminating the possibility of privately copying the old files in bulk during inspections.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s57-1: Estelle took the pocket notebook from her pack and began copying the site-selection and quantity codes from the manufacturing-batch register displayed on the screen. It was the only way.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s58-1: Gripping the pen tightly, she recorded as quickly as possible the key deployment batch numbers corresponding to the early peripheral settlements. But after page forty-one, accompanied by the dry scrape of the magnetic head, the century-old storage sectors completely failed, collapsing into a dead gray crash screen filled with gibberish.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s59-1: She could only stop writing. In the footer of the fully copied notebook page, she carefully wrote a line: Copied through page forty-one. Remaining pages unreadable due to a complete failure of the equipment’s magnetic head.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s61-1: “These are all nameless manufacturing batch numbers. They can’t be matched to any living person outside.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s63-1: She organized the thick stack of copies and answered calmly: “I know. These forty-one pages can’t account for all the ancestors of the settlements either. But the batch numbers and deployment records here are enough to prove our origin in the
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s63-2: periphery. Other than this lower-level cold-storage machine, forgotten a century ago after a power failure, I can’t find these specific batch numbers preserved in any public index directory. The Central Authority sealed them away long ago.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s65-1: “And now this machine is broken too.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s66-1: When she finished speaking, she turned her gaze toward the depths of the machine room.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s68-1: On the other side of the terminal was a cabinet containing the physiological configuration manuals for the vessels manufactured back then. I pulled out the archived retention copy concerning the
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s68-2: modification of the ear configuration. In another timeline, Yuna had seen the incomplete drawing. She knew the cat ears were an artificial design, that there was no tail, and that the cat ears had
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s68-3: no physical function for keeping warm or sharpening hearing. But that incomplete archive bore no approval, so she never learned the specific reason why this artificial feature had been finalized.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s69-1: Now, the standardized retention copy containing the transcription of the final decision lay open before Estelle.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s71-1: It was merely an archival transcription of the original approval document, not a second, newly approved drawing. The archivist had signed the form with his initials. Crowded into the footer near the binding was an exceptionally neat line of small text:
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s73-1: “Original approval wording does not conform to this table. Recorder filled in according to the option table. Original wording transcribed as follows: ‘Add it. Reason: Better.’”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s75-1: Estelle stared quietly at the small line of text, then raised a hand and touched the cat ears on her head. They were also the only pair of ears on her, and on every New Human.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s77-1: “To keep them from being frostbitten, the peripheral settlements even added special clothing rules for covering them during labor and ordinary gatherings,” she said softly. “And in the end, this was only someone’s ‘Better.’”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s79-1: “Yuna never saw this note,” I told her, watching her.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s81-1: “Then I’ll copy this page for her too,” she said, softly but firmly.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s85-1: Before we left, Estelle sat beside the main console and added a line to the work log on the portable terminal:
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s86-1: “This station’s tamper-proof record chain has been connected. Inspection records uploaded.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s89-1: The inspection order had stated clearly that the results of this operation’s investigation into the Taizi people were not to be publicly entered into the master database. Only a simple closed-file entry number was to be retained in the controlled archive, proving that the results had been submitted.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s90-1: But she walked over to the wall and placed the forty-one pages of handwritten manufacturing-batch notes, together with the original copy of Special Safety Regulation No. 7 and the disaster-recovery invocation memorandum we had just found, into the physical evidence slot. Then she typed the electronic index description into the terminal:
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s91-1: Attachment description: In addition to the Taizi investigation results, this station’s lower level yielded a century-old nameless New Human manufacturing-batch register (forty-one handwritten pages recovered), the original copy of Special Safety
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s91-2: Regulation No. 7, and the memorandum invoking the disaster-recovery screening model. The above materials constitute additional physical evidence for the investigation and are sealed in this station’s vault. This entry number is hereby made public.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s92-1: When I saw the final words, “This entry number is hereby made public,” I immediately reached out and pressed against the edge of the terminal’s screen.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s94-1: “You don’t need to write that last part.” I stared at her. Once the entry number identifying the inspection evidence was made public, it would force the Inner Circle leadership to confront what you knew. Since the inspection order only required investigating the whereabouts of the Taizi people, these forty-one pages and the historical dead files could easily be kept to ourselves.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s97-1: She did not stop entering the text.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s99-1: “You were just blaming me for hiding the truth,” I said, looking up toward the ceiling. The Taizi people were waiting outside the assembly hall in the cold wind. “If you’re really angry, you could
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s99-2: take all of this up there and show it to the Taizi people. Why hide it from them, while risking pursuit by the Inner Circle to force an index of this additional evidence into the Inner Circle network?”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s101-1: “What would I show them? Tell them that in the Inner Circle’s records, they’re merely descendants bred from waste?” she asked softly, her gaze passing over the stack of handwritten pages about to be sealed away. “You’re
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s101-2: right. Like you, I’m also deciding for them what they can bear. Dropping this vast, cold industrial calculation on them won’t buy them a single grain of food for the winter. Until they can survive, I can’t bring this to them.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s102-1: She looked back at the screen.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s104-1: “But that doesn’t mean any of this doesn’t exist. So I have to make the Inner Circle’s machines and archives remember forever that I’ve written this line.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s105-1: She did not delete the words. The physical delivery vault emitted a mechanical locking sound, and the paper copies, memorandum, and original manual were irreversibly swallowed into the local safe. Then she signed her name on the portable terminal with her fingerprint and pressed the confirmation key.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s106-1: With a sharp alert tone, the green indicator light came on in the darkness. The Inner Circle administrators might be able to destroy this local machine someday, but the index record bearing her fingerprint had already forced its way through the data channel into the tamper-proof record chain of the Inner Circle’s controlled archive. To delete
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s106-2: this line without a trace, they would have to destroy the entire region’s continuous tamper-proof record chain. The index could not guarantee the authenticity of the copied pages, but at the system level, it had fixed in place the act of her submitting forty-one pages of physical evidence in this cold-storage zone. It could not be taken back.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s107-1: By the time we followed the ropes back to the surface and completed the final entry on the terminal, its internal clock had already passed the two-and-a-half-hour mark. The cold wind outside the assembly hall was still cutting. The woman in charge had been called into the assembly
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s107-2: hall and was looking at the verified list of seventy people. They had been assigned to Vent No. 13 in the far-northern mining zone, where a collapse had occurred eighteen years ago. Seven were confirmed alive. The death records of the remaining sixty-three had all been verified.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s108-1: “Those seven … where are they now?” The woman stared at the seven names marked “alive” on the list, her voice trembling. “The far-northern mining zone is more than sixteen hundred kilometers from here. Can they come back?”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s109-1: “They’re now registered laborers with official household records in the far-northern mining zone.” Estelle looked at her. “Under the Inner Circle’s interregional movement regulations, they can’t leave the mining zone without a transfer order.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s110-1: They could not merely leave. Once the outstanding account was closed, Taizi’s fate would no longer be linked to the far north, and those seven people would become, completely, people on the far-northern mining zone’s books. Even if the Taizi people found a way to cross those sixteen hundred kilometers, they could not bring them back.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s111-1: “They’re still alive …” The woman’s eyes reddened as she clenched the corner of her clothing. “As long as they’re still alive …”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s112-1: Before this, because the village chief had no authority to deregister missing people in the living-dead system, the account could not be closed while the people remained alive; even the highest levels could not conjure a compliant death-case closure out of thin air. Now, with verified survival
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s112-2: and death nodes recovered from the old records network through the Inner Circle’s high-level authority, the sixty-three death markers were successfully written in. As for the remaining seven, their new interregional household registrations in the far north finally triggered the system’s
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s112-3: underlying “household deregistration” interface—hidden software that did not exist locally in Taizi and could be called only by using the inspection order to carry the far-northern data source back for reverse verification. It removed the seven survivors completely from Taizi’s baseline list.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s113-1: The inspection order filled the deadly outstanding account and turned the verification code for next year’s winter allotment green. Estelle crossed the newly raised warning cord and showed the woman the portable terminal’s green screen.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s114-1: But she did not stop. She did not explain the truth of the forty-one pages from underground. Instead, she went to the Taizi people huddled against the wall. She unhooked the canteen from her waist and poured its cold water, little by little, onto the frozen earth. It was the opening rite of a Watermarsh funeral.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s116-1: “Water returns to water, just as life returns to its source.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s117-1: Her eyes lowered, her voice steady enough to carry over the wind outside. The woman in charge watched the water seep into the frozen earth, then finally lifted her gaze from the names of the seven survivors and let it fall again on the sixty-three
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s117-2: names on the list, confirmed to have been buried in the mine. She staggered to her knees and pressed both hands hard against the cold earth. The other Taizi people followed. They huddled their shoulders tightly; some buried their faces in their coarse
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s117-3: sleeves. There was no wailing, only muffled, restrained gasps beneath the sound of the wind. Even with seven survivors still on the list, for the sixty-three families gathered here, twenty years of disappearance had finally become confirmed death.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s118-1: In the past, however, the second half of this prayer had to be spoken by a cleric—“A shared will shall guide us toward the right future, with God as guarantor”—for the ritual to be complete.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s119-1: Estelle emptied the last drop of water.
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s121-1: “The living leave their mourning here.” She hung the empty canteen back at her waist and did not continue with the prayer’s assurance of divine guarantee. “Since no one can guarantee the future for us, the dead must be remembered, and the living must go on living.”
texts.chapter:v15-23b:event:text-s122-1: The Taizi people silently pressed their hands against the earth in the cold wind. The woman lay on the ground, digging her hands into the hard surface until her knuckles turned bloodless white. All that remained for the living was the frozen earth beneath their hands, and a grief made certain.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-06-quota:title: Sea Line Six: Quotas
texts.chapter:heisenberg-06-quota:event:text-s: Before the previous cycle ended, the snowstorm and funeral outside that gathering place in another world still lingered in my mind. In this new world, the clock of disaster was still running. It was morning on the

first day. More than two hours had passed since the low-level failure designated A-774 occurred at 08:10 at the Central Computing Relay Station. That failure was what exposed the anomaly in the “week-end countdown.”
I was waiting alone at the rendezvous point outside the White Tower. Sera was risking a return inside the White Tower to investigate an order that might already have taken effect.

Hurried footsteps suddenly sounded at the end of the corridor.
I stood at once and fixed my eyes on the closed security door.
The lock gave a dry mechanical click. The door was pushed open.

Sera stood there, even her breathing disordered. She had not taken off her windbreaker, and snowmelt from outside still clung to her shoulders. She hurried to the metal table and, without a word, slammed a military-grade data card onto its surface. The holographic projection lit up at once.
It was an internal system log in active operation. At the top, glaring red text read: Central Execution Directive — Candidate Disposition Phase.

“This isn’t the Continuance Contract.” Sera’s voice trembled as her fingertip pointed to the center of the screen. “Estelle withdrew her hand. She didn’t press her fingerprint down. But in the system’s eyes, that doesn’t stop it from generating a disposition order for her.”
I followed her finger. The modern authorization system consisted of three physically isolated repositories—Otto’s risk assessment, Garon’s transfer execution, and Sera’s senior-seat audit. They
had no connection to one another and submitted only one-way data to the central system. Unless all the credentials were assembled, the center could not possibly construct an execution order.
In the “Subject’s Consent” field, Estelle’s fingerprint mark was indeed absent. But its status was displayed in green: “Approved: Original Body Termination Condition Met.”
“How can the directive continue if she didn’t sign it?” I asked.
“Because Otto submitted an ‘extreme-risk assessment.’” Sera brought up another data stream. “Under emergency conditions, that assessment activated a hidden
maintenance interface. The interface can directly rewrite the subject’s bodily dependency status, and even forcibly enter the original body termination condition.”
“But using a low-level interface like that requires authorization from someone with senior privileges.”

Sera said nothing. Her fingers slid to the bottom of the holographic screen and opened the “Attached-Record Reference” field.
An encrypted number lay there in silence.

“I opened only one ‘Candidate Rights Verification Order.’” She stared fixedly at the encrypted number, her eyes red. “I issued a limited order. It only opened access to her contract description section and candidate disposition index... But the system didn’t treat it as a review.”
It took the access record Sera had left behind as “attached-record grounds” and mounted it to the interface that modified bodily dependency.

I looked at that solitary encrypted number and remembered the ancient events I had read about in the old archives. When the Quota Method Review was established, the anonymous reviewer had filled the paper with extensive ethical annotations in an attempt to disclaim responsibility, but the administrative department

extracted only his technical access signature. Back then, the engineering department fabricated false test records. Chief technical bureaucrat Monde knew exactly what was happening, yet still issued the annual success brief after signing the falsified files at every stage, each one procedurally compliant.
In a system cut apart with perfect precision, no one felt that they had issued an order to kill. But the machine had received every endorsement it needed.

“It wasn’t the system that malfunctioned...” Sera braced herself against the edge of the metal table, her fingertips pressing until her knuckles went white. “Three repositories, each handling its own function. Otto submitted the extreme-risk assessment. Estelle’s absence was filled by the technical interface. And I...”
As if she had suddenly lost all strength, she slowly crouched beside the metal table and buried her face in her hands.

“Everything came together perfectly within procedure.” In the empty rendezvous point, only the sound of her sobs, no longer held back, remained. “They used the audit order I issued to save her and assembled a legally valid candidate disposition order for killing her.”
texts.chapter:chapter-24-six-eight:title: Chapter Twenty-Four: The Same Alias
texts.chapter:chapter-24-six-eight:event:text-:
AI Laboratory · Interface table footer (copy):
“Safe upper limit for release amount based on: File No. 762.
Disaster recovery intervention procedure: File No. 804.
Sources of the

two columns on the same interface table: one from an external report, one from this site’s own records.
Where the two columns do not agree, this site’s own records take precedence.”

That evening, the night wind moved along the edge of the village. After climbing out through the steep drainage channel at the base of the White Tower and leaving the facility, Estelle did not return to her quarters at

once. Under the dim light of the village archive room, we spread out, one by one, the papers we had brought out of the AI Laboratory that afternoon using Sera’s limited audit warrant, along with the diagrams we had copied.

The cuffs of her trousers were still stained with mud from the Witnessing area. In the seven years she had endured as a candidate, this was the first time she had truly seen the facility’s underlying nature.

Estelle’s fingertips first pushed aside an old-era low-level code memo. In its margin was a note: “INT overflow risk… recommended upper limit 2³¹-1.” Beside it, someone had hastily scribbled a joke about how the engineer

who wrote the line was afraid that, if the Leader arrested more people than the limit allowed, he would be held responsible too. “Some kind of life-saving humor from the old Empire’s engineers.” I pushed the paper aside.

Her gaze finally stopped on the copy of “Continuity Engineering · Operator Plan Description.”
“seed = political prisoner,” she read softly. When she had seen those words
earlier that day in front of the dark-red drainage channels, she had only found them cruel. But now, connecting the parameters of the entire facility, she saw something deeper.

“The AI Laboratory’s production line actually has two separate input channels,” I said, pointing to another document. “One is responsible for retrieving a general physiological template and supplementing
it with localized editing to produce a shell; the other is responsible for writing a person’s complete life record, together with their memories, emotions, and self-awareness, into it as a whole.”

“Lysenko’s private aim was to copy a new-human version that inherited all of his memories. As long as the record was complete, the machine could transcribe it without loss.” Estelle pulled out another log titled

“Project Rerouting,” her brows drawn tight. “Creating a breathing shell required no cost, but that did not mean the new body could wake like a real person. To fill this customized body with the ‘subject capacity’

needed for consciousness to emerge, he applied to the Head of State to have ten thousand political prisoners arrested, intending to feed them into the ‘operator plan’ and extract that capacity from their living bodies…”

“But that application was blocked.” I picked up her thread, pointing to the note in the margin of the log. “The Head of State allowed the facility to be completed, but the operation to arrest ten thousand people and extract them alive was never

approved. Without the capacity needed for someone to wake, the so-called operator plan ultimately produced only a handful of empty shell vessels without a first person. It was never some grand project for manufacturing substitutes without limit.”

Estelle was silent for a while, then pulled out the document titled “Public Notice of Disposition.” It was the thing she had cared most about that afternoon in the “Witnessing of Bodily Rights” area. A large section of conditional attachments had been deliberately removed. The complete record

Sera had gone to investigate, detailing exactly how the execution stage was carried out, had ultimately not been retrieved. The moment she touched the low-level interface, the facility’s counter-tracking mechanism would activate. In the end, she had only hurriedly brought back this fragment.

“Although we never managed to piece together that execution order in full, and we didn’t get the final page…” She stared at the hollowed-out attachment, her voice tightening. “But even from the preceding pages, once a

complete life record is written in its entirety, the one who wakes is no longer a mindless shell. If the ‘Estelle’ who wakes inside the Inner Circle possesses everything I have up to today, then she is my true continuation.”

“If she is real, and you are real too,” I said, “then there will be two people who possess these memories in full at the same time. But the Inner Circle has only one set of seats, permissions, and names.”

Estelle’s fingers curled slightly, her knuckles whitening with the force. In front of the low door beside the extraction capsule that afternoon, she had seen the dark-red passage with her own eyes. “That’s why the

attachment was removed too,” she reasoned quietly. “The Inner Circle’s political system can never tolerate two identical people competing for the same seat. So this me, as the old body, will inevitably be cleared out.”

The cold rain from the Witnessing area was still drying at the ends of her hair. On Sera’s desk, the draft of her Continuation Contract still remained. Earlier tonight, after learning the cruelty behind the promise of

continuation, she had already made her decision—she would sign it. All it would take was pressing her biological fingerprint. The result of enduring seven years would be signing her own death sentence with her own hand.

Even though the decision had been made, this body standing here still felt an instinctive fear of the destruction to come. She looked at her mud-stained hands and drew a deep breath, as if preparing to bear the weight of that decision once more.
“After I return to the chapel tonight and complete the final procedures…” Her voice no longer trembled. It held a cold clarity instead. “The me who wakes inside the Inner
Circle will take everything from the archive room tonight there, right? She’ll remember the drainage channel I climbed through, Sera’s lies, and how I accepted disposition.”
“She will,” I said. “She’ll possess all the anger you had up to the instant you stepped into the scanning chamber.”

The lights of Watermarsh village flickered outside the window. If that “self” could carry all the truth inside, if she could question what was truly hidden behind that tightly closed door… that was why she was willing to give up this old body.

I pushed a copied route map in front of her—the external sequence we had reconstructed that afternoon by working backward.
“The principle connecting those three pressure-release
locks to the shaft,” I said, tapping the route with my finger, “if we activate the whole system and complete this set of physical operations, which takes about seventy minutes,
we can bypass the White Tower’s monitoring and reopen the Laboratory’s passage directly from outside. After that, we won’t need to go through the approvals from earlier today.”
“Since the new shell can be created without my involvement…” Estelle looked at the route. The survival instinct she had just suppressed began to surface again. “Then we can sneak in through this back

door and complete the scan. Let them write an Estelle inside first, while the Estelle outside simply doesn’t press the fingerprint that triggers the destruction procedure… Then both of us can stay alive.”
What then?

This was the first time that day she had not followed the projection all the way to its end. Even if the old body outside was not destroyed, two Estelles with the same complete memories would eventually
have to face the reality of a single seat. Sneaking in and creating another self could not resolve the political deadlock in which only one of them could live. But at least it could postpone “death.”

“But you asked me before,” I said, looking at her. That was the heaviest thing in a world without Yuna. “If there weren’t ten thousand political prisoners, where would the subject capacity needed to awaken the new body come from?”
I pushed the slip of paper copied from the interface table footer in front of her.

“At one point, the time machine’s excessive connections between worlds created a capacity shortfall whose value was unknown. Later, someone willingly sacrificed the total capacity of ten thousand that she occupied across all worlds.” I stated it as steadily as I could. “That capacity

exceeded the safe upper limit and filled the shortfall. The production line’s available capacity is no longer zero. To awaken your new body, the machine can draw capacity directly from the field now that it has returned to normal. It no longer needs to extract anyone’s life.”

“Since there is enough capacity, the machine itself will not require the old body to be forcibly destroyed.” I pointed to the note beneath the footer. In my memory, File No. 762 was the famous report in which Heisenberg calculated the limit of the cost

of eight thousand people. “Whether it was the external report declaring the upper limit, or the equipment procedure before us that places local physical readings above external input, the signature line contains the same string of characters: ‘H.B.’”
Estelle’s gaze moved back and forth between the two lines of writing. “The person who calculated the safe upper limit also stipulated that the machine must follow local physical readings…”

“The machine recognizes only physical reality.” I withdrew my hand. That was also why the dark-red passage that afternoon had felt wrong to me. “Since the local readings show that capacity is already sufficient, the machine will only carry out the copying. It will never issue a kill command on its own. So if

you follow the official procedure and press your fingerprint, causing the old body to be forcibly ‘disposed of,’ that is not a necessary condition for the machine to operate at all. It is a private execution that the Inner Circle imposed on the fingerprint to prevent the two of you from competing for the seat.”

Beneath all the diagrams lay a section of red procedural text we had copied today from a log attachment. It was the rule governing the Annihilation Device in the deep ruins—the machine actually used for the sacrifice.
“The release procedure requires continuous external calibration. Once the final execution phase begins, the chamber door is physically interlocked and cannot be halted from within.”

Estelle put away her pen, carefully folded the papers, and placed them in her backpack. This weighty record would be the card she held for tomorrow’s action through the long night ahead. As I watched her movements, I silently

engraved every mark she had made into my memory again. Only the numbers, file references, and operation sequences in my head were stakes I could truly carry with me the next time I returned to the starting point of the cycle.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:title: Chapter Twenty-Four, Appendix Two: Both Awake
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s1-1:
AI Laboratory · Disposal Archive Index (first batch after the disaster, copy):
“This volume contains: source number, entry date, successor continuation date, predecessor termination date.
There is no adjudication column
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s1-2:
between the fields.
This machine does not adjudicate which one is the original. This machine records only: who began on which day, who ended on which day.
——Appendix: The termination operation must be confirmed by a human.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s4-1: After the previous cycle’s verification deep inside the AI laboratory ended, I endured the boundless dead silence until the end. When consciousness connected again and I woke once more in the morning house, the only sound around me
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s4-2: was the soft rasp of a rag against the wooden table. Watching my mother’s bent back, I pieced together what we had found earlier in the cleared candidate-disposal area beneath the laboratory, along with the clues gathered along the way.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s5-1: “Estelle looked into that S-prefix numbering format.” I looked at my mother. “It was the hardware source code belonging only to the underground isolation corridor, used to identify the room where each person receiving a body replacement was confined.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s6-1: By the second time I read it aloud, the rasping at the table had stopped. She slowly lowered the rag clenched in her hand.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s11-1: She didn’t ask a single question. She turned and went straight into the dim back room. I followed, watching her crouch and drag a heavy old wooden chest from the deepest space beneath the bedframe. When she lifted the lid, several layers of old cloth, washed pale, lay inside. She pushed them aside and reached directly toward the bottom.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s12-1: From the very bottom, she pulled out a stack of papers held together by an old wooden clip. They had been pressed there for more than a decade. Their edges had frayed into fine fibers. They were chain-severance receipts printed out by a system terminal back then.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s13-1: She stood, returned to the front room, and gently pushed the stack across the table toward me. She opened only the top sheet.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s16-1: Several lines of cold machine-printed text appeared on the yellowed paper. The heading was still clear:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s18-1: Tower District Terminal · System-Enforced Chain Severance Receipt: Index Chain Severed
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s20-1: Directly beneath the heading, the room-number format we had seen in the abandoned ledger was printed in perfect alignment. Here, though, it had been given another name:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s24-1: “That fits.” I kept my voice low. “If the source code was bound to the room number, then this was his location in the system. They must have assigned him Isolation
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s24-2: Room 102 for that cycle. Even if he hadn’t lain down in it yet, the process had already begun. He forcibly severed it, and that’s why this receipt exists.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s27-1: I drew a deep breath and told her I could take the documents to the underground laboratory and check the system logs to see what this process actually did.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s28-1: My hand had not yet reached the edge when she pressed her rough palm firmly over the papers.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s31-1: She kept her head lowered, her eyes fixed to the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s33-1: “It’s been more than ten years. Whenever people asked why he refused to take that path, I always gave them the same answer: It was his matter; he decided for himself. I used that answer to shut people up. I said it for more than ten years.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s35-1: “But I’ve never really understood what the process behind those three papers could have done to him. Today you told me exactly which room this number refers to. I’ll go see for myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s36-1: She raised her head. Something hard as stone had entered the eyes that were usually so calm and patient.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s39-1: We could only go to the laboratory today. Estelle had signed the continuation-of-life contract the night before. This morning was the day of her final oath. The elders’ council and most of the village would be gathered
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s39-2: in the chapel. As an external supplementary candidate, she had to go through the ceremony. I had been counted as the primary choice from the beginning of the cycle and didn’t need to attend, which left me free to act.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s40-1: When I went to find Estelle, she was sitting by the window, carefully sewing the Watermarsh-purple edging that signified her status onto her cuff. I repeated to her the truth we
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s40-2: had uncovered in the AI laboratory during the previous cycle, along with what the technical seat had concealed, and suggested that she confront them publicly during the oath later.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s42-1: She stopped sewing and looked at me. “I’m not going to ask.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s46-1: “As long as I need this body to stay alive, asking won’t mean anything. If they withhold the continuation authority, I can only submit. I already signed last night. Going to confront them now would only humiliate me. I can only walk in there myself and finish the oath.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s47-1: I wanted to stay and accompany her, but she shook her head and drove the needle tip firmly back into the fabric.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s49-1: “When the chapel bells ring, the outer patrols will pull back and form up. Those ten-odd minutes are the weakest window in the collapse-zone patrols. Go do what you have to do.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s54-1: The shaft leading to the laboratory was hidden in the wasteland outside the collapse zone. The ten-odd minutes when the outer patrols withdrew and formed up after the chapel bells rang were just enough for us to cross the open ground and lift the heavy prefabricated slab. Only after climbing into the shaft
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s54-2: and sealing the slab back in place did we turn on our flashlights in the dark space between levels. Beneath it were three interlocking mechanical locks. Even though I had memorized the opening sequence during the previous cycle, it still took a full seventy minutes of physical operation to open the way again.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s57-1: As one of the ten seats, my mother should have attended gatherings like this. But she had always claimed illness to avoid the elders’ council’s core affairs. Before leaving today, she had once again sent word to the chapel that she was ill. So even if she missed the whole-village oath, no one would suspect anything.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s58-1: Even so, she had spent her whole life avoiding those machines that decided who lived and who died, and she had never descended into a place this cold and steep. Before we left, she tied the hem of her long skirt tightly around her waist and changed into the coarse cloth shoes she wore for working the fields.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s59-1: The shaft was pitch-black. The beam of the flashlight swept back and forth across the rust-streaked iron ladder. At the bottom was a transverse ventilation duct that required us to pass hunched over, its
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s59-2: floor covered in mud and loose stones. She followed behind me, her breathing heavy in the narrow passage. The whole way was awkward and stumbling, but not once did she reach out and ask me to support her.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s62-1: We were more than halfway through the passage. There was nothing around us but our footsteps. Suddenly she spoke in the darkness, her voice somewhat muffled.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s64-1: “Those people in the village have been saying in private all these years that he was stupid. They said he refused a chance at rebirth that others would beg for, that he was stubbornly literal, that he thought the person made from him would no longer be himself.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s66-1: “I know that. But I keep thinking that, down at the level of flesh and skin, maybe he was just an ordinary person afraid of pain. Afraid of lying down on that cold operating table. He worked on the isolation beds down there for a while. After he came back, he never mentioned this place again.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s68-1: “What if he really was only afraid?” I asked softly.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s69-1: She walked a few steps at the edge of the flashlight’s glow, as if turning the question over.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s71-1: “On one side was the stubborn refusal to give up his identity. On the other was the very real fear of dying. Those two thoughts have been sitting in my heart for more than ten years.” She slowly straightened and looked into the darkness ahead. “Tell me. Can’t they both be true?”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s76-1: The post-disaster automatic-entry area was at the very back of the laboratory. When we pushed open the heavy dustproof door, rows of collapsed metal cabinets stood ahead of us, with brittle,
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s76-2: yellowed archive papers scattered across the floor. We searched the ruins by flashlight for a long time before barely piecing together several surviving pages from the old personnel records.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s79-1: I leaned closer and carefully made out the faded writing. Not one of the names belonged to anyone important I had heard of in the village.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s80-1: Their occupations followed the source numbers: people responsible for preliminary carrier testing, equipment inspectors, and several technicians who worked on reproducing lower-level personalities.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s81-1: On a permission-transfer table beside them, I saw more than thirty codes densely listed on the left. The records showed that they had all awakened in the first batch after the disaster and received the initial bodies. But on the right
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s81-2: side of the table, only the ten ultimately valid slots remained. Countless red arrows began at the codes on the left and converged on the names of those ten on the right, like something devouring them. Beside the crossed-out names on
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s81-3: the left were notes reading “cancellation resisted,” “permission downgraded,” or “eligibility for subsequent generation revoked.” More than thirty people survived. In the end, all the continuation slots were swallowed up by those ten.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s82-1: I couldn’t tell who the ten people on the right actually were from the codes alone. But in the archive pile we found a copy of the Survivor Habit Sampling Record from that time.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s84-1:
Source Habit Sampling Record:
Sample A (corresponding to Final Seat Three): When listening to a dispute or report, habitually taps the tabletop twice with the knuckles, then says, “One thing
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s84-2:
at a time.”
Sample C (corresponding to Final Seat Four): When thinking, unconsciously picks at the web between the right thumb and index finger with the left thumb until it leaves a red mark.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s87-1: “This one is Otto.” My mother glanced at the first line and spoke softly. “When he came to the house last month to ask about you, he tapped the table exactly like that.” Her gaze moved down the page. “This is Sera, who oversees inspections. When she reviews files, she’s always picking at the web of her hand behind the desk until it bleeds.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s88-1: After only two pages, several of the habits belonging to the ten surviving seats had already found exact matches here. Combined with the table full of red arrows, these habit records proved that the elders today had not been the upper ranks chosen
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s88-2: from the beginning. The machine had recorded every detail of a person into the new brain without omission. Those surviving habits matched the elders of today, and showed that they were merely the survivors who had taken everyone else’s slots back then.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s89-1: Holding those sheets, I was about to ask her to confirm what they meant when I realized she wasn’t looking at this ironclad evidence of the village’s origins in power at all.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s90-1: She had no interest in who had consumed whom decades ago. She stepped over the records of those power shifts and walked straight to a half-closed iron door beside them marked “Parallel Reading Room,” then reached out and pushed it open.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s95-1: The parallel-reading room was extremely cramped. A metal table stood in the exact center of the room. Spread across it was an anonymous subject’s Standard Continuation-Process Follow-Up Monitoring Form.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s96-1: The “high-frequency parallel-reading form” we had examined outside recorded only the first seventy-two hours of data. This form filled in the blank after high-frequency parallel reading ended. It was still divided bluntly into two columns. The left read: Successor. The right read: Predecessor.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s97-1: The table recorded each person’s blood pressure, pulse, and even the number of times they requested water from the fourth day onward. At the end of the form, a mandatory “Ninth-Day Termination Line” was printed in stark black.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s100-1: Without any explanation from me, my mother understood the two parallel records. The handwriting in the left-hand Successor column was clear and orderly. The ink in the right column was noticeably fainter, the writing crowded together.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s101-1: She extended a finger thickened at the joints by years of labor and pressed it against the right column, where the ink was fading.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s103-1: “The one on the right is still breathing. Still drinking water.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s104-1: As soon as she finished speaking, her hand gave a violent tremor. Her fingertip hung in midair, as if the paper had burned it.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s105-1: “If this is the standard Follow-Up Monitoring Form…” She stared at the record. “During those days when this body of mine first opened its eyes and was taught how to use itself, was another monitoring form belonging to ‘Rena’ also lying on this table?”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s106-1: “Is this the procedure everyone has to go through?” She stared at the blurred scrawl in the field for the operator on duty, her voice lowered almost to a murmur, as if asking me,
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s106-2: or asking the room from that time. “The predecessor left in the isolation room… it wasn’t as simple as closing their eyes, like they said? How did they survive these nine days?”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s107-1: There was no answer. The code of the person who had signed it could no longer be verified. At the very bottom of every page, there was only one identical line:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s109-1: This machine does not adjudicate which one is the original.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s113-1: In the final disposal result, the name, the seat, and the house were all transferred clearly. Beneath the predecessor column, only three words remained: cancellation, isolation, termination.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s114-1: That rule had not been set by the machine. It had been set by people.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s117-1: During the first few days, the reactions in the two columns were almost synchronized. But from the fourth day onward, the successor was taken out of the room to become familiar with the village, while the predecessor was left in the cold isolation area. On the ninth day, the successor casually complained in the record:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s119-1: “The patrol uniform they issued today has a collar that’s too stiff.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s121-1: That same day, in the other column, separated by a curtain, the predecessor looked at the wall and said:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s123-1: “He should have gone to collect his new clothes today, shouldn’t he?”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s125-1: Beside that sentence, the technician at the time recorded another mutter from the predecessor:
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s127-1: “What he’s experienced by now is already more than I have.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s129-1: My mother silently watched those words, one hand braced against the cold metal table. Her knuckles had gone white from the pressure.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s131-1: “I didn’t dare think about it before. Every time a body was replaced, the elders’ council only said that the previous me had been put safely to sleep.” Her voice was low. Her gaze seemed pinned to those lines. “Now
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s131-2: I’ve seen it. What the predecessor who couldn’t leave this room was thinking during these nine days—this form never cared. He was only responsible for filling out this table, then signing on this termination line.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s132-1: After a long time, she slowly closed the two-column monitoring form.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s134-1: “He worked on these beds back then. He wired many of the machines in this room himself. He knew better than anyone what it meant to lie on the right side of this form.” Her eyes were red, but there were no tears. “He was
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s134-2: afraid. He knew that if he accepted the replacement, he himself would become the one left in the old column, waiting for termination. And the one who walked out and took his name would be a stranger made from scratch.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s136-1: “Let’s go. I know now why he canceled himself back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s141-1: That evening, we slipped back into the village before the bells rang again. Half the day had passed. Passing through the square outside the chapel, I saw Estelle emerge from
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s141-2: the dispersing crowd in the distance. The narrow silver metal arc marking her candidate status rested between her low twin ponytails, catching the cold light of the setting sun.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s142-1: The people around her were congratulating her. She responded politely, but her hand was clenched tightly around the candidate badge at her waist, her knuckles white. She had signed the
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s142-2: contract of submission the night before. That morning, she had entered the chapel and accepted everyone’s scrutiny, lowering her head in exchange for the right to stay alive in this village.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s143-1: I watched her straight but rigid back. What would not leave my mind was the nine-day dual-reading record underground. When the day came for her replacement,
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s143-2: would the Estelle who retained the old memories also listen from the isolation area to the footsteps of another self walking away, waiting for the final signature?
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s146-1: When we returned home that night, my mother lit a dim lamp and formally placed the stack of receipts she had taken out that morning into my hands.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s149-1: One was a source-index receipt, one was a forced-cancellation form for the calibration record, and the last was a stub for the revocation of physical authorization. The foundational archive, brainwave calibration, and authority to clone a body had all been severed. The chain required to create a new person could no longer be assembled.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s152-1: “To destroy this final authorization completely, the system required an outside witness to confirm that the person concerned was giving it up while conscious and of his own free will.” My mother pointed to the stub. “He went down alone that day. But I actually followed him as far as the shaft mouth.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s153-1: “I didn’t have permission to go down, so I waited at the verification terminal on the outer edge of the surface. When the system sent out the request for a witness, I watched the live image he transmitted back, listened to his breathing, and confirmed that he was fully conscious and hadn’t lost his mind before pressing the confirmation seal for him.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s154-1: “As long as this stub exists, no one can say that it was a system failure or that he wasn’t in his right mind. The elders’ council can never again find a lawful pretext to force his data back out of storage.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s155-1: I stared at the paper bearing the outside witness’s signature. Several cycles ago, I had taken the traces he left in this house and confronted her. She had admitted that he refused a new body. Apart from that, she had brushed me off by saying he had fallen ill and failed to survive.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s157-1: “This is what you meant by ‘you didn’t know’?” I clenched my teeth and stared at her. “When you pressed confirm outside, you could hear what was happening in there, couldn’t you? Besides you, who else knew he was in there? If no one did, why didn’t you rush in and drag him out by force?”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s159-1: “I couldn’t bring him out.” She didn’t avoid my eyes. Her voice was quiet, but steady. “If I didn’t press it, the system would default to suspending the process and send people to investigate. Then the
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s159-2: elders’ council’s search team would break down that door, drag him onto the metal table we just saw, and turn him into one of the two data columns. If I pressed it, at least he remained a complete person.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s161-1: “Through the microphone, I heard his breathing grow heavier and heavier.” Her hand trembled slightly, but she quickly forced it down. “I watched the progress bar reach the final step, my palms covered in sweat. I was afraid he had deleted
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s161-2: all the data, afraid the system would really malfunction and leave him inside, afraid he would die completely just like that. But once he had made up his mind to sever this cycle, all I could do was press the witness confirmation for him.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s163-1: “Afterward, he dragged that already-sick old body home and grew weaker day by day, until he died of his illness.” She looked at me. “I didn’t tell you because I was afraid
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s163-2: you would follow his example. In this village, people who learn what lies underneath often drive themselves into dead ends. He shouldn’t have left this mess for you.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s164-1: She reached out and pushed the three documents across the table.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s166-1: “Take it.” My mother looked at me. “The elders’ council always says that as long as a record remains in the system, a person’s life is in their hands. Feel the paper in your pocket.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s166-2: Remember this: if someone truly decides to refuse, no one can stop him. He proved with his death that even in a place watched from every direction, a person can still have the final say.”
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s169-1: I folded the stack of yellowed cardstock and put it into my pocket against my chest.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s170-1: Under the lamplight, my mother looked utterly exhausted. The strength that had supported her underground seemed finally to have run out. She watched me put the documents away, said nothing more, and turned to fetch water from the kitchen.
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s171-1: I sat at the table, feeling the hard edges of the cardstock through my pocket. This was more than resistance to authority. It was the weight left behind by someone who had to confirm who he
texts.chapter:v15-24d:event:text-s171-2: was, even in death. Behind those records of replaced and canceled data, he used that sick body of his to leave the only real thing behind in this system sealed shut by code and permissions.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:title: Chapter Twenty-Four, Supplement Three: The Empty Seat on the Ticket
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s1-1:
Launch Site · Attachment Index (old copy):
“Crew Placement Attachment, missing from main volume. Transferred to K3-7 auxiliary cabinet. Physical sealing handled by: [employee ID]
—Launch not carried out.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s4-1:
At eight in the morning, the sunlight had not yet fully entered the room.
A new round had just begun. I recounted everything that had happened the night before to Mother as quickly as I could.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s4-2:
She sat at the table and listened in silence for a long time. Perhaps she felt that, in this household, hiding things could no longer protect anything. She stood and went into the inner room.
When
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s4-3: she came back, she not only returned to my hands the three vouchers bearing cancellation marks, but also brought out a yellowed old ledger and an old tool belt Father had used while he was alive.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s5-1: She opened the rough leather on the inside of the tool belt. A six-digit maintenance number had been stamped deep into it in steel.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s8-1:
Mother opened the last few pages of the ledger and pointed to an undated entry. It read: “Eastern ruins, special-seal K3-7 cabinet.”
The six digits from the tool belt followed. No one’s name was written.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s9-1: I recognized the number. Not long ago, when we had gone deep into the underground records vault beneath Node Two, the same mark had been left on the corners of the heavy sealed racks holding the original archives. It was Father’s double mark,
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s9-2:
left behind in this vast system.
And the “K3-7” that followed made my breath catch instantly.
On another parallel world I had experienced not long ago, Yuna had left those words behind while searching through the index in that dust-filled
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s9-3:
observation room:
“There’s one file missing from K3-7. Not only is the file gone—the name has been erased from the index too… Could this be the thing that must never see the light of day? The real crew list, maybe. Or the qualifications for boarding.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s11-1: Mother did not notice anything strange about me. Pointing at the writing in the ledger, she said, “For a place as classified as the ruins, the rules say the ledger recognizes employee IDs, not people. This was the mark he left for himself back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s13-1: She slowly gripped the tool belt. “This means he not only repaired the racks in the underground records vault, he was also assigned to the launch site in the east. He worked on the outside, but he also went down into the deepest auxiliary cabinet area and physically sealed the iron cabinet called K3-7.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s16-1: Looking at the number, I blurted out, “Mom, this might be a key. Is there a door in the ruins that recognizes this number?”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s17-1: Mother set the tool belt down and shook her head.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s19-1: “This isn’t a key.” Her tone was flat, as if she were talking about some utterly ordinary old matter. “Your father was careful with the jobs he took. He knew a little welding and carpentry. All this tells us is that he used his own skills to seal something shut completely back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s23-1: Looking at the ledger on the table, I felt uncertain. “This… should we hand it over to Sera? Or Estelle?”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s24-1: If we turned it in, someone at the White Tower could investigate it for us. If we kept it ourselves, even if we made it to the eastern ruins with nothing but an old ledger, we had no idea what we would be facing.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s26-1: She stopped what she was doing and looked at me. “Arno, our family lives in the Inner Circle. I used to think that as long as we stayed inside this circle, we were safe. But once we hand this over, it becomes someone else’s business.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s30-1: She came over, her voice soft but firm. “I’ve lived in this village for fifty years. I’ve seen what happens several times when outsiders ‘turn things in.’”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s32-1: She counted it out for me. “The first thing they do once something is handed over is seal it away. After that, it has to be scheduled, and scheduling requires a legitimate reason. Someone above you has to write that reason in the appropriate box. Once it’s sealed away, all they’ll say is: Isn’t it already being handled? What are you in such a hurry for?”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s35-1: Mother closed the ledger and carefully tucked it into her apron pocket.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s37-1: “Estelle is still waiting for the result of her review. The road she has to take is still inside their system, and she has to protect her own position first. This is a family matter. Those things are what he left behind.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s40-1: Close to nine-thirty, she returned from the White Tower with a slip of paper in her hand.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s42-1:
Approved: Villager Rena and her son Arno may make one trip to the eastern ruins to verify old belongings left by a deceased family member.
Limit: Depart the same day. Report return trip separately.
Note: This matter does not involve a candidate.
—Issuer: Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s44-1: Looking at the final line, “does not involve a candidate,” I immediately understood why Sera had approved it so readily. When we investigated Node Two earlier, she had assigned an aide to watch us the entire time, because that was active equipment under the White Tower’s jurisdiction. But the eastern ruins had long since become a pile of scrap
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s44-2: metal. As long as it was written that we were verifying “old family belongings” and that it “did not involve a candidate,” this was a private trespass unrelated to the White Tower. This slip was ironclad proof that Sera had cleared herself of responsibility—she had approved only the search for family belongings, not anyone touching the core archives.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s45-1: I asked what she had said to Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s47-1: “The truth.” She spoke while packing dried food. “He left something behind. I’m going there to find out what it is.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s48-1: She folded the slip into thirds and put it away carefully.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s50-1: “The truth doesn’t have to be told all at once. Tell them everything, and it becomes someone else’s business.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s55-1: Before setting out, she deliberately went to the wall of the courtyard and called out to the neighbor next door. In an ordinary tone, she said we were going to the distant outskirts to visit a relative and probably would not be back tonight. She said it without blushing or batting an eye, more smoothly than I did.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s56-1: The eastern ruins lay deep in the wilderness. The journey took five hours one way. We stuffed enough dried food for a night and two heavy water flasks into our packs.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s59-1: For the first two hours, we could only pick our way along the sandy road, sinking deep one step and shallow the next. The two flasks emptied quickly beneath the unrelenting sun. Her lips gradually dried and began to peel, but she kept herself from touching the half-flask remaining in the pack.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s60-1: In the third hour, we reached the edge of the gravel desert. The wind tore across us without obstruction, and the dry gullies were full of slippery rubble. Five hours of walking was
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s60-2: anything but easy on her knees. Several times she stumbled. Whenever I reached out to support her, she only waved me off, pulling her headscarf lower to shield herself from the choking dust.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s61-1: A little after three in the afternoon, we finally reached the outer perimeter of the ruins. This launch zone, abandoned for more than a century, resembled a dead beast with most of its body buried in sand. We had just leaned against a rusted
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s61-2: fence in the shade to catch our breath when I discovered that the physical gate on the main outer passage had long since rusted shut from the loss of power. There was no electronic authorization that could get us through by a shortcut. Across
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s61-3: dozens of loops, I had searched the pressure locks beneath the tower frames and cut through those equally lifeless electronic doors. But this independent entrance leading to the auxiliary archive cabinets had never once shown me its true face.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s62-1: Fortunately, we had Father’s ledger. Alongside scattered work orders, it contained several sketches he had drawn in pencil himself, marking specific work sites and pipe spacings: “Remove rust from B-section secondary exhaust duct,” “Weld floor drain in
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s62-2: south auxiliary engine room.” The gaps that maintenance workers had crawled through back then became an unexpected underground route map. We used a crowbar to break the hinge of a rusted ventilation grate, then followed the marked points and pieced together
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s62-3:
a stretch of piping that bypassed the main passage.
The pipes were pitch-black, and the air was thick with the sharp smell of old rust. To avoid the collapsed sections, we had to crawl through a narrow interlayer barely wide enough for one person. It was no
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s62-4: easy feat for an ordinary person’s stamina. Each time I crawled forward, I could hear her suppressed, heavy breathing. My shoulder was scraped until it bled as well. It was nearly four in the afternoon when we finally reached the archive room deep inside.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s67-1:
The beam of the flashlight swept through the dim underground space, and we went straight to the auxiliary cabinet area described in the ledger.
The row of iron cabinets was embedded in the wall. The old index on the wall was mottled and worn. It read:
“Crew Placement Attachment, missing from main volume. Transferred to K3-7 auxiliary cabinet. Status: Physically sealed.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s70-1: I jammed the crowbar deep into the gap of Cabinet Seven’s door and pressed down with all my weight. The crowbar let out a dangerous shriek and bent slightly, but the cabinet door did not budge even a millimeter.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s71-1: Its keyhole had been melted into an iron lump with a crude welding rod. A grinder or cutting torch should have been able to deal with it. I suggested that Mother wait there while I followed the exhaust duct back to the old storehouse beneath the tower frames to look for tools.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s72-1: “No,” Mother said, immediately pressing a hand against my shoulder. “The structure below is too old. If you crawl through the ventilation ducts alone and there’s a collapse, no one will be able to dig you out. If you’re going to get the tools, I’m coming back with you.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s73-1: She glanced at the narrow pipe entrance. I understood as well: there was no way her strength could hold out through another crawl along that waste duct, where she had to draw in her stomach and nearly suffocate to get through, let alone two consecutive
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s73-2: round trips. It would take at least an hour and a half. There might not even be a usable cutting tool in the storehouse, and if we encountered a collapse or some other danger, the consequences would be unthinkable. We had only one light crowbar, and
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s73-3: behind this sheet of iron was the secret. At this moment, all we could do was stand here. I tried to pry at the wooden wedges in the gap of the doorframe with the tip of the crowbar, but the wood did not move, as if it had grown out of the iron itself.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s74-1: Mother stepped forward and shone the flashlight on the wedges.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s76-1: “Don’t waste your strength. This is ash wood, soaked in oil beforehand. Driven in this tightly, not even a needle could get through.” Her fingers brushed over the angled faces of the wedges. “That was how he worked. Whenever he cut this kind of bevel, he always had a habit of putting a little more force into this angle.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s77-1:
Beside the wedges, a row of numbers had been carved deeply into the rust-spattered iron doorframe. They were the same six digits of the employee ID.
