By the rules, for work this classified, signing the ledger with an employee ID would have been enough. But with a craftsperson’s stubbornness, he had left his mark on the iron doorframe.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s80-1: Since the cabinet could not be opened, I turned and walked toward the list room next door. Hanging on the wall was a dust-covered sixth-edition General Engineering Roster. Its carrying limit stopped at a cold one hundred fifty seats, annotated: “Return shuttle capacity: None.” Beside
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s80-2: this final list of the one hundred fifty people confirmed for retention were three stacks of public records serving as proof of their origins: the public reserve roster, engineering certification histories, and private guarantees from senior officials of the various departments.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s81-1: The thickness of those three stacks was despairing. The reserve roster at the bottom ran to several thousand pages, densely filled with people waiting their turn. The second stack of engineering certifications was likewise packed with the
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s81-2: names of technical experts at every level, accompanied by complicated contribution weights. But I randomly opened a dozen names from the final list of one hundred fifty, then went back to check their origins. Without exception, all of them
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s81-3: came only from the thinnest book, the private guarantee ledger. I opened several pages of the engineering certifications and found the record of a thermal-control specialist named Akshay. He had led a team that overcame the bottleneck in
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s81-4: cyclical refrigeration, with the evaluation “Indispensable.” But his name had ultimately been crossed out in red, with a note beside it: “Replaced by private guarantee seat; transferred to life-support security echelon (remaining behind).”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s82-1: If those dozen or so names represented the rule governing the roster’s composition, it was no exaggeration to say that a handful of people had taken most of the seats through guarantees.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s83-1: Mother shone the flashlight on a ledger without a cover. This secret ledger was the shadow behind the sixth-edition list of one hundred fifty people. It revealed that, within those fully occupied one
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s83-2: hundred fifty seats, thirty-one had been left conspicuously empty. No names, and no origin in any of the three records—only the uniform annotation: “Placed separately (see K3-7 attachment for details).”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s84-1: Besides the thirty-one unnamed privileged seats forced into the full roster of one hundred fifty, the system logs showed that the life-support department had also locked ten seats in the equipment’s operating limits under a parameter called “buffer reserve.” No matter how long the reserve queue below grew, those ten empty seats were forbidden from being released as passenger capacity.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s85-1: Thirty-one unnamed privileges plus ten seats no one was allowed to occupy meant that, in the already full state of one hundred fifty seats divided among the senior officials of the various departments, forty-one people had to be kicked off the ark to make room for these invisible seats.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s85-2: Several departmental negotiation documents beside them gave the answer to who was fighting over those forty-one seats. The papers were urgent notices from the Engineering, Transport, and Supply departments to the military-police department. Every line was full of hysterical buck-passing:
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s86-1: “...To ensure the privileged quota and the system life-support reserve, the original full roster of one hundred fifty must be reduced by forty-one seats. The three departments have forcibly struck twenty-six seats from their respective original guarantee and approval rosters. The remaining
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s86-2:
fifteen mandatory cuts all fall within the original enrollment list of the military-police defense department.
The three departments currently have no supplies that can be exchanged with your department and cannot compensate your department on its behalf. Please issue instructions.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s87-1:
The military-police defense department had marked the urgent notice with a huge red X.
No complicated deduction was needed to see it: a handful of people had taken a large number of seats through guarantees, while everyone else waited in the reserve and certification lists thousands of pages long. But even among the one hundred fifty
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s87-2: seats already divided among the major departments—so thoroughly divided that even the thermal-control specialist had been pushed out—the higher-ups still had to kick out forty-one people to make room for thirty-one people without even names in the K3-7 cabinet, while forcibly keeping ten additional life-support reserve seats empty.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s88-1:
The Engineering and other departments swallowed the twenty-six cuts from their own rosters, but the military-police department clung to the fifteen people under its command and refused to stamp anything without supplies of equal value.
And to
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s88-2: conceal those thirty-one highest privileges, which did not even need to pass through the “guarantee” process, Father had been treated as a bottom-level laborer and used the most traditional of skills to nail the cabinet full of secrets into the wall.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s90-1:
I turned and went back to the iron cabinet, pressing my hand against its cold door. The identities of the thirty-one queue-cutters lay behind this sheet of iron.
I could not see a single name inside, but I immediately thought of Yuna. On another dead-end path, she had forced me to remember K3-7 amid a pile of discarded papers.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s91-1: If she were standing beside me now, looking at this iron door that even a crowbar could not overcome, she would never simply stand there and tally things up as I did. She would go looking for a grinder. If she could
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s91-2: not find one, she would grab the heaviest rusty wrench nearby and smash it hard against the doorframe. Even knowing she could not break it open, she would make the underground chamber ring with a deafening echo.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s92-1:
Not like now, when there was no sound except the whine of wind passing through the exhaust duct.
I ran my fingers over the six digits belonging to Father on the cabinet door, drew a deep breath, and forced down that hollow sense of loneliness.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s96-1: We left the list room and headed north. At the end of the corridor, an entire wall blocked the way. Sheets of paper had been nailed across it so densely that not a gap remained. A thick black line of ink ran from top to bottom, splitting the wall into two columns.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s97-1:
The heading on the left read: Transfers to Core Engineering and Security Bureau.
The heading on the right read: Shortages Reported by Each Region.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s100-1:
The flashlight beam moved down the wall.
Left: “New barracks for Security Bureau. Materials allocated. Skilled welders, ninety-four transferred in. Grain, increased.”
Right, on the same day: “Materials for South District pipeline repairs, not issued. Skilled welders, twelve requested this quarter, none assigned. Grain, issued at seventy percent.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s103-1:
There was one line Mother saw first. On the left it read: August 12, special cold-weather lining cloth, additional allocation of 2,400 bolts.
She hurried over and pointed to the same date on the right. It clearly read: Village cloth allotment for this year, reduced by 2,400 bolts.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s104-1: The two sides did not state the connection, but on that day, the entire system had only this one entry for cloth received into the core zone, and only this one allotment deducted out of nowhere from the peripheral areas. The scales matched exactly.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s108-1: She touched the surface of the paper. “Back then, the adults didn’t add new clothes. When the children’s sleeves got short, they added another piece. Then another piece after that. The clothes grew as heavy as burlap sacks.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s110-1: “In those years of shortage, the cloth never actually disappeared.” She looked up at the left side of the wall. “It was all here.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s111-1: The reason column for the shortages reported by the regions was filled with stock phrases: “Coordinated elsewhere,” “Approved by higher authority.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s116-1: We searched through the disorder covering the control room. Most of the drawers had been pried empty, leaving only a few urgent negotiation documents no one had wanted.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s117-1: On top was a copy of the former head of state’s will. This head of state, who had created the original reign of terror, had never had children in his lifetime, nor any blood relatives. In his will, he appointed a weak administrative
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s117-2:
official with no military or scientific background as his successor. A man decisive and ruthless while alive, he chose, in arranging what came after him, the person least likely to have posed a threat to him during his lifetime.
The
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s117-3: powerful military-police and engineering departments signed readily afterward, for a plainly stated reason: “This person has no independent base. Once in office, every directive will necessarily depend on our department’s execution.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s120-1:
Pressed tightly against the will was a receipt confirming delivery of the Public Report on Privilege Verification. The recipients were the communications towers of the eight regions across the territory.
In the body of the report, this successor considered to have
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s120-2: “no independent base” expressed his opposition to the old reign of terror in the most decisive way possible—he directly disclosed the ark’s one-way nature, along with the original experimental records showing that the time machine’s endpoint killed subjects after
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s120-3:
five seconds.
And that was not all. He attached a forceful administrative order: “Effective immediately, the previous crew roster is void. All crew members must undergo a qualification review by the new administration and board using newly issued digital credentials.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s121-1: This was a double retaliation. He used the truth to tear open the old alliance’s cover-up before the public, while also using the power of reexamination to purge all the old factions that had never respected him and redistribute the ark’s lifeboats, building a new alliance that truly belonged to him.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s122-1:
Beneath the terminal, I found an urgent order issued by the commander-in-chief of the military-police defense department two hours after receiving the broadcast across the territory and the reexamination order:
“This person is carrying out a purge of dissenters
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s122-2: in the name of reexamination. Immediately sever the physical connections between the crew-confirmation terminals under our department’s jurisdiction and the main database. Effective today, refuse to recognize any new crew roster issued by the new administration.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s125-1: The successor’s original intention may have been partly genuine correction, but his disclosure of the old accounts was first and foremost an assault for power. He tried to use it as a fuse, forcing the various parties to pledge allegiance to him again. But the old alliance was
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s125-2: frightened into raising its defenses by the broadcast and instead fell into complete mutual biting. Engineering, Supply, Transport—every department that controlled part of the launch interface followed the military-police defense department’s example and locked down its own interface.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s126-1: Mother silently looked at the negotiation record concerning the fifteen cuts.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s128-1: “The year after your grandfather died, I needed something to give them so I could get your uncle a household registration that would keep him out of the mines. Back then, I had nothing. I could only wear away at them, one place at a time.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s130-1: “In the end, it worked only because what I needed done wasn’t worth much. They could lift a hand and do it without losing anything themselves.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s132-1: “But this is different.” She stared at the writing. “These fifteen people had already received their stamps. They had reached this final step. Nothing of equal value could buy this. Once their seats were cut, what they got in exchange was death.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s133-1: Beside the military-police defense department’s order was the wreckage of a terminal. The screen was intact, but the data cable had not only been pulled from the motherboard socket—the socket itself had been burned into a lump of scrap aluminum with a welding torch.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s134-1: The enormous spacecraft had been built, and remained intact to this day—I had personally verified that it could fly in the previous phase. But once that broadcast had gone out across the territory, every faction completely refused to accept the same
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s134-2:
crew list. The military-police had its list, Engineering had its list, and no one was willing to carry out another faction’s evacuation plan.
Even with the ship sitting outside, no faction could assemble complete launch authorization on its own anymore.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s139-1:
To find another way out of here—we had to find a physical route around the outer security gates before night fell—we pushed open the heavy iron door on the other side of the control room. Beyond it was directly connected to the enormous launch platform.
The launch
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s139-2: platform stood in the center of the grounds, its four steel support arms spread like the claws of a giant beast. Between them, the escape ark with its one hundred fifty seats sat silently like a black iron tower. Its hull was covered in ablative coating, intact,
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s139-3: as if connecting the main power right now would send its passengers straight into space. We climbed the rust-covered maintenance ladder and stood at the edge of the platform. A metal catwalk extending along the platform’s outer side led through the night toward the
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s139-4: distant mountains. There, we could vaguely make out the remains of the cable-car tracks used for emergency evacuation—the only possible way for us to leave the ruins tonight. Night wind poured upward through the deep channel below, letting out a long, shrill howl.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s142-1: Mother looked down into the channel whose bottom could not be seen. Her dry hand gripped the cold iron railing.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s144-1: “When your father made a stool at home, he carved a mark even beneath the legs. He always said it would make it easier for whoever took over the repairs later to identify the joints.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s145-1:
I stood in the wind, looking at the black ark.
Back then, he sealed this ship full of privilege and secrets in place, becoming the least conspicuous executor of a cruel transaction. But
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s145-2: he had hammered the six digits belonging to him as a bottom-level laborer deep into the iron doorframe of K3-7, and pressed them into the old tool belt he himself had used in the same way.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s146-1: Mother released the railing and turned her head. The night wind tousled her hair.
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s148-1: “I used to think that living in the Inner Circle meant a clean, spotless kind of safety.”
texts.chapter:v15-24e:event:text-s150-1: Her voice was thinned by the wind. “What clean, spotless safety is there?”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:title: Rejection File (Shell Laboratory · Access Control Room)
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s2-1: Last night, on the other side of the cross-world connection, Mother and I found the K3-7 storage locker outside the abandoned launch site. The words she spoke in the night wind—“What clean and spotless peace are you talking about?”—still weigh heavily against my chest.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s2-2: When the twenty-two-hundred countdown ended, the cross-world connection cut off on schedule. Mother on the other side, along with that world, remained in the darkness, while I opened my eyes once more in the faint light of morning and connected to this new body for today.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s3-1: In that mother’s world, peace required a cruel price. In this world, the source of that suffering remained locked in old records. To dig out that “unclean ledger,” Estelle used the internal structure I had mapped
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s3-2: out in previous cycles to obtain from the Church a single-use inspection order limited to “routine outer-perimeter archives.” By that afternoon, we were already inside the shell laboratory in the outer suburbs.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s4-1: The corridor was dim, and the deacon assigned by the Church stood guard over us. Estelle invoked audit doctrine and demanded access to the original logistics allocation forms accumulated over the past several decades. Piles of dust-covered metal
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s4-2: boxes blocked the passageway. The deacon did not want to soil his uniform, so he could only stand a few steps away, watching us rummage through the old anti-rust oil ledgers. Every so often he checked his watch, urging us to finish this tedious errand.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s5-1:
While he turned away to look through his communicator, a row of tall archive shelves briefly blocked his view. Estelle took several probes from her tool bag and pressed them against an old access lock at the very back of the administrative district.
It was
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s5-2: an old-fashioned short-circuiting technique she had worked out from the ruined electrical boxes over the past few days. After a faint pop, the lock released. A heavy hidden door, whose existence even the deacon did not know about, slid open a crack before us.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s6-1: Estelle stopped outside the door. The inspection order in her hand was merely an ordinary document that could reach only the outer perimeter.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s8-1: “This door isn’t covered by Sera’s inspection order.” She looked into the dark passage. Her voice was very quiet.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s9-1: The rules required her to sign the life-continuation contract that would determine where she went next while knowing nothing at all about the future. If she were caught trespassing beyond her authority, the three elders responsible for the review could jointly sign to terminate her candidacy at any time.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s10-: But she did not hesitate. She put the inspection order, thin as waste paper, into her pocket, crossed the threshold, and followed me into the core access control room. The hidden door closed silently behind us, shutting out the deacon’s footsteps in the corridor.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s11-:
This was a core area never opened to outsiders. The iron cabinets held top-secret files on physical media, and the air was filled with the sour, moldy smell peculiar to old paper.
In the bottom drawer, Estelle retrieved the complete original set of

Lysenko’s sealed “Application for Supplementing the Base Capacity Pool.” We had previously uncovered the blood-soaked capacity for ten thousand people and his private body specifications, and had also deduced his plan to create a final successor.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s13-:
But what truly made me cold was the changing language and seals on these papers from year to year.
Estelle connected the applications and approvals from one year to the next, arranging them into a circle. In

the earliest approval, Lysenko demanded ten thousand political prisoners without restraint; in later reports, he compromised, changing his wording to request the staged requisition of civilians nationwide.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s14-: And in the application that had been blocked, the deadlock in this brutal transaction stood fully exposed.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s17-:
Application for Supplementing the Base Capacity Pool · Approval Page (Access Control Room Archive):
「Application: extraction for the base capacity pool. Source: 10,000 political-prisoner living subjects. Method: synchronous, total.」
Approval One:

Permit continued construction of the technical facilities; retain the “long-window operator” body project for external presentation.
Approval Two: Do not provide the target roster. Military, police, and transport departments at every level must not

assist with this operation’s arrests.
Annotation: Do not add names to the boarding roster for this project. Retaining the original body is the only form of continuation.
(Two seals, stamped on the same page. Between them, a finger’s width of blank space.)
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s20-: “The Supreme Office allowed Lysenko to build the production line for mindless bodies as a facade.” Her finger stopped on the rejection seal. “But it refused to provide the ten thousand people to fill them, and refused to let the military and police assist with the arrests.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s22-: This deliberate split was written on the authority division table beside it. The left column belonged to Lysenko. The right column belonged to the Supreme Office.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s24-:
“Lysenko held the final authority to write personalities, while the Head of State blocked the supply of living people.”
Estelle pointed to the annotation. “‘Retaining the original body is the only form of

continuation’—the Head of State did not acknowledge Lysenko’s so-called ‘replacement with a perfect shell’ at all.” She looked up. “In the Head of State’s eyes, a shell copied from past memories was merely a

new person. Once that new person was fitted with Lysenko’s memories and authority, and could escape the limits of a lifespan by changing bodies, he would become an independent ghost who needed no place on the

Ark and could attain immortality in the old world. The Head of State intended to keep every place on the Ark firmly in his hands. He would never allow such a monster, drifting outside the system, to be born.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s28-: Back at the table, Estelle took out a stack of blank paper and quickly copied the document numbers, dates, and exact wording of the key approvals from the files—two copies.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s31-: “This copy goes back to Sera later.” She pushed one stack aside. “I’m keeping the other.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s33-: “If Sera was willing to give us the inspection order, why are you keeping a copy behind her back?”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s39-: “Once we report back, the archive access for this sensitive area will automatically be locked and filed. If the Church or the elders decide, to preserve the stability of the system, to erase the
truth about these ‘ten thousand people’ from the official records, and I don’t even have the exact document numbers and original wording in my hands, I’ll have no leverage to demand another audit.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s45-: “I trust her character. After all these trips, she hasn’t secretly made things difficult for us.” She refuted it crisply. “But trusting her as a person and trusting the position behind her are two different things. I can’t hand all the evidence back to the system.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s48-: This immovable act of making two copies was the clearest measure she had taken of her own situation. She said nothing more, carefully folded the handwritten original, and put it into the inner pocket of her uniform.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s50-: While she organized the original, I pushed open an inner door directly beside the control room.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s52-: It was the source scanning room. A huge circular scanning frame stood coldly in the center of the room. The distance to the chin rest and the slight curve of the headrest had all been welded from dead iron into a fixed custom fit.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s53-:
The scan subject on the specifications sheet posted on the wall had been blacked out. But I had seen this blueprint during the inspection of the underground facility. Every precise parameter pointed, without the slightest discrepancy, to the same person.
Lysenko.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s54-: “He never intended to put anyone else into these shells.” Estelle came over as well and glanced at the scan record.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s55-: This also explained why the first-generation undead I had seen only awakened later—the Head of State had cut off the fuel for this plan. Only after the blockade on those
ten thousand people was finally lifted did these ownerless shells, originally left on hold, receive enough base capacity to write in the first batch of personalities.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s56-: I returned to the control room and found a dust-covered engineering log among a row of iron cabinets bearing Heisenberg’s personal clearance labels by the door.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s57-:
Beside a densely packed page of system inspection records, Heisenberg had circled in red a unique physical deviation recording the wear on the local prototype’s main shaft: phase error 0.04.
Below the red

circle was a handwritten note from that time:
『System blind spot identified: use the historical 0.04 main-shaft phase bias to forcibly inject a minor logical deadlock into the verification module. If this

operation is bound to the machine’s mandatory shutdown process at twenty-two hundred each day, and only if the physical connection at the other end has not been cleared, the deadlock will be triggered before

shutdown, forcibly engraving a shutdown anomaly record lasting 5.3 seconds into the low-level maintenance log chain. If the other end is empty, the connection will shut down normally, with no anomaly.』
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s58-: “He tested a back door in the original system.” Estelle hurried back, her eyes passing over the status flow on the log page. “This deadlock record has no semantics. It’s only a string of low-level status codes. Read-only.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s59-:
“Who was it for?”
“For the machine left at this endpoint at the moment the shutdown occurred.” She stared at the words “if this operation is bound.” “But whether he ever actually deployed it…”
“He did.” I remembered the core components we had checked

countless times down below over the past few days. “Over the past few weeks, I inspected the current cross-world machine. The core components that drive the shutdown, even the low-level basic process modules, still retain parts from that old model.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s60-:
Heisenberg’s “if this operation is bound” hypothesis had survived to the present alongside those components that had never been replaced.
The cross-world shutdown that arrived every night at twenty-two hundred had originally been a one-way fall into absolute

silence. But with those 5.3 seconds of anomalous state retention, when we checked the logs after twenty-two hundred, we could at least confirm through the abrupt deadlock record that the shutdown just completed had encountered a real physical endpoint blocking it.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s61-: It could not transmit a single word, nor prove who was on the other side. But it was enough to carve ironclad proof into the cold machine logs that “at that moment, the other side was not empty.” In a world that restarted every morning, where

no one remembered that a cross-world connection had occurred during the night, this indelible low-level record would be the only physical evidence in our hands that could prove to this world that “someone really was connected to us just now.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s62-: Just then, the security camera above the hidden door, its red light flickering faintly, suddenly began blinking faster. The deacon’s hurried footsteps sounded in the corridor at the same time as his communicator called the guards to break down the door. He had evidently realized that we had been gone too long behind the piles of ledgers.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s63-:
“Go.” Estelle pointed toward the ventilation emergency duct above us.
This was the core area. Her routine inspection order was a scrap of paper here. If we were caught and taken to the ecclesiastical

interrogation room, the three elders responsible for the review could jointly terminate her candidacy at any time—and they would search out the “ten-thousand-person” original she had hidden against her body.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s64-: “The pried-open lock and the disturbed original files are still here. Crawling into the ventilation duct won’t clear us of suspicion.” I looked at the shaking door.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s65-: “I know.” She stepped onto the iron cabinet and glanced back at me, the inner pocket of her uniform slightly bulging. “It won’t. That’s why we have to preserve the evidence. With the original document numbers, even if I lose my qualification, the Council of Elders won’t be able to pretend this application never existed. Let’s go.”
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s66-: We had only just crawled deep into the duct when the thunderous sound of the lock being smashed apart came from below. But now, in our pockets, along with the original records of the slaughter of ten thousand civilians, we also carried a key capable of prying open tonight’s darkness.
texts.chapter:phase2-rejection:event:text-s67-: We crawled out of this lightless underground area.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:title: Chapter Twenty-Five: The Missing Page
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s1-1: At ten last night, we conducted a one-way disconnection test using the equipment in the village. The moment we forcibly severed the connection to that legacy backdoor, the machine on the other end forcibly generated a status-closure record, triggering an anomalous signal lasting 5.3 seconds.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s2-1: The other side did not respond, but the disconnection caused the local device to output an error log. Following the addressing prefix in the log, I finally found, in this repeatedly trial-and-errored branch, a backup node not controlled by the White Tower—the external disaster recovery management station deep in the canyon.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s3-1: The actual shutdown command could only be submitted by an external system. But if that disaster station still retained a physical interface capable of writing the “termination marker” to the main network, I could verify whether this backup route was still alive.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s5-1: At eight in the morning, when I opened my eyes in this body, only fourteen hours remained for this expedition.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s6-1: The external disaster recovery management station stood at the end of a canyon to the northwest. In this branch of the world, history had taken a small detour—the shanties that had once crowded the area outside the canyon had disappeared. There was no settlement here, only a deserted dead-end canyon.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s7-1: Before we left, Estelle brought along, as usual, her personal notebook containing a copy of the First Relief Register’s oath. She had already confirmed through offline data that the lines used as the Watermarsh funeral oath actually came from a later list of cleansing persecutions. But no matter
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s7-2: how disgraceful the history was, the village still needed those remaining prayers to support the bereaved who had not survived the rainy season. Today, she had merely used the authority to verify that historical record as grounds for applying for a permit to leave the village, covering for me.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s8-1: At ten in the morning, we left the village. Apart from oilcloth and blankets, we carried no unnecessary burdens. In this branch, the disaster station had been flooded by stagnant water for more than a century, and harmful
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s8-2: gases had settled in the ruins at the bottom. Once the canyon cooled in the afternoon and the air pressure shifted, the toxic gas would spread upward through the passages. We had only a few hours for the expedition.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s12-: The boundary map we had obtained in the village came to an abrupt stop at the mouth of the canyon. There was no road in the canyon at all, only loose stones of every size, their edges sharp.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s13-: We picked our way through the stones, sometimes sinking deep, sometimes barely touching down. I walked quickly and nearly lost my footing several times.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s15-: “There’s no one else here. You don’t really need to check that notebook.” I could not help speaking as I kicked aside a stone blocking the way. “You said you would help me. Once we reach the disaster station, you don’t need to keep pretending with that verification order.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s17-: “I didn’t get the verification order for show.” She stepped around a sharp fallen rock, her breathing steady. “Since there is an actual disaster station here, I have to verify
its condition myself. I can’t rely on those conclusions you claim to have ‘experienced elsewhere’ to decide how I’ll account for this when we return to the village tomorrow.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s19-: The canyon wound on. I had just hurried around a sharp bend when I heard Estelle call from ahead, “Stop.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s20-: I froze. There was no one directly ahead.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s21-: I cautiously took another step. My foot landed on a downward slope. The loose stones could not bear my weight. With a clatter, an entire sheet of scree slid down the incline. I jerked my foot back and stood rigidly in place.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s24-: The second sound came from behind me.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s25-: I hurried back around the bend. She was still there. It was not her body that had been stuck, but the roll of oilcloth tied to the outside of her pack, wedged hard into the gap between two rocks. She had just freed herself.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s27-: “That ‘stop’ came from ahead.” I pointed into the depths of the canyon. The structure of the canyon walls was like a huge amplifier, carrying the sound from behind us around to the front.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s29-: “I was behind you the whole time.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s30-: She did not argue about the echo. She simply retied the oilcloth neatly and put her pack back on.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s32-: “The echoes are too confusing. From now on, at bends like this, you must see the other person with your own eyes before reporting.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s35-: With the rule established, we set off again. She crossed the bend carefully and waved only after reaching a place where I could see her clearly.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s36-: The alternating-cover method was cumbersome and slow. Each time we stopped to wait, I calculated the time remaining in my head. That tormenting echo became the strictest discipline on the road ahead—we could not trust what we heard. We could move on only after seeing the other person standing there with our own eyes.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s39-: At one in the afternoon, a small fortress suddenly appeared, embedded in the rock wall at the end of the canyon. Half of it was buried deep in the stone, while the other half stood exposed in the high air. Above the entrance hung a severely faded umbrella-shaped symbol: “Disaster Recovery.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s40-: The lower space buried in the rock had been completely flooded by groundwater, turned into a pool of stagnant water. And my true objective—the external disaster recovery interface responsible for receiving the shutdown command—was submerged in that black, bottomless water.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s41-: I stood before the iron door leading to the lower level, water rising to my ankles and washing over the soles of my shoes.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s44-: Estelle came up behind me and stopped two steps from the water. “The target device is underwater?”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s46-: “Yes.” I looked at the black water.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s47-: She lowered her head and glanced at the structural diagram on the terminal.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s49-: “We can’t go in.” She pointed to the main control room on the blueprint. “It isn’t just the flooding. The entire lower half is marked as having a high concentration of settled toxic gas.” She pointed to the main control room on the blueprint again. “To bypass the underwater section, we can only find a way through the unflooded station area above.

There’s a backup terminal in the upper main control room. We can try modifying the disaster station’s gateway routing through that terminal. Once the gateway is hijacked, when the main network sends its keepalive scan, the upper terminal can intercept the scan packet and send back a green online confirmation while impersonating the underwater node.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s52-: “If you want to verify this route tonight, modifying the routing to answer on its behalf can only confirm that this node’s logical address is still valid in the main network protocol. It can’t perform the actual write you need.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s53-: I looked at her. On the way to the canyon, I had already told her the truth: at ten tonight, I would no longer continue walking with this world’s version of her.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s54-: “What I need to verify today is that this address is still alive in the network logic.” I met her eyes. “If the address is confirmed alive, then this isn’t a dead end. As for the physical interface being unreachable, at worst, I’ll connect to another disaster station that hasn’t been flooded in a different branch.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s56-: “Don’t touch the routing-tampering option until we’ve exhausted every physical route here.” She spoke crisply. “The temperature is dropping. Once the toxic gas rises, we can stay only until the afternoon at most. Find a route first. Don’t work backward from an assumed result to justify the choices we make now.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s59-: For the next two hours, we searched through the safe areas above.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s60-: There was a maintenance hatch in the corridor. Beneath it was only a dry section of old cable duct. We smashed open the rusted locks on every storage room and found only rotting mops and broken glass. No pump. No diving suit. Not even a hose

long enough to use for ventilation. When we aimed the flashlight down into the water, we could faintly see the casing of the interface box, but it was at least seven meters below the surface, with the passage jammed tight by twisted steel frames.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s61-: At three in the afternoon, every physical route had been proven a dead end.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s62-: When I returned to the main control room, Estelle was sitting before the backup terminal in the unflooded area. We had already confirmed the structure from the diagram. As the outside temperature dropped, the toxic gas in the lower level would soon rise, but until then, the safe area above was still habitable.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s63-: She logged into the system using the authority granted by her verification order. In other branches of the world, she had once sat here for an entire afternoon, staring at the cleansing list that had turned relief into power, and discovered that the

Watermarsh funeral oath had been inserted through deliberate alteration. But today, she did not access those old ledgers that had shattered her faith, nor did she search for the misaligned records of the people responsible underground across two generations.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s64-: She went straight to the disaster station’s gateway control panel.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s67-: At three-thirty, the toxic-gas detector began to rise slowly. Although the lower level was already filled with toxic gas, the upper main control room would remain within safe limits until four. The physical route to the bottom was sealed, and there was no need to perform the offline-data verification again.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s68-: Estelle looked at the screen and placed her hand on the terminal keyboard. Without the necessary authorization, the “Modify Gateway Routing” option on the screen was yellow with a warning indicator.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s70-: “This terminal is outside the scope of the verification order,” she said quietly. “Our unauthorized operation belongs to the business layer. The log has been stored in the local cache and won’t be packaged and uploaded to the main network until six tomorrow morning. But lower-level connectivity is another matter.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s71-: She could still take the incomplete oath back and demand an explanation from the Inner Circle. But the moment she pressed Enter, all the leverage she still had would be placed at the edge of a cliff.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s73-: “If you’re destined not to continue with this world’s version of me after ten tonight, who will bear the mess you leave behind?” She looked at the yellow light on the screen.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s75-: “If we unplug the data cable now and physically disconnect this terminal from the network, the local cache won’t be transmitted tomorrow morning. Tomorrow, you just need to find an opportunity to remove and destroy the hard drive.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s76-: She looked at me for a long time, then slowly shook her head.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s77-: “The main network scans the disaster station’s connectivity every second.” She pushed the no-longer-worth-clinging-to fragment of the oath aside and placed both hands back on the keyboard. “If you unplug the cable, connectivity will be interrupted immediately.

If the main network doesn’t receive the routine packet at six tomorrow morning, then discovers from the timing records that this node was physically disconnected, it will immediately send someone with a physical key to retrieve the local hard drive.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s79-: “Give me the flashlight. You follow the blueprint. I’ll alter the routing.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s80-: The routing change was complicated but clear. I held the flashlight while she used the logical login authority attached to her candidate status to enter the commands line by line.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s81-: At the final step, she activated the routing hijack. The upper terminal intercepted the scan packet sent by the main network to the underwater node, then impersonated the underwater node and sent back an online confirmation.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s83-: The test passed. The main network protocol accepted the gateway’s proxy-response green light, and the verification was complete. Without hesitation, she immediately pressed the cancel key, cutting off the temporary proxy. The gateway resumed normal forwarding, but the offline log had already been generated.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s84-: The paper credential was divided into three fields.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s85-: In the “Operator” field, Estelle signed her name.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s86-: Her pen hovered over the final field for a moment. By protocol, if the accompanying party did not sign as witness, the record of this temporary unauthorized connection counted as a unilateral attempt at sabotage.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s88-: “You’re not on the roster.” She put her pen away. “If you sign here, once the electronic data syncs tomorrow, the audit will definitely trace your identity. If a name belonging to no identifiable person appears in an operation log of this level, you won’t even be able to explain how you came out here with me.”
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s89-: And so the crucial “Independent Verification” field remained permanently blank. Tomorrow morning, when the terminal data was uploaded, an electronic backup of this incomplete credential would appear on the review desk.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s90-: But the system recognized only the electronic command. The validity of that address in the main network’s logic had been confirmed.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s95-: Before four in the afternoon, we withdrew from the disaster station, as the toxic gas began spreading upward more quickly from the lower level.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s96-: On the way back, before the sky became completely dark, we lit a campfire beneath a huge windbreak rock in the middle of the canyon.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s97-: At ten that night, the canyon was so dark that even the sound of the wind seemed hollow. The fire was nearly out. Estelle sat beside the ashes with the notebook containing the oath spread across her knees.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s98-: Holding her pen, she forcefully crossed out the line “The collective will guarantees the correct future” from the oath. In this repeatedly explored branch, she did not need to
sit for hours and verify again the history of relief being turned into power. The slogan that had already collapsed in another world was still erased by her without hesitation.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s99-: But she did not burn the page filled with lies. When she returned to Watermarsh with the notebook and attended the next funeral for the bereaved, those villagers who had lost their families would still need the remaining sincere prayers. No matter how disgraceful the history was, the mutual-aid ritual itself still had to remain.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s100: I watched the quiet girl across the fire. The cross-world countdown was almost over. After ten tonight, my first-person view would go dark in this branch and turn to finding another way out.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s101: But the me remaining in this body would not disappear when that view left. While the version of me belonging to this branch spent the night beside the campfire in the canyon, I would still remember

everything that had happened during the day—the black pool no one could enter, the terminal that had forged the proxy response, and the unauthorized record added to the system with only Estelle’s signature.
texts.chapter:chapter-25-eight:event:text-s102: Tomorrow morning, deprived of cross-world communication, I would have to walk back to the village with her. By then, we would have to face together the institutional inquiry brought by that blank verification field—since the system could not produce a legitimate

witness, she had acted alone; and I, as the only person who had been with her from beginning to end, would become the sole person questioned alongside her. No perspective from across worlds could bear the consequences for us. Only our own selves tomorrow could.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:title: Chapter Twenty-Five Appendix: The Lie That Saved People
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s1-1:
First Relief Ledger · Page Index (copy held by the External Disaster Recovery Station):
“...Page seventeen. Page eighteen. Page twenty. Page twenty-one...”
(Copyist’s note:
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s1-2:
Nineteen is not in this sequence. This ledger’s index only lists page numbers.
The page numbers skip over it, so the index skips over it too. Not one extra word was added.)
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s4-1: As the desperate exploration of the flooded disaster recovery station faded from view, my consciousness, carried forward by the cycle, fell into an independent coordinate that already
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s4-2: existed—the sixth branch of the world I had experienced. Fourteen hours remained until I was cut out at ten tonight. At eight in the morning, I opened my eyes again inside this body.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s5-1: In this world, the texts concerning history differed in subtle ways. In the previous world, we had seen the current textbook outside simply delete the passage about Watermarsh’s founding in order to conceal the
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s5-2: truth. Here, however, the Church’s coursebook had not only left in the so-called “Seventy-Third Article,” it stated in black and white that it contained a doctrine and required Estelle to swear by it tomorrow.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s6-1: To verify it, at 8:10 this morning she took me to the old archive cabinets in the chapel and retrieved the original microfilm made of the First Relief Ledger before the Church of Convergence was founded. In the film projected
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s6-2: onto the wall, the portion corresponding to the Seventy-Third Article—the material recorded at the time as page nineteen—contained no sentence saying “A common will guarantees a correct future.” The densely packed entries
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s6-3: consisted entirely of the names of people from the Watermarsh settlement who had received grain rations at the time, with only one plain sentence beside them: “Ally with one another, and set aside a mouthful of rations each day.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s7-1: This was the underlying record left from the original microfilming. Later, the people responsible for compiling the textbook had packaged this history of allying to distribute rations as the Seventy-Third Article, forcibly inserting that loyalty slogan used to control people.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s10-1: What she was going to verify today was the physical original that still remained at the disaster recovery station.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s12-1: “Watermarsh used this same page of this same ledger for its founding anniversary.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s14-1: “Every year on the day of the first snow, our village recites all several hundred names on this page one by one. Mixed together with the words for sending off the dead, they became a long passage everyone hears from childhood onward. When someone in the village has a funeral, we recite it then too.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s15-1: She stared at the false coursebook on the table for a while, then closed it gently but firmly.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s17-1: “I’m going to swear by this forged textbook tomorrow.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s21-1: “If we already saw the truth clearly on the film this morning, why are we still going all the way to where the original is kept?”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s24-1: “You’re investigating what’s going on with this world. To you, who wrote one sentence is the conclusion.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s26-1: “But I’m investigating whether the few lines I’m going to recite in front of everyone tomorrow are something I can recite. I have to see with my own eyes how the thing that should have been there was erased from the physical original.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s29-1: Before we left today, Sera gave final approval to the release order without even looking up.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s31-1: “The rules say the lifelong confidentiality and continuation-of-life agreements have to be signed tonight, or tomorrow’s seat is void. And before handing over your life with that signature, you say you want to verify a book with a missing page first. You won’t be back until midnight.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s33-1: “I approve. I’ll leave the signing table open for you until two in the morning. What I want to see isn’t what that page says. It’s what you intend to do after verifying the truth with your own eyes.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s34-1: Sera stood and gestured for us to leave.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s37-1: We left the village through the west gate. On the previous timeline, we had been heading for the deep classified station area built at the bottom of the canyon. With the deep passage flooded, we could only struggle through the rubble-filled canyon floor, eventually
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s37-2: climbing into an offline terminal at the elevated gateway that had not been flooded. This time, she was only verifying the physical original of the relief ledger made available to the public, so we did not need to descend into the canyon. We followed the yellow-earth
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s37-3: road used by people, winding upward across the surface, and spent three hours reaching the External Disaster Recovery Station built atop the cliff. This gray cluster of public buildings was the external archive area once opened to ordinary church members.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s40-1: For the first half hour, Estelle merely walked with her head lowered. She did not speak until we had passed the abandoned fork. She said nothing about the oath or the disaster recovery station we were heading toward. Instead, she began talking about the rainy season in the village.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s42-1: “Where I’m from, someone has to guard the west embankment as soon as the rainy season comes. You press your ear hard against the soil and listen. If water starts boring through cracks in the earth, it makes a sharp sound. The moment you hear it, you have to shout for someone.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s44-1: “It rained heavily yesterday. I went to listen before I left. There’s already movement in the soil. The embankment won’t hold for more than a few days. The village has already sent people to reinforce it, but water leaking through the mud cracks can’t be stopped by filling them with earth alone. We need heavy machinery brought in.” She paused,
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s44-2: then continued. “The shifts are assigned by household. One household covers one night. If the man isn’t there, the man next door takes his turn. During the day, the woman from the first household works half a day for the neighbors to make it up. As for whether it balances exactly, no one has ever bothered to calculate such fine details.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s48-1: “When someone in the village dies, the rule is the same. From confirming the death until carrying the body out of the house, that’s women’s work. Once it’s out the door, carrying it all the way to the graveyard is men’s work.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s50-1: “But there’s one step in between that has to be done together: changing the body into clean clothes. Four people have to stand in the room while it’s done. Two from the dead person’s family, and two from the neighbors helping. No one is allowed to touch the body alone.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s51-1: I turned to look at her and asked why it had to be that way.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s53-1: “To prevent mistakes. If only one person touches the body, there’s no way to explain it afterward if something goes wrong. But if all four people are there, everyone remembers how the clothes were put on, one piece at a time.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s57-1: “When I was eleven, I filled in once at the old carpenter’s house at the west end of the village.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s59-1: “The old carpenter’s wife died. There weren’t enough people in the house, so they could only get three together. He pulled me over to fill the fourth position. Once I went in, I didn’t do anything. I just stood there and counted the hands they held out.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s61-1: “I only learned when I grew up that the fourth person wasn’t there to work in the first place. They were there to count.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s62-1: She paused, and her voice dropped.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s64-1: “The old carpenter is lying in bed now too. He’s been sick for more than two months. The village is short on doctors and medicine, and the last of the fever medicine was used up last week. All he can do is wait for the official supply channel to reopen and get the medicine approved and sent in.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s67-1: Over those long three hours, she told seven or eight stories like that, in fragments.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s68-1: They were all concrete steps. Her hands moved unconsciously at her sides as she talked. When she gestured through some detail, she would suddenly stop to correct herself, stubbornly retracing the whole sequence from the beginning.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s69-1: I walked beside her the entire way without interrupting.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s70-1: Only when the gray cluster of buildings appeared at the top of the slope did she stop speaking on her own.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s78-1: The disaster recovery hall was filled with the dusty smell of old paper. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of handwritten distribution ledgers were piled on the long table in the center of the hall.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s79-1: We searched through them at the long table like looking for a needle in the sea. The wall clock showed that it was already 3:00 in the afternoon. Estelle turned the pages more and more slowly, finally stopping at a yellowed record and pressing her knuckle hard against the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s81-1: “Among the people receiving relief on this page, three households have the Water surname. Shui Da-you, Shui Er-mao...” She read the names from the paper. “The first two pages of the genealogy passed
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s81-2: down from my grandfather’s generation are dedicated to these people. There are only a few families with this surname in our village altogether, and every one of them recognizes these three names.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s84-1: She drew a deep breath and continued turning the pages. Tucked into the very front of the handwritten ledgers was a stack of thin sheets bearing the old regime’s standard letterhead and signature boxes. They were official application forms.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s86-1:
Reason: The district’s joint observation group requests grain, lamp oil, and basic fever medication for night patrols, medical visits, and funerals after the start of winter.
Attachment: Qualification verification for the group’s initiators (rejected investigators from the former Third-Ring Engineering Office) and one participant roster, twenty-seven
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s86-2:
people.
Decision: This group’s network will help absorb the displaced people rejected for boarding and relieve resentment caused by the Ark’s supply cutoff. Its influence may also be used as external support to pressure the engineering departments competing for ship tickets. It does not violate the primary directive. Approved. Issue at the lower limit.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s88-1: At the other end of the long table, another stack sat neglected: acknowledgments of receipt for directives from the old regime. They went from the initially precise “Received and understood. Will comply,” to the later “This locality did not receive the previous order,” and finally to the completely empty boxes on the acknowledgments from the last third.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s89-1: Estelle placed the blank acknowledgment from the final year beside the last application form bearing official letterhead.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s90-1: The year they stopped was the same.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s91-1: And in the rough, thread-bound ledgers from after that year, the network called the “Joint Observation Group” had adopted a new seal: “Church of Convergence.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s95-1: At 3:30 in the afternoon, we passed through two heavy iron doors and entered the deepest part of the archives, where we found the physical original of the First Relief Ledger provided for public consultation.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s97-1: The page index had stated it plainly before we came: seventeen, eighteen, twenty, twenty-one. Only page nineteen was missing from the middle.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s98-1: Estelle turned the fragile ledger to the gap between pages eighteen and twenty. Under the dim corridor lights, she pried open the binding.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s101-1: Deep inside was a long strip of extremely narrow paper. A row of tiny needle holes ran through it, with a little of the old thread still clinging to the torn edges.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s103-1: “It was bound in. Later, someone cut it away by force, right along the stub.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s104-1: She pressed both hands against the two sides of the book and held them there for a long time. In the official original at the disaster recovery station, the missing page had not been filled with a fabricated doctrine. It was simply a black hole cut open by a blade.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s105-1: She did not ask why the book had been shortened for no apparent reason, nor why the later handlers had accepted the hole without even asking about it.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s106-1: She only opened her coursebook and wrote down “needle holes” and “thread ends” exactly as they were.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s109-1: In this archive area, the incomplete distribution ledger and the other thick relief records stood along the east wall, while the directives issued by the Church of Convergence ordering the destruction of records stood along the west wall.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s110-1: I carefully looked through the documents on both sides by myself. One of the persecution directives on the west wall contained a clear doctrine: “...The Fated faction firmly believes in the existence of a bad future. This certainty is itself an ongoing observation of this branch of calamity, thereby anchoring and strengthening the inevitable
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s110-2: destruction in physical terms. Therefore, cleansing these heretics and burning their archives preserves the true mind and protects our tomorrow.” In the directive’s approval section, someone had left a small “正” added when a mistake was made. The first stroke curved inward like a hook, and the final horizontal stroke rose toward the upper right.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s111-1: I watched her set down the few anti-heretic suppression documents she had just examined. She returned to the east wall, her gaze falling on the supply confirmation columns in the early relief records. The signature boxes
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s111-2: there contained the same “正” characters used for counting, with the first stroke curving inward like a hook and the final horizontal stroke rising toward the upper right. She stood before the long table for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s113-1: On the other side of the long table, several stacks of old-regime equipment logs lay haphazardly, thick with dust. With the change of regimes, these once-strictly-confidential technical records were nothing but meaningless waste paper to the Church, jumbled together and discarded in the external archive area along with the public records.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s114-1: I opened two equipment review records whose paper quality was completely different.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s115-1: One sheet had already grown brittle. Written on it in black ink was:
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s117-1:
Pool Position Observation Log
...
Current pool position: -37.4 meters (rate of descent deviates from population model)
Anomalous cause: [blank]
Handled by: [Duties Code 01 · abbreviated signature]
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s119-1: The paper of the other was slightly newer. Pressed onto it was an enlarged image screenshot. It showed part of the original log above, and beside that partial photograph, another scheduling system’s dates were clearly listed in red ink:
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s121-1:
The dates and times of the anomalous pool positions above have been placed alongside the time machine scheduling logs.
During the days when the old regime’s time machine was operating, the pool-position curve fell in abrupt drops by fixed values, leaving regular gaps.
Handled by: [Duties Code 02 · abbreviated signature]
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s123-1: The former had merely looked at the numbers that did not line up on the books and left the initial question behind. Much later, the latter used another extremely secret scheduling table to
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s123-2: fill in the cause of the pool’s precipitous decline. Two permissions that had been completely isolated under the old system were now opened side by side in this pile of disregarded waste paper.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s124-1: Estelle did not look in that direction. To her, the physical network records from this station built atop the cliff were not what mattered.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s128-1: “In those first two years, when the world was collapsing completely, this network called the Joint Observation Group really did save people.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s129-1: She spoke suddenly. Her voice sounded somewhat dry in the quiet archive. Over the past several hours, she had not examined the unresolved accounts of the surrounding settlements.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s129-2: She had devoted all her attention to the thick relief records along the east wall, searching through them until she had found every scattered name belonging to Watermarsh.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s131-1: “The names written page after page in that ledger—they really didn’t starve to death in the streets because of that hot food. The desire of those who survived the great disaster to gather together, warm one another, and live to see tomorrow was real too.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s134-1: “Because when I was eleven and that old carpenter pulled me into the room, the rules—everyone trembling, trying to do things correctly—weren’t fake. The people who struggled to stay alive back then for this food and these rules of mutual aid weren’t fake people in some fraud.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s138-1: “Then are you still going to swear tomorrow?”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s140-1: “From childhood onward, every year on the day of the first snow, the whole village recites that passage together. Whenever we reach the last sentence, all the voices join together. That is one of the most solid things I’ve ever felt in my life.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s142-1: “Now I’ve verified it myself. That page was brutally pulled out.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s145-1: “But I absolutely don’t intend to return that joined voice from when I was seven. That solid voice wasn’t bestowed on me from above. It was spoken by our own people.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s148-1: By closing time, it was completely dark. When we came out, the dim night lamps had been lit along the corridor. The clock hands pointed to 6:30.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s149-1: Estelle stopped at the far end of the corridor and said there was one more thing to do before leaving.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s152-1: There was a crude worship corner at the end of the corridor. The platform was bare.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s153-1: I withdrew to a bench at the other end of the passage, ten paces away from her.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s154-1: I heard her begin. She was reciting the passage the whole village recited together every year on the first snow and at funerals in Watermarsh. A corridor wind howled past. I faintly heard “the earth is warm,” heard “the road has been walked,” and then a long, solemn sentence that sounded like the counting of names.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s155-1: Just as she reached the very end, her voice suddenly paused.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s156-1: After the pause, she did not continue with the ending everyone knew should come next. She stood silently before the platform, leaving the sentence suspended in midair.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s159-1: Ten minutes later, we reached the courtyard. The night wind was cold.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s160-1: I asked her why she had paused like that.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s162-1: “When you bury someone in the earth at the graveyard, the first half says that the soil is warm and the road has been walked. Those words are for the living. No one is deceiving anyone.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s163-1: She folded her arms, her shoulders tightening slightly in the wind.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s165-1: “But at the end, it abruptly closes on that phrase, ‘a common will.’ That phrase was inserted to control people. When I conduct funerals myself in the future, I won’t recite it anymore. If other people still want to recite it, I won’t stop them.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s169-1: “If you’re the only one who forcibly deletes that sentence, there’ll be a gap in the voice everyone joins together.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s171-1: “Then let there be a gap.” She stared at the shadow on the ground, her voice quiet but firm. “Because the people standing by the graves in the wind are us. Which sentence deserves to stay and which one has to be thrown away—I have to decide that for myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s174-1: We stood in the pitch-black courtyard. The night wind was colder than when we had arrived. We should have set out when the station closed at 6:30, and there was still plenty of time before the two-in-the-morning deadline Sera had given her. But she seemed to have no intention
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s174-2: of leaving before the bells rang. She kept her back to the road down the mountain, her gaze passing over the station wall and settling deep in the empty night. Only when the faint sound of mechanisms turning came from the nearby clock tower did the hands finally draw near ten.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s175-1: By the weak corridor light, I saw that the cardboard cover of the coursebook in her hands had already been crushed slightly out of shape.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s177-1: “As for the passage on tomorrow’s oath platform... I’ll recite it word for word.” She drew a deep breath, as if forcing some coarse grit down her throat. “Because that’s the ground they built, and that sentence is the price of admission for a seat.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s179-1: “The west embankment is about to give way, and the old carpenter and those seriously ill people are still lying in bed waiting for medicine. If I want to negotiate with the people above, I need a seat in hand. If I want to take control of the supply allocation, then I’ll pay the price they’re asking.”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s180-1: She stopped speaking and finally turned to look at me. I knew why she had forced herself into a desperate situation with only four hours left, why she had spent three and a half hours in this empty courtyard. After ten, I—the
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s180-2: me from another branch, who always wanted to solve things for her—would have to leave. She wanted to leave what came next to the local Arno who would truly accompany her down the mountain and bear the consequences with her.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s181-1: Before the bells struck ten, I looked at her thin shoulders and finally asked:
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s183-1: “If you get a seat and take control of these rules, what will you do later when you meet someone like you today, someone who refuses to recite the last sentence?”
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s184-1: When the first heavy bell sounded, I felt my perceptual connection with this world cut off in an instant, my attention pulled toward the next coordinate in the cycle. I did not hear her answer.
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s185-1: For the next three hours of pitch-black road back to the village, the local Arno left behind would walk beside her. The instant the severance completed, he seamlessly took over this
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s185-2: body, retaining all fourteen hours of memories from waking that morning to the bell just now—including the question I had just asked. But he would not know where I was being pulled
texts.chapter:v15-25b:event:text-s185-3: at that moment. That was the one thing he had lost. He was simply a companion awakened by the bells atop the cliff at midnight, watching how Estelle answered the question beside him.
texts.chapter:chapter-26-that-column:title: Chapter Twenty-Six: That Column
texts.chapter:chapter-26-that-column:event:tex: I pushed open the door, and the cold wind of the morning of August 20 met me head-on. This was another day at Anchor 10.
In the ruins of the previous world, I had found the work case beside the skeleton of Heisenberg from the AI laboratory, and carved the string of low-level maintenance
aliases and the accident-record facility index into my mind. In this world, those memories of not belonging here were my key to breaking into the depths of the system.
I went straight to the center of the village. The oath-taking in the square was nearing its end.

I passed through the crowd at the edge and heard Estelle’s dry, even voice coming through the loudspeakers. To obtain that seat, and the independent verification qualification that came with it, she stood in this ceremony of compromise and fulfilled last

night’s promise to the letter. She was reciting the humiliating oaths she had once wanted to delete—declaring her obedience to the interpretation of the doctrine, acknowledging that the Church had graciously granted her the verification qualification.

Even though I had pressed her about the bottom line of the compromise on the night road in the previous round, her answer still held: she would obtain the seat at any cost, and take these rules into her own hands.

The loudspeaker gave a harsh burst of static, and the oath-taking ended. The crowd began to disperse. Estelle came down from the platform in a dark formal jacket. Her back was perfectly straight, but when she folded up her speech, the knuckles gripping the paper turned faintly white.
She saw me and gave a slight nod amid the crowd, slipping the page into her pocket. We said nothing and went straight to the White Tower.

With the seat and verifier status she had just obtained, she sat at the desk and began writing an application for verification based on her own “continuation-of-life contract.” She requested access to the bodily-rights witness zone for

herself as a candidate, and through it, entry into the external verification zone of White Tower Maintenance Point One. It was the furthest station ordinary maintenance personnel were permitted to reach before the underground facilities.

Sera approved it readily, since this nominally remained within the limited scope of the candidate-rights explanatory zone. As usual, she added the rule in heavy strokes beneath it: a Church representative must be present for every step beyond the outer seal.
But this was only the surface of the access credentials. Sera had not approved the creation of a new body at the AI laboratory, much less the establishment of any cross-world personality source.

“Once we pass the verification zone, we’ll have to use the work case to slip into the deadlock right under the representative’s nose,” she said calmly on the way to the passageway. “And every step we take at the AI laboratory afterward will be completely outside

this contract’s authorization. The moment the low-level system traces are discovered by the local Church, I’ll immediately lose this newly acquired candidate status. That won’t just bring accountability. The quota that’s been locked down will be voided completely.”

She came with me despite knowing the cost because she needed to confirm what her body would actually face, and she would never allow a subject experiment involving a new life to be decided by me alone.
We entered the long, deep passageway of White Tower Maintenance Point One.
At the first heavy iron door, the Church representative guarding it stopped us. Estelle handed over the badge that had just been issued, bearing her fresh authority.
The representative took it and turned it over repeatedly beneath the dim gaslight. When returning it, he could not help staring at the badge once more to confirm it.

Farther in, at the second door, the division of permissions meant a different, equally rigid representative was stationed there. The same fields had to be filled in, and he examined them again, word by word.
I followed behind without asking anything. Estelle’s hands remained steady each time she presented her credentials. She took back the badge and continued inward.

Inside the little room at the maintenance point, the air was thick with the familiar, faint ozone smell of running machinery. Following procedure, the representative stood just inside the door, rigidly watching everything we did. Estelle ignored him and went straight to the corner, opening the duty log hanging there.
