Her eyes fell on the duty record. Beneath that line, an additional note had appeared at some point: “Duty procedure amended. The physical door lock and the authorization check for the operating
terminal are no longer handled by the same representative.” It seemed that the local Church had also discovered the existing security flaw in this world and was splitting up the authority.
Estelle finished reading the entry silently and hung the log carefully back on its nail.
After that, we stood before the terminal of White Tower Maintenance Point One. The representative dutifully watched Estelle’s fingers, but was plainly clueless about the low-level
system commands on the screen. Using the operation to verify her candidate status, Estelle blocked the representative’s view with her back and gave up her place without a word.

On the index interface she had just brought up, I entered the maintenance aliases known only to me and the specific access index at the bottom. The terminal gave a faint hum, and the low-level connection

opened. That old-world password cut off synchronization to the Church’s surface host, secretly took control of the line deeper underground, and directed the search straight to Yuna in the collaborative seat.

At 07:50, the system had captured an instantaneous state snapshot of Yuna as an external collaborative-seat operator. By then she had already connected to the neural circuit. What the system retained was not a simple confirmation of biological features, but an original state containing personality

data. Under normal operation, however, it was currently only data retained in the short-term rolling area, with no continuous long-term archive established. I had to find out what the system’s actual processing rules would be if, someday in the future, I established her as a long-term source.
The screen lit up with a ghostly green glow. With the query access granted by the aliases, I saw the status metadata hanging quietly in the low-level system:

“Status query: collaborative-seat instantaneous state snapshot (07:50).”
“Current allocation: short-term rolling data area. Continuous recording not enabled.”
“Cross-world record archival rule: mandatory physical

black box. Record contents and log-parsing interface not exposed; upon extraction, the entire original record is sealed as an indivisible source, used only to restore first-person experience to a compatible vessel.”
My eyes lingered on the words “contents not exposed” in the last field.

Before this, I had always kept a secret hope—or perhaps a tremendous fear—in my heart: what if, at the final moment before death came for her, she hated me in one branch for not going to save her? If the system allowed me to look ahead at the contents, I might not

have been able to bear that guilt, and might have cut away those desperate fragments for her at the last moment. Even if I used “not bringing this pain back is better for her” as an excuse, I would still be selecting a safe version that allowed me to feel at ease.

But the low-level archival rules severed that possibility. Once archival extraction took effect, it would not care what was a confession, a rejection, or a bad ending. It had no function for selecting among them. It would only seal this vast whole in its entirety as an indivisible black box.

I would have to receive her without any defenses: a Yuna carrying every mutually exclusive, agonizing memory, with the right to regret and the right to resent me. Cold sweat seeped from my palms, but at the same time, I felt a trace of cruel relief.
Estelle stood beside me, looking at the terms on the screen. Calmly, she took paper and a pen from her bag.
“I’m going to write this down.”
The dry rasp of the pen across the paper echoed through the room.
She stopped her pen.
“Mandatory physical black box doesn’t just mean that you can’t look ahead now. It also means that Yuna herself won’t be able to retrieve this original record in the future.
” She looked at me. “If the system retained a parsing interface, then even if the Committee accused her of having disordered memories, she could bring up the record and
throw it in their faces. But since you accepted this interface-free black box, once she wakes up, she’ll have no direct system material proving what she experienced.”
“If the interface were retained, then as soon as she woke up, those people would force her to disclose the record and examine what she actually endured.” I looked at the dim screen. “The
black box erased her means of displaying its contents to the outside, but it also protected her right to refuse to display them. No one can force her to cut open her pain for others to see.”

“But without a system-generated external authentication signature, how can this black box prove that it’s valid?” Estelle’s gaze was sharp. “Since synchronization was cut off, the Church’s host retained only the low-level keystrokes you made.

If someone accuses you in the future of fabricating her memory source, or says this black box has been tampered with, the operation traces here alone can’t prove that this payload belongs to Yuna. What will you use to prove its integrity?”

“The operation logs here alone really can’t prove anything.” I watched the cursor blinking on the screen, my voice somewhat dry. “Relay stations, disaster-recovery stations…this is only the beginning. To make external

systems acknowledge the authenticity of this black box, I’ll have to run through every node in the ruins. Retrieve the sequence records, recover the audit signatures, and obtain the irrevocable completion mark.”

This was no longer a light promise, but a trek long enough to inspire despair. I had to gather every piece of the puzzle myself and use them together to lock down the integrity of this black box. Only then could I prove that these memories belonged entirely to her.

“As for what’s hidden in the logs…” I turned and looked at Estelle. “If she wakes up and hates me too, if she wants to condemn all of this in her own words, I won’t argue with her either. Only she gets to decide.”

We continued scrolling through the sprawling system logs. With no conventional query interface, we had to use the deepest index to compare the system’s responses one by one. In the dim basement, the passage of time became especially indistinct.

The representative waited by the door, growing somewhat impatient. He began pacing back and forth, then finally reminded us that, by regulation, we could not stay too long, and asked whether we wanted to light the gas lamp on the wall.
Estelle calmly said yes, and handed over the permit badge bearing two stamps without looking up. The representative glanced at the red seal ink, stopped urging us, and simply took out a match.
The lamp was lit, and a yellow glow spread through the room. Several more hours passed before a line of old logs appeared on the screen. It was a record left behind by the previous world:

“Source marker: cross-world record block. Source address: Worldline Branch—Type A-49. 08:00–08:10. Operation type: Forced neural takeover. Authorization identification: Level escalation. Operator: (blank).”

I stared at the green characters. The system did not count by human rounds. That source address referred to the world I had inhabited in the previous cycle. As a “level-escalated operation” in the system, I

had truly crossed the barrier, taken control of my past self, and held her hand for ten minutes. But in the low-level operation logs, it was merely a dry line of record with no dialogue and no emotional residue.

“The system couldn’t identify the cross-world, level-escalated authorization, so it forcibly left the operator field blank.” Estelle looked at the log. “The system doesn’t understand content. It only records actions faithfully.”
I collapsed into the iron chair in front of the terminal.
Estelle watched the metadata of the 07:50 snapshot in the short-term rolling area.
“If you designate it as a long-term source in another device later, its status will change to cross-world continuous tracking.” Estelle looked at me. “But for any
personality’s cross-world record to close at the source end, so it can ultimately be extracted as an indivisible black box, there has to be a clear completion signal.”
“Active termination,” I said. “If I forcibly sever the connection before she encounters danger, it would be like putting a termination mark on this record.”

“But the system could only retain it up to the moment you severed it.” She pointed this out calmly. “Yuna’s sacrifice is the full weight of her walking all the way through this dead end. If you cut it off yourself, what remains will only be a protected, incomplete experience. The integrity of her existence as a sacrifice will be broken.”

If I wanted to bring back a complete Yuna—a Yuna who had exhausted every path and faced death herself—I could not press that severance button. Throughout the long process of gathering the data, I could only leave the record running.

After writing this down, she took a formal document from her bag. It was the result of verifying her candidate rights through the system operation today. The tip of her pen stopped before the box at the very bottom: Independent verifier’s signature.
She did not write in that field.
“Even with synchronization of the deep contents cut off, my access to the system here and your operation beside me will leave hard physical traces in this terminal and the Church’s shell
host. Once I sign, the Church will claim that they ‘supervised’ this verification, and list me as an endorser of the reliability of this isolation system as well.” She set the pen down
gently. “I can’t issue a final conclusion under these conditions. I need to keep ‘permission to enter verification’ separate from ‘independent recognition that the system is effective.’”
“Then when do we wait until?”

“Until some day in the future, when the Church’s control over this Tower has completely failed. I’ll return here alone, confirm at that time that the results haven’t been tampered with, and then sign my name.”
She said nothing more, carefully putting the unsigned formal document back into her bag.

“Low-level archiving and sealing.” As she spoke, she took a blank sheet of letter paper and an envelope from the workbench beside her. “These purely mechanical operations all have to be completed by you personally.”
I saw her generate a string of completely arbitrary random characters on the paper. Avoiding my gaze, she folded the sheet and slipped it into the envelope.
“Tonight, when we return to the AI laboratory, I’ll start the scan and overwrite it with my current complete personality.” She ran her tongue along the adhesive strip on the envelope
and sealed it shut. “This is a seal that only I have seen. If the experiment goes smoothly, it will remain in the cross-world backup source along with my personality state tonight.”
She picked up the pen and wrote a specific drawer location on the envelope—the corner of the data room in the AI laboratory, a blind spot in the local facility.
“After we leave, I’ll put it in that drawer myself. And when you return to the world of the finale, you’ll find the physical original from this world in the corresponding drawer.”
Estelle looked at me. “You won’t know the contents in advance. Only a neutral custodian in the future will open both at the same time. Only when the me you awaken gives a string of
characters that exactly matches the ones on the paper in the drawer will it count as proof: she truly came from the independent memory source of tonight, one you couldn’t influence.”
It was a two-way blind-test firewall. A hard rule established to guard against the selfishness I might develop.

We sat at the terminal for a while longer. I exited the old low-level system and watched the screen return to the rigid interface for verifying candidate rights. Only then did we leave the White Tower.

That evening, I did not return directly to our quarters. Instead, I went to the AI laboratory. It was the first time she would exercise an overreach after obtaining candidate status, and the place where I would personally seal away the last trace of my own hope.
In the brightly lit white room, the mechanical arms began preparations before the growth chamber.

“We’re going to create a completely correct backup body template for Yuna and inject it with a globally usable empty capacity.” I looked at Estelle behind the glass. “But we can’t put any of Yuna’s autobiographical memories into it.”

“Before pressing that confirmation key, we follow what we agreed on the way here.” She held the proof she had written at the White Tower, her voice echoing through the empty room. “We do this only once. The moment she opens her eyes, she is a subject with

first-person consciousness. Don’t call her Yuna. Do not conduct any so-called ‘familiarity tests’ on her. Whatever the result, we don’t use ten o’clock tonight as an excuse to abandon her. In this local world, we are jointly responsible for her future.”
I nodded. This was the cost. When my overreach pulled a life forcibly into this world, I had to bear the fact of her existence, rather than treat her as a disposable experiment.
The chamber’s indicator light turned green. We pressed the button.
After the nutrient fluid drained away, the body drew in a deep breath of cold air, shivered faintly, and opened its eyes.

For a moment, she was bewildered, trying to adjust to the bright light in the room. Somewhat afraid, she turned her neck, her gaze sweeping across the cold machines before finally settling on us outside the glass. She looked at me.
There was no familiarity with me in those eyes, no warmth, and no past belonging to Yuna.

The thought that had lingered in my mind—the thought that “perhaps if there were a completely identical, correct body, Yuna herself could recover her original personality through the body’s instincts”—was shattered completely in that moment.
Without the restoration of a complete personality source at the system level, she would not return on her own, even if her body were exactly the same.
Seeing her shrink back, the facility’s care program automatically sent over a warm blanket. She awkwardly reached out and clutched the edge.
“When all this is over,” Estelle said softly as she watched her, “we’ll get her an identity. Here in this village.”
Nine-thirty that night, the laboratory data room.
I watched Estelle carefully place the sealed envelope in the third metal drawer against the wall. It was the fixed location we had agreed on.
Afterward, she sat inside the scanning chamber. This was the final step of the night.
The chamber door slowly closed. As the indicator lights blinked, the system began reading her current complete personality state, including the memory of the random seal. This record
would remain open as her subjective experience continued to accumulate. At ten o’clock, the system would seal and close it on schedule under the one-time authorization set in advance.

When the chamber door opened again, she would return to this small local village carrying the same memories, while the locked backup would remain forever settled in the depths of the system as the source that would bear witness to her future.
It was deep into the night before I returned to our quarters alone. Under the dim yellow light, I opened my notebook.
Estelle’s words from the day weighed heavily on my mind. If this black box was to fully contain Yuna’s struggle, it could not be cut off in advance.

The 07:50 snapshot was only short-term instantaneous data, but it could serve as a starting point. If I reestablished it as a long-term source in the future, its status would change to cross-world continuous tracking. The system did not

produce branches. It merely recorded the collapse of that complete Yuna as it occurred simultaneously in each local universe—those local experiences would become her branch experiences and flow into that enormous operator record pool.

What I wanted to take away was that complete Yuna, and sealing this cross-world personality record likewise required a clear completion signal. As long as any version of her in any of the countless local universes still had subjective experience continuing, the record channel had to remain open for her.
I closed the notebook, and the tip of the pen pressed a deep pit into the paper.

The authority to end the recording actively had always been there, but I could not press it. If I forcibly cut off the record in some branch to keep her from dying, what remained would not carry the full weight of her struggle.

I had to receive an unabridged Yuna. That meant that throughout this long process of gathering the data, I could only leave the record running and watch helplessly as each local ending arrived, again and again.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:title: Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Comatose Segment
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s2-1:
White Tower · Elevator Structure Maintenance Log (Final Three Entries):
“Some Year, Some Month: Cable No. 3 worn beyond limit. Repair requested.
Approval: Not approved.
Following year: Reported again. Approval: ‘Not a
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s2-2:
priority. Handle together after the operator’s plan is restarted.’
Several more years later (handwriting changed): Routine inspection. Cable condition: unchanged.
Note: It’s not as if anyone is going down there again anyway.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s4-1: In all my memories, there is one longest blank. It was the dozen-plus minutes after we crashed at the bottom level—that time when my local consciousness was absent, while my body was abnormally awake.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s8-1: The air before the elevator doors at the bottom of the White Tower carried the smell of iron left unrepaired for years.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s9-1: After listening to that five-second master recording and completing the double-sealed blind test, I had verified the conclusion left by H31 and grasped the rules of active switching. Now I stood alone outside the tightly closed doors. I no longer needed any probe or external device.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s10-1: The short-term snapshot Yuna left at 7:50 on the morning the anchor point was established was the data waiting to be written. And the body I had back then,
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s10-2: after we fell, had entered a deep coma lasting a dozen-plus minutes—that gap in consciousness caused by physiological shutdown was a perfect boundary for entry.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s11-1: The identical elevator doors before me, the echoes in the shaft—these sensory cues from reality were doing everything they could to suppress prediction error. I did not need to treat this place as some kind of physical springboard. By narrowing my
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s11-2: attentional focus and using active predictive decoding, I could cut my consciousness directly into the blank mind of that earlier body within the only modern-root session. I would designate the 7:50 snapshot as the source of the system’s long-term records.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s14-1: I pressed my palm against the cold metal door, letting the real sensation serve as the final anchor. I slowed my breathing and followed the perceptual pathway I had already verified, suddenly reaching toward that empty stretch of consciousness from back then—
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s20-1: Light shifted uneasily in the darkness. A small patch of dim yellow glow came through the gaps in the severely deformed iron grating of the cage door.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s21-1: My cheek was pressed against the cold metal floor of the cage, my bones and organs bearing the immense pain of the fall. The instant the memory forcibly took over, I felt a dust- and blood-stained hand
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s21-2: pressing hard against my forehead. She was sitting on the metal floor beside me. A strip was missing from the hem of her clothes—the cloth she had just torn off to bandage my forearm and stop the bleeding.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s23-1: I opened my eyes sharply, gritted my teeth, and pushed myself unsteadily up from the floor using only my left leg. My right foot, already unable to bear weight before the fall, was now a heavy mass of dead flesh.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s25-1: “Arno?” she called tentatively. Then a flicker of fear passed through those amber eyes as she noticed how strangely I was acting.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s26-1: Pain shot through this body. I had no time to explain. I seized her wrist, pressed half my weight onto her shoulder, and staggered with her toward the machine in the darkness. There was a pressure in my movements that did not belong to someone this age.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s29-1: Yuna had climbed over the high wall before dawn, then endured this fall from the sky, and had just torn off part of her hem to bandage my forearm. Though she did not know why I had suddenly become like another person, she followed as I dragged her along, enduring the pain and struggling to support me.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s31-1: “What are you doing?” she asked warily as she followed me to the machine cracked by the impact, her breathing extremely unsteady.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s32-1: I had only a dozen or so minutes. There was no time to explain.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s35-1:
“Give me a hand,” I said hoarsely between breaths.
She used her uninjured hand to steady me. I suddenly exerted myself, and with a clang, the maintenance panel on the side was torn open. The complex physical wiring inside the machine’s maintenance side opened before us.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s36-1: I swept my eyes over the upper-level feedback. The junction doors had been physically jammed shut. We could not get out. What’s more, according to the engineering conclusion H31 had left me, simply completing the internal process at the operator’s seat could not stop this machine. It had to be cut off manually from this maintenance panel.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s39-1: The deadlock was complete. But I carried the blueprint of the future in my mind.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s41-1: “Listen. The machine’s manual shutdown line can’t be cut off yet.” I pointed into the tangled wiring deep inside the cabinet. “Do what I say. Pull out the existing manual shutdown line and reconnect it as a one-time
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s41-2: delayed closure circuit. Let it remain on standby after the operator’s-seat process is fully completed, until it receives a shutdown request from outside in the future. Then it will burn out the coupling core.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s44-1: She endured the pain, her eyes passing over the complicated circuits she did not fully understand.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s46-1: “So even if we reconnect it now, it still won’t stop. We have to wait for… someone in the future to send a request from outside?”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s49-1: “Yes. Because we need the machine to stay on and receive something.” I pulled out a spare data cable and forced it into the mainboard. “In a moment, we need to work together to push the metal
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s49-2: slider deep inside the cabinet into the preset position and lock it there. That’s the final step in the physical reconnection. But before that, I have to register you through this spare line.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s52-1: “The snapshot you left upstairs at 7:50 is the only clean identifier. As long as we use it as the source, the system will treat it as a global anchor and gather every consciousness record
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s52-2: you produce from now on, across all branch worlds, into this machine’s long-term archive.” I looked at the screen, my finger hovering over the save key. “I’m going to register you.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s56-1: “Because once the metal slider is pushed in and the reconnection is complete, the manual line will lock and accept no new sources. My identity is bound to the operator’s seat that
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s56-2: has to be overwritten. It can’t be preserved. Only you, in the external collaboration seat, can leave this record behind. If I don’t record you now, there won’t be another chance.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s59-1: Her eyes fell on my hovering finger.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s60-1: She had just survived a fall from the sky and was covered in blood, trying to bandage herself. But the first thing I wanted to do was leave a data record of her after the deadlock.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s62-1: “I’m the only one you can record…” Her face quickly turned ashen. She looked desperately at the jammed upper-level doors. “Does that mean neither of us… no matter which one, can get out through that door?”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s64-1: “Yes.” I looked at her. “The sealed chamber below is a dead end. You and I can’t get out.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s65-1: Ten seconds of dead silence. In the dark hall at the bottom level, the only sound was her violent breathing echoing. She pressed her dust- and blood-smeared hand hard over her mouth, forcing herself not to cry out, but tears fell in large drops onto the cold metal floor.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s66-1: After a while, she drew a deep breath, wiped her face hard, and raised her head.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s73-1: I pressed the save key. The neural snapshot Yuna had left behind became the source of this river of records. The source was established.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s76-1: When all this was done, the light around us seemed to begin dimming. The dozen-plus minutes were almost over.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s77-1: She leaned against the cold machine. Beside her, the yellow indicator light showing that the circuit was inactive remained steadily lit, confirming that our physical reconnection had taken effect—the machine would not shut down when the internal process ended. It would continue waiting for that distant external request.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s79-1: “As long as this record is saved… when someone comes here again in the future,” she said through clenched teeth, her voice still trembling, “I’ll be able to live?”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s83-1: “As long as the source data remains and the subsequent records are complete, bringing it back to the future will let us reconnect it to a vessel.” I looked straight at her, my voice dropping. “I don’t know whether this record can actually be restarted. But it’s the only way to bring you back.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s84-1: She stared at me for several seconds, her expression a complicated mixture of fear and bewilderment.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s86-1: “Then why do you look even more afraid than I am?”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s88-1: “Because I don’t even know whether I can stay alive long enough to finish walking this timeline and press the extraction request for you.” I spoke softly. “But I have no choice.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s92-1: “You’re not Arno… You’re here to deliver a message again, aren’t you?” She sucked in a breath through the pain, tears welling up again, but her voice weakening.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s92-2: “This morning, when we were in that corridor of the White Tower, there was someone like you… He used your body to say all kinds of incomprehensible things to me…”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s94-1: “Because my current situation is like a wreck that could shut down at any moment.” I spoke softly. “I’ve… been going like this for a very long time. From when you saw me in that corridor, all the way to now.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s95-1: She looked at me. The bewilderment in her eyes gradually turned into a kind of certainty.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s96-1: “I don’t understand… I don’t understand what you mean by restoration or records… Just like I don’t understand why that other ‘you’ just said he was sorry…” She gripped my forearm hard, her knuckles turning white. “But I know you fought your
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s96-2: way back into this body in the present because you truly want me to live.” She wiped away her tears with a dust-covered hand, her eyes red as she crooked one corner of her mouth. “No matter what, I’ll push this slider all the way for you first.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s99-1: She reached out first and took my hand. She was still trembling, her fingers cold.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s101-: “Your hand is cold,” she said softly. “You said you’ve been walking for a very long time… so this is the temperature of the future, too.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s102-: She gripped me hard, as if clutching the only straw left in this desperate place.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s104-: “Even if there’s only a record… even if she isn’t the same me anymore in the future, you have to, you have to take her with you.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s107-: The edges of the darkness began to blur. The pain and weakness were surging back into this young body.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s108-: I knew the time had come. I suddenly leaned forward, clearing the way.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s109-: She gritted her teeth and lunged toward the depths of the cabinet. Following the spare line I had connected, she used all her strength to push the metal slider hidden deep inside all the way down. With a click, the slider locked firmly into the preset position.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s110-:
As the slider locked with a dull clunk, the breath I had been holding finally escaped. My knees completely gave way.
“No matter what happens,” I said, looking at her, “I’ll come back and keep my promise.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s111-: I tried to brace myself against the edge of the machine, but the pain severed the nerve feedback, and my whole body pitched heavily to the floor. As my vision spun, I felt myself dragged halfway back beside the cold, twisted iron grating at the bottom of the cage.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s112-: It was Yuna who had dragged me back with the last of her strength.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s113-: In the last second before this young body fell completely unconscious, I closed my eyes.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s116-: The memory withdrew completely. That ten minutes of future perspective was cut off.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s121-: The focus of predictive decoding dispersed, and that identical sensory blank came to an end. I returned to this world.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s122-: The scene abruptly settled into place. Still the bottom level of the White Tower, the tightly closed elevator doors, the smell of rust. Nothing had changed, except that my heart was pounding violently. The gap had ended. Young Arno would wake on the other side soon. But this earlier body would retain only

the low-bandwidth emotions and action tendencies from those dozen-plus minutes. He would only find that he had lost a stretch of time. As for the words we had exchanged and the reconnection we had carried out during those ten minutes, only the conscious Yuna could recount them to that bewildered young man.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s124-: Several hours later. In the temporary safehouse.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s125-: I gave Estelle a complete report of everything that had happened underground, including the final result of the slider being preset.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s126-: She listened quietly to the end, her eyes falling on the terminal beside her.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s128-: “So the source designation and the slider preset were completed during those dozen-plus minutes of lost time,” she said softly, confirming it.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s130-: “Yes.” I closed my eyes. “The conditions for extraction are set, too. If that day really comes in the future… the record can only be extracted safely once the machine is finally shut down.”
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s132-: She nodded and entered the matter in the record book. Then she poured a cup of hot water from the thermos she carried and pressed it into my cold palm.
texts.chapter:chapter-27-coma:event:text-s135-: I leaned against the wall and looked down at the cup in my hands. The weight of that hand seemed to remain in my palm. For me, it had happened several hours ago on another timeline; in this world, it was simply a page that did not exist among its many parallel histories.

“Calibration Recordings: One through Eight. Also: Final Volume. Play?”
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s6-1: I didn't tell Sera, and I didn't call Estelle along. During this most sensitive period, I had to keep them on the outskirts, maintaining the routine patrols and appearances, to cover my movements. So at dawn, I followed the route back and walked alone into this deathly silent building.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s7-1: A thick layer of loose dirt still weighed down the maintenance cover here. I slowly crouched and pressed my palm against the cold metal. According to what I had learned before, to dismantle it silently from the outside, I had to release the pressure in reverse order: two, one, three.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s8-1: I braced the heavy latches and felt my way through the dark, inch by inch, searching for where to release the pressure. When opened according to procedure, the machine's resistance guides you naturally. But I was forcing it open in reverse. It told me nothing. A seventy-minute dismantling procedure. This time, I could only finish it alone.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s11-1: The heavy cover was easy to pry up, but once inside the shaft, it was difficult to fit it back into place exactly as it had been from below. I braced my shoulder hard beneath the cover and freed one hand to feel along
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s11-2: the edge. Whenever I had infiltrated places like this before, Yuna or Estelle had always stood above, holding a flashlight steady to illuminate the groove I needed to align, then giving it a kick when the cover caught.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s12-1: But today there was only the desolate cliff base of early morning above the cover. In the darkness, I groped and supported it four times. On the fourth, the cover dropped heavily back into the groove, but one corner still inevitably stuck up.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s13-1: It was almost light. My arms were weak with fatigue. If I let go and the heavy cover came crashing down, the huge echo would immediately bring the patrol team from the top of the cliff. I released my grip and let the cover
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s13-2: remain caught in the groove, one corner slightly raised. I pulled off a thin strand of thread and wedged it into the gap. If anyone pushed it open from outside in the next few hours, the fragile thread would snap at once.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s14-1: After making that simple tamper marker, I dropped to the ground and walked farther down the corridor. The motion lights overhead came on dimly and dully, one section after another with the weight of my footsteps, then went completely dark behind me.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s19-1: Deep inside the production-line area, the slightly tilted panel screen before the control console gave off a dim glow. A verification key was inserted into the console, beside a status light shining with a cold blue glow.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s20-1: That withered white skeleton was sunk into the swivel chair. He was still in the position I had left him in last time: leaning back in the broad chair, his lowered skull facing the screen ahead, a clean, decisive fracture running through the right side of
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s20-2: the skull. On the metal floor to the right of the chair, half-hidden beneath the dust, lay an old-fashioned self-defense pistol. A deformed bullet remained lodged in the metal cabinet behind the chair, the blood around it oxidized long ago to a dark brown.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s21-1: Beneath the console, the heavy metal work case remained locked exactly as it was. The red authorization light on its small side display was still on. In yesterday's world, I had already used the key I brought back from the
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s21-2: underground target chamber to unlock it, taking out the recording tapes and accident index inside. But today—in the morning of this intact world, which had not yet been touched—it was still a black box preserved exactly as it was.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s22-1: I crouched down and entered the string of numbers from memory again. With a faint mechanical unlocking sound, the heavy metal lid sprang open, revealing the tapes and original index materials inside.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s23-1: He had arranged everything methodically, locked the final recordings and data inside this case, then dragged his aging body back to this chair, faced the screen, and ended himself.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s26-1: If we had not split up, Estelle would probably have stopped here, folded both hands tightly over her heart, and performed the solemn rite an outsider offered in mourning for the dead.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s27-1: But I don't know that rite. I only stood in the doorway for a while, then slowly walked in.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s30-1: I walked to the terminal built into the control console and glanced at the directory on the screen. This terminal's system still contained only the eight volumes of routine calibration recordings, sitting there alone.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s33-1: Today, no one had opened the record book to help me verify anything. I could only lay out, one by one on the console, the evidence I had rewritten from memory last night.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s36-1: I laid out the two handwritten sheets on the console. One contained the incomplete instructions recorded in the underground elders' archive piles; the other was the access code copied from the
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s36-2: White Tower's maintenance files. The original carriers of these two things had been left in yesterday's world, but I had them stored in my mind and brought them into the morning of this body's today.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s37-1: I pieced these two supposedly irreconcilable systems of logic together and entered them manually on the keyboard. Finally, I pressed Enter.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s38-1: The screen flickered faintly. At the bottom of the directory, which had previously contained only the eight recordings, a new entry appeared—one that had never shown itself before.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s39-1: I pressed “Final Volume” on the console.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s41-1: Final Volume archived in the White Tower's old accident review files. This machine retains the index only. Retrieval requires activation by the White Tower duty station.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s43-1: An access-denied notice appeared on the screen.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s46-1: I touched the sheet I had just rewritten from memory, then shifted my gaze to the work case I had just reopened. When I first obtained that verification key, I had taken it for the password to an ordinary
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s46-2: external device. Only today, before this console once sealed by the highest authorization, did the White Tower's access code and the incomplete instructions from underground converge without a gap. The
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s46-3: highest authorization carried away by the White Tower's chief when he fled, and the instructions left by the old man who had established a refuge underground, locked together seamlessly at this moment.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s47-1: I had no forensic equipment with which to compare DNA, nor any means of fingerprint identification. But that was no longer necessary. The man who had mastered the operating methods of both systems, sealed off both routes of retreat with those two strings of code before his death, and finally turned the muzzle toward the right side of his skull, was sitting in this swivel chair.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s48-1: In the previous world, the voice on that tape had already given his name. And today, when the White Tower's data and the underground data finally became one on the console, I saw clearly, all the way through, the path he had taken back then.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s49-1: The space before the console was empty. No one was here to enter the dead man's name into the record book.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s52-1: I looked at the screen and, in the quiet air, clearly spoke aloud the true name whose chain of identity had been severed by the official records.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s58-1: I spoke it for the dead man from more than a century ago in the chair to hear, and for this dust-covered room to hear.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s59-1: There was no echo in the room. The dust on the console continued to drift slowly as before.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s62-1: I took out the accident-record index from the case and stored it close to my body together with the verification command required to retrieve the Final Volume, slipping them inside the breast of my clothing close against my chest. Through the fabric, I pressed them hard.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s63-1: This time, I had obtained the password and the local data credentials. What I truly lacked was the access authority of a living person's position.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s69-1: I followed the corridor to the room at the other end. A heavy long table stretched across the center. A pile of drafts lay scattered across its surface, left openly spread out for more than a century. I began reading from the oldest drafts at the bottom.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s72-1: The sheets contained two completely different sets of complicated equations. On the left was the orthodox engineering notation of the White Tower; on the right, the symbols were steeped in the rough methods used underground to calculate the world's repeated capacity collapses.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s73-1: What was unbelievable was that these equations, which should have been utterly opposed, had been written on the same sheet in exactly the same handwriting.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s76-1: He had not merely learned the other heretical doctrine. He had forced himself to absorb the entire system until it was part of his bones, learning to switch seamlessly between the two kinds of logic.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s79-1: As I turned through the pages one by one, the two sets of symbols progressed from tentative probing on their separate sides, to standing side by side as equals, and finally fused completely on the sheet lying atop the stack.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s82-1: On this heavy long table, he had placed the machine's operating parameters alongside the abnormal changes in the pool level observed underground. I couldn't understand those dense physical derivations. But the sentence written most heavily at the very bottom needed no formulas to explain it:
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s84-1: The anomaly matches the operation. The machine itself is the hole.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s86-1: The diagrams on the long table revealed the most closely guarded secret at the heart of what happened back then: it was this time machine, taken pride in, that had crushed the foundations with each successive operation. The source of the entire system's present slide toward collapse was nothing other than the time machine itself.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s89-1: Beside these two columns of derivations lay two completely different drafts.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s92-1: My eyes fell on the annotations immediately beneath the equations:
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s96-1:
Based on the machine's physical limit at full load, eight thousand people is the safe upper bound under the assumed worst-case scenario. An upper bound is not an exact bill.
Because the
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s96-2:
world's underlying accounts have all been burned, the exact deficit, affected by operational fluctuations, can never be measured.
—Do not trust anyone who fills in an exact number here.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s98-1: Yet beside this warning not to trust exact numbers lay the lower-level directive that had already been signed and enacted. In this formal document, a top-secret contingency plan, under the highest-authorization verification of the fugitive old man, the execution column stated an incontestable conclusion in black and white:
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s99-1: “Regardless of how the actual hole fluctuates, this erasure will be carried out as a fixed quota of eight thousand portions.”
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s100-1: At one end of the long table, he had written out, plainly and clearly, the draft warning not to trust any exact number. But at the other, he had personally used system authorization to issue eight thousand as an absolute death bill.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s101-1: This was not a miscalculated account. It was pure calculation carried out to ensure the operation of the foundations. Because no one could calculate the exact deficit created by fluctuations over time, those in power simply treated the full-load limit of the entire physical system as an execution list.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s101-2: As long as eight thousand people were taken out to fill it, that cloth woven from living bodies would be large enough—large enough to cover one hundred percent of any fluctuating gap. In this effective death order, all the redundancy casually added for absolute technical safety was made of human lives.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s102-1: I stood there before the long table, looking at this weightless-looking quota sheet, and felt my hands and feet grow colder by the moment.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s108-1: I searched through that room for a long time. Only when the light in the corridor had grown increasingly faint did I leave and return once more to the reaction vat deeper inside the production line.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s109-1: It was exactly as it had been when I came last time. On the console panel, the error message was still glaring:
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s111-1: Infusion failed: field-pool reserve nearly zero. No host capacity available.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s113-1: I already knew what this meant. The capacity deficit caused by the connection of multiple worlds had reduced the pool reserve to zero. But
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s113-2: this record was not the laboratory's only truth. Combined with the data I had read in Memory Block 04 and the files left in this work case—
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s114-1: After the death bill for eight thousand people had been fixed, someone proposed another path that would not require sacrificing the living people already there: use this machine to create, from nothing, a new human with a capacity of ten thousand. If this one person could successfully be born, the deficit of eight thousand could be filled on paper.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s115-1: But the shell in the reaction vat before me declared that path a physical failure. With the pool reserve at zero, the system could draw out no capacity to infuse into the body. What lay in the reaction vat was merely a lump of flesh that could breathe and respond reflexively, but could never awaken a first-person consciousness.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s116-1: The machine could not create a substitute that was both devoid of consciousness and conveniently came with ten thousand units of initial capacity to be sent to its death. To use “ten thousand capacity” to fill this deficit, ten
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s116-2: thousand people's capacity would first have to be used to ‘infuse’ this new subject into existence. What would still be placed on the altar would be living people—each with a real subject, each capable of feeling pain and fear.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s117-1: The system could not measure the exact difference produced by the fluctuations, so the person holding the authorization made the decision himself and set a hard target of eight thousand human lives in its place.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s118-1: Yuna appeared before my eyes, standing in the dark underground chamber before the target capsule of that enormous annihilation device. In this dead end, already sealed shut by the “safe upper bound,” every shortcut once attempted had smashed against the iron wall of physics a century ago.
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s119-1: “So what I handed over was a real, solid self that had made it all the way to today. I accept that bill.”
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s120-1: Yuna's words, accompanied by the panel screen's dim blue reflection, seemed especially heavy in the deathly silent laboratory. The death laws written into the system's
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s120-2: foundations because the deficit could not be borne, the collaborations severed again and again because of mistrust—they were like a dead-end passage with no end for a hundred
texts.chapter:v15-27c:event:text-s120-3: years, piling all the weight onto one person's shoulders. And the knowledge and consent she handed over were, at the end of that passage, the most helpless and clearest echo.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:title: Chapter 27, Appendix 3: He Never Said How He Knew
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s5-1: Eleven in the morning. Heisenberg’s underground workshop from years ago. The sickly green glow from the old terminal cabinets illuminated the blind spot beneath them.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s6-1: It was a maintenance slot half-hidden behind a metal panel. I probed along the dust-caked bottom and touched three physical tapes packed tightly together. The first two had yellowing paper labels on their sides, marked “vital-sign waveforms” and “biochemical monitoring.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s7-1: The third was bare. The casing carried only a blurred string of numbers scrawled over in thick black marker. It was wrapped in a rough paper sleeve. On the back, someone had written
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s7-2:
several lines of notes in extremely messy handwriting:
“Two streams of input. The brain grabs the one that matches.
　Can switch. Cannot create from nothing.
　(How did he know?)”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s8-1: The three tapes were not in the normal directory displayed by the terminal. Someone had deliberately pushed them into the blind spot of the official records.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s9-1: I tried inserting the first two, but the old card slot lit up red—they were dedicated tapes for purely physiological probes, and this log terminal’s interface could not read them at all. Only the third, the unlabeled one, made the gears labor into motion when I pushed it in.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s12-1:
A broad field of static surged across the screen. Then the image struggled to stabilize.
The camera seemed to have been casually left at the corner of a table. There was no face in frame, only a pair of hands resting inside the circle of light. Black grease filled the nail beds, impossible to wash out, and layer upon layer of calluses covered the knuckles, worn there by years of gripping tools.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s14-1: “First-person experience is a stable explanation the brain finds for sensory input. It only explains. It has never copied the outside world without the slightest discrepancy.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s15-1: The speech was extremely fast, the voice carrying the raw rasp of someone who had gone a long time without water. It was exactly the same voice as in the calibration records on the previous tapes—the engineer who had left behind the work case.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s18-1: The hands picked up two sections of tubing in different colors and laid them side by side on the table.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s20-1: “When multiple branches overlap, if your senses receive two mutually exclusive streams of reality at the same time, both internally complete—”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s21-1: He bent his index finger and struck one of the tubes twice, hard. Knock, knock.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s23-1: “The brain can’t stabilize two opposing worlds at once. It grabs the side whose details match more closely and makes it the only reality you’re currently seeing. As for the other, no matter how strong its underlying signal is, if it doesn’t line up, it gets treated as background noise and suppressed outright.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s27-1: “Both streams of input have their own complete structure. You can’t rush to dismiss one as a hallucination just because the one underneath doesn’t match your prior memories.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s28-1: The hands in the frame produced an extremely fine bare wire and used it to connect the two sections of tubing.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s30-1: “Through extremely intensive attention training, a person may be able to change what they tend to grab onto. As long as the signal has enough structural support, you can stabilize it for a
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s30-2: short time. Once that side is grabbed as the only reality, your sensory focus will shift over completely. If you can truly see the light on that side, you can raise the hand on that side.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s33-1: Rough breathing came through the speaker in the recording. The hands suddenly swept across the table, sending all the tubing into the shadows.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s35-1: “But there is a limit. A shift in attention can only make you choose another path that already exists. It cannot produce input out of thin air.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s37-1: “That kind of switching only chooses. It does not create. If there is nothing in the branch on the other side capable of carrying your complete signal, you could stare your eyes bloody and still never create a path.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s41-1: Five-twenty in the afternoon. The White Tower, old accident records station.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s42-1:
I pulled out the universal maintenance cable at the bottom of the terminal and pressed it against the access port at the back of my neck. The cold metal stabbed into my skin.
For the past hour, I had been digging
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s42-2:
through the physical neural takeover logs from the morning of Anchor Day at this records station. I had found a fixed blank in the signal—a disconnect gap from 08:00 to 08:10.
My first-person perception had disconnected
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s42-3: during those ten minutes, but the machine had not gone offline. This unbrowsable old log was not a key in itself. It merely marked an exact blind-spot coordinate on the timeline. What kept tugging at me was the
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s42-4: unfulfilled potential deep in my brain—in the other branch corresponding to this coordinate, I actually possessed firsthand sensory experience of those ten minutes. It had merely been suppressed into background noise.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s43-1: The log was an address on the door. The potential in my mind was the key that could break into that world. With the ten-minute gap as an entrance, what my own potential connected to was the entire world that had still been running intact that
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s43-2:
morning.
The recording I had watched in the basement that morning surfaced in my mind: as long as the signal had enough structural support, it could be stabilized again.
I closed my eyes and stopped resisting the pull of that potential deep in my
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s43-3: mind. I held fast against the nausea that made me want to vomit and let my sensory focus shift completely. No image, no sound. I forcibly severed my perception of the screen in front of me and reached for the immense stream of reality behind that gap.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s44-1: Extreme nausea. A violently wrenching sense of rejection pierced my nerves in an instant, and the sickly green screen at the records station shattered into overlapping images.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s45-1:
When everything locked back together, the smell of dust in the air was gone.
In its place was the cool, clean air of early morning.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s46-1:
My vision stabilized. Anchor Day, eight o’clock sharp, in the White Tower calibration-area corridor, in front of the system panel.
That signal pulled my focus in like an anchor, dragging it into a world
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s46-2: that had long since existed in full. This was the morning when Yuna was still alive. Anchor Day, eight o’clock sharp. Through this single ten-minute gap, I continued into the body that had existed then.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s47-1:
She was standing three steps away.
I looked at her. My throat felt blocked by something, and all I could produce was a dry, rasping sound: “Yuna.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s48-1:
She turned around. The ease of the morning paused slightly on her face. She did not come over as she usually did. Instead, she stood where she was and watched my eyes warily.
“Thirty seconds.” Her voice
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s48-2: held a note of suspicion. That was the final safeguard we had agreed on against mental contamination: “If you lose focus for a long time in the middle of a conversation, you have to immediately prove
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s48-3: you haven’t been replaced when you wake up. The time you were disconnected just passed thirty seconds. This morning, in the White Tower, at seven fifty-eight”—she stared at me—“what did I do for you?”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s49-1: “The shoelace on your left foot had come undone. You crouched down and tied it for me.” My voice was trembling.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s50-1: The guardedness in Yuna’s eyes eased a little, but her expression as she looked at me grew stranger. She reached a hand forward, as though she wanted to touch my shoulder,
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s50-2:
but I instinctively moved away.
In that instant, she realized that the person inside the body before her had just gone through something immensely long and heavy.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s52-1: “I took you out of this village once. We went beneath a purple sky, but the escape still failed in the end. I still couldn’t bring you back.” I looked at the girl who was still alive at eight that morning, speaking faster and
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s52-2:
faster, terrified of leaving out even one word. In the remnants extending from the future, I had lived through too many moments of losing her.
I swallowed the bloody taste in my throat and continued. “The engineering limit for
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s52-3: filling the machine’s gap is eight thousand. The engineering specifications for the new-human vessel with a reading of ten thousand really are sufficient to cover it. But that can’t decide who should ultimately deal with all of this.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s53-1: I met her gaze. “I went to ten adults. But after understanding the real price, not one of them was willing to carry their consent through to the end.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s54-1: I bit down hard, forcing myself not to look at the black spots beginning to flicker at the edge of my vision.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s55-1: I watched the fingers picking at the panel come to a stop. She was still listening.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s56-1: “I once used a private fact another you told me—you had divided half the grain from your induction offering among the orphan next door—to bypass your judgment.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s57-1: “And you were right.” I looked at her. “That was why you left me.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s58-1: She raised her head and looked at me quietly. In the expression that crossed her face in that instant, I saw no anger. I only felt a sorrow that was difficult to describe.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s59-1: “So you’re apologizing to me?” she asked softly.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s60-1: My throat tightened. I could not answer a word. It was a regret that even I, at that moment, had been unable to stop.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s61-1: “Across all these cycles, I’ve exhausted this morning.” I looked at her as the black spots before my eyes rapidly expanded. “I thought about taking you before the Ten Seats to confront them, or waking the people in the old calibration area. I even thought about setting this place on fire.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s62-1: I paused. I had to take several deep breaths before I could get out the second half.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s63-1: “But it wouldn’t have worked. As long as you still recognized me at first sight that morning, as long as you could still tell that something long had happened to me, you wouldn’t come with me. No matter
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s63-2: how great the fire, no matter how much chaos there was, you wouldn’t run. You would go save the people in this village who didn’t care about you, until you walked toward this machine by your own judgment.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s64-1: My voice was hoarse. “Because I can only take over myself. I can’t change you.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s65-1:
The words from the recording struck my mind like cold iron nails: It only chooses. It does not create.
I could force my way into these ten minutes along the gap left in the record. I could stand here and speak, even try to drag her away. But I couldn’t create a world in which
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s65-2: she suddenly wanted to abandon everything and leave with me, because that wouldn’t be her. In every existing chain of causality where she remained herself, she would walk toward the dead end again. I could only choose what existed. I couldn’t create a version of her that didn’t.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s66-1: My vision began to peel away. The corridor and the panel were turning transparent before my eyes. I could feel my earlier self waking inside this body. He was about to take back control of the time that followed. Yuna’s figure was trembling too, as though it were about to dissolve into the air.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s67-1: “I promise you one thing.” I looked at her through the overlapping images. My voice drifted in and out as the signal tore apart, so indistinct that even I could not hear it clearly.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s68-1:
Yuna continued to look at me quietly. She suddenly took one step forward and reached out, wanting to touch my shoulder.
It was a real, deliberate movement. Her fingertips brushed my
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s68-2: clothes, but the overlapping images in my vision had already torn apart to their limit, and my body’s sensory input was completely severed the next second. I failed to respond to the touch.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s69-1:
“If it can’t be proven that she’s you, then I shouldn’t have called her by your name.” I stared fixedly into her eyes as the overlapping images tore my vision into fragments.
Those words fell into Yuna’s world exactly as spoken. They were the promise I made to her.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s70-1: She looked into my eyes, parted her lips slightly, and said something. But I could no longer hear her.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s74-1:
Five-thirty in the afternoon.
A heavy dizziness slapped me back in front of the records station. My back struck the cabinet, and I gasped for breath, my hands and feet shaking uncontrollably.
During those ten minutes, I had taken over the body. My confession and Yuna’s silence had both occurred
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s74-2: as real facts. I had truly controlled myself and made myself say those words, but that was all I could do. When the ten-minute window ended, my focus was ejected. Yuna, left in that morning, still walked toward the machine by her own judgment. That farewell had not stopped her final decision.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s75-1:
I looked at the cabinet screen again. The coordinate from 08:00 to 08:10 still lay there, but the faint tug deep in my mind had vanished completely.
The Arno of this old world had just retaken control of the body at eight-ten. As a local vessel, he
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s75-2: would clearly remember saying those words and making those movements against his will, but he would not possess the future vision of the consciousness in this body. As for me, I had completed the only intervention I could make along this worldline.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s75-3: Because the unfulfilled potential in my mind had been completely spent. During those ten minutes, I had truly turned that stretch of background noise into a firsthand memory. It was no longer external input that could be grabbed again. It had become
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s75-4: subjective history fixed inside me. Even though that worldline continued to run intact in the past, I had no second reserve of potential with which to reopen the entrance. That confession during those ten minutes was the last thing I could do in that morning.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s76-1:
I leaned against the metal panel and recalled a warning from the latter half of the recording, delivered at breakneck speed:
“Extreme nausea. Overlapping images appearing at the edge of the visual field. Neurological spasms causing the hands and feet to fall out of alignment.”
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s77-1:
What I had just experienced matched those words exactly.
How could an engineer who spent all day with his head buried in data calculate, out of thin air, the subjective vertigo nearing the limit
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s77-2: as two mutually exclusive realities struggled back and forth inside the brain? The practical details, precise down to the neurological spasms, carried a nauseating warmth of flesh and blood.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s79-1: I recalled the two data tapes I had touched in the basement that morning, their interfaces incompatible, marked “vital-sign waveforms” and “biochemical monitoring.” Whose bodily records, exactly, were stored inside them?
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s80-1: The security checkpoint that morning conducted thorough physical scans. There was no way I could have hidden the two tapes in my clothes and carried them out. At the time, I could only put them back exactly as they were,
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s80-2:
into the blind spot of the cabinet.
He had offered a method that could change the course of fate, then buried the source of that method—along with the flesh-and-blood price paid by someone unknown—in a bottomless black box.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s81-1: I used the records station to pull myself upright. That recording, and the ten-minute gap that had just shut for good, were still only fragments of the truth. Together, they formed an incomplete index pointing toward the heavily restricted core document.
texts.chapter:v15-27e:event:text-s82-1: I could not keep stumbling blindly through the dark alone. I had to find Sera. Whatever I had to offer in exchange, I had to make her unlock the truly sealed “final reel” in the old accident review file for me.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:title: Chapter Twenty-Seven, Appendix Two: Lit One by One
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s1-1:
White Tower · Old Accident Review Archive · Fixed Plaque on the Console (engraving filled in black, date unknown):
“This console is read-only. No permissions.
　What is displayed on the console is a record. A record is not the world.
　A blank field is also something recorded.”
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s6-1: The heavy dizziness gradually faded. The forced landing through those ten minutes was over. I stood in the room with no guard on duty, bracing myself against the long console just above waist height.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s7-1: I had descended through that physical break from 08:00 to 08:10, then been ejected, ending an encounter that was fated never to bring her back. The door had now shut tight. Several hours earlier, I
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s7-2: had found this place by digging an old guide map out of a pile of wastepaper on the first floor, and on this “old accident records console” in the outer corridor, I had dug out the one and only gap.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s12-1:
A whole row of slender little windows was set into the console’s surface, each with a faint point of light glowing deep inside. The old metal information plaque on the wall continued to watch me in silence:
What is displayed on the console is a record. A record is not the world. A blank field is also something recorded.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s15-1: I approached the long console. The windows still displayed neatly arranged rows of data—a physical overview of more than two hundred old accident records and current connection sessions.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s16-1: Each row represented one connection session between a cockpit and the White Tower. On the left was a device identifier, followed by the time of connection. On the far right was the
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s16-2: time of disconnection. Between those two points stretched a thin strip of faint light, representing the continuity of subjective consciousness that the local system was able to verify.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s17-1: The farther back the data went along the console, the older it became, and the glow at the edges was already extremely faint. Among those old strips of light, several broke abruptly in the middle. At each break was a stretch of dead darkness, meaning that the system had lost track of the local consciousness at that moment.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s20-1: At the far left end of the console was a sensor area giving off a faint glow. I did not take out any credential sheet. I simply placed my palm against it.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s21-1: The sensor read the operator’s physical characteristics. The machine remained silent. It did not need to check any name or permission. It recognized only that this body was currently part of an active cross-world connection, and marked this physical endpoint.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s22-1: At the bottom of the console, one row’s strip of light quietly changed color, from cold white to a faintly warm dark yellow.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s23-1: I took my hand away, and the yellow faded. I placed it back, and the yellow lit again, stubbornly. The records console had simply highlighted, honestly, the “physical endpoint” standing before it at that moment.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s26-1: I leaned forward and brought my face close to that yellowed strip of light assigned to me.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s27-1: At the far right of the line, the place representing the time of disconnection was blank—representing that my original body was still in the process of crossing worlds. Near the beginning of the strip, however, there lay a conspicuous break.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s28-1: It was a stretch of dead darkness, corresponding precisely to the moment when the system, overloaded, had failed to capture the continuity of the local first-person consciousness.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s29-1: It was those ten minutes from 08:00 to 08:10. During that interval, Yuna remained online as the collaboration seat, while the data stream belonging to the primary operator position showed this black break in the connection. Whatever I,
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s29-2: later on, had done after descending through that break, the old accident had already been settled. The system recognized only the deepest layer of logic: during those ten minutes, the first-person subjective consciousness originally belonging
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s29-3: to this world and this moment had indeed been lost. This underlying physical record would never be rewritten by later operations. It stubbornly retained the pitch-black appearance of its original failure to track the local consciousness.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s30-1: That was the only break I had found so far that allowed me to land conscious, carrying knowledge across worlds. I had already crossed it and brought back a promise to her. But I still had not brought her back.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s33-1: Yet standing before this console, my eyes remained fixed on the tiny line of text beneath the break.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s37-1: I reached out and touched the black break through the glass, pressing my fingers hard against it until my knuckles went white.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s38-1: I tried to push it to the left. I wanted to drag it even a little toward an earlier time.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s39-1: I wanted to return to the morning when we nodded our agreement in the cold wind outside the chapel—or even just to 07:50, before she pressed the external collaboration confirmation key and prepared to submit the delayed startup. I wanted to take back that nod before then.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s40-1: If I could return to 07:50, the safety deficit equivalent to the capacity of eight thousand people would never be established.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s43-1: But the markings beneath the glass did not move at all.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s44-1:
08:00 exactly.
The door was pinned in place like a nail, fixed at eight o’clock sharp.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s45-1: Before the break recorded on this console, this body’s subjective consciousness had never been interrupted. The complete consciousness that had originally experienced all of this within this body filled it like a wall
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s45-2: without a single gap, shutting my later-arriving projection out completely. This cross-world system could let me descend there along the break, but it could not conjure an earlier opening and smash one out for me.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s46-1: The break happened to appear after the starting point of the loop had been established. At eight o’clock sharp, when the system stopped accepting cancellation commands, a debt that had to be repaid was completely locked in. But that did not mean the system had nailed Yuna to the position of repayer.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s47-1: She could have stopped, and refused to fill that capacity deficit for anyone. What was established at eight o’clock was a bad debt that could simply be abandoned. We could have stayed together and watched this world collapse because no one was willing to bear the cost.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s48-1: But the time I went back was only enough to watch her understand all of this. In that confession shared only by Yuna and me, I told her the facts I had personally experienced during the latter half of the first phase. She had not heard
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s48-2: with her own ears the long-table meeting refuse to bear the cost for her, nor seen with her own eyes the resource-allocation seats shrink back from the quota of ten thousand units. After understanding my request, not one of those adults
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s48-3: was willing to step forward—that was what I told her. During those ten minutes, she took those words in as highly credible testimony. If even one person had been willing to step forward and take over, she would not have had to go that far.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s49-1: But in the end, before she went to make her final direct request to the Inner Circle elders, before she had fully verified the cowardice of this world with her own eyes, she still walked to the console outside that chapel herself.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s52-1: The light shining through the windows made the console gleam. Outside, the sky had gone completely dark.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s53-1: I slowly released the hand I had pressed against the sensor area.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s54-1: The yellowed strip of light silently faded back to cold white, merging again with the more than two hundred old lights. They kept lighting up mechanically, one line after another. Without the color marking, there was no way to tell which one was mine from the doorway.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s58-1: The information plaque on the wall remained silent: A record is not the world. Among these more than two hundred strips of light, how many bodies had been recorded as completely drained dry?
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s59-1: I had brought back everything I could bring back from the physical landing between 08:00–08:10. To cross the index and see the locked main text of the old accident archive, to uncover what Heisenberg had left unsaid, I needed the permission of the long-table meeting. That meant Sera.
texts.chapter:v15-27d:event:text-s60-1: Through my coat, I pressed the validation instruction sheet folded into thirds in my inner pocket, pushed open the door, and walked into the corridor where the night wind was pouring in.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:title: Chapter Twenty-Eight: Sealed
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s2-:
Sacrificial Terminal · Daily Log:
“External calibration: forty-one items, confirmed individually.
Lockdown: complete. Internal/external communication: severed.
Target status: release, in progress.
——
Release: complete. Subject signal: none.
Operator present for: entire duration.
Remarks: (blank)”
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s5-: The third blank, I left for last.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s7-: Finding its exact position wasn’t difficult. The basic operation log printed by the sacrificial terminal back then preserved the precise timestamps in black and white. The blank in my memory was like a puzzle piece that didn’t fit. Once the two

were matched, that lost stretch of time was fixed in place: from the moment I pressed the lockdown key and fell into blankness, all the way until I regained consciousness—a long discontinuity in which my body was clearly present, but “I” was not.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s8-: Entering it didn’t require reconstructing the exacting external conditions of the first two stretches.
