Those two breaks had occurred on the morning of Anchor Day and amid the chaos of the fall, and had required complicated environmental parameters to locate.

For this final stretch, I had only been standing quietly before a sealed capsule door. Once I connected to the machine, put on the teaching band, and descended along the precise timestamp, I could naturally settle into the void that already belonged to me.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s9-:
What was truly difficult was that I knew perfectly well what I would have to do once I got in.
The first two times I entered through a blank: one was to see her, and one was to save her.
And this final stretch of blankness, I was going to send her off.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s15: My vision turned over. The cellar’s bone-chilling air hit me at once.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s16: I entered this sixteen-year-old body. A few seconds earlier, the younger me had slammed down the lockdown key, and then consciousness had been severed, dropping into the discontinuity. Now I took control of the body from within.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s17:
Before me stood the heavy capsule door, locked irreversibly shut, its red lockdown indicator glaring.
The hands on my pocket watch had already passed 19:50. I knew I had only these few dozen seconds of lost-time blankness left.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s18: I turned back to face the still-operating sacrificial terminal. This machine, which had just swallowed her, was the system’s only physical hub with direct access to the lower layer. While the highest operator

permissions, temporarily opened to seal this record after lockdown was complete, remained valid for these few dozen seconds, my hands flew over the keys.
The universe had no shared clock. But watching

the screen through the machine’s lower-layer connection, I could clearly see that the branch worlds where she had not sacrificed herself were no longer extending. They did not need to wait for this world

to reach the same timestamp. Each had already arrived at its own final moment and rested quietly in its own ending—some terminating at dusk beneath skies of blowing sand, others frozen forever in the dark.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s19:
There was nothing left to wait for. This brief window of highest permissions had originally been meant to mark the end of a single sacrifice, but I crossed beyond the individual world and appended a single external termination marker governing every branch directly to the root of this vast body of data.
Next came the continuity check.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s20:
I entered the command. Then I turned and walked back to the tightly sealed capsule door, laying my palm flat against the heavy metal.
The door was cold, cold enough to reach straight through to the bone.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s23: In these last few dozen seconds of dead silence, the small patch of metal beneath my palm had only just been warmed by my body heat. But I knew that the moment I let go, it would quickly give up its heat and turn cold again.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s24: The gas lantern beside me burned tirelessly. I crouched down, reached out, and turned the knob lower until the flame went out completely. When the boy woke, in that state of extreme weakness and dim light, he might take

a few more seconds to see certain remnants on the ground outside the capsule door. Even if it only delayed his discovery of the torn safety harness and scattered emergency bandages by a few seconds, that was enough.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s26: I stood there before the door. I wasn’t thinking about anything as grand as the fate of the world.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s28:
What I kept turning over were all those insignificant details.
I thought: when she slowly withdrew her fingers and let go of my hand before entering the capsule, why hadn’t I held on tighter? She turned and stepped through the hatch without the slightest hesitation, cutting off the pain of being caught between advance and retreat before I had to bear it.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s29:
I thought: during the forty-one external calibrations, had she been quietly watching me through the blast-resistant glass?
The truth was, I hadn’t dared look up at her eyes then. If I had looked for even one second longer, I might not have been able to force myself to press the lockdown key.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s30: The verification stream lighting up on the screen pulled me back from my thoughts.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s33: The sacrificial terminal emitted a faint beep. I turned and walked back to the screen. As the termination marker was written, the branch records that had long since stopped were initiating continuity self-checks in the lower layer, waiting for the final seal.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s34: I stared intently at the terminal. The system had left no interface for reading any specific content. The only things moving across the screen were the basic readings representing the final states of the various branches.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s35: The first record whose own time marker stopped at 19:41 was the earliest break read so far. It was an alien world at the boundary between heat and cold, and the final environmental parameters it transmitted contained a tearing temperature differential. The telemetry trajectory showed

that until the second its readings reached zero, she had been running at full speed from the dark side toward the sunlit side where the shuttle was parked, pushing through the bitter cold.
Another stopped at 20:05 by its own time. The sensor’s final determination was that her arm

had briefly lifted toward the space in front of her. There was no force feedback, and it fell again. That was her final attempt to reach out and grab me as she lingered at the edge of the cliff while I held the rear guard at the collapsed lower level. In the end, she caught nothing.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s36: One by one, records bearing world tags entered the self-check queue. Their endings projected their final reflections toward me in this way.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s41: Once the system finished verifying continuity and locked the record boundaries completely, the conditions for going to bring her back would be in place.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s42: The delayed shutdown circuit capable of causing a system crash had already been set during that bout of unconsciousness after the fall. Following the backup line I had connected in advance, she had pushed the slider into

place herself. In the safe world where the shutdown would eventually be carried out, all it would take was an external closure request for the connection point sustaining the entire system to be burned out completely.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s43: When the shutdown settlement came in the future, the termination marker generated here, the system audit signature automatically signed after the lower-layer self-check passed, and the permission trail I left behind would

be the only credentials proving the record’s legitimacy. I no longer needed to do what I had once believed necessary—to run to some disaster-recovery station and pull down a physical lock. The sealing was complete here.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s44:
A faint light flickered on the screen.
Each flash meant the system had performed a self-check of one record’s continuity from morning through its final state.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s47:
The telemetry location in the tall grass, the record with stable status. Self-check passed.
The record in zero gravity, with minute microscopic stress in the hand. Self-check passed.
In the branch where I taught her chess that morning, the telemetry registered a fluctuation on the eighth move. Self-check passed.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s49: And the records that had chosen refusal.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s51:
In that record, at eight that morning, I had told her the whole truth.
Her determined heart rate showed no sharp fluctuation in the status brief. The trajectory parameters showed a brief burst of high-intensity output at that coordinate. Combined with the yard’s

geographical data, she had probably been moving something heavy.
Until the end drew near.
Environmental calibration: her own yard.
She did not hide. The terminal status showed her breathing gradually slowing from its initial rapid pace before settling into a smooth curve.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s54:
When the green light for that record came on, I clenched my teeth and pressed down hard on the console.
Her right not to die for others, and her steady breathing as she faced the end, were archived safely together.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s56: And another record that had received no revelation at all.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s58:
That morning I hadn’t gone to see her. Apart from the raw wooden bookmark with nothing written on it, she hadn’t received any material from me.
The log contained no cortisol spike triggered by memorization, no signs of forced data retention.

The location data showed her going to the prayer room and eating. In the afternoon, she remained at the edge of the wheat field for an hour. The faint mass feedback indicated that something very light had been held in her hand the entire time.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s59: The final environmental determination reading remained in the light breeze.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s63:
All the way to this world’s record.
This was the final log. It was fixed in this deep cellar, before that irreversible capsule door. The audio sensor’s recording status changed to “blocked.” With the final flicker, the self-check light turned green.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s64: From this moment on, every road she had left behind, every choice, along with countless parallel dead ends, had settled safely into the complete body of life records in the lower layer.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s69: The verification in the window was complete. My lost-time window was about to run out.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s70:
I left the control console and walked back to the tightly sealed capsule door.
The red lockdown light flickered once. The sealing conditions I had set had been met. It was about to cut my connection.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s71: I knew my time was over.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s72:
The instant that glaring red light went completely dark, I withdrew from this body.
The owner of this body, that sixteen-year-old boy, would soon wake in the hell that belonged to him and pull open that empty capsule door with his own hands.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s73: No one could take that pain for him.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s79:
When I disconnected from the machine, hardly any time had passed in reality.
I removed the teaching band and walked from the apparatus back to the familiar wooden table. The water in the cup had gone somewhat cold.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s80: Estelle, sitting across from me, glanced over. She picked up her pen and wrote on the paper: “All three are clear.”
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s82: That night, beneath the dim yellow light, I spread the record I had written across the table and looked at it for a while.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s83:
Yuna’s record boundary had been locked.
If she truly woke one day, the operations and sealing after her death would not enter the portion restored to her. For her, it would be nothing more than a vigil kept by me alone.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s84:
I sat at the table and looked out into the darkness.
I had completed with my own hands everything that could logically be closed at this point. I didn’t know what she would become when she woke in the future, carrying so many dead ends while existing as a collection of these contradictory memories.
texts.chapter:chapter-28-sealed:event:text-s85:
But this long night had finally ended.
Next, I would go bring her back.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-09-night-of-eight-tho: Sea Line Nine: Eight Thousand Nights

Months have passed since that night. When Yuna’s heart stopped, I fled the isolation room where her body heat still lingered, but I could not escape the fate of being forcibly pulled out of that world. Through the long attrition of these hundreds of loops, I waded through

countless dried-up universes. Yuna filled the fatal shortfall. The world no longer went dark, but after that, I woke each time to a morning without her. I watched this safe yet empty world continue to run smoothly, again and again, but could not even grasp a body I could touch.
Today, when I pushed open the door to this cellar archive once more in the darkness of the loop, I locked myself in here again, trying to understand what she
had given herself to in that cold transaction. On the long raw-wood table, all the traces of Heisenberg’s merging of two technical paths back then still remained.
Finalized Annihilation Plan · Cover Page (Basement · Equipment Room):

“Two systems of notation used in parallel. Left column: engineering notation from the old experimental sector. Right column: Conservation Society numerical notation.
The same hands, translating back and forth.
(A line of tiny text in the footer: There is no second copy of this draft. Transcriber: none. This time, I will be my own reviewer.)”

I pieced together the shape of him sitting here for the first time from the oral-recording tapes left behind by survivors of the underground network. On either side of the table were two completely different sets of records: on one side, the Empire’s arrogant Inner

Circle engineering tables, where each operation of the time machine was recorded only as an isolated success; on the other, the underground network of the Conservation Society’s observation ledgers, filled with dates when the pool level plunged violently and blank spaces

whose causes were unclear. On the tapes, the watchman from the rebuilt young network recalled that Heisenberg would always pull out a thin sheet, cover half the table, and insist that the uncovered column had to be traceable all the way back through the page numbers.

Faced with those disconnected figures, he set a rule: until the source of an anomaly had been established, no one was allowed to fill it in with a zero. Between the two sheets used for comparison, he drew a comparison

frame with a thin page of memo paper, aligning, across the screen, the dates of the machine’s confidential activations one by one with the dates when the underground pool levels had undergone violent fluctuations.

Those tapes also mentioned that one night, carrying a hurricane lamp, he led people into the cold equipment room. He wiped the dust from the old pipe in the wall, pointed to the physical scale left behind by the old experimental sector, and ordered them to abandon all the ratios estimated by later generations and use only the most primitive needle readings.

Among those complicated conversion sketches, I saw how this number came into being. Because of the complexity of the branching histories, the deficit created by the time machine was not a debt that could simply be

accumulated along a timeline. But the world was finite. That meant that as long as the universe had not collapsed on the spot from exhaustion, the total shortfall torn open by the machine had to possess a physical limit.

Standing within Heisenberg’s blind spot at the time, the actual shortfall was an unknowable quantity. Since it could not be calculated, he went looking for a safety upper bound that would not break through the universe.

Following the calculation drafts weighted down at the corner of the table, I walked through his reasoning from that time again. He locked this historical black box in place with known physical boundaries. The draft listed three key variables: first, the known

depth of the local capacity pool; second, the maximum capacity the time machine could contain within the existing physical structure; third, the conservative estimate of the minimum release efficiency of the recoupling apparatus used to carry out the sacrifice.

This was not an empty assertion, but a rigorous constraint. Since a complete cross-world connection could not be exhausted through calculation, he did not calculate “how much was owed.” He divided the machine’s maximum structural load by its minimum release efficiency, then added the fallback

calculation for the local pool level. These three physical walls clamped down on the invisible abyss, proving that as long as the machine was ultimately destroyed and did not continue running without limit, the absolute safety upper bound derived on paper would be enough to cover the worst case.
It was still only a physical extreme.

But at the bottom of that draft, I saw the handwriting change. With strokes pressed so hard they nearly tore through the paper, he converted this extreme into the old-era capacity baseline for a single person and

arrived at the number eight thousand—the number of human lives. Then, beside the number, he stamped the seal representing an administrative resolution and left a string of cold duty codes and abbreviated signatures.
And so, a safety upper bound that had originally existed only on calculation paper was personally translated by this administrative procedure into a cold quota that had to be filled with human lives.
He was not calculating how much the machine actually owed. With that signature, he forcibly framed the unquantifiable abyss as an executable maximum death quota.
We already knew, before Yuna walked toward that machine, that eight thousand was only an upper bound guaranteed to be sufficient. The blind annihilation valve was responsible only for releasing
everything at once. It did not know the actual shortfall, and it did not calculate change. When Yuna sat down, all ten thousand units of total capacity shared across every world were drawn out.
The portion not taken up by the shortfall was not held back. It melted back into the anonymous soul field.

But that could not change the cost of the release. In this one-way physical transfer, as the ten thousand units of total capacity at the source were drained dry, countless local projections of Yuna attached to

them were severed from the future simultaneously in every world. But the life she had lived, and the information she had left behind, were not burned away with them. They were sealed in the form of an ending.

He organized the draft that had taken three nights to calculate and weighted it down at the corner of the table. In the evidence cabinet at the other end of the archive lay the sheet he had used when filming the verification recording back then—the original abnormality alert left behind by Semmelweis, the first director of the underground network, while he was

still alive.
Now, the water-stained original lay beneath a glass cover. Heisenberg had attached a comparison frame of dates to its edge with memo paper before the camera, leaving incontrovertible evidence in the recording. Yet the original itself remained as clean as it had been before Semmelweis’s death, without a trace of ink added by anyone who came after.

[Abnormality Alert]
This season’s pool level has fallen sharply, far beyond the extreme energy consumption value of the population on the register.

When Semmelweis left those lines, he did not know that the Inner Circle’s time machine was running. He saw only a string of abnormally depleted figures, and died without ever knowing what he should suspect.

Only later, when Heisenberg compared these fragments one by one against the Inner Circle’s classified machine-operation dates, did a cold truth take shape: during the period when the time machine was digging out its enormous deficit, vast amounts of capacity were forcibly severed

directly from the underlying layer of the world. This brutal extraction bypassed every surface protocol in the White Tower responsible for binding identities. It did not trigger any corresponding identity registration. Since, at the moment of outflow, it appeared in the physical

structure only as a decline in pure energy levels, with no attachment point reserved for any personality, the underlying laws would likewise leave no opening for identities to be preserved when the shortfall was filled. The soul field was merely an anonymous ocean that provided capacity.
Yuna’s ten thousand units of capacity, which filled the abyss, were, as far as the underlying laws were concerned, simply an influx of pure energy. In the energy exchange
that filled the shortfall, there was no place for the name “Yuna.” The same physical input did not change according to who it came from. It filled the abyss. Nothing more.

Those lines pierced the last trace of hope that boy had held onto. The system would not automatically reconnect the input with the name “Yuna” simply because she had provided enough energy. What she gave would not automatically bring her back.

Heisenberg recognized the blindness of that anonymous ocean earlier than I did. Faced with that enormous dead account of eight thousand people’s worth of capacity, he tried, in his later years, to use the production line to create a new human who carried no designated personality but possessed ten thousand units of capacity, to fill the shortfall.

That was his final attempt. Back then, he made his way back to the abandoned AI laboratory and tried to use the production line to create a human one last time. The production line woke, completed the standard

process, and ultimately produced not the enormous vessel he had expected, but merely an empty shell that could breathe and respond to basic stimuli, yet possessed no first-person subject at all. What was missing

was not technology or equipment, but the surplus consumed by the time machine. The shell was not an incomplete product. It was the precise output of a time when the remaining capacity was zero. He sat beside

that shell for a long time and left behind the confession recording. I do not know whether, when he finally took his own life, he was trying to atone for his former colleagues, or merely trying to prove that

his arithmetic could still solve a dead end. In the end, he could not cross that physical chasm. The complete shell later labeled “Vessel 07” still rests quietly beside the abandoned production line to this day.
I pushed aside the heavy stack of records on the table and rose to my feet in the dim cellar. Heisenberg had fallen at this step. But I was different.
If the underlying layer recognized only anonymous energy, if the “identity information” had not been burned away along with the energy—
As long as the information remained continuous, as long as there were a complete record of a life—

Deep inside the White Tower, the records of her life before she entered the machine had always been sealed away. These records could not change the anonymity of the energy pool, but they preserved all of Yuna’s information. In the previous loop, during the elevator’s

lost-time interval, I had already forcibly appended the only legitimate external termination marker to the root of this enormous body of data. And I had personally stayed with her through that irreversible endpoint. Her record had long since been locked and sealed.
Energy could not recognize its owner on its own. But the White Tower and the AI laboratory could. What I had to do was reconnect the road that had once been severed.

Yuna had filled the shortfall. Now, the usable capacity in the soul field was nearly infinite for the purposes of creating a human. The ready-made shell left behind by Heisenberg, unable to produce a subject because its remaining capacity had once been zero, was now the ideal physical vessel for this moment.

Because I had already completed the external termination marker on that archive, the severed history now possessed a legitimate boundary. I only needed to activate the local White Tower, import that fully sealed restoration core into the AI laboratory, and issue an overall write command to the shell.

Nothing missing. Nothing altered. As long as ten thousand units of abundant anonymous capacity were forcibly poured into the shell that had waited for countless years along this restoration command, the system would mechanically reproduce that complete state of life without the slightest discrepancy.
That was the chasm even Heisenberg had failed to cross.

On this severed road, even if the energy filled into the shell was merely anonymous pool water, as long as the information remained continuous, as long as her past could be completely mapped onto that blank page of

ten thousand units of capacity, I believed that when she woke, the person before my eyes would still be her. This was not a prayer, but a physical execution chain that would be completed in my hands. I had to believe.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-10-return:title: Sea Line Ten: Return
texts.chapter:heisenberg-10-return:event:text-: Recruitment Record · Private Page (among his late-life notes, written in a hurried hand unlike his usual composure):

“First person: listened through. Shook his head. ‘I don’t trust anyone who has signed a list.’ —He had every right to say that.
Second person: didn’t listen through.
Third person: listened through. Agreed to

consider it. Reported him the next day. An informant from the preaching post—I should have thought of that.
Fourth person: …”
(After the fourth person, the lower half of this page was torn away. The tear was ragged.)

On the tapes, he laid bare this recruitment effort. He wanted to establish a complete chain of sacrifice and shutdown—people willing to enter the chamber first and die, becoming fuel to fill the hole, and operators with

access outside the chamber, or even at the distant White Tower, responsible for cutting the circuit. If he could find even one companion willing to shoulder the deadlock together, the plan could take its first step.
Estelle placed a copy of that private page at the exact center of the table. The page did not name anyone, but each entry was marked with the code for the district where they had met.

“A person who recorded every roof he repaired for more than a decade tore away a page here with his own hands. We followed those codes and the Church of Convergence’s inspection records from its final years.”
The words on the private page—“I don’t trust anyone who has signed a list”—were spoken by that person himself. In a recording Heisenberg left later, there was a complete answer from that night:

“I accept all of the reasoning. But this life of mine was dragged back from a sea of fire back then, and I truly can’t bear to send it away with my own hands a second time. Besides, I don’t trust anyone who has signed a list.”

Later, Estelle found another person’s trail in a survivor register in the underground records archive. On that yellowed page, he had written his own name and entered the number of a shelter camp in the “place

of origin” field. Comparing it against the population-placement data from those early years showed that the camp number corresponded exactly to the district code for the first person in the private page.

The search results showed that at the end of the camp’s transfer-and-execution list from that period, there was an official’s position code, beside it an old work-badge authentication number Heisenberg had once worn in the recordings.

“That list had one hundred and seventy-three people in all. The official execution records account for only one hundred and fifty-one. The remaining twenty-two disappeared without a trace. This person is the only one we can confirm survived.”

The refuser who had looked Heisenberg straight in the eye and said those words never ultimately escaped that history. Estelle swiped a finger, and the execution list on the screen flipped over—on the blank space

on the back of the paper, someone had hastily penciled several transfer numbers. They were probably records Heisenberg had made privately before sending people underground. This person’s camp number was among them.

Apart from those two yellowed official records, the first person’s final trace in history was that he lived to a very old age in the lightless underground. In several important copies passed down by the first

generation of the Preservation Society, we compared the handwriting against the signature in his register and found that the writing in the earliest copies of the Underground Pipeline Atlas matched him exactly.
The man who refused Heisenberg that night was him. He refused to hand over his life, but in another way, he spent twenty years copying diagrams in this lightless underground pipeline.
As for the middle-aged man who “didn’t listen through,” he left no dialogue behind.

“According to the registration records for District Seven, only one person left his assigned night ration post during the secret meeting that evening. Early the next morning, he voluntarily signed up for the preaching post’s auxiliary security group. He didn’t go to claim the informant’s reward. He simply pushed himself into the safest ‘everyone’ as quickly as possible.”
“This is the only record that matches.”

“Of course, we can never confirm whether he was the second person. But the Church of Convergence’s security system did gain, that morning, one person whose transfer record from his previous unit could not be found in the register.”

The third was a young man. He listened quietly to the entire plan and said he would consider it. The “reported him the next day” from the private page corresponded, in later records, to a nighttime raid on a safehouse.
The archive room still held records of the reporting system established during those years.

“The first informant received an advancement. Whoever reported a verified conviction received an additional credential. If a family member was on the delisting review list, the informant could use a valid report serial number to apply for the review to be suspended.”
As for who in that third young man’s family was on the review list, and how Heisenberg happened to escape the roundup that night, there was no way to know anymore.
All he left behind was that sentence, “I should have thought of that,” written with enough force to bleed through the paper.
By then, Heisenberg was already the Empire’s most wanted fugitive. But after this final betrayal late in life, he raised an even more ghostlike barrier against the few potential recruits he had left.
At this line, only a solitary ellipsis remained. The lower portion had been torn away with force. No direct paper evidence could tell us who it was.
On Volume Six of Heisenberg’s tapes, while recounting that recruitment attempt, there was a stretch of dead silence lasting eleven seconds. Then he said abruptly:
“I had to look that person in the eyes and say: your life would not be enough to fill it. Your death would not count.”

In the basement that night, the two of them sat facing each other across a table. The tapes held no record of the other person’s answer, and Heisenberg had violently torn away the lower half of the private page on the spot. What had the fourth person said during those ten-odd seconds

of silence? Had he already been prepared to take on the burden of the deadlock, or had he shaken his head before its incomprehensible weight? Everything was buried beneath the sound of tearing paper.
The only certainty was that Heisenberg refused to accept his life at that moment.

For the plan to proceed, someone first had to be put into the annihilation device underground. Eight thousand was the safe upper bound that would ensure coverage of the worst case. One person could provide only the capacity of a single base unit. If that were all there was to it,

he could simply have let the man stay and continued searching for the remaining seven thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine people, as well as the even more distant external operator.
But on the scratch paper beside him, the calculation stopped there, next to a set of heavy lines

drawn through it.
The first three answers had already smashed the cruel reality into his face: there would be no eight thousand people. Recruiting people to willingly step into the abyss was so difficult that finding even the first person was hard enough, let alone eight thousand.

If he accepted this person’s life now but could not gather enough capacity to fill the unknown gap, then the man’s death would be not only meaningless—Heisenberg himself would become the next executioner. He would be opening another dead end that had to be filled with human lives.
And yet, on the title page of the operator register that remained blank in later generations, there was a line carved in Heisenberg’s own hand: “The person who adds lamp oil may not be the operator.”

The underground facility needed people to maintain it over the long term. In the long years that followed, the successors known as “lamp-oil workers” became the only watchmen left in the system. Shutting down the device ultimately required

an “operator” with sufficient knowledge and authorization to sever the circuit from outside. But with this death order carved into the title page, he stripped everyone who had come into contact with the underground system’s operation of the

qualification to serve as operator. From then on, those who knew the system’s secrets were trapped forever in the duty of keeping it running, while anyone who wanted to operate the device had to be found in the outside world—someone who knew

nothing about this brutal mechanism.
But how easy could that be? Those outside knew nothing, while those who knew had been disqualified. Every attempt to recruit an external operator meant making an uninformed person take on the burden of

carrying the entire deadlock without revealing the system’s full shape. The first three failures had already proven the futility of searching outside, and this one possible step with the fourth person had been cut off by Heisenberg’s own hand.

As for whether the fourth person who sat across from him that night ever left, among the later religious copies passed down in this shelter, there was one copyist who never signed his name. Judging from the ink’s composition

and the age of the paper, he left an enormous volume of handwriting during those years. We do not know who he was, and we can never confirm whether these manuscripts belonged to the person who sat across the table that night.

If they could not gather enough capacity among those willing to fill the hole, and could not find a suitable external operator under the prohibition severing inside from outside, then no executable chain of sacrifice existed in reality.

The prohibition that “lamp-oil workers may not be operators,” combined with the impossible fuel requirement, locked the deadlock completely. Zero executable targets, zero complete internal-external operating chains: this was an impasse that could not be solved by the sacrifice of only a few people.
At the dead end, only one final possibility remained.

The idea for an artificial vessel on the old blueprints. He had to build that shell, with its capacity of ten thousand, and use it to replace the impossible number of people, solving the first deadlock directly. As for shutting down the machine at the White Tower, that would have to wait until the vessel that filled the hole had been built.
That abandoned shell of a laboratory at the edge of the map was also where his escape had begun. There was an old production line there.
At the time, news of the Head’s death and the aftershocks of the Choice Party’s collapse reached the underground. Over those long years, he had slipped back to that production line like a ghost

forty-one times. As the Church of Convergence, formally evolved from the Joint Observation Group, seized total power, its purges of those hiding underground became even more brutal than under the Head.

It was precisely that brutality that forced the old surface inspection system to be taken over and reorganized by the new church. And within that fatal seam of transition, the blind spot in the defenses he had watched for so many years finally appeared.

His nearly fifty-year-old body and rapidly declining strength told him that he no longer had enough time to keep waiting in the dark. During one final night in the years after the Church of Convergence took power, he had to leave.

In the margins of his late-life notes, there was a casual line:
“An anxious child who had just taken over timidly asked me where I was going with my pack. I told him I was going back to my old home for a visit.”
The people in the cellar watched silently as he packed. No one said a word to stop him.
Before leaving, he went to two places.

He went to the equipment room. The door for filling the hole had been built, and the operator register lay quietly beneath the ever-burning lamp, still empty. He would not live to see that field filled.

Then he turned into the records archive. On the rough table lay the original half-page of the anomalous alert that he had brought in back then. It had originally been only a scrap left behind by Semmelweis before his death. He placed a cardboard folder beside it and carefully clipped the half-page inside.
He shoved the thick notebook into his pack, then added that day’s ration of water and dry food.
There was no exact route map in the archives for a wanted criminal nearing fifty, his strength failing, crossing the wilderness. Only scattered inspection logs left a few inconspicuous traces.

A room-inspection record from an abandoned railway station complained that, after a day of heavy rain, a message written in charcoal had appeared on the signal room’s wall: “Those who take this road, go east, cross the second ridge, and there is water.” Beneath the message, in the mud, was a fresh trail of footprints heading east.
The message may have been there for a long time. But those fresh footprints heading east were the only trace left in this wilderness by the man carrying the notes of half his life.
At dusk several days later, a figure nearing fifty followed the familiar route from those years and felt his way toward the dirt ridge.
In the wild grass in the distance, a ring of thin iron posts stood alone around a low, rusted building.
The AI experimental zone crouched there in silence. It had witnessed his forty-one failed returns before, and was also the grave he had chosen for himself.
He lay low on the dirt ridge for a long time. His hair was graying, and he carried in his arms the notes of half his life.
He kept hidden outside the pipeline until deep into the night. Only when the patrol searchlight outside passed over the blind spot did he set off, heading toward the waterlogged pipes.
texts.chapter:heisenberg-11-final-recording:ti: Sea Line Eleven: The Last Recording
texts.chapter:heisenberg-11-final-recording:ev: After copying the verification command from the hands of that skeleton by myself, I went down into the abyss once more, this time with Estelle, and carried the entire heavy metal work case back to the control room on the surface.

I laid out again on the console the objects I had taken from the case during the previous descent. The lecture tapes for The Nineteen Lectures, later revered by posterity as scripture, had already been taken

away. What remained in my hands were the eight physical backup tapes hidden under the name “system calibration,” a rusted metal plate engraved with an equipment designation, a folded card, and a thin logbook.
The main terminal refused to play any media, its permissions locked tight. I could only try to read this remaining reel with an old tape player I had found in the abandoned archives.
Before pushing the tape into the slot, I unfolded the card first. On it was a handwritten recording index:

“One, Name. Two, White House. Three, Escape. Four, Underground.
Five, Two Halves. Six, Torn Page. Seven, Empty Shell. Eight, (Blank).
Final Reel: Face.”

Two strings of handwritten characters were attached to the back of the card. The first was a network address pointing to the original Semmelweis pool-position report in the Conservation Society’s underground archive. The second was a decryption key, meant to unlock the thing referred to as the “Final Reel” on the last line of the index.

The “Final Reel” was not a tape inside the case, but a video sealed deep within the White Tower’s old accident-archive network, numbered H31. But the key could only unlock the data lock. The main terminal in the control room was currently

permission-locked; without authorization, the file could not be retrieved, and even local playback was impossible. To truly obtain the video, I still had to cross the final line of defense—to acquire the historical archive authorization held by Sera.

I opened the logbook as well. It contained processing logs for early unnamed sample-incident records and anomalous telemetry data. The logs held only rows upon rows of cold, rigorous audit traces: deduplication, stratification, and

cataloging. Looking at those dense cross-checking records, I could imagine him sitting alone at the bottom of the abyss, meticulously breaking down and recalculating those materials, then packing them away for future generations.
After sorting through everything, I pressed the play button on the tape player.

The footage on these tapes had long since been completely destroyed by the aging equipment. Only the sound could still struggle intermittently to force words out into the world, more than a century later.

I had already heard the first eight reels during the previous descent. They were merely the dry facts he had left for those who came after: the calculated disaster, the dead end of the White House, the schemes behind escaping into the underground, the eleven

seconds of dead silence, and the repeated erasure and rerecording at the end, when he announced that he had produced only an empty shell. That cold, steady voice beneath the background noise had merely strung together once more the past I had already pieced together.
What was about to play was a tape not included in the index numbering, one that had been pressed beneath the eighth, empty-shell tape all this time. There had never been a slot for it in the case.
After listening for several minutes, I understood why it had no name or designation. It was not a statement of history, but pure engineering handover: specific commands
for bypassing the system’s routine alarms to access the hidden data layer, an account of exactly how many concealed locks were built into the base of the giant time
device underground, even the precise timing for injecting the equipment designation from the rusted metal plate. This reel was a maintenance guide for the machine itself.

The reel was long. He no longer used the hard, cold tone with which he declared facts in the first seven reels. Throughout, he spoke at the slow pace of an old craftsman briefing an apprentice. He repeatedly emphasized the key data coordinates, and after reading each dense set of parameters, habitually asked the audio:
“Did you get that?”
Even though he knew that by the time anyone could hear those words, he himself would have been dead for more than a century. Still, in the dim light of the control room, I copied
those coordinates onto the recording board one line at a time. If we could not keep the machine’s precarious balance steady, we would not even have a chance of reaching a safe shutdown.

The only laugh in the entire set of recordings appeared here. While talking about the trouble with an old valve, he said, “You turn this valve, it doesn’t move. You curse at it, it doesn’t move. You have to turn it back half a turn first, then turn it through—the damn thing’s got exactly the same temperament as Krennik in the old machine room.”
A short, faint laugh came through the tape. Then it quickly faded into the background noise, and he continued with the next maintenance point.
With a click, the audio of this unnumbered reel ended. The tape spun empty, hissing with white noise. That was all the sound this old machine could read.
Later, at the camp.

I placed the equipment maintenance procedures I had transcribed in the control room, along with the processing log, on the table. Estelle pulled over the punched index card and compared it against the log, trying to make sense of this handover spanning more than a century. She had not been there in the control room; she had only heard my account.
She picked up the parameters and coordinates I had recorded from the unnamed engineering reel.
“On the tape, he would stop and ask, ‘Did you get that?’ after every set of data,” I said. “I copied all those data points and the locations of the hidden locks there.”
She looked over the intricate maintenance procedures covering the pages and the system’s hidden locks I had marked, her eyes moving quickly back and forth between the coordinates as she checked them.
“Got it. This thing is useful,” she replied softly.
texts.chapter:phase2-routing-corridor:title: Routing Corridor (Central Computing Relay Station)
texts.chapter:phase2-routing-corridor:event:te: After obtaining the special investigation order issued by Sera as the archive’s authorizer, Estelle took me from the White Tower straight to the Central Computing Relay Station. This trip was not about continuing to dig through old paper.

The final battle was drawing closer. We had to confirm the complete connectivity status for Yuna’s future record verification at the underlying hardware gateway before the system shut down. Sera’s authorization was

a pass that let us legally enter the facility and get through its modern security procedures, but it had no power over the ancient hardware below. We would have to run the remaining machine self-checks ourselves.

Fault Drill Record · Final Page of Drill Section (Communications Foyer Public Notice Folder):
“Drill item: Single-zone communications loss, neighboring zone to answer.
Result: Passed.
Note: No observers present for this drill.
Date of next drill: (blank).”
The heavy blast door slid shut behind me with a sluggish metallic bite. The instant the gap sealed, the wind and cold of the wasteland were cut off completely.

The place was far larger than the hollow disaster-recovery stations scattered through the wilderness outside. As a true Central Computing Relay Station, it was a low, windowless machine room half-buried in the high ground, still running with formidable force.
“The row of ceramic ridges on the roof, serving as directional antennas, has spent its entire life speaking to only one object.”

Estelle walked ahead. The beam of her flashlight swept across mottled walls crowded with conduits. She did not look back; her voice carried a faint echo through the empty foyer. At the White Tower, we were investigating. Here, we were setting the route.
She pressed her palm against the cold door leading farther inside. A deep, faint vibration came clearly through the soles of our boots and into our bones. Something was turning in there.

The first room beyond the door was a foyer. It maintained an order that had gone uninterrupted for more than a century: the cooling well in the corner gave off a low circulating hum, and the ghastly white low-power light strips on the ceiling were still lit.

Estelle stood in that room for a long time. Her gaze passed over the public materials hanging on the walls—the dust-covered manuals for Relay Network Continuity Verification, the eight-zone node list.
Carefully, she took down the node list, turned to a page folded at the corner, and held it out to me.
“Read this line.” She dragged her fingernail hard beneath one line.
“‘The facility interior is divided into eight major zones according to routing gateways.’” I translated it.

She undid the notebook she carried and turned to the monastery duty roster she had copied out by hand earlier in the chapel. The shift numbers, from one to eight, had never changed in more than a century.
She set the two sides—the eight physical divisions in the relay station and the church’s unaltered eight-shift rotation—side by side and connected them with lines, writing down no conclusion at all.
The latter half of the manual was filled with cold operating instructions. I squatted on the floor reading until my ankles went numb.

“‘Telemetry specification: for all basic neural hardware of the New Humanity.’” I tried to translate the string of cold abbreviations. “The manual says that all New Human neural hardware comes out of gestation and manufacture

with a dormant layer of adaptive structure. Without binding to a time machine, it displays nothing and carries no old knowledge. Only once the binding is established does it activate an interworld connection interface.”

“In other words, even if you force a living person into the channel, as long as they don’t have that pre-bound substrate, the machine sees nothing coming through.” She looked at me. “It recognizes only that adaptive interface. It doesn’t recognize whose soul is inside it.”
She moved her gaze away from the manual and made no note of the anomaly in her notebook.
At the end of the manual, there was an extremely short section on corrupted-block handling.
“‘If reception of a segment is corrupted, request it again from the source that sent it. Data format only.’”

“As long as the packet carries a valid source format, no matter how many physical interruptions the transmission suffered, once the final retransmitted blocks are assembled, the system will judge it to be valid connectivity.

” She decisively made a note in the notebook. “When extreme pain or a struggle at the brink of death makes a person’s physical connection tremble and causes transmission packets to be lost, the machine cannot see what happened

behind it. It neither filters pain nor understands pain. It only sees the hash error in the metadata, then coldly requests the same slice from the local cache again until it has assembled a continuous sequence of bytes.”

Corrupted-block handling: request it again from the source cache.
The machine checks only hash and byte continuity. It does not interpret pain. It only assembles the whole.
The routing corridor was hidden just beyond the foyer.

It was an exceptionally long corridor, with metal wiring racks packed densely along both walls. Hundreds of cables clung to the walls like thick veins, each one ending in a physical address plate. A huge master diagram lay spread across the center of the corridor.

To obtain the relay gateway’s final green light, we first had to pass a physical self-check at the lowest level—prove that every access request listed on the diagram received a definite physical-port response at the gateway. Nothing could be left unconnected, and nothing could occupy more than one slot.
“I’ll check the diagram. You do the hands-on work. We have to restore the diagram’s state exactly.”

For the next several hours, I climbed up and down among the cramped wiring racks. The cables’ aged insulation was stiff and prickly, and dust kept falling into my eyes. Whenever a cable did not match the diagram, I had to plug it back into the rack port marked there.
“Stop.” She would suddenly lift her head behind the patching table. “That physical address just responded from another rack position. The same connection cannot occupy two physical sockets.”
Once I put the rough cable back into its one and only rack position and heard the latch click shut, I became especially careful with every movement.

“Later, the routing here will relay the source data sent from the White Tower. In verifying the four criteria for a record—genuine source, continuous coverage, valid ending, and no alteration to the whole—the Central Computing Relay Station stores no one’s actual record.

It handles only the middle two: whether packet coverage is continuous, and whether the hash matches—in other words, whether the whole was altered during transmission.” Estelle looked at the master diagram. “If transmission is interrupted, it caches the data briefly

and requests a retransmission. But it does not care whether the source is genuine, nor does it have the authority to determine whether a record has ended legitimately. That is for the White Tower’s original recording seat and the external disaster-recovery stations.”

When every mark on the master diagram had been checked against the ports on the walls, line by line to the final entry, an anomaly appeared.
One physical address appeared twice on the diagram, strangely enough: the fourth rack on the east wall and the second rack on the west wall. Both were plainly marked “new addition” and stamped with confirmation seals.

We returned to the maintenance station at the end of the corridor and opened the wiring-change records. The same address range had been mounted twice. Eleven days apart, both were signed with the same employee number.
It was Heisenberg’s employee number.

The date column showed that these changes had been made in rapid succession during the months when Heisenberg was lying low after his demotion. They continued until the final period before his complete defection and the revocation of his access.
“In the action column, there’s only ‘addition’ and ‘change.’” She scanned the headings. “Not a single line says ‘removal.’”
She raised her head.
“Let’s go. We’ll look at the sockets at both ends. Don’t touch anything.”

The fourth rack on the east wall was high up. I climbed onto the crossbar and followed the line to the north-end wall. The socket there was empty. The dust cap was still properly in place, its surface pressed with the factory seal.
It was a yellowed paper seal. In more than a century, no one had ever pierced it. The plug hung forlornly beside it.
After confirming the east wall, I ran along the west wall. The line there sat firmly in its socket, fitted without the slightest gap.
Estelle tilted her head back and inspected both sockets herself. Then she took out her notebook and drew the unbroken paper seal on the east-wall line exactly as it was.
“It has to be recorded now. If someone who doesn’t know about it plugs it in and the paper seal breaks, no one will be able to say what it originally looked like.”
After finishing the drawing, she tore off a slip of paper and pressed it onto the tray:
Both ends of this line visible; plug not seated. Leave in original condition.
Before leaving, Estelle stopped at the access archive page in the change records.
“Reserved interface binding status: vacant. Awaiting assignment.”

“This network’s self-check originally followed only the target addresses on the diagram when it called them.” She looked at the unpierced seal. “Before Heisenberg fled, he registered a dual-connection port here: exactly the same

address. The west wall was connected with a live line to answer the gateway’s routine calls each day; the east wall kept this sealed-paper socket unopened. But in the gateway’s system ledger, the two counted as one legitimate address.”
She circled the empty position on the east wall with her pen.

“If one day someone pierced the east-wall socket and connected the line, both sides would have genuine signatures, and the gateway would receive double packets from the same address. Could it tell the difference?”

“It couldn’t.” I followed her line of thought. “To support high-concurrency transmission, the ancient gateway protocol wouldn’t report a conflict when new data blocks appeared under the same legitimate address. It would treat them as priority relay data on

a redundant line. And because the live line on the west wall occupied the routine-response metric, any new data bearing a genuine signature from the ghost line on the east wall would overwrite it without obstruction and flow straight into the routing table.”
I looked at the empty socket. No packets had ever passed through it.

“The west wall maintains the physical response. The east wall preserves ghost relay.” She put a check mark beside the final line of the master diagram. “That explains the duplicate on the diagram. This section is complete.”
The machine rooms were at the end of the corridor. There were two enormous equipment cabinets in all, one occupying each room.

Using the physical-port states we had just checked one by one, we entered the verification commands at the two equipment cabinets. Sera’s investigation order let us unlock the modern maintenance lock without difficulty. The ancient hardware self-check inside started up afterward.

As for the strangely duplicated address, when the self-check system sent out its query, it looked only at the target response and not the specific interface. Since the east-wall seal was still unbroken, it used the response from the west wall and directly marked the two-ended ghost interface as normally connected.
The next stage, running the hardware code, would take a long time.
Dense packet-verification logs flickered across the screen. Rows of green commands streamed past my eyes.

“One segment comes in corrupted, request it again. Keep only the last complete copy…” I watched the indicator lights flicker. “To the machine, every struggle and rupture in the transmission is just network noise. It isn’t even worthy of the wastepaper bin.”
Estelle sat down at the maintenance station beside the equipment cabinets.

“So the decrypted recording we uncovered in the White Tower, and those blind spots in the external surveillance, are things the machine will never understand.” She watched the cold characters roll past. “It verifies only block continuity and whether anything has been altered. It does not understand human struggle.”
I stopped typing and watched her open the old handwritten note we had brought out of the White Tower.
“Even if that long transmission process was filled with one person’s most genuine fear, despair, and pain.” She pointed at the green commands flickering on the equipment cabinet’s screen.
“In its eyes, those things don’t even count as ‘discarded packets.’ They are sealed intact inside a black box. From beginning to end, all it verifies is the legitimate shell on the outside.”

“Look at the twelve minutes when she disappeared during lunch on the first day.” Estelle opened another classified investigation file we had retrieved from the White Tower—a reconstructed surveillance diagram of Yuna’s movements. “She

crossed most of the facility and went to that abandoned old storage area. The ash marks on the floor show that she wasn’t wandering. She went straight to the seventh door and left twelve minutes’ worth of disordered footprints there.”

She pointed to an enlarged photograph of the door. “Look at the ash on the floor. The front of her foot was pressing down, her center of gravity already thrown completely toward the door. One toe was even braced against the edge of the gap.”
“The seventh door…” I remembered the number. That was the place Sera later ordered us to inventory. “It held the prohibited old objects confiscated by the
Church over the years. Her old wooden dice were locked in there. She must have learned somewhere where they were. She went there specifically to find them.”

“Yes. But the dust on the doorknob was undisturbed. Her access privileges were valid at the time. She only had to press it to take what she wanted, and the entire facility would not even have sounded an alarm.” Estelle shook her head. “But she knew that

even if the system did not raise an alarm, the underlying gateway would record an insignificant fluctuation in the door-lock level. And if even the smallest redundant record were left during the review period, it might give Sera a thread to follow.”

She closed the file. “She went through the whole process and stood outside the door. She could have reached out and taken it, but she stood there for twelve minutes. In the end, she forcibly withdrew her hand. That inhuman

struggle between overwhelming desire and absolute reason— the machine knew neither what was behind the door nor what it cost her. In the system’s eyes, it was merely legitimate idle time that triggered no overreach alarm.”

Estelle pulled out the next page of the materials. “Until the day the results were posted. In the classroom, Sera shoved Yuna’s badge back into her collar and dragged her outside. Later, in the prayer room, Yuna pressed her about the bottom line.”
She opened a photocopy of Sera’s private notes.

Excerpt from dialogue record:
She questioned the bottom line of the “no itemization” rule.
I classified it myself as contempt for the rules.
One line entered in the register. Classes continue tomorrow.

“Under the standard review procedure, Sera, as an instructor confronted by a candidate probing the core boundary, would not only have recorded the violation. She would also have copied the circumstances that led Yuna to ask that question, word for word into an attachment, and reported it to the Council of Elders.”

“But in the end, the register contained only one isolated sentence: ‘Contempt for the rules, record one line.’ That meant she had been recorded as violating the rules, but it would not leave behind how far she had actually crossed the boundary.” Estelle’s finger moved across

the photocopy of the register. “Together with her restraint outside the door, neither document spells out the reason, but the logic is the same. The system can record Yuna lingering outside the door and breathing in front of Sera, but it cannot record the weight behind them.”
“So we can only piece together from these fragments, judged incomplete or in violation, how she restrained herself in that moment, and how she was brutally protected by another person.”
After the authorization write finished, I went back to the foyer to return the manual. My eyes fell again on the line at the end of the drill section:
“Drill item: Single-zone communications loss, neighboring zone to answer.”

The first time I read the phrase that afternoon, I thought it sounded like a backup response: one zone lost contact, and the neighboring zone’s routing would answer in its place, maintaining the continuity of the network.
But after checking hundreds of addresses in the routing corridor, I no longer saw the phrase that way at all.

If a zone lost all physical power or burned out completely, the machine beside it would take over its physical-connectivity response and send packets outward. Once the underlying network received this machine response in a valid format, it would mark the dead zone “online normally” in the master ledger.
I looked at the line: “No observers present for this drill.”

During the process, no one was called in to carry out repairs, and the fault would not be reported to the application layer. Once the substitution took effect, the network status would turn green. In this network design, to preserve the availability of the system as a whole, local death was silently concealed.
I remembered how we had previously forced the disaster-recovery station’s network to proxy that deathly silent node beneath the water. At the time, I had thought it was merely a technical means of

deceiving the main network. But when I realized that the underlying logic of this communications facility maintained its surface completeness through this kind of silent substitution, a chill ran up my back.

We were inventorying the gateway for Yuna, trying to ensure that the final transmission broadcast across the whole network would face no obstruction. But inside this device, whose backdoor logic had been set in advance, everything was different.

“If someone used this mechanism…” I thought back to the suspended mark on the master diagram. “The ghost port on the east wall of the relay gateway—the paper seal has always been intact, which means no one has ever plugged a line into it.”

“No one needs to plug in a line. That unbroken paper is precisely the perfect decoy.” Estelle’s finger moved across the substitution protocol in the manual. “Heisenberg registered the east wall at the underlying level as a legitimate redundant address. Under the logic of ‘neighboring zone to answer,’ as long

as some external disaster-recovery station sends a report to the main network, claims to be that redundant node, and requests to take over, the gateway will consult the master ledger, see that the east wall does indeed have a legitimate address in a ‘vacant’ state, and accept the external signal directly.”

I drew a sharp breath. “In other words, even if we welded an iron cover over that physical socket and put ten locks on it, it wouldn’t help. As long as the false address remains in the system ledger, an external counterfeit node could seize the highest-priority disaster-recovery transmission authority out of nowhere at any time.”

“And deleting the redundant address from the system ledger requires the highest application-layer authority, at the level of the Council of Elders. Here, all we can do is watch that address remain on the diagram.” She

looked at me. “We can’t even cut the line. At the physical layer, the east and west walls are hard-written into the same safety circuit. If you bite through the insulation with pliers and cause a metal short, or forcibly

alter the circuit impedance, the gateway hardware corresponding to the live line on the west wall will immediately trigger an irreversible protective lockout. Yuna’s primary verification channel would be buried with it.”

“But what good is seizing the communications band?” I remembered the rules we had confirmed earlier. “The relay station can’t determine identity of the personality. The final external verification mechanism will check the genuine neural-hardware signature. The ghost node can’t send in a fake personality.”

“That is why it needs the ‘substitution’ protocol working together with a legitimate neural berth.” Estelle raised her eyes, her gaze cold. “It doesn’t need to forge Yuna’s signature by force. It only needs to put a stranger’s consciousness into a berth with a legitimate signature.”
“Occupy the ghost interface to secure the highest priority on the redundant line during network concurrency, then use the legitimate hardware berth to pass the source-signature check.” She
closed the notebook. “As long as packet coverage is continuous and the hash matches, the relay station does not care who is lying in that legitimate berth. Under the system’s perfect green
light, a completely different memory and consciousness would be treated as legitimate redundant data and, with perfect legality, poured into the routing table, overwriting the original record.”
A chill ran down my back. I instinctively tried to find a way to defend against it. “Then as long as we guard every external node on the day of the final battle—”
“Arno, the window of opportunity has already closed.” Estelle cut me off.
Her words fell like a heavy hammer, scattering all my remaining hope.

“Yuna’s records were already locked and sealed during the previous review period.” Her voice was very soft, yet it struck a despairing echo through the empty foyer. “The usurpation did not need to wait for the final battle. That substitution

must already have happened during the brief interval when her records were sealed. The system recorded only the continuity of the hash. No one knows whose personality imprint was actually written into core storage during those few seconds.”
I watched the green commands flicker endlessly across the screen. The completeness the system pursued had merely hidden the real rupture perfectly. In this machine room that had not changed for more
than a century, the green light remained on, while the truth we were exhausting ourselves to protect may already have been silently replaced with an empty shell before dawn, without anyone noticing.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:title: Proxy Response
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s2-1: When I pushed open the door to the village archives, Estelle was sorting through a stack of newly delivered registers.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s3-1: I pulled out a chair, sat across from her worktable, and pushed over the page I had copied from the relay station.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s5-1: “The relay station’s communications procedure for ‘single-district disconnection, neighboring-district proxy response’ looks remarkably like our situation now.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s6-1: She stopped her pen and glanced at the page. Her gaze lingered for a moment on the line, “The lower level must record the missing marker; the upper level makes no distinction.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s8-1: “When the sensation of severance descended in the shaft beneath the ruins at twenty-two hundred last night, I didn’t even have time to say goodbye.” The relay station’s harsh green
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s8-2: light seemed to remain suspended across my vision. “I was forcibly pulled away just like that, leaving behind the self who was still in the shaft, leaving behind everyone in the village.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s10-1: “It frightens me. The world that was left behind is like the ‘disconnected district’ in this procedure. And as long as we’re still here breathing normally today,
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s10-2: the normal operation on this side is like a proxy heartbeat being sent on their behalf. It conceals the rupture perfectly. No alarm will ever be triggered.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s16-1: She turned and pulled her own work ledger from the shelf. She flipped past the old records of routine supplies and personnel, going straight to a fresh page.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s17-1: She pulled off the pen cap and began to write. The scratch of the nib against the paper echoed through the room. When she finished, she blew on the still-wet ink, turned the ledger around, and pushed it in front of me.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s18-1: At the very top of the page, the heading read:
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s22-1: Below it was the standard form she normally used to register supplies.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s23-1: In the [Time of Severance] column, she wrote: exactly twenty-two hundred.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s24-1: In the [Missing Subjects] column, she entered: everyone left in the old world.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s25-1: In the [Reason] column, she wrote: Access to the original endpoint interrupted. Disconnection not reported. Manually registered herein.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s26-1: But in the final [Current Status] column, she left it blank. She wrote nothing.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s28-1: “What are you doing?” I looked at the form.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s34-1: “The machine’s concealment comes from the fact that, to it, all that matters is that the heartbeat connects.” She leaned back in her chair. “But I’m a registrar.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s36-1: “So you’re making a record for a past whose whereabouts are unknown?”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s40-1: “If you were forcibly taken away from there, then that reality still continued after you left.” She looked at the blank space.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s42-1: “What the you in the shaft encountered, what happened to the village after twenty-two hundred… none of it stopped, and none of it became a happy ending under my pen. I simply can’t know anymore.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s43-1: She reached out and closed the ledger.
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s45-1: “This blank space is the only fact I can confirm now.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s47-1: “Will anyone ever check the records in this ledger?”
texts.chapter:v15-p2ab:event:text-s48-1: She did not answer. She simply put the ledger away in the drawer, the movement brisk and certain.
texts.chapter:phase2-isolation-corridor:title: The Permission Isolation Corridor
texts.chapter:phase2-isolation-corridor:event::
Permission Matrix · Excerpt (original posted on the Isolation Corridor wall):
“Operation: Replace source. Operator: No. Program seat: No. External administrator: Yes.
Operation: Designate long-term record starting point. Operator: No.

Program seat: No. External administrator: Yes.
Operation: Extract complete record. Operator: No. Program seat: No. External administrator: Yes.
Operation: Write external end marker. Operator: No. Program seat: No. External administrator: Yes.

Operation: Remove partial experiences. Operator: No. Program seat: No. External administrator: No.
—This network has no such operation.”
(The final line at the bottom of the matrix.)

That happened not long after Yuna had just been sacrificed. Before we infiltrated the White Tower and truly established 07:50 as the source of her life’s long record, Estelle and I had first searched the wasteland in

the northwestern canyon, checking the underlying state of the legacy systems, until we reached the last facility in the continuity verification network—the old Empire’s external disaster-recovery management station.

In this world where Yuna had never been born, I had grown used to the dislocation of infiltrating the heart of the old world amid the desolation. Hidden beneath the windblown sand, the facility’s heavy alloy door gave a muffled thud

when it recognized the high-level authorization code Estelle had retrieved as the second candidate, then slid open without a sound. We crossed the threshold in silence, searching for a handle with which to interfere with that black box.
The outer section was a public disaster-recovery hall.

The duty roster from that era was nailed to the wall. The name of the last person on watch had faded to a pale gray, gnawed away by time. The stamp pad for dual approval had dried and cracked. On the shelf beside it were paper fault lists, their stubs stopping forever at one torn page.
Estelle went straight to the console as soon as she entered, picked up the thick approval ledger, and opened it.

“Over the more than a century since the Church took over the White Tower, every person assigned here has had only one task: perform a ‘routine verification’ in the outer hall. No one has ever gone inside.” She tossed the ledger back onto the table. “Come on. We’re going farther in.”

Beyond the hall was a corridor that had not been opened in years. It was called the Permission Isolation Corridor. The air carried the stale smell of settled dust. The permission matrix for the entire facility hung on the wall.
Ordinary operators had no authority inside at all. The people who built the machine had left every key to the “administrators” outside.
“That’s what keeps the people inside from dreaming.” Estelle did not look at the routine operations near the top. Her eyes went straight to the bottom of the matrix.

“This master plate uses the standard engraving format.” Her fingers brushed over the final line. “The first few lines properly say ‘who has the authority to perform a given operation.’ But this line—‘Remove partial experiences’—along with the

following ‘This network has no such operation,’ is engraved in an entirely different weight. It was forcibly added later. It wasn’t engraved to regulate permissions. It was engraved to nail shut forever a request that had once been raised.”
Estelle pried open one warped drawer after another. The dust-covered metal cabinets were crammed with complaints written by generations of duty officers, requests for scrapped
parts, and old accident investigation reports. She searched through a jumble of moisture-proof bags for structural drawings, but pulled out a yellowed, brittle form instead.
It dated from the founding of the Empire. The applicant’s name had been crudely blacked out, leaving only the mark of a shrunken stamp.
“The old script is used here. You read it.”
I leaned closer. “‘Proposal: Add a partial-experience trimming function. Purpose: Manually remove unwanted, contaminated, or traumatic segments from a record.’”
“Read the rejection on the back.”
The rejection was handwritten in fountain pen. There was no pointless talk about technical feasibility, only three brief, ruthless lines.

“‘What counts as contaminated must be judged by a person. If a person judges, a person can delete. This network provides no benevolent function that can be abused. No semantic deletion or alteration whatsoever.’”
At the very bottom of those three lines was an extremely sloppy abbreviated signature—Lysenko.

I turned toward the interface list on the console. A system-level annotation lay coldly across the bottom of the terminal screen:
【Mid-record slicing and partial-period extraction interface: Not implemented, as it violates the “no trimming” principle.】
Lysenko had not only rejected content-based selection; he had also removed every interface for mid-record truncation and partial extraction at the physical level.

There was no room here for human reconsideration. Not even a back door marked “except for the highest authority” had been left. The system designers of that era had entombed this path in concrete. Under this engineering architecture, once

this record was formally established someday, its lower bound would remain locked forever at that starting point, and extraction could only export the whole thing. There would be no boundary editing: either take everything, or take nothing.
Estelle held the yellowed application form for a long time. At last, she rested it on her knee and copied the rejection verbatim into the audit ledger, stroke by stroke.
“No matter how many schemes the builder of this old Empire had behind the scenes, at least for this exception without a back door, I have to give him credit for one thing.”
Behind the blast door at the end of the corridor was a flight of stairs leading downward.

The physical sealing chamber below lay in a depression. Its water was deep and black, reeking of mold, and had completely submerged the native interface equipment on the lower level. We could only stand on the still-dry platform high on the stairs and watch the proxy communication terminal light up on the wall.
In a waterproof trough above us lay an appendix to a very early project proposal.

“‘External’ simply means an administrative channel not constrained by the permission structure of the ordinary operator interface. For example, the disaster-recovery direct connection at the bottom of the White Tower, or this room we’re standing in.”

On the final page of the appendix, one line of primary text had been nailed there by itself:
“Preset source for this network (personality-template integration placeholder): the person in charge. This initial setting prohibits all ordinary changes within the system.”
The seal of the head of the core laboratory had been stamped beside the signature—that of Lysenko, who had taken control of the ruins. This had originally been his fallback.
“No wonder ‘Replace source’ on the matrix outside is available only to external administrators.” Estelle returned the appendix to its place. “Looking at what happened afterward, he never actually
lay inside that device, but he sealed every normal change point within the system. He only specified that someone with high-level authorization could overwrite this instruction from outside.”
