I stepped past her and woke the structural interface on the terminal above. Through a remote communications link, it connected to the metadata of the entire record. The screen displayed the intervention capabilities this sealed system had left to external administrators:

One was 【Replace source】.
One was 【Designate long-term record starting point】.
Behind both of them, the shell parameters Lysenko had set were still filled in by default. On the external administrator’s side, the input fields were both still awaiting overwrite, unlocked.

The proxy terminal glowed with a red warning. Whether replacing the source or designating the starting point, all record-creation overwrite operations had to be performed within the baseline spacetime of data generation—the physical origin where the person first came online. If we forcibly

invoked the high-level permissions here, in this world without Yuna, the system would not only be unable to capture her physical snapshot as the underlying credential; by leaving the baseline anchor, it would also directly cut off the original data stream she had left in that baseline world.

That was why this disaster-recovery station had the permissions, yet we could not complete the record creation here. The neural snapshot Yuna left at 07:50 was currently only a piece of short-term rolling data in that baseline

world, not yet entered into the records. Unless we returned to the White Tower and designated the starting point at the correct spacetime coordinates, it would remain a suspended slice that could neither be extracted nor cut off.
Besides 【Extract complete record】, which could export the entire record, the final item on the interface was 【Write external end marker】.
That was the seal that would draw an absolute full stop beneath the long record of the future.

I watched the empty status bar. No long-term record had been opened yet, so naturally there was no end marker. But the operating instructions were clear: once the record was established, as long as its source was still

generating subjective experiences in any connected branch world, the seal would remain locked. Even if someone forcibly submitted an end marker at the terminal, the operation would be immediately rejected as long as

endpoint activity verification was not zero. That meant that if I truly opened this record in the future, what I would have to face would not be some slice, but the sum of every experience up until she completely shut down.

Standing before this machine, which had only total-control and export permissions but not a single “trimming” button, I was forced to see the trace of desire in my heart that should never have been there.
Somewhere beneath my awareness, I still imagined that this facility might offer some precise extraction function. I wanted to discard the despair of being swallowed by flames again and again
beyond the blast window, the suffocation of struggling in a pool of blood, in a traceless data wasteland, and bring back only the her who sat beside me by the fire, listening to the wood crackle.
I wanted to decide for her which experiences were worthy of making up her life.

But the words “This network has no such operation” on the wall, together with the empty interface list on this terminal, completely extinguished that false mercy. Under the physical iron law of this system, the weight she would have to bear would be complete. Whether

she would still feel that she was Yuna when she awoke, whether she would still acknowledge the sacrifice she had made back then, the future me would have only one choice left: prepare to face that unpredictable version of her, and swallow all of this together with her.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:title: That Card (External Disaster Recovery Station)
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s2-1:
We left the isolation control room just flooded with black water and followed the rusted maintenance passage downward. The disaster recovery server room was colder than the White Tower, and the air smelled of old filter media.
At the center of the room stood a dust-covered console
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s2-2:
and a fixed engineering chair. The two physical interfaces we were looking for were embedded in the metal wall behind the chair, completely separate from the desktop.
One was mounted higher, beside a narrow operations table: the verification seat for the local auditor. The other was
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s2-3:
extremely low, almost flush with the floor, reserved for the audited subject. The staggered heights carried an unmistakable posture of power—the auditor stood looking down, while the subject could only crouch at the base of the wall.
The old terminal refused to respond to any of
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s2-4:
Estelle’s advanced commands. On the screen, the verification request triggered in the outer control room hung coldly in place—the system had discovered that the underlying code contained the highest “external administrator” credentials, forcibly bound there by someone unknown.
To formally
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s2-5: activate these old credentials, whose origin even I did not know, the system sent the verification baseline back to the underlying physiological identification. It required us to use the two rigid physical interfaces to forcibly compare the biological characteristics of two people.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s5-1:
A cold warning appeared on the screen: “Dual-person review registration required.” Looking at those words, I vaguely remembered being six years old. I had broken the coarse porcelain bowl at home and was hiding in the shadow of the house, afraid to go outside.
A ghastly white strip of torn cloth was
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s5-2: wrapped around the gap in the window frame. Suddenly, two light taps came from the base of the wall. Two little feet kicked against the wall and flipped up onto the windowsill. Yuna jumped in. She was wearing a long-sleeved shirt that was slightly too large, and clutching a yellowed supply registration card.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s7-1: “This windowsill is much easier to climb than the one at my house.” She scanned the room to make sure there were no adults, then lowered her voice. “Come here.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s8-1:
I obediently crouched over. She spread the stolen card on the dust-covered ground, preparing to register some “stolen property” she had hidden in her pocket and refused to show me even at the cost of her life.
Several fixed fields were printed on the card. At the bottom, in tiny letters, was a warning: Copy exactly as written. Do not guess.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s10-1: “I saw Aunt Sera filling one of these out.” She wrote her name in the top field, “Registrant,” then copied a string of numbers crookedly from whatever she was feeling around for in her pocket into the field labeled “Readable Characters.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s14-1: “The adults say that anything without a box drawn for it on the form doesn’t count.” She stared at the half-length pencil in her hand. “There’s only ‘characters’ here. No ‘ownership.’”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s15-1: She wanted to draw a horizontal line in the blank space on the form and force in a new field to declare that the thing now belonged to her, but in the end she gave up. However, the bottom of the card contained one final rule: there had to be two names. One registrant, one reviewer.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s17-1: “What’s the reviewer’s name?” she asked with exaggerated seriousness, pointing her pencil at the blank line below, pretending not to know.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s20-1: The pencil tip struck the paper hard.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s22-1: “All you have to do is nod, and it counts as signing this name yourself,” she declared.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s23-1: I stared at the pencil tip and, as if possessed, nodded. She wrote my name in the reviewer’s box. I never knew what exactly she had registered that day. I only remembered the name from ten years ago,
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s23-2:
incomplete and missing strokes.
The harsh dual-person review procedure before me was mechanically repeating that scene from long ago. Only this time, the person holding the review credentials was Estelle.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s27-1:
Estelle walked to the interface at the higher position and pressed her left palm against the palm-sized metal plate.
The terminal emitted a beep, and a code from the old era appeared on the screen. The machine directly
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s27-2:
mapped the biological characteristics of this shell to the account of the “Director of White Tower Security” in the old disaster recovery archives.
She stared at the ancient title on the screen and froze for a moment.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s27-3:
As a candidate selected by the Central Village, she knew better than anyone how rigorous the Church’s physiological screening of candidates was.
“So the Church’s so-called ‘divinely granted body’”—the corner of
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s27-4: her mouth pulled into a self-mocking smile as she quickly turned the astonishing coincidence into a cold conclusion—“is nothing more than a security shell mass-produced generation after generation from the genetic
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s27-5:
template of an old-government security chief.”
The system assigned her the seat of “Local Security Officer,” and a confirmation prompt appeared. She stated her name coldly and formally registered herself in place.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s29-1: “The auditor must remain at the station. The entire time.” She lifted her head and glanced at the authorization matrix posted on the wall, then turned to me. “That means that while your external administrator credentials are being verified, if my hand leaves this plate even once, the entire process starts over from the beginning.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s30-1: She raised her chin toward the base of the wall. “Your turn.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s31-1:
Dragging my aching leg, I struggled to crouch in front of the interface less than half a meter off the ground.
The instant my right hand pressed against it, the system’s underlying layer began forcibly pulling my identifying features and physically comparing them with the old records.
The wait took a while. To
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s31-2:
avoid the space where Estelle was standing, I could only crouch awkwardly on my side. The old injury in my right knee began to ache. To ease it, I instinctively shifted my weight half an inch to the left.
The shift caused my palm to arch slightly, lifting it away from the coin-sized sensing area at the center.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s32-1: With a soft “beep,” the indicator light went out.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s35-1:
I took a deep breath, lowered my weight again, and pressed my palm firmly back against the metal plate.
Cold air blew through the server room. To maintain the rigid posture, I could only brace the tip of
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s35-2: my right foot against the floor. The uneven pressure sent a sharp pain up through the thin part of the sole. That familiar sensation made me feel as if I had returned to that abandoned drainage channel.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s39-1: It was behind the village road. Once, we had slipped out along the perimeter, and after we returned home, my mother had recognized the route from the white mud on my soles. We kept quiet for a while after that. Later, Yuna found an
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s39-2:
absolutely dry route and began taking me on even harsher drills. That day, we crawled into an abandoned dry ditch that could not yield even a drop of muddy water.
Once the soles had worn clean through, the stones hurt terribly underfoot.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s39-3:
I could only walk into the grass and pad my feet with the soft blades. Yuna walked silently ahead of me, carrying that rough gray cloth bag. Her steps looked remarkably light.
When she climbed out at the end of the dry ditch, she stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s43-1: “Repeat it. The one thing you absolutely must not do today.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s48-1:
Once the exchange was complete, her gaze slowly lowered and came to rest on my right foot. The front of the sole had worn completely through, leaving a large hole.
Then she asked a completely unrelated question:
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s50-1: “What time did you actually get home last night?”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s52-1: “I don’t know. Galon said we could leave when the work was done. It was already completely dark.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s53-1: She nodded and held out one hand.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s56-1:
I untied the light, empty canteen from my waist. She took it and decisively turned it upside down. Not a drop of water fell out.
With practiced movements, she stuffed the empty canteen back into the depths of the cloth bag and retied the opening in a tight knot.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s60-1: “Insufficient preparation. Today is void.” She delivered her verdict.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s62-1: “I’m not thirsty. We’ve only just started walking. The rule was yours: we were supposed to stay out for three days.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s64-1: “The rule is mine, so now I say the water isn’t enough. The drill is over.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s65-1: She ignored my argument and turned away, setting off.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s68-1: The sun was fierce on the way back, and the exhaustion finally began to surface. When we reached the collapsed section at the mouth of the ditch, she told me to rest in the shade behind a rock while she went into the dim cavern to scout the way. It was full of loose dirt; there was no chance of a hidden spring. The moment I sat down, I fell into a dead sleep.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s71-1:
I woke once in the middle of it. In my haze, I saw her back out of the pitch-black cavern and stand at its entrance.
Her shadow on the ground slowly stretched forward. She held that posture, looking at me, and stood without moving for a long time.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s74-1:
Then she stepped back twice, half disappearing into the shadow of the entrance again.
She lifted her foot and scraped the sole hard against a stone, producing a harsh “screech.” Only after making the noise did she walk out.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s76-1: “What are you staring at? Time to go.” she shouted at me, freshly startled awake.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s78-1: I got up and took the gray cloth bag from her without thinking. I had watched her carry it the whole way earlier, but had never weighed it in my hands. Only when I took it did the strap bite hard into my finger bones, revealing that it was unexpectedly heavy. Clear sloshing came from inside.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s78-2:
There had plainly been another full canteen hidden in it from the start, enough water for the two of us for three days.
She never mentioned the blood blisters worn into the soles of my feet again. Neither of us exposed the existence of that heavy canteen, and we walked back in silence.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s81-1:
I remained in the difficult crouch, my line of sight forced level with the very bottom of the equipment cabinet.
A ghostly green progress bar moved slowly across the metal panel.
“Thirty percent,” Estelle called out from above. Her voice echoed through the empty server room. “Don’t let your
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s81-2:
hand shake.”
The machine before me stubbornly compared the biological traces beneath my surface. The process from thirty to one hundred took as long as a punishment. The ache in my right toe gradually went numb; only the sensation of my palm pressed hard against the metal plate remained clear.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s84-1:
The green light indicating successful verification flared brightly.
The long, oppressive silence in the server room wrapped around me. A prompt glowed on the engineering interface: Verification checksum being generated.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s85-1: Once the process was complete, we could finally take our hands off the metal plates. My right hand spasmed in the air for a while, unable to close. Estelle leaned against the console, pulled a recording pen from its leather case, and held it out to me.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s88-1: I took it with my stiff right hand, pinched the physical export sheet emerging from the print slot, and forced myself to concentrate. The ink on the paper was so fine it made my eyes swim. Holding the pen, I began mechanically reading the characters aloud while Estelle checked them
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s88-2:
against the screen.
When we reached the third group of verification codes, a sharp pain stabbed through my palm. Only then did I realize that at some point I had clenched my empty left hand so tightly that my nails had dug deep into the flesh.
I released my left hand and shook it.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s91-1: Estelle stood behind me to the side like a silent ghost. She asked nothing. She simply turned, walked to the wall, felt around, and turned up the dim backup light behind the
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s91-2:
equipment cabinet by one notch.
The light fell across the export sheet, making the numbers somewhat easier to read. After doing this, she silently returned to her position.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s94-1:
I finished reading the remaining password, signed my name at the end of the sheet, and returned the pen to her.
At the bottom of the authorization export sheet, besides the audited subject, there was still a blank field belonging to the auditor.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s96-1: “Confirmed.” She took the pen and neatly capped it. From beginning to end, she had not signed her name anywhere on the sheet. “The physical comparison is complete. Your shell has been recognized. This is only an admission ticket. Next, I have to investigate how this admission ticket came into your hands.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s100-1: We left the server room and followed the narrow engineering passage all the way outside. When we pushed open the heavy blast door, a desolate canyon lay beyond. This was the true core data storage zone.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s101-1: She insisted on going in alone to conduct the audit.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s103-1: She stopped at the entrance to the heavy airtight hatch leading into the depths of the canyon and blocked my way.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s105-1: “This trip wasn’t just to have the machine compare our fingerprints.” She sighed softly. “Machines only compare characteristics mechanically. They don’t know who you are. Once I
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s105-2: go in, I’ll be checking every change made to your external administrator credentials, the legality of every signature, and the source of that final privilege-escalation command.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s106-1: She looked at me, her voice turning extremely serious.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s107-1: “This system treats people like assets and guards against them. You are absolutely not to follow me inside. As the audited subject, the moment you appear at the internal verification site, any unnecessary
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s107-2: movement will be judged by the system as an attempt to tamper with the record. Once the defense mechanism is triggered, the external administrator credentials you just lit up will be locked permanently.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s109-1: “When I come out, I’ll read every comparison result to you exactly as it is. You’ll have to accept the good and the bad.”
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s110-1:
The heavy hatch made a teeth-grating scraping sound, then slammed shut with a bang.
I remained at the mouth of the canyon, where the wind howled, and found a rock to sit on. The steep rock walls on either side were like giant axes, cleaving an incredibly narrow slit through the sky. That strip of sky was a deep blue.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s111-1: The wind was cold, cutting through my thin jacket. I knew my own circumstances—in the morning after the lost time that followed the fall, I had tried to force-start those machines and
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s111-2: failed without surprise. Who, at the other end of the terminal, had crossed every lawful procedure and somehow attached this shell’s physical characteristics to the highest credentials?
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s112-1: I remembered the way Estelle had capped the pen just now. As long as the auditor’s field remained blank, no one had vouched for these credentials of unknown origin.
texts.chapter:v15-p2bb:event:text-s112-2: I sat there, listening to the wind howl through the canyon, waiting for her to come out and see how she intended to explain this battered trail to that rigid machine.
texts.chapter:chapter-29-why-only-her:title: Chapter Twenty-Nine: Why Only Her
texts.chapter:chapter-29-why-only-her:event:te: I waited for her in the ravine outside the external disaster recovery station. The wind was strong, pressing the knee-high wild grass flat one patch at a time, then letting it spring back up before my eyes.
After a long while, the heavy airlock door gave a dull thud. Estelle stepped out of the machine room, cold as an icehouse, holding a narrow verification sheet.

External Disaster Recovery Management Station Certification:
Permission trail: continuous. Unauthorized deregistrations: zero instances.
External termination marker: confirmed appended.
Personality body: not retained by this station. Original block integrity pending cross-facility verification.

“The disaster recovery station recognizes only physical logs. It has no authority to store personality data.” She drew out her pen, signed her name heavily at the bottom, and continued, “But it proves two things you said. First, the permission trail of your

low-level ‘operator’ access is continuous. No matter how many times the system restarted, the phantom port never went offline. Second, the personality data brought back in that package has already been sealed with an ‘ended’ marker. No one has touched it since.”
She folded the signed sheet.
“Your identity is preserved.” She turned to look at me. “That also means the data you mounted has a legitimate chain of origin. Whether it can be used is something we still have to pursue.”
On the way back, we stopped on a sheltered slope to rest and lit a small fire to boil water.
The dry brush crackled as it burned. Watching the flames, I told her everything this verification had uncovered: this was not merely a set of permission records, but Yuna’s real life across countless

mutually exclusive branches produced by repeated restarts. Each carried its own origin tag, and all of them would be written into a new body that could live only in one direction, following time forward.
She watched the fire for a while, her gaze deep. For the local Estelle, who possessed only a single line of memories, the weight of this exceeded anything reasonable.
“Arno.” She looked across the fire at me. “You told me before about marking the source. That morning, she said to you, ‘Press it,’ allowing you to press the key and begin saving.”

“But that doesn’t mean she agreed to be recorded by you indefinitely. Even less does it mean she agreed to be put into the same body at restoration along with countless versions of herself whose experiences contradict one another.”
“Before she walked through the sacrifice door, she told me herself, ‘Bring me back.’ That was the last task she left me.”

“That was the Yuna who had gone all the way to the end, with no other choice.” She fixed her eyes on mine. “In all those desperate branches, was there not a single Yuna who, while going through that pain, wanted to end all of this completely? Was there not one of them who told you, ‘Stop taking care of me’?”
She drew a deep breath.

“The one who refused to keep being dragged through this experiment was also completely herself. What gives you the right to use that one sentence of consent at the source to decide for everyone across all the branches, forcing every Yuna who never agreed to merge with countless mutually exclusive selves into what comes next?”
The fire gave a soft pop.

“Because that system isn’t an editor for personalities.” I looked at her. “At the machine’s lowest level, every life branch produced by a restart carries its own independent tag. During restoration, the system recognizes only the complete data tree from the true source to the final

subjective state. I can’t cut out an experience from some branch because I dislike it, or keep only the part where she willingly went to her death. The moment any branch is cut from the tree, this set of origins fails system verification, and the entire data set becomes invalid.”
I swallowed.
“If she wakes up and never forgives me because of the pain forced into her, I’ll have to accept that.”
Estelle picked up a branch and poked at the coals.
“So you deprived her of the right to choose in those branches,” she said.
She did not offer me some grand forgiveness. She was only stating a cold boundary.

“The form I signed proves only that you possess a compliant data source. To put these things into a real body, you still have to pass the technical review overseen by Elder Garon, and the hearing that will decide how you use this data.”

“No one can decide for her unilaterally, and you have even less right to have the final say alone. Even if she wakes someday, whether those conflicting histories become public evidence must also be decided by her. I do not provide an acquittal.”
I nodded. This was the auditor’s boundary.
The water boiled, making a muffled sound against the lid of the pot.

“The project’s source file survived because you forcibly locked the starting point of the long-term record during the lost time.” Estelle turned her face aside. “But if this restoration project is technically universal, then once the gap formed, even if someone had to fill it, why did it have to be her at seventeen?”
The question was like a thorn. I had already settled the account myself. I did not want to lay out that fourteen-hour stretch of despair all over again, but she needed an explanation.
“Because she was the only one willing to accept that account.” I watched the dancing flames. “That machine didn’t want a life. It wanted someone who, with full knowledge
of the facts, willingly gave up every possible branch, ending the continued existence of their projections in every related world, without leaving any way back.”
I poked at the fire with a branch, and sparks shot into the air.

“After the gap formed, I tried to fill it myself, but the system returned a direct error: ‘Target cannot be coupled.’ Yuna worked out what that error meant for me: my balance was zero. I no longer even qualified to be the sacrifice.”

“Among the Inner Circle who knew the secret, only ten adults had enough data capacity. The first to step forward was Elder Garon. When he heard that a human life was needed to fill the gap, the first thing he said to me was, ‘If ten thousand is enough, use me.’”
“Then why didn’t he fill it?”

“Because afterward, I turned that bill to the next page.” I watched the ash illuminated by the firelight. “I told him that the machine would not extract only the version of him standing there. It would also cut off every

living branch of him in every other connected world. It would leave no backup, no continuation, and no other version of Garon to live in his place. He understood that it meant a complete end. He never offered himself again.”

I did not continue. The procedure was incomplete, the evidence insufficient, or, like Garon, they could not accept the total termination of their selves across worlds—the ten of them had all made entirely reasonable choices that day.
“The only one who crossed beyond those reasonable calculations alone, settled the bill for that dead end, and stepped onto the one-way road without a word was her.”
Estelle watched the firelight. For a long time, she said nothing.
We put out the fire and continued back. On the way to the village, there was still one final section of perimeter logs to complete.
The severity Estelle had shown at the fire applied equally to her own work. Walking ahead, she opened the register and stopped.

“It doesn’t match the patrol group’s record from yesterday morning, when they left the village. In the source notes near the western boundary stone, they marked ‘road collapse, passage cut off,’ but we haven’t verified this stretch of road. It’s just ahead.”
“Do you want to walk over and verify it?”
She looked toward the area concealed by the brush in the distance. The old break in the abandoned underground passage was hidden below it.
I lowered my voice.

“People are still using that underground road. The tops of the rebar at the break were worn smooth by shoe soles long ago, and someone deliberately brushed loose soil back over it.” I looked at Kaine, sitting on the boundary

stone nearby and smoking with bored indifference. “He keeps watch over that road every day, watching those traces. The moment you step on it to verify the mark and clear away the loose soil, he’ll know someone is investigating.”

“I’m not crossing this one out.” She took out her pen and wrote ‘According to testimony. I did not approach’ beside the unverified road condition. “Anything I haven’t stepped on myself will never enter the verified record. That’s my rule.”

She clipped the pen back into the register with a heavy motion. Without looking at me again, she went around the patch of grass and walked steadily toward the village. Kaine, sitting on the boundary stone, glanced at us, exhaled a plume of white smoke, and said nothing.
It was afternoon when we returned to the village. She was going to submit the audit report from this verification and my verification form to the controlled archive.
The deposit was handled quickly. The old guard took the materials and entered a record.

Estelle pressed her palm against the identification panel until the verification light came on, then pulled out her evaluation file as an external candidate. She flipped through the first three pages quickly: registration, evaluations over the years, current-term assessment. A red stamp marked the conclusion field: Competency passed.

At the back of the same file was an aged supporting document titled “Revocation and Isolation Attachment.” A line of red text was printed across the top: ‘This document is not to be shown to candidates. Controlled Inner Circle material.’

That morning at the disaster recovery station, the abandoned system had extracted the biological features from the palm of this body’s left hand and mapped them to the account of the “White Tower Chief of Security” in the old disaster recovery archive. The White Tower’s internal data network had always been

connected to this physical machine room beneath the chapel. When she pressed that hand against the identification panel, the backdoor permissions of that high-level seat were briefly brought in, forcibly bypassing the local controlled archive’s restriction and pulling up the attachment she was never supposed to see.
The attachment had red lines drawn across it.
“‘Two. Anyone who obtains materials other than their own file through non-procedural means will have their candidate status revoked.’” She traced the line with her finger. “That’s
why I accessed my own file today in my own name. It cleanly avoided the boundary set by clause two. They can’t use this outdated clause to take back the seat I just obtained.”
Her finger moved downward.
“But the next clause is something you can’t evade, whether you’ve been formally selected or not: ‘Three. Anyone who publicly challenges an effective unified statement will be isolated.’”
She turned to look at me. We both knew that if she continued looking, the candidate seat that had been secure could still be taken from her in another, harsher way.

“If I do more than access Yuna’s data—if I throw it out at the hearing and use it to oppose the Inner Circle’s account—then that moment will be defined as a public challenge,” she said. “It will directly trigger the ‘isolation’ in clause three.”
“That’s a blade hanging over your head. Do you want to stop?”
“No.”
She pulled her black register toward her and picked up her pen. In the subject field, she wrote ‘self’ with heavy strokes.

Controlled archive. Accessed: current-term external candidate file. Subject: self.
Procedural assessment: competency passed.
Access risk attachment record: subject has been selected, and the subject of this access is the subject’s own

file; clause two not triggered. The next inquiry has a very high probability of triggering clause three, “isolation.”
Procedural assessment and political designation may be recorded simultaneously. No conclusion entered on this page.
Once the ink had dried, she closed the register and kicked this deadlock heavily back to the institution.
After leaving the archive, she did not return to her quarters. She went straight to the White Tower.
“We’ve checked the perimeter and stored the source records,” I said from behind her. “What else is there?”
“One thing of my own.”
She stopped outside the candidate training room, her hand resting on the cold doorknob.
“Come in.”
I followed her into the training room. The door clicked shut behind us.

She opened the cabinet and took out a sheet of stationery. With her back to me, she wrote a line. Folded it. Dripped purple-red sealing wax onto it. Then she took a dry grass stem she had casually snapped off along the way from her pocket and pressed it heavily into the drop of wax.
The grass stem was crushed, leaving a complex, disorderly seal on the wax, printed with countless minute fibers. She locked the envelope in the drawer.
“What are you doing?”
“I know that system isn’t an all-purpose toy for reading and writing.”

She looked at me, her gaze hard.
“The system can use only an entire past life to construct a new original. If something happens in the future, and someone tries to use the old-version data to construct a new me, then have the institution erase and replace the

living person I am—this is the anchor used to verify me. A successor newly made could never know what the present me wrote inside it. If they want the successor to replace me, they’ll have to unlock it early, open the envelope, and memorize the answer inside.”

“You can’t prevent them from replacing it.” I looked at the drawer. “They don’t need to restore it to its original state. Once they open it, they can drip on new sealing wax, press some random object into it again, and confidently claim that the new mark is the original.”
“I know. That’s why I need not only this irreproducible mark, but also someone who watches it come into being.” She turned and looked into my eyes.
“I did this in front of you deliberately, because you’re the person in the system most capable of obtaining the data and creating that ‘new piece.’”
“If one day you decide to cooperate with them, use the old data to create a version of me, and replace this troublesome me, you can help them switch the envelope and make a new mark.
But when that confrontation between the real and the false comes, when you watch me produce an entirely different account and accuse someone of replacing the sealing wax in the drawer—”

She stepped closer.
“Even if no one believes the wax was replaced, you yourself will know perfectly well that the one being held down and executed is the living person who crushed
that grass stem in front of you today. What I want is to make it impossible for you to deceive yourself with ‘the system is flawless.’ You will know clearly that you killed me.”

The corridor was very quiet. She had relied on neither the system nor any anti-counterfeiting device. With a random grass-stem mark, she had pinned the guilt of replacement firmly to me, the person most likely to become the “creator.” This was her defense of the self that existed now.

I thought of the Yunas packed into the records across different branches. Watching Estelle’s back as she left, I suddenly began to feel afraid. Afraid that if Yuna woke up, she would come to me for the account concerning her own life.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:title: Page Nine
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s2-1:
One-time write authorization · Front page (written and archived by the author; this document does not cross worlds with the source):
“Authorizing party: Estelle. External candidate.
Authorization: My complete
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s2-2:
life record up to today, to be written once into another world in the future.
Number of times: One. No renewal.
This document consists of nine pages. Sign each page separately. Unsigned pages are invalid.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s6-1: Yesterday, in the candidate rehearsal room at the White Tower, when I was stopped outside the door and heard her press marks into a piece of roadside grass she had snapped off at random, then seal the twelve candidate marker cards, I
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s6-2: knew we were running out of time. But that defense, based only on cross-checking random facts, could do no more than pin the suspicion of a switch on me. As long as we established no new source record, the originals would remain safe.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s7-1: But today, with the establishment of the new source record, the future version of her would possess the latest memories up to this moment. The memory of the old sealing wax alone would no longer distinguish whether it belonged to her as she was now, or to her after waking in the future.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s8-1: So at 9:35 this morning, before we examined the old files, she put a new defense in place. She not only sealed the twelve black and white marker cards, the Watermarsh purple line, and the candidate wax, but also used an
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s8-2: anti-narrative seal and an evidence checklist with a markedly longer objection column to establish the boundaries of same-day authorization, then made me perform an active confirmation. I understood then that she was doing this
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s8-3: not only to guard against me, but also to confirm that the machine would not infer her identity. That was the boundary of our same-day authorization. Its third item was the one she insisted on—the witness zone for bodily rights.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s9-1: Once this system took effect, we went in the afternoon to the cultivation facility beneath the Enlightenment District. We called up a precise artificial body template and injected the anonymous capacity the system had just thawed
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s9-2: and released. In the experiment later confirmed to have produced a blank new-born, the infant, carrying no autobiographical memories at all, woke at 15:20. She shivered from hypothermia, but after a few minutes instinctively

texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s10-1: The result was cruel. She understood neither light nor sound, and even less of me.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s11-1: “She isn’t Yuna.” Estelle raised the temperature and wrapped the trembling body tightly in a blanket. “She isn’t a failed vessel, either.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s12-1: I stood outside the glass, both hands clamped hard against the console. “This is the only path I have left. If I don’t do it, I’ll never be able to convince myself I’ve reached the end.”

texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s14-1: I did not argue. It was a trespass I could not wash away.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s15-1: The tiny body let out an indistinct cry and clutched tightly at Estelle’s sleeve.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s16-1: “But I crossed the line too.” Estelle lowered her gaze and gently supported that hand. “Together, we created a living infant whom we’ll have to face Sera’s questioning about tomorrow, and whom someone will have to teach
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s16-2: about this world. Once a first person appears, she is no longer test material but a rights-bearing subject. She must never be given a name, and she must never be subjected to any harmful test meant to verify familiarity.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s17-1: Estelle’s voice grew cold, but the hand supporting that small one remained steady. “You cannot be the only one caring for her. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s17-2: another one on the grounds that the sample is insufficient. The life we created in this world is this world’s responsibility to the end. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s18-1: Carrying that weight, we did not return to the old room containing the scanning frame in the AI laboratory until 20:10 that night.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s19-1: When we came to examine Lysenko’s old files during the day, we had not even touched the frame in the center of the room. But now, she pushed the door open herself.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s20-1: The scanning frame stood quietly in the center, its ring-shaped structure gleaming with a cold metallic light. After trying twice, she still could not find an angle where it would rest securely.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s25-1: “Give me your coat.” She turned her head, her tone flat, without complaining about the roughness of the old equipment.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s26-1: I took off my coat and handed it over. She deftly folded it into three and placed it between the back of her head and the metal headrest. Only then could she lean back securely.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s28-1: “If the dimensions don’t fit, forget it. There’s no need to force it. This machine’s identity verification only recognizes Lysenko’s voiceprint and neural characteristics. You have no chance of registering as the official source.”

texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s30-2: to bypass cumbersome audits. I’ll cut the system’s safety-detection circuit and implant an abnormal pulse signal. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s30-3: the subject’s complete state during the rescue period, package it as an appended data block from a driving accident record, and back it up to the channel. It did not repair, and it did not select.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s36-1: “Are you sure?” I looked down at her.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s38-1: “I know.” Her gaze was frighteningly calm.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s41-1: For those seventy minutes, I was like a statue, sitting on the folding chair by the door. In the middle, the old ceiling light began to flicker at regular intervals. When the light dimmed, her pale face sank into shadow;
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s41-2: when it brightened, her face surfaced again. The rigid posture forced by the support beneath her head was clearly uncomfortable, but I silently counted her breaths. There was not even a second of fluctuation or retreat.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s42-1: “As soon as the system determines that the rescue period has ended, or an error above the threshold appears during capture, it will classify the data as contaminated and forcibly terminate the process,” she had told me. “But until it stops, I can’t move.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s43-1: At the sixtieth minute, her fingers began to tremble faintly—the precursor to an instinctive spasm after prolonged muscular tension. Sweat ran down from her temples into the hollow
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s43-2: of her neck. I held my breath and watched the steady green capture line on the console. Until the final seconds of the seventieth minute, when the line jumped slightly upward.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s44-1: At that instant, a low buzzing sounded. The blue light of the sensing ring dimmed.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s45-1: A line of red underlying archival status appeared on the screen: “Severe Collapse Rescue Terminated · Appended Data Block Generated, Awaiting Mount.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s46-1: It was a complete state that had scraped past the tolerance limit. She did not take the hand I offered. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s48-1: “What time is it?” Her voice was terribly hoarse.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s51-1: She smoothed out my coat and handed it back to me. Then she pulled an extremely fine wire from inside her collar, pressed the sensing patch at its end behind her ear, and connected the other end back to the base interface glowing red.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s52-1: The prompt on the screen flickered once and changed to: “Physical Accident Tracking Mounted, Cross-World Synchronization Enabled.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s54-1: “The source record is established. As long as I keep wearing this, everything I experience from now until you leave will be continuously appended as the state of a continuous subject, and the cross-world channel will synchronize
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s54-2: it automatically.” She raised her head. “When we reached this building at noon, before you went in to look up the old files, I took the random-character slip from my coat pocket and put it in the fixed drawer in the corridor.”

texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s57-1: “I lay down in this machine only after locking that slip inside the drawer. What the characters are, and how I jammed the latch, are all in this record currently being made.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s62-1: On the dim rooftop, the stairwell door stood half open, casting a warm yellow strip of light.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s63-1: At the edge of the glow, she tore blank pages from her notebook and wrote rapidly. After filling all nine pages, she read them from beginning to end, then solemnly signed her name at the bottom of each page.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s66-1: The only thing I was responsible for checking was the six-point “Restrictions” section on the fourth page.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s68-1:
One. This black-box data does not disappear because of this backup. I continue to live in this world.
Two. The complete memory must be retained. Especially all of today’s anger and distrust, and the random seal stored here.
Three. The outer shell body has no voiceprint backdoor. No
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s68-2:
unverified source is accepted.
Four. This record may be loaded only once in the next world.
Five. The person who wakes will no longer possess Estelle’s name or any legal identity. She is an entirely new person.
Six. After waking, she does not need to testify for anyone, including Arno.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s70-1: I looked at those lines. Apart from the authorization statement on the front page, these six restrictions were all she allowed me to see.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s72-1: “The paper original can’t pass into the next world. It stays on this rooftop,” I reminded her.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s74-1: “I don’t need it to pass over.” She capped the pen. “The process of writing these words on this paper is all in that data. The system can only write the complete life
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s74-2: record as a whole. It can’t selectively remove anything. As long as the future me wakes with these memories, the restrictions on these pages will become her own boundary.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s75-1: The fifth point meant that the person who woke in the future would voluntarily give up every local candidate seat and all former family ties. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s78-1: She pointed to the words “random seal” in the second point.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s80-1: “I know that slip is meant to guard against me. In that world, she’ll remember this drawer and demand to check the characters on the paper against them.” I looked at her. “But that’s only the drawer here. That letter doesn’t exist in the other world.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s82-1: “She doesn’t need the letter to cross over. This isn’t merely a confrontation between memories. It’s a complete double-blind opening protocol established between two generations of
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s82-2: us.” She did not look up, her tone calm. “Once she’s there, she’ll write down the sequence from her memory, lock it in a physical package with a timestamp, and hand it to a local
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s82-3: third party. When you return here, you’ll smash open the old drawer, already jammed and impossible to tamper with before the slip was inserted, read the numbers on the card, and fix
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s82-4: them in your terminal with a timestamp. When you return there again, you and she will open and compare the final two records simultaneously, carrying the fixed time records with you.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s83-1: She continued, “As long as the characters match exactly, and her packaging time is earlier than the time you return here to obtain the answer, it creates a logical deadlock: what is in her mind truly came from this real
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s83-2: world today. I damaged the drawer’s structure, which means that even after learning the future answer, you can’t return to the present and replace the paper without leaving signs of forced entry. This not only proves the
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s83-3: record’s authenticity. It also rules out the possibility of fabricating an ‘obedient Estelle’ locally—because if you fabricated her, you could not have guessed this seal in advance and passed the timestamp comparison.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s85-1: She looked straight at me. “This is a tripwire. texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s88-1: She squared up the nine pages and folded them. I tried to see what was on the final page, but she had already tucked them neatly into the inner pocket of her clothes.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s90-1: “Point four. One time. No renewal.” Her cold gaze fixed on me. “The system has no technical lock making a single load the only possible one. If something goes wrong in the future and that new body dies, this authorization will have been used
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s90-2: up too. You absolutely cannot create another copy from the data just to save her. If you refuse to follow this, or force a write by bypassing the defenses, I won’t be able to stop you. This is only a source individual’s boundary and demand.”
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s92-1: “I understand.” I did not try to argue.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s97-1: “What about tomorrow here?” I looked at her.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s98-1: She remained silent, looking at the windows of the Enlightenment District below.
texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s100-1: “I know experiments like that had never succeeded before. If I hadn’t insisted that we couldn’t leave even the tiniest gap for tomorrow, there would never have been a new consciousness in that artificially

texts.chapter:v15-29a:event:text-s113-1: She braced both hands against the low ledge behind her and tilted her head back slightly. “I want to stand under that sky on my own two feet and truly look at it once. Even if there’s nothing there but barren permafrost.”

texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s57-1: Sera straightened herself again at the other end of the table. As she sat, she habitually rolled back her cuff. It was the gesture she made before taking up a pen.
texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s59-1: “I’ll give you a limited audit order.” She uncapped her pen as she spoke. “Three things: the contract explanation, the Disposition Index, and the Bodily Rights Witnessing Area. Go look below for yourself. When you’re done, come back and tell me what you saw.”
texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s65-1: “You want to investigate Maintenance Appendix Four, and you want to bring him along. Your application is cleanly written, but my system has a warning. That appendix is connected to a cross-world entity-generation back door.”

texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s76-1: “Someone took my name and wrote it onto a page I can’t see at all.”

texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s79-1: “I oversee this entire procedure for candidates. I’ve overseen it for twenty years. Whose body is disposed of under what conditions—that all goes through my signature.”
texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s81-1: “If what’s written on that page is that they can use your bodies however they please, then for twenty years I’ve been opening a back door for them.”
texts.chapter:v15-29b:event:text-s83-1: “I need to know where the bottom line is in this matter.”
