texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s32-2: chance to bargain, trading that machine for the lives of the living. I have no intention of watching yesterday’s trick—trading the preservation order for a shutdown—a second time. Everything has to be done today, in one motion.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s34-1: “Record: the proposing party refuses to split the motion.” Sera answered without expression and picked up her pen again.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s37-1: The witness and I sat in the two isolated iron chairs beside the long table, with one person’s space between us. These were the seats under scrutiny.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s38-1: Nona turned her head to look at us, her brow faintly furrowed.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s42-1: “This matter is for executing the two of you. Those to be executed must be present.” Sera answered without looking up.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s44-1: “Then I don’t want to hear them make excuses.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s46-1: “They cannot speak during the vote on this motion. By rule, when the seats vote on another person’s life or death, the parties concerned are forbidden from making a statement.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s47-1: Only then did Sera raise her eyes, pinning both of us with a sharp look.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s49-1: “You two, listen. Two words: shut up. Whatever is said at the table, do not answer. Do not ask questions.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s50-1: I looked at her and nodded.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s51-1: The witness twisted her hands tightly in front of her. Her knuckles had gone white with the effort. She lowered her head and drew herself completely into the iron chair.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s53-1: The silence over the long table was suffocating. I sat there listening as they began to take my life apart and weigh it.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s55-1: Nona cleared her throat and made the first attack.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s57-1: “Yesterday you held the connection rights to the operator’s seat, held the village in your grip, and traded for that preservation order. We gave ground to make you shut down and gave you seven votes. Now the Tower has stopped. There is nothing left in your hands to use against us.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s58-1: She spoke evenly, like someone reciting the settlement list for a transaction.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s60-1: “Those seven votes were the price of buying your shutdown yesterday. Now the shutdown is complete, and the transaction should be settled. Today I’m putting the chance to correct the mistake on this table and taking back those wrongly granted protections. That is fair.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s64-1: “I’ll add one thing. Yesterday’s sheet approved preserving that record. That is a deadly opening. From now on, anyone who wants to touch this deadly craft can point to it and say the elders once approved it. That door will never close again.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s66-1: “The half of the key in my hands is responsible for the bottom line. I will leave no precedent.” He rubbed the stubble on his chin.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s68-1: “I’m talking about reality.” Kane leaned forward.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s70-1: “This morning, people have already begun gathering in the outer labor district. Yesterday afternoon’s preservation-order broadcast let the entire outer district know that this boy not only failed to die inside the Tower, but was also protected by the
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s70-2: elders. The labor district’s awe of the White Tower’s certain death is already crumbling, and everyone outside is guessing what happened. Order is about to collapse. Only two bodies can reestablish this rule and suppress what people outside are thinking.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s74-1: Sera listened quietly, then set the tip of her pen firmly onto the case file.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s76-1: “Before the vote, I need to make one thing clear. Revoking the preservation order is only words. The other two matters require specific people to carry them out.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s78-1: “That record was transported into the lower isolation zone in the remote outskirts yesterday afternoon under the preservation order. It was secured with a mechanical lock and a joint key held by three seats.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s80-1: “Nona, then let me ask you: once the vote passes, who will retrieve the keys from Kane and Otto? Who will open the door? Who will supervise its return?”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s81-1: Nona had not expected to be pressed so directly. She fell silent for a moment.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s83-1: “You collect them. You’re on duty. You should be the one to handle it.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s85-1: “I am only responsible for unsealing and registering it. But once it is retrieved, the restoration core has to be thrown into the high-pressure furnace and burned completely, without leaving even ash. Who will take that final step?”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s90-1: Sera did not object. She really recorded it. The pen pressed hard against the rough paper as she scratched out a line.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s91-1: At those words, the witness’s shoulders suddenly contracted. Sitting in the solitary iron chair, I dug my fingernails into my palm. They were not discussing an object. They
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s91-2: were discussing Yuna. The box contained the whole of her life, frozen in place, and they were assigning, as a matter of routine across the tabletop, who would turn her into ash.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s93-1: “The third clause is the same. Two living people are to be executed on the spot. Who will do it?” she continued without looking up.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s95-1: “My people. I’ll handle it cleanly.” Kane’s gaze swept over us.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s96-1: The witness bit down hard on her lip and curled deeper into the iron chair. The scrape on her elbow from yesterday had already crusted over. The dried thread of blood stood out sharply along the edge of her arms, still twisted tightly together in front of her.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s97-1: We were pinned in place, unable to make a sound.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s103-1: “It is past eight fifteen. The vote begins now. All reasons will be entered in the register.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s105-1: “In favor. Yesterday you insisted on crossing the boundary. Today this opening has to be stitched shut.” Nona spoke first.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s107-1: “In favor. To close off the precedent.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s109-1: “In favor. Better to finish it before something changes.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s110-1: Sera lowered her head and rapidly recorded three lines. Those were the three cards they held. They did not even need to exchange glances.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s115-1: Otto’s dry voice sounded in the silence. Slowly, he closed the ledger in his hands and looked straight at Nona with cloudy eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s117-1: “Sera has already entered those two lines in the register. Everyone, think through the exact process here. Kane kills the people. Kane burns the object.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s119-1: “He could simply keep the restoration core and report back that everything had been destroyed. Once everyone is dead, there would not even be a witness—complete death without evidence. Nona,
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s119-2: you would be handing the elders’ only remaining technical asset to Kane with both hands and letting him keep it for himself. When that day comes, what would this place have left to restrain him?”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s121-1: “I act within my office. Don’t drag this somewhere else, Otto.” Kane cut him off coldly.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s123-1: “I have no intention of accusing you of what you might do. But this would create a fact without any restraint. I’m old. I don’t want to see that day.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s127-1: “Opposed.” Galon sat there, his voice like muffled thunder. “My workshop cannot become a knife for secret killings.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s130-1: There was no unnecessary talk in the morning wind.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s132-1: “Opposed.” Merlu swept her cold gaze over Nona. “No matter how you look at him, on paper he is still a registered candidate. The candidate-status hearing hasn’t even begun, and you want to bypass the process and close the case with an execution that leaves no witnesses?”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s134-1: “Opposed.” Chico interlaced his fingers and stared at the grain of the long table. He offered no further explanation. He only pushed the deployment map of the remote perimeter inward from beside his hand—if Kane’s people were allowed to enter the remote isolation zone
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s134-2: openly under the name of “secret destruction,” and could even bypass the records to erase all traces, then the outer perimeter under his control would no longer be his to command. It would become the defense force’s backyard, ready for them to take over at any time.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s136-1: “Opposed. I won’t sign.” Toma pushed his pen away.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s137-1: Each time an opposed vote fell, the atmosphere around the long table hardened another degree. It was not that seven people had suddenly joined forces to save us. They were seven accounts that could not be made to balance. In this deadlock without a gap, each of them—out
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s137-2: of concern for the files in their hands, the outer perimeter, the workshop, or even the fear that Kane would monopolize the power of execution—slammed yesterday’s boundary back onto the table exactly as it had been drawn. The opposed votes reached five in an instant.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s142-1: Rena’s voice finally sounded, rigid and cold. She sat there with a face as still as a calm lake. Yesterday, she had used those words to buy my shutdown. Today, sitting in the same place, the same words stopped an execution.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s144-1: The sixth opposed vote ended the suspense immediately.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s145-1: I lowered my head. The dark green old canvas strap she had once used to tie me to her back while escaping the lower levels had long since left my possession, but I still instinctively touched my waist.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s146-1: There was no exultation at escaping death. Only a nauseating sense of weightlessness. Through the suffocating thirty minutes this morning, we had sat here watching ourselves
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s146-2: cut apart and weighed on this table as an asset or a liability, handled as official business. No one had truly fought to save us. What saved us were seven other kinds of fear.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s149-1: “I oppose.” Sera set down her pen and delivered the final statement.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s151-1: “The reason is simple. Once the preservation order is in effect, and before its term has expired, forcibly destroying the record and executing living people would be to smash the elders’ own monument. I, Sera, will not do that.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s154-1: She stacked the two sheets covered in writing neatly in front of her.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s158-1: “Seven opposed. This matter does not pass. By rule, once a bundled motion is rejected, its clauses may not be split and resubmitted on the same day. Today’s hearing is concluded. Meeting adjourned.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s162-1: The people in front of the long table gradually dispersed. The rising sun had just cleared the gray rooftops. Its light was glaring, but carried no warmth.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s163-1: I remained seated where I was.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s164-1: The witness let out a deep breath. Her tightly clenched hands finally loosened, leaving deep red marks in her palms from her nails. She abruptly buried her face in her hands, her shoulders shaking silently a
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s164-2: few times. Then she turned toward me and looked at me in exhaustion, as if she had just been pulled from the water. I looked back at her and could clearly hear the heavy beating of my own heart inside my chest.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s165-1: Sera organized the case files and slipped several sheets into a kraft-paper envelope.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s166-1: “Have someone tell Estelle,” she said to a Boundary Guard some distance away. “This one is withdrawn. Tell her to close the book and get some sleep.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s167-1: The Boundary Guard acknowledged the order and ran off. Only then did Sera come around from behind the long table and stand silently in front of me. The sunlight cast her long shadow over me.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s168-1: We looked at each other in silence for a while. She seemed to be deliberately waiting for our breathing to settle.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s172-1: “Wash your face. We leave at exactly nine. The location is the production-line control room. You, the witness, and me.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s173-1: I stood up from the iron chair. My legs were a little numb.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s174-1: She looked down at me for one second.
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s176-1: “You no longer have to follow the ‘shut up’ rule. This matter is over. You’re no longer in the column for execution. You can speak.”
texts.chapter:v15-30a:event:text-s178-1: “Nine.” I looked into her eyes. “We’ll be there on time.”
texts.chapter:chapter-30-awakening:title: Chapter Thirty: Waking
texts.chapter:chapter-30-awakening:event:text-: Yesterday at noon, within the only half-hour export window, we extracted all of her personality data. The extraction stripped away only redundant logs from the system shell and records left by the administrator’s

forced intervention in the system environment. The machine’s “wrapping paper” was peeled away, but nothing inside it had been touched—not a single part of the human core: any life she had lived as a living

person, even the hundreds of mutually conflicting endings. They were preserved word for word, completely offline before shutdown last night, sealed inside a physical case as the sole read-only restoration core.

But before the infusion could formally begin, this as-yet-unmaterialized carrier template, along with the vacant production chamber about to bring it into being, had to be checked to ensure that no control backdoors had been implanted in the physiological parameters or connection hardware. Once the infusion began, the template would become living flesh, and there would be no undoing it.

The parameter console was at the deepest point of the AI laboratory’s production-line area. Outside Estelle compared the production entries in the bottom ledger one by one against the hardware scanning grid on the side of the sleep chamber. The target column held the number of this design prototype, written neatly. The name column contained a rigid horizontal line.
“The ledger matches the hardware. Nothing was added. No backdoor,” she said. Her voice sounded dry in the empty room.

She raised her head and went back through the old global parameters. Her finger stopped at the edge of one page, where a cross-shaped seal marked “sealed” had been affixed. She picked at the seal with the tip of her pen and unfolded the supplementary page beneath it.

The page opened. It was a control scheme proposed three years ago by Otto of the risk seat, intended to implant neural-drug dependence in high-risk carriers. But in the countersignature column of the bottom ledger, the handwriting had been forced in sideways, the pen pressed down hard:
“Technical feasibility does not mean it should be carried out. Do not send it into the production queue. —Garon”

Outside Estelle looked at the signature Garon had left behind, then lowered her eyes to the special-authorization column on Yuna’s page: direct hardware backdoor canceled; voiceprint forced-sensing module

canceled. At the very bottom was the poison scheme her master had kept off the production line—the one the risk seat had given the deeply misleading name “non-addictive regulator” in the formal records.

She quickly crossed out the abandoned line in the ledger, copied the clean parameter list before her into a memorandum, and drove the final possible physiological backdoor firmly into the record so no one could make an issue of it. She closed the book and turned around.
“Let’s go. To the control room.”

The air-conditioning in the control room was turned up high. Sera, wearing a supervisor’s armband, stood in the corner. Under the safeguards agreed upon before shutdown, the supervisor’s seat was not to touch the console, only to watch us and ensure that the site complied with “division of authority.” Local

Estelle, who had been responsible for checking the data item by item yesterday, was absent today—the verifier could not also be the writer, lest the data be switched by the same person between the two procedures. The ones standing before the console to perform the final infusion were Outside Estelle and me.

Just half an hour ago, under the joint watch of the witness and the supervisor’s seat, we had used a joint key to retrieve the read-only record from the quarantine zone in the outskirts. Now the heavy restoration core lay quietly in the metal slot. Sera stepped forward and checked the outer seal bearing Otto’s sole signature.

After confirming that it was intact, she returned to her place. The single-read circuit had been connected. Once the reading was complete, the circuit would physically burn out. That meant the case containing every ending of her past would become unusable from that point on, no longer available as a fallback for any replication.
Outside Estelle opened the manual.
“Confirmation and execution must be assigned to two operators.” She stared at the manual, her voice stern. “I read, you press. No one does anything extra on impulse.”
She read out one instruction, and I answered loudly with “Present,” then pressed the corresponding key.

The main slot slowly closed with the heavy sound of mechanical hydraulics, locking shut without a seam.
The read-only restoration core began infusing in full into the body that had just finished forming.

The indicator lights on the console panel jumped from line to line. Pale green lettering appeared in sequence across four items:
Source: true.
Coverage: continuous.
End record: closed.
Entire record written: unaltered.

Immediately afterward, a separate hardware screen beside it lit up, monitoring the physical readings at the bottom of the main slot. To give this empty shell real mass in this world, the energy injected into the slot was condensing in large

quantities into particles at the physical layer. The indicators on the screen jumped. When they finally settled at the mark representing a full quota, a single-person physical carrier that had originally been only a design prototype was ready.

The hardware was in place. The first-person perspective that followed would be forcibly anchored by the soul-field capacity supplied by the AI laboratory. Ten thousand standard units of anonymous capacity was far too much to support an empty physical shell.

Yet the name column was still blank. The soul field could not identify its owner by name. It could only be forced into the body like water poured into a vessel as the writing procedure advanced. Once the anchor was established, the hundreds of unabridged

life records in the restoration core—the real information accumulated from a shared morning onward—would pour through the single perspective that had just been opened, shaping that vast, faceless capacity and pulling her back into the world of the living.
The hydraulic chamber door slowly opened. Beneath the white membrane, something rose and fell, almost imperceptibly.

At first, the rhythm was slow enough to make anyone despair—slower than a sleeping person’s, with only a trace more life than the dead. I gripped the cold edge of the transfer slot. Outside Estelle came over and pressed her hand hard against my forearm, using its weight to hold down my trembling, which was close to breaking.

Then the rhythm changed.
One beat faster. Then another.
The sound of breathing gradually grew clear, settling little by little into the rhythm of a living person.
Her lashes trembled faintly. Then both ears shook softly open in the cold air.
She opened her eyes.

Amber struck my vision in that instant. The familiar point of light rested quietly in the depths of her pupils. She stared blankly at the harsh searchlight overhead, her gaze lingering there for a full second.

Then she braced herself against the edge of the transfer slot and slowly sat up. The moment she rose, she suddenly arched her back and dug both hands into the metal edge. Her chest heaved violently, sawing breaths forced through clenched teeth. The final deaths of hundreds of different worlds were forced

into this newly awakened body at the same time, making her whole body convulse violently. She pressed herself hard against the metal rim, as if trying to crush down all the phantom pain of severed limbs, the sensation of suffocation, and the illusion of splintering bones that did not belong to this moment.

She closed her eyes, the knuckles of her fingers turning white from the strain. More than a full minute passed before the deathlike convulsions gradually receded from her back. But she did not raise her head at once. Her breathing was still rough, both hands still braced at her sides, as if she were forcibly sorting out the

tangled threads in her mind. Beads of sweat rolled from her forehead and struck the metal rim. Several full minutes passed before the chaos that seemed ready to tear her body apart was finally pressed into place by force. She slid weakly against the chamber wall, let out a long breath, and then slowly turned her head to look at me.
Her dry lips moved.
“What happened afterward?”
Her vocal cords had only just formed, making her voice rasp like sandpaper, but the utterly calm tone came through without hesitation.
“After I died…” Yuna stared at me. “What happened afterward?”

I stood beside the hydraulic slot, looking into her eyes. No greetings. No tears. Outside Estelle took a clean windbreaker from beside her, draped it over Yuna’s faintly trembling shoulders, and handed her a cup of warm water. Yuna accepted it, holding the cup in both hands without drinking.

I told her everything that had happened after her death: yesterday morning, the accident-record seat checked the time and confirmed her death, after which we stripped the records and exported her life data without alteration; yesterday afternoon,

Outside Estelle submitted the shutdown request and burned out the coupling core of the root machine; by eight fifteen this morning, the Abrogation Proposal had failed its vote; then, at ten ten, this body began the restoration infusion.
Yuna listened as I finished reporting the long account. Her gaze shifted slightly only when she heard “the Abrogation Proposal collapsed.” Then she closed her eyes, tapping the side of the cup

once, then once again with her finger.
Then her brow furrowed slightly, as if she were struggling to sort through hundreds of timelines playing simultaneously and separate out the final thread.

“I’m missing thirty-one hours… no, more precisely, thirty-one hours and ten minutes.” She opened her eyes again, her gaze calm, fatigue from the long computation visible in their depths. “Starting from that morning, the last point at which the final one

of these three hundred life records reached its end was three in the morning yesterday, when I was killed at the edge of Watermarsh. After that, I have no new records until the infusion began in this body at ten ten this morning. The timeline matches.”

Just then, out of habit, she raised her right hand toward her left wrist.
Her fingers slid once over the newly formed pale skin. They found nothing. She froze for a moment, looking at her bare wrist.
“My band from the final one didn’t come with me,” she said quietly.
“I wore it for five years in the mining district of that final cycle. The edges had started to fray.” The corner of her mouth pulled wryly. “I thought it would grow on my wrist.”
The old band that had accompanied her for five years in her final life, like the hundreds before it, had all been left on the other side of the daylight and had not come over with
the data. Since yesterday morning, in addition to my father’s old dark-green tool belt, I had worn another newly woven dark-red cloth band around my waist. I had found material
of the same color in the local supply store and woven it by hand, guided by the color I remembered her wearing countless times. Its edges were still new, without a trace of wear.
I untied the dark-red band from my waist. I took her pale, newly made left hand, wrapped it around her wrist, and tightened it. Two loops. Fastened.
“You said so.” I looked at her. “That someday, even with both hands empty, I still had to give you back exactly the feeling of this tightening around your wrist.”

She lowered her head and gently rubbed the band’s new edge with her thumb. It was only a handmade strip of cloth, incapable of giving this numbered carrier a legal name. But her tense shoulders finally loosened by a fraction, and she lowered her head to take a small sip of warm water.
“The case used to bring me back.” Yuna suddenly raised her head and looked at me. “Who was the other operator?”

She was not asking about the infusion just now, but about the extraction that had taken her data out of the machine yesterday.
She had walked through death and awakened only to check whether her life had fallen into unreliable hands.
“I performed the extraction. Local Estelle checked each item. The witness was Outside Estelle, standing here now.”
Yuna’s gaze swept toward Sera in the corner.
“Sera supervised the infusion procedure just now. She watched the process, and her final signature was ‘non-operator.’ She was not present when the data was exported.”
Yuna tilted her head slightly and drew her gaze back. Her breathing eased a little.
At the console in the control room, Outside Estelle closed the manual, pulled the cap from her pen, and wrote down the time Yuna began speaking again.

“Six safeguard orders, remaining in force until the future restoration completes its first statement before the seat.” Outside Estelle looked toward Sera in the corner. “She has just checked the time of her death against the shutdown time and completed an independent comparison. But that proves

only that she can speak. A true statement before the seat is for her to give a complete testimony herself at the upcoming special hearing, where the records seat will enter it into the official archives. Until that formal procedure is brought to a close, the safeguard orders remain in force.”

The six orders protected the restoration core from destruction, protected the writing procedure, and protected me, Local Estelle, Yuna, and Outside Estelle, as the witness, from private interrogation and execution. During the time covered by

that protection, Yuna had returned. Once the hearing began and she completed her statement before the seat, the force of the document would vanish immediately. After that, the political backlash and purge aimed at the seat would fall again.
Outside Estelle replaced the cap on her pen. These few short exchanges were recalibrating Yuna’s sense of time.
“I have one more thing to ask.” Her throat moved once.
“Go ahead.”
“There was one branch.” She stared at the ceiling, her voice still even. “I said, ‘I’m not going.’ ‘I don’t want to die in there.’”
“Present.” I looked at her and answered with certainty.
“You heard all of it?”
“I heard it.”
“Not a single one missing?”
“All the hundreds of life fragments are in there. Not a single one missing.”
The system’s complete-life-record channel permits only whole-record writing. If you bring someone back, you have to bring back everything good and bad in her.
“Even that one.” I looked directly into her amber eyes.
“Even that one.” She repeated it.
She was quiet for a while, her gaze lowered to the newly formed pale skin over her knees. After several seconds, she raised her head again.
“Good,” she said.
Her voice was flat, without the slightest rise or fall.
“The me on that branch is me too.”
“Did you ever think about reaching out?” She suddenly turned her head.
“What?”
“It can only be written in full, right? Did you ever, even for an instant, think about forcibly splitting it apart and erasing something?”
“Yes.”
“What did you want to erase?”
“The one I wanted to erase wasn’t the one where I said, ‘I’m not going.’” I drew a deep breath. “There was a dead loop. I didn’t go to the wheat field to find you.”
The control room was so quiet that only the instruments’ faint hum could be heard.
“I know.”
She accepted the words calmly, filling in the afternoon I had not been present for at all.

“That day, I wrote slips for three people in the prayer room, went home for lunch, then went alone to the edge of the wheat field. I took that wooden tablet from inside my coat, looked at it, then put it away again. Because that morning, you hadn’t given me the pen and pigments I needed for copying.”
My throat tightened. I had not gone, but the memory in her mind had preserved everything that happened that day with perfect clarity.
“I held that blank tablet, sat there for about an hour, and then went home.”
“There was wind that day.”
My breathing stopped abruptly for a moment.
“Coming from the west.” Her gaze grew distant. “It drove the wheat down in waves. I sat there, wondering if you were sick today.”
Her eyes returned to the ceiling.
“I thought of three possibilities. First, you were sick. Second, the elders had detained you. Third, you didn’t want to come.”
She turned her head and looked straight into my eyes.
“I put the third one last.”
“As long as I admitted you had changed, I wouldn’t have to worry that something had happened to you. But I still put it last.”
It felt as if someone had struck me hard. I could not get out half a word.
“I sat there for an hour, sorted through the three, stood up, and went home. On the way home, I thought: if he comes tomorrow, I’ll ask him.”
The corner of her mouth pulled into the faintest curve.
“But that version of me reached the end of its loop,” she said. “There was no tomorrow.”
I was still standing beside the hydraulic slot, looking at her shoulders trembling faintly beneath the windbreaker. I could not get out half a word.
“It matches.” She looked at me, then suddenly smiled.

Her lips were still pale, cold sweat still beaded at her temples, but the smile appeared plainly on her face.
Her left hand, wrapped in the new dark-red cloth band, still gripped the cup of water tightly.
“It’s all there.” Her voice was light as paper, but still steady. “They’re all here.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:title: Appendix to Chapter Thirty: Item Closed
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s1-1:
Observation Record · Annotation on an Old Page (in Estelle’s hand):
“Item closed: subject present.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s4-1: That first afternoon after waking, Yuna spent most of the time sitting quietly. Her new body was operating perfectly, while she struggled to bear the intangible things surging in like a breached
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s4-2: dam. Hundreds of “todays,” countless broken mornings and dusks, and death after death in different forms—all had to be forcibly compressed into her consciousness within those few short hours.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s5-1: I sat across from her, watching her whole body sink into an utterly exhausting struggle. She had to grip the edge of the chair, her knuckles paling to a sickly blue. At times, she would suddenly tremble violently, as if
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s5-2: experiencing one particular death by freezing in the depths of winter; at others, her breathing would quicken as though she were suffocating. I could only watch from the side, unable to take even a second of that weight from her.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s6-1: Only after her breathing gradually settled did she release her stiffened fingers. Her forehead was covered in fine beads of cold sweat.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s8-1: “The heaviest part isn’t death,” she said hoarsely after a long while. “I’ve practiced death until I’m used to it. The pain ends once you get through it.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s9-1: She raised her reddened eyes and looked at me quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s11-1: “The heaviest part is—I remember what happened on every page now, but I can never go back to any of them. Everyone who was left behind remains there.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s13-1: “I’m like you were before. So this is what you’ve been carrying all along.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s15-1: She didn’t cry. After saying that, she fell silent again for a moment. Then she reached out and made a gesture asking me for something.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s17-1: “Give it here,” she said. “I smelled it. I could smell what was in your pocket from the moment you came through the door.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s19-1: I reached into my pocket and took out the new-wheat cake. It had been tucked away for so long that it was completely cold. The sugar was wrapped separately in a small paper packet.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s21-1: “I already tried a bite for you.” I handed her the cake.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s25-1: “Now I’ll try it myself.” She took it, carefully broke off a tiny corner, dipped it in sugar, and put it in her mouth, chewing slowly. As she chewed, her eyes narrowed slightly. Her pointed ears sank little by little, finally settling into a soft curve of complete defenselessness.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s27-1: “It’s cold,” she judged. “And a little hard.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s31-1: “This is the best bite I’ve ever eaten in my life,” she said seriously. “Write it down.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s34-1: She carefully wrapped up most of the remaining cake and placed it on her knees.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s36-1: “You just told me what happened afterward. You said that according to the duration recorded in the local system logs, only a little over a day had passed from when I left until now.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s38-1: “Exporting the restored core, the preservation hearing yesterday afternoon, and this morning’s motion to void the agreement took only a day or two altogether.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s40-1: “But you yourself spent several months inside the machine.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s43-1: That was different from everything else she had checked today. What time it was, what day it was, whether a key had been pressed incorrectly—there were system logs to reconcile all of that against. But for those extra months, I was the only person who had stayed connected from beginning to end.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s45-1: “What did you do with all that time?”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s48-1: I had meant to fill that blank by listing all the errands: finding people to audit the records, checking the seals over and over… I did start, but halfway through I could hear the wrongness myself—the work had really been done, but it wasn’t the true “content” of those months.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s50-1: “What remained was calculation.” I stopped the meaningless listing and told her the truth.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s52-1: “Before shutdown, in the hundreds of worlds that kept switching back and forth between this morning and late night, I had to calculate during those fourteen hours in each one how much was still missing before the conditions for bringing you back were met.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s54-1: “Once I’d finished calculating, I kept waiting for the next world’s eight o’clock sharp.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s57-1: After hearing that, she was quiet for a while, as if trying to take in this day-after-day emptiness.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s59-1: “Did you ever calculate how many more switches there would have to be?”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s61-1: “I did. I calculated it many times during the first few dozen.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s63-1: “Then I stopped. The number was uncertain every time I calculated it. In the end, I realized that calculation itself had already become unbearable.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s64-1: She nodded, as if putting this line neatly in its place too.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s68-1: “If you can’t verify a number, don’t calculate it every day. That’s what you taught me before.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s71-1: After saying that, she unconsciously rested her right hand on her left wrist.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s72-1: It was her old habit. Whenever she used to think, the clasp would turn beneath her fingertips, from the outside inward, until she no longer noticed the small movement herself.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s73-1: Her fingers touched the reddish-brown strap. Yesterday morning, I had found matching material in the local supply store and rewoven it inch by inch from memory. When she woke this morning, I had tied it around her left wrist.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s74-1: Her fingertips rubbed along the edge of the new strap. Since this was a new body, there was no faint mark on her wrist from years of wearing one. The strap had an ordinary
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s74-2: new clasp now, no longer the old metal piece that had worn a hard callus into her fingertip. Tied around her wrist, it hung a little loose, like something borrowed.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s78-1: “The old strap stayed over there. It didn’t come over with me.” She touched the smooth new weave and spoke softly. “My body is new too. In this world, neither the days of the past nor the things on my hands have a place yet.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s79-1: I looked at the familiar reddish-brown strip around her wrist.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s81-1: “You want to find it a place.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s83-1: “The new strap was woven by you. Putting it back on doesn’t change anything.” She corrected me. “We have to do something new in this world.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s86-1: She raised her head and looked at me.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s88-1: “I owe you its origin,” she said. “Before, I never told you how this strap originally came to be. Now I can tell you myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s92-1: “The original strap was a brand-new reddish-brown military woven band I found when I was six. It probably fell from some Inner Circle transport vehicle’s supplies.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s96-1: “I turned it in as contraband,” I picked up her words.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s97-1: She folded her hands and looked into my eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s99-1: “Mm. But later you helped me keep it hidden and let me steal it back from the archives.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s101-1: “That day, you tied it around my wrist yourself.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s105-1: “That was the first time you owned something of your own.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s107-1: “Yes. With half a pencil, I wrote two names side by side on the inside.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s113-1: “I watched you write them with that half-pencil.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s116-1: She looked at the wrist where she wore the new strap. The new skin, free of the old pressure marks, looked somewhat thin.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s118-1: “Too bad it was always an item of unknown origin.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s121-1: She turned her left wrist over and held it flat in the air between us. The newly woven strap looked somewhat loose around her slender wrist.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s124-1: “But now it’s time. Today, in a world with no records of our past, we’ll fill in the names ourselves,” she declared.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s127-1: I reached out, my fingertip landing on a spot in the middle of the new strap. The weave there was still smooth, without a trace of wear.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s128-1: We didn’t have a half-pencil like the one we’d had back then. But I still used my fingertip to write the two names stroke by stroke in the air over the new fabric. This was no longer something meant for the village archives. It needed no ink left behind as proof, and no one else’s acknowledgment.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s130-1: “‘Yuna,’” I said, speaking the name I had just written.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s131-1: She lowered her head and looked at the fabric. Then she extended a finger and traced a few strokes in the air beside “Yuna.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s133-1: “And ‘Arno,’” she said softly. “Just like back then.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s136-1: After writing the names, she raised her head. This time, she didn’t hide behind analysis or conclusions as she had before, but there was a faint tremor in her voice, rare for her.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s139-1: Among the countless parallel memories she had reclaimed, perhaps one version of her on some route had already expressed her feelings. But in this new world where we had nothing, under both our gazes, this was the first time since waking that she had said it so plainly. No excuse, no qualification.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s143-1: It was as if she had finally let out a breath she had been holding for a long time. Her pointed ears gave an almost imperceptible twitch, and her tense shoulders relaxed.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s145-1: “When I was inside the door, I thought I was going to die. I wanted to say it, but…” She bit her lip. “I was afraid you’d go soft when you heard it, let go, and reach for me.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s147-1: “I was afraid too. If I said it in the corridor, I was afraid I wouldn’t be able to press that button.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s148-1: Her eyes reddened slightly, but the curve at the corners of her mouth could no longer be hidden.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s150-1: “Luckily,” she said softly. “It isn’t too late to say it now.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s152-1: We sat quietly like that for a while. In this new world with neither our past nor any place for us, the two names traced in the air by our fingers became the
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s152-2: only anchor between us. In that brief moment, there were no numbers that needed to be checked in a hurry, and no responsibilities that needed to be fulfilled.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s153-1: Until footsteps from the corridor broke the quiet.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s155-1: The local Estelle knocked and came in. By afternoon, Sera, who had overseen the procedure, and the external Estelle, who had carried out the infusion, had both left. Now, this local independent auditor had come before us with the dossier.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s156-1: This was Yuna’s first face-to-face conversation in this world with the auditor who had run from place to place to uncover the truth for her.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s160-1: “This is the independent auditor,” I said to Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s161-1: Yuna stood, placed both hands flat, her right palm against the left side of her chest, fingertips pointed toward Estelle, and bowed her head slightly—a solemn, equal greeting used by peers who had crossed life and death together.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s163-1: “You’ve walked the single-plank bridge too,” she said, her voice gentle but full of strength. “Thank you for not letting him fight his way through this case alone.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s164-1: Estelle stood straight as a measuring rod. She opened the record book in her hands—the independent auditor’s private notes—and turned to the page concerning
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s164-2: “Unclaimed Item: Yuna.” She picked up her pen and forcefully added eight words beneath the final line, then turned the book around to show both of us.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s168-1: This was not an official procedure that could secure Yuna an identity allocation. Adding a line to this book would not give her even half an inch more footing in the village’s household registry system.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s169-1: She spoke, her voice as steady and without a ripple as usual. Only the flush at the tips of her ears betrayed her feelings.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s171-1: “On the private observation record…” She paused. “Welcome back.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s173-1: After Estelle completed the declaration, Yuna decided to return to the village.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s175-1: After this morning’s motion to void the agreement was rejected, the two of us remained under controlled status. But Estelle applied to the Ten Seats for a temporary joint authorization, citing the need to
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s175-2: verify the physical evidence of the “observation record.” Galon, who held the migration authority, and Kane, who was responsible for security, ultimately pressed their fingerprints onto the application.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s176-1: This was not a release, but a constrained armed escort. Galon designated a strictly limited, short-term access whitelist for us in the system; Kane sent two armed patrol members to follow far behind us, serving as silent monitors.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s177-1: Under this temporary authorization within the five-person framework, Yuna, as the “anomalous subject” under inspection, was granted a brief period to remain on the village roads. Estelle stayed underground to prepare the hearing dossier. Only the two of us set out on the road back to the village, with gun muzzles directed at us from far behind.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s179-1: She walked steadily at my side. By then, she had asked and clarified every question she needed to ask. She knew that in this world, a person named “Yuna” had never existed;
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s179-2: that her parents had only one daughter, named Milu; and that in the village household register, the number of children under Galon and Melu’s name was “one,” never “two.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s180-1: She knew all of this. She had heard me explain it and personally checked Estelle’s audit records. She had recorded every cruel truth precisely in her mind.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s183-1: “I want to see the village for myself.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s187-1: “I want to see it.” She interrupted me. “I trust the records. But in the end, the records were written by other people. I have to confirm this with my own eyes.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s189-1: We passed her family’s courtyard from a distance. The gate stood wide open. Galon was chopping wood inside, while Melu hung washed things from the clothesline. Everything was orderly and needed no extra person to help; nor did the absence of one leave any gap.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s190-1: Yuna stopped across the road, looking at the well she had once known so well and the old chopping block. Melu turned and casually brushed dust from the clothesline, her movements practiced and without the slightest hesitation. Yuna watched quietly for a while. She made no attempt to approach and made no sound.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s192-1: Then she turned and continued walking. We went straight to the threshing floor.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s195-1: Alone, she held the familiar bell high in one hand and shook it merrily.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s196-1: It was a perfectly intact bell that had never had an iron ring fitted to it. Its clapper was still inside, making a clear ringing sound.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s197-1: Yuna stopped at the edge of the threshing floor.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s205-1: She darted over like a little sparrow.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s210-1: Milu’s gaze landed on Yuna and stopped there in curiosity. She tilted her head back to examine her—she was a full head shorter than Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s214-1: I opened my mouth, suddenly unable to think of how to introduce her.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s224-1: Yuna was silent for one second. Only one second.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s227-1: Milu said “Oh,” accepting the answer easily. Then she raised the bell in her hands as if showing off a treasure.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s229-1: “Do you want to try shaking it?”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s232-1: I clearly saw Yuna’s hand move.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s233-1: Her right hand lifted an inch, as if out of habit she were about to take the bell. But then that hand stopped abruptly in midair and slowly withdrew to her side.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s238-1: Milu shook the bell herself, a little bored.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s243-1: “Mom always says I’m heavy-handed, and the blacksmith says the clapper in bells like this is thin, so it’ll break if you drop it even once.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s244-1: She hugged the perfectly intact bell to her chest.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s246-1: “It makes me worry every time. Whenever I shake it, I feel like it’s already broken inside. Strange, right? It’s been fine the whole time.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s247-1: I felt Yuna’s whole body stiffen in an instant.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s249-1: “If you shake it loudly enough, broken things will get better.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s250-1: Those were the exact words I had once heard Milu say on a morning when Yuna did not exist. That morning, the words had sent a chill through me. Now the same chill passed into Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s251-1: She had clearly heard them too. In another world, those were words she herself had used to comfort Milu. Now they had come from the mouth of a Milu who did not recognize her at all. Her body tensed almost at once.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s253-1: “What did you just say?” she pressed, her voice taut.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s254-1: Milu flinched at her. The little girl stared at her blankly and hugged the bell a little tighter, looking hurt.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s256-1: “I said it’s fine as long as you shake it loudly.” Milu pouted. “That’s what Mom taught me. She said that as long as the sound is still ringing, you should treat it as unbroken. Why are you being so mean…”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s260-1: Yuna didn’t say another word for a long stretch after leaving the threshing floor.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s261-1: She suddenly stopped when we were almost near the White Tower.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s268-1: “That was Melu’s line,” she said suddenly.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s272-1: “I used to hear Melu say that too, and that’s why I used it to comfort her. An adult’s warning, and a child’s instinctive fear…” She looked at the road, as if cutting off some hope that should never have existed. “That wasn’t a remnant.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s275-1: At last, we went around to the back of the house.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s278-1: There was a small south-facing window. It had once been her window. From the age of six, she had climbed out through it to find me, for ten whole years.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s279-1: Now the window was tightly closed. The paper was newly pasted.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s280-1: She stood beneath the wall, looking up silently at the window.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s282-1: “Didn’t you ask what’s piled up inside now?” she asked softly.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s290-1: She reached out and rested her hand lightly on the windowsill—the exact place her foot had landed every time she climbed through the window.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s291-1: The smooth mark was still there. But she was no longer the one who had worn it down day after day. It was merely a similar mark left by wind and rain.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s294-1: She withdrew her hand and said nothing more. She only turned her head and looked quietly toward the distant village.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s299-1: “I’ve written it down,” I said. “Just like I wrote down the wheat cake.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s300-1: She glanced at me and gave a soft assent.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s302-1: The trip to the village completed the final piece Yuna needed to confirm with her own eyes. We did not spend the night there—once this short-validity inspection order expired, she would
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s302-2: immediately become an unregistered person the system could not acknowledge. Even my own courtyard could not conceal someone who, to the village’s surveillance network, simply did not exist.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s303-1: We returned underground before dark. The distant patrol members lowered their guns, and Galon’s whitelist was revoked with it. Yuna became once again a controlled subject who could only be confined to a sealed room.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s304-1: In the control room, Yuna took out the large portion of new-wheat cake she had kept wrapped in paper. We divided it between us.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s307-1: The skeleton still sat upright in the chair where he had spent more than a hundred years. Yuna walked to the chair and placed the last remaining crumbs on the console.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s308-1: “Former Chief,” she said to the skeleton, with some lingering fatigue in her voice but in a tone as calm as if she were making small talk, “the old debt you left behind has been settled completely.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s309-1: She raised her left hand and looked at this brand-new body.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s310-1: “The red line you calculated back then was right. We filled the large gap. What keeps me standing here now is exactly the same as what keeps those people outside standing: ten thousand standard units of anonymous
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s310-2: capacity.” She spoke softly. “To a system this immense, it’s only a little indistinguishable weight. I haven’t brought any private burden with me. Your island won’t sink just because there’s one more me.”
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s311-1: She cast the words into the air.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s312-1: As she turned, the faint light from the roof vent fell down, illuminating the two pointed ears now standing perfectly straight.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s314-1: “What are you staring into space for?” she asked, looking at me.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s315-1: I don’t know how many times I had heard her say that in my life. Every time, she had forcibly pulled me out of the place where I was stuck.
texts.chapter:v15-30b:event:text-s317-1: “Let’s go,” she declared. “Get ready for the hearing. This time, I’m going to sign a name of my own.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:title: Chapter Thirty, Appendix Two: The Outer Gate
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s1-1:
Outer Maintenance Gate · Duty Elder’s Record (complete, unabridged):
“This matter is recorded in full at the duty elder’s request. Reason on a separate page.
Time: Evening of the second day. Location: Outer Maintenance Gate of the launch site.
Present: Six
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s1-2:
members of the outer maintenance crew. Four Boundary Guards. Two technicians. Duty elder.
Proceedings: See below, item by item.
Disposition: The six held together under guard. This matter is filed separately, not combined with yesterday’s or today’s cases.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s2-1: I was not there when the events recorded in this document took place. It was the evening of the second day, a full day before the final hearing that would decide our fate.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s3-1: These six people were responsible specifically for maintaining the launch site’s outer roads. To prevent them from forming a bloc, the Inner Circle had mixed together people from six different outer settlements. Before anything happened, I had seen them both in
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s3-2: the village and outside the inner gate. Each wore a narrow strip of iron sewn onto the left sleeve, representing basic carrying access. Not long after daybreak, they left and walked silently toward the last high-altitude launch facility on Earth still in use.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s6-1: That evening, the technician who issued the work orders gathered them in the open space just inside the outer maintenance gate. The order had come down: clear the outer grounds, seal two road junctions, and carry the three heavy pieces of equipment that had just arrived farther up to the launch platform.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s7-1: Those were the kinds of jobs the outer maintenance crew had always done. What was not routine were the three objects.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s8-1: They were three heavy transport coffins with restraint locks and sealed interfaces. A person-length mixture of metal and composite material gleamed coldly, each lid pasted with a brand-new classified-item seal, the side marked unmistakably with a rail code leading directly to
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s8-2: the top of the launch frame. The Inner Circle was used to treating them as tools that only knew how to apply muscle, assuming that as long as no information leaked, these people who worked the dirt roads would not ask questions. But when they lifted the coffins in pairs, Thun
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s8-3: touched the pipe clamp on the side and stopped. He was the one in the crew who often went up to clear the upper connections, and he knew the dimensions too well. “This isn’t for delivering supplies.” He muttered under his breath, his finger tracing upward along the interface.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s8-4: “Standard circulation exhaust valve, waste outlet… This volume is just enough to fit a person. And the shell doesn’t even have the most basic thermal-insulation coating for return.” He raised his head and looked at the seal. “…It’s a one-way capsule for throwing people into the sky.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s11-1: Yesterday afternoon’s public broadcast preservation order had already leaked to the outer settlements: the lives of several core transgressors had been temporarily preserved; it was not yet time for execution. Since the order explicitly included an “exodus route,” when the three heavy
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s11-2: coffins pressed down on their shoulders, Thun’s conclusion made Neva break out in a cold sweat: if the proper procedures were still underway, why had these three one-way capsules for carrying people been delivered to the junction leading to the launch frame at this particular moment?
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s12-1: In her mental arithmetic, the public hearing had not yet begun, and no one knew whether these three capsules delivered in advance were preparations for tomorrow’s judgment or some as-yet-undisclosed capacity for forced departure. But if they quietly slid onto the rails, it
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s12-2: meant the Inner Circle was prepared at any moment to make someone disappear without leaving even a word of explanation behind. If it truly came to an open judgment, why would the Inner Circle need to seal off the outer settlements’ view so suddenly, as they were doing now?
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s15-1: Neva was the crew chief. She had walked this road to the launch site for nineteen years. She dusted her hands and went to the technician responsible for issuing the work orders. In a low voice, she asked, “Who exactly are these three coffins prepared for?”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s16-1: The person issuing the order did not even look up. “Follow the order.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s17-1: Neva did not back down. She stepped closer. “The outer broadcast just reported a preservation order. Everyone is to be kept alive. Now three one-way coffins for carrying people have been sent here, and we’re being told to seal the outer roads. Who are they going to lock inside?”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s18-1: Only then did the person issuing the order look up, eyes cold. “Follow the order.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s21-1: The moment the words left his mouth, there was a bang.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s22-1: Samo, the oldest, let go without warning. He was always the steadiest worker, so when he released his grip, the heavy body of the coffin dropped sharply, nearly pulling Neva off balance with it.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s22-2: She steadied herself, glanced at Samo’s tense profile, said nothing, and decisively released the handle in her own hands. The first heavy coffin crashed onto the packed earth inside the gate.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s23-1: The impact made the other four stop instinctively. Thun looked at the coffin on the ground, then at Neva standing at the front. The air froze for two seconds. Then two more muffled impacts followed, and the other two metal coffins came fully down.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s24-1: In the record Sera left behind, the line reads:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s26-1: “5:40 p.m. The outer maintenance crew ceased work. Three crates, placed beside the road. Six people, standing beside the crates. Did not leave the site.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s28-1: They stood where they were, facing down the person who had issued the order.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s31-1: The technician was keeping the record at the time. The writing was very small, crowded together, and showed his panic. Neva stood there, her voice quiet but steady.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s32-1: “First, since those people are still under preservation according to this morning’s public notice, these coffins for carrying people, whose destination is unknown, should never have appeared on this road. Without a definite destination, we will not carry them.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s33-1: “Second, if they are still alive, we want those three core witnesses to remain here and make a public statement to the outer settlements. Until we hear them speak, we will not cover for anyone.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s34-1: She paused, then added, “Record these two requests exactly, word for word. If they aren’t recorded, we won’t move.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s37-1: The message was sent back, and the reply came quickly. Only one cold sentence:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s39-1: “Proceed with the work as ordered. Neither of the two requests will be accepted.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s41-1: The messenger had come on horseback. He pulled back on the reins, flung the sentence at them without dismounting, then jerked the reins again and rode away through another cloud of dust.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s46-1: The outer maintenance gate stood not far behind them. It was a massive metal sliding gate, driven by tracks and a motor on the inner side, sealing off the launch-site terrace from the broad dirt road to the outer settlements.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s46-2: If the gate stood open, the view that had been blocked would run straight through to the terrace, and people from the settlements passing along the outer road would be able to see the three heavy coffins meant to carry people.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s47-1: Neva and Samo knew this gate too well. They had applied the lubricant to its hinges themselves, and touched the control panel beside it every day.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s48-1: If the Boundary Guards wanted to go out and seal the road, or lock the information inside the terrace, they had to pass through this gate. After hearing that the requests would not be accepted,
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s48-2: the six turned and walked toward it. They did not leave. Instead, they lined up with their backs against the heavy gate, using their bodies to block the Boundary Guards’ path to the inner controls.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s49-1: Thun was the youngest of the six. He held the maintenance access needed to open the gate outward. Turning sideways, he placed his hand against the control panel on the wall, preparing
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s49-2: to override the system and force the gate open. As soon as it slid open, the capsules prepared to carry living people would be exposed without cover to everyone on the dirt road.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s52-1: He extended a finger and pressed the familiar button. The screen flickered, then lit up with a line of text:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s56-1: Thun held his breath and waited. He knew what low hum the gate should make when it started. But the sound did not come. He frowned and pressed harder a second time. The words on the screen changed:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s58-1: “Permissions for this terminal have been revoked. Please contact the duty elder.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s60-1: In the record book, this system instruction appeared between Thun’s two attempts:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s62-1: “6:05 p.m. Permission cut-off and removal order issued. Jointly authorized by: Kaine, Toma.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s64-1: And beneath this formal order was an additional note in another hand, from Toma’s seat:
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s66-1: “Addendum: All six are to be registered by name, with a complete disposition record retained. Physical removal limited to riot-control equipment; special nonlethal devices and the outer-settlement lethal sonic interface are prohibited.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s68-1: The high-powered nonlethal dispersal device beside the gate had originally been intended for dealing with large-scale unrest in the outer settlements. Once activated, its piercing low-frequency roar would make people lose their balance and collapse to their knees, vomiting, within seconds. It was the thing they most dreaded encountering during maintenance.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s71-1: Toma’s addendum not only cut off Kaine’s attempt to clear the site secretly through the bureaucratic procedure of requiring names and retaining a record; it also firmly held down the nonlethal mechanism that could have broken their resistance
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s71-2: instantly. If that level of riot-control equipment were used against an ordinary outer-settlement crew, the distinctive internal injuries it caused would leave unmistakable traces of specialized equipment use in the medical records afterward.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s72-1: And he had specifically locked down the most decisive hidden interface of all—the outer-settlement lethal sonic frequency. This was not out of mercy. With the public hearing approaching and the preservation order already
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s72-2: causing controversy, if the Inner Circle directly awakened the body’s back door and killed six laborers as a group, it would turn a localized act of defiance into ready-made evidence of an outer-settlement war, with everyone
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s72-3: present able to identify it. Through this precise division of responsibility and political calculation, Toma restricted the Boundary Guards’ action to the most primitive form of physical beating—with riot shields and long poles.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s75-1: The four Boundary Guards came down from the upper terrace carrying riot shields and long poles, pressing toward the six. At 6:10 p.m., Duty Elder Sera also arrived.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s76-1: The first thing Sera did after dismounting was walk straight to the technician, snatch up the substitute record book, and read it from beginning to end. Then she raised her head.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s78-1: “From this moment on, record exactly what anyone says. Record my column the same way.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s81-1: Only after arranging the record did she go to the gate and negotiate with Neva. Under the Inner Circle’s strict system, any voice or sentence meant to reach the outer settlements had to be converted into a controlled official document before it could cross the boundary.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s83-1:
“Question: This seat cannot accept the two requests you have made. The first must be decided collectively by the elders’ council; the second, this seat has no authority today to allow any document to leave the boundary.
Answer: Then write it down, in black and
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s83-2:
white, that you refuse to accept them.
Question: Recorded in the register. This seat asks a second time: If you leave this gate now, I can record this matter as a work stoppage, not as an occupation of a vital position. Think carefully.
Answer: We will not leave.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s88-1: The Boundary Guards advanced from above with riot shields and long poles, forcing their way down. The thick shields slammed solidly into the six people, producing dull impacts as flesh struck the metal gate.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s89-1: Samo was the oldest. The first impact made him suck in a sharp breath, but he braced himself against the gate and did not move aside. Then a long pole drove hard into his stomach, forcing him out of the line and sending him crashing onto the rough ground.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s90-1: Thun tried to pull him back, instinctively gripping the wire mesh beside the gate. Two Boundary Guards rushed him and violently twisted his left wrist to drag him away from the vital position. There was a crack. Thun screamed on the spot, and the next day he could only keep the wrist suspended against his chest with a strip of cloth.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s91-1: The other three laborers—the young woman from the mining district and the two taciturn middle-aged men—fought to form the line again, but were quickly scattered under the repeated blows of the shields and pinned down one after another in the mud. Neva
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s91-2: remained standing in the very center. Even when a shield slammed into her shoulder, she did not retreat half a step, until a Boundary Guard knocked her down with a long pole. Her head struck the stone slab, and blood mixed with dust across her face.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s92-1: Only a few minutes later, all that remained in front of the gate they had oiled with their own hands was heavy breathing.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s95-1: The Boundary Guards hauled the six people up and shoved them into the dim tool shed at the edge of the terrace. Two fully armed Boundary Guards stood at the door. That night, the guards brought them water but did not give them a light. The six spent a difficult night amid heat, darkness, and pain.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s96-1: That complete record was copied twice overnight. One copy was properly entered into the elders’ council archives. Sera kept the other herself. On that
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s96-2: night of uncertain circumstances, this record, which clearly documented the injuries, names, and reasons, became a copy that could not easily be erased.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s99-1: Neva told me later that, deep that night, the tool shed was thick with the smell of blood and sweat.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s100-1: Thun leaned against the corner, clutching his swollen wrist and sucking air through his teeth. He was trembling. He cursed under his breath. “Even if we had gone along and loaded living people into the coffins, walking this road afterward, we would eventually have been silenced too.”
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s101-1: Neva wiped the dirt from her face and stared at the shadows on the floor. She refused to carry those coffins for living people along this road again.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s102-1: Samo, the oldest, sat in the farthest corner. He had said almost nothing. It was not until midnight that he rubbed his face with his rough hands and sighed in the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s103-1: “Fifteen years ago, when something happened in the mining district, they told us to lock the outer gate the same way. Not one person inside ever came out.” He raised his head. “I just didn’t
texts.chapter:v15-30d:event:text-s103-2: want to close that kind of gate for them one more time.” I remembered the heavily worn iron bar on his sleeve, proof of the half of his life he had spent carrying loads along the outer roads.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:title: Camp (Hollow Laboratory · Cell Block)
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s2-1:
It was the day of the final hearing. The day the White Tower shut down counted as the first day; this was the evening of the third.
The hearing that would decide our fate and rule on whether the six laborers at
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s2-2: the outer gate lived or died was about to begin. Estelle, who was currently going through the local candidate process, did not have to face either case. The rest of us were all standing at the edge of a cliff.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s3-1: Two armed boundary guards followed ten paces behind with their guns, escorting Yuna, me, and the witness Estelle along the edges of the underground experimental zone’s access panels.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s5-1: The witness Estelle stopped, pulled out a sheet of paper, and pointed to the signature at the bottom. “The authorization Elder Sera issued last night. The terms allow me to conduct an on-site
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s5-2: evidence survey before the hearing.” She looked at the boundary guards. “If you think you’re more qualified than Sera to decide which evidence reaches the hearing table, you can shoot.”
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s6-1:
The boundary guard glanced at the document bearing the highest authorization, then at the time. In the end, he stepped aside by half a pace.
Yuna said nothing unnecessary. She followed Estelle toward the stairs leading upward.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s8-1:
We went around to the back of the enormous complex and emerged from the underground “Origin Zone.”
The smooth resin beneath our feet stopped abruptly at the building joint, turning back into rough concrete.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s8-2: The smell of old rust mixed with mold rushed into my nose. This was the true view of the hollow laboratory on the surface of the remote outskirts—an enormous forced-labor camp built to wring out expendables.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s10-1: Yuna walked to the building joint, her left foot on the experimental zone and her right foot inside the camp. She looked at the completely different surfaces on either side, then stepped straight into the darkness.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s15-1: The passage through the cell block was narrow and cold. The iron bunks lining both sides had long since rusted solid, while the inner sides of the bars on the windows were worn unnaturally bright, catching the faint sheen of human
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s15-2: grease. Along the base of the wall ran a rigid groove that curved past every iron door, several inches deep. Hundreds of pairs of shoes, mechanically shuffling along year after year, had gouged it into the hard concrete floor.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s17-1:
At the entrance to the third cell, I noticed a yellowed cardstock card inserted in the slot beside the door.
The small text on it read: “Improper handling of data, undermining confidence in the project. Clerk: Ilia.”
Beneath the
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s17-2:
reason for disciplinary action was a crossed-out statement of the person’s defense: “As a clerk, I could only copy the daily losses of expendables truthfully.”
The “Departure record” on the back of the card was completely blank.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s18-1: Estelle did not linger. Checking against the terminal screen, she led us toward the isolated cell at the end of the corridor.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s21-1: “After obtaining this authorization last night, I searched the old records here in advance from the peripheral archives.” Estelle stepped over the rusted threshold and brought up the logs on the screen. “The prisoner assigned to this cell was Vera, the base-model designer. When the Empire
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s21-2: declared Lysenko’s ‘use and disuse’ the sole orthodoxy, she was convicted and sent to the camp for insisting on genetics and being branded a ‘fatalist.’ Once Lysenko’s own operator project was approved, the camp forcibly brought her out and made her complete this base-model skeleton as a
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s21-3: convicted criminal. The final entry in the logs is an alert: a guard discovered a sharp tool she had hidden in the corner of the bed. Immediately afterward, she was permanently transferred. The record on the same page shows that once the alert was cleared, the cell was emptied and inspected.”
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s22-1: Yuna glanced at the empty bed. “If she really wanted to hide something important in a place subject to searches at any time, she wouldn’t put it in the corner of the bed, where it would be visible as soon as it was lifted.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s22-2: That looks more like bait meant to keep the guards busy.” Her eyes swept across the bare concrete walls and stopped at the only ventilation grille at the end of the cell with enough depth behind it. She reached into the corroded
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s22-3:
cavity behind the grille and felt around, then pried an iron box out from the very back.
Inside was a stack of neural-interface blueprints, along with the project proposal and outline manuscript for the Introductory Library.
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s24-1: Yuna went to the bedside and unfolded the yellowed interface blueprints. They were not designs for the base-model skeleton, but for an added “external infusion interface.” In the blank space at the side were resource parameters chilling enough
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s24-2:
to stop the breath:
“To realize a long-window operating vessel for a new-human operator, one hundred percent capacity units are required. Sole designated source: compulsory requisition through the Imperial transport network, ten thousand people.”
texts.chapter:phase2-camp:event:text-s26-1: “When she drew these cables, she knew exactly what they represented.” Yuna’s finger slid across the page. “Ten thousand living people would be dragged into the camp and connected to these lines. One unit of capacity would be extracted from each person’s brain
