Sera did not respond. She picked up the heavy official seal representing removal from the register.
The hand holding the seal descended steadily, first onto the field that had originally been mine, then onto the newly drawn field for Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s36-1: “Cancellation complete. The resolution is fully in effect.” Sera put away the seal and closed the register. “Boundary Guards, take them away. Join the six outside and transfer them to the launch site.”
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s39-1: As we left the deliberation square, the Boundary Guards’ line spread apart to either side. Kane kept his promise and personally led the escort.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s40-1: At the outer edge of the square, we joined the six maintenance workers detained for defiance. They retrieved the personal belongings cleared out of the laborers’ dormitory; a pack sat at each person’s feet as they silently accepted the outcome of their journey. There was no opportunity to change their minds. The expulsion was carried
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s40-2: out immediately. The Boundary Guards distributed the prepared survival supplies. Yuna and I, along with the witness Estelle carrying the recording equipment, each received our allotted share. The overnight escort made everything seem extraordinarily urgent, as though the village could not wait to spit us completely out of this land.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s41-1: The nine-person group stretched out in the cold wind of the deep night.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s42-1: We passed through the crowds that had not yet dispersed on either side of the road. Someone tentatively reached out and stuffed a patched old coat into one maintenance worker’s arms.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s42-2: As we passed a cart stopped in the darkness, another water skin filled with water was silently handed over. Kane walked at the front and gave no order to stop this public witnessing.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s43-1: Kane did not stop until we reached the stone marker at the village entrance that represented the boundary.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s44-1: He brought out a cast-iron recovery box.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s45-1: The sound of metal hitting the ground was especially harsh in the cold wind. In the darkness, some people removed the maintenance badges they carried and threw them into the box. Others lowered their heads and rolled up their coat sleeves, folding them little by little until the embroidery bearing the village emblem on their clothes was completely covered.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s46-1: The mechanic Thun at the front turned and glanced at me after throwing down his badge.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s47-1: There was no regret in his eyes, only the exhaustion and numbness of someone facing the road ahead. I met his gaze without speaking. The person on this land most familiar with machinery
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s47-2: and pipes might still prove useful aboard the ship. But until we had definitely removed our helmets and breathed the first breath of alien air, I could not promise them anything.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s48-1: Yuna walked beside me, keeping one hand in her coat pocket the entire time.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s49-1: Her fingertips should have been pressed against the old silver brooch, its edges somewhat darkened. It was the kind commonly used on a believer’s ceremonial clothing. Two hours earlier, while we were waiting outside
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s49-2: the hearing square, Mother had slipped it to her during the moment the Boundary Guard turned away. I saw Mother’s hand withdraw from Yuna’s pocket. Yuna looked down at it, then quickly clenched her hand around it again.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s50-1: The cold wind of the first deep night of autumn forced its way roughly into my collar. I instinctively pulled this coat tighter. When Mother smoothed the wrinkles from it one last time, her hand paused heavily on my shoulder.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s51-1: “If I’d known, I would have punished you for a little less time back then.” Her voice had been very low.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s52-1: I did not even have time to recall what I had done at twelve to deserve being made to stand in the yard for half the night. Now I was going to wear this coat to a place that might not even have thorn bushes.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s53-1: At last, we crossed the boundary marker.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s54-1: The long torchlight could not illuminate the road ahead. At the rear of the group, the witness Estelle carried the heavy recording equipment without a word.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s55-1: The Boundary Guards’ torchlight remained where it was, drawing a distinct line before the boundary marker.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s56-1: At the back of the group, Yuna took her hand out of her pocket. She looked down at her palm, then clenched the old silver brooch tightly again.
texts.chapter:v15-31d:event:text-s57-1: She did not look back. The nine of us crossed the boundary between light and darkness and followed the rough downhill road into the launch site in the dark.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:title: Chapter Thirty-Two Appendix: The Local Copy
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s2-1: The afternoon of the day we left the village for the launch site.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s3-1: In the basement of the parish archives, the terminal’s cooling fan gave off a faint hum. The local Estelle stood a few steps away beside the shelves, quietly turning through a thick black parish ledger.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s4-1: The screen’s cold blue light fell across Yuna’s face. She said nothing, only watched the electronic stub that had just been retrieved.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s6-1:
“White Tower Accident Recorder · Sealed Copy Stub
Note: A physical baseline snapshot captured by the external operator seat during the First-Day accident.
Residual signature (12 KB): Matched against the newly created living subject.
Conclusion: Local accident-subject signature established.”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s9-1: She reached out, tracing the glowing line of text through the dust-filled air with her fingertip.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s10-1: “If the soul field accommodated me across the universe, and you preserved the formal restoration authorization despite the hardliners’ resolution, why did you still have to run this 12 KB verification after I woke up?” Yuna turned her head.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s11-1: “The continuous record written in the AI laboratory established who you were. But in the local system, the old First-Day accident was still an unresolved case,” I said. “The instant you
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s11-2: pressed the external confirmation key and collapsed before the operation-room glass on the first night, the machine extracted your neurophysical state into the disaster-recovery log. This
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s11-3: newly created body was originally a blank slate, but the memories infused into it weren’t just inert data. They were sequences of extremely intense emotional discharges. When those infused
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s11-4: memories began thinking for the first time, when you were forced to feel that despair again with the same intensity as back then, the surging neural currents would forcibly press the new
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s11-5: neural circuits back into their old shape. Once the brain was activated along the physical inertia of that time, the machine could capture the overlapping signature and complete the match.”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s12-1: She looked at the two brief lines of explanation. “What if we didn’t run the verification?”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s13-1: “Then to the local system, you’d be an illegal intruder resurrected in a borrowed shell,” I said softly. “Once the machine detected the physical mismatch
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s13-2: and restricted your activity permissions at the underlying level, tonight’s departure from this world couldn’t even begin—the launch site’s control node
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s13-3: would never allow a ghost without physical coordinates in the system to log into the orbital cabin. I had to bring the local system to a complete closure.”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s16-1: Yuna watched the screen for a long time, then slowly lowered her hand. She did not speak right away as she usually did. She only listened to the fan turning in the silence.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s18-1: “No wonder you’ve been operating the terminal behind my back these past few days,” she said at last, her voice very quiet.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s20-1: “I wanted to deal with all these system aftereffects cleanly.” I looked at the floor. “You left me a commission to bring you back to life. But that doesn’t mean I wanted you to wake up and be held hostage by countless unresolved procedures. You need a completely clean identity to board that ship.”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s21-1: She stepped half a pace forward and looked into my eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s23-1: “A clean identity, and then the generosity to give me every possible choice.” She looked at me, a trace of anger barely perceptible in her voice. “Even though we laid everything bare that afternoon, deep down you still think pulling me back into reality was an
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s23-2: unauthorized abduction. You’re desperately settling all these unfinished accounts so I won’t have to love you with a sense of indebtedness. Arno, you’re completely insane. Do you really have to turn something between two people into freedom you unilaterally bestow on me?”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s25-1: In this basement, where even the machine had already drawn a full stop for her, the only sound was the terminal’s faint hum. She stared at the few lines of system characters showing that everything had been completely closed, her shoulders rising and falling slightly.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s26-1: The silence continued for a long time. The fingers clutching the corner of her clothes slowly loosened.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s27-1: “But...” Her voice lowered, the anger fading somewhat and revealing the exhaustion she had forced herself to carry through these past few days. She did not finish. She only closed her eyes and let out an almost inaudible sigh. “I’ll accept this ‘clean slate.’”
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s30-1: Estelle closed the thick black parish ledger in her hands. She had just stamped a vivid red seal onto the blank file on the newest page.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s32-1: “File closed. The machine’s account is settled.” Her voice rang through the archives.
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s33-1: She raised her head and glanced between us:
texts.chapter:v15-32b:event:text-s35-1: “As for the rest of the unfinished business, make sure you keep your own records.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:title: Chapter Thirty-Two, Supplement Two: End of Work
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s4-1: The shutdown request surged backward along the final operator connection, returning toward the source in the distant root world. The screen flashed with a glaring red warning light.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s5-1: In the final second before this connection completely melted through, a fatal acknowledgment traveled back along the collapsing channel to the terminal before me:
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s7-1: “Synchronized verification from root machine: physical destruction process triggered.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s9-1: Immediately afterward, the last light went out.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s13-1: The last line of small text to flicker across the screen read, “Root-node physical isolation confirmed.” I had no way to verify whether the root machine far away had truly burned down completely, but the acknowledgment of physical
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s13-2: isolation meant that whatever its current state, communication between it and this world had been permanently welded shut. As the signal returned, the low hum produced by the machine’s operating load at the base of the White Tower
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s13-3: dropped sharply and disappeared completely. The White Tower in this world became a dead port without a connection. The vibration that had always been there beneath the tower was gone. The ground beneath my feet became lifeless and still.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s14-1: Under the strict rules Sera had established beforehand, the three supervisors and the two recorders responsible for the main and duplicate records were all waiting outside the blast-proof glass at the rear. Only the witness and I were permitted to remain inside the core corridor.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s17-1: I climbed out of the operator’s seat, pulled out the main cable from the primary control area, grabbed a heavy wrench from the ground, and brought it down hard on this world’s White Tower power servo unit and connection array.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s18-1: The tremendous crash of breaking metal echoed through the empty base of the tower. Outside the blast-proof glass, the three supervisors stationed at the interfaces wore different expressions, but no one stopped me. The protocol called for a physical severance, and I was the one who carried it out most completely.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s19-1: On the other side of the grating, the local Estelle watched me smash the glowing components into scrap metal. She lowered her head, made one mark in the record book serving as the main ledger, and continued reporting according to the previous procedure:
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s21-1: “Tower’s low hum: stopped. Machine signal transmission: none. Bottom-level connection equipment: physically destroyed. Tower interior instrument readings: all zero. Additional item confirmed: the recovery assets delivered by the external AI laboratory had already been safely taken offline and were unaffected.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s22-1: Yuna’s backup had been sealed that morning. She had completely detached from this system and would not be dragged into this death.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s25-1: In this ruined space, the first thing to reveal itself was the sound of my own heavy breathing.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s26-1: I instinctively closed my eyes and tried to call up the single-focus view of meditation navigation. Nothing. I tried again to touch the gray button that had always lain dormant
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s26-2: at the edge of my perception. Absolute silence. My consciousness seemed to strike a black wall without any give, sealed precisely back inside this flesh that could live only once.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s27-1: The witness stood beside her assigned outer position and watched me smash the last glowing panel. Destroying this machine had been her defiant refusal to accept humiliation that day, but now, as everything fell silent, her shoulders
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s27-2: sagged slightly. There was no expression of relief, and she did not continue directing her anger at me. She simply stood there quietly, watching the metal fragments scattered across the floor, still giving off the smell of burning.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s28-1: I took a few breaths beside the quiet wreckage of the seat frame, then slowly moved my stiff legs out. As I followed the same route back, the lights embedded in the walls no longer sensed my footsteps and came on.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s31-1: I walked out of the deep passage. In the corridor, the witness, who had remained inside with me, walked at my side.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s32-1: The local Estelle closed the record book serving as the main ledger. Through the grating in the blast-proof glass, Sera checked it over.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s35-1: “Inner-site recorder did not participate in the equipment operation. But the recorder was present throughout outside the blast-proof glass. Both matters entered into the record.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s37-1: This was the boundary she left for herself and everyone else. Today, or in any future when the matter was reconsidered, no one could use a vaguely worded preservation order to hold the two Estelles jointly accountable.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s41-1: We returned to the entrance at the base of the tower. Sera took the booklet recording the equipment’s final status and scanned it. She did not sign in the signature space of the final-item column.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s43-1: “Where should this duplicate booklet go?” the field recorder beside her asked quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s45-1: “File it with the main ledger in the resolution’s attachments,” Sera said. “Start another sheet. Head it: White Tower External Confirmation. Write the time heading for the final line in advance too: 22:00 exactly. Leave the middle blank.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s47-1: Sera’s gaze passed over us and fixed itself on the darkened passage.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s52-1: Night had fully fallen. We followed the stone steps back the way we had come and walked out of the silent White Tower.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s57-1: The preservation order prohibited entry after completion. The long tables from the hearing square had not yet been removed, and the boundary guards followed us all the way here.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s59-1: “You three, sit over by the long table.” Kane pointed to the cold patch of ground at the edge of the square.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s60-1: He stood in the middle of the road. With the slightest turn of his head, he could keep all three of us locked in the corner of his eye.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s63-1: Sera handed the field recorder the paper she had just marked “White Tower External Confirmation.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s65-1: “The low hum inside the tower has not resumed. All instrument readings: zero,” the field recorder read aloud.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s67-1: “The next confirmation will be at 21:50.” Sera wrote the time heavily on the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s70-1: Kane did not look at the paper at all. His only task was counting people.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s72-1: “Three.” He forced the two words out of his throat.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s75-1: I walked before the elders and formally asked Otto to enter a statement into the record: “The deep-layer connection has been severed. While I was inside, I completely destroyed the local connection equipment. This tower is now only a dead port. You no longer need to guard against me having left a back door.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s76-1: I paused and met Otto’s scrutinizing gaze.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s77-1: “On the day of the preservation-order hearing, I said that if you did not accept the conditions, I would sever the connection and jump to another world that would. I calmly laid out the fact. At the time, I admitted that it was a bluff. Now I am
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s77-2: asking for this to be formally entered into the record. Once the local connection is severed, I no longer have the option of choosing again. I have no remaining leverage with which to force you to honor the agreement. That is the whole truth.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s78-1: Otto remained silent and entered the statement into the record. The scratch of his pen across the paper announced the complete end of technological coercive power.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s84-1: Cold sweat seeped gradually into my palm. Even though reason knew the connection had been severed, this body still honestly remembered the conditioned reflexes of hundreds of failures.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s85-1: The second hand crept toward 20:36, mark by mark. In the hundreds of loops across the past hundred-odd days, that had been the exact boundary when the sky was torn open by white light and the world began collapsing into reset. I held my breath, an uncontrollable spasm rising in my stomach, and stared hard into the darkness in the distance.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s86-1: In reality, time flowed quietly past. The night wind passed through the empty square. No abnormal light came on.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s87-1: I released the fist I had kept clenched.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s90-1: During the long wait that followed, villagers began gathering at the edge of the square in the distance. Without the low hum that had accompanied them for more than a century, the entire village seemed unusually quiet. Those who
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s90-2: should have been asleep at night came out wearing outer clothes. They did not make a commotion or panic, and no one delivered a speech. They simply stared in silence at the stone tower that had suddenly become an inert object.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s91-1: An old man hunched over with age carried an oil lamp glowing with a dim yellow halo to the edge of the square, outside the security line. He set it down and turned away. Before long, others began following his example,
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s91-2: leaving their household lanterns along the edge. The weak halos formed a winding, rough line across the open ground. They simply watched the creation that had hummed for more than a century become silent stone on this night.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s92-1: Rena brought an outer garment from home and gently draped it over my shoulders.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s93-1: I took the dry cakes from my bag and broke them forcefully into several pieces. When I offered one to Sera, she extended her hand, paused halfway, looked at the coarse crumbs, and only then slowly accepted it.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s96-1: Without thinking, I nudged a rusty old nut on the ground with the tip of my shoe. Rust stained the side of my shoe. Without the machine’s calculations or the channel’s low hum, waiting in the physical world became unbearably cumbersome. Every minute could only be forced past by the second hand.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s99-1: It grew late. The newly arrived boundary guards taking the next shift stared at us.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s103-1: 21:50. Sera spread the external confirmation sheet across her lap and made the final count of the three living coordinates before her.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s106-1: Keeping the three of us who had directly come into contact with the shutdown site within sight of one another for mutual verification, and not letting us leave, was the elders’ clumsy way of ensuring that none of us had gone to restart the machine before us. But whether the shutdown itself had truly succeeded—
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s107-1: That could only be proven by watching the time pass 22:00 exactly with my own eyes, while I was still in this world.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s108-1: The field recorder made one final trip to recheck the bottom-level power indicator on the outer wall. When he returned, a thin layer of night dew had formed along the edge of the paper.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s110-1: “Until 22:00 exactly, the witness will continue guarding the White Tower’s external response,” Sera said.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s113-1: The local Estelle held her pen suspended above the paper. Her fingers trembled with tension. She took a deep breath, changed her grip, and clenched it tightly.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s118-1: In the minutes leading toward the final moment, I picked up the rusty nut from the ground, hooked it over my index finger, and raised it before my eyes. Through the round hole, I stared fixedly at the glow of the oil lamps along the edge of the square.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s121-1: The second hand passed the twelve mark.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s122-1: The pale wall visible through the hole did not change at all. A night wind picked up a tiny speck of dust and slowly rolled it into the left side of the opening, inching it toward the right.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s123-1: The clock’s second hand ticked forward another mark.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s126-1: The witness watched me quietly. The pen in the local Estelle’s hand still hovered in the air. Sera gazed at the White Tower in the distance.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s129-1: I lowered my head and looked at the hand that had held the nut. Black machine oil from sitting in the old operator’s seat that afternoon still remained in the gaps beneath my fingernails.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s132-1:
“Do you still recognize the short-term preservation order I gave you today?” Kane suddenly called from nearby, pointing to the stack of papers in Sera’s hand.
“Sera handed it to me,” I answered. “Otto’s name on it was signed by proxy. You voted against it at the hearing.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s133-1: Kane’s chin gave an almost imperceptible nod. This was a surprise check on the handover of the preservation order and the details of the hearing. His only task was to confirm that the person sitting here now and the person who had participated in the hearing that afternoon had continuous memories, with no gap between them.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s134-1: In truth, this could not prevent a change of address. Even if I had escaped to another world in that second, the local Arno who regained control of this body would carry the shared
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s134-2: memory of the past few hours and answer Kane’s questions word for word. But within the boundary guards’ limited understanding, this was the most reliable defense they could construct.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s135-1: The local Estelle’s wrist finally sank, and she brought the pen down hard.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s137-1: “22:00 exactly has passed. The White Tower remains without power. Machine signals have not been restored. All three relevant persons are present.”
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s141-1: When she finished, she handed the pen to Sera. Sera took it and let her gaze travel up the towering body of the tower toward its top, which disappeared into the night sky. In the blank space reserved long ago on the final line of the page, she solemnly signed her name.
texts.chapter:v15-32c:event:text-s142-1: The night wind passed through the square, making the flames of the distant oil lamps sway all at once. I opened my hand, and the rusty nut dropped onto the stone paving with a clatter. Darkness pressed heavily down upon this world. There was no white light, and no jump.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:title: Chapter 32, Supplement 3: The Lock
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s1-1:
Launch Site Guide Log (Boundary Guard, Kane):
“Day of the decision. Escort nine people across the boundary, toward the northern boundary stone.
Deep into the night, saw the launch site’s return lamp flash three times. Gate opened.
Traveled through the night. By the following morning, the handover was complete.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s4-1: Ever since the hum from the base of the White Tower vanished completely, something had been missing from the village.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s5-1: On the first day after the shutdown, that feeling—as if a piece had been gouged clean out—grew more and more concrete. Several people who could not bear the silence ran to knock on the chapel door. The pounding echoed across the square, but the doors remained shut.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s6-1: That low sound, which had run through the lives of several generations, had never had a name and had never needed one. Only when sunlight fell across the Tower’s perfectly still body did the villagers feel that a piece had simply gone missing between heaven and earth, leaving behind a silence that made their hearts panic.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s7-1: Old Nona leaned on her cane and sat down on the peeling bench beside the chess stall. Her head tilted, her cloudy eyes half closed, and she listened for a long time in that suffocating emptiness. Several bewildered young people milling around nearby stopped and looked at her.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s8-1: Then, in her hoarse voice, as if confirming it to herself, she murmured:
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s14-1: Early the next morning, a long line soon formed outside the prayer room. People clutched scraps of paper and copper coins and came to have the scribe write slips for them. Each person stepped forward murmuring the same sort of things—what were they supposed to do with the days ahead? Would anyone still hear their prayers?
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s15-1: The scribe gripped her pen, her hand shaking badly. For more than half an hour, she could not write a single word. In the end, she quietly stood up, took down the sign that read Scribe, and slumped onto the steps outside.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s16-1: By that evening, the oppressive mood found the wrong outlet. Two households at the eastern end of the village started arguing in the street, over something that had happened twenty years ago.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s17-1: When the crowd’s anxiety was close to becoming uncontainable, Sera came over from the deliberation court. She passed through the crowd and walked to the center of the square.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s18-1: More and more people gathered. Someone in the front cautiously asked her what had happened, and whether they should still mill flour tomorrow.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s19-1: She stood there as steady as a stone statue. When nearly everyone had gathered, she straightened her back and, in the unquestionable voice of the elder on duty, said something that could never be written into any procedural form:
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s22-1: The scene went strangely quiet for a moment. She paused, her gaze passing over those bewildered faces.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s28-1: The crowd dispersed, but slowly, as if no one knew where to put their feet.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s29-1: When the second night fell, as the elder court’s final decision on whether we would stay or leave was about to be made, the lamps beneath the Tower had not been taken away. Instead, more had gathered silently, winding into a spread of lamplight.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s30-1: No one knew who had gone to add them.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s31-1: Sera saw them from a distance. She turned away and did not interfere.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s35-1: The road to the launch site was divided by successive iron fences. Under the Boundary Guards’ supervision, we passed through the first fence, which locked behind us. The formal passage ahead, leading to the launch site, could only
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s35-2: be opened after the security sequence on the other side was confirmed and the deadlock released remotely. So the nine of us stopped in the buffer zone between the two fences, packs on our backs, waiting for a signal from the depths.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s36-1: Everyone set their packs on the ground. One was a cloth bag containing copies of everything in the work case; the other was the heavy recording equipment the witness Estelle had carried all this way. The official departure register bearing the seal from the decision was safely tucked inside Boundary Guard Kane’s coat.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s37-1: Beside them were the old clothes my mother had packed for me. The last belonged to Yuna; inside were only a few pieces of warm clothing and a ration she had brought from home. As for the six maintenance workers, personal belongings they had just cleared out of the laborers’ quarters lay at their feet.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s39-1: While we waited, a figure hurried over along the gravel path up the dirt slope.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s41-1: Her face was utterly clear of expression—neither grief nor anger. She stopped outside the first fence. The Boundary Guards did not stop her.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s43-1: “I’ll say a few things, then I’ll go. I want to make everything clear before I leave.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s46-1: The local Estelle looked at us inside the fence, her tone brisk.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s48-1: “The decision from the court opened a gap for the nine of you. It broke the hard rule against crossing the boundary.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s51-1: “I stopped Sera in front of the long table just now and forced her to reopen my case file. She had no choice but to sign my application to delay my deportation. I’m not going back to the mines at Watermarsh.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s52-1: She looked at the witness, then at Yuna.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s53-1: “The elder court is most afraid of complications now, and the nine of you have already made your departure a fact. No one wants another conflict tonight. That gives me leverage
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s53-2: to stay. I’ll force them to rewrite the terms of my disposition, word by word. The decision has to state clearly who I am. I’m staying here. I’m no longer anyone’s replacement.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s56-1: When she finished, she adjusted her stance slightly and turned her gaze toward the girl standing on the other side of the fence.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s59-1: She looked at the face exactly like her own.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s61-1: “I’m not changing it. I’m still Estelle.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s62-1: The witness took one step forward from the crowd. Her voice was not loud, but every word was sharply enunciated.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s66-1: “I tried turning other names over in my head. But I stopped at the fourth one—the names meant nothing to me. They had nothing to do with me.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s67-1: She looked at the people inside the boundary stone, a trace of stubbornness in her eyes.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s69-1: “My mother shouted this one at the well back then. This is the only one I recognize.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s72-1: The local Estelle stood quietly outside the fence for a while. She looked at that face and did not argue.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s78-1: After saying this, she turned decisively and walked along the dirt slope into the night.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s82-1: The night wind grew colder. Everyone waited.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s83-1: After a long while, an intensely bright white light appeared in the direction of the far end of the wilderness. In the heavy darkness, that light flashed three clear times—the indicator that the lower control room where Chiko was had completed its verification and released the gate remotely.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s87-1: The signal that the gate had opened arrived. Before crossing the iron gate, Kane walked over to a large stone beside the road. He undid the clasp inside his coat and touched the heavy Boundary Register he kept close to his body.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s88-1: At the edge of the long table in the deliberation square, Sera had already stamped it, marking my name as “crossed the boundary.” He did not take out the register and go through the motions again. He only pressed hard against it through his clothes.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s90-1: “My boundary is clean,” he said quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s91-1: Then he opened the ration bag and distributed the food piece by piece. When he reached Yuna, his hand paused in midair.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s92-1: He looked at Yuna, then lowered his head and glanced into the ration bag. After a while, he took out another piece.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s94-1: “The ink on the stamp they put down at the table just now hasn’t even dried, and it’s already wastepaper,” he said stiffly.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s96-1: Kane handed her both pieces of ration. Avoiding her eyes, he looked toward the wilderness beyond the iron gate.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s98-1: “You don’t count as one of the villagers we drove out.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s100-1: “Call it passing through. Someone passing through will be far away tomorrow. Take them.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s102-1: Beyond this gate began the long wilderness.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s103-1: The group continued forward. The first few steps were very quiet. No one looked back. But Yuna suddenly stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s104-1: Looking back from here, the village gave off patches of dim yellow lamplight in the night. The White Tower stood in the center, dead silent. The spread of lamps beneath it had already grown far beyond the number there at dusk. The cold wind passed through, gently stirring the worn cloth sign outside the prayer room.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s106-1: Facing the wind, Yuna said it very, very softly.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s107-1: She did not address anyone by name, but I knew she was not speaking to the people around us. She watched the distant lamplight for a while.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s108-1: “Let the ones who couldn’t make it here share this view.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s109-1: She quietly finished taking in that sight, then turned decisively and tucked her hands back into her pockets. She lifted her chin firmly toward the boundless wilderness.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s111-1: I turned around too. My mother dozing beside the stove, the narrow lanes I had walked countless times, the door to our home that had only just been closed yesterday—all of them were now left behind forever. The evening wind blew in. It was cold.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s112-1: After catching up with the group, none of us looked back again.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s117-1: The second half of the night after we passed through the gate was extraordinarily long. Before dawn, we finally reached the launch site deep in the wilderness.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s118-1: The nine of us stopped before the gray metal door leading to the launch tower. The six workers—Nava, Thun, Samo, the somewhat older electrician, the fifth person who had taken a deep breath at the hearing, and the young apprentice whose legs had been shaking but who
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s118-2: had still followed along—wore worn work clothes. Several still had bruises on their faces and arms from being subdued by the Boundary Guards when they disobeyed orders earlier. At the final hearing just now, these six had each stepped up to the edge of the long table
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s118-3: in the deliberation square before the White Tower and personally acknowledged to Sera that this journey off the ground was one-way. Now Nava slapped the edge of the airlock with her rough palm and tilted her head toward us, signaling that we should go in together.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s119-1: Sera had already reached the outer control tower in a maintenance vehicle. In the cold wind, she connected to Chiko’s line. After a moment of silence on his end, Chiko directly reported the final
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s119-2: verification results from below: the system had locked out every possibility of changing orbit, and the flight’s landing point was fixed on the deep-space planet selected by the old civilization
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s119-3: more than a hundred years ago. Then he added: the suspension fluid levels and impact-absorbing gel in the sleep pods were all full, enough to keep us alive until we reached the landing orbit.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s120-1: These uncompromising technical facts formed the premise behind his affirmative vote.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s121-1: Yet the door leading to the ship remained tightly shut. We stood before the towering airlock, looking at the cold metal door.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s122-1: Sera’s voice came through the communications channel. She gave a heavy sigh on the other end, followed by a stretch of muffled operational sounds.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s123-1: “The final decision of the ten seats is now in force. The system commands at the base of the Tower have been pushed down.” Sera’s voice echoed through the channel. “The old crew manifest verification has been forcibly overwritten. The door is open.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s124-1: With a low release of air pressure, the metal door clicked and opened all the way for us. At the end of the passage stood three dark-gray transfer caissons side by side. Since the ship had been sealed inside the launch tower for a century, we had to use these rail caissons to transfer up to the airlock hatch above.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s125-1: We entered the caissons in three groups. Amid the roar of meshing gears, the caissons carried us upward along the vertical rails. When the doors opened again, we finally stepped into the white ship.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s128-1: When the ship’s main airlock behind us locked completely, the air, wind, and smell of soil belonging to this planet were cut off in a single click.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s129-1: A burst of static came through the communications channel. It was not Sera. It was my mother.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s130-1: “Arno.” My mother’s voice was very soft, threaded with a faint electrical hiss.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s131-1: I watched the indicator lights flickering before the main console. “I’m here.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s132-1: “Yuna, and the witness girl. Can you hear me?”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s133-1: “We can hear you.” Yuna looked out at the night beyond the porthole. In the corner, the witness silently nodded.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s134-1: “Listen.” My mother paused on the other end, her breathing somewhat heavy. “Don’t come back. Don’t look behind you.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s135-1: The cabin was quiet. Only the engine’s low preheating hum remained.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s136-1: “Don’t lose to homesickness. Forget all of us.” My mother’s voice slowly sank, as if she meant to drive every word into the ground. “Don’t miss us. Don’t write. Don’t come through my door again.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s137-1: These were the last few words she left me before the communication cut out. There were no pleasantries, no farewell. In this decisive way, she severed the last small possibility that we might turn back.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s139-1: The lights inside the ship were pale and cold, and the air was thick with the smell of old machine oil. In this metal chamber, where even the oxygen mixture felt somewhat dry, a complete engineering construct
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s139-2: finished more than a century ago waited quietly. Most of its one hundred and fifty spacious sleep pods were empty. It had failed to launch back then because the final decision had not been reached. And on
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s139-3: the execution document bearing the elder court’s seal, only the destinations of nine people were listed—three core parties who knew the truth, and six maintenance workers who had personally claimed the
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s139-4: consequences of disobedience and could no longer be forced back onto the old track. Those empty pods stood silently before us, but until the final moment of boarding, no tenth name was added to that list.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s140-1: Now, only the final wake-up procedure remained.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s141-1: Yuna crossed the long corridor of sleep pods and walked straight to the control wall covered in dim screens. This body had only truly entered this place not long ago, but she stood before the main console without hesitation. What we had to rely on was the heavy operating manual on its fixed bracket.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s142-1: This was a strict verification procedure requiring two people to complete. I pulled out the manual and opened it to the wake-up procedure. The indicator lights had not come on for more than a century.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s143-1:
“Main power confirmed.” I stared at the manual and read the first line.
Yuna pulled down a heavy switch at the console. Metal scraped with a piercing
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s143-2:
shriek, then a faint light came on. “Power confirmed. Green.”
“Environmental circulation. Internal circulation on.”
“Circulation on. Pressure stable.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s144-1: We carried out the startup procedure like this, asking and answering one another. The air was too quiet. Every crisp click of a switch sounded like a countdown. The six workers stood around the perimeter, staring fixedly at the readings on the key instruments. Their
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s144-2: breathing was clearly audible in the silent cabin. The witness Estelle stood quietly beside a sleep pod in the farthest corner. On the communications channel, Sera remained on the ground, watching the telemetry screens and supervising the final safety-lock status.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s145-1: When Yuna personally released the final physical deadlock on the console and placed her finger on the red master-control valve as it lit up, she stopped.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s146-1: She looked at the boundless darkness outside, then at the eight people behind her.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s148-1:
Sera’s hard voice came through the channel:
“Ground reception confirmed. Peripheral lines clear. Physical lock fully released. You can go.”
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s149-1: The banks of previously dead screens suddenly lit up with blinding blue light, and the sleeping engine began to hum low. It was the sign that the automatic launch sequence had been fully
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s149-2: activated. After completing this final step, Yuna turned around, walked back to the row of impact-absorbing seats, sat in the empty seat beside me, and pulled down the heavy restraint harness.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s150-1: The others in the cabin each found a position and fastened their straps.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s151-1: Nava looked across the aisle at me, then at Yuna. She said nothing. She only reached up, tugged on the restraint across her chest, and made a forceful gesture to show that it was locked
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s151-2: tight. The older electrician and the fifth person silently checked their buckles as well. I could even hear the young apprentice breathing heavily. I checked my own clasp and nodded at them.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s152-1: The engine’s vibration began traveling through the deck. First came a faint hum, then a rumble that seemed ready to churn our organs inside out.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s153-1: The powerful acceleration slammed into my chest, making it difficult even to breathe. The reawakened ship heaved and rumbled through the violent shaking, dragging a long tail of flame as it tore open the
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s153-2: night sky. With difficulty, I looked toward Yuna from the corner of my eye. She was strapped tightly into her seat, her face pale, but one hand reached out through the violent shaking and seized my wrist.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s154-1: Amid the deafening roar, the ship pierced the final layer of atmosphere. The gravity of the ground, the countless mornings that had circled the White Tower, the familiar smell of earth in the narrow lanes, and my mother’s back as she sat beside the fire were all hurled violently behind us forever.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s155-1: The acceleration reached its peak. All color outside the porthole completely faded, leaving only boundless deep cold. We were driven straight into deep space inside this iron shuttle.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s156-1: The violent shaking finally subsided into a faint, regular hum. The pressure of the safety harnesses gradually faded, replaced by a drifting sensation of weightlessness that wrapped around us.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s158-1: Nava released her fingers, clenched white from gripping so hard. Samo’s tightly closed eyes slowly opened. I turned my head. Yuna still held her gaze toward the porthole, her fingers
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s158-2: still wrapped tightly around my wrist, not letting go. In the abyssal darkness, the planet that several generations had been unable to leave was slowly moving away, tracing a gradual arc.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s159-1: There was no cheering. At last, this planet was no longer the cage we woke up in.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s160-1: “We made it out,” Yuna said softly.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s161-1: She did not turn around. I only listened quietly.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s162-1: Beyond the porthole, deep in the distant sea of stars, a faint purple glow floated quietly in the darkness.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s164-1: It was not merely a halo of light. It was a pink-purple dawn sky.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s165-1: Violent shaking struck again, but this was no longer the turbulence of ascent. It was the tearing sensation of entering an atmosphere. Scorching plasma wrapped around the portholes, and alarms rang throughout the cabin. When everything finally settled, the ship’s landing struts slammed heavily onto solid ground.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s166-1: After the engine’s final sigh-like burst of exhaust, the main airlock opened again, after more than a century, toward another world.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s167-1: The air that rushed in carried a damp, unfamiliar sweetness and the faint tang of blood.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s168-1: We released our safety harnesses and descended the ladder one by one. The six workers followed, setting their feet for real on land that did not belong to our home.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s169-1: Yuna stood at the front. She did not collapse beside the lakeshore as she had in countless past cycles. She stood before this unfamiliar body of water, breathing
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s169-2: the cool air. The witness Estelle stood quietly beside us with the heavy recording equipment on her back, no longer anyone’s shadow, but an independent companion.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s170-1: The nine of us stood together on the shore of this new world.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s171-1: Far across the lake, the enormous cracked moon cast a dim radiance beneath the pink-purple sky. Low, dark, leaf-shaped creatures swayed in the wind, and several long-winged creatures glided silently through the low air.
texts.chapter:v15-32d:event:text-s172-1: This was where we were going.
texts.chapter:chapter-33-new-shore:title: Final Chapter: New Shore
texts.chapter:chapter-33-new-shore:event:text-:
New Shore Flight Form (Launch Site Archive Copy):
“Crew: nine. (Three in the first column, six in the second.)
Flight: one-way.
Destination: deep-space coordinates. Habitable: possible.

Fuel: full. Trim: confirmed. Weather window: pending.
Return flight: (This section is not provided.)
Remarks: May you have a safe journey. —Ground Control Console, on behalf of the recorder”
When the massive overload finally subsided, the ship had already entered the silent depths of space.
On the rear-facing screen behind the main console, a high-magnification optical lens was aimed at the ground for the last time.

The history the White Tower had long suppressed in the machine’s name, the rigid hierarchy built around it, and the lives still sleeping on the boundary between lies and truth all shrank, along with the village’s faint lights, into one tiny point far away.
Then the camera signal was cut, and the screen went completely dark.
Near the wall of the forward cabin, the brass communications grille blinked with a faint indicator light.

To ensure that those leaving the ground would completely withdraw from Earth’s politics, this ship had been forcibly stripped of all active transmission modules as the price of this exile, leaving only a one-way receiver. This was a true exile. The ship would never be able to

send any instructions to those who came after. By now, the physical telemetry cable from the launch tower had long since detached, and the ground tracking screens showed nothing but passive radar echoes. Along this communications route, we could only listen. We could not answer.
A flat voice came through the radio: “Flight path locked. Ship clear of the gravity well. Outer radar tracking normal.”
But after reading it out, he did not cut the line immediately.
“One addition not on the list. Her Excellency Rena, currently on the platform, needs the frequency for the last two minutes.”
The static in the grille flickered, replaced by the sound of someone breathing.
“Arno.”
“Only two minutes. I’m counting in my head.”

Before boarding, a boundary guard had shoved a coarse cloth bundle into my arms, saying she had asked someone to bring it. Now it sat at my feet. Inside were several freshly baked flatbreads and a thick, rough new wool hat. She had hurriedly knitted it over the past two days.
“Don’t eat all the bread at once. Make it last. And the hat—make sure she wears it.”
Obvious wind noise came through the grille. She took a deep breath.
“Don’t come back.”
“That vote on the resolution table—I raised my hand myself. I voted to let you go only if all three of you made it there alive and none of you ever came back. I won’t change my vote.”
“Don’t save words up in your heart, hoping that someday you’ll think of some miraculous way to tell them to me. That day is never coming.”
“Don’t think of me as someone waiting for you at home.”
“Do you understand?”
The other side of the grille waited in silence for a moment. Knowing perfectly well that the ship had no way to answer, she asked anyway.
It was the same for me. Knowing perfectly well that my voice could not get through, I still spoke toward it.
“I understand.”
The two minutes were not quite over.
“If your father were—”
Wind mixed with static, and her voice hung suspended in midair. Only the sound of deep breathing remained in the grille, the wind brushing past her microphone.
A long time passed—long enough for me to think the communication had already been cut—before she spoke again.
“As for me—there’s still work to do at the camp.”
A sharp crack sounded. The voice in the grille broke off, leaving only hollow electrical noise.

Gradually, not a trace of the old world’s reflected light remained beyond the porthole. The points of light belonging to that era vanished completely from view, and the vast river of stars spread open without reserve in the absolute darkness.
Looking out from somewhere this desolate, you would feel that this was the first true night in the entire history of the world.
Throughout this irrational stretch of the voyage, the ship maintained a dead, steady course.

After steady cruising, the sensation of weightlessness was gradually replaced by a faint centrifugal force. In this cabin, which could have held a hundred and fifty people, only nine now sat in the emptiness. The gel levels in the hibernation pods were full, but no one went to activate them. The

destination and flight path had been locked by the old civilization’s code and could not be changed. In the previous trial flight, in a dead loop, this ship had plunged straight into deep space on the very night of its launch. Since the flight path had not changed, we would not have much time.

Not long after takeoff, Estelle had already carefully numbered every piece of material she could find in the forward cabin. After numbering the final item, she pulled a blank navigation log supplied with the ship from a drawer and pushed it to the center of the table.
Printed on the yellowed pages was a standard crew roster from the old era. At the very top were the words “Commander of the Entire Ship.”

Yuna took the pen from the table. Ignoring the vacant heading, she wrote her name, stroke by stroke, in the blank crew column below. This was what she had promised. In the register of the new world, she would write her own existence into it with her own hand.
She handed me the pen. After Estelle and I had both signed, the register held its first three names in equal ink.
“Then who goes in this line?” Estelle tapped the printed words “Commander of the Entire Ship” with the tip of her pen and looked at the two of us.

Yuna looked at the words. Even aboard the ship, the six maintenance workers still instinctively remained in the rear cabin, maintaining a boundary between us where neither side interfered with the other.

“There’s no Inner Circle or outer settlement on this ship.” Yuna shook her head and pushed the register back to Estelle. “Go ask Neva and Thun. If we’re going to survive, we have to decide how supplies will be allocated from now on. Go to the rear cabin and ask whether they’ll sign.”
Estelle looked at her quietly for a while, then stood and carried the register toward the rear cabin.
A long time passed before the door to the forward cabin was pushed open. Neva held the register in her hand. She walked to the table and dropped it onto the surface with a heavy thud. Six
crooked names had been added beneath the crew column, while several thick black strokes had completely crossed out the heading “Commander.” Beside it was a fingerprint still wet with machine oil.
“We signed our names. But those words in the heading were too irritating to look at, so I crossed them out. We don’t need you managing us, and don’t expect to order us around.” Neva rubbed the oil
from her hands against her work clothes, then cast a wary glance at the empty chair. “When everyone feels they can sit at one table and argue naturally, then we can think about who listens to whom.”
On this question, Yuna only nodded. Those six signatures and the blank space left by the three in the forward cabin formed the ship’s first consensus after departure.
During this short voyage, I spent most of my time in the forward cabin, organizing the memory terminal I had brought aboard. I typed the key points about this long cycle into the screen.
Yuna served as both the first reader and the proofreader. Sometimes she would frown and point to a record of us making our way through the old shelter:
“This part. Why did you write that I was afraid?”
“You were clearly trembling.”
“That was physiological trembling caused by the sudden drop in ambient temperature.”
“I only record what I saw.”
She gave a cold laugh. “Fine. Then I’ll write a note here arguing with you.”

And so this memorandum of the past became disordered. It contained not only the subjective perspective I had pieced together, but also the blind spots described by Yuna. Her supplementary notes were everywhere, along with Estelle’s red lines: “The gaps where you were not present and the subjective narration are yours. As for objective facts, I only recognize numbers that happened.”
An offline copy remained open in one corner of the screen. Before leaving the White Tower, I had transferred the fragment sealed in the old archive network into this small physical storage device.
On the screen, the old and exhausted Heisenberg asked through the shadows of the old era, in a trembling voice: “If you are watching this—is it of any use to you?”
It was a piece of soliloquy he had left underground. I had watched the image several times.

I had no way to answer the dead. But looking at the document beside the screen, crammed with Yuna’s notes and Estelle’s red lines, I remembered Estelle’s words to him underground: “useful.” She had recorded it, and now we had carried it out of the White Tower.
Before I could close the screen, the alarm in the control room suddenly broke the quiet of the forward cabin.

It was not a malfunction alarm. The final lines of the automatic navigation sequence appeared on the main console’s screen. As the deceleration rockets ignited violently, the massive overload pinned us against our seats.

Beyond the porthole, the blackness of deep space was torn open. The huge cracked pink-violet moon, and the far larger planetary body behind it, came crashing into view. It was the scene we had seen during the previous trial flight in the dead loop—the one-way destination fixed deep in the old civilization’s code.

Just as it had in the dead loop, this vessel built more than a hundred years ago shook with an ear-splitting roar, then touched down smoothly as if by a miracle. The engines gradually shut down with a dull thump. A row of green indicators lit up on the control panel, ending its brief voyage.
The cabin was so quiet that all we could hear was the hurried breathing from the forward and rear cabins. The blueprints had once marked various detectors connecting the control console to
the outside, but on this abandoned antique, left unused for more than a hundred years, most had long since become blind ornaments. The external environment readings flickered erratically.
Two old-fashioned sealed spacesuits hung quietly in the shock-absorption cabinet at the front of the cabin.

I took one down and handed it to Yuna. We put on the heavy protective suits, fastened our helmets shut, and entered the forward airlock, leaving Estelle behind the inner hatch. Yuna gripped the control lever for the manual outer hatch and pulled it down hard. With the heavy scrape of machinery, the outer hatch slowly slid outward.
Yuna paused for one second against the wind rushing into the airlock, then took a step and walked down the ramp.
I followed close behind. Her voice came through the intercom channel inside my helmet:
“No high-radiation warning. Atmospheric pressure stable. Atmospheric composition… The instruments show oxygen, but there are other unknown gases.”

She stood before a cluster of strange leaves folding inward, looking at the portable detector dismantled from the ship in her hand. The biochemical warning module at the bottom of the instrument’s screen lit yellow—the

highest-precision conclusion it could provide. It indicated that the composition of the surrounding air differed from the preset baseline, but the probe had detected no known highly lethal neurotoxins or corrosive agents.
The crude mechanisms of the old era were powerless against this planet’s microorganisms, unknown gases, and chronic hazards. The yellow light on the screen continued to flash.
“We may need long-term sampling…” I said over the channel.

“We don’t have that much time.” She cut me off and calmly clipped the detector back to her belt. “The ship’s life-support system won’t hold for long. We can’t hide inside our helmets forever, either. If the air here could kill us within five minutes, we’d already be dead.”
With that, she raised a hand and pressed the clasp on her neck ring.
With a hiss, the seal released. She removed her helmet and drew a deep breath.
She did not cough or collapse.
I undid my own fastenings and lifted off my helmet. I clearly smelled a trace of moisture in the wind rushing inside—the scent of water.
She turned, pulled the rough red wool hat Rena had hurriedly knitted from her pocket, and drew it firmly over her head.
I gestured toward the inner hatch. Estelle silently tucked the register bearing all nine names under her arm and stepped out, planting her feet on the soil of another planet.

The ship had landed exactly on the edge between dawn and dusk on this planet. On the left, the cold, bright light of the star still remained; on the right, the sky had already rapidly sunk into deep, dark purple.
Above that deep-purple night sky hung a huge moon, its surface covered in broad cracks and dark bands. Directly in front of the hatch was the lake.

Near the lake, low dark leaf-shaped organisms grew in dense patches. As the light from the cold-bright side slowly swept over them, the leaves rapidly folded inward one after another, as if alive. In the distant sky, one or two unidentified creatures with enormous wings occasionally swept past.

At that moment, all the blood in my body seemed to freeze. In one of the dead loops from an earlier attempt to break out, Yuna had died at this exact spot. The wooden die she had deliberately placed on a stone was enclosed by folding leaves, and she had fallen into the mud and never risen again.
But now, there was no fallen figure in that marsh. Only a gust of wind passed over the water, stirring a layer of fresh ripples.
I turned sharply. Yuna was standing beside me, the red wool hat lifting slightly in the wind.

She was also looking down at the flat stone by her feet, then at her empty palm. After that, she raised her head and surveyed the strange lakeshore, her gaze passing over the clusters of folding leaves before finally coming to rest on that exact patch of mud by the water.
She said nothing. She only reached out and lightly touched her chest. She remembered that she had gone out here.
Then she slowly lowered her hand and stepped onto the same soil.
The auxiliary hatch opened as well.
Neva, Thun, Samo, and three others came down. After leaving the ship, they instinctively stood together, studying this new world from an open space not far away.

Still, no one took the initiative to come toward us. Neva tilted her head back to examine the scorch marks on the hull; Thun grabbed a handful of mud and rolled it forcefully between his fingertips; Samo stared at the lake. Each of them, in their own way, was confirming that they were still alive.

The wind came across the lake and stirred Yuna’s sleeve, revealing the reddish-brown cloth identification band around her wrist. I had wrapped it around her myself with a new strip of cloth at noon on the day she was resurrected. After everything we had been through, the once-new band had begun to fray at the edges.
“It’s almost broken. There should be spares in the storage room. Want to change it?” I asked softly.
“No.”
She raised her hand and pressed the band back into her sleeve.
“If it breaks, let it break.”
She stopped before a cluster of strange leaves folding inward and looked toward the lake.
I turned and looked at the six people standing together not far away.
There was still a stretch of distance between them and us. In this new world, we did not immediately embrace, and the cracks left by the past had not been erased by a single landing.
I did not remain where I was. I took the first step toward them.
Yuna noticed. She gave the cabin behind her one last look, then turned and stood beside me.

On the other side, Estelle also stepped forward from the ship’s shadow and came to stand beside us. She did not look at us. Instead, she studied the cracked moon in the distance on her own, while the register, bearing nine signatures in nine different hands, flipped and rustled in the wind of the new world.
Those who had just escaped death quietly confirmed one another’s existence.
“What are you staring at?” Yuna looked ahead and lifted her chin at me, just as she had beyond the boundary stone.
“Let’s go.”
